en: The Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra with the commentary Darpaṇa:
[Salutation] to Him who is capable of protecting the world through the love of Ramā, and whose joy of face— the Vedas— is produced by the extraction of the mass of Vedic hymns stolen by Madhu.
I bow to Hayagrīva, who abounds in unbroken bliss, who dwells within the lotus-hearts of all people, and who destroys the forest of the works of this author for the sake of removing its afflictions.

Since the production of an effect is not observed even from a thousand concurrent means of accomplishment when there is a single obstacle, the author composes at the beginning of his work a benedictory verse in the form of praise to the Blessed One—performed to remove obstacles to the desired undertaking—for the purpose of instructing his disciples, saying: "Śrīlakṣmīramaṇam. Here, the word *lakṣmī* ending in the genitive case is compounded with the word *ramaṇa*, which is derived from the root *ram* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, the compound *śrīsahita* is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term-omitted) compound, because [compounds] such as *śākapārthiva* belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups). Its inclusion is intended to indicate that the Blessed One is the cause of the creation of the world precisely when He is endowed with Śrī. Regarding the word *naimī*: from the root *ṇu* meaning "to praise," although the pronoun *asmad* (we) is not explicitly used, there exists a coreferential relationship (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the implied meaning of that pronoun in the sense of the agent, which is the referent of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*). Consequently, the third person singular of the present tense (*laṭ*), which indicates the current action, is employed.

In the rule "asmadyuttamaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.107), the term "sthāninī" is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Praise (*stuti*) is an activity conducive to a cognition characterized by the quality of being superior. That alone is the meaning of the verbal root in this context. Because the Beloved of Lakṣmī (*lakṣmīramaṇa*) is the substratum of the result—which is the cognition that constitutes the meaning of the root—he possesses the status of the object (*karman*).

And thus, according to the view of the Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇa), the meaning of the sentence is: "An operation in the form of the current use of the word [‘Śiva’], which has as its substratum something non-different from myself, and which is conducive to a cognition characterized by the possession of excellent qualities based upon the beloved of Śrī, Mahī, and Lakṣmī. Now, one might ask: since Śiva is more worthy of worship as the initiator of this treatise, why was an auspicious invocation consisting of his praise not performed? To this, he says: "having the form of the lover of Gaurī."

By means of the term *svarūpa-pararūpa*, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the word *gaurīramaṇa*; from that, the suffix *iti* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), based on its ending in the vowel *a*. There is no impossibility regarding this possessive suffix, because the author of the *Bhāṣya*, while citing the usage *asubvataḥ* as an example under the rule [Pāṇini 5.2.127], did not disregard such a construction—namely, "that whose own form (*svarūpa*) is Gaurīramaṇa. Indeed, a twofold usage is observed in such instances:
"To Śiva, who has the form of Viṣṇu," and "To Viṣṇu, who has the form of Śiva," and so forth.

And thus, the meaning is that [the Lord] is non-different from that [the Absolute]. The proof for this is precisely the Puranic passage cited here. Furthermore, since the diversity of effects is necessarily governed by the diversity of causes, the Lord’s assumption of various forms—wherein specific qualities are predominant—in order to account for the diversity of effects such as the protection of the world, does not constitute an ultimate ontological difference. Therefore, the sense is that Śiva’s being the object of praise is not untenable.

The phrase "from which" (*yataḥ*) reveals the possession of supreme qualities; for, according to the final view [of the author], since Brahman as qualified by *māyā* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is applied to the material cause based on the technical designation of "ablative" (Pāṇini 1.4.30: *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*). Because the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is used, the option provided by Pāṇini 2.3.25 (*vibhāṣā*) does not apply. Thus, the meaning is "from which material cause. The construction is: "the entire world, in the form of *sphoṭa*, undergoes illusory manifestation (*vivartate*)."

That from which an object (*artha*) bursts forth—that is, becomes manifest—is called *sphoṭa*; it is the word (*śabda*) consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*). The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) by virtue of its frequent application (*bāhulaka*). That which is formed or defined (*rūpyate*)—that is, determined—is *rūpa*, meaning the object (*artha*). In a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) of these two, ending in the singular neuter, the meaning is "the nature of the signified and the signifier. This is based on the Vedic scripture (*śruti*): "I shall unfold name and form" (*nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi*). The meaning is that this [universe], being made the object of immediate proximity, undergoes *vivarta* (illusory manifestation), which is to say, it is produced; this is because of the prefix attached to the verbal root.

[Objection: But since the Śruti, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," teaches that that which consists of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is eternal, how can it possess the quality of being born? To this he says: [the word] *jagat* is correct by virtue of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) "pṛṣat" in the sense of "that which exists" (*vartamāne*). Thus, through the etymology "it goes" (*gacchati*) or "it disappears" (*tirodhatta*), disappearance (*tirodhāna*) is expressed; and by the rule that "whatever disappears manifests," manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) is necessarily implied. Therefore, that [manifestation] alone is the meaning conveyed here by the prefix [in *jagat*].

And thus, although this [Brahman] is eternal according to the sentient being, there is no contradiction with the aforementioned scripture because its manifestation as name and so forth is admitted; nor is there a contradiction with that [scripture] which teaches origination, such as "From that, from this very Self, space was produced," since anything consisting of name and form can arise from something else. He says "all" (sarvam) in the sense of "as much as exists," because origination is merely an illustration for preservation and so forth. By this, there is obtained the status of being the object of praise for the exalted attributes—such as being the creator of the world—which serve as the delimiters of that [Brahman].
And in this regard, the scriptural authorities are such passages as: "From which indeed these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter when they depart."

According to another view, the ablative case in *yataḥ* denotes a causal condition (*nimittahetutā*). The meaning of the verbal root *tud* preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-* is "origination," which consists in connection with the first moment [of existence]. Now, one might object that since entities such as space (*vyoman*), which are included within "all" (*sarva*), are beginningless, how can they possess origination? To this he says: "the world" (*jagat*), meaning consisting of the stationary and the moving. Thus, since the etymology "that which goes" (*gacchati*) and "that which perishes" (*naśyati*) indicates perishability, and since there is a necessary rule that a perishable entity must be produced, its origination is not contradictory. This is the intended sense.

In this context, the term *sphoṭapada* refers to that which is understood through scripture, inference, and direct cognition. By the etymological derivation "that whose form (*rūpa*) is such [as described]," it should be understood as an epithet of the Blessed One meaning "one whose form is *sphoṭa*. The rest is as before. Alternatively, in order to demonstrate and specify the nature that delimits his state of being worthy of praise, he qualifies him with the term *sphoṭarūpa*; according to the etymology to be explained later, the meaning is "one whose essential nature is the illuminator of all objects."

Establishing that very point, he shows another delimitor of its status as an object of praise with the words "yataḥ" (from which). The meaning is: from which material cause (*upādāna*), or, by virtue of the suffix *tasi* having the sense of all case endings, upon which substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). And "vivarta" is an unreal transformation (*atāttvika-anyathābhāva*). That is to say, it is the state of being the object of a cognition characterized by another form, while not abandoning its own prior form. Furthermore, the word "jagat" (world) refers, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), to name and form (*nāmarūpa*).

And thus, the meaning is that upon whatever substrate this entire world—consisting of the elements, the senses, and so forth—appears in its respective forms. Even though the world has been shown to be sublated by the scriptural text, "There is no diversity here," its appearance is governed solely by the existence of the substrate; therefore, it is logically possible for [Brahman] to be the illuminator of all objects. Furthermore, because Brahman, whose own nature is never lost, undergoes a *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) in the form of the world, there is the realization of its supreme attribute of being changeless.

And in this context, the meaning is that such scriptural passages as "Everything shines only after Him who shines" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14), which establish His immutable nature, are to be understood as authoritative evidence.

Here, the figure of speech *hetu* (cause) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the sentiment of love (*rati-bhāva*) directed toward the Blessed Lord. Having praised Him as the material cause of the universe, the author now praises Him as the object of the knowledge that is the means to liberation and as the ornament of Śeṣa, the commentator of this scripture; he then prays for the realization of the entire established doctrine set forth in this work with the words "aśeṣa" (entirety). The "fruit" (*phala*) is the intended goal of the undertaking. He uses the word "aśeṣa" because the capacity to bestow some minor fruit such as heaven is common to other deities as well. Thus, by the term "aśeṣa," even the fruit consisting of liberation (*apavarga*) is included.

Because the state of being its giver is contained within [the Lord], it possesses a quality that makes it uniquely sought after, as there is no other means to achieve it. He clarifies this very point with the words "in the ocean of existence" (*bhavābdhi*). This is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) wherein "existence" (*bhava*) itself is the "ocean. Because it is difficult to fathom—being overwhelmed by desire, greed, and so forth, which are like crocodiles and other sea-monsters—the superimposition of the nature of an ocean upon existence is made. By this, the difficulty of crossing over existence is suggested. "Crossing over" (*taraṇa*) means reaching the opposite shore; "in that" is the meaning. A "boat" (*tarim*) is the means for that.

Although, by the etymological derivation "that by which one crosses," the meaning of the word *tari* (boat) is the instrument of crossing, it has nevertheless been explained as referring solely to the substantive (the boat itself) so that there may not be a redundancy—since the act of crossing, which is not a constituent part of that [substantive], is already obtained through the proximate term [in the compound]. This means: "having as its object the knowledge that is the instrument of liberation. And in the Vedāntic view, liberation (*mukti*) is the attainment of one's true nature simultaneously with the cessation of ignorance.

If it is argued that since the cessation of ignorance is not distinct from its locus and its very nature is already established, it is impossible for that cessation—being of such a nature—to be accomplished by the knowledge of reality, we say no; for, just as for the opponents [the Naiyāyikas], the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is established, so too the cessation of ignorance can be an object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in the sense of being common to both "acquisition" (*yoga*) and "preservation" (*kṣema*). Further details should be sought elsewhere.

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that liberation (mokṣa) is the absolute destruction of suffering. Regarding this destruction, "absoluteness" means not being co-temporal with any suffering that has the same locus as itself. It is precisely here that the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is of use. Alternatively, they say that liberation is the manifestation of eternal bliss, since the substantive portion [of the self] can only arise through its own specific causal complex.

The compound *śeṣaśeṣa* is a genitive tatpuruṣa (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*) with a karmadhāraya as its final member. This is then compounded with the word *lābha* (attainment) in the analysis *lābhāya idam* (this for the sake of attainment), where the word *lābha*, ending in the dative case, is joined with the word *artha*. [In this context,] *Śeṣa* refers to Patañjali, because he is a partial incarnation (*aṃśa*) of Śeṣa. Thus, the meaning is: "for the sake of knowing all the established doctrines (*siddhānta*) set forth in the Bhāṣya spoken by Śeṣa. As for *Śeṣabhūṣaṇa*, it means that of which Śeṣa (the Infinite One) is the ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*).

Since Śeṣa is his ornament, his prayer is for the attainment of the established doctrines taught by Śeṣa; thus, because of the employment of a significant substantive (the subject), there is the poetic figure *parikarāṅkura* here, which serves as an ancillary to the *rasa* of devotion toward the Lord. Demonstrating the superiority of his own work over other treatises for the sake of the engagement of discerning readers, he first shows the subject—which must necessarily be shown among the subject, purpose, relationship, and qualified student—by saying "from Pāṇini," etc., and "the Goddess of Speech who possesses the male form."

This is an epithet of the Father (Brahmā). It is either a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *vāgdevatā* (the Goddess of Speech) having as its first member a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*—meaning "she whose nature is that of a male"—or else the word *pumbhāva* ends in the suffix *ac* (added after the sense of possession, i.e., matvarthīya), meaning "one who possesses the state of being male. Thus, the meaning is: Sarasvatī, who has manifested a male form. Regarding the phrase *dvaitadhvānta* (the darkness of duality): it refers to that which is known in two ways—that is, an object of knowledge characterized by contradictory dual attributes. Alternatively, *dvitā* is the state (*bhāva*) of being two.

Since even a substratum (dharmin) can possess the nature of being a positive entity (bhāvatva) with respect to various contradictory properties through the relation of being a qualifier (prakāratā) determined by a single subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) residing in itself, the referent of the word "dvitā" is indeed the substratum. In that context, "dvaita" refers to a cognition consisting of doubt. Alternatively, "dvitā" is the state of being two or many—that is, plurality; and "dvaita" is the cognition related to that [plurality]. This is because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), only the non-dual Brahman is accepted, and thus [the term] refers to a cognition that apprehends plurality which is sublated by scripture (śruti).

The meaning is as follows: false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), which is synonymous with ignorance (*avidyā*) and consists of specific functions of the organs, is itself the "darkness" (*dhvānta*) or "gloom" (*tamaḥ*). Because it conceals reality, its removal is the one primary fruit of that [work]. The sense is that for those who are not qualified [for higher knowledge], it produces a cognition directed toward one side [of the two alternatives], whereas for the qualified, it bestows a cognition resting upon pure Being (*sanmātra*); thus, the Goddess of Speech in her human form effects that removal. *Ḍhuṇḍhi* refers to Gaṇapati; the word "having bowed" (*praṇamya*) is to be supplied.

"Established doctrines" (*siddhāntān*) means those doctrines determined by the author of the *Bhāṣya* and others; "by means of arguments" (*upapattibhiḥ*) means by means of logical reasonings consisting in the presentation of probative evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*). "Refute" (*dūṣayet*) means by means of arguments consisting in the presentation of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

By this, the superiority of his own work over other treatises is implied. Thus, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) presented here is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of grammar; the purpose (*prayojana*) is the knowledge thereof; the relationship (*sambandha*) is that between the taught and the teacher; and the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is one who desires to know the established doctrine—these three [along with the work itself] are also effectively shown. He states the purpose of the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) performed at the beginning of the book and its composition by means of the words "prāripsita" and so forth, omitting the phrase "for the sake of completion" (*samāptaye*).

By the statement "for the pacification of obstacles," it is indicated that for auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), whose fruit is inferred from the extraordinary and unobjectionable conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), the fruit is indeed the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*). This is because the learned do not perform auspicious rites with the aim of completing [a work] in a future birth; therefore, since the causal relation between the auspicious rite and completion must be postulated as residing in a proximity (*pratyāsatti*) inherent in the body, and since such completion is absent in the case of an atheist's completion [of a work], completion cannot be the [actual] fruit. Rather, [the fruit] is simply the effect in general.

Since the absence of an obstacle (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is the cause [of completion], the utility of the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) lies solely in the removal of obstacles such as those that are difficult to dispel; it does not extend to the actual completion itself, because the latter is established by other means through the destruction of impediments (*vighna*). Furthermore, it is indicated that completion arises from the collection of causes already established elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "recollection of the Serpent" (*phaṇismaraṇa*), "Serpent" refers to Śeṣa. This is because, according to the Lord’s own statement, "My abode is named Śeṣa," the recollection of him serves to ward off obstacles.

The word "recollection" (smaraṇa) is used to indicate that auspiciousness (maṅgala) possesses various forms through its divisions such as salutation (namas), praise (stuti), and so forth. The phrase "he promises" (pratijānīte) should be understood as having the result of a formal promise (pratijñā), namely, the focused attention of the disciples.

In response to the expectation regarding the agent of extraction (*uddharaṇa*), he says "by us" (*asmābhiḥ*) in the root text; the remainder is "it is stated by means of the verses composed by Hari and others. In that context, since the *sphoṭa* generates the cognition of meaning and the expectation is satisfied by that alone, even though the *vākya-sphoṭa* (sentence-sphoṭa) will be established as the final conclusion in such passages as "the *vākya-sphoṭa* is the ultimate [reality]," nevertheless, because it is impossible to grasp the convention (*saṅketa*) for every individual sentence and because explaining it through that method is difficult to accomplish by a simple means, the words are divided there [in the sentences] by way of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Even among those [words],...

Having likewise analyzed the portions consisting of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), and having established them through imagined positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the author] shows that even for those respective meanings, the *padavastu-sphoṭa* and *varṇa-sphoṭa* are accepted for the sake of carrying out the grammatical process (*prakriyā*) within the treatise composed by the Great Sage (*maharṣi*), which explains correctness (*sādhutva*) by means of making known the beginningless linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) regarding the names of bases and suffixes. Then, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is primary in a sentence—which consists of a collection of nominal and verbal endings and whose primary element is the meaning of the finite verb—the author states at the outset in the root-text (*mūla*) the following in order to define that very [meaning]: [The original Sanskrit text follows here.]

In the phrase "of the result and the operation," the word "root" (*dhātu*) is qualified by the term "are remembered" (*smṛtāḥ*); this is because they are presented with different case-endings. For there is a rule that the words expressing the qualificand and the qualifier must agree in number, provided that the number intended by the case-ending following the word expressing the qualificand is not incompatible with the number of the qualifier. Precisely for this reason, expressions such as *nīlo ghaṭāḥ* ("blue pots") are not grammatically correct.

However, when there is an intention to express that [number], as in "The Vedas are authoritative" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*) or "The meaning of a word consists of genus, form, and individual" (*jātyākṛtivyaktayaḥ padārthaḥ*), there is indeed a difference in number. But since there is no reason for such an intention in the present case, the *Bhūṣaṇasāra* shows the syntactic connection by changing the number in the phrase "the verbal root" (*dhātuḥ*). Now, that which is understood to be the purpose for which the Veda or worldly usage proceeds—that is its "fruit-ness" (*phalatvam*), which means being the object of a desire not dependent on another's desire. As Hari said: "That object for the sake of whose accomplishment roots such as *pac* (to cook) are commenced..."
That [liberation] is their primary fruit; gain and so forth are not the purpose. Thus it is said.

Even in the rule *svaritañitaḥ*, the word *phala* (result) is well-known to refer only to the primary result intended as the goal of the activity. Thus, if such a result were denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then at the stage of the operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*), the rice grain would lack the status of an object (*karman*) because it is not the locus of such a result denoted by the root; furthermore, that which is the locus of the result produced by that operation would incur the same [undesirable] consequence. Therefore, he says: "The result is softening and so forth. The intention here is that, according to the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the world, the word *phala*...

Even though such meanings are presented here, the intent is strictly toward technical (paribhāṣika) meanings; otherwise, the linguistic usage regarding transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) and so forth would be difficult to justify. Its essence (*tattva*) consists in being the object of a presentation produced by that verbal root, while being produced by that verbal root, or else it consists in being the meaning of that verbal root. "Being produced" (*janyatva*) means being the object of a cognition whose qualifier is "being produced. By this, there is no over-extension (*aprasaṅga*) to [universals] such as existence (*sattā*).

The qualifier [“that which is denoted by the verbal root”] is included to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the separation (*vibhāga*) and so forth produced by the operation of the object of motion (*gamyādi*) and the like; and the positive term (*satyantam*) is included to eliminate over-extension to the operation directed toward that object. Furthermore, this definition remains intact for [results such as] softening (*viklitti*) and the like, because it is established by universal experience that even these are understood in that very form as being the denotable objects (*śakyatā*) of the relevant roots such as *pac* (to cook) and the like, and because they are understood even by one who does not know their status as verbal roots (*dhātutva*) and so forth. This is the intended meaning.

Others, however, define it as follows: when used in co-occurrence with a verbal suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), [an action] possesses a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) that is determined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of that same verbal root, while being produced by the meaning of that same verbal root. Whether this "producedness" (*janyatā*) is superimposed (*āropita*) or non-superimposed (*anāropita*) is another matter. Both conditions are included to exclude the status of being a "result" (*phala*) for the disjunction and the conjunction respectively, within the meaning of "falls," which consists of a conjunction produced by a disjunction.

They argue that since the fruit (phala) appears as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in a verbal root denoting action (*karmākhyāta*), the co-occurrence with a suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) is required to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) there; however, this is to be considered, because a consistent definition of "fruit" has not been established. Furthermore, since it will be stated later that conjunction produced by disjunction (due to its being partless and perceptible) lacks the status of being the meaning of the verb *patati*, the counter-example (*vyāvartya*) is unestablished; more on this will be said further on.

Now, [it may be argued that] being an operation (*vyāpāratva*) is not "the state of being an action that brings about a result," because that would involve the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), since the very nature of an action is what constitutes it; furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence that even the operation of a staff and the like would become the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Nor is this an acceptable consequence, because it will be stated later that agency (*kartṛtā*) belongs only to the substratum of the operation which is the meaning of the root. Consequently, if the staff and such were denoted as the agent by the verb, then in expressions such as *daṇḍena devadattaḥ pacati* ("Devadatta cooks with a staff"), the third case ending would not occur after the word *daṇḍa*, and instead, the first case ending would have to occur.

Because the two designations (*saṃjñā*)—agent (*kartṛ*) and instrument (*karaṇa*)—cannot coexist due to the rule *ā kaḍārāt* (P. 1.4.1), the intended designation of "instrument" would be sublated by the subsequent designation of "agent. Furthermore, if being an "instigator" (*prayojakatva*) were defined as direct causality, then in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), the operation of the agent would fail to be the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), since that operation produces the result only through the mediation of the instrument's operation.

If that [causality] were common to both producers and non-producers, then since even the act of purchasing rice is an action that brings about the result [of cooking], it would follow that one could use the expression "Devadatta cooks" even at a time when he is merely buying rice; furthermore, it is impossible to define such a "causality-as-bringer-about" (*prayojakatva*) that is excluded from acts like the purchase of rice. For this very reason, the definition well-known in other systems—namely, "being the producer of that which is produced by it"—is not [the correct one].

If that which is delimited by those [actions] were the meaning expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then the usage ‘*pacati*’ (he cooks) would occur only at the stage of the final contact with fire that directly produces softening (*viklitti*), and not even during stages such as placing the pot on the fire; for those [earlier stages], being established otherwise [than through softening], do not produce softening. Therefore, he says: "But the operation... (*vyāpārastu*).

In the expression "sādhyatvena," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes a qualifier. Thus, the meaning is that *vyāpāratva* (the nature of being an operation) consists in being the object of a denotation whose mode (*prakāra*) is "being-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyatva*), and which is not prompted by co-utterance with another word. The status of being a mode and the status of being the determiner of the objecthood (*viṣayatānirūpakatva*) attributed to the denotation are metaphorical. In short, it means being the object of a cognition in which such "being-to-be-accomplished" is the mode.

In expressions such as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), since even jars and the like are perceived as being in a state of accomplishment (*sādhya*) when used in conjunction with the root *kṛ*, the phrase "not caused by the juxtaposition of another word" is added as a qualification of the perception in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is because, in the absence of that juxtaposition, they are not perceived as such. Since the entire complex of actions beginning from placing [the pot] on the fire up to taking it off is perceived as something to be accomplished even without the juxtaposition of another word, its status as the aforementioned operation (*vyāpāra*) remains intact; thus, the denotability of roots such as *pac* (to cook) with respect to that which is delimited by such an operation is not untenable—this is the intended meaning.

He refutes the notion that the meaning already stated was merely his own invention by saying "and it has been said" (*uktañca*) up to "all" (*yāvat*). The meaning is "everything. He explains each of these categories in detail with the words "established" (*siddham*) and so forth. "Siddha" (established) refers to that which possesses a presently existing destruction, as in "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*) and similar cases. "Asiddha" (unestablished) refers to that which is other than past—namely, the present—and that which possesses a corresponding prior non-existence, as in "he cooks" (*pacati*) and "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*). The phrase "by way of being a goal to be accomplished" (*sādhyatvena*) means by its nature which is about to be described. "Is denoted" (*abhidhīyate*) means it is the object of a cognition characterized by that mode. There is a variant reading: "is intended in some cases" (*kvacid vivakṣyate*).

By this, the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word "action" (*kriyā*) has been demonstrated. He also states its etymological meaning (*yaugikatva*) with the word "resorted-to" (*āśrita*): because it has as its nature that which is resorted to in the form of a sequence—that is, because it consists of parts arranged in a prior and posterior order. Since its constituent parts, from placing [the pot] on the stove up to taking it off, arise in succession, it is designated by the term "action. However, where an operation does not consist of sequential parts, one must either accept the conventional meaning alone or resort to the superimposition of priority and posteriority.

The result (*phala*) also appears in that same manner through the superimposition of the priority and posteriority belonging to the operation (*vyāpāra*) of its own producer. This is the intended meaning: for this very reason, the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) is established for that which denotes only that [result]. Although there is an appearance here as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), how else could words such as *stoka* [in the expression] "a slight cooking" (*stokaṃ pākaḥ*) function as the object (*karman*)? Nevertheless, the intention is that in those cases, while the state (*bhāva*) presented by the verbal root is subordinate, the state presented by the primary *ghañ*-affix is indeed established (*siddha*).

He states the established meaning with the words "tathā ca" (and thus). Regarding the phrase "kriyāntara" (another action), the underlying intention (*āśaya*) is as follows: *sādhyatva* (the state of being an object to be accomplished) is that which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) in a cognition from which arises the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) for another action; or it is the state of being distinct from that [already accomplished] nature, or the delimiting factor for the absence of the capacity to arouse such an expectation residing in the cognition. However, the cognition of *sādhyatva* itself does not act as an obstacle to the expectation, because that [expectation] simply does not arise due to the absence of its already established causes.

Nor should it be argued that when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is presented as the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*)—in the form of a property that does not give rise to an expectation for another action—the co-occurrence of another action would be impossible due to a lack of expectancy in cases such as "If one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, he would attain happiness," because there is no such expectancy there either; for even in those cases, the presence of the word *cet* (if) gives rise to the necessary expectancy. Furthermore, the conventional designation of words like *hiruk* as having "action" as their meaning is merely because they serve as qualifiers of action alone. For this very reason, case-relations (*kāraka*) do not co-occur with the meaning of *hiruk* and similar terms, since their meaning lacks expectancy for another action.

In reality, however, just as there is an expectancy for a probandum (*sādhya*) when there is a cognition of something already established (*siddha*), once the meaning of a root such as *pac* (to cook) is understood as being a probandum, the expectancy "What is its means? arises; thus, the nature of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*) is simply the state of possessing a property that delimits the capacity to arouse the expectancy for a means. For this very reason, the subsequent passage beginning with "taking this very [factor]" is consistent; otherwise, in cases such as *pacati bhavati*, since the aforementioned form would be absent, that inconsistency would be evident. And it has been said by Hari: "Among things fit for usage, an object that is established (*siddha*) should be understood through qualifiers."

"And prior to the connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the action (*kriyā*) does not arise at all. It should be noted that even the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *suṭ kāt* is consistent with this view, for it is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) that brings about the action. However, some maintain that because of the continuous usage of the term "he cooks" (*pacati*), there exists a universal (*jāti*) such as "cooking-ness" (*pacitva*). Thus, action is precisely the universal residing in a series of multiple individual instances. Its state of being "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) is mediated solely through its individuals. Like the *sphoṭa*, its manifestation occurs through successive moments.
Some say that the universal (jāti) is an action residing in multiple individuals;
though it is unachievable in its own form, it is perceived as if it were achievable through the medium of the individual.

They say that the *Vākyapadīya* is the authority here regarding this view. By the phrase "possessing that form" (*tadrūpavattvam*), he states the synonymy between the words "being a process to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) and "not being an existent entity" (*asattvabhūta*). The phrase "this very [thing]" means precisely that state of being an existent entity (*sattvabhūtatva*) as defined by the *Nirukta*. The term "not being an existent entity" (*asattvabhūta*) is intended to convey the meaning of the *Nirukta* definition: "A verb (*ākhyāta*) has the action as its primary meaning. An individual (*vyakti*) that has attained the nature of an existent entity is denoted by nouns (*nāman*).

This is the first half [of the verse]. Regarding the word *bhāvaśca* ("and the state of being"): the particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), meaning "only the state of being as previously described. By this, there is an exclusion of that which has become a substance (*sattvabhūta*). Regarding the phrase *tiṅpadaiḥ*: by the natural force of the plural number, it means "by words ending in verbal suffixes" (*tiṅanta-pada*); the meaning is "it is expressed" (*abhidhīyate*), i.e., "it is made known" (*bodhyate*). To the word *abhidhīyate*, the ellipsis is "primarily indeed" (*prādhānyenaiva*). Consequently, there is no fault even if words ending in primary suffixes (*kṛdanta*) express a state of being that exists as a substance. Some maintain that the phrase *tiṅpadaiḥ* refers specifically to the verbal forms of the bhāva-vṛtti (intransitive/impersonal) voice.

"And this" means the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is perceived as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). "Expressible" (*vācya*) means it is incapable [of being expressed] by verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook). "Because it is established by experience" (*anubhavasiddhatvāt*): for this very reason, when fire is ignited by fanning or other means, one who has grasped the expressive power (*śakti*) [of the word] does not use the expression "he cooks. As for the disagreement (*vipratipatti*) regarding whether it is sacrifice (*yāga*), desire (*icchā*), or knowledge (*jñāna*), the point is that it arises solely from the nature of one's own understanding.

The sense is that "having multiple meanings" (*nānārthatva*) does not consist in possessing a single property that serves as the delimiting factor for the denotative function (*nirūpakatāvacchedaka*) which is itself delimited by various distinct properties (*nānādharmavacchinnaśakti*). This [definition] remains intact in the case of roots such as *pac* (to cook), etc. It should be understood that if one takes the "resultant portion" (*phalāṃśa*) into account, this very status is indeed acceptable even to the opponent who raises the objection. In the phrase "of a particular cognition, etc. (*buddhiviśeṣādeḥ*), the ellipsis is to be supplied as "by way of the relation of being the deliminator of the objectivity (*viṣayatāvacchedakatva*) determined by itself. That is to say, it means "the state of being the deliminator of the objectivity of a particular cognition."

The point is this: the cognition of Caitra and others through their respective forms, such as "Caitra-ness" (caitratva) and so forth, is established by universal experience. And that [cognition] is untenable without a property that serves as a unifier (anugamaka-dharma) for Caitra-ness and the rest; therefore, accepting a property that unifies them—namely, being the delimitor of the object-sphere of a particular cognition—the denotative power (śakti) of words like "that" (tad) resides in Caitra and others as delimited by those respective [unifying properties].

Furthermore, because the property of being the delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) for the object-sphere of a particular cognition is treated as a mere adventitious indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no possibility of Caitra-ness and the like appearing in verbal cognition under that form. Polysemy belongs only to those [words] whose denotative function (*śakti*) is determined by a single common property that delimits the locus of the function despite being delimited by various non-uniform properties; it does not belong to those [words] such as "that" (*tad*). This has been established elsewhere in the analysis of the denotative function of words like "that," and the same should be understood here as well.

[Objection: Since it is impossible for successive operations—which are momentary and perishable in their prior and posterior sequence—to coalesce, the action consisting of them cannot be a unity; therefore, the statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *praśaṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.69), namely "and [the suffix is used] when there is a single action," would be inconsistent. To this, he says: *ākhyāta-*. The reading without the case-ending (*nirvibhaktika*) is correct. The meaning is that it also establishes the unity of the action conveyed by the verb (*ākhyāta*). In the reading with the case-ending (*savibhaktika*), the locative case is to be understood as a locative of domain (*vaiṣayika-adhāra*), taking into account the implied action of cognition (*jñāna-kriyā*).

The phrase "unity of a specific cognition" (buddhiviśeṣaikyam) means taking as the unifier the unity consisting of a specific cognition in the form of a synthesis (saṃkalana). Thus, the sense is that the sequence (paurvāparya) resides in the parts, while the unity resides in the whole; it is by taking these two that their connection is established. He presents the authority for this with the words "And it has been said."

The meaning of the verse is as follows: with respect to this collection of successive operations, that which is subordinate (guṇabhūta) and characterized by its constituent parts appearing in their respective forms—a collection whose non-difference is conceptually constructed by a unifying cognition (saṅkalanātmakaikatvabuddhi)—is designated as "action" (kriyā). In this context, the word "by cognition" (buddhyā) is used because there is no real, substantial aggregate of operations that perish in each moment. The term "having examined" (nirūpya) implies "in brief," and so forth.

Intending to state that the meaning of the suffixes (pratyaya) as qualifiers must necessarily be explained after the explanation of the primary meaning of the base (prakṛti), and that this follows by the principle of "occasional connection" (avasara-saṅgati), he says, "the meaning of the *tiṅ* [suffixes]. The phrase "because it is obtainable from another" implies the maxim: "The meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained from anything else.

By this, it is indicated that the objection raised by the Naiyāyikas and others—that if the agent (*kartṛ*) is defined as one possessing effort (*kṛti*) or activity (*vyāpāra*), there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (*gaurava*) in assuming multiple efforts and activities as the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatā-avacchedaka*)—is merely a manifestation of ignorance regarding our own position.

Now, if the substratum (*āśraya*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), then "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) must be stated as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Since that [substratum-ness] is non-different from its own nature and is manifold due to being delimited by various relations, there would be a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*); therefore, he says: "And the delimitor of the denotative capacity... The phrase "will be explained" implies that this is the occasion for defining the meaning of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*). Thus, the point is that since a uniform [property] in the form of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) will be explained there, the defect resulting from multiplicity does not apply in that case.

Intending to refute the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and others by means of powerful evidence, and wishing to establish that the agent and the object are indeed denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but). [The objection is: "But surely, according to the rule that 'whatever causes the cognition of something denotes that thing,' the very cognition of the agent and the object produced by the verb (*ākhyāta*) is the proof. To this, he replies with the words "pratīteḥ" (from the cognition), which is to be construed with the word "sambhavāt" (because of the possibility). He states the reason for this possibility with the phrase "by means of indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*).

Now, if the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) were to indicate the substratum (*āśraya*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the manifestation of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) would be untenable; yet, if one were to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for it there in order to justify that manifestation, then secondary indication of the substratum would be impossible due to the contradiction of two simultaneous functions (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, if there were secondary indication of the substratum of the productive operation by virtue of its being the substratum of the productive operation, the primacy of the productive operation itself would be lost. Therefore, he says: "by implication" (*ākṣepāt*). The meaning is: "implication" refers to an apparent inconsistency (*anupapatti*), and [the substratum is understood] from that.

For instance, according to the *anvitābhidhāna* theory, since words present their meanings only as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is impossible for the *bhāvanā* denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*) to be a qualifier itself; therefore, it [the *bhāvanā*] necessitates the postulation of a substratum (*āśraya*). Alternatively, this is established through inference. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The *bhāvanā* understood from the verbal form is dependent upon something [as its substratum], because its capacity is apprehended as being a qualifier, just like the 'pot-ness' (*ghaṭatva*) understood from the word 'pot'."

However, being cognizable by the same cognition [as the object] is not an implication (ākṣepa), because when the substratum appears as "the object of knowledge" (prameya), the productive urge (bhāvanā) does not appear; and because when there is a cognition of the productive urge generated by the word "productive urge," the substratum does not appear.

Now, one might object: since the cognition of the substratum is established by experience even without the recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) and so forth, the appearance of the substratum cannot be accounted for through implication, because such an appearance occurs only occasionally.

Furthermore, if its manifestation [of the substratum] is established according to the aforementioned method, it would follow that the predominance (*prādhānya*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in the cognition produced by the verb is untenable; for, at the time of grasping the word-potency (*śaktigraha*), it is presented merely as a qualifier, just like "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Moreover, this point cannot withstand scrutiny. Therefore, he says: "or from a word ending in the nominative case. The meaning is that the cognition of the substratum is established from the very word "Caitra" or the like, which is co-occurrent (*samabhivyāhṛta*) and ends in the nominative case. Thus, the intention is that the failure to cognize the substratum does not prove that the potency of the verb resides in the substratum.

Regarding the word "mānam" (proof): although it would have been more appropriate to reply that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must necessarily possess a denotative power (*śakti*) in that context for the purpose of manifesting the substratum as the locus (*āśrayatvena*), nevertheless—given the view that the verbal root (*dhātu*) has power over the result and the operation (*phala-vyāpāra*) while the verbal suffix has power over the substratum—the substratum is obtained merely as a substratum [and not specifically as the locus]. Consequently, the specific power of the verbal suffix intended by [the author] regarding the substratum in general is not established. Therefore, it should be understood that this aphorism (*sūtra*) is cited as evidence specifically to refute that view.

One might raise the objection: "Since this sūtra does not contain the word 'agent' (kartṛ), how can it serve as proof for the fact that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) denotes the agent? He dispels this doubt with the words "atra hi" (for here). One might further object: "This sūtra teaches that the power to denote the agent and so forth belongs only to the *lakāra*s (the abstract substitutes), not to the verbal suffix itself. To this he replies: "bodhakatārūpām" (in the form of being a signifier); the meaning is "in the form of being a generator of cognition. This statement is made in order to refute the view that the power resides only in the substitutes (*ādeśa*) and that the substitutes convey the meaning by means of recollecting the original forms (*ādeśin*). How this is so will be explained later.

The sense is as follows: since it will be established that, according to the theory of *varṇasphoṭa*, the expressive power belongs to the very phonemes being heard, the sūtras such as "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) can serve as valid means of proof for the expressive power of the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), provided one determines that their purport lies specifically in the apprehension of the power of the *tiṅ* suffixes and so forth. The phrase "the nasal *n*, the visarga, etc. refers to instances such as "rāmān" and "rāmaiḥ. The expression "in the case of the agent and object words" is to be understood as continuing from the previously mentioned [context] beginning with "obtained through the recurrence," and so on.

The phrase "regarding [the words] *kartṛtva* and *karmatva*" is intended to refer to the theory that the word-meaning is the universal (*ākṛti-śakti-vāda*); the underlying thought is that the designation is primarily focused on the abstract state (*bhāva-pradhāna-nirdeśāt*). The meaning is as follows: since the root *kṛ* denotes effort, the word *kartṛ*—which ends in the suffix *tṛc* derived from that root and signifies the agent—is a denoter of the substratum of that effort; therefore, by means of the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) following it, there is the cognition of a subordinate property (*upadharma*) in the form of the effort which serves as the qualifier of the primary meaning of the base.

The meaning is that "action-ness" (karmatva) is the result, because the term *karman* is technically defined as the substratum of the result of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*). As for the phrase "it should be suspected," the sense is that, by the force of that very sūtra, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verb (*ākhyāta*) for the agent and the object is not established.

The term *darśanāntarīyā* means "belonging to another system of philosophy. Here, *darśana* refers to a philosophical system such as Nyāya; *anyad darśanam* is "another system," and that which arises therein is *darśanāntarīyā*. The suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *gaha*. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that because the verb *pacati* is analyzed as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the root *pac*, while the *tiṅ*-suffix expresses the operation (*vyāpāra*). In their view, since the operation is not obtainable from any other source, there is no obstacle to the prescription of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in that regard.

Although, according to the aforementioned method, even if the capacity (śakti) for the operation (vyāpāra) is established, the statement that "the term *karman* indicates the capacity for the result" remains untenable; nevertheless, it is absolutely necessary for the sake of establishing the distinction between what is directly denoted (*abhidhāna*) and what is not (*anabhidhāna*). The sense is that the dual manifestation [of the operation] must somehow be resolved. The phrase "of the *kṛt*s" means those suffixes designated as *kṛt*, such as *ṇvul*, *tṛc*, and so forth.

Now, one might object that the rule "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*) itself is the proof for the existence of expressive power (*śakti*) there; to this he replies: "And because of the rule 'kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent' (*kartari kṛt*)," and from that very sūtra, the term "agent" (*kartari*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here as well. Thus, the word "agent" in the preceding sūtra refers only to the substratum (*dharmiparatva*), whereas here, if it were to refer to the property (*dharmaparatā*), then even there it would have to refer to the property alone. He states this very point: "It shares the same acquisition and security. Here, "acquisition" (*yoga*) is the obtaining of what was not yet obtained, and "security" (*kṣema*) is the preservation of what has been obtained.

And thus, by the same logic, if one accepts that the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) establishes that the *bhāvanā*—which cannot be obtained from any other source—is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), then the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) must likewise establish that the *kṛt* suffixes have the *bhāvanā* as their meaning. If it is argued that this is not so because the *bhāvanā* is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) alone and therefore the rule *kartari kṛt* does not establish that power for the *kṛt* suffixes, then it follows equally that the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* also does not establish the power of the *bhāvanā* for the verbal suffix; such is the sense.

Now, it might be argued that even if the word *kartṛ* (agent) in the preceding sūtra refers to the substratum (*dharmin*), there is no aforementioned defect, because that term, as it is carried over (*anuvṛtta*), can be made to refer to the property (*dharma*) by resorting to the governing context of "words" (*śabdādhikāra*).

Furthermore, if it is considered that the recourse to the governing rule of *śabda* (the word itself) occurs only when there is an indicator (*gamaka*), and that in the present case there is no evidence for such a recourse, even then—since both positions, namely that "capacity (*śakti*) is the *kāraka*" and "that which possesses capacity (*śaktimat*) is the *kāraka*," are established in the original treatises (*ākara*), and since the distinction between the *tiṅ* and *kṛt* suffixes is based on the adoption of one of those alternatives—even when resorting to the governing rule of *artha* (the meaning), the attainment of the intended meaning remains entirely unimpaired; hence he says "api ca" (furthermore), and thus, regarding the fixed alternative...

The sense is that, since [the alternative] would lack authoritative basis, it is logical that [the sūtra] has only a single purpose. Now, if the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) does not denote the operation (*vyāpāra*), how can that operation be understood from it? To this he says: "of the productive activity" (*bhāvanāyāḥ*). The phrase "like *kṛt*-suffixes, etc. uses the suffix *-vat* according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*; the meaning is "as in the case of *kṛt*-suffixes, etc. By the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of primary derivatives (*taddhita*) prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

And thus, in your view, since the verbal root does not denote the operation (*vyāpāra*), the *bhāvanā* implied by the agent denoted by the *kṛt*-suffix becomes an object of cognition; the point is that the same applies to the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as well. "That being the case" means: given that the *bhāvanā* is not directly expressed (*avācya*) by the verbal suffix. "Of that *bhāvanā*" refers to its primacy, that is, its status as the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*). The meaning is:

just as in the theory that "the word-meaning is the universal" (*jātiḥ padārthaḥ*), the individual (*vyakti*) implied by the universal is the primary element, so too the *bhāvanā* implied by the agent will be established as the primary element.

One might suspect that the fact that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes *bhāvanā* (productive activity) will also follow from the "explanation" (*vivaraṇa*) included among the means of grasping word-potency; this is addressed by the phrase "of the explanation of *bhāvanā*. Since "explanation" consists in the statement of a term's meaning by means of another synonymous term, in the present case, because the verbal suffix in "he cooks" (*pacati*) is explained by the word "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*) as "the productive activity of cooking" (*pākabhāvanā*), the meaning is that the suffix denotes *bhāvanā*.

He states that because a paraphrase (vivaraṇa) follows one's own specific understanding, no definitive conclusion regarding the meaning can be reached by it alone. The sense is this: since we observe that for the expression "pacati" (he cooks), there is a paraphrase as "the act of cooking having a single agent" (*ekakartṛkā pacikriyā*), there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*) to determine whether the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) lies in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) or in the agent; thus, the meaning remains indeterminate. Regarding the term "itaretarayoga-dvandva," it is stated as such because, whereas in a *samāhāra-dvandva* the collective whole denoted by the final member is paraphrased by the word "ca" (and), here it is not so.

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of a *dvandva* compound such as "dhava-khadirau" (the Dhava and Khadira trees), the conjunction (*ca*) found in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) explains the "concomitance" (*sāhitya*), which is not denotable by the individual words of the compound. Furthermore, this "fitness" (*yogyatā*) consists in possessing the form that serves as the cause for syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Thus, it has been stated—assuming that even the concomitance of word-meanings (*apadārthasāhitya*) appears here as the cause for the connection with duality (*dvitva*), just as "being other than perforated" (*chidretaratva*) appears as the cause for the fetching of water in the sentence "fetch water with a jar"—that there is a manifestation of such concomitance.

In that regard, since *sāhitya* (conjunction) is not experienced as something distinct from duality (*dvitva*) and so forth, and since it is presented [to the mind] solely through dual-number endings and the like, the function of *sāhitya* does not reside in each individual word constituting the compound. As for the alternative view that this very [conjunction] is the analysis (*vivaraṇa*), that will be discussed later. The phrase "because of equality" means that one can likewise say that the analysis of the verb by means of the word *bhāvanā* is also an analysis of something that is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*). The sense is that both [theories] are equal in that an analysis following one's own particular understanding does not determine the actual meaning.

Now, if the verb denotes the agent, then it would be untenable for the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), which is implied by that [agent], to possess primacy. Nor should it be argued that primacy is already established—as in the case where an individual is implied by a genus according to the theory of form (*ākṛtivāda*)—because there is a disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration. To explain: the *bhāvanā* must be implied by the agent as that which defines its own nature, since agency is impossible for one devoid of *bhāvanā*. Consequently, because its status as a subordinate factor is established by the very cognition that apprehends the agent, primacy is impossible, just as it is with the action (*kṛti*).

However, since a substance (dravya) understood as the object to be delimited by its genus (jāti) is implied in that very same way, it appears as the primary element; thus, for the sake of this primacy, it is necessary that the efficient force (bhāvanā) be the expressed meaning. With this in mind, he states another objection beginning with "kiñca" (furthermore). The phrase "because of the observation of non-difference connection" means that such a cognition as "the current activity has Devadatta as its single, non-different agent" is accepted by the grammatical tradition (Ākara). The phrase "in accordance with that" means in accordance with the requirement of non-difference connection.
The meaning is that [the requirement of] "necessity" (āvaśyakam) is because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of denying such an experience as is actually felt.

"Restrictive factor" (niyāmakam) means that the causal efficacy of the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by a word ending in a particular case-ending toward a verbal cognition—wherein the relation is the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) determined by a subject-ness (prakāratā) delimited by the relation of non-difference (abheda-saṃsarga) residing in the meaning of a noun ending in that same case-ending—is already established in cases such as "nīlo ghaṭaḥ" (the blue pot). And "that" (tacceti) means the possession of identical case-endings (samāna-vibhaktikatva), which is the cause for the cognition of non-difference; this refers here to examples such as "devadattaḥ pacati" (Devadatta cooks).
He shows instances where there is a deviation from such a rule through the passage beginning with "By means of Soma" (somena), etc.

One might object: "In this sacrifice, since Soma is construed only as the instrument (karaṇa), how can there be a deviation from the stated rule? If so, we say no; for if Soma is construed as the instrument in the production of the sacrifice (yāgabhāvanā), then the sacrifice itself must also be construed as the instrument. Consequently, if both were enjoined—namely, "One should bring about the desired result by means of Soma and by means of the sacrifice"—it would result in the fallacy of sentence-splitting (vākyabheda).

If *soma* were the instrument of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) toward the fruit—just as the sacrifice is—the sacrifice would consequently become subordinate, which is untenable because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice; furthermore, since the efficient force denoted by the suffix connects with the sacrifice expressed in the same word as its instrument, the expectancy is satisfied, making it impossible for *soma*, which is expressed by a different word, to connect as the instrument.

If one accepts the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) as "one should perform a sacrifice with *soma*," although there is no logical inconsistency regarding *soma* being for the sake of the sacrifice—since it connects precisely as an instrument (*karaṇa*)—nevertheless, the impossibility of connecting that which is presented as the instrument of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), which is the meaning of the suffix, as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) remains unavoidable. Therefore, the established doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas is that there is no contingency of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), because the word *soma* functions through a metaphorical indication of its quality (*sattvārtha-lakṣaṇā*) to enjoin a qualified object: "One should bring about the desired result by means of a sacrifice possessed of *soma*.
In this regard, the sense is that a deviation from the stated rule is unavoidable.

The meaning is that even in the case of "stokaṃ pacati" (he cooks slightly), there is a non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the referent of the word *stoka*, which has a different case-ending, and the fruit produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root. Now, it might be argued that having the same case-ending is the sole condition for the cognition of a non-difference relation between the meanings of two nouns; this is why, in the rule of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), only the dual number is mentioned. Furthermore, the status of being a noun (*nāmatva*) will be explained later. In the present instance, since the relata (*anuyogin* and *pratiyogin*) are not the meanings of nouns, the aforementioned fault does not apply; therefore, he says "rājapuruṣa" (the king's man).

Although the fact that [the verbal suffix] denotes the agent is already established—even in cases such as "Devadatta cooks," where, just as in "one should sacrifice with Soma," the possession of the same case-ending is not the governing factor but rather the requirement for the connection with the intended meaning—nevertheless, the example involving two noun-meanings has been adduced with the intention that, despite the linguistic capacity (*vyutpatti*) [of the suffix] to have two noun-meanings as its object, the deviation [from the rule] remains unavoidable.

This is according to the view of the Naiyāyikas, for they accept that in a *karmadhāraya* and a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, either the denoted or the indicated meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) undergoes a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) with the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). However, it should be understood that in our own system (*svamata*), since we accept the theory of "abandoning one's own meaning" (*jahatsvārtha-vṛtti*), there is no relation whatsoever between the meanings of the preceding and succeeding members; thus, the aforementioned grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) has no application here. This [point] is also illustrative of the *ṣaṣṭhy-artha-bahuvrīhi*.

Others, however, say that because the condition of being non-compounded (*asamastatva*) is also a qualifier of the nominal element (*nāmāṃśa*) in the aforementioned etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the cases mentioned. More will be said on this later. "Co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) means the two words express a single object. "Of those that are etymological" (*yaugikānām*) means of those that function by virtue of their constituent parts (*avayavavṛtti*) alone. "Because of the non-attainment of denoting a substance" (*dravyavācitvānāpatteḥ*) means because of the non-attainment of having the power [to denote] a substratum (*dharmin*).

The meaning is that "thus" (*evam*) refers to establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) solely through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or alternatively, that it means "in this very manner. Regarding the phrase "such as *vaiśvadevī*," the words "because it would not result in denoting a substance" (*dravyavācitvānāpatti*) are to be supplied. The implication is that, in such a case, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the section concerning the *bālabāla* [or *bālābalā*] sacrificial offering.

For instance, it is heard in scripture: "One pours curd into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; [the whey] for the Vājins. Herein arises this doubt: does this scriptural statement enjoin a single ritual action characterized by both qualities (*āmikṣā* and *vājina*), or rather two distinct ritual actions differentiated by their respective qualities and deities? [The opponent argues: Because they are connected with the food (*vāja*) in the form of *āmikṣā*, the Viśvedevas are the "Vājins"; referring to them, the quality of *vājina* (whey) is enjoined.

Therefore, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the Vaiśvadeva is a single ritual possessing both qualities. In the statement "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevyāmikṣā*), the connection with the deity expressed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is a direct, scriptural (*śrauta*) connection; however, in the statement "The *vājina* for the Vājins" (*vājibhyo vājinam*), that connection is established through syntactical context (*vākya*). Even though there is a dependence on another word, because only a word whose meaning is non-different from one's own is required, there is no sublation of the scriptural nature of the connection. But where there is a dependence on a word with a different meaning, only there does the syntactical context (*vākya*) function as the allocator.

And thus, the statement "the curdled milk (āmikṣā) belongs to the Viśvedevas" is not an injunction of the accessory substance *vājina* with reference to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice already enjoined, because that sacrifice has no further expectancy since its requirement for a substance is satisfied by the scripturally prescribed (*śrauta*) material. Rather, it is an injunction of a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*). Furthermore, the phrase "to the Vājins" is an injunction of a previously unknown deity; such is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

Furthermore, if the *taddhita* suffix possesses the capacity to denote only the relationship with the deity, then—since the application of both the *vājina* and the *āmikṣā* by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*) is equal—the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the relationship with the deity regarding the substance *āmikṣā* is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) would be contradicted. For, if one were to take up the substance *āmikṣā* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and then establish its relationship with the deity, there would be no inconsistency in that relationship being based on direct scriptural statement; thus, it would be improper to assume that the *taddhita* suffix has the meaning of a substance.

"From the acquisition of instruction"—this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes logical reasoning (*yukti*) as well. For instance, just as from the word "pot" there arises a cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*), so too is it universally established that from words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) there arises the cognition "one who possesses a connection with a staff. In that case, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the mere relation would be the denotation of the suffix *-matup* and others. It is for this very reason that the capacity of the suffix *-tva* to convey a relation is consistent in the expression "Devadatta’s possession of cows" (*devadattasya gomattvam*).

In cases such as *ghaṭatvam* ("pot-ness"), since the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is that which serves as the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*), just like the pot-ness itself which is the meaning of the base, one should not raise the objection: "How can there be a cognition of the particular [entity] or the relation from that [suffix]? For that [particular] appears precisely as a qualifier with respect to the aspect of the individual (*vyakti*) implied by it.

Thus, even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed with the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), such as in the analysis "one year belongs to her" (*ekam hāyanam asyāḥ*), and also in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) signifying a deity, such as in the analysis "the Viśvedevas are its deity" (*viśve devā devatā asyāḥ*), it is observed that the relationship itself is the predominant factor; therefore, it is determined that this relationship alone is what is expressed by the compound formation (*vṛttivācya*). And it has been said:
"In whichever external referent (*anyapadārtha*) a *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed, since that too is the meaning of the suffix, the relationship holds the position of predominance."

Nor is there an impossibility of cognizing the relatum in expressions such as "gomān" (possessor of cows), because that is possible through the implication (*ākṣepa*) of a relation that rests upon both [relata], just as in the case of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the relation itself. Furthermore, since a non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*) relation alone cannot be the meaning of a nominal suffix (*vibhakti*), and since the *matup* suffix and others prescribed after such a suffix would then fail to convey a cognition of such a relation—resulting in the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the non-connection of gender and number—one must, out of respect for the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*), admit that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in a substantial relation alone.

And in this way, let the substance itself be the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*); why should the relation not be something obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*)? Furthermore, if the possessive suffix and its like were to have "relation in general" as their meaning, they would result in being synonyms for words such as "relation" (*sambandha*), and thus it must be accepted that they denote a specific relation. And that [specificity] consists in being defined by the particular relata—the correlate (*anuyogin*), the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Furthermore, it should not be argued that there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for that [relation] even when one of the two relata—the *nirūpaka* (the defining locus)—is obtained by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), merely for the sake of manifesting the form of the *anuyogin* (the related term) as the *nirūpaka*. For words such as *matup* (possessive suffixes) have as their denotation only a relation that has not yet become a substance (*asattvabhūta*). Precisely for this reason, although relations are manifold and lack gender (*aliṅgaka*), words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) appear in the singular number and possess various genders; this is because such usage is observed only when the relata themselves possess those respective properties.

And thus, because a connection with gender and so forth is impossible for the possessive suffix (*matup*), the related entity is implied by those very [suffixes], just as the agent and so forth are implied by the number of the verbal meaning (*ākhyātārtha*).

In reality, however, even the state of being "unsubstantial" (*asattvabhūtatva*)—defined as the non-connection with gender and number—is established by the sense of the genitive case and the like; for it is impossible for the gender, number, and so forth belonging to the meaning of a suffix to connect with that very same meaning of the suffix, given the etymological derivation of "suffixes" (*pratyayānām*) as those which are "attached to" (*prati + ayana*) the base. Therefore, a relationship that is unsubstantial is not denoted by the genitive case.

As for the objection that it is cumbersome to postulate a power (*śakti*) in a substance in order to account for the manifestation of the relationship between the qualificandum and the qualifier, that too is not correct; for while the perception of a relation requires the manifestation of all its substrata, this is not the case in verbal cognition, whereby the cumbersomeness of postulating such a power might be suspected. Therefore, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the power of the *matup* suffix and others residing therein. This has been explained in greater detail elsewhere.

And thus, since there exist grammatical injunctions and numerous supporting arguments establishing that words such as *ekahāyanī* denote the relation itself, their denotative power (*śakti*) resides in that very relation and not in the related entities; this is the "indivisible meaning" (*akhaṇḍārtha*).

Consequently, the meaning is that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Regarding the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*: for instance, it is heard in scripture, "He purchases Soma with a reddish, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: should the word *aruṇim* (redness) be construed by breaking the context and inserted into the [general] context, or should it be connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys)? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: If it were connected with *krīṇāti*, then by virtue of that connection, it would become an instrument for the act of buying. However, since that which is formless (*amūrta*) cannot be such an instrument, it has no connection with the act of buying; therefore, it should be inserted into the context as something entirely separate.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: since it is improper for words to enter into a context when a connection with proximate word-meanings is possible, and because words such as *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) denote substances, they can easily be connected with that [substance]; thus, through that [substance], they also achieve connection with the meaning of the verb "to buy" (*krīṇāti*), and therefore their status is indeed that of being constituent parts of the sentence. But this is untenable, because derivative words (*yaugika*) such as *piṅgākṣī*, by the reasoning already stated, have relation as their meaning and do not denote a substance by means of them.

Furthermore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is also untenable; for the relationship between the meanings of the words *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old) is likewise incorporeal (*amūrta*), and thus it cannot possibly serve as an instrument for the act of buying (*krīṇāti*). Consequently, the status of being an instrument for buying cannot be obtained from this sentence. Moreover, since there is a suspicion of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) regarding *āruṇya* (redness) itself, the very foundation of the argument is weak. Furthermore, there is no decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) to establish that the two *bahuvrīhi* compounds and the word *aruṇa* are equally capable of enjoining a substance through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), such that one could claim that only the *bahuvrīhi* compounds etc. enjoin the substance and not the word *aruṇa*. This will be explained in greater detail later.

"By the aforementioned method" means by the postulation of a relational indication (*sambandhi-lakṣaṇā*). "As elaborated" means that the elaboration has already been stated for the most part. "In the *Bhūṣaṇa*" refers to the present context, as well as on the occasion of defining the power of compounds (*samāsa-śakti*). By the phrase "having defined the word-meaning," the connection between the definition of word-meaning and the subsequent definition of sentence-meaning is indicated. The result of this, however, is the comprehension of the preceding and following portions of the text as a single syntactic unit (*ekavākya*), which possesses a single purpose and results in knowledge.

Some, however, state that the purpose [of stating the connection] is the removal of the cognition of inconsistency, which is caused by the suspicion that [the text] is the incoherent prattle of a madman. And that [connection] is of six kinds, consisting of the property that delimits the capacity to generate the desire to know (jijñāsā) which prompts the statement of immediate succession. As it has been said:
"The relevant context (prasaṅga), the introductory topic (upoddhāta), causality (hetutā), and likewise the occasion (avasara)..."
"When there is a single purpose to be accomplished, a sixfold connection is desired. Thus [it is said].

In this context, *upoddhāta* (the introductory or preparatory discussion) consists in being conducive to the subject at hand, as delimited by the time of reflection conducive to the accomplishment of that subject. Here, "conduciveness" should be understood according to the specific case, in forms such as being a constituent part (*ghaṭakatva*) or being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*). In that regard, the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) is useful as an existing entity in its own right (*svarūpasat*), while the other factors are useful when known.
