The same applies hereafter. *Prasaṅga* (the incidental or consequential discussion) consists in possessing a property that serves as the delimitant of the state of not being fit for neglect, as delimited by the time of recollection. Its status as a cause (*hetutā*) is well-known.

*Avasara* (the opportunity) is the necessity of being stated at the time when the student’s obstructing desire to know has ceased. *Nirvāhakatva* (the state of being a facilitator) consists in the production of a single effect; it is a form of *prayojakatva* (causative agency) common to both a cause and its delimitors. *Ekakāryatva* (the state of having a single effect) is the effectness of one thing, which is both the state of being produced (*janyatā*) and the state of being an object of a produced cognition. Some examples will be given right here, while others are to be inferred by oneself.

As for the examples of objection (*ākṣepa*) and so forth, which are well-known as types of "connection" (*saṅgati*) in other systems, they are included within these very categories; thus, there is no possibility of their being additional. In the present context, however, the connection is one of "occasion" (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) between the meaning of words (*padārtha*) and the specific sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) consisting of the relation between those word-meanings. For instance, once the word-meanings have been defined, since there is generally no word-meaning that remains unconnected, there arises a recollection of their mutual relation in a general form.

Then, because a cognition whose qualifier is a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) generates a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*), the student has a desire to know the specific property in the form of the question, "What is their relation? Thereafter, for the purpose of making that known, the student employs speech. Following that, the teacher possesses the knowledge of the student's desire to know.

Then, upon the knowledge of the object of inquiry, from the cognition that [the teaching] is a means to a desired end, there arises through the production of the striking of the throat, palate, and so forth, the denotation of the sentence-meaning in the form of a specific relation by the teacher, which results in the cessation of the student's desire to know. Since the generality residing in the relation is the delimitor of the state of being not fit for neglect, and since that [generality] exists in what possesses it (the specific relation), the definition is applicable. In this manner, the definitions should be applied elsewhere as well.

Regarding the term "viśeṣaṇe" (in the qualifiers), the meaning is that they are the modes (*prakāra*) by way of the relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). He states the reason why number (*saṅkhyā*) is what causes its connection with the agent or object denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), namely: "because it is presented by the same suffix" (*samānapratyayopāttatvāt*). By this, it is suggested that since direct syntactic indication (*abhidhāna-śruti*) within the same word is stronger than sentence-level context (*vākya*), it is improper for the number to connect with the meaning of the nominative case-ending while abandoning its connection with what is presented in the same word; the sense of the phrase is "because it is the object of a presentation produced by the same suffix."

In the view that the optative suffixes (*laḍ* etc. are denotative, since the property of being an object of the presentation generated by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) also exists in time (*kāla*), he qualifies that [presentation] as having the agent or the object as its object, in order to avoid a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that respect.

And so it is said: "tathāca" (and likewise). In order that there be no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is a number such as singularity (*ekatva*) in expressions like "the jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*), the term "meaning of the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātārtha*) is included within the scope of the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). To exclude [such cases] from a cognition where time is the qualifier of that [verbal suffix's] meaning, he uses the word "number" (*saṅkhyā*). In this context, he refutes the Nyāya position—intended to demonstrate his own view that the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are the meanings of the verbal suffix—by means of the phrase beginning with "naiyāyikānām" (of the Naiyāyikas), taking the occasion to do so. The phrase "due to connection" (*anvayāt*) means that it is logical for two things denoted by a single word to be connected with a single referent; this is the intended sense.

He says "number" (*saṅkhyā*) because the cognition of the tense and mode of the meaning of the verb does not depend upon the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case.

He says "not being a qualifier of another" (*itarāviśeṣaṇatva*). This means: "not being included in [the state of] being a qualifier of something other than the meaning of the nominative-terminating word. Thus, the meaning is that the cause is a mental presence whose object is a meaning that has not attained the status of being a qualifier of another. And so, although the meanings of "moon," "eating," and so forth are the meanings of words ending in the nominative, there is no deviation [from the rule], because they are qualifiers of the similarity (which is the meaning of *iva*) or of the act of going, and so on; this is the sense. He says "included" (*ghaṭita*). The meaning is: "that which is not the object of a cognition that does not have that [qualifier] as its object."

This means, in short, that [the object] is the locus of a causal capacity whose delimiting condition (*avacchedakatā*) is not interrupted [by another]. Furthermore, "not being a qualifier of another" (*itarāviśeṣaṇatva*) means not being the intended object of the status of being a qualifier of another. Consequently, there is no fault in cases such as "Caitra cooks," where—according to the maxim of pigeons on a threshing floor (*khale kapota-nyāya*)—there is no intermediate cognition of the form "similarity belonging to Caitra"; for even though Caitra possesses the state of not being a qualifier of another (insofar as he lacks the status of being a mode (*prakāratā*) relative to anything else), this does not undermine the fact that, despite not being a qualifier, he is indeed the intended object of the status of being a qualifier.

Thus, the established meaning is as follows: with respect to verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) where the relation is the qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) of the number of the meaning of the verb, the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), through the relation of qualificandness residing in an object that is not the intended focus of the intention to have something else as a qualifier (*itaraviśeṣaṇatvatātparyāviṣayārthavṛtti*). In cases of the impersonal verb (*bhāvākhyāta*), such as "It is slept by Caitra" (*caitreṇa supyate*), there arises a cognition such as "Sleep having Caitra as its agent. To avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—since the aforementioned [nominative-generated] qualifier would not connect with the sleep which is the meaning of the verbal root—the phrase "ending in the nominative case" is used as a qualification for the word.

If it is further considered that, even so, in cases such as "Caitra alone cooks, not Maitra," there would be an impossibility of number-concordance because Caitra is a qualifier of "otherness"—which is a part of the meaning of the particle *eva* in the form of an exclusion of connection with another—then the meaning of the nominative case-ending must be qualified by the fact that it is not the intended object of the mere qualification [of the verb].

The summary of that view is as follows: since there is no purpose in introducing even the remaining portion [of the subject], and because in the stated instance Caitra is the intended object of reference by way of being both the primary qualificand and a qualifier, there is no inconsistency in the connection of number.

"Excessive complexity (*atigaurava*). The meaning is as follows: when postulating a capacity (*śakti*) for an action that is obtainable through other means, it is already complex to include the condition of "being produced by different words" (*vibhinnapadajanyatva*) in the causal factor for the cognition of number-concomitance (*saṃkhyānvayabodha*). However, if one includes the condition that the referent of a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntapadārtha*) must not be the intended object of being merely a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatvamātra*), then there is excessive complexity. "This too" means that even the aforementioned simplicity (*lāghava*) regarding the presented causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) [is undermined].

Even though, according to that view, there is a rule that number must necessarily co-occur with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), and since no verbal suffix ever produces a cognition of the co-occurrence of number with anything other than the productive operation, the state of being a cognition of the co-occurrence of the productive operation is a pervader of the state of being a cognition of the co-occurrence of number; therefore, when the effect is to be produced, the causal complex delimited by the pervaded property requires the causal complex delimited by the pervading property.

Since that [cognition]—consisting in the presentation of the meaning of a nominative-terminated word qualified by qualifiers such as "having as its sole purport the status of being a qualifier" and "not being the object of the purport"—is absent in that case, there is no possibility of a deviation (vyabhicāra) therein; therefore, there is no occasion to include the aforementioned qualifier within the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) for the causal capacity for the connection with number in order to exclude it. Nevertheless, according to the view that the power [of the verb] resides in *kṛti* (effort), in order to prevent that [undesired] consequence in the aforementioned case, there would be the burden of including the aforementioned qualifier within the delimiting condition for the causal capacity for the cognition of the connection with *bhāvanā* (productive activity).

In our view, however, since the referent of the nominative case must function exclusively as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the meaning of the verb, that which has already been conjoined as a qualifier to one [element], such as the moon, lacks further expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) and thus cannot be conjoined as a qualifier to another. Consequently, there is no deviation from the stated rule, and therefore the cumbersome introduction of a qualifying term intended to prevent such [deviation] is unnecessary. With this in mind, it was said: "this too. Further details should be sought elsewhere.

Regarding this, the moderns (navyas) say: The burden of postulating such a causal relationship—which would result from establishing that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the property [of action] by means of the aforementioned collection of arguments reinforced by parsimony—is of no consequence, because it is "phalamukha" (dependent on the result). Furthermore, it is necessary to admit the coreferential connection (*anvaya*) of the number and other properties denoted by the verbal suffix with the object of comparison, such as the moon.

In that case, if one does not accept its connection [with the verb], the sentence would result in having an incomplete meaning due to the lack of a property that serves as the basis for similarity. However, in the case of the act of eating and so forth denoted by the suffix -ktvā, there is no over-extension because number and other such properties are simply unfit for connection. Thus, in our view, there is not even a trace of a fault. Having established that the agent, the object, and number function as qualifiers, he explains that time also functions as a qualifier with the words "But time... and so forth. The phrase "in the operation" (vyāpāre) means "in the operation which is the meaning of the verbal root."

Now, one might object: since the rules such as "the *laṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of the present" (*vartamāne laṭ*), which delimit the temporal power of the verb (*ākhyāta*), do not employ a word denoting "operation" (*vyāpāra*), how can time be a qualifier of the operation that is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*)? To this, he establishes that [qualification] by the authority of those very rules, saying "tathā hi" (for instance). The meaning of "that" is the word "verbal root" (*dhātu*). The meaning of "the meaning of the verbal root" is that which consists of both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). This is because of the indication of meanings such as "in the sense of existence" (*sattāyām*) and because of the authority of the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*. By saying this, he makes it known.

The phrase "like the word ‘san brāhmaṇaḥ’" means that [the verbal root] appears as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the cognition produced by the verbal root, due to its predominance (*prādhānya*). By the particle *eva* in the expression "only the operation" (*vyāpāram eva*), the result (*phala*) is excluded. By stating "due to its predominance," it is implied that in those systems where the result is predominant in the case of a verb in the passive voice (*karmākhyāta*), the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs with the result alone. The term "makes one grasp" (*grāhayati*) means that it causes [the listener] to understand [the operation] as the qualificand of the specific time denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

The sense is that this follows from the maxim "Because qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of another," and because there is a rule that the meaning of the suffix must invariably be construed with the qualificand (viśeṣya) produced directly by the base (prakṛti). The sense is that [the agent or object] is [connected] through the proximity of being presented by the same suffix, as indicated by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ. The phrase "lest there be [the undesired application] in 'pacati'" means that the agent exists [therein]. The same applies further on. Nor is it the result (phala).

However, some maintain that the verbal root has distinct powers for the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of these two being construed as the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), because it is a general rule that such a construction occurs between two things presented separately. Furthermore, it would be cumbersome to assume that a cognition produced by a specific verbal root acts as an obstacle to the construction of those two [as subject and predicate]. Therefore, the power of verbal roots resides in the operation delimited by the result, and in the result delimited by the operation.

Furthermore, the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with specific suffixes denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) serves as the regulator for the cognition of those respective meanings. And this theoretical complexity (*gaurava*) is not a defect, because it is supported by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇikatva*). Thus, in the case of an active verb (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*), the operation (*vyāpāra*) is primary; however, in the case of a passive verb (*karma-ākhyāta*), the result (*phala*) is primary. When something is primary, temporal relation (*kāla-anvaya*) is construed with that. Since both [the operation and the result] are presented as primary from the word "root" (*dhātu*) in the Sūtra, there is no room for the aforementioned restriction.

Alternatively, even when the fruit has not yet been produced, the expression "it is being cooked" (*pacyate*) is justified by the superimposition (*āropa*) of the presence of the fruit upon the cooking process that has already begun; this is like the usage "he cooks" (*pacati*) at the time of placing the pot on the fire, based on the superimposition of the whole upon a single part. And regarding this superimposition, perception itself is the proof. As for usages such as "Devadatta cooked" (*apāci devadattena*) when the fruit exists but the operation has ceased, they say this is because the state of being past (*bhūtatva*) is constituted by the occurrence of production.

Others do not accept this; for if one were to admit such a connection (anvaya) between two [words] that have been presented separately, then there would arise the contingency of a relationship between the subject and the predicate even among the horse, the sun, and so forth, which are presented by the word *hari* when it has multiple meanings. Therefore, in that case, one must follow the principle that the causal factor (*tantratā*) is precisely the presentation generated by distinct words. And since that [distinct presentation] is absent in the present instance, how could the occurrence of such a connection be established? Furthermore, there is no evidence for the verbal root (*dhātu*) having the power (*śakti*) to denote both such a result and an operation (*vyāpāra*), and there is also the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).

It is clear to the discerning that explaining the aforementioned usages through superimposition (*āropa*)—on the grounds that a specific property (*viśiṣṭadharma*) serves as the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—is truly a resort of those with no other way out (*agatikagati*). Furthermore, by following this view, one would also be adopting the position of others (*paramata*) in asserting that "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) consists in being connected with origination (*utpatti*). Anticipating and refuting the objection regarding the connection of the time denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) with the operation (*vyāpāra*), he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). The reason given is "because of the existence of effort" (*yatnasattvāt*); that is, since the operation in the form of effort exists in its present state, there is no sublation of the object [of the cognition]. For me, however, because the result (*phala*) has not yet arisen at that time, there is no possibility of such an application [of the term "present"] occurring.

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of application" (*aprayogāt*): one might object that even if effort (*parayatna*) is imperceptible because it lacks the cause consisting of a heterogeneous conjunction with the mind and inherence in its substratum, once it is understood through inference—either by taking bodily movement as the subject (*pakṣa*) or by using that [movement] as a logical mark (*liṅga*)—one would still rise up; thus, the consequence of such an "application" (*prayoga*) is unavoidable and difficult to resolve. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by accepting the consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), stating: "by some movement, etc. (*kiñcicceṣṭādinā*), which means "by the action of some part of the body"; "in the understanding of that" (*tadavagatau*) means "in the inference of effort."

The formulation of the inference (*anumānaprayoga*) is as follows: "Devadatta’s activity is produced by effort, because it is an activity, like my own activity. Alternatively: "This person possesses an effort conducive to rising, because he possesses a distinct type of activity, like myself. In this context, the causal relationship between activity and effort serves as the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*). Since the relation of being delimited by its own locus (*svāśrayāvacchedyatva*) functions as the delimiting relation for the probans (*hetutāvacchedakasambandha*), there is no fallacy of the unestablished nature of the probans (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

Others, however, avoid the aforementioned objection in a different manner. For instance, even though an effort made by one whose body has been paralyzed by rheumatism (āmavāta) is directed toward the purpose of rising, it does not produce that result; therefore, the aforementioned grammatical application does not arise. For this very reason, the usage in such cases is simply "he exerts himself for the sake of rising" (*utthānāya yatate*).

Furthermore, to prevent the application of expressions such as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) or "he cooks" (*pacati*) during stages such as the construction of an altar or the purchase of firewood when the intended purpose is a sacrifice or a meal respectively, it must be accepted that the relation [between the action and its result] is specifically a form of "causality" (*prayojakatā*) consisting of an essential connection (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

That is to be considered: for having that as its object means being the object of a desire dependent upon a desire for that [result], since a desire for a means is dependent upon a desire for the result. And being a means is nothing other than being a motivator (*prayojakatva*). Otherwise, how could there be a desire for that? In the present case, the usage of "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and so forth would be unavoidable. Therefore, one must simply accept that the relationship between the result and the operation is precisely that of being directly produced and being the producer; by that much alone, the aforementioned usage is precluded.

In the present context, although there is no production [of the action] due to the absence of a cooperative cause in the form of power (*śakti*), the usage "he rises" (*uttiṣṭhati*) is indeed intended because the status of being a direct producer (*sākṣājjanakatva*) in the effort is unassailable. Furthermore, since that [effort], understood as the meaning of the verbal root in question, possesses the nature of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), it is impossible for it to be the objective (*uddeśyatva*) at that time. It is with this very intention that the author of the *Sāra* stated: "when there exists an effort conducive to rising.

For this reason alone, when there exists an effort which is the meaning of the verbal root in question and is conducive to cooking, the usage is simply "he cooks" (*pacati*); otherwise, however, one says "he exerts himself for cooking" (*pākāya yatate*).

In reality, the intention of the author of the Sāra is that the usage *uttiṣṭhati* ("he rises") occurs when there is a desire to express merely the operation (*vyāpāra*) in the form of an action (*kṛti*), which is the meaning of the verbal root; however, it does not occur when there is a desire to express that collection [of factors] consisting of effort, capacity, physical movement, and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood that even the usage *tadotthānāya yatate* ("he exerts himself for the sake of rising at that time") is easily accounted for.

He summarizes with the words "and thus" (*evañca*); by the particle *eva* in the phrase "only the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇam eva*), the possibility of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-artha*) being the qualificand is excluded. By the phrase "the productive activity itself" (*bhāvanā eva*), the meaning is that it is specifically the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu-artha*). Here too, by the word *eva*, the result and the agent (which is the meaning of the verbal suffix) are excluded. He raises the objection regarding a contradiction with established grammatical usage (*vyutpatti-virodha*) with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). "Elsewhere" refers to cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"). The word "observed" (*dṛṣṭam*) implies that if one were to accept the primacy of the productive activity as the meaning of the verbal root, there would be a contradiction with that [established usage].

Having established that the fourfold types of words—nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles—are taught under the heading "bhāvapradhānam," these two sentences serve to define the characteristics of nouns and verbs. Here, the construction is: "the verb (ākhyātam) has action (bhāva) as its primary meaning. According to the literal sense, the definition of the subject (*uddeśya*) consists of its connection with the word *yat*, its being mentioned first, and so forth.

This is because of the statement by the learned: "In verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), that which is mentioned first is intended as the subject (*uddeśya*)," for otherwise the intended meaning would not be obtained. For this very reason, the statement in the original treatise (*ākarokta*)—"The prior mention of the word *vṛddhi* is for the sake of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalārtha*)—is consistent. The same applies hereafter. Furthermore, since the purport (*tātparya*) of the definition is determined to consist in the communication of the primary meaning of the action (*bhāva*) as delimited by the property of being a verb (*ākhyātatva*), there is no defect even if, by the power of words (*śabdamaryādayā*), an additional identity between the meanings of the two terms in question appears from the definitional sentence (*lakṣaṇavākya*).

The delimitor of the denotatum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is *ākhyātatva*, which consists in being a *tiṅ*-ending suffix; for this is precisely what is determined to be the primary denotation of the word *ākhyāta* in such rules as "a verbal suffix [is compounded] with a verbal suffix" (*ākhyātamākhyātena*). Furthermore, this is supported by the commentary on the current Nirukta passage, which states: "The four meanings of a verbal suffix are the action (*bhāva*), time (*kāla*), the factor of action (*kāraka*), and number (*saṅkhyā*); among these, the action is the principal. By this, those who claim that the rule merely establishes that the *tiṅ* suffixes have the action as their principal meaning are refuted.

Furthermore, it is impossible for a single finite verb (*tiṅ*) to simultaneously convey the fourfold set of meanings—beginning with "being" (*bhāva*)—that are referred to by the word *tat*. "Being-ness" (*bhāvatva*) here means "the state of being produced. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*aprasakti*) to the view that the verbal suffix conveys a cognition qualified by a specific result (*phala*), which is the case for the object (*karman*). Since the property of being the primary conveyor applies only to nouns (*nāman*), and the property of conveying "being" (*bhāva*) is over-extended to nouns such as *bhuktvā* (having eaten), the specific qualification is employed to exclude those cases.

And predominance, due to its immediate presence, is determined solely by the meaning of the suffix whose base is its own designator. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as "pāka" (cooking) in expressions like "kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ" (cooking with wood), which generate a cognition possessing a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in the suffix-meaning of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Nor does it apply to nouns ending in the default singular number or those ending in suffixes such as *tavya* (gerundive), for it results in this: the state of conveying the intention (*tātparya*) that possesses a qualificandhood determined by a modehood residing in the meaning understood from a finite verb (*tiṅ*).

However, that [nature of being a non-qualifier of another] is not [the definition], because it does not exist in the action denoted by "cooks" (pac-) and so forth within sentences such as "he cooks, he exists" (pacati bhavati), and thus there would be an over-narrow application (avyāpti) to the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) in "he cooks. Furthermore, since the view that the suffix *ktvā* denotes prior time will be refuted later, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the stated definition to what is not its intended object.

The claim that there is no over-extension [of the term *bhāva*] because the *Mahābhāṣya* states, "An action expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix appears like a substance," and thus, through the transfer (*atideśa*) of substantiality (*sattva*) as in the case of "cooking" (*pāka*), the nature of being an action (*bhāvatva*) in the form of something yet-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) is absent, is not correct. For, according to the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) which explains what is correct, the transfer of that [substantiality] would apply only to that action-expressed-by-a-*kṛt*-suffix where the connection with gender and so forth is established by experience, such as in the case of the action expressed by the suffix *-ghañ* in "cooking" (*pāka*).

However, in the case of the sense of the suffix *ktvā*, because there is no experience of gender (*liṅga*) and so forth, it is improper to extend those properties [of verbal endings] to it; furthermore, since it will be stated later that, by virtue of being an indeclinable suffix (*avyayakṛt*), it merely restates the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, "having action as the primary element" (*bhāvapradhānatva*) results in the definition: the state of expressing an action which possesses a subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of a verbal ending (*tiṅartha*). By this, the verbal endings (*ākhyāta*) found in sentences such as *pacati bhavati* ("he cooks [and then] exists") are subsumed; in some cases, however, [this property] consists in the absence of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) determined by a subjecthood residing in another action.

The argument that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases where the action denoted by roots such as *pac* (to cook), although it serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the root *bhū* (to become), nevertheless appears as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) when not co-occurrent with it, has been refuted. This is because the present definition is more cumbersome than the one previously stated due to its inclusion of the concept of "absence" (*abhāva*). Furthermore, since primacy (*prādhānya*) will be defined in the subsequent definition specifically as being the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), it is logical that the same should apply here as well. Moreover, this very point of my interpretation is supported by the Bhāṣya statement: "That which has existence as its primary element" (*bhāvapradhānam*).

Regarding the phrase "sattvapradhānāni" (those in which substance is predominant), here too, as before, one should conceive of the relationship between the subject and the predicate. The delimiting factor for being a *lakṣya* (the thing to be defined) is "nounhood" (*nāmatva*), which consists in having the form of an inflected word whose base is a *kṛt*-affix or the like. This is because the *Mahābhāṣya* states: "The base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), and the inflection (*vibhakti*)—this is a noun; and existence (*sattā*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), and number (*saṃkhyā*) are the meanings of a noun. Furthermore: "A verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its predominant meaning, while a noun (*nāman*) has substance as its predominant meaning. For when one is asked about an action, one explains it with a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*): 'What is he doing? 'He cooks.'"

When asked about a substance (*dravya*), one indicates it by means of a *kṛt* [suffix]—as in the example "Which Devadatta? The one who is a cook"—according to the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra *praśaṃsāyām*. In that context, the word *kṛtā* means "by a nominal stem ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Even though a *kṛt* suffix denotes a substance, it cannot be used in isolation according to the maxim *na kevalāḥ* ("not alone [are suffixes used]"), and this is also supported by the natural sense of the word *vibhakti* (nominal ending) found in the aforementioned Bhāṣya. This is stated while relying on the view that words are derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*); therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to nouns and the like under the view that words are innate (*avyutpattipakṣa*).

He states the definition: "sattvapradhānāni" (those in which substance is predominant). The analysis of the compound is: *sattva* is substance (*dravya*) having the definition to be stated hereafter; that in which this is predominant is [the name]. The meaning is that the definition of a name (*nāman*) is the capacity to convey an object characterized by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in gender and so forth. Since the property of "having an object as its qualificand" (*viśeṣyārthakatva*) would over-apply (*atiprasakta*) to particles (*nipāta*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*), the qualification ending in "determined by a modehood" (*prakāratānirūpitatva*) is included to exclude them.

Since the rule that the cognition of an individual must have a property (dharma) as its object necessarily entails that it is qualified by having a genus (jāti) as its qualifier, the inclusion of that [genus] would not prevent over-extension; therefore, it is not included. Furthermore, the over-extension to arbitrary names (yādṛcchika), which are not covered by the delimitors of the objects of definition (lakṣyatāvacchedaka), is to be avoided simply by adding the qualification "other than those" to the definition. Likewise, the non-application of the definition to words ending in suffixes that merely restate the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) is also to be avoided by restricting the delimiters of the objects of definition.

In this regard, even the conventional usage of the term "noun" (*nāman*) is figurative, based on the fact that [words] end in nominal suffixes (*sup*); such is the intended meaning. The definition of prefixes (*upasarga*) and so forth will be stated later. Regarding the phrase "beginning with *bhū*": for instance, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) there states—“What then is this mode of expression: ‘he cooks and exists,’ ‘you cook and exist,’ ‘he will cook and exist’? This very mode of expression means that the actions of cooking and so forth are the agents (*kartṛ*) of the action of existing. By this, the primacy of the action of existing—which has the actions of cooking and so forth as its agents—is explicitly established.

The point is this: if one accepts that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*), then—because it would be contradictory to its own inherent meaning—it could not be construed as a qualifier of another word-meaning. Consequently, due to the lack of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), the actions such as *pacati* (cooking), which are qualifiers of the verbal suffix meaning, could not be construed with the action of "becoming" (*bhavati*). Thus, there would be no contradiction at all in their mutual opposition. By the phrase "the sūtra and so forth," the inclusion of the sūtra "praśaṃsāyām" is intended.

Now, does it not follow from the Nirukta’s statement, “The verb (ākhyāta) has the action (bhāva) as its primary meaning,” that in the case of verbal suffixes (liṅanta), the predominance of action—which is synonymous with *bhāva*—is established? And according to the Naiyāyika view, in the case of an agent-verb (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*), this [action] is the agency (*kartṛtva*), which is effort (*kṛti*); whereas in the case of an object-verb (*karma-ākhyāta*), it is the objectness (*karmatva*), or rather, the substratumhood (*āśrayatva*) as defined by that [objectness]. This is because they accept that the meaning of the verbal suffix, other than number and time, is designated by the term *bhāvanā*. However, in the case of an action-verb (*bhāva-ākhyāta*), since the suffix merely restates it, the action is simply the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root; and its predominance is relative to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

This Bhāṣya passage is also the source for those Mīmāṃsakas who maintain that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the mere result (*phalamātra*), based on the proximity of being conveyed by the same cognition (*samānapratyayopāttatva*). However, if one accepts the connection with time, which is the meaning of the *laṭ* suffix and so forth, then that [cognition] is also required. Furthermore, in the aforementioned Bhāṣya, the referent of the word "action" (*kriyā*) is precisely the *bhāvanā* as accepted by them; for this very reason, it is stated simply that "one explains action when asked about it by means of a *tiṅ*-suffix," and not "by means of a *tiṅ*-ending form."

The proof for the view that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the *kṛtya* (the action to be accomplished) and so forth is found in the section of the *bhūvādi* sūtra which asks, "How is it known that this is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and this is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? Therein, the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "When 'he cooks' (*pacati*) is uttered here, a certain word is heard: the word *pac*, ending in *c*, and the suffix *ati*. A certain meaning of the suffix is also heard; it is understood as the softening (*viklitti*), the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), and singularity."

When "he reads" (*paṭhati*) is said, some word is lost, some arises, and some persists: the word *pac* is lost, the word *paṭh* arises, and the word *ati* persists. As for the meaning as well, some is lost, some arises, and some persists: the act of cooking (*viklitti*) is lost, the act of reading (*paṭhikriyā*) arises, and agency (*kartṛtva*) and singularity (*ekatva*) persist.

"Therefore we conclude: whatever word disappears, that is its meaning; whatever meaning disappears, that is its word. Whatever word arises, that is its meaning; whatever meaning arises, that is its word. Whatever word is constant (anvayin), that is its meaning; whatever meaning is constant, that is its word"—so says the Bhāṣya. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa notes that because the suffix *ati* was postulated by certain earlier teachers (*pūrvācāryas*), it is stated that *ati* is a suffix.

In cases such as *pacyate* ("it is cooked") and *paṭhyate* ("it is studied"), the fact that even the object (*karman*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is determined for the same reason [as in the case of the agent], namely by the equality of the underlying logic based on the stated positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, the definition in the *Nirukta*, "the action is the primary element" (*bhāvapradhānam*), was formulated with the intention of relying on the view that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) qualified by all the factors of action (*kāraka*) and their numbers, as is evident from the natural drift of its commentary. For this very reason, when defining the characteristics of nouns (*nāman*), there is no mention of the factor of action (*kāraka*) as being the meaning of the noun; the intention behind that is that since the factor of action is obtainable from the verbal root, it does not constitute the meaning of the noun.

Nor should it be argued that, on the authority of the Bhāṣya on the *Rūpapsūtra*, although there is evidence for the existence of singularity in an action, there is no proof for the existence of duality and so forth; therefore, how can the aforementioned connection be established? For, according to the method to be explained by the words "But others... (*pare tu*), it is possible for that [number] residing in the *kāraka* to be superimposed upon the action there. Just as time and number are indicated (*dyotya*), the *kāraka* is also indicated, because the underlying logic is the same. If one were to accept that the *kāraka* is the meaning of the suffix, then—as in the cases of *pācakaḥ* ("cook") and *pakvaḥ* ("cooked")—it would result in the *kāraka* being the primary meaning.

This is because the criterion for a category distinct from *jāti* (universal) being a qualifier is precisely its status as being indicated (*dyotya*). For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "striyām," the view that gender (*liṅga*) is denoted (*vācya*) was rejected out of fear that it would result in [gender] becoming the primary meaning. If that which is denoted were not a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), the inconsistency of that [rejection] would be quite evident.

Nor does it follow from the aforementioned theory that, as in the case of the cognition of the object (*karman*) in "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of the verbal root (*dhātu*) expressing an action qualified by *apādāna* and other *kārakas*. For while the accusative and other case-endings occurring in grammatical co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) and so forth are indicators (*dyotikā*), others [such as prepositions] are different. Indeed, being a suffix whose base is itself (*svaprakṛtika-pratyayatva*) is not the sole determinant for being an indicator of its own meaning; otherwise, it would not apply to prefixes (*upasarga*). Rather, the determinant is being either a suffix or a particle (*nipāta*) that occurs in grammatical co-occurrence with itself.

And this [definition] remains intact even for the case of a case-ending following words such as *taṇḍula* (rice). For if the substance were the meaning of the noun (*nāman*) without being qualified by number, it would follow that number itself appears as the meaning of the noun; therefore, it is necessary that the noun has the substance as its meaning, which is why [the definition] excludes that [number]. For this very reason, the fact that the term *kāraka* in the Bhāṣya passage—"The four meanings of the verb (*ākhyāta*) are the action, time, the kāraka, and number"—has an unrestricted application is also consistent.

If it is further considered that the aforementioned description of the intention is not tenable because it has never been observed anywhere for a case-ending belonging to one stem to indicate the meaning of a different stem, even then its application [to the verbal suffix] is justified by taking the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) to be the action qualified by number, tense, agent, and object; for it is possible for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) alone to indicate such an action.

Nor should it be argued that such an intention indeed exists, because it is supported by the parsimony resulting from the postulation of the causal relationship described in the *Vākyapadīya*. For such a view cannot be relied upon even by those who trust the statements of the *Cakṣuḥśruti* during the stage of linguistic analysis (*prakriyā*), let alone by the followers of Akṣapāda who are adept at discerning the meanings of stems and suffixes. To illustrate: if an action qualified by its factors (*kāraka*) were the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the injunction "the suffix *la* [denotes] the object" (*laḥ karmaṇi*) would result in being rendered purposeless.

Nor does it [the suffix] possess the capacity to express the illuminator (dyotaka), because if that were the case, the same would apply to the *śānac* suffix and others as well, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the agent and other factors would also appear there as qualifiers of the action.

Furthermore, in expressions such as "Caitra cooks," there is no evidence for the superimposition (āropa) of the number residing in Caitra onto that [action]. For, under the view that [the verb] is denotative (vācakatā), since the appearance of that [number] in the factor of the agent (kartṛ) is accepted, the validity of the usage is established; thus, it is improper to assume its invalidity. Moreover, even if duality and so forth exist there by way of the relation of being located in what is itself located [in the agent], they cannot function as qualifiers because they do not serve to differentiate; consequently, the state of being qualified by them is impossible there. Indeed, a pot or the like, which is the substratum of duality, is not conventionally referred to as "two. This will be explained further below.

Furthermore, since the agent and the object are merely parts of the meaning of a word (*padārthaikadeśa*), it is impossible for Devadatta and others to be construed with them, according to the linguistic maxim that "the meaning of one word is construed with the meaning of another word. Even if such a construction were admitted, there would result the undesirable consequence of neuter gender—just as in the case of words like *stoka*—because the agent would function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in a relation of non-difference (*abheda*) with the meaning of the verbal root. Moreover, since the agent presented as a qualifier of the action lacks a specific expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), questions such as "Who? or "Of what kind? would be logically untenable when the verb *pacati* (he cooks) is uttered.

For the author of the treatise will indeed state: "The agent, being subordinate [to the action], is not capable of grasping the negation as its own adjunct. Therefore, by virtue of this very authority, those who roar with the claim that the agent is denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*) and that it serves as a qualifier of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) are refuted; for the aforementioned rule is shown to apply only when the suffix has an indicative function (*dyotakatā*), and because from that [rule] one obtains precisely the predominance of the suffix's own meaning.

Nor should it be argued that even under the view that *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is denoted by the suffix, the aforementioned objection remains as difficult to resolve; for it is possible for the agent—who is presented either through a confusion regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) or through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—to possess expectancy.

Furthermore, since the requirement that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), there is no possibility of the number [denoted by the suffix] being construed [with the agent], because the causality of the presentation generated by the base as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) toward a cognition qualified by the number—the meaning of the case-ending—is absent in the case of the agent and so forth.

The assumption that the presence of the agent or object denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is a cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the number belonging to the meaning of that suffix is likewise rooted in dogmatism; for when two word-meanings are construed as the locus and the located, such a relation depends upon their being presented by distinct words. Furthermore, since the agent denoted by the case-suffix is not a substance (*adravya*)—as it lacks gender—it is impossible for number to be construed with it, in accordance with the maxim: "And because subordinate factors (*guṇa*) exist for the sake of another."

In my view, even though it [the suffix] does not connect with the meaning of its own base due to semantic incompatibility (*ayogyatā*), the rule that it must connect with the meaning of the base remains intact, according to the maxim: "Even a minute distinction is determinative."

Furthermore, if the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) were to denote the agent, then with the intention that "the act of going has as its agent a person non-different from one related to the king," there would arise the undesirable consequence of the usage "The king goes, the man" (*rājā puruṣo gacchati*), by wishing to express the king as the agent through a relationship such as owner-and-owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), just as in the case of "The king’s man goes" (*rājñaḥ puruṣo gacchati*). Nor would there be the occurrence of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in that instance, because that [genitive] occurs only when the meaning of the suffix is intended to be the primary qualifier (*viśeṣya*) of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

This will become clear further below. Since the agent, who is the meaning of the verb, is not the meaning of a nominal stem or a verbal root, it lacks even the status of being an object of the grammatical derivation rule: "between that which is the meaning of a nominal stem and that which is the meaning of a verbal root."

Nor should it be argued that, for you as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage *caitrasya pacati* ("Caitra cooks") because of the phrase *caitrasya pākānukūlā kṛtiḥ* ("an effort conducive to cooking belonging to Caitra"); for there is an absence of mutual expectancy (*parasparākāṅkṣā*) since the meaning of the genitive case requires a nominal referent, whereas the effort denoted by the verbal suffix requires a subject expressed in the nominative case. Furthermore, everyone accepts the use of the genitive ending when there is an intention to express Caitra’s relation to the cooking, as in the example *guruvipratapasvidurgatānām* ("of the teacher, the Brahmin, the ascetic, and the poor").

Therefore, let the learned understand that the citation of the definition [of verbal roots] regarding the primacy of the meaning of the root-action over the meaning of the verbal suffix is entirely futile.

In expressions such as *pacati bhavati* ("he becomes cooking"), since it is accepted that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) meaning "becoming" (the *bhāvanā* consisting in being the locus of the verbal root's productive activity) is construed with the verbal root *kṛ* (productive activity) which is favorable to the act of cooking, one understands that the agenthood of becoming resides in the productive activity qualified by cooking. Consequently, because that [agenthood] is obtained even for the action denoted by the root *pac*, the statement in the Bhāṣya—"Verbal roots like *pac* are the agents of the action of 'becoming'"—is explained: the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the cause; thus, in the compound, it means "actions whose cause is the verbal roots *pac* and so forth," i.e., actions whose meaning is the operation denoted by *pac* and other such roots.

Furthermore, because we either derive from that [statement] the meaning that "verbs become possessors of agency as determined by the activity of becoming (bhavana-kriyā), which is of the nature of an action (kṛtyātmaka-vyāpāra)," or because we accept such a state of syntactic unity (ekavākyatva), there is no contradiction even with the Bhāṣya located in the sūtra *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*.

Moreover, precisely because of the authority of such a commentary (*bhāṣya*), just as in your view the understanding of the verbal root-meaning as a qualifier (*prakāra*) is caused by the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by the root, so too in my view, the understanding of the *bhāvanā* denoted by the suffix (*ākhyāta*) as a qualifier is caused by the mental presence of *bhāvanā* generated by the *tiṅ*-suffix, through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). Thus, the aforementioned syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is easily established.

It should not be argued that if the aforementioned understanding is accepted, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) would result after words such as *caitra* because the agent is not understood by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); for, since the occurrence of the meaning of the verbal suffix produced by the *tiṅ*-suffix is a cause for an understanding whose qualificandum is the meaning of the nominative (*prathamā*) ending, and since it is accepted that *caitra* is conjoined with that [verbal meaning] through the relation of locus (*ādheyatā*), it appears precisely as the primary qualificandum. Thus, because there exists therein an "expression" (*abhidhāna*) consisting of the understanding of the effort (*kṛti*) as a qualifier in a portion other than the substratum, the occurrence of the third case-ending is impossible.

Nor should it be argued that even upon the mere utterance of "Caitra cooks," there would result the unwanted consequence of Caitra being construed as related by way of the relation of "being located in" (ādheyatā); for we must also postulate that the presence of the mental representation of the activity (bhāvanā), which has become the qualificandum (viśeṣya) of the meaning of the verbal suffix (tiṅ), is a cause for a cognition whose qualifier (prakāra) is the meaning of the nominative case-ending. Consequently, the aforementioned fault does not arise.

Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of "caitre pākānukūlā kṛtiḥ" (in Caitra there is an effort conducive to cooking), the application of the locative case in expressions such as "caitraḥ pacati bhavati" (Caitra is cooking) would be unavoidable; for the rule for the locative is prescribed only when the locus-ness (*ādheyatva*), which serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root, is intended to be the primary qualificand of the nominal stem-meaning. Furthermore, in these cases, locus-ness is not intended to be presented as a mode (*prakāratayā*). And this has been stated with the intention that the cognition has the effort, which is the meaning of the verbal suffix, as its primary qualificand.

In reality, even if one accepts that in sentences such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*) or "Caitra is cooking" (*caitraḥ pacati bhavati*), the cognition has the meaning of the nominative case as its primary qualificand, there is no loss of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). This is because it is possible for the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the act of cooking—which is itself construed with the state of being the agent of "becoming"—to appear as a qualifier within the scope of Caitra.

By this, the objection that "if one accepts a cognition having *kṛti* (effort) as its qualificandum, there is complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating that the presence of the *bhāvanā* denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is the cause of a cognition in which the meaning of the nominative case-ending is the qualifier" is irrelevant, because we accept that it [the effort] is construed precisely as a qualifier. Anticipating a lack of conviction in this, he says "moreover" (*api ca*). Regarding the phrase "due to non-difference connection" (*abhedānvayāt*), this is stated according to his own [the author's] habitual inclination, even though in his own view the agent is the meaning of the verbal suffix.

However, it should be noted that in the Naiyāyika view, since effort is the meaning of the verbal suffix, it is construed with the referent of the nominative word solely through the relation of being its substratum (*āśrayatva*).

The phrase "established by the Bhāṣya" means that it is established by the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *karmaṇā yam*, which states: "Action (*kriyā*) is also a 'made' object (*kṛtrimaṃ karma*), for even an action can be desired through another action, such as the actions of seeing, praying, and so forth. In your view, since the intermediate sentence-meaning "the deer possesses an effort conducive to running" arises there, the act of running is already occupied by its agent. Consequently, because there is no further expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣyeṇa*) for it to be construed elsewhere as a qualifier, it is impossible for it to be construed as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing.

However, the cognition to be accepted must be of the form: "The deer, which possesses the activity conducive to running, is you who are the locus of perception. And thus, because there is an absence of syntactic unity (ekavākyatā)—defined as the capacity to produce a single cognition having one primary qualificand—the contradiction with that [other cognition] is unavoidable; this is the sense.

[Objection: But surely there is no fault as stated, because the deer—which possesses the volitional effort (*kṛti*) conducive to running—is connected with the object of seeing precisely by way of being the *karman* (object). [Response: To this he says, "by the first case-ending" (*prathamānta*), meaning "in the attainment of the status of *karman*"—that is, in the attainment of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) by way of being a *karman*. The connection of the deer with the act of seeing through the relation of *karman*-hood is impossible, because it would contradict the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that "the meanings of nouns and the meanings of verbal roots [are not directly connected]," and because it would contradict the forthcoming demonstration regarding the application of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*). This is the intended sense.

The meaning is that because the object (*karman*) is not expressed here by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the rule "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), which falls under the governing heading of "when not already expressed" (*anabhihita-adhikāra*), remains fully operative.

The meaning of "evam" (thus) is that [the objection applies] when there is the contingency of a second case (*dvitīyā*) following the word *mṛga*. The intention of the objector is this: since the rules for the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* specify that they must be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the agent of the present tense (*laḍ*), if the word *mṛga* were in the second case, that [suffix] would result; therefore, the second case will not occur. The author refutes this with "evamapi" (even so), with the underlying thought that the occurrence of the *śatṛ* suffix is not what prevents the second case; rather, it is the expression of the object (*karman*). Since the absence of such expression exists here, the second case is unavoidable. Thus he provides the resolution.

Regarding the phrase "because it would lead to an impossibility": the meaning is that if one were to accept the deer's connection with the object of the verb "to see" (dṛś), then the sentence "Look at the running deer" (adhāvantaṃ mṛgaṃ paśya) would be the only appropriate form.

Now, one might object: from Jaimini’s sūtra, "A single sentence consists of a single meaning, provided that there is expectancy if it were divided," it follows that when a passage is split, its status as a single sentence is established by its generating the cognition of a single meaning while possessing expectancy. In the present case, since the word *tam* (him) creates an expectancy for *kam* (whom), and since the two sentences in some way convey a single meaning—namely, the perception of a deer as the object of an action conducive to running—there is no risk of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). To this, he says: "As stated... (*ukteti*).

"Adhyāhāra" (supplying) means the mental connection (*anusandhāna*) of a word that was not previously mentioned but is required by the context. "And because of the consequence of non-connection" (*ananvayāpatteḥ*) means that even if the pronoun (*tatpada*) refers to the deer or to the deer possessing the volition conducive to running, it would be impossible for such a running action—which is the desired object of the root *dṛś* (to see)—to appear from that sentence as the object of the act of seeing. He concludes with "And this" (*etacceti*), meaning: and in order to strengthen the refutation consisting of the impossibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) within the system of those who accept a cognition where the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*) is the primary qualificandum.

The sense is that it is not to be respected because it is afflicted by the aforementioned defects. He states the refinement of his own view with the words "but rather" (*kintu*). To exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the result (*phala*), he specifies the objective-ness of the presentation (*upasthiti-viśeṣyatā*) as being "delimited by the nature of productive operation" (*bhāvanātvāvacchinnā*).

Now, one might object: even in your view, there arises the contingency of violating the rule that a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) generates a cognition where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the primary qualificand; to this he replies, "behold. The implication is that the stated rule applies to objects other than this [specific case].

But surely, there is an application [of the verb] in the sense of seeing, where the meaning of the sentence—namely, the form of a deer qualified by the agency of running—is the object. Thus, there is no contradiction with the grammatical rule "between two nominal meanings," because a sentence is not a nominal stem (*nāman*). For this very reason, there is no resulting occurrence of the accusative case suffix (*dvitīyā*) from that [sentence]. Furthermore, since the running, which serves as the qualifier, also acquires the status of being the object upon the understanding that the thing qualified by running is the object of seeing, there is no failure to obtain the intended connection.

In cases such as "Caitra cooks and exists" (*caitraḥ pacati bhavati*), the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) has already been established in the manner previously described. Thus, one might ask: what is the reason for following that [view] regarding the proposed causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)? To this, he says "dig" (the direction/way). Its meaning is as follows: by establishing sentence-syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) in this manner, one fails to obtain the intended connection (*anvaya*) that is sought to be conveyed through word-syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*), which is the consensus of the author of the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, if the objecthood (*karmatva*) of a jar qualified by "blue" were intended to be expressed in a sentence such as "He knows the blue jar" (*nīlaṃ ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), the use of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) would be untenable.

On this point, the Naiyāyikas argue: there is no violation of the unity of the sentence (padaikavākyatā), because it is accepted that the deer—which is already constrained by its status as the agent of the action of running—is construed with the object of the act of seeing (*dṛśya*) through the relation of being the object (*karmatā*). And "being constrained by that" means being the intended object of the speaker's purport (*tātparya*) by virtue of being connected to that [action].

Nor should it be argued that, since the rice (*taṇḍula*) could also be construed with the verb through the relation of objecthood (*karmatā*), the usage "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*) would result; for we do not accept the general construal of the meaning of a noun with the meaning of a verbal root through relations such as objecthood and the like, but rather [only] when [that meaning] is already restricted by being the agent of another action. And this is not the case with the rice, whereby it could have the relation of objecthood with the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook).

For this very reason, the expression "the wood makes a heap of ashes" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasmarāśiḥ karoti*) is not used, because the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) is not already occupied by the heap of ashes. However, in expressions such as "the wood is made into a heap of ashes" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasmarāśiḥ kriyate*), even though the action is already occupied by another [grammatical] object (*karmatva*), [the agenthood of the wood is expressed] due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpattivaicitryāt*).

If one does not accept that [the action] is a relation to that [object] in that context, then due to the consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), the cognition produced by that sentence would fail to remove the doubt—such as "Is this a transformation of the wood, or a transformation of something else?"—just as the cognition produced by the two sentences "The wood is destroyed" and "Ash is produced" does not. This and other points have been elaborated elsewhere.

And thus, since the status of this as a single syntactical unit (*padaikavākyatā*) is established here without any difficulty, the claim that the cause for the cognition of the manner of the productive operation (*bhāvanāprakārakabodha*) is the presence of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) within the productive operation is entirely without proof. Nor does there follow the consequence of a second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) after the word *mṛga* (deer), because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not intended to be the qualificand of the nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārthaviśeṣyatayā*). For this very reason, there is no possibility of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) there either; for the rule "the genitive is used in the remaining cases" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*) prescribes that [genitive] only when the relation (*saṃsarga*) is intended to be the qualificand of the nominal stem-meaning.

In the same way, this should be understood in cases such as "the pot does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*). However, in that instance, the nominative case (*prathamā*) applies only to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Nor is there any inconsistency in the usage "he knows the blue pot" (*nīlaṃ ghaṭaṃ jānāti*); for since the pot is not precluded from being the agent of another action, it is impossible for the status of being an object (*karmatā*) to function as a relation (*saṃsarga*) with respect to the action denoted by the root *jñā*, which has not itself attained the status of being qualified by another [primary] object. [As in: "Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the supremely virtuous crane at Pampā. (*paśya lakṣmaṇa pampāyāṃ bakaḥ paramadhārmikaḥ*)

In such cases, the word "exists" (*asti*) must be supplied as an ellipsis. However, in reality, the attempt to derive a cognition from examples such as "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*) by means of this analogy does not withstand scrutiny; for since a cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of the verb "to cook" and whose relation is the connection with the objecthood (*karmatā*) is unestablished, such an inference is impossible.

If it is argued that such a cognition is well-known in cases like "He cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*) through the relation of objecthood (*karmatva*) denoted by the case-ending, then [we reply]: since the knowledge of the word-sequence *pacati* as co-occurring with the word *taṇḍula* ending in the second case is the cause of such a cognition, the very absence of that [cause] makes the occurrence of the [alleged] consequence impossible. As it has been said: "Only that kind of result which is established in some instance can possibly be entailed."

By this, the objection—that in the case of "paśya lakṣmaṇa," the *asti* (is) must be supplied because of the force of the word *api* in the Bhāṣya statement, "The root *ās* (to sit), when followed by forms of *bhū*, is used even when not explicitly applied," which yields the meaning that *asti* is supplied only in the absence of another verb that completes the sentence; whereas in the present case, since the act of seeing (*darśana*) exists as the verb that completes the sentence, there is no evidence for its supply, and thus its connection through the relation of objecthood (*karmatā*) is untenable—is irrelevant.

And when it is stated thus, in the presence of a word ending in the nominative case, a cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of that nominative-ending word generally arises without impediment. For this very reason, in the sentence "Whosoever twice-born man cooks the food of a Śūdra, he is exceedingly censured," the fact that the pronoun refers back to the *dvija* (twice-born man)—who is the primary referent—is easily accounted for.

Objection: In the view that the primary meaning of a sentence has the object denoted by the first-case suffix as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), in examples such as *caitrau pacataḥ kalpam* ("The two Caitras cook somewhat"), since the word ending in *-kalpa* is a noun (*nāman*), it would follow that it must share the same gender and number as the first-case words *caitra* etc., which denote its qualifiers; furthermore, it would follow that the action (*kṛti*), which is the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*), must enter into a relation of non-difference (*abheda*) with the Caitra who is the first-case referent. Response: This is not so, because derivative suffixes (*svārthika*) generally serve to indicate contempt or other qualities residing in the property that delimits the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*). In the present case...

This is because the suffixes *kalpa* and so forth indicate the slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāptatva*) residing in the action that delimits the meaning of the base; and it is appropriate that they end in the neuter singular, as they express the state of being slightly incomplete in a manner consistent with the property that delimits the meaning of the base, whether that property be existent or non-existent.

The claim that "there would result an abheda-anvaya (non-difference relation) of its referent with Caitra because [the word] *kalpādi* and [the word] *anta* share the same case-ending and function as names" is to be rejected as the prattle of a fool; for the abheda-anvaya of the denoted agent (*lakṣyārtha*) with the agent is desired, whereas the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) simply does not connect due to semantic incompatibility (*ayogyatva*). Furthermore, they say this is because the grammatical rule includes the qualification "provided there is no sublation" (*asati bādhake*) in order to prevent over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "the jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*) or "the cloth" (*paṭaḥ*).

In this regard, the following appears: for the Naiyāyikas, when there is the co-occurrence of a word denoting an agent in the nominative case, there generally arises a cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of that nominative case. However, in some instances—such as in the sentence "Look, the deer runs"—due to the requirement of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), there arises a cognition whose qualificandum is the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). To explain: in accordance with the syntactic unity in such cases mentioned by the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*), it is postulated that the cause of a cognition having the *bhāvanā* expressed by the verbal root as its qualifier is the presentation of the *bhāvanā* produced by that verbal root.

For the Naiyāyikas, however, this is exactly the same: in a cognition where the verbal suffix (tiṅ) meaning—the productive operation (bhāvanā)—is the qualifier by way of the relation of being the object (karmatā), there is the requirement for the presentation of the productive operation derived from the verbal root (dhātu). Furthermore, in accordance with the syntactic unity of the sentence "Devadatta cooks, [and he] exists," the requirement for the presentation of the verbal suffix meaning—the productive operation—is likewise postulated for a cognition where the agent, which is the meaning of the nominative case-ending, is the qualifier.

Thus, in the case cited, when the effort conducive to running qualified by the deer is construed as the object (*karma*) with respect to the meaning of the verb *dṛś* (to see) through the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatā*), the resulting sentence-meaning comprehension is: "You are the locus of the seeing of that action which is the effort conducive to running residing in the deer. Furthermore, because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) conveyed in respect to the effort qualified by running culminates in the running itself—according to the maxim *saviśeṣaṇe hi* [when there is a qualification, the operation applies to the qualified]—the intended meaning is also successfully obtained.

Nor is there a second fault regarding the word *mṛga* (deer), because the status of the deer as the object (*karman*) is not obtained from this sentence. And thus, even in the case of "pacati bhavati" ("he is cooking"), since the cognition is that "the present activity (*bhāvanā*) based on the agent, which is the meaning of the nominative ending, is qualified by the act of cooking," the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*) is not compromised there either. Consequently, the unity of the sentence (*padaikavākyatā*) stated by the author of the Bhāṣya is easily established even in the Nyāya system without contradicting the maxim "between the meanings of the base and the suffix. Enough, then, with describing the views of others.

The author states the conclusion with the words "ityevam" (thus). The meaning is that [the view holds] both for the case where the presence of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) denoted by the verbal root is the cause of a cognition whose qualifier is the agent (*kartṛ*)—which is the meaning of the verb—and for the case where the presence of such a result (*phala*) is the cause of a cognition whose qualifier is such an object (*karman*). The term "*bhāvanā*" here refers to the "present" [action], and so forth. Furthermore, the description of a cognition having the *bhāvanā* as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the case of an object-verb (*karmākhyāta*) is made in accordance with the views of the ancients.

The moderns (navyās), however, argue that since it is observed that there is a cognition where the fruit of the action is the qualificand, it is logical that even in the case of the accusative suffix (karmākhyāta), the cognition must likewise have that [fruit] as its qualificand. In this way, the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*)—that the meaning of the suffix is directly connected with that which is the qualificand of the meaning of the stem—is not contradicted. For this very reason, the form *putrīyati* does not occur in the sense of "he desires a son" (*iṣyate putraḥ*), because the meanings would be different; rather, it occurs only in the sense of "he desires for himself a son" (*putram ātmānam icchati*). This was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *supa ātmanaḥ*.

Otherwise, the statement regarding the difference in meaning between the two would be inconsistent, since in both cases there would be a cognition having the *vyāpāra* (operation) as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In our view, however, the difference in meaning is clear: in one case the *vyāpāra* is the qualificand, while in the other it is the result in the form of desire (*icchārūpa*). Furthermore, a suffix denoting the object (*karmani pratyaya*) is difficult to obtain from a *kyaj*-derived stem, because such stems are intransitive (*akarmaka*).

And Kaiyaṭa has stated: "When the fruit of the action is primary, then only the sentence itself is desired—as in 'he desires a son' (*putram iṣyate*)—and not the form ending in *kyac*, because that [denoted by *kyac*] is intransitive and thus no suffix for the object can arise. And so they say that there is a contradiction [in the opponent's position] with the statement: "the present softening (of the rice) which has a single substratum produced by the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)."

In the case of a verb expressing an action (*bhāvākhyāta*), the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) alone is the qualificand, as that is how it is experienced. The *tiṅ*-suffix is merely reiterative; however, by virtue of being in the present tense (*laṭ*) and so forth, it conveys time. Number, however, is not its meaning, because there is no possibility of its number being construed with it due to the absence of the causal factor consisting in the presentation of a meaning such as the agent (*kartṛ*). Nevertheless, according to the maxim "not [used] alone," the singular number is used solely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), based on the established principle: "The singular number shall be applied as the general rule. As it is said: "When the time is right for a rendezvous, those who lure the deer become bewildered."

Regarding the passage, "They sit in the posture of camels; they lie down like those who have been slain," the ancients maintain that the use of the plural number is due solely to the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya.

The moderns, however, hold that the status of the singular as the default (autsargika) applies only when there is a specific indicator (gamaka), such as in the case of its derivation from an indeclinable (avyaya) by the rule "avyayād āpsupaḥ. For this very reason, in the absence of the sūtra "ṅyāpprātipadikāt," the Bhāṣya raises the objection that the suffixes might be derived from verbal endings (tiṅanta), and resolves it by stating that this is not the case because number has already been expressed by the verbal ending itself.

According to the method you have stated, even though that [number] residing in the *kāraka* is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), it is not expressed as residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Consequently, since the singular number is unavoidable—either because it is the default (*autsargika*) or because it cannot be precluded—the inconsistency is quite evident.

The rule *dvyekayordvivacanaikavacane* and others also forms a single syntactical unit with the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*. Its form is simply this: "The *l*-suffixes occur when there is an object (*karman*) and so forth; and in their place, *ti*-suffixes and others occur when there is singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. For in that context, there is no [rule] such as *dvitīyā karmaṇi*, by which one could perceive that number is a qualifier of the *kāraka* (participant in action). Furthermore, there is no evidence for [the necessity of] repetition [of the word *karmaṇi*]. Therefore, in all cases, number is construed only with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).

When the expectation arises as to "of what [is there] oneness and so forth?", it is appropriate that the connection be with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) because it is the one immediately present. Furthermore, since [terms] such as "in the object" (*karmani*) serve as qualifiers with respect to the thing to be enjoined, they have no connection with number according to the maxim "and because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another. Moreover, since the expectation "of what object? exists for [terms] such as "in the object," the connection of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) with that [object] is already established. Even in the case of an action (*kriyā*), oneness certainly exists, as evidenced by the commentary on the *rūpapa* sūtra which states, "the action is one."

And thus, because it is construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), the singular number [is used]. However, duality and so forth—belonging to the factors of action (*kāraka*) expressed by the *tiṅ* suffixes that follow it—are superimposed there; thus, dual and plural endings are established in the case of *tiṅ* suffixes expressing agent or object. For this very reason, there is no doubt regarding duality and so forth in the factor of action (*sādhana*), because the superimposition of number residing in the action is caused by the cognition of the factor of action. Since, in accordance with examples such as "many cook" (*anekaḥ pacati*), you too must admit the superimposition of number upon the factor of action, its construction (*anvaya*) also occurs only with the meaning of the base.
