In the present context, regarding such examples as *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante* ("those who have been killed lie down"), the reason why there is only the superimposition (*āropa*) of [the action] belonging to the [agent] who has been killed, and not that belonging to another, is rooted precisely in the inherent nature of the power of the verbal root (*dhātvartha-śakti-svabhāva*). For this very reason, the dual number and so forth occur in the impersonal passive (*bhāve*). As it has been said:

"Even though the action (*kriyā*) denoted by the verb is one, it is differentiated in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) by the number residing in the grammatical factor (*sādhana*), but the differentiation consisting of gender (*liṅga*) does not exist therein, for that [gender] resides in the [substantive] substrate."

And thus, they say that there is parsimony in the view that the semantic representation (upasthiti) generated by the verbal root is the cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the verb; this maintains a single cause-and-effect relationship and preserves the grammatical rule that "suffixes [denote their own meanings]."

Others do not accept this, because since the general singular number (*autsargika-ekavacana*) serves the purpose of maintaining the conventional rule (*samaya-paripālana*), there is no need for an expectancy for an indicator (*gamaka*) therein; thus, the statement "only when an indicator exists" is redundant. Furthermore, as for the citation from the *Bhāṣya* on the *ṅyāpprātipadika* sūtra as an indicator, that too is exactly so, because that very *Bhāṣya* indicates the absence of any general number (*saṃkhyā-sāmānya-abhāva*) with respect to the action (*kriyā*).

To explain: in the absence of the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, the apprehension that a case-ending (*sup*) might arise after a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) would have to be raised either by taking the number of the *kāraka* (the meaning of the suffix) or by taking the number residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Among these, since the meaning of the base is of the nature of a non-substance (*asattva*), its connection with number is impossible; thus, only the apprehension based on the number residing in the *kāraka* remains. That [apprehension] is refuted by the statement "because it has already been expressed by the verbal suffix" (*tiṅoktatvāt*). For, since the observance of the linguistic convention has already been accomplished by the verbal suffix itself, there is no possibility for that [case-ending] to apply, and thus its refutation is not even required.

This is because, by the natural force (*svārasya*) of rules such as *sup-tiṅ-antaṃ padam* and *tiṅ-ṅatiṅaḥ*, and rather than implying the knowledge of the aforementioned meaning, it is more appropriate for that rule to indicate the absence of the default singular number (*autsargikaikavacana*) after a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).

Even the Bhāṣya statement, "and there is one action" (*ekā ca kriyā*), does not indicate oneness in the action itself, but rather merely the absence of any general number (*saṃkhyāsāmānyābhāva*). Otherwise, how could the commencement of this statement be meaningful when the purpose would already be served by the common use of the singular number? Furthermore, by saying "by the capacity to establish plurality in the object of comparison," it is effectively stated that [the same applies] "by the capacity to establish duality and so forth in the *kāraka*. Thus, just as in the expression *hataśāyikāḥ*, where the plural number serves to establish plurality in the object of comparison, in the present case there is no basis for establishing duality or the like in the *kāraka*; therefore, the superimposition (*āropa*) of such a number is impossible.

Nor can that [number] be understood from the dual ending in expressions such as *caitramaitrau* (Caitra and Maitra), because it is absent in cases like *caitro maitraśca pacataḥ* (Caitra and Maitra cook), and because that [number], being already connected with Caitra and others prior to its connection with the *kāraka*, cannot itself be connected with a *kāraka*. Furthermore, in the case of an abstract verb (*bhāvākhyāta*), a dual ending is impossible because no *kāraka* denoted by a subsequent *tiṅ*-suffix is established. Moreover, when there is the expectancy "of what is there singularity?", it is only logical that this relates to a fit object of inquiry; for since action (*kriyā*) is non-existent, the expectancy for a delimiting factor is impossible, and thus the claim of its connection [to number] therein is refuted.

This is because the very fact that the cognition of number as qualifying a *kāraka*—established by the universally accepted inquiry "Who? Who? (*kaḥ*, *kau*) and so forth, which arises immediately after the understanding produced by sentences such as "he cooks" (*pacati*)—would otherwise be untenable, serves as the proof for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) and so forth.

Even in the case of the verbal root (*dhātu*) of a word such as *uktavākya*, although the action denoted by the verb (*ākhyātārthakriyā*) is one and lacks any general plurality of number, it is nevertheless perceived as if manifold in certain instances due to the multiplicity of agents, objects, and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction [with our position]. Furthermore, this is because the principle that "the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root" is not established through the very nature of the word (*śabdamaryyādā*). As for the rule "and because subordinate elements (*guṇa*) exist for the sake of another," it applies only when the principal element (*pradhāna*) is already capable of being construed.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa and others have accepted that the number expressed by the verbal suffix (tiṅ) is construed only with the *kāraka* (participant in the action). Thus, it should be further inferred by oneself that, except for the usage of the Bhāṣyakāra himself, the dual and plural numbers in the impersonal passive (*bhāvākhyāta*) are indeed ungrammatical.

The sense is that the restriction—"non-difference (abhedānvaya) occurs only between two elements with identical case-endings"—has already been refuted by the phrase "by the agent and so forth, which are the meanings of the verb. Suggesting that even in the case of intransitive verbs, other scholars must also accept that the verbal root denotes both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), he states the manner of verbal cognition using the example "the jar perishes" (*ghaṭo naśyati*). To address the expectancy for its operation, he says "And that... (*sa ca*). The qualification by "counter-positiveness" (*pratiyogitva*) is to be understood through the relation of "determinateness" (*nirūpakatā*).
The meaning is that the operation conducive to that [destruction] is simply the bringing together of those [causes].

"From this very reason" means that since the object is not merely destruction, for this very reason the operation (vyāpāra) also consists of the respective causal complexes (sāmagrī) which have as their result destruction qualified by the state of being a counter-correlate (pratiyogitva). Furthermore, because the result and the operation share the same locus, there is no transitivity (sakarmakatva). It is precisely for this purpose that the term "qualified by the state of being a counter-correlate" has been employed.

In the view of those for whom destruction (*nāśa*) alone is not the meaning of the verbal root, since destruction exists eternally immediately after its own production, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the form *naśyati* ("is being destroyed"); furthermore, because that [destruction] cannot be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of its own annihilation (*dhvaṃsa*), the use of the form *naṣṭa* ("destroyed") would be untenable. To indicate this, the demonstration of usage across the three times is presented by the phrase "when that exists," and so forth. The Nyāya position, however, will be discussed in the analysis of the meaning of the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix.

By indicating that the transitivity (sakarmakatva) of verbs such as *jānāti* (he knows), which have objects as their referents, would be untenable if one does not accept that they signify an operation distinct from cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth, he demonstrates the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) according to his own view in the passage beginning with "Devadatto jānāti" (Devadatta knows). He states the meaning included by the word "etc. (*ādi*) as "desire and so forth" (*icchādi*). In some versions, the reading is simply "in cases such as *jānāti*" (*kvacijjānātītyādau*).

"And that" means: an operation conducive to knowledge. Since the conjunction of the self and the mind is always readily available for its pursuit, he says "at last," meaning in the absence of that [other operation]. "It is the very substratum itself": the sense is that even though it (the self) is partless, its status as an operation is to be established by superimposing parts upon it.

By way of introduction (*upoddhāta*), he says "nanu" in order to determine that particles such as *śatṛ* are *dyotaka* (indicative). [Objection: According to the linguistic maxim (*vyutpatti*) that "a word uttered once conveys its meaning once," there can be no simultaneous cognition of two meanings; therefore, he says, "like the cognition of the agent alone. The word "alone" (*mātra*) is used for restriction. The meaning is that it generates the apprehension of *tātparya*, which consists in being uttered with the intention of conveying a specific meaning. For this very reason, the mention of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and so forth in rules such as *kartari śap* is purposeful.

Otherwise, since the agent and other roles would be understood through the very substitutes for *l* prescribed by the rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), those [other rules] would clearly be redundant; this is the intended meaning.

"In the root, [there is] the operation upon the fruit"—here "therein" (tatra) means "in those two things presented by the verbal root. With the intention that the locative case in "phalavyāpārayoḥ" is used for selection (*nirddhāraṇe*), he explains it as "the fruit," etc., in the *Sāra*. "Deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) means: in the presence of *ya*-class suffixes and the like, and in the absence of *śa*-class suffixes and the like. He demonstrates this very point by stating, "when there is a desire to express the agency of the object," and so forth; for even when *ya*-class suffixes are present, the substratum is not understood as being connected to the fruit, whereas even in the absence of *śa*-class suffixes and the like, the substratum is connected to the operation, which is the meaning of the *tiṅ* suffix.

The intention to express that [the suffix] is for the purpose of highlighting an excellence of ease (*saukaryātiśaya*) means that there is an intention to regard as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) the very operation consisting of contact with fire and so forth residing in the rice (*taṇḍula*), since that alone produces the result.

In reality, however, it has been stated previously that even the result appears as an "operation" through the superimposition of temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) belonging to the operation that produces it; thus, the meaning is that there is an intention to regard the result itself residing in the rice as the operation. Regarding the phrase "from the means" (*sādhanāt*): the sense is that because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the suffixes *taṅ* and others are not indicators (*dyotaka*).

"By the phrase 'in succession' (*kramāt*)," etc., means by the word "etc. (*ādi*) found in the root text [referring to] "the object, the agent, the locus, and so forth. The phrase "of the general [object], etc. is an explanation of "in succession. Intending to show that the status of being an object (*karmatva*), as determined by the meaning of a transitive verbal root (*saviṣaya-dhātu-artha*), ultimately results in being a "locus" (*viṣayatva*), he says "of the locus" (*viṣayaka*). He says "transitive" (*sakarmaka*) because suffixes such as *yaṅ* (passive) occurring in co-utterance with a transitive root indicate the object (*karman*) and so forth; however, in cases such as "the rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ svayameva*), the suffix *yaṅ* and others are not of that nature, but rather are due to extended application (*ātideśika*).

The point is that there is no deviation [from the rule] in that case, because the status of being an extended application (*atideśa*) established by the rule *karmavatkarmaṇā* has been settled as the final doctrine (*siddhāntita*) in the *Ākara* (the Mahābhāṣya). "Common to the state" (*bhāvasādhāraṇā*) means: prescribed by rules such as *yag* for the *sārvadhātuka* affixes when the sense is either a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*). By this, there is an exclusion of those prescribed by rules such as *dīpajana*. "In this way" (*evam*) means: in the manner described above.

One might object: "Since it was promised in general that a verbal root denotes both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) by the rule *nanu phalavyāpārayoḥ*, it would have been more appropriate to establish that [denotation] through logical arguments in the very next moment, rather than after the determination of the sentence-meaning; for by that point, the desire to know [the specific nature of the root's meaning] would have already ceased. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the maxim of the needle and the kettle" (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāyena*).

Thus, when it is understood that the result and the operation generally constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), and the locus (*āśraya*) constitutes the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the sense is this: because the sentence-meaning itself is easier to explain—and because there is less disagreement regarding the doctrine to be refuted—it is what the students first desire to know. In the phrase "in those ending in *laṭ* etc.," the term refers to the verbal roots by means of an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*. Thus, the meaning is "in the verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) and *pac* (to cook)" in examples like *yajeta* and *pacet*. "Non-denotability" (*avācyatvam*) means the absence of being a determinant of denotability. By the phrase "Prabhākara and others," the Naiyāyikas are included.

Although activity (*vyāpāra*) is accepted by the Naiyāyikas as the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the point is that in their view it is not designated by the term *bhāvanā*. The word *vyāpāra*—which explains the first half of the verse beginning with "Activity is *bhāvanā*, that very [activity]" and which denotes the object defined by the previously stated characteristics such as "by its subordinate parts"—is explained by words such as *bhāvanā*. The meaning is that since the explanation (*vivaraṇa*) has the same referent as that which is being explained, it is established that the verbal root expresses *bhāvanā*.

In this regard, since the pronoun brings about the identity between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), it may take the gender of either one; for this is observed in many instances such as "That which is coolness is indeed the nature of water. Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the feminine designation "she" (*sā*). Even if it were masculine, its grammatical correctness would be established by the elision (*lopa*) according to the rule *so'ci lope cet*. Alternatively, let it be the very *bhāvanā* itself that is referred to by that word.

Now, one might object: "This may indeed be the case if the verbal root (*dhātu*) has 'operation' (*vyāpāra*) as its meaning; but what is the proof for that? Anticipating this doubt, the *Sāra* demonstrates the proof by analyzing the root through the verb *kṛ*: "He cooks" (*pacati*) means "he produces cooking" (*pākam utpādayati*). [Objection: Even though it is stated that "the action (*kriyā*) which is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is also remembered as 'production' (*utpādanā*)," the status of the action as *bhāvanā* is already established; why then is the word "operation" (*vyāpāra*) employed? To this, he replies: "And the word 'operation'... Thus, the term is formed either through the instrumental derivation (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*)—meaning "that by which one operates"—or through the abstract nominal derivation (*bhāva-vyutpatti*)—meaning "the act of operating."

The term "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is employed so that all operations conducive to the result, such as placing [the pot on the fire], may be understood as *bhāvanā*. However, since the term "action" (*kriyā*)—like the word "effort" (*kṛti*)—could potentially signify mere effort, it would follow that by defining it merely as such, one would not obtain the status of *bhāvanā*. This is the intended meaning. "For this very reason" means precisely because blowing and so forth are denoted by the verbal root in their respective forms. "Established for all" means that for this very reason, when one says "he cooks," no doubt arises as to whether he is performing the act of blowing or not; this is the intended meaning.

He refutes the objection of a bystander who might think that, following the method of the Naiyāyikas—who have rejected *vyāpāratva* (the nature of operation) as the delimitor of the denotatum of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) and established *kṛtitva* (the nature of effort) as such—likewise, for the verbal root (*dhātu*), *kṛtitva* alone will be the delimitor of its denotation (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). This is addressed by the words "And not thus for these... and so forth; the word "not" (*na ca*) is to be construed with the word "correct" (*sādhvī*). "For these" means for [properties] such as *adhiśrayaṇatva* (the nature of placing on the fire). "Due to prolixity" (*gaurava*) means because of the consequence of prolixity in [assuming] them to be the delimiters of what is denoted by the verbal root. The sense is that they are more cumbersome than *kṛtitva* and are manifold in number.

The phrase "its delimitant" (tadavacchedakam) means the delimitant of being denotable by the verbal root. Now, if the meaning of the verbal root were only *kṛti* (volitional effort), then in cases such as "the chariot goes," that [meaning] would be sublated because it is absent in the chariot; thus, such usage would be untenable. To this, he replies with "the chariot goes," etc., by the words "from the operation," etc., whereby both *āśrayatva* (substratum-ness) and *pratiyogitva* (counter-positive-ness) are included. This is because in examples like "he knows," etc.—and by the word "etc. one should include cases such as "the jar perishes"—since substratum-ness of destruction is sublated there, one must recognize that the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) applies specifically to counter-positive-ness.

The term "the Naiyāyika method" is employed because of a similarity in the following sense: for in their investigation of the meaning of the verb (ākhyāta), they have accepted metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) in the operation (vyāpāra) and direct denotation (śakti) in the effort (kṛti); since this argument has been established by them, it is likewise to be established by me. Thus, the word "method" (rīti) is used on account of this resemblance, but the intention is not that one should adopt their view in other respects.

With the intention that the meaning is established by the very cognition supported by parsimony (*lāghava*) and not by parsimony alone, he reveals the invalidity of that [Mīmāṃsaka] method according to the Mīmāṃsaka tradition, stating "of the state of being the delimitor of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedakatvasya*). Thus, the sense is that, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the primary denotative power (*śakti*) is delimited even by a heavy property (*dharma*), just as it is by the nature of effort (*kṛtitva*) in the case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, the primary power will be established in those [heavy properties] through inference.

[Objection: But surely, in view of their being produced (kṛtitva), it is precisely their heaviness that constitutes the subverting factor; therefore, he says "of those two," meaning of the two [properties]: being the delimitors of capacity (śakyatāvacchedakatva) and being the delimiters of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedakatva). [Response: Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of a seed" (bījābhāvāt): since a light property that is co-extensive with [the heavy one] is possible, and because the principle that "there is no [recognition of] that [heavy property] when a light one exists" does not apply here, if being a delimiter is a specific type of essential relation (svarūpasambandhaviśeṣa), then since that very nature (svarūpatva) exists even in heavy properties, what is untenable?

If, on the other hand, it is over-extensive (*atirikta*), then its inclusion as a property of the Guru (*gurudharma*) is also necessary. This is because of the common usage that "being on the bank of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgātīratva*) is the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatā'vacchedaka*), and because the condition of being included within the category of delimiters of occurrence (*vṛttyavacchedakakoṭipraviṣṭatva*) applies equally to both cases. If such usage were based on a definition of "delimitor-ness" (*avacchedakatva*) consisting merely in not being under-extended or over-extended (*nyūnā'tiriktavṛttitva*), then the implication is that this would have to be the case everywhere.

One might object: "Surely we do not claim that it [the effort] is the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) merely on account of parsimony (lāghava), but rather because there is evidence for it. To this, he raises the doubt with the words "na ca" (but not). By stating "by the word *karoti*, which has the meaning of 'effort'," he suggests—through the very act of providing a gloss—that the meaning of *kṛñ* as "effort" is already established; for even though the cognition of being produced by an operation (*vyāpāra*) is the same for both a jar and a sprout, the linguistic convention of "done" (*kṛta*) versus "not done" (*akṛta*) applies only to the jar, thereby proving that *kṛñ* signifies effort. The phrase "from the gloss" (*vivaraṇāt*) means from the statement of words that convey that specific meaning.

The meaning is as follows: the mere root-meaning (*dhātumātra*) is denotative of that which is qualified by effort (*yatnatva*), because—absent any subverting evidence—it possesses the meaning conveyed by the verb *kṛ* (to do) when it is qualified by effort; for whatever word conveys a meaning that is qualified by a particular property is denotative of that [property]. This is because analysis (*vivaraṇa*) functions as a means of grasping denotation through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*), just like words such as *kalaśa* (jar), which convey the meaning denoted by the word *ghaṭa* (pot) when the latter is denotative of that which is qualified by "pot-ness. The reading is: "the meaning is effort alone" (*yatna evārthaḥ*).

The reading "effort alone (*yatna eva*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix" contradicts the context under discussion. Here, "meaning" (*arthaḥ*) refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthaḥ*). By the particle *eva*, the expressibility of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is excluded.

Only when the root *kṛ* (to do) has "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning is there any possibility that any verbal root whatsoever could have that same meaning. He states that this [claim] is like a flower in the sky by saying, "the chariot performs going," and so forth; since effort is sublated in non-sentient things such as a chariot, such usage would be untenable. Therefore, the root *kṛ* does not have "effort" as its meaning, but rather has "activity" (*vyāpāra*) as its meaning. Thus, the sense is that through this analysis, it is established that the verbal root has "activity" as its meaning.

One might object: "In the usage 'the chariot goes' (*ratho gacchati*), since the root *kṛ* (which expresses the meaning of the verbal root) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for the activity [of going], there is no loss of its denoting effort. To this he replies: "by means of seeds, etc. The point is this: since the usage of *kṛ* for activity is so frequent, it is logical that its primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in that very sense; therefore, because of the explanatory analysis (*vivaraṇa*), one must necessarily accept that the verbal root has activity as its meaning.

In this regard, the following should be noted: even according to the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), the verbal root *pac* and others have their denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to activities such as blowing [on the fire] only in the general form of "activity" (*vyāpāratva*), because they are explained by the root *kṛ*, which signifies activity in general. And thus, since even "effort" (*kṛti*) is included under the category of "activity," statements made here and there—such as "the ghost arose from me" (*mattaḥ bhūtam*) rather than "it was done by me" (*mayā kṛtam*)—are consistent. However, the cognition of these roots in their specific forms can be accounted for through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which is delimited by those specific forms. This is in accordance with the saying of the learned: "Secondary indication occurs when there is a cognition of something in a form other than its primary denotation."

For this very reason, at the occasion of demonstrating the meaning of the sentence, there is a connection with the word *vyāpāra* (operation), which denotes operation in general, as it is used to designate "the operation conducive to softening" (*viklitti-anukūlo vyāpāraḥ*) and "the operation conducive to cognition" (*jñāna-anukūlo vyāpāraḥ*). He introduces the root text, "Because *kṛñ* would result in being intransitive," with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "Inexpressibility" (*avācyatve*) means "incapability [of denotation] by the verbal root. "The accusative case would occur" (*dvitīyā syāt*) because [the object] would be the locus of the fruit consisting of production, which is the meaning of the verbal root.

One might object: "Even though in the sentence *ghaṭo bhavati* there is an understanding of agency (*kartṛtva*) consisting in being the locus of the effort (*kṛti*), since there exists an agency consisting in being the locus of the operation denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) which is connected with the fruit denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), this necessarily sublates [the status of] 'object' (*karmatva*). Therefore, the application of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) does not arise in such instances; otherwise, even the L-suffix (*lakāra*) used for the agent would fall into unaccountability. Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it with the words *na ca*. Just as in the case of *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*, the same contingency of the accusative case would apply here in *ghaṭo bhavati* as well.

In my view, however, because the designation "agent" (kartṛ-saṃjñā) based on being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root (dhātu-upātta-vyāpāra-āśrayatva) is more powerful, it sublates [the other], and thus there is no occurrence of that [undesired designation]; this is the intended meaning.

He states the manner of refutation: "Anugata" (concomitant) means common to both the sentient and the insentient. "In your view" (*tvadmate*) means in your own doctrine. "By being difficult to state" (*durvacatvena*) means by being impossible to define. He explains that very point: "Of being the substratum of activity" (*kṛtyāśrayatvasya*); the sense is that this [definition] is under-extended (*avyāpti*) to the insentient. Or, "of being the impeller of the causal complex" (*kāraṇacakraprayoktṛtvasya*); the sense is that it consists in being the motivator of all the factors of action (*kāraka*) denoted by the verbal root. Having thus rejected the Nyāya position, he addresses the Mīmāṃsaka: "Of the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*).

In the expression "only the factor" (*kārakamātra*), the word "only" (*mātra*) has the sense of "entirety. This is because every factor (*kāraka*) is the locus of some action whatsoever that is conducive to the meaning of the verbal root; the point is that being a factor consists precisely in being a generator of action.

Now, even though in non-conscious entities the agency (*kartṛtva*) consisting in being the locus of volitional effort (*kṛti*) is sublated, the definition that determines the technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is simply the state of being the locus of an operation intended as the object of the speaker’s intention, characterized by independence from the operation of another. And this operation is, in some cases, volitional effort (*kṛti*), and in others, mere conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth. It is precisely the locus of such an operation that constitutes the meaning of the term *svatantra* (independent) in the rule "The independent is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), due to the force of the formulation of that very rule.

This has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *kārake*: "In a state of conjunction with the principal [factor], the cooking pot is dependent; in a state of separation, it is independent. But what is the principal? The agent (*kartṛ*). How is it known that the agent is the principal? Because when all the *kārakas* are present, it is the agent who brings them into operation. The meaning of this is that in examples such as *sthālī kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati* ("the pot cooks with wood"), it is the pot itself that is intended to be expressed as the primary subject. This will be explained further below.

The refutation of the objections raised against the Mīmāṃsaka position will also be stated [later]. And thus, since the status of being an agent (kartṛtva) is unimpeded for such an operation residing in the jar itself when independence is intended, there is no contingency of the accusative case; therefore, he says "apica" (furthermore).

The phrase "having its own meaning as its fruit" (*svarthaphala*) excludes over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to verbs such as *jīvati* (to live), because the fruit is qualified by being the locus (*āśraya*) which does not enter into the scope of the delimitors of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Likewise, the "own meaning" (*svārtha*) should also be qualified by the absence of the state of having an unintended object (*avivakṣitakarmakatva*). Therefore, there is no such [over-extension] to the root *smṛ* when it is the base of a bhāva-lakāra (impersonal construction) accepted as having an unintended object. As for the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), it will be discussed later. The sense of the statement "it is impossible" is that, in this way, it is necessary for a verbal root to denote an operation (*vyāpāra*).

"Anyatamatva" (being one of several) means that, having specifically selected roots such as *paci* (to cook), there is a distinct difference [in their definitions]; "tattva" (thatness) means the common property of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*). Regarding "because of observation": for instance, since the root *ji* (to conquer) is accepted as intransitive in the sense of "overpowering" and transitive in the sense of "diminishing," if this were included in the definition of a transitive root, it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to that intransitive sense; conversely, if it were not included, it would result in under-extension (*avyāpti*) to that very same sense of "diminishing. This is the meaning.

Although there is no fault in defining transitivity by taking each root as qualified by its respective object according to the method described above, nevertheless, it should be understood that the intention [of the definition] is to include all those roots simultaneously—given the traditional rule "this illustration is manifold" (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*) and because a commentary has been composed for each specific case—since it is impossible to grasp all such roots at once. The phrase "all this" (*tadetad*) refers to the collection of objections stated previously.

One might object: "How can the statement 'lest *kṛñ* become intransitive'—which is intended to refute that *kṛñ* has 'effort' (*yatna*) as its meaning—be taken as intending the point already stated? Anticipating this doubt, he clarifies the manner of that intention with the words "the sense is this" (*ayam bhāvaḥ*). By the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "mere result" (*phalamātram*), there is an exclusion of the "operation" (*vyāpāra*). By the phrase "in 'he does' (*karoti*) etc.," there is an inclusion of all verbal roots whose meanings possess an object.

The term *tanmātra* means "only that which has the form of effort and so forth as its object"; the phrase "the consequence of being intransitive" (*akarmakatāpatti*) implies that if the operation (*vyāpāra*) were not denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), it would be subject to the aforementioned definition [of action]. Some, however, say that the phrase "the consequence of being intransitive" is intended specifically with roots such as *kṛñ* (to do) which have the agent as their object, since those alone are the ones under discussion; thus, they argue, there is no lack of established precedent for that. [The phrase] "in the manner stated" refers to the following.

The meaning is: "in the manner already stated," that is, by means of the definition consisting in "the state of being a verbal root different from those roots that possess an object" (*sakarmaka*). For, according to the literal [definition], if a verbal root does not denote an operation (*vyāpāra*), it would be impossible to establish its status as intransitive (*akarmaka*)—which consists in denoting an operation that is coreferential with the fruit of its own meaning. Now, one might object: since it is currently unestablished that all verbal roots whatsoever denote an operation, the counter-positive (i.e., *sakarmaka* roots) is unestablished; therefore, the establishment of the meaning you have proposed is equally impossible to assert.

If it is argued that there is no fault in the aforementioned explanation because the notion of "one of many" (*anyatamatva*) has already been refuted by [the author] himself, and thus it is impossible for it to be grasped by the word used [in the definition], we say: No. This is because even for those who maintain that the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) here is its result (*phala*), they must admit that transitive roots such as *nī* (to lead) have as their meaning a result consisting of an action residing in the goat or other object, which is conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Furthermore, since it is well-known in the world that the action residing in the goat produces the result in the form of conjunction, and since this action is a "process" (*vyāpāra*), it is possible—by taking roots whose meaning is such an action, or by taking causative (*ṇyanta*) roots—to somehow establish the definition. Therefore, there is no fault in the stated explanation.

But surely, by this much it is established that roots such as *jñā* (to know) and *kṛ* (to do) have activity (*vyāpāra*) as their meaning, yet not all roots [do so]. Therefore, he explains the word *kṛñ* as referring to all roots: "the root *kṛ*" (*kṛñ iti*). The word *kṛñ* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all roots; thus, by means of a non-abandoning indication (*ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā*) based on the common property of being a root—applying to both the primary sense (*śakya*) and the indicated sense (*lakṣya*)—it conveys all roots. And thus, since it would follow that all roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*), they do not have only the result (*phala*) as their meaning, but rather have activity (*vyāpāra*) as their meaning as well; such is the sense.

The term *akarmakatā* (intransitivity) means that it belongs to all verbal roots other than those previously mentioned [as transitive]. He states "sakarmakatā" (transitivity) because if being transitive were defined solely as denoting an object (*phala*), then all roots would be transitive without distinction.

In reality, the proof that a verbal root (*dhātu*) has "activity" (*vyāpāra*) as its meaning would only be established by the aforementioned reasoning if the definition of transitive roots—namely, "that which has its own fruit as its result" (*svārthaphala*) and so on—were applicable to all transitive roots without exception. But this is not the case, because the definition fails to apply (*avyāpti*) to roots such as *śīṅ* (to lie down) when preceded by prefixes like *adhi*. Consequently, roots such as *bhū* and others would fail to attain the status of being verbal roots. Furthermore, in expressions such as *maitreṇa pācayati* ("he causes Maitra to cook"), the agency (*kartṛtva*) of Maitra and others would likewise be untenable. It is precisely for this reason that statements such as "the causative suffix *ṇic* is prescribed after a root whose original impulsion (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, in the sense of the primary action" are logically consistent; such is the direction of the argument.

Now, one might object: "The passage beginning with 'lest *kṛñ* become intransitive' is not intended to refute the Mīmāṃsaka position; for that [position] will be refuted later by the words 'therefore, the root *karoti*' etc., and because they do not admit that *kṛñ* has effort as its meaning. Nor is it intended to refute the Naiyāyika position, since the Naiyāyikas admit that both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are denoted by the verbal root. As it is stated in the *Ākhyātavādadīdhiti*: "Or let the result and the operation remain as two distinct meanings of the verbal root."

The point is this: if the verbal root (*dhātu*) were to signify an operation delimited by a result (*phala*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the result appearing in two ways within the verbal suffix denoting the object (*karmākhyāta*); therefore, it is more appropriate that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in those two [the root and the suffix] separately. While there is a disagreement among certain logicians regarding the result being expressed by the verbal root—since its appearance is possible through the verbal suffix denoting the object or through the accusative case—the former view remains superior.

Furthermore, if this passage were intended merely to prove that the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone has the sense of "operation" (*vyāpāra*), then the root would result in being intransitive; thus, one should have simply said, "It does not mean the mere fruit," rather than saying "of *kṛ*. Due to this lack of satisfaction, he introduces the original text with the words "Or else" (*athavā*) as having another purpose.

The meaning is that [the author] has explained it by intending to provide a commentary on the first half [of the verse], having established [the point]. The word "that" (tat) means "the state of being denotable by a verbal root. The phrase "of *jānāti*, *karoti*, and so forth" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all verbal roots whose meanings involve objects, excluding those whose meaning is effort (*yatna*). By the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the expression "mere action" (*kriyāmātra*), there is an exclusion of the result (*phala*).

The view of the ancient Naiyāyikas is that transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*) generally denote either an operation delimited by a result (*phala*) or both a result and an operation as distinct entities; however, verbs such as *jñā* (to know) denote only the operation of cognition and so forth. As for all intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*), they do not have a result as their meaning, because no such result is experienced from them; rather, they denote only the operation.
The point is that if, according to the method to be explained, the verb *kṛ* (to do/make) has a result as its meaning, then by the same logic, it would be established for all [verbs] as well.

Now, one might object: "If the root *kṛ* does not denote a result (*phala*), how can it be intransitive? To this he says, "The point is this. By the phrase "denoting [the result] and so forth," he includes both the Naiyāyika position—that a root is transitive when it denotes a result that is non-co-referential with its own meaning-activity (*svārtha-vyāpāra*)—and the view that it is transitive when its meaning is an activity delimited by a result (*phalāvacchinna-vyāpāra*). If one does not admit that roots such as *jñā* (to know) and others have the result as their meaning, then the term "exclusion" (*uccheda*) would mean "over-narrowness" (*avyāpti*). However, if one does not admit that for all such roots, it would mean "impossibility" (*asambhava*).

Thus, it should be understood that the statement "the root *kṛ* is intransitive," and so forth, demonstrates the counter-argument (*vipakṣabādhakatarka*) against the inference: "the root *kṛ* denotes the result [of an action], because it is transitive, like the roots *pac* and others."

In reality, however, the first half [of the verse] itself establishes that the root denotes both the result and the operation (*vyāpāra*), by demonstrating its explanation as "the operation is *bhāvanā*, and that is precisely it. For it is quite clear that if the root’s denotation of the operation were unestablished, the mere explanation of the word "operation" (*vyāpāra*) by means of terms such as "*bhāvanā*" would not establish it. Therefore, its expressed meaning must be understood solely through explanations such as "he cooks," "he acts," "the *bhāvanā* of cooking," or "such a production. And it has been explained in exactly this way by the author of the *Sāra*.

And thus, since the root *kṛ* (to do), which signifies activity (*vyāpāra*), is explained by words such as *pāka* (cooking), which signify results such as softening (*viklitti*), it is established that both are the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). In this context, regarding roots such as *jñā* (to know) where the Naiyāyika disagrees about the result-component, the statement "the root *kṛ* is intransitive" (*akarmaka*) and so forth was stated as a supporting argument for that very point. However, against the Mīmāṃsaka who asserts that no verbal root expresses activity, the passage beginning with "therefore, [it is said] 'he does'" (*tasmāt karoti*) was stated precisely to establish that [point].

Although the support of the rule *kṛñaḥ* and so forth applies even to one who disagrees regarding the aspect of activity (*vyāpāra*), nevertheless, since the transitivity of a verb is established otherwise even without [the verb] having activity as its meaning—given that the analysis (*vivaraṇa*) itself is subordinate to the finite verb (*ākhyāta*)—that text is nonetheless necessary.

The modern Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that transitive verbal roots have their denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to: (1) the fruit (*phala*), and (2) those operations intended as its producers (*tajjanakatvena vivakṣita-vyāpāra*). These [powers] reside in those things delimited by various respective properties (*tattaddharmāvacchinna*) which are subsumed under the property of being co-locational (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the property that serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the expectancy for a means (*sādhana*)—which is itself indicated (*upalakṣaṇībhūta*). This is because it is possible for those operations intended as the producers of the fruit to possess distinct properties.

However, where what is intended to be expressed is the suitability for the result belonging to that which is delimited by a single property alone, the [denotative] power of the verbal root resides in that very thing so delimited; for there is no royal decree that the denotative power must reside in the aggregate alone in every case.

As for the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "this is what is called action" (*kriyā nāmeyam*), it refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as accomplished over a long duration of time; thus, there is no contradiction therein. Otherwise, one would have to resort to the imposition of a "resortless" interpretation in all cases. Furthermore, it is precisely those [long-duration meanings] that are designated by the term "operation" (*vyāpāra*). Although the property of being an effort (*kṛtitva*) is a property co-extensive with such a [long-duration] property, it does not serve as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the meaning of roots like *pac* (to cook), because it is not accepted as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*) in that respect.

For this very reason, those who are proficient [in the language] never employ words such as *yāga* (sacrifice) or *pāka* (cooking) with that [effort] as their intended meaning (*tātparya*), nor do they derive a cognition of an effort toward cooking from such usage. By this, the view that the *tiṅ*-suffix possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) for that [effort] is refuted, since it is already obtained from the verbal root itself by virtue of being an operation (*vyāpāra*).

However, it is possible for the objects of verbs such as *jñā* (to know) to be both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) that brings about that result, namely the cognition itself. In the case of the root *kṛ* (to do), however, the meaning consists of both "being something to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) and "effort" (*yatna*). Consequently, the status of being a primary object (*mukhya-karmatva*)—defined as being related to the result of that verbal root's meaning—is established without obstruction for things like a pot. Likewise, the status of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*), defined as having a result that resides in a locus different from its own [the effort's] locus, is also established. But for intransitive roots such as those denoting effort, the meaning is simply the operation itself, consisting of an effort delimited by various specific properties.

In the case of the expression "yatate bhojanam," the verbal root does not admit the effort as its primary meaning (śakyatva), because such usage is not standard; furthermore, when "yatate" is uttered, there is no expectancy for an object (karmākāṅkṣā). However, in the case of roots such as *śīṅ* (to lie down) when preceded by prefixes like *adhi*, there is indeed a conventional metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā) regarding the result, since *śīṅ* and other such roots do not convey the result in all instances. And the utility of rules such as "adi-śīṅ-sthāsām" [Pāṇini 1.4.42] is solely to capture the beginningless intention (*anāditātparya*) regarding that meaning. As for the term "kartṛ" (agent) here, because the root *kṛ* conveys effort, the word "agent" is not used naturally (*svārasataḥ*) with reference to insentient things.

And thus, for the sake of accounting for the cognition of the agent in expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), it is necessary that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) in the effort (*kṛti*). This is because the effort, which is the meaning of that suffix, can be logically understood as being construed with the meaning of the nominative-terminated word through the relation of substratehood (*āśrayitva*). However, in cases where such a cognition is not established—as in "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*)—there is, accordingly, a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) either in the operation (*vyāpāra*) or in the state of being a substrate (*āśrayatva*), as the case may be.

By virtue of the sūtra "the agent is one who acts independently" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), since the status of being an agent is defined as belonging not only to the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root but also to its counter-correlates, there is no impossibility of understanding [the agent] as the agent. Where there is co-occurrence with a word ending in the nominative case, and where the intention is focused solely on the action (kṛti) as the qualificand, there the cognition has that [action] as its qualificand. Furthermore, the meaning of the term *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed") is simply "when not already conveyed."

However, since non-cognition [of the agent] regarding an object distinct from the substratum is precisely the cognition of the meaning of the suffixes *kṛtya* and so forth as qualifiers, there is no inconsistency in the distinction between what is denoted and what is not denoted. Furthermore, in cases such as "Caitra cooks," since the cognition of the agent can be accounted for solely through the power (*śakti*) of the effort (*kṛti*), it is improper to postulate a separate power for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Since there is no designation of an operation (*vyāpāra*), the aforementioned property of softening (*viklitti*) and so forth cannot be accepted as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*); thus, a separate power is indeed unobserved.

The status of being a fruit (*phalatva*) has indeed already been determined previously. This being so, they say that any objection that might arise in certain cases will be disregarded. Thus, it is concluded that because the definition of transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) and so forth is untenable otherwise, it is necessary that the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses both meanings.

However, those who maintain that the capacity [of a verb] consists merely in its activity (vyāpāra) argue as follows: "Transitivity" (sakarmakatva) is the state of having a meaning that is construed with the meaning of the second case (accusative) and so forth. This is because, when co-occurring with verbs such as *pac* ("to cook"), the second case has the sense of "softening" (*viklitti*) and the like; whereas, when co-occurring with verbs such as *jñā* ("to know"), it has the sense of "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*) and the like. Thus, they say that being construed with that [meaning] remains intact for the object of the action. Anticipating and refuting the view of those who claim that in connection with verbs such as *jñā*, objects like "a jar" possess only a "figurative transitivity" (*gauṇakarmatva*), he says: "Not so" (*na ca*).

"Secondary" (*bhākta*) means that by which the primary meaning is "shared" (*bhajyate*), i.e., crushed or served; thus, *bhakti* is *lakṣaṇā* (indication). By this [secondary sense], because the primary meaning is concealed and yet required as a constituent factor for its own cognition, it is called "derived from that," hence "secondary. Even though it is secondary—that is, even though it is based on *lakṣaṇā*—the point is that since the scripture's purpose is fulfilled by taking the primary transitivity (*sakarmakatva*), there is no evidence for such a function in a figurative sense.

Regarding this, he states a worldly example: "Not indeed," and so forth. Others maintain that since the application of the designation "King" to a domestic priest or similar person occurs only figuratively because they perform his duties, and since the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*)—which was established elsewhere as being restricted to word-meanings where a specific form is employed to bring about a specific meaning, such as in the case of *mahadbhūtaścandramāḥ* (the moon has become great)—prevents the substitution of *ā* [for *a*] there, it does not fall within the scope of that [principle] here.

According to some, "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists precisely in having a meaning that connects with the meaning of the technical grammatical designation "object" (*karma*). This is because the previously mentioned definition cannot be obtained through the linguistic constraint (*śabdamaryādā*) from the word *sakarmaka*—which means "together with an object"—and consequently, the cognition [of transitivity] would not arise from the word *sakarmaka* in rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi ca*. "Intransitivity" (*akarmakatva*), on the other hand, consists in having a meaning that does not connect with that [designation]. For this very reason, the use of the past passive participle suffix *-kta* in examples such as *adhyāsitā bhūmayaḥ* ("the lands were sat upon") is justified. They further state that since connection (*anvaya*) consists in a relation between separately presented meanings, there is no fault in cases such as *jīvati* ("he lives").

This very position has been adopted by those who maintain that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists in the denotation of an operation delimited by a result (*phala*), since everyone accepts that the result possesses the status of the object (*karman*), and because the property of having a meaning connected with a result exists in all transitive verbs.

If it is considered that the aforementioned definition is not possible because [the action and the result] are objects of a single presentation (*ekopasthiti*), then, according to the theory of distinct potencies (*pṛthak-śakti-vāda*), there is indeed no fault; for since the word *avacchinna* (delimited) refers to the relation, the meaning of the verbal root as an operation related to the result in its capacity as an object (*karmabhūta*) is well-established. It should be noted that by not accepting the result as the meaning of intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*), there is no room for the faults of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) or under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "the stages have been occupied" (*adhyāsitā bhūmayaḥ*), the justification has already been established as previously explained. Now, one might object: from the root text *karmavat syād yagādyapi*, the meaning obtained is that "there should also be *ya*-class affixes and so forth, just as in the case of the object (*karman*). Since that [application] is sublated and not intended to be expressed, he says: "by the phrase *karmavat syāt*. This means that what is prescribed by the Sūtra is indicated. That is to say, that which is ordained by the Sūtra is indicated.

Even if the word *karman* (object) were presented by the sūtra through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as being included within its own [denotation] based on the literal sense, there would still be the consequence of its non-connection with the phrase "that which has *yag* [passive endings] and so forth. It is precisely for the sake of conveying this that the term *syāt* (would be) is included within the scope of the illustrations (*lakṣyakoṭau*). The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, is that because it does not reside in a jar—due to the absence of residing in jars alone—there is an absence of having an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyakatva*). "In this way" means: when one accepts that the root *kṛ*, in the sense of "instrument," signifies effort (*yatna*) together with its production (*utpatti*), in accordance with the requirement for the treatment of the object like the agent (*karmavadbhāva*).

In the phrase "of *jānāti* etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes [verbs such as] *gam* (to go) and others. By the phrase "due to the destruction of the veil" (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*), the word "etc. includes [actions such as] conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth. By the term "necessary" (*āvaśyakam*), it is indicated that if one were to accept cognition alone as the result (*phala*) in those cases, then since the jar and other objects would not be the locus (*āśraya*) of that [result], their status as the "object" (*karman*) would be untenable. Furthermore, how even the destruction of the veil can function as a result in the case of past objects and the like will be explained in the *Sāra* itself during the determination of the meaning of the accusative suffix (*sub-artha*). The sense is that the status of being a transitive verb (*sakarmakatā*) would not be established, because the previously stated definition—namely, that [the action] has its own result in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*)—is impossible in that context.

In reality, however, it is more appropriate that the root *jñā* signifies the result in the form of cognition itself. This is because the *Bhāṣya* states, "There is no occurrence of the action in the object for those roots whose state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*)," which implies that for such roots, the result of the action does not reside in the object alone. Consequently, by accepting that "having the action reside in the agent" (*kartṛsthakriyakatva*) means having a result common to both agent and object, one must necessarily admit that "having the action reside in the object" (*karmasthakriyakatva*) consists precisely in having a result that resides in the object alone.

In that regard, if the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*) were the result, then in that view, the status of being an action (*karmavadbhāva*) would be unavoidable, just as it is with [actual] actions. Furthermore, this very position was adopted by the author of the treatise himself when demonstrating the mode of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in such cases as "he knows" (*jānāti*), where he shows that it is an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to knowledge, desire, and so forth. As for the doubt and its resolution in the present context, it is clear in the *Sāra* that they are intended according to the first alternative (*prathamakalpa*) mentioned by the *Bhāṣya* and Haribhadra.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the aforementioned theory, since knowledge does not inhere in objects such as jars, it is impossible for those objects to be the "object" (*karman*) of the verb *jñā* ("to know"); nor that there would be a loss of its status as an intransitive verb due to the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the knowledge, the operation conducive to it, and its substratum; nor that its being a "state residing in the agent" (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) would be untenable. For, based on the experience in the scientific treatises (*śāstra*) that "knowledge is in the jar," one accepts that the object possesses the status of being the substratum of knowledge by virtue of being its objective domain (*viṣayatā*). Thus, the first objection is refuted.

This is because, in that case, there is an absence of non-objecthood (*akarmatva*) as defined by the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) involving the relation that delimits the result; and since the second [definition]—by way of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) and inherence (*samavāya*)—subsists in both the object and the agent, it is not at all defective. More will be said on this point later.

Let us return to the subject at hand. The point is this: why should it not be the case that "the jar acts by itself"? For here, just as the jar is the locus of the fruit consisting of its own production (*utpatti*), it is also the locus of the fruit consisting of the removal of its concealment (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*). Now, one might ask: what is the authority for the rule that the status of being treated like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) applies to objects that are produced (*nirvartya*) or modified (*vikārya*), but not to objects that are reached (*prāpya*)? To this, the root text says: "The established conclusion is here," referring to the commentary on the sūtra: *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyāḥ*.

The meaning is as follows: since the term *dhātu* (root) is carried over from the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ*, the phrase "by the action expressed by the root" is obtained through that inclusion of *dhātu*. Consequently, in examples such as *sādhvasi chinatti* ("he cuts with a good axe") and *sthālī pacati* ("the pot cooks"), where the agent possesses an action equal to that of the instrument or the locus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) precisely because the operation, though actually present, is not expressed by the root. Thus, the inclusion of the word *karman* (object), which would otherwise be redundant, establishes the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it serves to characterize an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*).

To demonstrate that the status of being the "agent of action" (*karmasthakriyatva*) is possible only when the object (*karman*) is distinct from the agent, [the author] first states the classification that will be explained later for the sake of easy understanding: "The desired object" (*īpsitaṃ karma*). Although it would be more appropriate to say that there are three types of objects—since even the undesired, such as the hated (*dveṣya*), is included within these very categories—the venerable Hari [Patañjali] stated: "Among those, it is considered threefold; and that [desired] is the most desired (*īpsitatama*)."

It should be understood that because [the author] has analyzed [the categories] separately in such passages as "ityādinā," he has stated the same here accordingly. Regarding "prāpyatva" (the state of being reached) and so forth, these two definitions will be explained when the meaning of the *sub*-suffixes is determined. The phrase "it will be explained" means by the verse beginning with "kriyākṛtaviśeṣāṇām. He demonstrates the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [definition] in order to show that the cause for the treatment of an object as the agent (*karmavadbhāva*) is the fact that the action conveys a distinction residing in the object—that is, the action is "object-located" (*karmastha*). This is shown in the passage beginning with "nahi."

Regarding the statement "he presses the *soma*," it is classified as a *vikārya* (object undergoing transformation). Now, one might object: since the first two types of objects involve actions residing in the object (*karmasthakriya*), they fall under the scope of the rule for *karmavadbhāva* (the object being treated like the agent); however, how can the case of "he presses the *soma*" be subject to the definition of a *vikārya*, given that the original material (*prakṛti*), the *soma*, is not perceived here to undergo transformation? As it has been said: "But when there is an intention to express the original material, it is a *vikārya*. If it is asked what is meant by "intention" in this context—namely, that it refers to [the intention] of its being a transformation—the answer is as follows: its validity is established by the intention to express the *soma* as the original material (*prakṛti*) with respect to the powder, which is a portion of the pressing process consisting of the act of pulverization.

Others, however, maintain that the definition of the *vikārya* (the object of transformation) is "that which produces a result that causes the destruction of its own substrate"; with this intention behind the definition, the term *soma* is designated as a *vikārya*. For instance, the meaning of the root *su* (to press) is an action conducive to a disjunction that destroys the conjunction that constitutes the originator [of the substance]. In the present context, the word *soma* is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇika*) to refer to its parts. Thus, they say that since the conjunction that originates the substance—which resides in the parts denoted by the word *soma*—is destroyed by the disjunction produced by the action denoted by the verbal root, it is logically established that it is a *vikārya*.

By the phrase "capable of being known," it is stated that the capacity for a cognition characterized by a specific property produced by an action (*kriyākṛtaviśeṣadharmaprakārakapratītiyogyatva*) is the cause for the application of the *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment as an object). In the view of the ancient Naiyāyikas, however, the application of *karmavadbhāva* in the present case is established through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the root *kṛñ* as denoting effort delimited by the result consisting of origination (*utpatti*). Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) mentioned; the meaning is that there is no occurrence of *karmavadbhāva*.

In the view of the ancient Naiyāyikas, however, since expressions such as "he produces knowledge" (*jñānaṃ karoti*) are not employed, the verbal root *kṛ* (to do/make) has its primary denotation (*śakti*) exclusively in respect to the result (*phala*) and effort (*yatna*), both of which are objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Consequently, because it is universally recognized that there arises in respect to a jar (*ghaṭa*) and the like a cognition characterized by the specific property of being something to be accomplished, and because the fitness for such a cognition remains unimpaired therein, the application of the *karmavat* rule (treating the object as if it were the agent) is established without any difficulty.

Furthermore, if the definition of "that which possesses an action" (*tatsthakriyaka*) were taken to mean "having as its meaning an action that bestows a specific quality upon the agent," then—as stated in the aforementioned Bhāṣya—there would be defects such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is because a specific quality in the form of fatigue is observed in the agent of actions like *pac* (to cook), whereas it is not observed in the agent of actions like *jñā* (to know). Regarding this, [the Bhāṣya] states: "The observation of a specific quality is established where there is an action;
however, the determination of action for others is fashioned by words alone."

If it is argued that by the latter half of Harika’s verse (*harikārikā*), an emphasis on those very two definitions mentioned previously is intended, even then there is no harm. For, just as the definition of *karmasthakriyaka* (verbs whose action resides in the object) includes the condition of being distinct from roots such as *jñā*, and the definition of *ṣopadeśa* (roots taught with the marker *ṣ*) includes the condition of being one of the group beginning with *ṣvaṣka*, so too the definition of *kartṛsthakriyaka* (verbs whose action resides in the agent) includes the condition of being distinct from roots such as *jñā*. Consequently, the status of *karoti* as *karmasthakriyaka* and the status of *jñā* and others as *kartṛsthakriyaka* are both logically established.

For this very reason, Hari also employed the word "śabda" (word) in the phrase "constructed by words alone," because the meaning is that [the difference is] by means of words and by the specificities residing in the objects conveyed by those words. He sets forth the reasoning of another philosophical system: the mention of "roots" (*dhātūnām*)—as in the case of *tyaji* and *gami*—is an elliptical expression for all such roots. The sense is that the consequence would be synonymy (*paryāyatā*), since the definition of synonymy consists precisely in having a power (*śaktatva*) delimited by the same delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the roots *tyaj* (to abandon) and *gam* (to go) have as their meanings respectively operations characterized by disjunction (*vibhāga*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*)? And thus, since the definition of a synonym includes the qualification "not being characterized by anything other than that [specific operation]," the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not arise. [Response: To this he says: "Even though they are characterizing marks" (*upalakṣaṇatve 'pi*). Being a characterizing mark (*upalakṣaṇatva*) consists in being the object of the denotative power (*śakti*) while not being the object of the denotative power as the object of the cognition produced by that word; [this is so] because [the operation] is the cause [of the cognition].

And thus, since there is no distinction between conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) in being produced by the operation directed toward their own objects, there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) to establish that conjunction alone—not disjunction—is the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the operation denoted by the root *gam* (to go). Consequently, if both were taken as indicators, the aforementioned undesirable consequence would be unavoidable; therefore, the meaning is that the potency (*śakti*) must necessarily reside in the result (*phala*) itself.

In this regard, in examples such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), since the very fact of being the correlate of the result—consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth—is the decisive factor for the dative case, it is easy to state that conjunction alone serves as the defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the action of going; furthermore, since [the usage] is otherwise justified through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the aforementioned method is not correct. This lack of satisfaction is also indicated by the two authors [of the commentary]. He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*); the meaning is: because of the consistency of the arguments stated above.

The meaning is that there is no dispute at all, because the state of being intransitive (*akarmakatva*)—defined as the verbal root denoting an operation co-referential with the fruit of its own meaning—is untenable without the verbal root denoting a fruit. Now, one might object: "Transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) is exactly as previously stated, and intransitivity is simply being a verbal root different from that; therefore, the aforementioned untenability does not arise. To this, he replies: "Because in the [Dhātu] lists, such as 'bhū sattāyām', it is the fruit itself that is specified. The meaning of "for this very reason" is: precisely because every verbal root denotes a fruit.

The phrase "having two meanings" (*dvyartha*) means that the term "two meanings" refers to both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*); this is the intended sense. Now, one might object: let the Bhāṣya statement "the root *pac* has two meanings," by virtue of its mention of *pac*, serve as proof for the fact that transitive roots denote the result; however, it does not apply to intransitive roots. To this he says "dig" (direction/illustration), because if that were the case, the mention of "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth as meanings would result in being purposeless.

The general meaning of the direction [of the argument] should be understood as follows: since, by virtue of the common capacity of their verbal roots (*dhātu-sāmānya-śakti*), an operation (*vyāpāra*) can be understood from verbs such as *bhavati* just as it is from *pacati* and so on. Now, one might raise the following objection from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsakas: "By the explanation that 'the operation is *bhāvanā*, and that alone [is it],' there is no definitive determination that the operation is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthatā*), because it could equally be argued—on the basis of the analysis 'he cooks' = 'he performs cooking'—that it is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārthatā*). It is with the aim of resolving this Mīmāṃsaka doubt that the author introduces the root text with the words "In this way" (*evam*), etc.

The term *vācyatva* (denotability) means being the object of the cognition produced by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). Thus, even through the analysis "the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) conducive to cooking," it follows that the word *pacati* denotes the efficient force conducive to cooking. For if taken according to the literal sense, once it is determined by such an analysis that the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses the efficient force, the subsequent passage—"But that [efficient force] is indeed denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)"—would be inconsistent. Anticipating the objection that the maxim "the base and the suffix [convey the meaning]" is subject to deviation in the case of number and so forth, he says: "For when that [suffix] occurs... (*tadāgame hi*).

And with the intention that "that which is the primary element is the meaning of the suffix" is the form of the maxim (nyāya), upon examining the root sūtra, the form of the maxim "that which is the meaning of the suffix is the primary element" is obtained.

For instance, it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the singularity conveyed by the singular suffix a qualifier of the sacrifice, or is it a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root? Since the object denoted by the word "animal" is subordinate (*guṇa*) to the sacrifice, if one were to perform the sacrifice using as many animals as possible, the primary act would be repeated, resulting in the failure of the primary act. Because the repetition of both the subordinate and the primary is untenable, if the injunction were for an animal qualified by singularity, then—since singularity would be a qualifier of the animal and not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice—that singularity would indeed be unintended (*avivakṣita*). This is the sense [of the argument].

When the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position has been raised by the sūtra, "In that case, oneness is not a subordinate factor of the sacrifice, because the object [of the number] is subordinate," the sūtra of the final conclusion (siddhānta) states: "But it is perceived as being like the word; for when that [word] is present, its cognition is seen, just as it is with others. The meaning is as follows: "Like the word" means it is perceived in the same manner as that which is denoted by the word. For oneness is indeed seen when that [word] is present—that is, when there is the occurrence of the singular number. Therefore, it is understood as the primary element, just as it is with other factors such as the "red" [cow] and so forth.

Alternatively, "in its arrival" (*tadāgame*) means "in its oneness" (*tat-ekatvam*). In the rule *āgame*—specifically in the rule *dvyekayoḥ* which prescribes the singular number—it is perceived as the meaning of the suffix in the form of the singular; that is to say, it is understood as such, unlike other [grammatical categories] such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth.

And thus, by virtue of the proximity consisting in being conveyed by the same cognition, that which is connected with the instrument (karaṇa) denoted by the case-ending first undergoes syntactic connection with the action, according to the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, and subsequently with the meaning of the stem. Consequently, through the understanding that "the sacrifice has both the animal and its singularity as its instruments," it is realized that singularity is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice; therefore, the sacrifice is not performed with multiple animals—this is the point of that [discussion].

And "predominance" (prādhānya) consists precisely in not being a qualifier of the meaning of the base (prakṛti), since the application of the rule [P. 1.4.54] occurs by taking up the meaning of the suffix; thus, the portion "that which is the meaning of the suffix" constitutes a factor of that rule. It should be understood that in the present case, because there is no cognition of *bhāvanā* in the absence of a verb (*ākhyāta*), its manifestation is as non-predominant, and this is how it connects [with the definition].

[Objection: Is it not the case that the very difficulty of defining "having an object" (*sakarmakatva*) and "transferred agency" (*anugat kartṛtva*) is the flaw in this view? [Response: To this he says, "And thus" (*evañca*); the meaning is: "and when the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is the denotation of the verbal suffix. Thus, when cooking has begun but the result has not yet arisen, in response to the question "Has the cooking occurred?", the answer "It will occur" (in the future tense) leads to the conclusion that the Mīmāṃsakas intend for the result alone to be the denotation of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "the consequence of such usage" (*prayogāpatti*), since the result—which consists of the action denoted by the root *gam* (to go) ending in a *lyuṭ* suffix and having the nature of conjunction—exists in the village, there would follow the validity of the usage "the village possesses going" (*grāmo gamanavān*), just like the usage "the village possesses conjunction" (*grāmaḥ saṃyogavān*). This principle should be inferred for subsequent cases as well. Regarding the phrase "due to the non-arising of the result" (*phalānutpāda*), it is stated that such usage is not accepted by anyone when the result has not arisen; however, it is said that [such usage] occurs "because of the existence of the operation" (*vyāpārasattve*). Regarding the phrase "there is no consequence of [saying] 'it is becoming'" (*bhavatīty-anāpattiḥ*), the meaning is that because the action denoted by the word *pac* (to cook), namely softening (*viklitti*), is not present [at that moment], there is no such consequence.

The intention is as follows: since there is no contradiction with the actual state of affairs at the time the result is produced, such a usage is desired; thus he says, "there is the contingency [of the verb being used]," because he intends for the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to be the mere result, setting aside the aspect of the operation (*vyāpāra*). However, the answer "it will come to be" (*bhaviṣyati*) and the explanation "he produces cooking" (*pākam utpādayati*) are given from that perspective.

The term *anukūla* (conducive) is used to indicate that this is the view of those who maintain that a word denotes the qualified entity (*anvitābhidhānavādin*), thereby praising its suitability. "There is no inconsistency" means that since the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by suffixes such as *lyuṭ* and *ghañ*—which are prescribed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*)—is sublated in the case of [the object] such as a village, the aforementioned undesirable consequence of grammatical usage does not arise. The point is that because the operation denoted by *ghañ* and other suffixes, which is conducive to softening (*viklitti*), is construed with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and so forth as its agent (*kartṛ*), there is no occurrence of the aforementioned inconsistency in usage.

One might raise the objection: "Since it is observed that *kṛt* suffixes prescribed by the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67)—as in examples such as *paktā* and *pācaka*—have the agent (*kartṛ*) as their meaning, it is difficult for the *ghañ* and other suffixes prescribed therein to have the activity (*vyāpāra*) as their meaning; therefore, the grammatical injunction *bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18) serves its purpose in teaching that [the *ghañ*] has that [activity] as its meaning. Anticipating this doubt, he provides an illustrative example consistent with his own view: "like the verbal suffix denoting the agent" (*kartrākhyātavad*). The meaning is as follows:

just as in your own view the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) prescribed by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve ca...* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) has the activity as its meaning, so too it is possible for the *ghañ* and other suffixes prescribed by *kartari kṛt* to have the activity as their meaning.

The phrase "and because of the occurrence of contradiction" (*virodhāpattiśca*)—the word *ca* here functions as a reason; thus, the meaning is that since there is futility (*vaiyarthyam*), there follows the occurrence of that contradiction. This is merely a stylistic variation in expression.
