Alternatively, the meaning is that it would result in a contradiction with your own established tenet (*siddhānta*), which holds that suffixes prescribed for denoting abstract states (*bhāva*) merely serve to restate the meaning of the verbal root and have no purpose other than ensuring the grammatical correctness of the usage. The term "explanation" (*vyākhyānam*) is further clarified by the word "elucidation" (*vivaraṇam*).

Therefore, "that too" means that even the analysis of *pacati* as *pākaṃ karoti* (he does cooking) is included; by the word "even," the maxim *prakṛtipratyayau* (the base and the suffix) which is about to be criticized is also collected. However, the separate analysis of the verbal root (*dhātu*)—just as the operation (*vyāpāra*) among the number, time, and operation [denoted] by the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is analyzed by *kṛñ*, and number and so forth are analyzed by the following *tiṅ* suffix—is likewise possible for the operation that is the meaning of the verbal root; thus, it does not prove that [the operation] is the meaning of the finite verb.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra: "How is it known that *pac* and other such roots denote action? Because they stand in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *karoti*: 'What does he do? He cooks (*pacati*)'? By this, it is clearly understood that even the analysis (*vivaraṇa*) belongs to the verbal root alone; such is the intended meaning. As for the root text "pakvavān," since it lacks the status of being an analysis of the verb *karoti*, he explains it as "in cases such as *pakvavān*" and so forth. He clarifies precisely the lack of connection [between the two] with the words "this is the intended meaning," etc.

"Sahārtham" means "having a connected meaning. "Brūtaḥ" means "they indicate. Between those two—the meanings of the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya)—the meaning of the suffix is that which is the qualificand (viśeṣya) in the apprehension of the function of the suffix; it is "predominant," meaning it possesses the status of being a qualificand as determined by the mode-of-being (prakāratā) of the meaning of the base.

He demonstrates, by means of dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*), the causal relationship established through such linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*). The meaning of the phrase "by way of being the qualificand" (*viśeṣyatayā*) is that [the suffix] is a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) through the relation of being the qualificandum as determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) of the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*). The remainder of the phrase "it is the cause" (*hetuḥ*) is "through the relation of being the qualificandum" (*viśeṣyatāsambandhena*).

"According to the method stated in the Aruṇādhikaraṇa" means that it was stated there that the redness (*āruṇya*) denoted by the word *aruṇayā* first connects with the other action as an instrument (*karaṇa*), whereas its connection with the meaning of the noun stem (*nāmārtha*) occurs subsequently (*pārṣṭhika*). "As will be explained" means according to the method to be explained in the determination of the meaning of case-endings (*sub-artha*), where—since the state of being a factor (*kārakatva*) consists in being a generator of an action—it is understood that [the factor] generates an action; and then, in determining what the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the connection with a factor is, [the point will be made].

The phrase "mere relation" means that in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the verbal suffix *yajeta*—which expresses both the root-meaning (the sacrifice) and the meaning of the verbal affix (the productive operation or *bhāvanā*)—establishes only a general relation between them. However, this verbal suffix has no function, such as denotation (*abhidhā*), in conveying the specific relation between those two in the form of an action-agent relationship (*kriyākārakabhāva*), because there is no word present that directly denotes such a specific relation; this is the meaning.

And so, in the case of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the cognition is that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is related to the sacrifice (*yāga*), not that the productive activity has the sacrifice as its instrument (*karaṇa*); similarly, in the present case, the cognition is that the agent is related to the cooking (*pāka*). This is the intention of the objector, who argues that an action is required only when there is a cognition of a relation [of the agent] with [the object] through [its] status as an object (*karman*) and so forth. He says, "due to the lack of compatibility" (*yogyatā-virahāt*), meaning that such a relational cognition is impossible because the fruit (*phala*) is incompatible [with being an agent] by virtue of its being a result (*kārya*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that semantic competency (*yogyatā*) consists in the presence of the meaning of one word in the meaning of another? And that [competency] exists in the present case, since the form "being related to cooking"—like "being the motivator of cooking"—is present even for a non-agent; therefore, he says: "of having the form that is the motivator of the connection. Thus, if semantic competency were merely the state of being delimited by the delimitor of the meaning of one word within the meaning of another, then since the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) of a jar exists with respect to fetching water, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of even a perforated jar being an instrument in that act.

In our view, however, the property of being a pot other than one with a hole is the determinant of the application of the fetching of water; thus, in such a pot, there is the application of such fetching, and therefore there is no contingency of its application [to a leaking pot]. Now, an objection is raised: in the case of "fetch water with a pot," since the pot possesses the property of being a pot other than one with a hole, what is the delimitor of the factorhood (kārakatva) in the present instance, by the absence of which the contingency of non-application is alleged? To this he replies: "For it is action-ness itself... [and so on].

[Objection: "But surely there is no fault, because since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is implied by the agent [denoted] by the *kṛt* suffix, it is easy for [actions] such as cooking (*pāka*) to be construed as its object (*karman*). To this, he says: "In reality... It should be understood that the intent of the *sūtra*—"That which is the primary meaning is the meaning of the suffix"—is that whatever is primary is the meaning of the suffix, and that the maxim "upon the addition of that [suffix]" is the basis for the sense "whatever is the meaning of the suffix. Since in examples such as *aja* ("goat"), there is a clear deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—because the referent of the word *aja*, which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), is not the meaning of the suffix—he disregards that [first alternative] and demonstrates the deviation only in the second alternative: "*aja*..."

Regarding the acceptance of this [objection], he says: "of the female goat, etc. (chāgyādeḥ). The meaning is either "of the female goat, etc., which is qualified by femininity," or "of the femininity residing in the female goat, etc. The point is that if something already construed as a qualifier in one context were to be construed again as a qualifier in another, there would be a lack of syntactic expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*). Consequently, in cases such as "bring the female goat" (*chāgīm ānaya*), it could not be construed with the objective case (*karmatva*) or other kārakas; and in cases such as "the female goat goes" (*chāgī gacchati*), it could not be construed with the agent (*kartṛ*) denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), because the referent of the word "female goat" (*chāgī*)—namely, the femininity residing in the goat—is incompatible [with being an agent].
Furthermore, in the reading "and because of the non-attainment of primacy for the female goat, etc. (*chāgyāder anāpatter ca*), the meaning is "because of the non-attainment of predominance."

[Objection: But would that linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) not be entirely useless? To this he says, "But rather... (*kiṃ tu*). Thus, the meaning is that such linguistic usage has as its scope only *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes, and not all suffixes (*pratyaya*) in general; therefore, on the strength of that [usage], it does not follow that the verbal root's meaning (*ākhyātārtha*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*). [Objection: But how, then, can there be a cognition (*bodha*) where the operation is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)? To this he says, "By way of being the qualificand, etc. (*viśeṣyatvādinā*). Thus, cognition follows linguistic usage, but linguistic usage does not follow cognition.

And thus, for those who accept such a linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*), there is understanding in that very manner; however, for those possessing a different kind of competency, there is understanding otherwise—this is the intended meaning. He clarifies this very point with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). Regarding the phrase "having as its qualifier the delimitor of the denotability" (*śakyatā'vacchedakaprakāraka*): by reflecting on the sūtra of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, "metaphorical transfer is a superimposed action" (*lakṣaṇā''ropitā kriyā*), one obtains that metaphorical transfer (*lakṣaṇā*) consists precisely in the relation residing in the object of the superimposition of the delimitor of denotability. Therefore, in the expression "the hamlet is on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the referent of the metaphorical transfer is perceived precisely as the Gaṅgā itself; for this very reason, from that [perception], there arises a suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of qualities such as coolness and purity.

And in such instances as "A creeper has indeed grown on the mountain," the intention is that the cognition produced in the form of a golden creeper alone is what evokes aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).

For the Naiyāyikas and others, the denoted meaning (lakṣyārtha) appears only through the form that delimits its relationality (*sambandhitāvacchedakarūpa*). For this very reason, in cases such as "the face [of the moon] shines and [the moon] trembles," the justification for the cognition of fear—which is produced by the shining—is possible only through the form of being a flame (*jvālatva*) and so forth, which delimits its relationality. If one were to accept that the denoted meaning is cognized through a form that delimits its denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), such as "shining-ness" (*kacatva*) and so forth, the aforementioned impossibility would be evident. Furthermore, that which delimits denotability is not what delimits denotability-in-virtue-of-lakṣaṇā;
*lakṣaṇā* occurs when something is known in a form other than its denotable form.

The meaning is that this is because of the contradiction with the statement of the learned (Abhiyukta). According to the view of the Navyas (the Neo-logicians), who accept that "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists in a word's lack of capacity to produce a cognition of syntactic connection when another word is absent, they admit that a verbal cognition arises from such a sentence as "ghaṭaḥ karmatvam" (The pot is the object) at a time when there is the knowledge that the word *ghaṭa* lacks the capacity to produce a cognition of connection due to the absence of the word *karmatva*. With this in mind, the term "of the Navyas" is used. The phrase "lacking expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣam*) has the ellipsis "with respect to a cognition [of the relation] through the relation of locus-ness" (*ādheyatā-saṃsargeṇa bodhe*).
"For this very reason" means: precisely because cognition follows the rules of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

"Because it follows linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*)" means because it is dependent upon the apprehension of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). For linguistic convention follows cognition; indeed, cognition does not follow linguistic convention. Therefore, authoritative scholars maintain that when there is a superimposition (*āropa*), one seeks its cause, but it is not the case that a superimposition occurs simply because a cause exists.

The meaning is as follows: because the object (*artha*), being perceived as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and so forth, is the referent of another cognition; and because [the word] possesses a linguistic convention that conforms to the cognition which serves as its own qualifier. Others hold that even though Pāṇini did not accept the restrictive rule "the meaning of the suffix is the primary [meaning]," the principle that "whatever is the meaning of a suffix is the primary" was accepted by Jaimini in the sūtra *tadāgame hi* (Jaiminisūtra 1.1.24); and since this is faultless, the stated causal relationship [between the suffix-meaning and the primary status] is also beyond reproach, precisely because of the qualifier.

With the intention that the implied meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*) possesses primacy—according to the logical principle expressed as "for when that [meaning] arrives" (*tadāgame hi*)—he says: "for when that [meaning] arrives. He explains that this is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*); the meaning is that it deviates from the rule "the neuter with a non-neuter" (*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*), which requires the formation of a neuter compound in the singular. He clarifies this very point with the word *kṛñ*. By the particle *api*, the previously mentioned form *pakvavān* is also included; for in that case, although the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is implied and thus cognized, there is a possibility of deviation because it is not the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*).

The meaning is as follows: since one understands from the word "what was done? (*kiṃ kṛtam*) that there is a desire to know the object of the operation (*vyāpāra*), and because the word "cooked" (*pakvam*) does not convey that [object], it is untenable for it to be the answer; therefore, while it is certain that [the suffix] conveys the operation, it cannot be the meaning of the suffix (as the primary referent), and thus there is no deviation [from the rule].

"Vivaraṇam" (explanation) here refers specifically to that which takes the form of a question and answer. For the sake of making this understood, why is there no mention [of the definition]? Otherwise, since the word "kṛta" alone is not commonly known in the world as an explanation of the word "pakva," the objection that the definition would be over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) would be incoherent. The phrase "it would be denotable" (*vācyā syāt*) means it would be denotable by the suffix (*pratyaya*).

The word "api" (also/even) does not merely serve to include what was stated previously, but rather intends to state another point as well; thus he raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely), the sense being that the aforementioned undesirable consequence is actually desired.

He clarifies the meaning of the conjunction "api" with the words "tathā ca. The term "ubhaya" means both the verb (ākhyāta) and the primary derivative (kṛdanta). "In common" (sādhāraṇyena) refers here to a specific co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra). "From the cognition" (pratīteḥ) means from the cognition of the productive urge (bhāvanā). "Common to both" (ubhayasādhāraṇa) means that, by virtue of being a constituent part, it is woven through both types of usage.

Thus, in both types of formal arguments (*prayoga*), it is established that the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone is the denoter of *bhāvanā* (efficient force), because its status as a verbal root is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of its expressive power (*śaktatā*), which is simpler (*lāghava*). It is not so for the *tiṅ* or *kṛt* suffixes, because the status of being a *tiṅ*—which is non-uniform (*ananugata*)—as a delimiting factor of expressive power would involve complexity (*gaurava*), and because of mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The sense is that there is no possibility of the aforementioned undesirable consequence occurring.

[Objection: But surely, since the status of "being a verbal root" (*dhātutva*) as the delimiting factor of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedakatā*) has already been refuted, the aforementioned criticism cannot be subsumed under the meaning of the word "also" (*api*). To this, he replies: "According to your view" (*bhavadrītyā*). He says "according to you" because, in his own system, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*). By the phrase "because it is the meaning of the suffix" (*pratyayārthatvāt*), it is indicated that among the two previously mentioned doctrines, this very one is the one accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas; and it has been explained accordingly.

It should be understood that the demonstration of the contradiction of that principle (*tannyāyavirodha*) in the introduction is based on the intention that, since the status of being the meaning of an affix (*pratyayārthatva*) and predominance (*prādhānya*) are generally co-extensive, and since one gains from that [co-extensiveness] the proof that what is predominant is the meaning of the affix, this [predominance] would be untenable if [the action] were expressed by the base (*prakṛti*). The phrase "another proof" (*sādhakāntara*) refers to [the argument] beginning with "if the verbal root denotes the operation" (*dhātor vyāpāravācakatve*), and so forth.

The point here is not that the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) is established as being the activity (*vyāpāra*) solely through the explanation in the form of a question-and-answer sequence—namely, "What is to be done?"—but rather, since such an explanation in the form of a question-and-answer sequence has already been introduced, he says "in the phrase 'what is to be done' (*kāryamityatra*)" to indicate why the word *kim* (what) is mentioned. Regarding the suffix *ṇini*, the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "under the governing rule 'bhūte' [Pāṇini 3.2.84], by the sūtra 'karaṇe yajaḥ' [Pāṇini 3.2.85]. The meaning is that these include the suffixes *ṇyat* and so forth.

The phrase "without action" (kriyāyogam antareṇa) implies that since only those things connected with an action possess the status of *kārakas* (factors of action), if the verbal root (*dhātu*) did not denote an operation (*vyāpāra*), then in expressions such as "the pot is to be made" (*kāryyo ghaṭaḥ*), the designations of *karman* (object) and so forth—which are prescribed under the governing rule "with reference to a *kāraka*" (*kārake*)—would be impossible in the case of the pot and other such entities. Consequently, the impossibility of applying the suffixes *ṇyat* and others prescribed therein necessitates the implication of an action by the verbal root; the sense is that this is just as the impossibility of Devadatta's corpulence implies his eating at night. He states this very point in the words: "without action."

Regarding the term "gamyamāne" (in the case of the being-understood), the phrase "even in the absence of a word that presents it" and so forth is to be supplied. "In the event of its occurrence" means that the formation of suffixes denoting the agent or the object is possible by taking the action itself as being understood. In that context as well, this applies specifically to the verbal forms (*ākhyāta*) designated as *tiṅ*.

The phrase "due to the requirement of agreement with gender and number" refers to examples such as *pācakaḥ* (the cooker). The word "necessary" (*āvaśyakam*) has the term "in the case of a *kṛt*-suffix" (*kṛtau*) as its ellipsis; the meaning is that the status of being the expressed object (*vācyatva*) of the agent, as defined by a *kṛt*-suffix, must necessarily be accepted. By that agent. The phrase "by implication" (*ākṣepāt*) means "by way of defining its essential nature," and so on. The word "cognition" (*pratyaya*) means "understanding. The word "of that" (*tasya*) means "of that [status of being] the expressed object."

"Due to incapacity" (asāmarthyāt) means due to the failure to bring about the cognition of a qualified meaning; that is to say, because there is no mutual expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*). In the view that maintains that the verbal root denotes the operation (*vyāpāra*), the capacity characterized by mutual expectancy is easily established: for the two actions denoted by the roots contained within the distinct words *trāta* and *bhinnā*, there is an expectancy for the agent and object *kārakas*, and the agent and object presented by the words *hariṇā* and so forth have an expectancy for the action by virtue of being *kārakas*. Thus, the mutual expectancy is well-formed.

The point is that, according to your view, a compound would be untenable because of a lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*), just as in the case of "the king’s man is Devadatta’s wife" and so forth. This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) regarding the case-endings of the *kāraka*s.

"Taking the supplied action" means taking the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is the sense of the verb "to do. "Capability" (*sāmarthya*) means that, by accepting the understanding "it was split by means of those [teeth]," capability is established by taking the supplied meaning. He provides an example for the acceptance of capability by taking the supplied action: "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*) and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: even in cases such as "annaṃ vyañjanena" (rice with condiment), since these are word-derivations (*padavidhi*), they fall under the scope of the *samartha-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding semantic competency). Consequently, if one were to assume the ellipsis of an action such as "pouring over" (*upasecana*)—lest the prescription of a compound (*samāsa*) for words like "dadhi" (curd) which are inherently incompetent (*asamartha*) become purposeless—the injunction [of the compound] would still be rendered futile. This is the sense of the phrase "due to the futility of the injunction."

The meaning is as follows: since the root *kṛ* is accepted as having the sense of "activity" (*vyāpāra*), agency (*kartṛtva*) defined by that activity exists directly in Hari; therefore, the rule [of the suffix -ta] is satisfied without the need for supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Consequently, there is no evidence for the application of that rule in cases such as *haritrātaḥ* by resorting to a capacity mediated by a supplied action.

The word "kṛtam" is stated to indicate that if one does not accept that the root *kṛ* has the meaning of "activity" (*vyāpāra*), then even a supplied sense would fail to provide the required semantic fitness, and thus the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) itself would become useless. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as "śarakṛtam" (made with reeds) are included, which are instrumental *tatpuruṣa* compounds.

However, some argue that in cases such as *haritrātaḥ* ("protected by Hari"), one takes the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) implied by the agent expressed by the third case-ending (the instrumental) associated with the root *kṛ*; whereas in cases such as *nakhair bhinnaḥ* ("split by nails"), one takes that operation which is supplied through the force of the instrument. Since the semantic competency is thus established, they claim that this lack of competency cannot serve as a proof for the verbal root's denotation of the productive operation. Furthermore, they maintain that even if the root *kṛ* signifies the result, there is no lack of semantic competency in the compound. This [view] is to be considered.

The sense is that "being connected to a single action" (*ekakriyānvayitva*) alone is the factor; since this is observed in examples such as *dhavakhadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees"), it is precisely this—either directly or indirectly—that serves as the motivator for a compound even in other cases. The underlying point is that in the case of *asūryampaśyāḥ* ("those who do not see the sun"), since it will be explained that the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) which is connected to an action, the sun (*sūrya*) also functions as an object (*karmakāraka*). Thus, because it is connected to that [action], the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) asserted by you exists there as well.

The phrase "having made all clay" (*kṛtasarvamṛttika*) implies that the word *mṛttikā* (clay) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), while the entire object (*padārtha*) functions as the patient (*karman*), because both are construed with the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to make). This is the intended sense. He says "furthermore" (*kiñca*) because splitting the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*) does not lead to any undesirable consequence. Regarding the phrase "in the event of the non-attainment of agency" (*akartṛtāpattau*), the ellipsis to be supplied is "because [the agent] would not be the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātārthavyāpārānāśrayatvāt*). In our view, however, since [the agent] possesses agency by being the substratum of the activity denoted by the base of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is no such inconsistency; this is the intended sense.

[Objection: But surely, even if Viṣṇumitra is not the agent, the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is easily obtained there simply by intending to express his status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*). [Response: To this, he says: in the example "he causes [Viṣṇumitra] to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamayati*), according to the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* (Pāṇini 1.4.49), the designation of object (*karman*) is prescribed only for that which is connected with the result produced by the operation residing in the primary agent. Since, in your view, Viṣṇumitra is not the agent, the village—which is the locus of the result produced by his operation—would likewise not be an object; consequently, the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) would fail to apply after the word denoting the village. This is because, if Viṣṇumitra were an instrument...

And there is the impossibility [of the suffix] *ṇic*. The point is that if one accepts that only that which is the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root is the object (*karman*), then in the case of a causative form (*ṇijanta*) such as *pācayati*, it would be the object of the causative operation alone, and not the object of the root *gam* (to go). To the objection that this might be an accepted position, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). By the phrase "by this," the meaning is: by the refutation of the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) of the locus of the operation expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). In the case of a causative form such as *pācayati*, "both" means the two operations belonging to the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*). "Because of being the locus of those" means because of being the locus of the two operations expressed by the verbal suffix.

The sense of the phrase "it has been rejected" (*apāstam*) is as follows: even if the agenthood of Viṣṇumitra is established by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denoting two operations, since that agenthood is expressed by the suffix itself, a third case ending would be difficult to obtain after the word *viṣṇumitra*, just as it is after the word *devadatta*. Likewise, because both [Viṣṇumitra and Devadatta] are equally substrata of the operation denoted by the suffix, there would be the undesirable consequence of abolishing the conventional usage of the "principal" (agent), which would contradict the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "and [the suffix is used] when there is an instigator" (*hetumati ca*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the locus of an operation that is either the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) or the meaning of the verbal root? In our view, since the mere result is the meaning of the verbal root as listed in the *gaṇa*, Viṣṇumitra would also be difficult to exclude from agency because he is the locus of the operation expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) which is conducive to that [result]; therefore, the aforementioned inconsistency does not arise. To this, [the author] says "furthermore" (*kiñca*): Since being the locus of the operation expressed by the verbal suffix is a property that is universally present (*kevalānvayin*), it lacks the capacity to distinguish [the agent], and thus the verbal suffix must necessarily be qualified by its presence within that specific sentence.

And thus, in sentences such as "Caitra is a cooker" (*caitraḥ paktā*), which lack a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), the failure to include the agent denoted by the *kṛt* suffix would be unavoidable; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Since the *Mahābhāṣya* states that 'the verb *as* [is understood] with the present tense endings,' the use of a finite verb is necessarily implied there, so the aforementioned consequence does not arise. Furthermore: "Agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the substratum of an activity, whether that activity is expressed by a suffix prescribed after a verbal root or is implied by it."

Furthermore, because the term *dhātuvihita* (prescribed by a verbal root) serves as a qualifier for the suffix (*pratyaya*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the substratum of an operation that is the meaning of the instrumental case (*karaṇatṛtīyā*). In the aforementioned instance, since it is the substratum of the operation implied by the agent denoted by the primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*), the stated fault does not arise; hence he says "dig" (and so forth). Its meaning is as follows: in a sentence whose purport is the exclusion of others, the necessity of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is absent, and thus the method already described is more sound. Moreover, rather than defining agency (*kartṛtva*) in such a manner, it is more appropriate to define agency simply as being the substratum of that [operation] by accepting that the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is an operation (*vyāpāra*), on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), and so forth.
"Being one's own invention" means being the object of a rootless (nirmūla) conceptualization of one's own.

This [definition] is stated while adhering to the literal sense of the term *hiruk*; however, since its meaning lacks connection with time (*kāla*), it cannot be a "verbal action" (*kriyā*). But it should be understood that if only that much were stated, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms such as *āṇavayati*, because if those were considered verbal roots (*dhātu*), they would result in grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) by virtue of falling within the scope of the grammatical treatise. In the phrase "if only that much were stated," the word "only" (*mātra*) excludes the component "denoting a verbal action."

Fearing that this might be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says "And thus" (*tathāca*); and in order to indicate that the word "yāḥ" is in the accusative case, he says "you see" (*paśyasi*).

*Lakṣaṇapratīti* (the cognition of the definition): that by which a correct word (*sādhuśabda*) is characterized—that is, explained—is the *lakṣaṇa*, namely, the Sūtra. By metaphorical extension, even that which is *lākṣaṇika* (derived from a rule) is called *lakṣaṇa*, because it depends upon the consideration of that [rule]. For example, the form *pā* derived from *pai* is slow to present itself to the mind because it depends upon the consideration of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇā*). However, that which is *pratipadokta* (stated in its own specific form) is read without reference to a particular case-ending; it presents itself quickly because it does not depend upon the consideration of a rule.

Just as the form *pā* is derived from the root *pibati*, so too, the quality of being quickly presented (*śīghropasthitikatva*) is the reason for accepting a term as it is explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*). This quality exists only in the case of *yā* as listed in the *gaṇa* [of pronouns], because in the case of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), one must depend upon the application of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇānu-saṃdhāna*). By the phrase "in *avyaye vā* etc.," the inclusion of the prefix *su-* (in *suvikalpa*), as well as *mā* and *māṅ* (the two forms beginning with vowels), is intended. One should not suspect that the prefix is excluded because it is not read in the section on the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva-prakaraṇa*), for even there, the technical designation of being taught with a *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśatva*) exists in order to include roots such as *ṣidhu*.

The phrase "there would be usage" (*prayogaḥ syāt*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication) for usages such as *suvati*, *māti*, and *mimīte*. This is because, since roots such as *ṣūṅ* (in the sense of "the birth of living beings") and *māṅ* (in the sense of "measuring") exist, it would be impossible to determine [which one is intended] based on mere usage. However, there is no fault in stating the condition "when it exists" (*satyanta*), because the meaning of the verbal root (*vācyārtha*), such as a mental alternative (*vikalpa*), lacks the nature of an action (*kriyātva*) due to its lack of connection with times such as the past. This is the underlying intention (*bhāva*). [Regarding the term] "restrictive" (*niyāmaka*).

The meaning is that if the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) were intended only for those [words] recited in the *gaṇa*, then the specification of their meanings would result in redundancy; therefore, it is made known that only those which have their meanings specified possess the status of a verbal root. Regarding the phrase "of that specification of meaning": the meaning is that because there is no instruction—that is, no recitation—of the meanings, such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth.

The phrase "due to the acquisition of modernity" means that it is understood to have been composed by Bhīmasena and others. Thus, regarding the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*, it is stated: "The mention of 'measure' (*parimāṇa*) should be made; for why is this so? Is it that the word *bhū* alone receives the designation 'root,' and not the word *bhū-edha*? Even though the indication of the meaning was indeed composed by the author of the Sūtras, as seen in the rule *cuṭū*: "Since he recites certain roots with the augment *num* attached, such as *ubundi* in the sense of 'observing' and *skandi* in the senses of 'motion' and 'drying'."

It is stated in the Bhāṣya that "this rule [P. 1.3.2] is prompted by that [fact]. Nevertheless, the sense is that because the indication of all verbal root meanings (dhātvartha) is not the work of Pāṇini—due to the authority of the two Bhāṣyas—that indication does not serve as a restrictive rule. Regarding roots such as *culump* and those beginning with *stambh*, their status as verbal roots is established by the rule "kāsyanekāca ām" and by the inclusion of the marker *u*. The meaning is that [the action] is indeed the meaning of the root, and thus it is simply the result (*phala*). Consequently, the point is that this sūtra does not fail to establish that a verbal root has the sense of an activity (*vyāpāra*).

Regarding "in the case of origination" (*utpattau*): as in the case of the origination of a sprout from a seed and so forth, that [objection] is avoided by the fact of beginninglessness; this is one point. Or, as in the case of "Caitra’s son is Caitra" and so on, because even there, the second [designation] would be untenable without the first origination. Regarding "in the case of cognition" (*jñaptau*): this is well-known in rules such as *halantyam*. Regarding "because it would result in an inconsistency": as in the case of the relationship between container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) between earth and water, since everyone accepts that both exist through a mutual relationship of container and contained.

The meaning is that, in the present context, since there is no sublation (bādhaka) to the fact that the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is indeed an action (*kriyā*), or that action-ness (*kriyātva*) is the meaning of a verbal root, it would follow that it is improper to offer a refutation against that [position]. "Anyatamatva" means the state of being distinct from those [roots] other than *bhū* and so forth.

[Objection: "In our view, since an action (*kriyā*)—in the form of a collection of parts arranged in a temporal sequence—is the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is possible for the result (*phala*) to be designated as an 'action' by superimposing that sequence upon it. But in your view, since you do not accept that an action is the meaning of a verbal root, how can such a designation apply to it? To this he replies: 'Because it is the meaning of a verbal root' (*dhātvarthatvāt*). The sense is that, just as there is the designation of 'result-ness' (*phalatva*) in that case, the designation of 'action-ness' (*kriyātva*) also arises because one accepts that being the meaning of a verbal root is the determinant (*prayojaka*) for it."

The phrase "stated in the Bhāṣya and elsewhere" means that [the term] *abhūvādi* is stated in the Bhāṣya and so forth regarding the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the Vṛtti and other works is intended. "Of this very [word]" means of that which expresses action alone. By the particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of those that denote merely the result. The reason for its not being expressive of this [action] is "due to the absence of the cognition of action"; "of those not expressive of this" means of those not expressive of the operation (*vyāpāra*). "The consequence of not being a verbal root (*adhātutva*)"—the sense is that this consequence is not desired, because it would follow that suffixes such as the *lakāra* could not be produced from it.

The meaning is "in the aspect of the dharma which is the nature of the fruit. Because of the employment of the word "aspect" (aṃśa), since the substratum (dharmin) has a form constituted by its attributes (dharmas), and because in the case of intransitive verbs the fruit resides in the agent, the fruit is also an "aspect" of that [agent]; yet, since there is dispute only regarding its status as something to be brought about (bhāvyatā), he says "by way of being something to be brought about," which means "by way of being produced by the efficient force (bhāvanā). This amounts to saying: "when the activity whose goal is the fruit is what is desired to be known. For this very reason, he will later say: "that which is on the verge of perishing."

He demonstrates that which resides in the speaker's intention precisely through the form of a question and answer: "Has he gone from there or not? Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule for roots meaning "to go" when they are intransitive (*gatyarthākarmaka*). By the word "question" (*praśna*), the fact that the state of being about to happen (*bhāvyatva*) is what is desired to be known (*jijñāsya*) is implied. Thus, the form of the question is: "Has he gone, or has he not? (i.e., "Is it the case that he has gone, or not?").

"Application" (*prayoga*) means a sentence that resolves a doubt. Regarding the phrase "is indeed perceived," the ellipsis is "by the verbal root. Now, from the sentence "Has he gone from there or not? it is understood that what is desired to be known is either the state of being the locus of an activity conducive to disjunction with a limit such as the house, or the absence thereof.

Even if it is accepted that the word "asti" (is) denotes an operation (*vyāpāra*) through great effort, [the response] would still be merely an operation conducive to the existence (*sattā*) whose agent is Caitra and so forth; how, then, could these two constitute question and answer? For instance: when a sentence conveys the relation of an object qualified by a certain property (*dharmāvacchinna*)—which is the object of inquiry—with another object qualified by a certain property, as understood from the interrogative sentence, then that sentence is the answer which makes known the relation of the object qualified by that [inquired-after] property with the object qualified by that [other] property. As they say: "That by which the relation of the object of inquiry is understood..."

"That which follows it is called the answer (*uttara*); otherwise, it is termed a semblance (*ābhāsa*). For example, in response to the question "From what [is this] a jar?"—which seeks to establish the relation between the jarness-qualified object and the property sought to be known—the sentence "A jar [arises] from a staff" serves as the answer by establishing the causal relationship between the staffness-qualified cause and the jarness-qualified effect. In the present case, however, the appropriate answers would be "He has gone" or "He has not."

Furthermore, since it is not understood from the aforementioned question that the operation (*vyāpāra*) which establishes existence is what is intended to be known, how can this [verse] serve as an answer? Even if that were the case, since the word "with effort" (*yatnena*) is employed in both the preceding and following sentences, the status of being an answer is established solely through the cognition that [existence] is produced by the effort (*yatna*) presented by the word "effort"; therefore, the fact that the verbal root (*dhātu*) has "operation" as its meaning is not established thereby. Hence, he says: "In production, etc."—the ellipsis to be supplied is that the phrase "all the more" (*sutarām*) implies that [the verbal root] has "operation" as its meaning.

In this context, since the cognition of the substratum (*āśrayatā*) is established according to both schools of thought, that very cognition is what is designated as the "operation" (*vyāpāra*) because it is the object to be accomplished. Furthermore, the sense is that the temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*), which in the view of the opponent belongs to time, is merely superimposed upon that [cognition], just as it is superimposed upon existence (*sattā*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that even there, the assumption that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the locus (*āśrayatā*) is rooted in mere dogmatism? For even if [the suffix] has the sense of mere origination (*utpatti-mātra*), one obtains the understanding of the intended meaning—namely, "an origination occurring in the recent past, having redness as its locus. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "Of that alone" (*tasyā eva*): the meaning is "of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) alone. By the word "alone" (*eva*), the result (*phala*) is excluded. How this is so has been stated in the *Sāra* itself. "Because of its prescription" (*tad-vidhānāt*): because of the prescription of the *laṭ* and other suffixes. In this regard, he also cites the consensus of Hari: "for the sake of distinguishing actions" (*kriyā-bhedāya*).

The word *tumarthāt* [in the sūtra] is in the dative case, or it denotes the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*) according to the Vārttika. "To distinguish the action" means to qualify it. "Time" refers to that which is understood through the *laṭ* (present) and other suffixes; the word "exists" (*asti*) is to be supplied. The meaning is that time, as expressed by the *laṭ* and other suffixes, is the differentiator of the action alone. Number, however, in the form of a case-meaning, is the differentiator of the entire meaning of the verbal base and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). According to another view, it should be understood as the differentiator of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the nominal stem. Thus, this applies when the verbal root expresses the operation (*vyāpāra*).

Regarding the phrase "mūle-aśeṣabhāvāt," the word "remainder" (śeṣa) is to be supplied. A "state" (bhāva) is that in which something exists; thus, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the term "state of remainder" (*śeṣabhāva*) signifies having a locus distinct from the result. This is an indication where the state itself is the primary referent. Therefore, from the negative compound ending in the singular ablative case, the understanding of the meaning arises as "due to the absence of non-distinctness of locus from the result. He states the established conclusion in the *Sāra*: "The result of the meditative cultivation... [referring to] the essential nature of the co-occurrence in the same locus of the result with a single locus.

Because it is accepted that [the cognition of the object] obstructs the clear manifestation of the *bhāvanā*, its perception is not clear. And "as if clear" means not being overwhelmed by the perception of the result; this is the sense. Thus, regarding the view that roots such as *asti* (to be) have action (*vyāpāra*) as their meaning: "because of being restricted to a result" means because of being pervaded by a result (*phalavyāpyatva*). This amounts to saying that being expressive of *bhāvanā* is pervaded by being expressive of a result. The reason for the consequence of these roots having an object (*sakarmakatā*) is that we observe roots like *pac* (to cook), which express both the result and the operation, to be transitive; this is the underlying idea.

[Objection: If it were the case that the result and the operation residing in the same locus is the criterion for being intransitive (*akarmaka*), then verbs such as *gam* (to go) would also incur the status of being intransitive, because the result and the operation of their meanings reside in the same agent. Therefore, [the author] explains: "in the sense of residing in one alone. "Residing in one alone" means: while not occurring in anything other than the one, it occurs in that one. In this context, since there is no purpose [for including the qualifier], he omits the substantive portion and states the intended meaning: "residing in different loci" (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*). And "difference" here should be understood in relation to the locus of the operation.

Thus, the final definition—that of being expressive of a result which does not reside in the locus of its own [verbal] operation—applies to the definiendum; for in that case, the fact that the operation consisting of existence (sattā) resides in the subject alone remains unimpaired. This is the intended meaning.

Now, an objection: in the *Mūla*, by the phrase "when there is a difference of substrata (*dharmibheda*) for those two," it was stated that transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in either expressing an operation whose locus differs from the locus of its own fruit, or expressing a fruit whose locus differs from the locus of its own operation. In this context, "difference of locus" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) means not residing in the same substratum as that [fruit]. Consequently, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to roots such as *grāma* (to go to a village), because the operation and the fruit of that root do not lack the property of residing in different substrata from one another; therefore, the *Bhūṣaṇasāra* explains it as "difference of substrata" (*āśrayabheda*).

Thus, the point is that there is no inconsistency, because in the first definition, what is introduced is the state of not occurring in a locus other than the agent, while in the second, it is the state of not occurring in a locus other than that [agent].

He also cites the consensus of Hari regarding the fact that the root *as* signifies both the result and the operation—stating "and it has been said"—where "is designated" means "is conventionally treated as. "Because of inclusion" means "because of being included within the scope of the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root."

The sense is that since there is a rule of concomitance (*anvaya-niyama*) only between two things presented separately, the property of being *sakarmaka* (having an object) defined as "having an object whose meaning is connected with the meaning of the word designated as *karman*" has no scope there [in the case of *ātmānaṃ dadhāti*]. Following his own stated definition, the author of the *Sāra* explains: "by the factor of the fruit" (*phalāṃśena*), which means because the operation conducive to that [fruit] shares the same locus (*ekādhikaraṇya*) with the fruit consisting of the act of holding (*dhāraṇa*) having oneself as its object.

Regarding the inquiry as to why there is no *sakarmakatva* by virtue of the object that is one's self (*ātmarūpa-karman*), the wise should discern whether this proposed solution is susceptible to the fault of being elliptical (*udakṣara*).

One might object: "In cases such as 'he knows himself' (*ātmānaṃ jānāti*), there is an under-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of transitive verbs just stated, because the operation intended by that [verb] and its fruit (the cognition) do not lack coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); furthermore, there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of intransitive verbs beginning with 'having the same locus as the fruit,' etc. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution starting with "he knows himself," etc. "The inner self" (*antarātman*) refers to the self delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); "the bodily self" (*śarīrātman*) is that [self] delimited by the body.

Thus, even though the Self is one, since the grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is easily established by taking the difference imagined through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body, there is neither under-extension (*avyāpti*) nor over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the stated definitions. To this he says: "having different substrata" (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*). The phrase "of that which has become non-existent" (*asattvabhūtāyāḥ*) means that which is characterized by a property that does not give rise to an expectancy for another verb. "That" (*tat*) means the contingency of being perceived in that form. "Expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix" (*kṛdabhihita*) means the meaning of a *kṛt*-suffix.

The phrase "like a substance" (*dravyavat*) means that it appears or shines forth in a manner similar to a substance—that is, to the meaning of a noun. This signifies that it assumes the properties of a substance, namely gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*). Alternatively, "substance" (*dravya*) refers to that which possesses the state of being established (*siddhatva*), characterized by the capacity to give rise to an expectation for action (*kriyākāṅkṣotthāpakatāvacchedaka*); thus, "it appears like that" means it manifests as something already established.

Consequently, the point is that when the absence of the probandum (*apādyavyatireka*) is determined by such a commentary, it is impossible to avoid the undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) because one must admit its validity (*prāmāṇya*) as the cause of that determination.

With the intention that the sentence is the "referent of another word" (anyapadārtha) by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, "that in which there is a verbal form (*ākhyāta*) such as *śabdādi*"—he says "paśya" and so forth. [The examples are] from the two verbal roots ending in *tiṅ* suffixes, *paśya* and *dhāvati*. The status of being an illustration is appropriate because *dhāvati* functions as the means (*sādhana*) and *paśyati* conveys the action (*kriyā*); for this very reason, he will later state: "This much, however, is the difference. The explanation "prakṛtyādi" is found in the *Vivaraṇa*. His point is that the term *ākhyātaśabda* is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

He states the reason for this misinterpretation in the passage beginning "in the case of 'pacati'": thus, since the meaning of the form of the *tiṅ* suffix in "pacati" and so forth is already obtained by the word "ākhyāta" alone—which is conventionally established as denoting *tiṅ* suffixes—the inclusion of the word "śabda" would be redundant.

In my view, however, because it serves to establish that [the word] as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is logical that the term *ākhyātaśabda* refers to a sentence composed of two finite verbal forms (*tiṅanta*). The point is that even though the two parts of words such as *pacati* reside respectively in the state of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), a *dṛṣṭānta* (example) is impossible here because an action is not understood from them as a means (*sādhana*). He clarifies this very point with the phrase "in the form of a means" (*sādhanarūpatā*). The remainder of the sense is: "by the base-form (*prakṛti*)"—that is, in cases such as *pākaḥ*.

[Objection: But surely, since these two differ in that one possesses gender and number while the other does not, how can there be the relationship of example (dṛṣṭānta) and subject of the example (dārṣṭāntika)? To this he says: "This much [is] at most. The meaning is that since similarity is intended on the basis of possessing some property or other, the aforementioned defect does not apply.

If it is argued that, since the meaning of "running" (the action) cannot be connected as a *kāraka*, its non-existence—defined as the lack of connection with a *kāraka*—would be compromised, [we reply]: in that case, by qualifying it as "not being the locus of an action," its aforementioned nature of non-existence remains intact even when it is connected as an agent through being the locus of the agent's operation, as an object through being the locus of the result, or as an agent or an object [in general]. And it has been said: "The action is not joined with gender; the action is not [joined] with the loci of *kārakas*.
This very [lack of connection] is to be determined as its nature of non-existence."

In the view that "non-substantiality" (*asattvabhūtatva*) consists in possessing a property that does not give rise to an expectancy for another action (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣānuttthāpakatāvacchedakadharmavattva*), the aforementioned defect certainly remains. However, when it is refined as consisting in possessing a property that gives rise to an expectancy for a means (*sādhanākāṅkṣotthāpakatāvacchedakadharmavattva*), there is no defect anywhere. The phrase "in such a designation" (*tathābhidhāne*) means in the cognition [of the object] by way of the aforementioned nature of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*).

In the expression "of the rice" (*odanasya*), the word *odana* refers to the rice grains (*taṇḍula*) and so forth; otherwise, since the meaning of the word *odana* would be only that which has already been cooked, it would follow that its connection with cooking is impossible, resulting in a contradiction of its meaning. "Of the genitive case in the sense of the object" (*karma-ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*) means of the genitive case itself as having the capacity for the object-role (*karmatva*). "Because of being a means of knowledge" (*mānatvāt*) means because of being a means of knowledge in the form of an apparent inconsistency (*anupapatti*).

The point is that since a word ending in *ghañ* denotes only an already established state (*siddhabhāva*), and because there is a rule that factors of action (*kāraka*) must necessarily connect with an action whose nature is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyasvabhāvakriyā*), the boiled rice (*odana*) would not be a factor of action; consequently, it would not be an object (*karman*), and thus the genitive case would be untenable. Therefore, this very fact serves as the proof for its denoting an action whose nature is yet to be accomplished. The phrase "due to connection with an action" (*kriyānvayāt*) means due to the indirect connection (*paramparānvaya*) with the sense of the verb *bhavati*, which is supplied (*adhyāhṛta*) and has the nature of something to be accomplished.

[Objection: But surely, since *odana* exists as something capable of being the locus of the fruit of the meaning of a *kṛt*-affix—being thus suitable for a *kṛt*-affix—how can there be this inconsistency? To this he says: "Not by common usage" (*na loka-*) etc. This was stated for the sake of ease of resolution. For, by proximity, only that which is the agent (*kāraka*) of the meaning of a verbal root obtains the status of the object (*karman*) when it is the locus of the fruit of that verbal root's meaning. Consequently, although the meaning of the verb *bhavati* is an action, since the meaning of the word *pāka* (cooking) is also an action, *odana* cannot even be established as the object, because it lacks the status of being the locus of the fruit of the meaning of that [specific] action.

If it is argued that in those cases there need not be a genitive of agency (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī*), since the usage can be accounted for by the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) alone, we say no; for if the usage were possible everywhere through the genitive of relation (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*) alone, the rules such as *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) would become redundant.

If it is argued that its necessity must be admitted—both for the sake of accounting for the well-established cognition of the objecthood (*karmatva*) as the qualifier in expressions such as "the creator of the world" (*jagataḥ karttā*), and for the sake of ensuring the application of rules like "a *kṛt*-suffix follows a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*" (*gatikārakopapadātkṛt*) in the case of compounds—then the point is this: what purpose does it serve in the present context? It is as good as hidden from view (*pāṇipihita*).

One might object: "If the meaning of the base of a nominal suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is an action that has not become a real entity (*asattvabhūtakriyā*), then since it is possible for firewood (*kāṣṭha*) to possess instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) as determined by that [action], the expression ‘*kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ*’ (‘cooking with firewood’) would result even without supplying the verb ‘to be’ (*bhavati*). Anticipating this objection, he dismisses it by conceding the point, saying: “In this manner... (*evaṃrītyā*).

Others, however, maintain that in the case of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), just as a single entity possesses the status of "fatherhood" and "brotherhood" due to the difference in its relata, so too the single action denoted by the verbal root—such as "running"—is presented through the two aspects of being the "end to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) and the "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) due to the difference in its relata, namely the suffixes which express them; it is not that two distinct actions are presented by those two aspects.

The word "evam" (thus) means that just as in expressions such as "the cooking of rice," because the status of the rice as the object (*karman*) would otherwise be untenable, the operation (*vyāpāra*)—which is unreal (*asatya*) in the sense of being non-existent—is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*); so it is here. He demonstrates the untenability [of the theory] if such a result were not denoted:

"For this very reason" [means]: otherwise, such usage would be untenable; however, if such a result (phala) were the denotatum (vācya), then by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (vyapadeśivadbhāva), it would possess the status of an object (*karman*) by virtue of being related to itself. Consequently, the use of the accusative case after words such as *stoka* (a little) in coreferential constructions is justified. In that context, the genitive case prescribed by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* does not apply to *stoka* and the like, because in that rule, by association with the word *kartṛ* (agent), only an object that enters into a relation of difference (bhedānvayin) is understood.

For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *pūjānātpūjitam*, it is stated that the rule for the elision of the suffix *matup* was initiated in order to establish forms such as *dāruṇādhyāpakaḥ*—meaning "one who teaches in a harsh manner. Otherwise, if the compound were formed with a word ending in the sixth case (genitive) prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*, its purposelessness (*vaiyarthya*) would be evident; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Others, however, maintain that under the governing rule *ojaḥ-saha-am̐bhasā vartate*, the mention of the word *tat* (that) in the accusative case in the sūtra *tat-prati-anu-pūrvam īṣad-alpam-kūlam* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that "the accusative is used after an adverbial modifier" (*kriyā-viśeṣaṇād dvitīyā*), but not for the status of [words like] *stoka* and so on as objects (*karman*), because a result (*phala*) cannot be the locus of its own result.

And thus they say that there is no possibility of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arising from words denoting such [an action], because it has already been stated. The meaning is: "the state of being a *sādhya* (that which is to be accomplished) consists in possessing a nature that does not give rise to an expectancy for another action," and so forth; the point is that since [the action] is presented through a nature that does not give rise to an expectancy for another action, its connection with another action is impossible.

Because [the gender] would be present in that form, there would be an inconsistency in cases such as "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" (see, the deer runs); therefore, he says "stokaḥ pākaḥ" (a small cooking). The point is that if the *ghañ* suffix did not convey the action in its accomplished state, then words like "stoka" expressing a qualifier of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) would result in being assigned the gender of the verb, a pronoun, or the neuter gender. He clarifies this very point with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). By the phrase "etena" (by this), the meaning is: by establishing that the *ghañ* suffixes and others denote an action that has reached the state of accomplishment.
The word "mātra" (mere) in the expression "prayogasādhutāmātram" (merely for the grammatical correctness of usage) serves to exclude the status of being a denotative power (*vācakatva*).

Regarding the statement of the Neo-Naiyāyikas: since verbal roots are not the base (prakṛti) for case-suffixes (*sub-vibhakti*), it is untenable for the meanings of those suffixes—such as number and objecthood—to be construed with the meaning of the root. Consequently, one must admit that even a word ending in *ghañ* (e.g., *pāka*) denotes action (*kriyā*), just like the verbal root itself. However, if one were to admit that the suffix-meanings are construed with only a portion of the base-meaning, then there would arise the undesirable consequence of such usages as "he sees two cooks" (*pacantau paśyati*) in cases where duality and so forth are precluded from the agent of cooking, while they are not precluded from the act of cooking itself.

Furthermore, there is the drawback of complexity (gaurava) in the case where one understands that the cognition of a word following a verbal root having the sense of "something" as its property is an obstacle to the comprehension of the syntactic connection of a case-meaning with the meaning presented by that verbal root. And thus, wherever one understands that the cognition of a word following a verbal root having the sense of "something" as its property is an obstacle to the comprehension of the syntactic connection of a case-meaning with the meaning presented by that verbal root, there is complexity.

And thus, where there is an intention (*tātparya*) regarding the mere verbal root—as in the case of "cooking" (*pāka*) and so on—there the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) alone is used after a word like *stoka*, which expresses a qualifier of that [root-meaning]. However, where there is an intention regarding a complex formed by a *kṛt*-suffix, a word expressing a qualifier of that [complex] must indeed have the same case-ending as it. Having stated this view from the *Kātantra-pariśiṣṭa* and the *Ḍhakṛt* (as the opinion of the Navya-naiyāyikas), he refutes it with the words "not so" (*na ca*), citing the reason "due to prolixity" (*gauravāt*).

[Objection: Since it is established that *ghañ* and other suffixes prescribed for nominal action (*bhāva*)—just like verbal action (*bhāva*) expressed by a verb—merely restate the meaning of the root, it is necessary, as a last resort, to accept that the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) of the *ghañ*-ending form is the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), in order to justify the previously mentioned usage. To this, he says: "Not so, because of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*). The sense is this: rather than accepting a cumbersome sequential order as the delimitor of expressive power, it is more appropriate to take *ghañ*-ness itself as that [delimitor], in accordance with the grammatical rule, for the sake of justifying the aforementioned usage.

Now, even if *ghañ* and other suffixes do not denote an operation (*vyāpāra*), since the word "action" (*kriyā*) in the rule "the second case ending after an adverbial modifier of an action" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇād dvitīyā*) refers to that which does not convey the meaning of cooking (as opposed to the verbal root), there would be no contingency of a second case ending after a word expressing such a modifier in cases like "a slight cooking" (*stokaḥ pākaḥ*), because the cooking conveyed by the verbal root lacks the aforementioned qualifier. To this he says "dig" (the direction/method). Its meaning is as follows: this would indeed be so if the rule "the second case ending after an adverbial modifier of an action" were an independent injunction.

However, that is merely a restatement of the meaning already established by our own position; for if it were otherwise, the term "a little" (*stokam*) would not be applicable according to your view. Thus, the phrase "in the action" (*kriyāyām*) means "in the action which is the object of the instigation. He provides proof for the impossibility of the *nighāta* accent if there were no connection with that [action], stating: "on account of the requirement of the *nighāta*. [He then states: "in a single sentence" (*samānavākye*).

The meaning of the entire passage is as follows: according to the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*, which states that "a sentence consists of a verb along with its qualifiers," a verb (*ākhyāta*)—whether directly or indirectly—conveys an action (*kriyā*) connected with another word-meaning (*padārthāntara*). Consequently, if the meaning of a vocative case were not connected to the action, then in examples such as "O Devadatta, you speak" (*tvaṃ brūhi devadatta*), that [connection] would be absent; thus, because the rule "in the same sentence" (*samānavākye*) would apply, the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) resulting from the vocative being treated as a stem (*prakṛti*) would be untenable. This is the purport of the whole.

In this context, regarding examples such as "I shall give you rice from the *śālī* grains," the phrase "by way of a series" (*paramparayā*) is used to establish that [the word] "of the *śālī* grains" (*śālīnām*) and so forth reside within the same sentence. This principle is common to cases such as "he cooks, [and thus] he exists. In the present case, however, since the vocative functions as a subject to be restated (*anuvādya*), and since that which is restated requires a predicate (*vidheya*) to complete its sense, and since the status of being a predicate resides in the action (*kriyā*), it is appropriate for the meaning of the vocative to be construed with that very action; thus, the fact of residing in the same sentence remains intact—this is the intended meaning.

"Awakening" (*bodha*) here refers to speech whose agent is non-different from the instigation directed toward Devadatta, which has as its object an activity conducive to becoming face-to-face. Regarding this, he cites the consensus of Hari: "And it has been said," etc. The meaning is that the vocative word is what is to be understood by that [instigation]. The term "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*) means [it qualifies] through an indirect relation consisting in being the object of an instigation directed toward oneself. For the remainder of the sentence "vrajāni" (let us go) is "jānīhi" (know/understand). They define "addressing" (*sambodhana*) as the mere act of making one who is already established [in existence] face-to-face.
For a person who has attained the stage called "Abhimukhī" is indeed employed in spiritual practices.

Thus, by stating "it is employed" (*viniyujyate*) in another *kārikā*, [the author] indicates that its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is understood only with the action that is the object of the instigation (*pravarttanā*). Since the very object of the instigation is the object of the action directed toward it, the relationship between the subject to be addressed (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) is obtained through the constraints of semantic relation (*saṃsarga-maryyādayā*); therefore, the meaning is that there is a pause (*nighāta*) due to their forming a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*). The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) here, however, is as follows: "The knowledge which has me as its agent and going as its object is the object of the instigation directed toward Devadatta, who is the object of the address.
The phrase "according to the manner of the Sūtra, Bhāṣya, etc. means according to the manner stated in the Bhāṣya on the *sūtra* *bhuvādi-samartha*.

The phrase "it may indeed be so" means [it applies] to the word *devadatta* when it is addressed. The intention here is that by supplying the word "know" (*jānīhi*) as a supplement, the aforementioned principle remains intact because the word *devadatta* stays within the same sentence. Regarding this, he cites the agreement of the author of the Sūtras with the words "according to the Sūtra, the Bhāṣya, and so forth," which means according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*.

This agreement concerns both the aspect of being part of the same sentence and the aspect of accentuation (*nighāta*). However, there is no agreement regarding the Bhāṣya [in its entirety], because [the Bhāṣya] rejects the mention of the term *atiṅ* (non-verbal).

[Objection: "In that case, there is no consistency in rejecting the inclusion of *tiṅ* [in the definition of a sentence], because it is necessary there to prevent the occurrence of *nighāta* (elision of accent) in examples such as *pacati bhavati*; for in such cases, there exists a 'unity of sentence' (*ekavākyatva*) consisting in the expression of an action connected with a *kāraka*, which is common to both nominal endings (*sup*) and verbal endings (*tiṅ*). [Reply: This is not so, because the intention is that although the aforementioned unity of sentence exists there, the specific kind of unity of sentence defined by the author of the Vārttika—as consisting in having only one *tiṅ* actually heard—is absent in that instance.

And thus it has been stated: since there is an absence of such syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) in the aforementioned instance, the non-application [of the rule] is certain; therefore, the mention of the finite verb (*tiṅ*)—which indicates the possibility [of its application]—is precisely for the purpose of signaling that the *nighāta* (accentual suppression) must indeed occur. He clarifies this very point with the words "according to the Vārttikakāras," which refers only to them. With the phrase "in reality," he speaks from the perspective of one who adheres strictly to the literal wording of the Sūtra. As Helārāja has stated: "Even when there are many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) that are mutually expectant, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*);
thus, the prohibition of *nighāta* after finite verbs becomes meaningful."

The phrase "at the occasion of the commentary on the *Vākyapadīya*" is to be understood as the ellipsis (*iti śeṣaḥ*). It should be noted that the statement "even in his view, this indeed occurs" is based on the intention that only the status of being a *nirukta* (etymological) or *laukika* (ordinary) sentence serves as the cause for the occurrence of the *nighāta* (tonal suppression).

"Repetition of birth" [is the meaning]. For this very reason, when an action occurs only once, one does not say "he cooks twice. In expressions such as "he eats five times," words like *pañca* (five) refer to the production of the number; the suffixes *kṛtvasuc* and others are merely indicators (*dyotaka*) of that [number]. The sense is that the meaning indicated by those [suffixes] is construed with the action (*kriyā*). This explains why the technical designation applies only to those things that are construed with the action, as seen in the examples beginning with *apādāna*. In some places, the reading is exactly like that; it is clear.

Others, however, maintain that the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) arises from the etymological derivation [of the term] shown in the later commentary (*uttarabhāṣya*) as "that which brings about the action" (*karoti-kriyāṃ nirvarttayati*). For this very reason, in expressions such as "he asks the Brāhmaṇa’s son the way," the Brāhmaṇa does not possess the status of a *kāraka*, because he is rendered superfluous by the son. Consequently, these [participants] are construed with the action. Once it is known that something is a generator of an action, the question "What is that action? would arise; furthermore, since the action itself requires a generator, it is more appropriate for the [participant] to be construed with that very action.

For this very reason, in rules such as *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*, the word *kāraka* is understood to refer to the [specific] grammatical relations (kārakas) such as the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth. However, they say that in the rule *kārake*, the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative (*prathamārthe*). Because it has been stated thus, in the commentary on the example *brāhmaṇavat*, the understanding from the expression *brāhmaṇavad adhīte* is that the study is performed by the same agent as the study whose agent is a Brāhmaṇa; that is, the study is equal to that of a Brāhmaṇa. In that context, since the suffix *vat* prescribed by the rule *tatra tasyeva* conveys a relation with both substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), it was stated in the root text that [the word *brāhmaṇa*] is in the nominative case.

The meaning is that, because of the rule [of interpretation], the word *dhātu* there refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); for otherwise, in the case of "He saw while dwelling" (*vasan dadarśa*), the understanding would be something like "the act of seeing whose agent is the agent of past dwelling."

The word *pratiṣedha* (negation) is derived from the root *sajj* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule of *bāhulaka*. Through the etymological analysis—“that whose nature is an absence (*abhāva*) which has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) that which is brought about (*prasajjya*) or produced (*āpādya*)”—its meaning is that of an absence. The point is that [the opponent’s view] would lead to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because, in cases such as “Do not bring a Brāhmaṇa,” the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with the Brāhmaṇa and so forth through superimposition (*āropa*). The phrase “from the cognition of negation” means “from the cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)”;
thus, the intention is that such a cognition itself serves as the proof for the fact that the aforementioned meaning of the negative particle is construed with the action (*kriyā*).

However, if the referent of "you" (*yuṣmad*) and so forth were construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that [negation], then because there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—defined here as the denoter of the agent expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*)—the use of the second person and so forth would be untenable; furthermore, since the absence whose counter-correlate is the referent of "you" is a single entity, the use of the dual number and so forth would be untenable. To indicate this, it was stated: "not you cook, nor do you two cook. Likewise, if one accepts that the agent of the action is the absence whose counter-correlate is Caitra, then the fact that Caitra is the agent of the cooking would be contradicted.

However, according to your own view, if the meaning [of the verb] were the existence of an activity conducive to cooking (*pākānukūlakṛti*), then since there would be no factor to determine the status of the person (the agent), there would occasionally be the undesirable consequence of the middle or highest person endings. To indicate this, it was stated: "Caitra does not cook. For this very reason—that is, because the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys an absence whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is the action—[the sentence is so constructed].

"Such an application" means an expression of the form "the jar is not being produced. The sense is that during the state when the jar exists, there is an absence of the activity conducive to production having the jar as its agent; however, according to your [opponent's] view, since the jar is non-existent [at the time of production], there is an absence of agency with respect to the activity conducive to production, and thus the aforementioned usage would be untenable. This is the underlying point.

Since it is certain, according to the aforementioned method, that the negative particle (*nañ*) necessarily conveys an absence whose counter-positive is an action, it is appropriate—even if the status of being the agent of the jar's absence is not understood within the meaning of the verbal root in the sentence "the jar does not exist"—to disregard such a cognition and accept the cognition of the absence of the jar's existence; this is because of the force of the causal relationship to be stated hereafter. Thus he says, "And so," and explains that very point with the words beginning "for not... (*nahi*).

[Objection: But in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground," where there is no co-utterance with a word expressing an action (*kriyāvācaka*), how can the negative particle (*nañ*) convey an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is an action? To this, he says: "And thus... [and] "is to be supplied" (*adhyāhāryam*). The sense is that, according to the *Mahābhāṣya*—starting with the rule "*astiḥ bhavantīparaḥ*"—even in the absence of another action, the completion of the sentence is understood by taking the action "to be" (*asti*).

The meaning is as follows: since it has been established—on the basis of examples such as "na tvaṃ pacasi" (you do not cook)—that the cause of a verbal cognition delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhitva*) is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a verbal root, related through the relation of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāsambandha*), with respect to the absence residing in the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) which is itself related to that cognition through the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāratāsambandha*); therefore, for the sake of accounting for the understanding [of the sentence] here as well, the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the verb "is" (*asti*) is necessary.
