Now, if it is accepted that the absence which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) holds primacy in a sentence-meaning cognition, then one must likewise accept that the absence consisting of the exclusion (*bhedātmaka-abhāva*) of that object also holds primacy, since there is no difference in their status as absences. And if this were so, then in forms such as *asarvasmai*, the grammatical operations triggered by its being a pronoun—such as the replacement with *smāy*—would be untenable, just as they are in *atisarvāya*.

Because from the word *asarva* there arises the cognition "distinct from all," the referent of the word *sarva* is subordinate (*upasarjana*) with respect to the aspect of difference; and since a technical name (*saṃjñā*) has been established [for the group beginning with *sarva*], those whose meanings are subordinate to a technical name are excluded from the group beginning with *sarva*. Furthermore, in rules such as *anekam anyapadārthe*, the use of the singular number after the word *aneka* would be untenable; therefore, he says: "The remainder... (*śeṣam*).

Indeed, just as in cases such as "nanu tvam pacasi" (surely you are cooking), since it is accepted here too that the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as an indicator of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is no inconsistency regarding the person (*puruṣa*) because there is no contradiction in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the referent of *yuṣmad* and that which is different from it. Furthermore, since number (*saṅkhyā*) is not contradicted therein, there is no inconsistency regarding the dual number either. However, since such a causal relationship [between the indicator and the indicated] lacks any basis in authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), how can compliance with it serve as a regulator for the necessary ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*)?

In cases such as "the pot is not produced," where the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), we shall explain later how there is no inconsistency. Thus, in instances such as "there is no pot on the ground," there is no obstacle to the cognition that "there is an absence of a pot residing on the ground"; therefore, he says "the rest" (*śeṣam*). Consequently, when the cooking is not performed by an agent distinct from the referent of the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*), there is no undesired consequence (anāpatti) regarding the usage "you do not cook."

In the view that [the particle *nañ*] indicates exclusion (*paryudāsa*), one must therefore accept that its meaning is indeed a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); thus, by the reasoning already stated, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is necessary—this is the meaning of the remaining words. The Nyāya position on this matter will also become clear in the very same context, specifically during the commentary on the verse: "Whether it be the qualifier or the qualified, let it be determined according to logic," under the heading "An Investigation into the Meaning of *Nañ*. This is the remainder of the sense.

The meaning is as follows: it will be stated that in the rule *etattadoḥ*, by the inclusion of the term *anañ-samāsa* (non-negative compound), it is indicated that even those words listed in the *gaṇa* which express meanings that have become subordinate (*upasarjana*) within a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) still possess the status of being members of the *sarvādi* group; thus, there is no inconsistency in what was previously mentioned.

Likewise, in the case of *aneka* in the phrase *anekam anya*, the singular ending is used in accordance with the word *sup* (which expresses the suffixes) acting as the substantive; and in examples such as *sevyate 'nekayā*, the singular is used because it conveys the understanding that the service is performed toward each individual woman. Therefore, there is no inconsistency in that either; this is what will be stated.

The meaning of "tadyoga" (connection with that) is "connection with the action" (*kriyānvaya*), because it results in the attainment of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). This is the underlying intention: by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*, the seventh case (*saptamī*) is prescribed after a word denoting the substratum of an action that indicates another action. Because the term "bhāvalakṣaṇam" (the indication of an action) is employed, the meaning of the seventh case—in the form of being an indicator—must connect specifically with the action. Therefore, in examples such as *goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ* ("He went while the cows were being milked"), one understands that the time which is the locus of the act of milking serves to delimit the act of going.

The meaning is that the entire preceding sūtra applies there as well. Thus, when disregard (*anādara*) is implied, the sense is that the sixth and seventh case endings prescribed by that [sūtra] are grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) only when used in connection with a verb, provided they denote that which possesses an action which serves to indicate another action. Now, one might object: even in the absence of a connection to an action for the aforementioned [words], their grammatical correctness in the form of "capacity" (*śaktatva*) is easily obtained; therefore, he says, "its nature" (*tatsvarūpam*), meaning the nature of grammatical correctness.
The phrase "will be stated" implies that this will occur at the occasion of defining grammatical correctness.

The meaning is that correctness (*sādhutva*) is not the capacity [to convey meaning], because comprehension arises even from corrupt words (*apaśabda*); rather, as will be stated, it is a genus delimited by the productivity of merit (*puṇya*), which is manifested solely by grammar. And in the present context, since that [correctness] is manifested by grammar only in those [words] connected with an action, the implication is that anything other than that is simply incorrect (*asādhutā*).

[Objection: "Is it not true that by the root text stating 'let [the suffixes] be restricted solely to action,' their grammatical correctness (sādhutva) is obtained only when they are construed with an action? Indeed, this is so; nevertheless, since the word 'action' (kriyāpada) is used in the Bhāṣya even for the result (phala), their grammatical correctness is justified even through construction with the result of the meaning of the word 'action,' whether directly or indirectly. Therefore, the aforementioned method does not prove that a verbal root denotes an operation (vyāpāra). Anticipating this doubt, he reveals the intended meaning with the words "The point is as follows" (ayam bhāvaḥ). He says "generally by the word 'action'"; thus, the abundance of usage is the cause for the existence of a conventional sense (rūḍhi). This is the meaning.

"Conventional" (*sāṅketikī*) means that which is manifested by convention; the meaning is "established usage. The reason for this is stated as "occurring only in certain instances. Regarding that, he states the restrictive factor: "it is etymological" (*yaugika*), because it is derived through the sense of "being produced by an operation" (*vyāpāreṇa niṣpadyate*); such is the intention. "Without regard" (*anapekṣya*) means without taking into account the powers of the stem and the suffix. "Precisely for this reason" (*ata eva*) means precisely because the name-word (*saṃjñāśabda*) is stronger due to its independence in application.

"In the ninth" means in the ninth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā; thus it is said: for regarding the *rathantara*, there is a scriptural injunction, "One sings that which is in the *yoni* on the two following verses. In this regard, since the *bṛhat*-yoni is recited after the *rathantara*-yoni, should the *rathantara* be sung upon the latter? Or, because "na tvā vā manyate" is recited in the subsequent section (*uttaragrantha*), should it be sung there? When this doubt arises, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it should be sung in both places due to the lack of distinction. [The Siddhāntin replies: In the subsequent section, the word "uttara" functions as a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

It is well known that in the *Bṛhadyoni*, because the word "Uttarā" is stronger—due to its being etymological (*yaugika*) and its application being independent of prior texts, as it follows from the force of being subsequent to them—it was determined in the ninth [book] that the fear [of contradiction] applies only to those verses beginning with "na tvā vā manyate," and the sense here is that it is the same in this case as well.

Now, one might object: "Is there not firm evidence for the claim that the verbal root has a conventional (*sāṅketikī*) power with respect to the act of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), whereas its usage with respect to the fruit is etymological (*yaugika*), such that the introduction of the aforementioned topical discussion would be possible? For [the word 'sacrifice'] can generally be explained as being etymological as well. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

The meaning is that "tathābhūtāni" (being such) refers to qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇas*). The intention is that this is observed in cases where an agent is expressed by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Regarding the phrase "guṇānām" (of qualities): because qualifiers are for the sake of another—that is, because they assist others—and precisely because of this equality, which is their common characteristic (*samānadharmatva*), there can be no mutual relationship between them; such is the meaning of the logical principle (*nyāya*).

And thus, just as the factors of action (*kāraka*) are construed with the qualified productive activity (*bhāvanā*) because they assist the result, so too do the *kārakas* themselves—whether directly or indirectly—construe with that very [activity]; otherwise, their very status as *kārakas* would be untenable. The point is that they do not construe with the result, because [the result] lacks expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*). He also sets forth a common worldly maxim in support of this: "For a beggar... and so forth.

The form *anviyanti* [is derived from] *vīganti*, where the prefix *pra-* is elided. The phrase "the Mīmāṃsakas also" implies that, according to the aforementioned reasoning, they have established that the presence of the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) generated by the verbal root is the cause for a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the *kāraka* (participant in action). The expression "kāraka, etc. includes time, which is the meaning of the suffixes such as *laṭ*. The term "subsidiary" (*guṇabhūta*) means being a qualifier of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffixes such as *-tṛc*. By this, it is shown that the previously stated reasoning does not apply there.

"In that very [context]" means "in the bhāvanā which is the meaning of the verbal root. It has been explained at length that there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the *kārakas* with the objective portion (*phalāṃśa*), because even in the Mīmāṃsā school, such a connection is unestablished; for it has been stated therein that since a *kāraka* cannot be connected to another *kāraka*, the sacrifice—which is the form of the result—cannot be connected to the action as an object (*karman*).

The meaning of "because it is not observed" (*adarśanāt*) is that, according to the maxim "for every sentence is completed by an action," one does not observe there a lack of expectancy for syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha-nirākāṅkṣatva*) in the absence of an action such as "exists" (*asti*) or "knows" (*jānāti*). In that case, a sentence such as "Caitra is handsome" (*caitraḥ sundaraḥ*), which is expectant of an action, would result in being ungrammatical (*asādhutā*).

The dissatisfaction that the [meaning] is established merely by the connection with a portion of the fruit (*phalāṃśa*), and thus the status of being the denoter of *bhāvanā* is not obtained, is indicated by the phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*). The meaning is as follows: having stated the argument in favor of the connection of the aforementioned eight [factors] with *bhāvanā*, he now states the argument against it, which consists in the presentation of subverting reasons (*bādhaka*). In the reading "the argument himself" (*svayamupapattim*), the word "himself" (*svayam*) indicates that the reasoning to be stated next is not based on any external source.

Now, if it is argued that since words ending in vocatives and the like are grammatically correct only when they are construed with a verb, how can there be a connection of the similarity—which is the meaning of the suffix *vat*—with the mountain in examples such as "The mountain possesses fire, like a kitchen"? Or how is it that in the case of "There is no pot on the ground," the locative sense of being located on the ground connects with the negation (*nañ*) denoting absence? To this, the author of the *Mūla* says: "If [the relation] were also in the subject (*pakṣe*). Here, "subject" refers to the locus (*dharmin*)—such as a mountain—which is the qualificand of the cognition produced by the thesis-statement and in which the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is doubted; "kāraka" refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth.

The meaning is: "in the case of *nañ* and so forth," [it refers to] the absence of the meaning of *nañ*, and in the case of the meaning of other nouns. He clarifies this very point in the *Sāra* with the words "the mountain possesses fire" and so on; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in *nañ* and so forth" (*nañādiṣu*), the meaning is "by the word 'and so forth'. He explains that very point further with the words "in such cases as these," which means "in cases such as 'a pot on the ground' and so on."

The meaning is that the cognition [of similarity] occurs as "the mountain is similar to the kitchen," or "the jar is absent from the ground," or "there is an absence of the jar on the ground. By the grammatical rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.115), the suffix *vati* conveys similarity residing in the action; and by the rule *kārake* (Pāṇini 1.4.23) governing the seventh case (*saptamī*) in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it is understood that the seventh case is grammatically correct only when it relates to an action. Therefore, it was stated [in the commentary], "if... (*yadi*).

The meaning is that you must abandon your own established tenet according to which: regarding the dative case in the phrase *puṣpebhyaḥ* (in the rule *caturthyāḥ*), the dative prescribed by the rule *spṛherīpsitaḥ* (*Pāṇini 1.4.36*) conveys its own meaning only when construed with the object expressed by the verb *spṛhayati* itself, and not with an object expressed by another word or one supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*), because such a construction would contradict the grammatical injunction.

The term *arddhajaratīyam* is formed by adding the suffix *cha* (which functions as *-ya*) according to the rule for words beginning with *gaha* (Pāṇini 5.2.107). Its meaning is "resembling a half-old woman"—that is, following the grammatical rule in some instances and not in others. Thus, out of fear of the contradiction consisting in the abandonment of one's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), even in this case the proposition (*pratijñā*) must be accepted as "the mountain ought to possess fire," and not as one devoid of a word expressing an action; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the aforementioned rule. As for what should be said regarding cases such as "there is no jar on the ground," that has already been stated.

And it will be stated [later] that "more than this" is the sense; in the expression *kṛtapūrvī*, the state (*bhāva*) denoted by the suffix *kta* (which is prescribed for expressing a state) refers to the state of having attained a dwelling (*siddhāvasathāpanna*). With the intention that the action expressed by the root-meaning is the qualifier of that [state], he introduces the root-text with the words "In this way," etc. By the phrase "in the agent, etc.," the inclusion of the state (*bhāva*) is intended; by the phrase "of the suffixes *ktvā*, *tumun*, etc.," the suffixes themselves are meant. "It is connected" means that, as previously stated, the presence of the verbal activity (*bhāvanā*) produced by the verbal root serves as the cause for its being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in relation to the cognition of the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth.

Regarding the expression *kṛtaḥ pūrvaṃ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made previously"), since the suffix *kta* here denotes the object (*karman*), the use of the accusative case after the word *kaṭa*—which falls under the rule governing "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) objects—is untenable; for a *kta* suffix denoting the action itself (*bhāva*) is as rare as a flower in the sky when used with a transitive verb, due to the restrictive rule *tayoreva* (Pāṇini 3.4.69). For this very reason, it cannot be a *kta* suffix denoting the neuter action (*napuṃsake bhāve*) either.

If it is asked how, in that case, the aforementioned statement regarding the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*) is justified, they say here: because the action (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed in its specific form beforehand, the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*); thus, when the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), the resulting form is compounded with the word *pūrva*, and by the rule "sapūrvācca," the suffix *ini* is added. It should be understood that such intentions and non-intentions of expression apply only to cases like *kṛtapūrvi* and so forth, as established by the authority of the Bhāṣya, and not to other instances.

The phrase "by means of *in* and so forth" means "by means of those [suffixes] whose meaning is the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. In reality, however, in the case of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), it should be explained that the action, which is subordinate to another meaning—whether that other meaning is the sense of the suffix whose base (*prakṛti*) expresses itself, or something else—is [connected] with objects such as the mat (*kaṭa*) and so forth. Therefore, there is no inconsistency with the present subject matter regarding the agent of the sense of *in* being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) within the usage *kṛtapūrvī*, because from that [usage] one understands "an agent of an action performed at a previous time," and such an action is subordinate to the agent who is the sense of *in*.

Nor can this [suffix] have *bhāva* (the action itself) as its governing referent, because it is not employed independently. Furthermore, it is not the case that from the analysis (*vigraha*) "this has previously been done by him," the resulting cognition has the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as its primary qualificand; for if that were so, it would follow that the suffix lacks a *vigraha*, which would contradict the fundamental rule. This is because, when a suffix follows a verbal root that merely restates the meaning of the root, it is the action denoted by the root—which does not serve as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix—that is perceived; thus, it is more appropriate that the agent, who is enjoined by that suffix, should be the primary qualificand. Otherwise, it would result in the suffix being subordinate (*anupasarjana*), just as in the case of *pacatikalpam*.

For this very reason, the grammatical usage in such expressions as "he has gone to eat" (*bhoktum gataḥ*) is justified; because a suffix prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*) that does not denote an agent merely restates the meaning of the verbal root, and since the action denoted by that root is by nature purely in the state of being accomplished (*sādhyamātra-svabhāvatva*), and because it lacks [the quality of] being a subordinate attribute (*aguṇatva*). Likewise, although it is stated that "kṛt suffixes used with indeclinables denote the abstract state," there is an experienced difference between the meaning of the *ghañ* suffix in usages such as "cooking" (*pākaḥ*) and the meaning of suffixes like *tumun*; therefore, suffixes such as *tumun* also have as their meaning the abstract state of being purely in the process of accomplishment. This is explained in detail elsewhere.

In the phrase "in mere *vṛtti*," the word "mere" (*mātra*) has the sense of "entirety. The reason given is "because it will be stated later," which refers to the passage beginning with "in a compound, indeed, [the meaning] is distinct," etc.; the intention is that in that context, the word "compound" (*samāsa*) will be explained as referring to *vṛtti* in general. As for the question "how [is this so]?", the intention is that in examples such as *gataḥ* ("gone"), since there exists a *kṛt*-derived *vṛtti*, it is impossible for the object to be construed with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) which is a constituent part of the referent of the word *gata*—namely, the agent of the act of going—and thus the illustrative example is unestablished.

In cases where there is a constant requirement for a relation (*nityasāpekṣasthala*), there are two positions. Regarding the example "Caitra’s teacher’s house" (*caitrasya gurukulam*), one position is that the qualifier, such as Caitra, is construed with the qualified object, such as the house, through a relation mediated by the teacher (*guru*). This has been stated by Hari:

"For those [words] whose connection is with a whole, such as 'the teacher’s house' (*gurukula*), they are joined with that which possesses it [the whole] after having touched its parts. This is the first position.

In the case mentioned, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a relation defined by the whole (*samudāya*); and since the relation with the whole is mediated through its parts, it follows by implication that the qualifier touches upon the part as well—this is the meaning [of the rule]. Another view, however, holds that the genitive in "Devadattasya" denotes a relation defined specifically by the teacher (*guru*) and so forth, and its connection occurs only there. And it has been said: "All words denoting a relative (*sambandhi*) are always compounded when they are dependent;
for that mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), which exists in the sentence, is not lost even in the compound."*1* *1 This verse is traditionally attributed to Bhartṛhari.*

The word *nityam* (always) connects with the meaning of the term *sāpekṣa* (dependent). For the meaning of the verse is this: since that mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) which exists in separate expressions such as "the teacher of Devadatta" or "the family of the teacher" is not lost even in a compound, the rule applies. The linguistic maxim (*vyutpatti*) that "a word-meaning connects with another word-meaning" has as its scope cases other than those of constant dependence (*nityasāpekṣa*). This is the intended sense. With reference to the last of these positions, he provides the resolution: "In the case of those that are constantly dependent... (*nityasāpekṣeṣu*).

The point is as follows: since properties such as "heaviness" (*gurutva*) are invariably determined by another correlate, when that [property] is presented, there necessarily arises an expectancy for its correlate (*nirūpakākāṅkṣā*). Just as in the case of the word-meaning of "Devadatta" and so forth, this expectancy must be satisfied; likewise, in the present case, there is an expectancy for the means (*sādhana*)—namely, "what is the goal (*sādhya*) consisting of the act of going?"—and for the sake of satisfying this, the connection with an objective factor (*karmakāraka*) such as "the village" is necessary. Therefore, there is no lack of consistency with the example. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as "his leaves were cut off by arrows" (*śaraiḥ śātitapatraḥ*) are included.

He clarifies what is to be understood by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the introductory phrase "In this way, in cases such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ*": here too, what is included by the word "etc. is *bhuktvā pākaḥ*. The meaning is that one should understand that in the action denoted by the root *pac-* (to cook), which has become subordinate to the state (*bhāva*) expressed by the suffix *ghañ*, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the action of eating and so forth, which is the meaning of the suffixes such as *tumun*. In instances involving forms ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes, an action characterized by the states of being non-existent (*asattva*) and existent (*sattva*), brought about through the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), is denoted.

In that context, because it serves as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the action denoted by the *ghañ* and other such suffixes possesses primacy. For this very reason, the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*) is possible by taking up that action whose nature consists solely of what is to be accomplished (*sādhyamāna*) through the root-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). Although the suffix *ṇvul* might be possible when there is a subordinate word (*upapada*) consisting of an action characterized by the aforementioned properties, the point is that expressions such as "the agent has gone" (*kārako gataḥ*) are simply not used.

The modern grammarians (*navya*), however, argue that because the rule prescribing the *tumun* suffix states "when [another] action is for the sake of an action," proximity (*pratyāsatti*) yields the understanding that the two actions must be of the same kind; consequently, since the meaning of the suffix whose stem does not denote itself cannot lack the nature of being merely something to be accomplished (*sādhyamātra-svabhāvatva*), and because there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified between those two—the meanings of the stem and the suffix—it follows that [the suffix is not used]. This has been indicated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *upapadam atiṅ*.

However, where there is a mention of that which signifies merely an action, there it is said that [the suffix is used] even from a word denoting merely an action; thus, *suktvā* and so forth are used even in connection with *gata-pāka* and the like.

Their intention is as follows: in instances involving suffixes such as *ghan*, both a positive and a negative action—characterized respectively by existence and non-existence and standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified—are presented by the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). Among these, the action denoted by the suffix is primary. Thus, although the action presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses the nature of being merely something to be accomplished (*sādhyamātra*), because it is subordinate with respect to the meaning of the *ghan* suffix, suffixes such as *tumun* do not apply there.

In this regard, the following must be considered: because the suffix *tumun* would be unavoidable when joined with a word ending in a suffix that does not take the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as its governing factor (*adhikārīya*), [the definition of *kṛt* must include such a restriction]. Furthermore, even in the rule prescribing the suffix *suC*, it is necessary to understand that suffix as being qualified by the aforementioned characteristics. For since the action that serves as each respective qualifier has the nature of a mere process toward completion (*sādhyamātra-svabhāvatva*), if one were to express its production, the occurrence of *suC* in the expression "two cookings" (*dvau pākau*) could not be prevented. Nor can one accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because the employment of the word for action (*kriyāpada*) would be redundant; as will be explained later, the action is already obtained through the force of the word "repetition" (*abhyāvṛtti*) itself.

Furthermore, on the occasion of commenting on the verse of Hari, "In that [context], the action is [present] as the thing to be accomplished" (*sādhyatvena kriyā tatra*), there is a contradiction with his own statement: namely, that just as a single person appears as a teacher or a maternal uncle due to a difference in relations, so too a single action appears due to a difference in its expressive relata in the form of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*); thus, he accepts the non-comprehension of two actions.

"An over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)" means that, according to one's own view, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying suffixes with the sense of *kṛtvas* (times) by taking a subordinate action (*guṇībhūtakriyā*). "Between two actions" (*kriyayoḥ pūrvakāle*) means from a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting an action occurring at a time prior to the interval between two actions. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "the suffixes *tumun* etc.," suffixes such as *ktvā* are included. Regarding "being prescribed," since it is stated that "suffixes added to an indeclinable denote the abstract state" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*), the word "abstract state" (*bhāva*) is to be supplied as the remainder; for it will be explained later that properties such as being the object of reference for a prior time appear [in the cognition] as relations (*saṃsarga*).

By the phrase "repetition" (*dvirvacana*) and so forth, the inclusion of double usage, double arrival, and so on is intended; the sense is that in those cases, the suffix *lyuṭ* or *ghañ* is observed when the action has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*).

"But [this leads to] an over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*) means that there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of such usage as "simultaneous cooking" (*sakṛtpāka*). "Because of non-denotation" (*anabhidhānāt*) means because it is not employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). "Of that very [action]" (*tasyā eva*) means of the action itself, which consists of a collection of parts arranged in a temporal sequence of before and after. By the word "only" (*eva*), substances and qualities are excluded, since those two arise only once. The point is that for an action, even a single one, repetition is possible at its occurrence, because it is admitted that an action characterized by distinct cessations (*nivṛtti-bheda*) is what is denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*).
"By implication" (sāmarthyāt) means by the force of employing the word "repetition" (abhyāvṛtti). And "implication" (sāmarthya) consists in its having the sense of implying that [repetition].

Although the status [of being the object] remains intact for that [action] when it is presented by a verbal root as "mere thing to be accomplished" (*sādhyamātra*), there is nevertheless no fault; for the word *sādhyamātrasvabhāva* refers to "mere thing to be accomplished" as a subordinate element of the aforementioned suffixal meaning, according to the reasoning previously stated. "Such" (*tādṛśī*) means "of the aforementioned form as presented by the suffix *ghañ*. "By etymological derivation" (*vyutpattyā*) means "because of the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya, who is intent on providing an explanation. "Indicative proof" (*jñāpakam*) means "in the form of the usage by the author of the Sūtra."

The sense is that it is like the expression "those who have already slept are sleeping. The phrase "they say" implies "the graspers of the essence" (sāragrāhiṇaḥ) as the ellipsis; by repeating "they say," a lack of full satisfaction (asvarasa) is indicated. The reason for this is that even if the word *krayāpada* were intended to convey the stated meaning, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would not be avoided; therefore, it is more appropriate to regard it as being solely for the sake of clear comprehension.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), it is held that it is improper to justify well-known worldly usages such as *dvirvacana* (reduplication) by following technical *jñāpaka*s (indicatory marks), when their occurrence can be prevented simply by not resorting to such denotations. The meaning is this: the power (*śakti*) in the form of denotative capacity (*bodhakatā*), which is established by the statement "of the senses toward their respective objects" and so forth, remains entirely uncontradicted even in the case of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); for it is from this that the cognition of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) arises. Regarding the phrase "concerned with correctness" (*sādhutvapareti*): thus says Hari— "This very tradition of Grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) has as its purpose the knowledge of correctness (*sādhutva*)."

In that context, "in the knowledge of correct words" means by way of being a delimitant (*avacchedakatayā*), that is, as the delimitant of the capacity to produce understanding residing in the knowledge of correct words. "Even in the theory of a distinct denotative power (*śakti*)" means that correctness (*sādhutva*) is not the possession of denotative power (*śaktatva*), because even incorrect words produce understanding; rather, it is the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*), as will be explained later—this is the sense even in the Siddhānta view.

The meaning is that there would indeed be ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) regarding the productive drive (*bhāvanā*); for even when the *bhāvanā* is understood through a misconception of the expressive power (*śakti*) derived from a verbal suffix, its ungrammaticality in that context would still necessarily follow. Accordingly, the Author of the Bhāṣya stated in the *Paspaśā* section: "When the relationship between word and meaning is established," [the rule] "one should speak with correct words (*sādhu*), not with incorrect ones (*asādhu*), constitutes a restriction (*niyama*), just as in the case of 'one should go' (*gamyeta*) versus 'one should go' (*gamayet*)."

And thus, when a particular sequence of phonemes is accepted by any one of the authors of the grammatical sūtras as being the cause for the cognition of a particular qualificand endowed with particular qualifiers, that word possessing such a sequence is correct (sādhu) in that specific cognition and not elsewhere. For this very reason, it is consistent that the word *asva* is not correct when referring to a horse, but is correct when referring to one who possesses no wealth (*niḥsve*); and the word *aśva* is not correct when referring to one who possesses no wealth, but is correct when referring to a horse (*turaga*).

To the objection that this might be incorrect, he says, "And thus," by means of the phrase "in the sacrificial rite. This indicates that because such scriptural injunctions as "One should not speak untruth, nor corrupt speech" are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of a sacrifice, there is no sin in using [corrupt forms] elsewhere. The sense is that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is not taught by the authors of the Sūtras and others as denoting the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), since they teach it solely as denoting the agent (*kartṛ*).

The Mīmāṃsaka raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but surely). "In your view" means in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). Regarding the statement "one should not speak untruth," which is heard in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there arises a doubt: is this prohibition for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), or is it for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)? In resolving this, since the agent is understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in the word "vaded" (should speak), it is determined that [the suffix] denotes the agent; furthermore, this is established by the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ," which shows that the suffix *la* has the sense of the agent.

Since speaking is primary as the object of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*), speaking is first of all for the sake of the person; therefore, the prohibition is also for the sake of the person. This is because the word "one should speak" (*vadet*), by restating the act of speaking as the counter-positive of the prohibition, conveys it precisely as being for the sake of the person. Furthermore, since the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys that such speaking—namely, speaking untruth—is a means to an undesirable end by indicating its contrary nature, and since no other kind of speaking untruth is present [in the cognition], [the prohibition applies only to that].

For this very reason, it is parsimonious (*lāghava*) to hold that this same [Vedic] source also serves as the basis for the prohibition of speaking found in the *Smṛtis* which is taught outside of a specific ritual context (*anārabhyādhīta*). Otherwise, one would incur the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) by having to postulate another, separate prohibition pertaining to human ends (*puruṣārtha*) as its source. Thus, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), according to the maxim "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise," the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) alone is the denotation of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), while the agent (*kartṛ*), being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) with the efficient force denoted by the suffix, is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) and therefore possesses no expressive power (*śakti*) in that regard.

The traditional rule (smṛti) beginning with "laḥ karmaṇi" etc., being in syntactic agreement with the rule "dvayekayoḥ," is intended solely to express that number. Furthermore, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks," grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with "the cow is white" is established only through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā); thus, the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) does not denote the agent. Consequently, since the agent is not presented by direct audition (śruti), he does not serve the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha); rather, it has been determined in the *Kartradhikaraṇa* that he serves the purpose of the ritual (kratvartha) based on context (prakaraṇa).

He restates that established prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "by the verb" means by the *tiṅ*-suffix; "and that" refers to the context (*prakaraṇa*); "contradiction with scripture" means opposition to the nature of scripture which is independent [of other means of knowledge].

For instance, there are six means of application (*viniyojaka*) here: direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*). When these come into conflict regarding a single object, since their simultaneous application (*samuccaya*) is impossible, it must be stated that one of them conveys the meaning while the other does not. And since that [non-application] occurs when the weak is set aside by the strong, the great sage Jaimini, in response to the inquiry as to which possesses weakness, composed the aphorism: "In the case of a collision among direct assertion, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding, because of the remoteness of the purpose."

Regarding the "relative weakness" (*pāradaurbalya*) when there is a "conjunction" (*samavāya*), that is, a simultaneous occurrence in one place of the [means of proof] beginning with direct audition (*śruti*): *para* means "subsequent," i.e., that which is recited later. Thus, the meaning is that among these, whichever is subsequent in relation to another is the weaker.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "due to the remoteness from the purpose" (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). This means due to the remoteness of the purpose—that is, the applicator such as *liṅga* (indicative power) and so forth—because they occur later; that is to say, because their status as applicators is understood with a delay relative to the preceding [means]. In this regard, the examples for *śruti* (direct assertion) and the others are as follows: "Direct assertion is an independent utterance. Independence (*nirapekṣatva*) consists in having a validity that does not depend on the validity of other [means of proof], as in the case of: "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*).

In this context, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)—expressing that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in being the recipient of a result produced by an action—establishes that the rice grains (*vrīhīṇām*) are subordinate to the act of threshing (*avaghāta*), independently of anything else. Indicative power (*liṅga*) is the capacity to illuminate a specific meaning; for example, in the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*), its application (*viniyoga*) is to the act of cutting because it illuminates the meaning of that act. A sentence (*vākya*) consists of words that, through mutual expectancy, culminate in a single unified meaning.

For example: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of Aśvin, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer thee, acceptable to Agni. Here, by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the portion whose meaning is directly connected to the act of offering (*nirvāpa*) is employed; and by virtue of its syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the portion beginning with "at the impulse of the god Savitṛ" is also applied to that very same act. When words have attained the status of a sentence, their connection with another sentence—driven by the necessity for another function—is what constitutes *prakaraṇa* (context), which is defined as the culmination of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

For example: "He offers the fuel-sticks" (*samidho yajati*). In this case, regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, because of its reading within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it serves as a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*) to fulfill the requirement of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*). This is the order of position (*sthāna-krama*). And that [position] consists in the recitation in close proximity (*sannidhi-viśeṣa*) to multiple [mantras] that have been transmitted. For instance, in the mantra "Thou art curd" (*dadhyasi*), the *āgneya*, *upāṃśu*, and *agnīṣomīya* sacrifices are recited in sequence. Among those, the application (*viniyoga*) of the two—the *āgneya* and the *agnīṣomīya*—is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone.

In the case of the mantra *dadhi ras*, however, there is no application based on gender (*liṅga*) or other such factors; rather, because this mantra is recited in the same section where the Brāhmaṇa prescribes the Upāṃśuyāja, its application is through the Upāṃśuyāja-anumantraṇa by virtue of the power of the sequence (*krama*), which is the strength of the connection with the name (*samākhyā*). For instance, in the case of "the office of the Hotṛ" (*hautra*) or "the office of the Udgātṛ" (*audgātra*), and so forth—since these are the duties of the Hotṛ, etc., by the force of the etymological connection (*yoga*) that "this is the *hautra* of the Hotṛ"—the rites designated by names such as *hautra* are to be performed by the Hotṛ and others.

Examples of conflict (*virodha*) and so forth are as follows: when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the direct statement is stronger, while the indicative mark is weaker because of its remoteness from the purpose. For example, regarding the verse beginning with *kadācana starīrasi*, there is a direct statement (*śruti*) enjoining it: "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī [verse]. From the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, its capacity to manifest Indra—it appears that this verse is enjoined for the worship of Indra, since it is impossible to enjoin elsewhere that which does not manifest [that deity]. However, by the direct statement, it is understood to be for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire.

The accusative case in *gārhapatyam* indicates that the primary meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is subordinate (*śeṣitva*) with respect to some action, because it signifies the state of being the recipient of the desired fruit produced by that action. Similarly, the instrumental case in *aindryā* indicates that the primary meaning of its base is subordinate with respect to an action, because it signifies the status of being the most effective instrument (*karaṇatva*) toward that action. Thus, there is a contradiction between these two.

In this regard, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Scripture (*śruti*) effects application only by depending upon the knowledge of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). Indeed, even a thousand scriptural injunctions are not capable of applying what lacks capacity; therefore, because the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger, this [mantra] is applied to the worship of Indra. In accordance with that, the accusative case-ending must be explained as having the sense of the locative: "Indra is to be worshipped by means of this [mantra] in the vicinity of the Gārhapatya fire. This is the final conclusion.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) requires its own inherent capacity (*svarūpasat-sāmarthya*), but not even the knowledge of that capacity; for if it did, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would become stronger. Since the application (*viniyoga*) of that [statement] occurs only when it already exists, its cognition arises subsequently through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*). The indicative mark (*liṅga*), on the other hand, depends upon direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) for its application. For from the indicative mark, one does not naturally understand by itself that "Indra is to be invoked here," but rather only that "Indra is such-and-such."

And thus, on the strength of the context (*prakaraṇa*), because it is otherwise inexplicable that a verse capable of manifesting Indra [is used], the indicative power (*liṅga*) would lead one to postulate a direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) stating, "Indra is to be approached by means of this [verse]," through which the application (*viniyoga*) would occur. Therefore, while the indicative power is still engaged in the process of postulating such a scriptural injunction, the application is already established by the directly perceived scriptural injunction; since the context has thus become devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), by what inexplicability could a scriptural injunction be postulated?

Therefore, because direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, when its capacity is interpreted in accordance with it, it is determined that the word "Indra" has the *gārhapatya* fire as its intended meaning, by virtue of denoting the locus of supreme sovereignty. An example of the conflict between direct statement and context (*prakaraṇa*) is as follows: regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice for one desiring stability, the direct statement—"One desiring stability should recite twenty-one [verses]"—establishes that the twenty-one recitations of the *sāmidhenī* verses are subsidiary to that [sacrifice]. Consequently, since the requirement is satisfied, the context—which would otherwise establish the fifteen *sāmidhenī* recitations as subsidiary—is sublated.

Other examples of conflict (*virodha*) should be understood from other sources; they are not elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity. Thus, the distilled meaning is as follows: Scripture (*śruti*) is stronger than all else because it is independent. As for indicative mark (*liṅga*), however, it is stronger than sentence (*vākya*)—which is separated by two [steps]—because it is separated by only one [step] in the matter of application (*viniyoga*). The same should be inferred for the others as well. But name (*samākhyā*), being separated by five [steps], is the weakest of all. Therefore, in the present case, the sentence must be inferred through the context (*prakaraṇa*), which is satisfied by the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

By that [indirect indication], there is the indicative power (*liṅga*); by the indicative power, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*); and by that [statement], the application of the prohibition against speaking untruth to the sacrifice. As long as the context (*prakaraṇa*) has its function initiated for the purpose of constructing a syntactical connection (*vākya*), so long as the application of that [prohibition] to the person is established by the direct Vedic statement of the verb—which is perceived to have the agent as its sole meaning—it follows that even a constructed syntactical connection and the rest are of no consequence; thus, in case of conflict with the direct statement, they are sublated. This is the meaning, the sense being that the indicative power and the others are weaker than the direct statement according to the manner described.

He explains [the intention]: "The meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), however, is a qualifier. Thus, although the agent is presented by the hearing of the verb (*ākhyāta-śruti*), he does not appear as primary like the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), such that one might suspect the prohibition has the person as its purpose; rather, he appears solely as a qualifier. And since that which is presented in such a way has no further expectancy for other qualifiers, there is no connection of the agent with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) through direct audition (*śruti*); therefore, there is no sublation of the context (*prakaraṇa*) by direct audition here. With this intention, he clarifies [the point] with the words "as his own limb," which means "as his own qualifier."

[Objection: In that case, the prohibition would never have the status of a scriptural human goal (*śrauta-puruṣārthatā*), because even in the case of "One should not eat *kalañja*," the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected to the agent according to the aforementioned method, and thus it is [only] scriptural. [Response: If it is argued that—even though the agent is not primary—the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) residing in the agent is primary; therefore, when that [force] connects with the meaning of the negative particle, the agent denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) also connects through that medium, and thus there is no inconsistency in its being a scriptural human goal—then the same applies to the present case as well. To this, he says: "Or let it be so. (*astu vā*)

Regarding the performance [of the rite], one must not say "this is not so" (i.e., it is not the case that the prohibition "one shall not speak untruth" is a duty of the person connected to the sacrifice). For if it were a duty of the person connected to the sacrifice (*kratuyuktapūruṣadharma*), then because the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the primary [agent], the avoidance of speaking untruth would apply only to the principal agent. On the other hand, if it were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then since it does not depend on a specific agent, the avoidance would be established for both the sacrificer engaged in the sacrifice and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Thus, one might ask how this distinction is made. It is explained by the fact that, through both direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), there arises the understanding that the absence of speaking untruth has as its agent the person who is connected to the sacrifice.

This is because the intended meaning of one who says "connected with the sacrifice" (kratuyuktā) is that there is no evidence for the cognition [of the word] as having the performer of the sacrifice as its denotation.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "While yawning," and so forth. This mantra-injunction is heard within the very context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice: "One who is yawning should recite: 'In me, may skill and wisdom [dwell]'. Here, a doubt arises as to whether this mantra-injunction is a duty for the person in general (*śuddhapuruṣadharma*), or rather a subsidiary element of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) by way of being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the person engaged in the sacrifice. In this regard, based on the syntactical connection (*vākya*), this is understood as a duty for the person yawning, because the suffix *śānac* (the present middle participle) expresses the agent.

However, by virtue of the *prakaraṇa* (context), [the act] is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice; and since *prakaraṇa* is weaker than *vākya* (syntactical connection), it is more appropriate that this is indeed a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*). Furthermore, when there is a desire for a result, a result mentioned in the supplementary portion of the sentence—namely, "He supports his very self through prāṇa and apāna"—is postulated according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra*. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: there is a relationship of sublation and being sublated (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) when there is a conflict between *vākya* and *prakaraṇa*, but in this case, no such conflict exists.

Since the word *jañjabhyamāna* denotes the agent, and such a person exists even within the sacrifice (*kratu*), it is possible for [the prohibition] to be an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) by way of being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that person. Furthermore, in this way, there is no burden of postulating a result presented by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Thus, when considering relative strength (*balābala*), since contradiction is indeed appropriate, just as the recitation of the *jañjabhyamāna* formula—by virtue of both sentence (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)—is a duty of the person associated with the sacrifice, so too in the present case, the prohibition against speaking untruth (*anṛtavādana*) is appropriately a duty of the person connected to the sacrifice by virtue of both direct statement (*śruti*) and context. And it has been said by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda:

The sense is this: even though [acts such as] resorting to women, eating beef, and so forth serve human ends, they are intended as prohibitions that are auxiliary to the sacrifice, by virtue of depending on the context (*prakaraṇa*). As for the phrase "it has been explained in detail," the detailed exposition has already been stated.

[Objection: "But how can this be so? Since verbal cognition arises even without the knowledge of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, since the nature of correctness as being 'possessing expressive power' (*śaktatva*) will be refuted later, [how can it be the cause]? To this he says: "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*). The phrase "the determination of its absence" means the certainty of incorrectness (*āsādhutva*). For even when that [correctness] is certain, one observes cognition arising from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). Thus, the sense is that there is no obstacle to the cognition of *bhāvanā* from the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*).
Thus ends the first section, the Determination of the Meaning of Verbal Roots and Verb Suffixes, in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the verbal suffixes (lakāra).

Having defined the general meaning of the *lakāra*s, and once the desire to know that [general meaning] has been satisfied, the author states "pratyekam" (each one) to indicate the *saṅgati* (logical connection) of the occasion for defining their specific meanings, based on the knowledge that they must necessarily be explained. The phrase "of the ten *lakāra*s" means those enumerated in the sequence beginning with *laṭ*, *liṭ*, and so forth. Even according to the view that the substitutes (*ādeśa*s) possess the denotative power, the fact that they have those meanings remains intact; for, by superimposing upon the substitutes such as *tiṅ* and others—which reside in them—the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatā*), they are prescribed as having those meanings. This is the intended sense.

The meaning of "the state of being commenced but not yet completed" is: the state of possessing the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of some already destroyed parts while not yet possessing the final part characterized by its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). The two words/phrases [in the definition] are used respectively to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to future and past actions. He applies the definition to the object of illustration with the word "pacati" (he cooks). The sense is that only a collection of sequentially ordered parts, which is the object of a cognition whose mode is "being something to be accomplished" (*sādhya*), constitutes an action (*kriyā*).

The phrase "tadīti" means "the state of being present as previously mentioned. Although the *Nirukta-bhāṣya* states that the four meanings of a verb (*ākhyāta*) are "state" (*bhāva*), "time" (*kāla*), "case-role" (*kāraka*), and "number" (*saṃkhyā*), and thus it appears that the status of being present and so forth belongs only to time distinct from action (*kriyā*), nevertheless—since that [time] in its unconditioned form cannot be cognized as being present and so on, and since it is necessary to state that status by taking recourse to the action which serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—it should be understood that the status of being present and so forth is stated to belong to the action itself.

In reality, it is only a fragmentary time (*khaṇḍakāla*), consisting of such units as the *daṇḍa* muhūrta, that is denoted by the suffixes *laṭ* and others through its state of being present and so forth. And the "presentness" residing therein is simply the status of being the locus of the employment of the respective word. Furthermore, because these [present times] are subsumed under the category of being the locus of word-employment according to the maxim of "that and so forth" (*tadādi-nyāya*), there is no infinite multiplicity of denotative powers (*śakti*). If, however, it is considered that even this [explanation] fails to account for the empirical fact that the cognition of each specific time occurs as "that specific time," then let it be that the denotative power of *laṭ* resides precisely in that which is delimited by those specific temporalities (*tattatkālatva*) as they are indicated by the property of being a sub-class of temporality residing in the locus of word-employment.

The undesirable consequence that expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) would apply even before the commencement of the action or after its completion is to be avoided by accepting a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the occurrence [of the verbal suffix], qualified by two conditions: (1) having a substratum that does not possess a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) residing in itself, and (2) having a substratum related to the action in question that does not possess a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) residing in itself; this is done through the relation of "inherence-in-a-locus" (*ādheyatā-sambandha*).

However, in cases where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is indeed an indivisible action (*akhaṇḍakriyā*), there is no fault [in the definition] because that [action] connects with [the time] solely through the relation of pure superstratum-ness (*āgheyatā*). Regarding the phrase "or being distinct from past and future," the word "or" (*vā*) indicates a lack of preference, because this [second] definition is more cumbersome than the previous one; furthermore, since future-ness (*bhaviṣyattva*) is itself composed of present-ness (*vartamānatva*), the apprehension of future-ness would require the apprehension of present-ness, and the apprehension of present-ness—which consists in being distinct from what is delimited by future-ness—would require the apprehension of future-ness, resulting in a circular dependency (*anyo'nyāśraya*). The same circular dependency should be understood to apply when taking past-ness (*bhūtatva*) into account as well.

An objection is raised: "But where [the meanings] such as being the locus of existence (*sattā*) and so forth constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is a failure [of the definition], because since those are impartite (*akhaṇḍa*), it is impossible for them to possess the aforementioned 'presentness' which is composed of parts. To this, he says: "The self exists" (*ātmā asti*). "Because of impermanence" (*anityatvāt*) means: because, by virtue of having parts, they are both counter-correlates of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and counter-correlates of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). "Of that qualified" (*tadviśiṣṭasya*) means: of the object consisting of existence and so forth, as qualified by impermanent royal actions and the like.

And thus, although that [existence] is absent in an object consisting of mere existence (*sattā*) and so forth, its presence is not untenable when that object is qualified by the aforementioned qualifiers, because one can take the qualifying portion into account; this is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, in the phrase "qualified by that" (*tad-viśiṣṭa*), since it is *anityatva* (non-eternality) itself that is immediately proximate and thus referred to by "that," the sense is that the suffix *laṭ* denotes existence (*sattā*) and so forth by superimposing the state of being present upon such an action. He refutes the notion that this is his own invention by stating, "For it has been said. The meaning of "the locus of the root *sthā*" is that [the time] is qualified by such an action consisting of [the act of] staying through the relation of being the substratum (*ādheyatā*); this is the intention behind the word "of them" (*tāsām*). By this Bhāṣya passage, as well as by the statement beginning with "in reality" (*vastutas tu*), the validity of the aforementioned interpretation alone is established.
Because in every action, it is precisely time—characterized by the definition already stated—that is obtained as the locus of inherence.

"...is differentiated from another. All generalities of the meanings of verbal roots, such as "cooking" (paci) and so forth, are "differentiated from another"—that is, by another factor such as the speaker of the present tense relative to themselves; they are "differentiated," meaning they are excluded [from their own scope]. However, regarding the phrase "the Self (ātmā)," the word *ātman* and its synonyms here signify the existence of the Self (*ātmasattā*) and so on. It "does not waver" because, being eternal and partless, it lacks the connection with the aforementioned qualifiers and thus does not become an object of the inference of difference (*bhedānumiti*). Consequently, the usage "the Self exists" (*ātmā asti*) would be untenable; this is the meaning of the first half-verse.

He provides the formal conclusion: "Therefore," meaning that because it is impossible for a category distinct from the particular (*viśeṣa*) to be inherently excluded [from others]. By the phrase "mountains and so forth," the inclusion of the self (*ātman*) and other such entities is intended.

"By means of another form" (*pararūpeṇa*) means by means of the form—i.e., the property (*dharma*) such as "presentness" (*varttamānatva*)—of another object, such as the activity of a king; thus, the meaning has already been stated: that [the verb] is differentiated. Regarding the phrase "darkness existed" (*tama āsīt*) and so forth, the meaning is that these are to be applied because of the superimposition (*āropa*) of "pastness" belonging to a past action, and because of the superimposition of "futurity" belonging to a future action, as in "I shall be" (*bhaviṣyāmi*). Demonstrating that both positions are established in the authoritative sources (*ākararūḍhatā*), he states the justification for the position that the verbal suffix (*ādyotakatva*) indicates [time], beginning with "And that" (*tac ca*). "Of a general action" (*kriyāsāmānya*) means of that which expresses an action occurring at a general time.

The meaning is: "in that qualified" refers to an operation (vyāpāra) qualified by the present time and so forth, or qualified by presentness and so forth. By the phrase "of *laṭ* etc.," the inclusion of *liṅ* and other suffixes is intended.

"Because of their utility"—and that has been established previously. Thus, since *ti* and other suffixes indicate [tenses] such as the present by virtue of being the substitutes (*ādeśa*) for *laṭ* and so forth, there is no cognition of a present action in cases such as *apākṣīt* ("he cooked"). The point is that, since the understanding of an action qualified by those [tenses] is possible through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the verbal root—which possesses the power (*śakti*) to denote action in general—with respect to those specific [temporal] qualifications, it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate denotative power (*śakti*) in them for [tenses] such as the present. Adopting the position that they are denoters (*vācakatva*), he says: "By means of positive and negative concomitance," and so forth.

Nor can it be argued that the denotations of the agent and so forth are set aside by the maxim of "the curd for Kauṇḍinya," because the delimiters of the respective capacities (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) differ. Furthermore, if this were the case, the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* would become devoid of scope, since in other instances there could be a sublation by meanings such as the injunction (*vidhi*) and so on; this is the underlying sense. Otherwise, if positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) were not the means of apprehending the capacity, there would be the consequence of its total disappearance; the sense is that in all cases, the cognition of what is intended to be the meaning of each respective suffix could be possible through the base (*prakṛti*) alone.
More will be said regarding this in the *Subarthanirṇaya*.

The meaning is that by the two rules—"in the past" (*bhūte*) and "the *laṅ* [suffix] is used for what is not of today" (*anadyatane laṅ*)—those respective words are understood through syntactic continuity (*anuvṛtti*). Regarding the statement "there is no use of the *liṭ* [suffix]," the sense is as follows: because the stated meaning would be sublated, and because doubt regarding whether something is "not of today" and so forth does not arise after the cognition produced by the understanding of "he cooked" (*papāca*) and similar forms, it must be admitted that these two [properties, "not of today" and "past"] also appear as qualifiers of the action-component within the cognition produced by that sentence, just like "pastness" (*bhūtatva*).

And since that [appearance] is untenable without either denotative power (*vācakatā*) or indicative power (*dyotakatā*), it is necessary to admit that the *liṭ* suffix possesses such power. This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "remoteness" (*parokṣatva*) consists in being the object of a cognition other than perception? And since [the properties of] being heard or inferred exist even in the case of the action of perception, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using such expressions as *papāca* ("he cooked") [even for an action witnessed by the speaker]. To this, he says: "And remoteness... Since the state of not being an object of perception as it is literally heard is absent in the case of an action brought to mind (*upanīta-kriyā*), the use of expressions such as *papāca* would be untenable there; therefore, he says: "I perceive directly. The meaning is: the state of lacking an object that is worldly and witnessed by the testimony of the cognition "I perceive directly."

In the aforementioned case, even though there is the status of being an object of perception (*pratyakṣaviṣayatā*), the absence of such a distinct type of objecthood (*tādṛśavilakṣaṇaviṣayatvābhāvavattva*) remains intact; thus, there is no inconsistency. "Perception" here should be understood as that which is apprehended by the speaker of such words.

If it is objected that, since direct (aparokṣa) knowledge is observed even from words such as "You are the tenth," the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is inappropriate for an action involving a sense-organ connection with the object of such word-generated knowledge—this is not so. For even in that case, the direct perception of being the tenth occurs through the mind alone, assisted by verbal knowledge, and not from the word itself; because, in the absence of sense-organ contact or other factors that determine ordinary objective presence (*laukika-viṣayatā*), it is impossible for the word to possess such [objective] character.

Therefore, it is entirely consistent that it is stated in the *Gītā-bhāṣya* that the mind—purified by the teacher’s instruction such as "That thou art" and by [the disciplines of] tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*)—is the cause for the vision of the Self.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, “this is what is called action” (*kriyā*), the ellipsis is to be supplied as: “that [action] is cognizable through inference. Action is that which is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is the object of common usage such as “he cooks” (*pacati*) and so forth; because it consists of a collection of many successive operations occurring in a temporal sequence (*pūrvāparībhūta*), it is therefore “entirely unseen by another”—meaning it is not at all perceived by another person through the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), and thus is not an object of the knowledge produced thereby. The phrase “consolidated into a mass” (*piṇḍībhūtā*) implies that because the constituent parts perish so rapidly, there is no such thing as a stable mass.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [action]?", he says: "Directly," meaning it is to be inferred from effects such as softening (*viklitti*). "Otherwise" means if one does not admit the direct perception of action even in its constituent parts. "It appears" means that the aforementioned object itself becomes the object of our cognition.

But surely, even the constituent parts (*avayava*) of an action are, like the action itself, beyond the reach of the senses. Just as the sub-parts of cooking, such as pouring water and so forth, are themselves composed of further parts, those too are denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*) only in their collective form. That part which is delimited by a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) is not denotable by the root; rather, it is denotable only as the essence of a collection of parts. This is because that which is denoted by the root consists of a sequence of dependent stages. Thus, an action, being of the nature of both existent and non-existent [in its successive parts], cannot be grasped by the senses whose objects must be presently existent. As it has been said: "Because they exist and do not exist in succession, they do not form a collection in their own individual natures."

"They enter into a relationship with the eyes and other [senses] through objects that are real entities. Thus, even the meaning of the *bhāṣya* passage "never seen" (*atyantāpūrva*) is simply "not seen," whether in its individual form or as a collective whole. For this very reason, in the *bhāṣya* on the rule "the present tense suffix *laṭ* is used for the present time" (*vartamāne laṭ*), it is stated: "The present time exists, but it is not perceived, like the movement of the sun"; the word "by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder of that statement.

And thus, from that [statement], it is clearly perceived that actions characterized by the state of being present are indeed imperceptible. However, in cases such as "Look, the deer is running," there is no fault whatsoever, because in such instances the verb *dṛś* (to see) has the sense of "cognition," or the verb *dhāvati* (is running) refers to the result [of the action].

Furthermore, if a constituent part were perceptible, then—just as in examples such as *prakṛtaḥ kaṭam* ("he made a mat"), where the suffix *kta* is justified by taking the non-perceptibility of the whole based on the non-perceptibility of the parts—the rule *parokṣe* ("in the case of what is not perceptible") would find its scope by taking the non-perceptibility of the whole based on the perceptibility of the parts. Consequently, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) found in the Bhāṣya would be rendered baseless. Therefore, out of dissatisfaction with this, he states another view: *vyāpārāviṣṭānām* ("of those [actions] entered into by an operation"). Thus, the meaning of the sūtra *parokṣe liṭ* ("the *liṭ* suffix occurs when the agent is not perceptible") is: the *liṭ* suffix occurs after a verbal root denoting an action whose agent is not perceptible and which is entered by an operation that is past and not of today.

The sense is that in the example *ayaṃ papāca* ("this one cooked"), although there is no lack of direct perception (*apārokṣya*) on the part of the agent at the time [of speaking], the usage is justified because there was a state of indirectness (*pārokṣya*) during the phase of the action. The phrase "they also say thus" (*ity api vadanti*) implies a disregard for other opinions; the word *api* is used here because those who follow the Bhāṣya consider the previously stated view to be merely superficially attractive—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

On this point, the Naiyāyikas say: It is indeed correct that a technical action (*pāribhāṣika-kriyā*), which consists of a collection of parts arranged in a temporal sequence (prior and posterior), is not perceptible, because such a collection does not exist as a real entity; furthermore, the natural sense of the Bhāṣya statement "having become a mass" (*piṇḍībhūta*) makes it clear that the collection itself is what is understood [to be the object]. However, the claim that even its constituent parts are beyond perception contradicts universal experience, since the causes of perception—such as inherence in that which is conjoined with the eye (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyukta-samavāya*)—are present there. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of even jars, books, and the like being imperceptible, which would result in a great contradiction.

Furthermore, there is the universal consensus that "I am directly perceiving the act of placing [the pot] on the fire. If such a perception were not a proof for the existence of the object, it would result in the total collapse of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "This is indeed an action," its meaning is that this [action] consists of the form of the object of cooking and so forth, which possesses parts; thus, there is no contradiction with that. Regarding the phrase "of those existent and non-existent," it means "consisting of parts that are present and absent"; since its intent is to establish the mediacy (*pārokṣya*) of an action whose nature is a composite whole, there is no contradiction even with the words of Hari.
Otherwise, for one who asserts that "action has the nature of being both existent and non-existent," the contradiction would be quite evident.

Since time lacks perceptibility, even the citation of the Bhāṣya as a supporting authority for its restatement cannot establish the indirectness (pārokṣya) of its parts; for even in the case of the current example "the mat" (*kaṭam*), since the usage is justified by taking the pastness of the parts alone, there is no evidence for superimposing pastness upon the whole, and thus the cited analogy is inconsistent. Furthermore, the attempt to render the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) baseless by superimposing the perceptibility of the whole upon the perceptibility of its parts in the case under discussion is rooted solely in one's own misconception.

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya demonstrates through the example "Look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*) that the verb *dhāvati* possesses the status of being the object of the root *dṛś* (to see), which has as its domain worldly objects. Otherwise, how could such a usage not occur for one situated inside a house? For there would be no obstruction to the deer’s running being the object of knowledge, insofar as it consists in being the object of a cognition whose agent is the deer. Furthermore, if *dhāvati* were to mean the result in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it would follow that it is not a verbal root (*adhātu*), because it would lack the expression of an operation (*vyāpāra*).

Furthermore, if one attempts to establish the status of [the action] as a *kriyā* by superimposing a sequence of prior and posterior stages upon the activity of its own cause, the consequence of its non-perceptibility remains exactly as it was; thus, this argument amounts to nothing. Therefore, the previously stated view alone is free from objection. For this very reason, the author of the text also indicated his lack of conviction in that position by using the expressions "api" and "vadanti. Regarding the phrase "due to distraction and so forth," the meaning is as follows: just as in the case of "I indeed prattled while intoxicated," the action is perceived indirectly (*pārokṣya*) because the mind is not present due to intoxication and the like, so it is here.

Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of the *liṭ* [perfect tense]": here it should be considered that actual remoteness (*pārokṣya*) and so forth are not the determinants for the *liṭ* and other suffixes; otherwise, in the example "He occupied Ayodhyā, which is pleasant in all seasons," the use of the *laṅ* [imperfect tense] would result in being ungrammatical. Rather, that [remoteness] is intentional (*vaivakṣika*). As the author himself will state later: "The *laṅ* is used when there is an intention to express the past as not belonging to the current day; in that very case, if there is an intention to express remoteness, the *liṭ* is used."

In the present context, since there exists the intention to express the non-recent past (*anadyatanatva*)—which results in the cognition that [the action] was accomplished without effort and was accomplished quickly—and likewise the intention to express indirectness (*pārōkṣya*)—which results in the cognition "I shall do this in such a subtle time that even I cannot perceive it directly"—the possibility of the application of the *liṅ* suffix is established.

Regarding the term *anadyatana* (non-current day), the authors of the Vṛtti and others maintain that the current day (*adyatana*) is a day characterized by the latter half of the past night combined with the former half of the coming night; non-currentness (*anadyatanatva*) is the state of being at a time distinct from this. Kaiyaṭa, however, stated in his commentary on the rule for the *luṅ* tense that the current day is the day joined with the final watch of the past night and the first watch of the coming night.

In this regard, the following should be noted: when there is a desire to express merely the state of being past (*bhūtatvamātra*) regarding what is not of the current day (*anadyatanabhūta*), then only the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is used. Thus, in cases such as "he cooked yesterday" (*hyo'pākṣīt*), since the *luṅ* is employed when there is a desire to express merely the state of being past, and the non-current-day status is subsequently understood through its connection with the word "yesterday" (*hyaḥ*), the *luṅ* is not ungrammatical.
