Similarly, regarding the future not of the current day (*anadyatanabhaviṣyat*), the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix is used when there is a desire to express merely the state of being future. In the case of "the deity will sacrifice tomorrow" (*śvo yakṣyamāṇe—devatā yakṣyati*), the non-current-day status is subsequently understood.

Others, however, say that because the sacrifice along with its constituent parts (*sāṅgayāga*) is to be accomplished over a period of two days, the time consisting of those two days as its locus lacks the quality of being "non-immediate" (*anadyatana*); thus, since there is no occasion for the *luṭ* suffix, the use of the *laṭ* suffix is justified, as in the example: "O fisherman, from today onwards my celibacy (*brahmacarya*) shall begin."

Now, one might object: in the statement "I alone existed first, I exist now, and I shall exist," since the existence denoted by the verbal root is contradicted by the fact that its present prior absence has a counter-positive (i.e., the present moment), the future suffix cannot apply to express that meaning; therefore, he says "And that [future-ness] consists in... The reading is: "the state of possessing a time of origination that is the counter-positive of a present prior absence."

And thus, for those who follow the literal meaning [of the rule], since the time—which is the substratum of the operation directed toward that object and which consists of non-eternal royal actions and so forth—possesses "futurity" in the form of being the counter-positive of the present non-existence, the application of the *luṭ* suffix is justified by taking that very [time] as the basis.

Others, however, raise this objection: "In the view of those for whom the meaning of roots such as *naś* (to perish) is mere destruction (*nāśamātra*), if future-ness consists in being the counter-positive of a present prior non-existence, then there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage 'it will perish on the day after tomorrow' (*paraśvo naṅkṣyati*) regarding something whose destruction is to occur tomorrow. This is because that destruction, which is the counter-positive of a present prior non-existence, exists at the time of 'the day after tomorrow'."

Nor should it be argued that there is no risk of such an unintended application because the future time [of "tomorrow"] is admitted to be construed with the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) that constitutes its futurity, and since that [prior absence] is sublated by the actual prior absence of that [destruction], the aforementioned usage would not arise; for if that were the case, the usage "it was destroyed tomorrow" would be untenable even in the instance of something whose destruction is to occur tomorrow.

Since there would be a contradiction regarding the connection with tomorrow’s time in the case of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that destruction, he says: "And its nature... Here, the inclusion of the word *samaya* (time) is intended to mean that time is the meaning of the suffixes such as the present tense marker (*laṭ*), but it is not included in the definition itself, because there is no purpose for it; rather, it is sufficient to define it simply as "having an origination whose counter-positive is a presently existing prior non-existence. However, where origination itself is the meaning of the verbal root, it should be defined without including that [prior non-existence], lest there be the undesirable consequence of the origination appearing in two ways.

Thus, they introduce [the discussion] by stating that since the occurrence of tomorrow’s time is sublated in the production (utpatti) which constitutes "futurity" in this context, there is no possibility of the aforementioned undesirable application [of the suffix]. However, for those who maintain that [the root] denotes both the result and the operation (*vyāpāra*), there is no inconsistency because the existence of the counter-positive of the present non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) with respect to the operation is not sublated; this was stated previously.

In this regard, the following should be noted: in cases such as "A pot will exist here today," the specific place, time, and so forth are construed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) only with respect to the arising (*utpatti*), which is the meaning of the verbal root. Now, one might object: [Why not construe them] with the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) that constitutes futurity, or with the arising itself? If that were the case, then in a situation where a pot is destroyed due to the destruction of its shards, there would arise the undesirable linguistic usage: "The destruction of the pot will occur here in these shards. This is because the prior non-existence of the pot's destruction—which consists of the counter-positive (the pot) itself—would indeed exist in the shards. Similarly, [this would apply to] what is to happen tomorrow today...

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the usage "it will exist," because its prior absence exists at the present time. Likewise, if Maitra were to arise tomorrow in the courtyard and depart the day after tomorrow, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "Maitra will exist in the courtyard the day after tomorrow," because Maitra, being one who has arisen, exists in the courtyard and exists at the time of the day after tomorrow. However, according to our view, even though he exists at the time of the day after tomorrow, there is no fault, because his arising does not occur at that time.

In expressions such as "the jar will be" (*ghaṭo bhaviṣyati*), when conjoined with a verbal root whose meaning is origination, the relation of "future-ness" (*bhaviṣyatva*)—which does not include origination—is construed [with the object], because this is more parsimonious (*lāghava*). This is because the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of words like "clay" is accepted to reside in that very future-ness which excludes origination. As for the secondary referent (*lakṣyārtha*) which includes origination, there is no inconsistency even in the view of other schools, since it is construed with destruction in cases such as "it will perish" (*naṅkṣyati*). Furthermore, in the case of "it will be," there is no possibility of the objection that origination would appear twice.

According to the Vaiyākaraṇa school, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) here is: "An operation (*vyāpāra*) residing in a jar, which is conducive to an origination that is the counter-positive of a present non-existence.

Regarding the rule *vidhyādyāśiṣi* ("the optative and so forth [are used] in the sense of injunction and benediction"), a benediction (*āśis*) is the desire of the speaker of a word ending in the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) or others, directed toward the welfare of the person being addressed. For example, in the phrase *bhavatu te* ("may it be yours"), the cognition is: "An act of becoming (*bhavana*), whose agent is the grace of Śiva, which is related to the state of being the object of my desire directed toward your welfare. The term *etayoḥ* means "of these two," namely the *leṭ* and *loṭ* suffixes; the term *trayāṇām* means "of the three," namely the *leṭ*, *loṭ*, and *liṅ* suffixes.

The phrase "by that very determination" means by the determination of the meaning of the *liṅ* suffix which is about to be explained. Since the word *hyaḥ* (yesterday) is conventionally established as denoting the day immediately preceding the current one, and since that [day] constitutes the time-referent of the *laṅ* suffix, the *laṅ* would be untenable for an action occurring on a day separated by one interval; therefore, he says "non-remote" (*anadyatana*). Thus, the word *hyaḥ* indicates "non-remote" merely by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) through its quality of being non-remote, and so there is no room for the aforementioned objection. This should be understood similarly in the case of the expression "to happen tomorrow" (*śvo bhāvinī*).

The understanding [of the sentence] "asya putraḥ" (his son) is: "an operation conducive to the production of this person's son, which has as its agent [the son], which is related to him, and which occurs at a time other than the present, being the counter-positive of a destruction existing in the present. However, in cases such as "adhyāsta" (he studied), the use of the *laṅ* suffix is justified by the intention to express merely the past non-present time. Since the *liṅ* suffix is understood from the Sūtra to have injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth as its meaning, one might ask how instigation (*preraṇā*) and the like can be the meaning of "injunction"; therefore, he says "therein," meaning "among those [meanings]," and "injunction is instigation," meaning that the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) is a synonym for "instigation" (*preraṇā*).

In order to refute the view of those who assert that the nature of the optative suffix (liṅ) and other such words is instigation (preraṇā), [the author] demonstrates the true nature of instigation with the words "of a servant, etc. (bhṛtyādeḥ).

The meaning is this: that which, by being the object of a cognition, generates an inclination toward action—that alone is *pravartanā* (the impelling force). And it is precisely the property of being the means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) that possesses such objectivity; for it is universally agreed that inclination arises from the knowledge of that [end] through either one's own or another's cognition, and not from the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, since inclination does not arise from a cognition whose object is those suffixes. If, with respect to the speaker, it becomes the object of an impelling cognition directed toward a person of inferior status, then it is called *preraṇā* (instigation).

But that which is designated by terms such as "invitation" (nimantraṇa) and so forth is of a different nature. Thus, it results that "instigation" (preraṇā) is an activity conducive to the engagement of a subordinate agent—who, due to ignorance of the means to his own desired end, has not yet engaged—in an activity directed toward that means. More will be said on this later.

An example from the Veda is: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), and so forth. According to the grammarians’ school (*vaiyākaraṇa-mata*), the cognition is that the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of a sacrifice, whose agent is non-different from the one desiring heaven, is the means for attaining a desired end such as heaven. Furthermore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the status of being a means to a desired end belongs to the productive urge only for the one who desires heaven. Having formed the intention "I am such [a person]," the engagement of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) in the sacrifice and other rites is thereby accomplished. As for the worldly example, such as "Bring water," the cognition is to be inferred by oneself.

He explains "invitation" (*nimantraṇa*) and so forth according to his own view: "the performance of an injunction" (*niyogakaraṇam*). From such expressions as "one invites a Brahmin," there arises the understanding of a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) that generates activity directed toward the Brahmin; thus, in this context, the meaning of the term "injunction" (*niyoga*) is activity, and its "performance" (*karaṇa*) means the operation conducive to that [activity].

"Obligatory" (*āvaśyaka*) refers to things such as meals for those who have taken refuge (*śraddhabhojana*), and likewise "instigation" (*preraṇā*) means "incitement" (*pravarttanā*). The phrase "of this [person], such as a daughter's son (*dauhitrādi*)" and so forth; that is to say, an activity conducive to the engagement of one who has not yet engaged in it. For example: "May you please eat here," and so on. "Permission to act at will" (*kāmacārānujñā*) means an activity conducive to engagement with a desired object, which results in the prevention of engagement elsewhere by one who is already engaged according to their own desire.

For example, in cases such as "Sit here," "Begin what has been started," or "Do that which is beneficial," when activity toward sitting and other such actions arises from the cognition that they are means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), the absence of activity toward anything else follows by implication. An action preceded by honor (*satkārapūrvaka*) is the meaning of the term *adhīṣṭa* (solicitation); that is to say, in the context of activities such as teaching, an action that is preceded by respect and is favorable to the disposition of the person addressed is the referent of the word *adhīṣṭa*. This very same [action] is called *abhyarthanā* (request). For example: "May you teach the boy."

Among the [properties] stated, being the means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and being favorable (*anukūlatva*) should be understood as being included within the defining scope (*avacchedakakoṭi*) of that which generates inclination toward action (*pravṛttijanakatā*).

“Deliberation” (*sampradhāraṇam*) means the desire for a determination regarding the fact that one of two presented actions is a means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). For example: “O sir, shall I study the Veda or logic? The understanding [of this sentence] is that the person addressed, characterized by the relation of being the object of the speaker’s own intention, is the locus of a desire for a determination whose qualifier is the fact that the production (*bhāvanā*) of either the study of the Veda or the study of logic is a means to achieve a desired end. The same applies to subsequent cases. An injunction (*vidhi*) is an instigation (*preraṇam*); “instigation” here means the act of prompting (*pravarttanam*).

To explain: for one who has not yet acted, it is the communication of the fact that something is a means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) when the means to that desired end is unknown; that is to say, a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or similar form, which is not prompted by [mere] desire, and whose object is the cognition of such a status as being a means to a desired end characterized by the intention to bring about a specific result, is designated by the two terms "command" (*ājñā*) and "instruction" (*upadeśa*). He states this very point with the words "of a servant, etc."; by "etc.," students and others are included. In this regard, a worldly example is: "May you bring water," and so forth. A Vedic example is: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and so forth.

"Invitation" (*nimantraṇa*) is defined as "the act of inviting. By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that by which one is enjoined" (*niyujyate 'nena*), the meaning is that the referent of the word "invitation" is an activity conducive to an injunction (*niyoga*).

(The phrase "it is obligatory" refers to occasions such as a *śrāddha* feast. The term "instigation" (*preraṇā*) implies [the instigation] of a daughter's son (*dauhitraka*) and others. Thus, the result is that "invitation" consists in making known to a daughter's son and others that a mandatory *śrāddha* feast and so forth is a means to achieve their desired end—for example: "May you please eat here. Regarding "acting according to one's own will" (*kāmacāra*), the meaning is the communication that for one who engages in acting according to their own desire regarding what they themselves long for, [that action] is a means to achieve their desired end.

The purpose of the activity of one who gives permission—expressed as "let it be as it was here"—is to communicate that the object of this activity is a means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), by way of obstructing the activity of others. This applies to such expressions as "do as you have begun," "perform that," and "act for your own welfare. All such cases are included as illustrations of this principle.

An operation preceded by *kat* means an operation such as teaching and so forth that is preceded by respect; the meaning is the communication of [the action] as a means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). This very thing is conventionally termed "entreaty" (*abhyarthanā*). An example is: "May you teach the boy. "Inquiry" (*sampraśna*) means deliberation (*sampradhāraṇa*). "Prayer" (*prārthanā*), however, is the communication of one's own desire regarding the giving of an object one wishes for, such as: "May I obtain food. "This fourfold" means the fourfold beginning with injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth.

"Because of parsimony" (lāghavāt) means that it is because of parsimony in postulating that [the aforementioned common form] is the delimiting factor of denotability (śakyatā'vacchedakatva). Although it is universally established that meanings such as the injunction (vidhi) are understood from injunctive sentences, the intention is that since it would be cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate each specific form as the delimiting factor of denotability, it is more appropriate for the aforementioned common form alone to be the delimiting factor of denotability. Regarding this, he cites the consensus of Hari (Harisammati), saying "And it has been stated."

The phrase "of what kind of differentiation" (*kimbhedasya*) means "of the distinctness [of the differentiation of powers] according to their respective forms"; the underlying sense is that power is not admitted to exist as such [independent] forms. If so, why was it formulated by the author of the Sūtras in that manner? To this he replies: "By logic" (*nyāya*); "logic" here means "power," and the meaning is "for the sake of its derivation" or "for the sake of its apprehension."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the apprehension of the capacity (*śakti*) of the instigation (*pravartanā*) in its aspect as "instigation-ness" (*pravarttanātva*) occurs only with respect to that very property which is co-extensive with the optative suffix (*vidhi*) and so forth? To this he says: "For the sake of elaboration" (*prapañcārtham*). He explains that from the word *pravartanā*—which is derived from the root *vṛt* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *yuC*, according to the etymology "that which causes activity" (*pravṛttikaraṇa*)—there is obtained the sense of "an operation conducive to activity" (*pravṛttyanukūlavyāpāra*). Thus he says: "And [the nature of] instigation-ness... The phrase "the state of being the delimitator of the object-sphere" (*viṣayatā'vacchedakatvam*) means "the state of being the delimitator of the mode" (*prakāratā'vacchedakatvam*). And the phrase "and that" (*tacca*) means "and that aforementioned state of being a delimitator."

The phrase "that very thing" means "the status of being a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) alone. By the use of the particle *eva* ("only/very"), there is an exclusion of such factors as "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*). Furthermore, "desirability" (*iṣṭatva*) consists in being the object of a desire presented by a word co-occurring in the same sentence. In the case of the injunction "One who desires heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), since heaven possesses the quality of being the object of the desire presented by the term "one who desires heaven," its desirability remains intact. It is precisely by this [definition] that all desired objects, such as heaven and so forth, are subsumed.

If it is argued that since activity does not arise from the mere general cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), one must instead maintain that there is a cognition of being a means to heaven in its specific forms, such as "heaven-ness" (*svargatva*) and so on—and if it is further considered how the motivating cognition can be established from an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*) when the status of being a means to a desired end in those specific forms is not understood from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*)—then one must conclude that the injunctive power (*śakti*) of the injunction resides in the state of being a means to that which is delimited by those [specific forms] like "heaven-ness," having subsumed them under the property of being a delimiter of desirability (*iṣṭatāvacchedakatva*). And thus, it is not [the case that...]

Furthermore, there is a multiplicity of meanings for the injunction (vidhi), just as in the case of "tadādi" (the word "tat" and its derivatives). And because it is accepted that the property-limiting factor (*iṣṭatā-avacchedakatva*) functions as a mere adventitious indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no risk of heaven-ness (*svargatva*) and other such properties appearing in their specific forms [as the objects of desire].

Now, one might object: "In the injunction *'One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma'*, the fact that the Jyotiṣṭoma is a means to heaven must be conveyed by direct denotation (*śruti*); however, this is not possible, because [the relation] is inconstant (*vyabhicāra*), since heaven arises even from the Vājapeya sacrifice, and because a specific universal (*vaijātya*) can only be postulated at a later time and is therefore not present beforehand. If this is argued, we say no. It is like the understanding in such cases as *'He knows the jar as being a substance'* (*ghaṭaṃ dravyatvenaiva jānāti*), where there is the comprehension of a cognition having "substance-ness" as its qualifier and a particular individual qualified by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as its objective.

By the Vedic injunction (*śruti*), sacrifice is understood as being the counter-positive of an absence that is co-located with some particular individual instance (*vyakti*) which serves as the substratum for the state of being heaven (*svargatva*). Alternatively, there is no fault whatsoever in [interpreting] it as simply having existence at a time subsequent to the sacrifice, by way of co-location with the state of being heaven. For this very reason, they maintain that the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) is "the state of bringing about a desired end" (*sādhyeṣṭakatva*). In that regard, however, the fact of its being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhatva*) is to be inferred at a later time, once it has been determined that the injunction intends to incite activity (*pravṛtti*).

And thus, just as there is no contradiction between the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) nature in the case of the *grahaṇa-śrāddha* and similar rites, so too there is no contradiction between the obligatory and optional (*kāmya*) nature in the case of the daily *śrāddha*, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), and so forth. Therefore, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) and according to the logic of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, one should offer the *śrāddha* day after day, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors: "Those who constantly perform the twilight prayers with firm vows... [and so on].
With their sins shaken off, they go to the stainless world of Brahmā.

Thus, the fruit is postulated as being precisely the satisfaction of the ancestors and the attainment of the world of Brahmā, which are presented by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Although elsewhere the causal relationship between the sacrifice and heaven is established through a co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting of inherence (*samavāya*), nevertheless, on the authority of the stated scriptural passage, that relationship between the Śrāddha rite and the satisfaction of the ancestors must be postulated through a co-location consisting of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) and inherence.

However, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the agent does not produce the satisfaction of the ancestors, because it has a different locus [than theirs], and because [if it did], the heaven of the ancestors and so forth would result from the destruction of that merit through actions performed after the *śrāddha* or by touching water and so on. But if the ancestors are liberated, then let that [merit] be postulated as residing in the performer himself. For this very reason, the elders say: "The fruit ordained by the scripture belongs to the performer; this is the general rule."

The human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is to be conceived either as the prior non-existence of suffering (*duḥkhaprāgabhāva*) or as the non-occurrence of transgression (*pratyavāyānutpāda*). And its status as a means [to that goal] is common to both *yoga* (the acquisition of what is not yet possessed) and *kṣema* (the preservation of what is already possessed). This is because when a compulsory rite (*nitya*) is performed, there is a rule regarding the non-occurrence of transgression, and when it exists, the prior non-existence of suffering is necessarily present.

Thus, activity would occur toward even a compulsory rite because it is taught as being such [a means]; for this reason, in the *sarvaśakti-adhikaraṇa-pūrvapakṣa-sūtra*, the Bhaṭṭas have explained that since the human goal to be realized is equal in both cases, just as a desired result is capable of being accomplished, so too is the compulsory one.

If it is argued that, since the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), and since the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the use of the instrumental case in the phrase "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" (*jyotiṣṭomena*) would be untenable—this is not so. For there is no room for such a doubt under the view that "the substance (*dravya*) is the factor of action" (*kāraka*). Even under the view that "the capacity (*śakti*) is the factor of action," although the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) consisting in being the producer of the object to be brought about by the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) residing in the operation of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is indeed denoted, the instrumentality residing in the sacrifice itself is not denoted; therefore, its use is justified by the word "Jyotiṣṭoma," which stands in grammatical apposition with it.

In order to establish that injunctions such as "one should not eat *kalañja*" are indeed prohibitions (*niṣedhavidhi*), it must be understood that when a negative particle (*nañ*) is co-occurrent with an injunction, the injunction possesses the capacity to signify that [the action] is a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhana*). This [undesirable end] also connects with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The negative particle (*nañ*) serves merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Thus, the cognition is: "The eating of *kalañja* is a means to an undesirable end. Alternatively, the cognition has the absence (negation) signified by the negative particle as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because it is determined that the negative particle intends the cessation of the injunction. By this [absence], since the status of being a means to an undesirable end is implied for that which is connected to one's own self, the cessation from that [action] is logically established; such is the sense.

Although it might be argued that—since one observes no inclination toward (1) bringing down the lunar orb (which is a means to a desired end but produces a powerful undesired result), (2) an aimless goal (which does not entail a powerful undesired result), or (3) eating food mixed with honey and poison (which is a means to a desired end in the form of satisfaction and is achievable through effort)—it is necessary to include these [undesired results and so forth] within the definition of the objective scope (*viṣayatā*) of the motivating cognition, and therefore the Vedic injunction must necessarily express the [balancing of] the pros and cons (*vidhi*) in order to justify its capacity to motivate—one raises this objection in order to refute the view of the Naiyāyikas, beginning with the words "Even though... (*yadyapi*).

This is the state of being the delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) for the objecthood of the motivating cognition (*pravartakajñāna*). He states the reasoning for its praise: "of that cognition," meaning that activity is observed even toward what cannot be accomplished by action because of the cognition of it; this is the sense. He refutes [this] with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). "From worldly experience alone" (*lokata eva*) means from ordinary means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*); the sense is that it is not possible [to establish it] through that, according to the maxim: "The meaning of a word is indeed that which is not obtainable otherwise. In reality, however, according to the stated maxim, it is only when a power (*śakti*) is obtainable through another word that [the word's own power is established]; otherwise, the power of no word at all would be established, since everything would be cognizable through means of knowledge other than the word itself.

Furthermore, if properties such as being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) were denotable independently on their own, then the aforementioned method might indeed be capable of refuting [the theory of denotation]. However, since those properties are accompanied by the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of being the delimitors of the object of the motivating cognition (*pravartaka-jñāna*), it is there that [denotability] resides. And since this secondary characteristic is unique to "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*), who can deny that denotative power (*śakti*) which is established even in that case? Let the wise themselves determine this.

As for the point that, even when the fact that [an action] is achievable through effort is understood from the Veda, an incapable person does not engage in a sacrifice and the like; therefore, it must be asserted that knowledge of that [action] as qualified by the "madaṃśa" (the element of capacity) alone is the cause of engagement.

Furthermore, the view that "the sacrifice is achievable by my effort, because it does not possess a property incompatible with being achievable by my effort, like a cooked meal achievable by my effort"—and that therefore its status as an object of verbal expression (*śakyatva*) is not established through inference alone—is incorrect. This is because, since the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) must also have the "I" (*mad-aṃśa*) as its object to be effective as an instigator of action, even if one were to admit a denotative power (*śakti*) for the term [in the injunctive] regarding its being a means to a desired end, the failure to obtain that [cognition] from the injunctive sentence would remain unremedied, and thus its capacity to instigate action would still be untenable.

If, however, it is considered that there is no necessity for inference because the injunction (vidhi) possesses the capacity to produce cognition through its repetition for each individual, and thus, by that very means, it can function as an instigator by communicating to that specific person that [the act] is a means to achieve the desired end—then the same applies to its being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*). Consequently, if the injunction lacks the power to convey the quality of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), then in the case of the prohibition "One should not eat *kalañja*," the phrase "one should eat" would not communicate that eating is a means to an undesirable end; thus, its status as a prohibitive injunction (*niṣedhavidhi*) would be untenable. This applies there as well.

The power of the injunction (*vidhiśakti*) must be accepted. Furthermore, "strength" (*balavattva*) consists in being distinct from the suffering that is inseparable from the arising of the desired object. Therefore, there is no logical impossibility of engaging in actions that are accomplished through effort. Nor is the aforementioned point established by the maxim "action is painful," for it is impossible for there to be an action that produces pleasure alone; and if such a thing were ever possible, then its strength would have to be defined simply as not being inseparable from the arising of the desired object.

By this, the prattle of certain [scholars]—to the effect that, on the view that the knowledge of being "not followed by a powerful undesirable result" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) is the sole cause of activity, there would be no occurrence of activity toward an action accomplished through great effort (such as Vedic study), because greater suffering arises; and furthermore, since even a small amount of suffering might be "powerful" due to some cause or other, it is impossible to define a consistent "powerfulness"—is thereby refuted. Thus, there is no possibility of that [knowledge] being the capacity of the injunction (*vidhi*).

Now, by the reasoning stated above, the cognition that [an action] is not a means to what is undesired does not function as an instigator because it concerns something undesired; rather, in order to establish the validity of sentences such as "one should not approach a forbidden woman" and "one should not eat vegetables," it must be asserted that the cognition of its not being a means to that [undesired result]—specifically in the form of hellish suffering and so forth—is what functions as the instigator.

If it is argued that there would thus be an infinite number of powers (*śakti*) and that the apprehension of these powers (*śaktigraha*) would be impossible, we say no. There is only a single power of the optative suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) directed toward a collection of absences (*abhāvakūṭa*), each of which is delimited by the property of being a means (*sādhanatā*) to hell and so forth, as characterized by the property of being a delimitor of the object of aversion (*dveṣaviṣayatā'vacchedakatva*). Because this characterizing property is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), once the property of being a delimitor of the object of aversion is set aside, what is cognized is simply the non-means-ness (*asādhanatva*) delimited by hellishness and so forth.

In some cases, the non-achievement of hell is understood, while in others, the non-achievement of enjoyment is understood; in this matter, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) alone is the restrictive factor.

Nor should it be argued that if one accepts a too-broad indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), then "knowability" (*prameyatva*) itself might serve as such an indicator due to its equal applicability; for since the non-achievement of pleasure and so forth cannot be the meaning of an injunction, "knowability"—which is common to those [undesirable things]—cannot function as an indicator.

It is not appropriate to assume that a property common to both [the desired and the undesired] serves as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the two, just as a property common to things that absolutely do not produce [an effect] serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of causality. Nor is it correct to argue that there is no fault even if the meaning of the injunction is the non-means-ness of pleasure and so forth—on the grounds that such a cognition does not arise simply because there is no intention [to convey it]—for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of modern speakers using the expression "one should not eat" with that very same intention.

Therefore, the refined view of the ancient Naiyāyikas—which holds that the injunctive suffix has its denotative power (*śakti*) in such an absence (an *abhāva*) that is subsumed under the property of being an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the nature of being a means (*sādhanatātva*) to hell, etc., as characterized by the delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) of being an object of aversion—is now refuted by adopting the perspective of the moderns [the Navya-Naiyāyikas]. The phrase "balavadaniṣṭa... means that the knowledge of not being a producer of a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭājanakatvajñāna*) is not the cause—meaning it is not the cause of inclination (*pravṛtti*). In some places, the reading is exactly as it stands.

And thus, the sense is that its object (the honey-mixture) cannot be denoted by an injunction. He states the reason for its not producing activity: "by the absence of aversion. In the case of eating food mixed with honey and poison, since there is knowledge of it being a means to what is disliked (*dviṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), activity toward that which is the object of aversion is prevented. Since the absence of aversion toward a particular object has already been established as an inhibitor (*pratibandhaka*) of activity directed toward that same object, and since the required invariable antecedence (*niyatapūrvavartitā*) is necessarily established through the status of the absence of an inhibitor, [activity] is accounted for by the absence of aversion alone.

The meaning is that the cognition of something not being a means to a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭāsādhanatvajñāna*) is not a cause [of action], because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) by that [other factor].

Now, one might object: since the causal status of the cognition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekasahacārajñāna*) is equal in both cases, the otherwise-establishment of this [cognition] by that alone is unavoidable. To this he says: "the believer" (*āstika*). And he is one who accepts the existence of the next world (*paraloka*). This qualification is employed because for one who does not accept that [next world], the cognition of [an act] as a means to hell (*naraka*) is impossible. He says "the lustful" (*kāmuka*) because, for a believer, there is necessarily an aversion toward an act due to the cognition of it being a means to hell, and thus activity [toward such an act] would be impossible. And its [lust's] nature is the possession of intense passion (*utkaṭarāga*).

Intensiveness (*utkaṭatva*) with respect to passion (*rāga*) consists in a specific nature of the [passion] itself, or a specific type of objectivity (*viṣayitā*). The phrase "of activity" (*pravṛtteḥ*) refers to [activity] such as approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*), and so forth. By the expression "in the state of absence of aversion" (*dveṣābhāvadaśāyām*), the deficiency of the causal complex for aversion (*dveṣasāmagrīvaikalya*) is indicated. This is to be understood both because the cognition of being a means to what is disliked (*dviṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), qualified by the absence of the causal complex for intense desire (*utkaṭecchāsāmagrīvirahaviśiṣṭa*), is the cause of aversion with respect to its object, and because such a causal complex acts as an independent inhibitor.

"And because of deviation," thus [the phrase] "it is not the cause" is connected with what precedes. For this very reason, in the case of the injunction "One desiring to perform malevolent magic should sacrifice with the Śyena," there is no sublation of the meaning of the injunction; for since the cognition that [an action] is not followed by a powerful undesirable result does not function as an instigator, the status of being the object of that [cognition]—namely, its being the meaning of the injunction—is simply non-existent. This is the sense. He concludes: "Therefore... By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only the state of being a means to the desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatvam eva*), there is an exclusion of both "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and "not being followed by a powerful undesirable result" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*).

The sense is that the former [the means] is understood through worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*) alone, whereas the latter [the end] is not the object of the motivating cognition (*pravarttakajñāna*).

"Motivation" (*pravarttanā*) means the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. "Because it is a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭābhyupāyatvāt*) means because it is a means to achieve a desired goal. "The other" refers to being achievable by human effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and so forth. "In actions" refers to those in the form of sacrifices and the like. The meaning is that [the end] is not the motivator for persons, nor is it the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) as an object in the production of activity residing in the cognition. In other words, it is not that which is denoted by the optative suffix and so forth within sentences such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason.
The meaning is that they designate by the term *pravartanā* (the impelling force) precisely that which is the cause of activity and the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of its causality.

Others, however, maintain that although the cognition of "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" is not the actual motivator—since it is otherwise established through the absence of aversion—the cognition of "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatā*) is universally established as the motivator; therefore, it is necessary that this [cognition] be the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*), as its object.

Nor can it be argued that there is a lack of evidence for its being the cause [of activity], because one might say that activity toward what cannot be accomplished by effort (*kṛtyasādhya*) does not occur simply due to the absence of the cognition that it cannot be accomplished by effort, since such a cognition acts as an obstacle. For, if the cognition that something cannot be accomplished by effort were the obstacle, then one would have to state that the non-existence of the property of being accomplishable by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), as well as the perception of properties pervaded by or delimiting that non-existence, are also obstacles; rather than postulating all those absences as causes of activity, it is more parsimonious [to posit] the cognition of being accomplishable by effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) as the cause.

This is because simplicity is much more evident in [the former] case of being a cause, and because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of activity occurring at all times, since the absence of the cognition that something is to be accomplished by effort exists always.

Furthermore, if the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is the motivator [of action], there is parsimony (*lāghava*), because one need not postulate that the causal complex for activity directed toward cooking and the like acts as an inhibitor with respect to a mental perception of the absence of a cognition qualified by having "being achievable through effort" as its qualifier and "cooking" as its substantive object. This is because at the time of such a causal complex for activity, a determinate judgment (*nirṇaya*) having "cooking" as its substantive object and "being achievable through effort" as its qualifier is necessary; and since that [judgment] exists as a real entity (*svarūpasat*), it is accounted for simply by its established status as an inhibitor of the aforementioned mental perception of the absence of the cognition.

In your view, the assumption that such a mental [cognition] acts as an obstacle to the causal complex for such an activity is clearly cumbersome. Likewise, there is simplicity in not assuming that the causal complex for activity directed toward cooking acts as an obstacle to the mental [cognition] "I am one who possesses the knowledge that cooking is to be accomplished by effort," which is qualified by invalidity.

At the time when there is a mental complex (*mānasa-sāmagrī*) possessing such a qualified objective state (*viśiṣṭa-viṣayatā*), the aforementioned cognition must necessarily be overwhelmed by a cognition of its own invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-jñāna*). Consequently, there is simply no possibility of a conjunction between that mental complex and the complex for activity (*pravṛtti-sāmagrī*)—which consists of a cognition having "being achievable through effort" (*kṛti-sādhyatva*) as its qualifier and "cooking" (*pāka*) etc. as its qualificandum—provided that it is not overwhelmed by a cognition of invalidity.

In your view, since there is no obstacle to the confluence of the causal complex for such an activity—which consists in the absence of a cognition having "being achievable through effort" as its qualifier and "cooking" (or the like) as its qualificand—and the causal complex for such a mental [perception], it is necessary to postulate that the causal complex for such activity acts as an inhibitor of that mental perception; thus, the resulting complexity is quite evident. They say that by this very same method, the causality of the absence of the cognition that something is a means to an undesirable end, and so forth, must also be refuted.

The teachers, however, maintain that the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Since a sacrifice is understood to be momentary, it is impossible to communicate [its status as a means]; thus, even its being an indirect means (*paramparāsādhanatva*) is impossible because the intermediate link (*dvāra*) is not present. Furthermore, the requirement of "fitness" (*yogyatā*), which consists in being a factor that necessitates the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) that prompts verbal cognition, is absent in that case. Moreover, a general cognition of being a means is impossible to assert, because there is a rule that when one specific instance is cognized, the cognition must have a qualifier other than that [specific instance] as its mode (*prakāra*).

Furthermore, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is not understood as something to be performed; rather, it is established elsewhere that a seeker of a desired end understands only that which is the means immediately preceding the desired end—other than the desire itself—as what is to be performed. Therefore, it is only the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), acting as the mediating means that exists immediately prior to the desired end, that can be understood as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*).

And "being an effect" (*kāryyatva*) consists in being the object of an effort (*kṛti*). In that regard, when there arises an expectancy for the locus and the object of the effort—which serves as the qualifier—the sacrifices are connected as the object, and the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) as the locus. Since pleasure, the absence of pain, and so forth are known through ordinary means of knowledge, and since even the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is understood by the Veda to be the object of an effort, there is no room for doubt regarding its lack of authority; therefore, it possesses that status [of being an effect]. Thus, in the case of the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the understanding is: "there is an *niyoga* (obligation) whose object is the sacrifice and which is the object of the effort of the one desiring heaven."

In this context, the "objectivity toward the sacrifice" (*yāgaviṣayakatva*) of the unprecedented result (*apūrva*) consists precisely in its being the intended object of the volition directed toward the sacrifice. When the sacrifice is the object of such a volition and the person is its locus, the delimiting factor for that relation is the state of being the cause of the unprecedented result. That itself constitutes the semantic competency (*yogyatā*). Just as in the sentence "Bring water with a jar," the competency-determinant is the state of being a jar other than one with a hole, which is understood through the ellipsis of words such as "jar" in cases like "not with a jar"; so too in the present case, it is understood through that very potency by virtue of the means of knowledge based on material implication (*aupādānika-pramāṇa*).

It is not correct to argue that the theory of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be abolished if one accepts the apprehension of an impossible object through the very power of that [word], for we maintain that only that which conveys a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by its own power conveys all the constituent objects required for its own establishment.

Furthermore, in cases such as "There is a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the words *gaṅgā* and so forth do not convey the connection [of the meaning] through their own primary denotative power (*śakti*), whereby there would be scope for the figurative means of knowledge (*aupādānika-pramāṇa*) to bring about the cognition of all the constituent meanings required to justify that [connection]. Moreover, "indication without abandoning one's own primary meaning" (*ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā*) is not established in our system. Thus, the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is one who understands the task as his own; and since the one desiring the fruit presented by the co-occurring words is such a person, in the case of a rite to be desired, the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is the person to be enjoined.

And thus, since human activity is possible when directed toward an *apūrva* (unseen potency) revealed by the Veda, "being a means to a desired end" cannot be the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*). For if its denotative power (*śakti*) were based on being a means to an object of desire, the motivating cognition would not be established; and if its power were based on being a generator of heaven, it would result in the fault of multiple meanings (*nānārthatā*). Furthermore, that view is beset by logical alternatives (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, for one who lives in purity at the prescribed times and observes the rules regarding lunar and solar eclipses, there arises the understanding that "this is an injunction for me concerning the twilight bath (saṃdhyā-snāna) as a constant (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) duty"; thus, there is no expectation of a fruit. However, in your view, since no fruit is heard of in such injunctions as "one should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun" or "one should perform the twilight worship daily," the sublation of the injunctive meaning would result.

For me, however, in the case of Vedic ritual, a person engages in action solely with a view toward the *apūrva* (unseen potency) taught by the Veda, because it is that very *apūrva* which the Veda declares to be the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the attainment of the fruit is merely incidental. For this very reason, they say that engagement even in obligatory rites (*nitya*) is justified by having that [unseen potency] as the objective.

However, others do not accept this; for since the cognition that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatvajñāna*)—which is universally acknowledged in the world as the motivator—is sufficient to account for the instigating power of an injunction by postulating the injunctive force (*vidhiśakti*) upon the fact of its being a means to a desired end, there is no evidence for the view that the mandate (*niyoga*) is the denotation of the injunction. Indeed, such a mandate would only be postulated because the status of heaven as a means [to liberation] as taught by the Veda would otherwise be untenable. Furthermore, that mandate is not previously present [in experience], such that the apprehension of the injunctive force could occur with respect to it.

Even though there is a rule that when a specific [particular] is sublated, a general cognition must have something other than that as its qualifier (*prakāra*), there is no obstacle to understanding [the Veda] as having "being a means" in general, rather than "being a direct means. Furthermore, the delimitor of fitness (*yogyatāvacchedaka*) for such being-a-means is the *apūrva*, which constitutes the intermediary link. Thus, since the requirement is satisfied by the very capacity to be a means to heaven, even if the *apūrva* is presented through the force of the *aupādānika* (implicative) means of knowledge, it need not be the denotable meaning (*vācya*) of the word.

If the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is not present [to consciousness], how could the Veda teach even its status as an indirect means? Thus, this is on an equal footing with the question of how the apprehension of a word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) can occur when the *apūrva* is not present.

Likewise, it is not the case that one who desires [a result] understands that the unmediated *apūrva* (transcendental result) is what must be performed as the means to that desire; for it is the very knowledge of being a means to the desired object (*kāmyasādhanatā*) that prompts action, and not even the requirement of its being unmediated, because such a restriction would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and lack any proof (*mānābhāva*). Furthermore, we observe that one seeking satisfaction engages in activities such as fetching water, which are merely instrumental to that end. It has already been explained how the apprehension of the capacity to be a means to a desired object occurs. And it has also been demonstrated how engagement in obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites takes place, even though the *apūrva* is not something directly achievable.

On the contrary, that [theory] is even more difficult to establish for you, because it is fruitless and results solely in suffering. This is because it has been determined that the knowledge of something being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is the cause of activity in general. Furthermore, if the object of activity is not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then the apūrva cannot possess the nature of being "to-be-accomplished" in the sense of being desired; thus, activity directed toward it would be impossible. Since activity toward what is understood to be fruitless cannot be produced even by a thousand Vedic texts, the claim that there is activity toward obligatory rites (*nitya*) simply because they are taught by the Veda is nothing but a deception of students.

For this very reason, in the eighteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, the purifying nature of sacrifice, charity, and austerity is declared by the verse beginning with "Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are action," which signifies that even though the avoidance of sin (*pratyavāya-parihāra*) was not explicitly mentioned, these acts yield their fruit when performed without aiming for results such as heaven.

Furthermore, just as a worldly injunction such as "one should cook" prompts action by making known its status as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatva*), a Vedic injunction also prompts action through that same capacity; therefore, once the function of knowledge is established, it is entirely without proof to postulate a potency (*śakti*) in an unmanifested *apūrva* (unseen merit) that has not been presented [by the text].

Upon hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others, there arises a necessary cognition that "this [suffix] impels me"; therefore, a function synonymous with "impulsion" (*preraṇā*), termed "denotation" (*abhidhā*), is the meaning expressed by the optative suffix and the like. Because it does not correlate with gender or number, and because it resides in the instigator (*pravarttaka*), it is designated by the term "function" (*vyāpāra*) and by the term "instigation" (*pravarttanā*). Since it possesses an object by virtue of being an impulsion, its "impulsiveness" (*preraṇātva*)—established as the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) by being the delimitor of the meaning of the root in verbs such as *prer*—is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

And that activity, because it is possible in the world, is simply a particular intention residing in the person who instigates [the action]. And in the case of being such an instigator, it consists in being the utterer of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. But in the Veda, since an utterer is impossible, it resides in the very form of the word ending in the optative suffix and so forth; and its status as an instigator consists in being independent while being the utterer of the optative suffix and so forth. For even though a foot-soldier instigated by a king may be an utterer of the optative suffix and so forth, he is not designated as an instigator.

"Independent" (*svatantrā*) means that by means of that [word], which is neither hostile nor spoken by an unreliable person, there is an inference of its being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) regarding its own object; and from that, the activity of the person to be prompted (*prayojya*) arises. Regarding the hostile statement "Eat poison," since the status of eating poison as a means to a desired end is not understood, [the word] is qualified by "spoken by an unreliable person. Even with a statement spoken by an unreliable person such as "Eat poison" or "Do not eat in his house," there is no inference of its being a means to a desired end in that case. Therefore, the qualification "neither hostile" (*adviṣṭā*) is included; because the intention regarding the subject of eating poison is characterized by the speaker's aversion, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Or rather, let it be that since no other operation is experienced when used in conjunction with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, that [causation] is everywhere of the very nature of the word ending in the optative suffix. For this very reason, in response to the question, "Why does the causative suffix (*ṇic*) not occur in the expression *pṛcchatu māṃ bhavān* (May your honor ask me)?", the answer is: "Because [the agent] is not an agent (*akartṛtvāt*). The suffix *ṇic* occurs in the instigation of one who possesses an action, whereas the imperative (*loṭ*) and so forth occur in the instigation of one who lacks an action. The meaning is that in the rule *tatprayojakaḥ*, the word *tat* refers to the agent as being engaged in an operation.

Moreover, even if the agent were somehow to exist, there would still be no fault; for it has been stated that since the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is expressed by the *loṭ* suffix, the *ṇic* affix will not occur. Consequently, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is obtained precisely as the act of impelling (*preraṇā*). This is also because it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "vidhinimantraṇa... that "injunction (*vidhi*) means impelling (*preraṇa*). Therefore, the meaning of the injunction is not the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth.

They say that even from the common worldly usage, "Since this is a means to achieve what you desire, therefore you should do it," the word [the optative suffix] does not have the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*), because that would result in redundancy (*paunaruktya*). For even if the intention of the statement is to convey that [the act] is a means to achieve the desired end in every respect, there would still be the consequence of the non-connection (*ananvaya*) of the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*). And this [position] is for the most part merely a restatement of the Bhaṭṭa school's view; for in the Bhaṭṭa system, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*) called *abhidhā*.

And that [efficient force] is, as previously stated, merely a specific intention residing in the person who employs it in the world; however, in the Veda, since no other [agent] is possible, it resides solely in the word ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. And because it is inherent [in the word], it is therefore designated as "verbal efficient force" (*śābdī bhāvanā*).

Since *bhāvanā* (productive operation) is twofold—verbal (*śābdī*) and objective (*ārthī*)—according to the distinction between word-meaning (*śabda*) and object-meaning (*artha*), that which is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is designated as the "objective productive operation" (*ārthī bhāvanā*). Because it possesses the nature of *bhāvanā*, the verbal productive operation (*śābdī bhāvanā*), which is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), also has an object. Since every *bhāvanā* is characterized by three constituent parts—the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—and since the verbal productive operation is understood as having an object, there arises an expectancy for what is to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) in the form of the question, "What should one bring about? In response to this, by virtue of the proximity of being conveyed by the same suffix, the meaning denoted by the verbal suffix—which consists of an activity directed toward its own object and is characterized by the three constituent parts—is [the answer].

The *bhāvanā* presents itself as the object [of desire]. This very [desire] is designated as the "expectation for the end" (*sādhyākāṅkṣā*), because it possesses an object precisely through the objective state known as "being the end" (*sādhyatā*). And thus, when its status as the end is understood, the cognition of the word containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth connects with it as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in response to the expectation for the instrument (*kenākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, being an instrument consists precisely in bringing about that which is to be produced by the *bhāvanā*; for even an axe and the like are instruments only by virtue of bringing about the act of cutting, which is itself accomplished by the operation of a person. This very *bhāvanā* is called the "expectation for the instrument."

According to the maxim "action is painful," when a person fails to engage in an activity due to aversion toward the means or through laziness and the like, the praise consisting of the excellence of the act—generated by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) through the removal of such aversion by making known its possession of a commendable fruit—serves as a cooperative cause; this is called the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance).

Thus, when the object is understood through the excellence of the three factors of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises the expectancy, "What should one cultivate? In response to this, because of the connection with words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), heaven is connected as the object to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), in the sense that "one should cultivate heaven. Although that activity has renunciation as its object, nevertheless, because it does not consist of happiness and thus is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and because it presents itself only as the instrument (*karaṇa*), it cannot be the object to be cultivated.

For this very reason, the third case ending occurs after words such as *jyotiṣṭoma*, which are in grammatical apposition with that [injunctive suffix]. When there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "by what means?", the sacrifice (*yāga*) connects as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Its status as an instrument has already been explained. Furthermore, regarding the expectancy for the "how-to" (*kathaṃ-bhāva*)—which consists of the expectancy for auxiliary factors—the collection of ritual acts such as the sacrifice named *samit* (as understood from sentences like "He offers the *samits*") connects as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). This should be further ascertained from other sources. As it has been said:
"The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others express one thing alone, namely the *abhidhā-bhāvanā* (the productive energy of the word);
but the *arthātmabhāvanā* (the productive energy of the object) is another, and that is the domain of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)."

"The denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is that very [activity] called verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*); its objective is the activity of the person; the cognition of the relationship [between the sacrifice and the result] is its instrument (*karaṇa*); and encouragement (*prarocanā*) is employed as an auxiliary. This is the meaning stated. In this regard, the distinction between the previously mentioned view and the Bhaṭṭa school is as follows: in the Bhaṭṭa view, the operation known as *abhidhā*, which is the meaning of the Vedic optative suffix, is inherent in the word and distinct from it. However, in that [other] view, [the efficient force] consists of the word itself ending in the optative suffix and is common to both worldly and Vedic usage. As for the possession of an object (*saviṣayakatva*), it is not distinguished in either of the two views.

On this point, they say: the power (śakti) itself, as determined by denotation (abhidhā), the optative suffix (liṅ), and so forth, is [the cause of action], and not some other operation (vyāpāra) inherent in the word distinct from those, for there is a lack of evidence [for such]. Since it has already been established that the injunction (vidhi) is the instigator of activity, there is no inconsistency in that [view]. Otherwise, one would have to postulate a single operation inherent in the word that is distinct from the word itself; and for that [operation], which is not established as a cause either for its own occurrence or for the occurrence of another, one would have to assume its status as a cause in that capacity.

Furthermore, since it is already established that a word—by virtue of its nature as an instigator and its capacity to convey an operation residing in another—is what conveys [the meaning], the Bhaṭṭas would have to postulate that it also conveys an operation residing in itself and possesses an object; thus, the prolixity [of such a view] is evident.

Even if instigation (*preraṇā*) is the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*), since a general term must ultimately resolve into a specific one, when seeking that specific nature, it is most appropriate to say that it is simply "being a means to a desired end" (*samīhitasādhanatva*). This is because without the injunctive suffix having that as its meaning, the capacity to incite action (*pravarttakatva*) would be impossible. Furthermore, the notion that "cooking is the object of the instigation," which does not involve the idea of being a means to a desired end, is contrary to common worldly experience in terms of its power to incite action.

Indeed, it is universally established that no one, even if impelled by a thousand scriptures, will engage in action without knowing that it is a means to achieve their own desired end. Furthermore, there is no rule whatsoever that the performance of a sacrifice produces its fruit solely through an operation residing in itself, for this is contradicted by the case of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. Therefore, the claim that the denotative power (*abhidhā*), which is the object of the cognition generated by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like, possesses the capacity to incite action independently of the knowledge that it is a means to a desired end, is utterly devoid of reason.

Even for one who maintains that the word itself possesses the power of impulsion (*preraṇā*), it must be admitted—by the reasoning already stated—that its status as an instigator occurs only through the inference of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) regarding that object; and this is not possible in the case of Vedic injunctions.

By supporting this with the Śruti passage, “This Veda—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda—is the very breath of that Great Being,” they accept that the Vedas are produced like a breath; consequently, the aforementioned inference does not apply because it lacks the qualifying attribute of being "spoken by an authoritative person," which consists in being uttered by one possessing true knowledge. Likewise, its having an object (saviṣayatva) is contrary to all systems, as it would be distinct from the specific qualities of the Self.

Furthermore, instigation alone is not the cause of activity by virtue of its independence, because it is subject to deviation in the case of independent activity; and because this would contradict the *Bhāṣya* on the *Hetu* Sūtra, which establishes that the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatājñāna*) is the motivator, stating: "All these act for the sake of their own welfare."

Furthermore, since the Bhāṣya on that very sūtra states, "What purpose does the instigation of the one to be prompted serve, such that it clings to the intentions [of the prompter]?", this makes it known that even the instigation (preraṇā) which is the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇic) lacks independent power to incite action. Consequently, because it is impossible for a Vedic injunction to have instigation as its meaning, and because its capacity to incite would otherwise be untenable, one must accept that its meaning is indeed "being a means to a desired end" (iṣṭasādhanatva).

And thus, since even worldly injunctions (*laukika-vidhi*) can be established as motivators through that very capacity [of the word], there is no need for that [intention] either; the hypothesis that intention alone is the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) is refuted by the very rejection of the teacher’s view to be mentioned later. As for the *Bhāṣya* statement "injunction is instigation" (*preraṇā*), it refers to the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) which is the object of the motivating cognition, based on the etymology: "that by which one is impelled or set in motion. This is because a cognition is a motivator precisely by virtue of having that [means-to-a-desired-end] as its object.

Furthermore, as for the citation of the *Bhāṣya*—"May you question me"—and so forth, which serves as a support for that [position], even that is not contrary to our view; for by means of that, the fact that the instigation (*preraṇā*)—consisting of the employment of words ending in the *loṭ* suffix and the like, which is designated by the term "incitement" (*pravartanā*) because it generates the knowledge that prompts action—is established as the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), but not as the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) either, since a difference in meaning has already been demonstrated.

By the statement "because there is no agent" (*akartṛtvāt*), [the author] also demonstrates that there is no contradiction, since the analysis (*vigraha*) of *gamayati* as "he impels one who is going," and of *pṛcchatu* as "he impels one who is asking," shows that the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not a cognition conducive to an activity directed toward the meaning of the verbal root which lacks a connection with an agent. Thus, the absence of such an agent is established.

Furthermore, the argument beginning with "athāpi" (even so) belongs only to the proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*), because the meaning of the suffix denoting an injunction is understood as being inherently future by its very nature. At that time, since the prompted agent (*prayojya*) is devoid of activity, agency (*kartṛtva*) is impossible; likewise, regarding the claim that the imperative (*loṭ*) expresses instigation (*preṣaṇā*), this is also incorrect because the instigation signified by the imperative appears only as a qualifier of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*). If one intends to express instigation as the primary object (*viśeṣya*), the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is unavoidable, since instigation is not perceived as the primary object from a word ending in the imperative when it qualifies the verbal root-meaning.

Furthermore, this would result in the complete collapse of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Statements such as "This is a means to achieve your desired end" are intended solely to communicate that something is a means to a desired end; for, on the view that the status of being a means to a desired end constitutes the injunctive force (*vidhitva*) by virtue of its being an instigator (*pravartanātva*), there is no possibility of redundancy. Moreover, in the system of the Naiyāyikas, since an operation consisting of an effort (*kṛti*) is not the meaning of verbal roots like *pac* (to cook), there is no occasion to charge them with redundancy even if they maintain that the injunctive meaning is the status of being a means to a desired end.

In reality, however, since the Bhāṣya states in many places that *preraṇā* (impulsion) has the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*), it is appropriate—on the authority of that—to maintain that its nature as an injunction consists precisely in the employment of words ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.

As for the Veda, by accepting its human origin on the strength of such scriptural passages as "From that sacrifice, from which all was offered, the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born," and "The Creator fashioned [the world] as before," one must establish the inciting power of the injunction through the inference of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) in an identical manner for both worldly and Vedic contexts; thus, everything is consistent.

The Teacher [Kaiyaṭa], however, maintains that the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) is the intention of the self (*ātma-abhiprāya*). This is because the optative (*liṅ*) in the middle and first persons—such as *pākaṃ kuryāḥ* ("you should cook") and *pākaṃ kuryām* ("I should cook")—has as its meanings specific types of desire (*icchā-viśeṣa*), namely command (*ājñā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), permission (*anu-jñā*), inquiry (*praśna*), and supplication (*prārthanā*); and since it is appropriate for the first person as well, its power (*śakti*) resides in desire alone. Among these, a desire that produces fear is a "command" (*ājñā*). When directed toward one who is to be entreated, that which manifests the speaker's favor is "entreaty" (*adhyeṣaṇā*). A desire that indicates the absence of prohibition is "permission" (*anu-jñā*). But that which prompts a subsequent [action] is "inquiry" (*praśna*).

The distinction is that "prārthanā" (supplication) is the desire for attainment (*prāptīcchā*). Thus, in the case of the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the understanding is that the sacrifice is the object of the desire for attainment residing in one who desires heaven.

Alternatively, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is simply the desire [of the agent] regarding what ought to be done. In that case, there is an inference of its being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). For example: "For me, who desires heaven, the sacrifice is a means to a desired end, because it is the object of a desire conveyed by an *liṅ* suffix uttered by a trustworthy person (*āpta*) as something to be done, just like the food my father intended for me to eat. To exclude the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*)—since even the eating of poison is an object of the desire of some trustworthy person (such as God) insofar as it is achievable through an effort (*kṛtisādhya*), yet it lacks the property of being a means to a desired end—the phrase "conveyed by the *liṅ* suffix" is included.

In the Vedic context, however, the authoritative person (*āpta*) is indeed God (*īśvara*). Regarding Him, they say that the injunction (*vidhi*) itself is the proof—just as the presence of a pregnancy in a maiden is proof of union with a man.

Yet even this is not so; for since it is necessary that the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) and so forth be the cause of activity in order to prevent engagement in what is unachievable, fruitless, or undesirable, the occurrence of activity is accounted for simply by accepting that "being a means to a desired end" and so forth are the meanings of the injunction. There is no evidence for the intention of the authoritative person (*āptābhiprāya*) to be the meaning of the injunction, because no one's activity is ever observed to arise from the mere cognition of being the object of the authoritative person's desire without the cognition of being a means to a desired end.

Furthermore, since there is deviation in the case of independent activity, it is impossible for the knowledge of the intention of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) to be the motivator; enough said on this point. Let us return to the subject at hand. This has been explained in detail; the meaning is that the refutation of the view that the knowledge of being unaccompanied by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) is the motivator, as well as the determination that the knowledge of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is the motivator, has been established. The detailed exposition, however, is essentially as previously stated.

The phrase "by the word *ādi*" (and so forth) means by the word *ādi* as used in the expression "in incitement (*preraṇa*) and so forth. Regarding the sentence "one who should threaten a Brāhmaṇa," the understanding is that there is a hundred-year torment resulting from such an attempt at killing, which has as its object the Brāhmaṇa who is the objective of the attempt at killing initiated by a particular agent. This is because the suffix *liṅ* is prescribed here for the abstract state (*bhāva*) of the two meanings of the verbal root, according to the rule: "The *liṅ* [is used] in the sense of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumat*)."

The sense is that since the Veda possesses authority by virtue of either inciting to action or restraining from it, when it is understood that [the passage] is intent upon the cessation of the effort to kill, the injunction "therefore one must not leap over" is inferred. Intending to show that the word *mātra* has the sense of "entirety," he says: "in the general sense of the past. By this, he indicates the scope for the *laṅ* and other suffixes when a specific [past tense] is intended to be expressed, stating: "the *luṅ* [is used] in the past. The meaning is: having taken the governing rule "in the past," [it follows] from the sūtra "the *luṅ* [is used]."

Is it not the case that "pastness" (bhūtatva) consists in having an origination that is the counter-positive of a present destruction? For this very reason, even during the state when the destruction of a jar is still present, the expression "the jar is destroyed" is used, because its origination possesses a present destruction as its counter-positive. And thus, where the root-meaning itself is origination, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the origination appearing in two ways; therefore he says "here," meaning in the rule *bhūte* [Pāṇini 3.2.84]. [The phrase] "present," etc., [is explained as follows]: [Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary argument regarding the definition of "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) and its implications for the verbal root *bhū* ("to be/originate") in grammatical rules.]

Nor is the aforementioned fault applicable; for in our view, since verbs such as *naśyati* (perishes) signify an operation conducive to destruction, and since the temporal relation is established as residing precisely within that operation, there is no possibility of that [fault] arising. Furthermore, because [the meaning of the suffix] is not constituted by origination (*utpatti*), a dual manifestation [of the action and its result] is impossible. In fact, it should be understood that, in order to justify the usage "the self existed" (*ātmā āsīt*), it is necessary that the meaning of the *laṅ* suffix includes pastness (*bhūtatva*) as well, just like futurity, and that this pastness is necessarily constituted by origination. The phrase "in the action" (*kriyāyām*) means "in that [action] which is conducive to the result."
