By the use of the particle *api* in the phrase "even when [the action] exists" (*vidyamāne 'pi*), it is indicated that if one were to accept the temporal connection with the *kāraka* (participant) denoted by the verbal suffix—on the grounds of its proximity as being presented by the same suffix—then the aforementioned usage would be untenable.

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that because the meaning consisting of mere non-inclusion of origination (*utpatti*) is simpler (*lāghava*), the word *bhūta* has its primary denotative power (*śakti*) precisely in that sense. Nevertheless, they argue that in cases such as *naśyati* ("is perishing"), since no operation other than destruction (*nāśa*) is experienced, it is necessary for the suffix to have a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) toward a meaning consisting of origination.

"Past with regard to the future" means that when the meanings of the two roots related as cause and effect are understood to be either past or future. By the phrase "due to the relation of cause and effect, etc.," the word "etc. includes relations such as capacity (*śakti*) and so forth. Regarding this, he provides an example for the future sense: *suvṛṣṭiśced abhaviṣyat*. Here, there is an understanding of the relation of cause and effect between two aspects of the very same root-meaning, distinguished by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of their being agent and object; however, in the subsequent example, the distinction is that those two are different in their essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The mention of the cognition having "the supreme absence" (*paramabhāva*) as its qualificandum is for the purpose of demonstrating that both verbal root meanings possess a future state. However, the following verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is more appropriate: "An operation conducive to the softening (*viklitti*) residing in rice, which is produced by a future flaming residing in a locus non-different from fire."

The term "prayojya" (that which is caused) is an expression of being caused by the absence of an operation; its mention serves to demonstrate the causal relationship between the kindling of the fire and the cooking of the rice, based on the rule: "That whose absence is caused by the absence of another is produced by that [other]. Thus, in the present context, once it is understood that the absence of the cooking of rice is caused by the absence of the kindling of the fire, the causal relationship between their respective counter-correlates becomes easily understood. This is the intended meaning. Such being the case: "If this pair, whose beauty is mutually desirable, had not been brought together..."
In this pair, the Lord’s effort to fashion the forms of his subjects would have been fruitless.

It should be understood that [the author] would have said "mañ" or "uñ," and would have followed the rule for *yaṇ* and so forth. One should understand that [the examples] such as "if Devadatta had not existed" are to be explained in this manner; thus he says, "in this way. And this [suffix], meaning that which is prescribed by the rule "laṭ for the present tense" and so on, applies even to other meanings—namely, to the sense of "fitness," "praise," "proper time," and so on. In these cases, such as the present tense and others, the expressive power (*śakti*) consists either in the form of a convention (*saṅketa*) or in the form of a distinct category of meaning (*padārthāntara*), whereas in the case of the sense of "fitness" (*ārhadyartha*), it is otherwise.

"Anubandhakrama" means the sequence of suffixes (anubandhas) beginning with 'a'. Now, an objection may be raised: where there is no perception of a suffix such as *tiP* and so forth, there is an inconsistency in both positions—whether [the word] is expressive (*vācaka*) or indicative (*dyotaka*). This is because, since the expressive or indicative element is absent, it is impossible to account for the cognition of "present time" and so on. To this, he says "dig" (direction/indication). The meaning of that is as follows: under the view that "the word (*pada*) is expressive," expressiveness is superimposed upon it through the conceptual division of base and suffix; thus, it is the power of the word itself [that conveys the meaning].

It is explained as follows: where the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is not heard [in the utterance], there the expressive power for that meaning is attributed to the suffix alone which is heard. As they say: "That which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided. For this very reason, in cases such as *vyatise* and *iyān*, the understanding of the meaning of the root arises from the suffix alone.
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) in the *Bhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. 2.

Intending to first explain the meaning of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is subordinate to the meaning of the word ending in a suffix (*subanta*), and because [the latter] requires an action (*kriyā*)—a connection based on the context of the occasion—he says, "The meaning of the *sub* [is as follows].

"The substratum (*āśraya*) is the meaning" means that it possesses a state of being a substratum not delimited by any particular attribute (*dharma*). Consequently, there is no contradiction even though the meanings of the fourth and fifth cases—the intended object (*uddeśya*) and the limit (*avadhi*)—are themselves of the nature of a substratum. He states the proof for the second case having the substratum as its meaning with the words beginning "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

Now, one might object that according to the literal meaning of the rule *kartur īpsitatamam*, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is established only for that which is the qualificand of the desire to obtain something related to the agent, and not for that which is the locus of the result produced by the action; therefore, he says: "by virtue of possessing the result produced by the action. The intended meaning is this: the word *īpsitatama* is derived from the root *āp* (to obtain) with the desiderative suffix *san*, followed by the past passive participle suffix *kta*, and finally the superlative suffix *tamap*, which serves to indicate the excellence of the primary meaning of the base.

And because of its connection with that [agent], the genitive case is used for the agent according to the rule "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67). Thus, since the agent is presented [in the cognition], the definition of the object (*karman*) results as follows: it is that which is the most desired object of the agent's intense desire—desire residing in the agent and characterized by the mode of being connected to a result produced by an operation—by means of its own operation. Consequently, that which is the substratum of the result produced by the action attains the status of being the object.

If it is argued that when the object is already established by the root itself—as in the case of the suffix *san* prescribed for desire by the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*—then since the root ending in *san* (which signifies the desire for pervasion) incorporates the object in the form of pervasion, it becomes intransitive like the root *jīv* (to live); how then can there be the formation of a past passive participle (*kta*) with an object from such a root? It should not be said so; for in the definition of being an "object" as "that which is incorporated within the meaning of the root," the specific qualification is that the meaning of the root [ending in *san*] does not require any other object than the one belonging to the root that serves as the base (*prakṛti*) of the *san*-suffix. Thus, the object of the base root is indeed the object of the derived root.

Because the stated state of being intransitive (*akarmaka*)—due to the requirement of another object—is impossible in the case of a desiderative form (*sannanta*), it must be understood that although the desiderative, being a complex formation (*vṛtti*), lacks the status of being transitive (*sakarmaka*) insofar as it does not have an object coreferential with its own constituent meaning, it nevertheless possesses transitivity by virtue of having an object coreferential with something external to that formation.

Thus, since that [action] also consists in being expressive of an operation that is non-co-referential with the fruit of the root-meaning by way of the relation delimiting the state of being a fruit (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), there is no impossibility of the accusative suffix (*karmapratyaya*) following roots such as *iṣ* ("to desire"). Even for the root *jighrati* ("to smell"), there is indeed a requirement for another object distinct from its own meaning, namely an object such as a flower; for a flower functions as an object (*karman*) because it is construed as the qualifier (*prakāra*)—as determined by a relational subject-objectness (*viṣayatā*) residing in itself—within the ordinary objective relation (*laukika-viṣayitā*) defined by the act of smelling.

In the case of the expression "rādhyati kṛṣṇāya" (he seeks [fortune] for Kṛṣṇa), since its meaning is "he deliberates upon the auspicious and inauspicious [fate] of Kṛṣṇa," the action of the auspicious and inauspicious—which is already included within the root-meaning—does not require another object; thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition of intransitive]. However, in the case of verbs such as "bubhūṣati" (he desires to be), since the action of "becoming" and so forth—which does not require another object—is included within the scope of the delimiter of the root-meaning, their intransitivity is quite evident.

Thus, it should be understood that just as in the usage of the *bhāṣya* "svar-yate," where the object of the modification of form (*rūpa-vikṛti-karman*) requires the proximate word-form as the base object (*prakṛti-karman*), the suffix denoting the object is justified from the causative (*ṇijanta*) of the root *kṛ*. Some, however, maintain that although a verb ending in *san* and so forth is intransitive because its meaning is subsumed within the verbal root's meaning, the suffix denoting the object is justified from it by taking the transitivity of its base.

[Objection: But even so, how can that which you have stated—which does not include "desired" (iṣṭa)—be the definition of an object (*karman*)? To this he says: "It is thus connected" (*tathāyuktam*). Since the conventional usage of the term "object" applies without distinction even to things that are hated (*dveṣya*) or indifferent (*udāsīna*), it is appropriate that the definition be one common to all of them. If, however, its definition were restricted only to that which includes "desired," there would be the fault of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding objects that are hated and so forth. Therefore, the sense is that for the sake of being common to all these cases, this [definition] alone is fit to be adopted. "In this very way" (*evameva*) means "in exactly this manner."

[Objection: But if the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) has the meaning of "object" (*karman*) as stated, then in examples such as *hariṃ bhajati* ("he worships Hari"), it would be untenable for Hari and so forth to appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) as being "desired to be reached" (*īpsita*) and so on; therefore, he says: "Regarding [the states of] being desired and undesired. The phrase "by the absence of appearance" means by the universal absence of such experience. [Objection: In that case, let the Sūtra simply state that "an object is that which is the substratum of a result produced by the action"; why then does he say: "Only regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*)"?

This is the intended meaning: although the technical designation [of *karman*] would be established for both the desired (*īpsita*) and the undesired (*anīpsita*) without distinction by the formulation of the rule "the locus of the fruit produced by an action is the *karman*," nevertheless, in examples such as "he wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the boy—who is intended as the recipient of the fruit produced by the action—would also incur the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) by the specific rule "of verbs meaning 'to ward off'" (*vāraṇārthānām*). However, the rule [defining *karman*] is intended to apply to cases such as "he worships Hari" (*hariṃ bhajati*).

To avoid that [objection], the state of being "most desired" (*īpsitatamatva*) is included within the scope of technical definitions (*saṃjñā*). Consequently, the subsequent sūtra is intended to provide the technical definitions for "aversion" (*dveṣa*) and "indifference" (*udāsīna*), which were not previously obtained; thus it is said, "so it should be stated. Now, one might object: even so, just as with the ablative case, the accusative case does not denote the mere substratum (*āśrayamātra*), but rather something specifically qualified. To this, he says:

And so it is said: "The substratum alone. By the particle *eva* ("alone"), there is the exclusion of the qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*) from being the denotable meaning (*śakyatva*). Now, one might object: since the nature of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) consists of the specific individualities (*svarūpa*) of those respective things, and thus differs from one substratum to another, how can it serve as the delimitor of the denotable meaning (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), given that only a recurring, common property (*anugatadharma*) can function as such? To this, he says: "And that [nature]," which means "and the nature of being a substratum. It is of the nature of an indivisible power (*akhaṇḍaśaktirūpa*). Here, "power" (*śakti*) refers to a property (*dharma*); that is to say, it is a property whose form is not composed of other categories of existence (*padārtha*).

The meaning is that its existence as a distinct category is established—just like "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and so on—due to the consistent usage of the term "substratum" (āśraya) and because the word "substratum" possesses a delimitor of its denotative capacity (śakyatāvacchedaka).

The Naiyāyika, however, [argues]: it is impossible for a substratum-hood (*āśrayatā*)—whose nature is restricted to being determined by something other than itself—to function as a unifying factor (*anugamaka*). Furthermore, even the property of being a delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) cannot serve as a proof for its being a partless entity (*akhaṇḍatva*), because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "being either one or the other" (*vibhinnānyataratva*). Thus, the second case-ending does not have "substratum" as its meaning, since that is already obtained by the verbal root itself, and because the substratum is not experienced from that [ending] as distinct from the meaning of the root. Rather, its meaning is simply the occurrence (*vṛtti*) in that which is connected with the result (*phala*).

Regarding the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case affix occurs when there is an object"), its purpose is to convey the intention (*tātparya*) that the second case suffix following [a noun] is used when it is construed with the "residing-ness" (*ādheyatva*) that culminates in the fruit (*phala*) of the action; thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, because it serves as a grasper of the beginningless intention and thereby indirectly grasps the expressive power (*śakti*), it is not redundant. However, "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) is not what is denoted by that [suffix].

Since it must be admitted that the connection with the result occurs through the relation of being the determiner (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*) alone, and since being a determiner is not a restrictor of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), it cannot be a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence; thus, [the sentence] "The bird goes to the ground" is not a violation of the rule regarding the case-ending, because in the view that "potency is the instrument" (*śaktiḥ karaṇam*), such a violation would be impossible. They say this because even the property of being the locus (*ādheyatā*) is a property of the instrument by virtue of being its determiner.

The meaning is that the technical designation "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*) applies because [the rice] is the substratum of the softening (*viklitti*). By this, it is stated that "object-ness" consists in being the substratum of a fruit of the action denoted by the root, which is distinct from the substratum of the operation denoted by that same root and is brought about by that operation residing in the agent. This is what will be stated later: "because of the aforementioned state of being brought about. In examples such as *agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the boy away from the fire"), the qualification "residing in the agent" (*kartṛgatatva*) is introduced for the operation in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the fire and other such things.

The meaning of the root *vṛ* (in *vārayati*) is an operation conducive to the absence of an operation that is itself conducive to conjunction. In examples such as "Caitra goes to the village," the term "residing in a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇa*) is used to exclude Caitra and others [from being the object]. This "residing in a different locus" means having its locus in something other than that [the action], and not merely not residing in that locus; for if it were the latter, there would be no application [of the definition] to the village and so forth, since [the absence of the operation] does not exist in conjunction. Furthermore, because such a locus qualified by that "residing in a different locus" does not exist in Caitra and others, there is no possibility of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

In expressions such as "he ties a horse to the beans" (*māṣeṣvaśvaṃ badhnāti*), the property of being the meaning of the verbal root in question (*prakṛtadhātvarthatva*) is a qualifier of the result [of the action], in order to exclude the beans—which are the substratum of the eating prompted by the tying—from being [the object]. Furthermore, the status of being "in question" (*prakṛtatva*) must be specified in each particular case. However, in cases such as "he eats rice with milk" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), the accusative case does not occur because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not intended to be expressed; for even when one who has already finished his meal proceeds out of a desire for milk, the state of being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) can still apply to the milk.

Now, since opponents accept that the root *kṛ* (to do) signifies merely effort (*yatna*), how can "origination" (*utpatti*) be the meaning of the verbal root in question? To this he says: "of origination. Thus, because it was previously established that *kṛ* has as its meaning the fruit consisting of origination, there is no lack of consistency in the sense. By stating "because it is the meaning of the verbal root," the impossibility of jars and the like being objects (*karman*) if *kṛ* signified mere effort is also implied as a defect. The phrase "the removal of concealment" (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*) is according to the view of the ancients.

However, in the view of Niṣkṛṣṭamatī, since the result in the form of knowledge exists in the jar and so forth by virtue of being its object (*viṣayatā*), it should be understood that they possess the status of an object (*karmatā*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence [of the verb] being intransitive, because there is no co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to the relation that delimits the nature of the result. As for the Nyāya school’s position, the manner in which jars and the like possess the status of an object in such cases has already been explained during the analysis of the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*).

[Objection: Granted that the destruction of an obscuration produced by cognition is possible in the case of an existing jar; however, since it is impossible in the case of a future or a destroyed jar because there would be no substratum for such destruction, the status of these jars as objects (*karmatva*) is untenable. To this, he says: "past and future" (*atītānāgata*). He provides the reasoning for accepting their status as substrata there with the words: "otherwise" (*anyathā*), which means: if the destruction of the obscuration were not admitted in those cases. The phrase "as before" (*yathāpūrvam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action of knowing (*jānāti*). It is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "not exceeding the meaning of its constituent parts" (*padārthānatikrāntau*); that is, "without deviating from what was previously [known]."

The meaning is as follows: "That in which there is no transgression of prior cognition" refers to the state of the existence of a jar. At the time when the jar exists, the cognition of that moment functions to remove the veil over that jar; however, at a past time, a modern cognition does not produce such removal. Since there is a transgression of the prior [cognition] due to its failure to produce that effect, and because the object—the absence of a cognition that has not transgressed the prior [state]—is uncontradicted, it follows that such usage would result in invalidity (aprāmāṇya). This is the sense.

The point is that if one accepts the production of the destruction of the veil by a new cognition regarding a jar that has already passed away, then because that [new] cognition does not transcend the previous cognition, the absence [of the jar] is sublated by it, and thus its invalidity follows.

[Objection: But when a jar has perished, how can it truly have that [cognition] as its locus? To this he says: "of the past, etc. By the word "etc.," the future is included. The sense is: just as for the Naiyāyikas, in accordance with experience, they accept that [the past object] is the locus of cognition by way of being its object (*viṣayatayā*), so too is it for us. [Objection: Granted that there is the cognition "the past jar is the object of cognition," let the past jar indeed be the locus of cognition by way of being its object; however...

However, since such a proof is not found in the case of [the theory of] being the locus of the removal of obstructions (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*), he says: "Because the effect exists" (*satkāryya*). He demonstrates this very point: according to the Śruti, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone," the collection of effects existed previously in a subtle form. According to the opponent's view, however, its manifestation occurs through connection with the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) intended as the producer. Its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is simply its abiding in a subtle form within the cause. It is designated as "it will come to be" only in that state.
Therefore, that which has fallen away from its state and has not yet attained the quality characterized by manifestation is said to be "born"; however, that which has attained manifestation exists.

[Objection: But if that [pot] exists at all times, how can there be the conventional usage "it does not exist" or "it is destroyed"? To this he says: "the admission of concealment. When concealment is manifested by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that manifests concealment, the conventional usage "it does not exist" or "it is destroyed" occurs. However, when that [concealment] has attained its sequential development, the usage "it is being destroyed" occurs; such is the established tenet of the Satkāryavāda (the doctrine that the effect pre-exists). The point is that even though the pot is concealed in the present case, it exists in a subtle form; therefore, it is easily obtainable as the locus for the result, which consists in the removal of the veil.

He raises an objection (*nanu*) in order to clarify the previously stated definition of "extracted objecthood" (*niṣkṛṣṭa-karmatva*). The phrase "of disjunction" (*vibhāgasya*) is to be understood as "produced by action," and so forth. Now, one might argue that even if the technical designation of "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*) is sublated by the subsequent designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*), the actual state of being an object (*vāstava-karmatva*) remains unsublated therein; thus, such a usage [with an accusative] could still occur. To this he replies: "In the production of the second case ending" (*dvitīyotpattau*). This is said with reference to the present context, because the production of a case-ending denoting a *kāraka* is governed solely by that [designation]. Otherwise—that is, if the designation were not a regulator—[such a usage would follow].

The second [reason] is because of the occurrence [of the same state]: the point is that just as in the sentence "He causes Kṛṣṇa to go to Gokula," there is the status of being the locus of the fruit—which is the action of the verbal root consisting of an operation conducive to the conjunction produced by the operation signified by the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—so too in the sentence "He has Kṛṣṇa cook the rice with [fuel]," there exists therein the status of being the locus of an operation conducive to the softening (*viklitti*) produced by such an operation.

The meaning of "verbal cognition" (*śābdabodha*) is that the verbal cognition is: "an activity residing in Caitra, directed toward a conjunction, performed by Caitra, and occurring in the present. The underlying intention is that this [cognition] is not sublated, as its object is uncontradicted. The phrase "for those who have such a linguistic competency" means for those who maintain that the apprehension of the locus (*āśrayopasthiti*) is a cause of verbal cognition through the relation of being the qualifier (*prakāratā*) as determined by the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) of the fruit, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The intention is that cognition conforms to one's own respective linguistic competency.

Since there is no experience of a verbal cognition whose object is the operation of the agent Caitra as the performer of the action of going—as in the sentence "Caitra goes to the village"—he says, "Or let it be stated... [that] there is another causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). The point is this: by postulating a causal relation in general, one avoids the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by qualifying [the object] as "not having as its locus the operation denoted by the verb in question. Since the cause is the presentation of such a locus, there is no occurrence of such a verbal cognition. The term "co-occurring" (*samabhivyāhṛta*) means "pertaining to the subject at hand" (*prakṛta*).

The phrase "because it has already been largely stated" (*uktaprāyatvāt*) refers to the beginning of the passage starting with "the status of being an object (*karmatā*) [arises] because it is the locus of the softening (*viklitti*) which is the meaning of the verbal root. Since the verb *gam* (to go) was not mentioned there separately, the word "largely" (*prāya*) was used. However, in reality, it should be understood that by defining "fruit-ness" (*phalatva*)—as the state of being the object of a presentation produced by that verbal root, while being produced by the meaning of that same root—the definition of "object-ness" as "being the locus of a fruit that resides in a different substratum from the operation" already precludes over-extension (*anatiprasaṅga*). Therefore, one should note that the aforementioned qualification does not need to be inserted separately.

He introduces the Naiyāyika position in order to refute it, saying: "The Naiyāyikas, however... The phrase "the first fault" means the contingency of such usage as "Caitra goes to Caitra. The phrase "the second [fault]" means the contingency of such usage as "Caitra, who is going from Prayāga to Kāśī, goes to Prayāga. The expression "being the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root" is stated according to the view of those who maintain that the meaning of a verbal root consists of an operation delimited by a result (*phala*).

And thus, according to that view, the meaning of the accusative case ultimately results in being "the state of being an object" (*karmatva*), which consists in possessing a fruit delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The meaning is that, regarding the causal relation, a distinct cause is postulated: the cognition produced by the verbal root (*dhātujanyopasthiti*)—standing in the relation of being a qualificandum delimited by the nature of productive activity (*bhāvanātva*)—is the cause of the verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) with respect to the property of "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*), which is the meaning of the accusative, through the relation of being a particularity (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by its own mode (*prakāratā*).

[Objection: Since difference (*bheda*) is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) property, everything is "other" (*para*); thus, even Caitra’s action is inherent in something other than Maitra. Therefore, even if one accepts that [the action] is denotable by the word [‘para’], the aforementioned fault remains as it was. To this, he says: “And ‘otherness’ (*paratva*)... Due to the diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—namely, the action—connects with “otherness,” which is a part of the referent of the whole word, as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). In the present case, because there is a contradiction in the action that produces Caitra’s conjunction being inherent in something other than Caitra, the expression “Caitra goes to Caitra” is not used.

And where there is a conjunction of two wrestlers due to the actions of both, although the action of one wrestler—which produces a conjunction residing in itself—subsists in something other than itself (the second wrestler), there is no such usage as "the wrestler goes to himself" (*mallaḥ svaṃ gacchati*). This is because such an action is obstructed with respect to itself; for even if the subsistence in something other than itself does not appear in the action of oneself that produces a conjunction residing in oneself due to its unfitness, a verbal cognition is still possible by taking as its object the fact that the action produces an unobstructed conjunction, just as in cases such as "one should sacrifice while practicing exorcism" (*abhicaran yajeta*).

It should not be suspected that the usage "he goes to himself" (*svaṃ gacchati*) would be unavoidable on the grounds of its having that as its intended meaning; for it is nowhere accepted that there is a cognition—dependent on the accusative case—that produces a result while not having the aspect of being "inhering in another" as its object, and such a cognition requires the presence of the causal complex for the manifestation of that aspect, which is absent in the present case.

Now, since even "self" is distinct from what is delimited by duality, in order to prevent the usage "he goes to himself," one must maintain that the meaning of the base of the accusative case is construed with the meaning of the verbal base through the relation of having a counter-correlate delimited by the delimitor of the base-meaning.

Likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the invalidity of sentences such as "Caitra goes to the substance" (*caitro dravyaṃ gacchati*) and "The wrestler goes to the wrestler" (*mallo mallaṃ gacchati*), because the action residing in Caitra, the wrestler, and so forth, is not co-referential with that which is delimited by the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) or the property of being a wrestler (*mallatva*)—which are the delimiters of the meaning of the base of the second case (*dvitīyā*). Furthermore, even when the specific individuality (*tad-vyaktitva*) is not presented [by a word], verbal cognition is established by experience; therefore, it is impossible for the relation to occur through a counter-correlativity delimited by that specific individuality, and there is an absence of any word capable of presenting that specific individuality.

Furthermore, there is no evidence that a counter-correlativity delimited by one property can have a relation delimited by another property; for the cognition of an absence qualified by its counter-correlate is invariably governed by the rule of apprehending a "qualified-qualificand" (viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya).

As stated by the author of the *Dīdhiti*: "The manifestation of an absence qualified by its counter-correlate does not transcend the limits of the cognition of a qualified-qualificand. If this is argued, then the meaning of the accusative case is the state of not being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the difference connected with the verb. Since the meaning of the verbal base is understood as residing in the difference [rather than in the object], the aforementioned undesirable consequence and logical inconsistency do not arise.

Furthermore, when used in conjunction with the negative particle *nañ*, by virtue of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), in expressions such as "Caitra does not go to Caitra," there is understood the absence of being the delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the difference from that object, as qualified by its occurrence in the meaning of the base of the accusative case. In some instances, such as "Caitra does not go to the village," there is understood the absence of being a generator of conjunction (*saṃyoga-janakatva*), which is the meaning of the verbal root, as qualified by its occurrence in the meaning of the accusative case; this is understood in relation to the action (*kriyā*).

However, those who maintain that the occurrence of the stated undesirable consequence is avoided even without accepting that the meaning of the accusative case is the "delimitingness of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in its own locus," by instead accepting that the action (kriyā) is construed with the result—such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—which is qualified by its occurrence in the sense of the verbal root, through the two relations of being the generator and being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in its own locus; in their view, because a relation that does not regulate occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*) cannot be a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absence, the negative particle (*nañ*) in the aforementioned instance [cannot negate such a relation].

Otherwise, there would be the impossibility of understanding the absence of conjunction, and there would be a contradiction with the *Dīdhiti*, which states that "the meaning of the second case-ending is 'inherence in another'.

Thus, the refinement of the Naiyāyika position regarding the sentence "Caitra goes to the village" is as follows: Caitra is the possessor of an effort conducive to an action (*kriyā*) which produces a conjunction residing in the village, and which is the delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference residing in the village.

Here they raise an objection: since it has been established that the negative particle (*nañ*) in a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) must be construed with the action as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), how can the negative particle in such expressions as "Caitra does not go to the village" (*caitro grāmaṃ na gacchati*) convey the absence of the production of conjunction? For it has been said:
"That is to be known as *paryudāsa* (relative negation) where the negative particle is connected with the following word;
but *prasajya-pratiṣedha* is where the negative particle is connected with the action."

The meaning of the second half [of the verse] is that where the absence, which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), becomes related by way of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) to the action—the operation denoted by the verbal root. Therefore, when a negative particle occurs in conjunction with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), it is logically correct that there is only a cognition of the absence whose counter-correlate is the action; however, it is not [correct] to assume the absence of the result in the action, the absence of the case-meaning (*vibhaktyartha*), or the absence of the finite-verb meaning in the meaning of the nominative (first-case) subject, because the established grounds for such [meanings] are lacking.

On this point, they say: "When, upon the utterance of the negative particle (*nañ*), the state of being delimited by a certain property (*yaddharmmāvacchinnatva*) in that which is delimited by another property (*yaddharmmāvacchinne*) is apprehended through a particular relation (*saṃsarga*), then, upon the utterance of the negative particle, the absence of that [latter] thing—delimited by that [former] property and having as its counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*) that which is delimited by that relation—is understood in that which is delimited by that [former] property. This is a matter established by the experience of all people, as formulated by the author of the *Dīdhiti* when he stated: "The connection of the counter-positive and the absence share the same locus of application (*tulyayogakṣema*)."

And thus, in the case of "Caitra goes to the village," when the negative particle (*nañ*) is not co-uttered, there arises a cognition of the action as possessing the property of being a generator of conjunction qualified by the denotation of the accusative case; when that negative particle is co-uttered, how can the resulting cognition of the absence of that [conjunction] in that [action] be prevented? Nor can it be denied on the grounds of a causal deficiency, because the presence of the object capable of being construed with the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—as the cause for the verbal cognition through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the mode (*prakāratā*) of the absence which is the meaning of the negative—is present in the action.

However, the presence of the verbal root-generated upasthiti (cognitive presentation) of an action is not the cause for a cognition [of negation] by way of the relation of being a non-mode (aprakāratā) qualified by a qualificandum-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*); for otherwise, sentences such as "Caitra does not go to Caitra" would result in being invalid, because since a counter-positive consisting of an act of going having Caitra as its object and Caitra as its agent is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), it would be impossible for the negative particle to convey its absence.

In my view, however, although an action performed by Caitra produces a conjunction residing in Caitra, the property of being the delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of a disjunction residing in Caitra does not exist in that action; thus, because the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys the absence of that property, the validity [of the cognition] is established. For this very reason, it is also necessary that "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) be the meaning of the accusative case.

Nor should it be argued that, even in your own view, since Caitra is not the object (*karma*) [of the verb], how can the use of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) be justified after a word denoting him in the aforementioned instance; for in the sentence "Maitra goes toward Caitra, not [toward] himself" (*maitro gacchati caitraṃ na caitram*), the use of the accusative is justified because there is no contradiction regarding both meanings of the accusative—the possession of a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by Maitra's action, and being the locus of the conjunction belonging to him. More will be said on this point later.

Furthermore, because of the common usage that "Caitra is not the object" in sentences such as *caitro gacchati* ("Caitra goes"), the nature of being an object (*karmatva*) must be defined as follows: it is the state of being the locus of a result of the verbal root's meaning which is (a) distinct from its substratum, (b) brought about by an operation of the verbal root's meaning that is excluded from the agent (*kartṛ*), and (c) [in the case of transitive verbs] related to all [aspects of the action]. In this context, although both the result and the operation are obtainable from the verbal root, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others must be admitted for the following reasons: first, for the relation of subsistence (*vṛttitva*), which ultimately results in the property of being the counter-correlate of a difference (*bhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatva*); and second, for the property of having different substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). This is because these meanings cannot be obtained through any other means. Let us now return to our main subject.

"Conducive to softening" (*viklitty-anukūla*) refers here to an action inherent in something other than the rice grains (*taṇḍula*). He refutes the literal interpretation with the words "We do not accept that," and so forth. Now, one might argue that the heaviness [of the definition]—which includes the property of being inherent in another (*parasamavetatva*)—is not a fault, because without it, over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) cannot be avoided. To this he replies: "Why [should there be] over-extension? The meaning is that even if one accepts as the meaning of the accusative case the status of being an object (*karmatva*), defined as possessing a result which is delimited by the meaning of the verbal root produced by an action inherent in another, the over-extension remains exactly as it was. He states that very point with the example "He causes Kṛṣṇa to go" (*gamayati kṛṣṇam*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "due to the occurrence of a second [accusative]": if the aforementioned status of being an object (*karmatva*) were the sole determinant for the production of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) upon the occurrence of a second [object], then in the sentence *gamayati gokulaṃ kṛṣṇam* ("He causes Kṛṣṇa to go to Gokula"), since the aforementioned objecthood—defined relative to the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—exists in Kṛ�ṣṇa just as much as the objecthood defined relative to the meaning of the causative suffix that has *pac* as its base, there would result the undesired consequence (*āpatti*) of a second case-ending even in usages such as *pācayati* ("He causes [him] to cook") when used with a word denoting the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*). Therefore, one must accept that it is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) itself that is the cause for the production of the second case-ending.

And thus, since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is already avoided by that very designation, the view that there is a direct expressive power (*śakti*) for the second case-ending in that context is redundant; this is the intended sense.

[Objection: Surely, it is precisely such *kārakatva* (the status of being a factor of action) that is the regulator for the occurrence of the second case (*dvitīyā*). Even though that [status] exists in Kṛṣṇa in the aforementioned instance, there is no undesired consequence because the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthāśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) teaches that this status is not intended when the root is in the causative (*ṇijanta*) and differs from those roots whose meaning is "motion" (*gati*) etc., which were mentioned. This is because, as will be stated later, it is the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) alone that regulates the production of case-endings. [Response: To this he says: in the expression *taṇḍulaṃ pacyate*, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the existence of the *karmatva* (objecthood) defined by you as the regulator for the second case in relation to the rice (*taṇḍula*). However, in the view of our own school (*manamata*), there is the designation of agent (*kartṛsaṃjñā*)...

The sense is that there is no occurrence of that [karmasaṃjñā] because it is precluded by the technical designation *kartṛ* (agent). By the phrase "not inherent in anything other than the rice," it is indicated that the state of being softened (*viklitti*) possesses the quality of being produced by an action inhering in another. By the phrase "because of being the locus of the meaning of the verbal root," the existence of the designation *kartṛ* is made known. "By the very manner stated" means by the manner stated in the passage beginning with "those who have such a linguistic proficiency"; the sense is that there is an absence of the cause, which consists in the presentation of a locus that is not the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal root.

[Objection: "But even in our view, the aforementioned undesirable consequence (prayogāpatti) does not arise; for in that case, since it is admitted that the fruit (phala) appears as merely an operation (vyāpāra), the rice (taṇḍula) lacks the status of being a locus of the fruit that delimits the meaning of the verbal root. Furthermore, even in your own distinct view, the fruit is accepted as an operation by superimposing a temporal sequence (paurvāparya) onto the operation. To this, he states another refutation: "because of the state of being dependent on another" (parasamavetatvasya).

The phrase "iṣṭānvaya" means for the sake of the appearance—i.e., for the sake of obtaining the connection—of the desired [element], namely the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha), with the action; specifically, for the sake of obtaining the connection of "otherness" (paratva), which is one part of "being inherent in another" (parasamavetatva) through the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā), and of "inherence in another" itself, with the action by way of being its locus (āśrayatā).

The meaning is that there is excessive complexity (*atigaurava*) in postulating that the presentation of the locus of the action (*ādheyatva*), which depends on the accusative case, is the cause—via the relation of being a qualifier—for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*); and likewise, that the presentation arising from the verbal root is the cause—via the relation of being a qualificandum delimited by its operation (*vyāpāra*)—for a cognition whose qualifier is "being inherent in another" (*parasamavetatva*). This is because such a theory would require the assumption of causal relations for numerous instances.

In my view, however, there is no over-extension because, within the portion of the operation that is the object of the presentation of the operation—which possesses a causality established for the verbal cognition having the result as its qualifier—there is the inclusion of the qualification of "not occurring in what is denoted by the base of the accusative case. This is the intended meaning.

But [one might object]: in cases such as "Caitra and Maitra go to each other," since the activity denoted by the verbal root resides in the referent of the base of the second case (the accusative), there would be the undesirable consequence that the result does not reside therein; therefore, he says "clearly" (*spaṣṭam*). Thus, by the phrase "not residing in the referent of the base of the second case," what is intended is the state of being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in the referent of the base of the second case. Consequently, in examples such as "they go to each other," even though it is sublated that the action does not reside in "each other," [the definition remains valid].

It has been stated therein that there is no impossibility of the connection with the result (*phala*), because the status of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of a mutual difference (*parasparaniṣṭhabheda*) remains uncontradicted.
He states the classification of *karman* (object) made by Hari: "And that" means that *karman* is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the result produced by the action.

The phrase "that which, being non-existent, is born" is based on the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*). However, the phrase beginning with "or, being existent," etc., follows the Sāṅkhya doctrine. Immediately after [the word] "manifests" (*prakāśate*)—

The reading in the *Vākyapadīya* is: "But when the material cause (*prakṛti*) is intended [to be expressed], it is called *vikārya* by some; otherwise, it is called *nirvartya*. Otherwise, if one were to demonstrate the *vikārya*—which has not been characterized by its general property—in its specific form, there would be the fault of shifting the meaning (*arthāntaratā*). Its meaning is as follows: according to certain well-known teachers, when the material cause is intended to be expressed, that which is to be produced is called *vikārya*; otherwise, when it is not so intended, that which is to be produced is called *nirvartya*. This is the sense.

In such cases as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), although the material cause such as clay (*mṛd*) exists, it is not intended to be expressed as undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmin*). However, in cases such as "he makes ashes" (*bhasma karoti*), it is indeed intended as such, even though that [material cause] does not exist.

Although the state of being "to be produced" (*nirvartyatva*)—derived from the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) as "that which is brought about" (*nirvartyate*) or "that which is accomplished" (*niṣpādyate*)—is present even in the case of the "object to be modified" (*vikārya-karman*), as in "he cooks rice-grains into boiled rice" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*), there is no fault here. This is because we intend to define "being produced" in its technical sense (*pāribhāṣika*) as "the state of being brought about while being presented by a word that is not co-occurrent with a word denoting a material cause. As it has been said:

"Whether existing or non-existing, that for which a transforming material cause (*prakṛti*) is not relied upon is declared to be *nirvartya* (that which is produced). Here, "for which" refers to the object of the transformative action; "is not relied upon" means it is not employed, or rather, it is not intended to be expressed. The rest has been explained. The definition of *vikārya* (the modified), however, is: being characterized by the manifestation of a state of material cause while possessing as its fruit either a specific result brought about by the action or the production of something previously non-existent. In examples such as "he makes a jar," although there is a production brought about by the action in the *nirvartya* [object], there is no over-extension [of the definition] because the relation of material cause and modification does not appear therein.

The definition is consistent because the primary action (*prakṛtikarman*) lacks such a qualified existence, while the modified action (*vikṛtikarman*) serves as the locus for such an origination. In such cases, it is necessary that the verbal root (*dhātu*) signifies an operation that brings about two results. This has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The root *pac* has the sense of *hi* (to split). Otherwise, since even intransitive roots possess the property of having a single result and a single operation, there would be the undesirable consequence of the specific qualification being redundant.

Others, however, state that based on the Bhāṣya—"the root *pac* has two meanings"—the meanings of *pac* are both softening (*vikledana*) and production (*nirvarttana*), as evidenced by the gloss of "he cooks rice-grains into boiled rice" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*) as "softening the rice-grains while producing the boiled rice" (*taṇḍulān vikledayannodanaṃ nirvarttayati*). Thus, in the present case, the understanding is: "An operation conducive to the arising of the boiled rice, which resides in [the agent], and which is itself an operation conducive to the softening residing in the rice-grains. They say that this should be inferred similarly for cases such as "he turns wood into ash" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasma karoti*).

That is incorrect; for since the cognition of the manner of the activity (*bhāvanā*) cannot arise—given that the requirement for such a cognition is the presence, through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), of an apprehension produced by either a *kṛt* suffix or a verbal root within the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*)—and because it is possible for two results to arise from a single action alone, it is inappropriate to assume that the cognition generated by that sentence has two operations (*vyāpāra*) as its objects. This is because, according to Kaiyaṭa on the *rūpap* sūtra, one understands from the word *ākhyāta* only an action characterized by a distinction of cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Furthermore, if the root *pac* were to signify two distinct operations according to the Navya (Neo-Nyāya) view, it would be impossible to convey duality in the action; consequently, the occurrence of a dual ending in the sentence "Caitra cooks rice-grains into porridge" (*caitras taṇḍulān odanaṃ pacataḥ*) would be unavoidable.

In reality, however, *vikledanam* means softening or dissolution, while *nirvarttanam* means simply production, because both these words end in the abstract suffix *lyuṭ*. Thus, the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that the meaning of the verbal root is a single operation conducive to two results. It should be noted that the claim by some that it signifies two operations is based solely on the misconception that those two words end in *lyuṭ* derived from a causative (*ṇijanta*) base.

Although it would have been more appropriate to state that the object to be modified (*vikārya*) is of two kinds—namely, the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*)—nevertheless, with the intention that once the twofold nature of the modification is understood, the status of being a modified object is already practically known even regarding the material cause, he does not mention that [distinction] and instead divides the modified action (*vikṛtikarman*): "by the destruction of the material cause" (*prakṛtyuccheda*). By this, it is implied that the nature of being the material object (*prakṛtikarmatva*) consists in the absence of something to be accomplished by the action and the possession of the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakadharma*).

In such instances as "he makes a mat from *kāśa* grass," "he makes a garland from flowers," "he makes earrings from gold," "he makes a jar from clay," "he reduces wood to ashes," and "he cooks rice-grains into porridge," there is an absence—brought about by the action—which has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) the *kāśa*, wood, and so forth, characterized by their prior state and consisting in a specific mode of existence (*viśiṣṭasattvarūpa*). The application of the definition to each respective base (*prakṛti*) consists in the fact that the *kāśa*, wood, and so on, possess the property of being delimited by the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of that [absence] characterized by the prior state.

In all cases where there is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*), since the presence of the qualification of such a counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakavaiśiṣṭaya*) would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the phrase "accomplished by action" (*kriyānirvāhya*) is used to mean that it is accomplished by the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verb in question. In some instances, the qualified absence—which brings about results such as ash or cooked rice—is produced solely through the destruction of the substratum (*dharmin*), such as wood or rice grains.

In other instances, even while the substratum exists, the non-existence qualified by a prior state consisting in the absence of a specific arrangement, such as a mat or a garland, is brought about by the action, resulting in the production of that mat-arrangement or the like.

The term *sambhūtam* means that which possesses an origination brought about by the destruction of its material cause (*prakṛti*). And this [term] is connected with the word *bhasmavat* (like ashes); the word *kāṣṭhādi* (wood, etc. is a separate word [from *bhasmavat*], otherwise wood, gold, and so forth would incur the status of being the fourth [category]. By the phrase *bhasmavat*, the meaning is that other collections of transformations (*vikāra*) also exist by virtue of their similarity to those [ashes]. And this similarity consists precisely in having an origination brought about by the destruction of the material cause. The same applies hereafter as well. Thus, the meaning is that it is a transformation (*vikārya*), such as wood, ashes, and so on, which has entered into the state of being both material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*).

It culminates as follows: thus, in the case of "He turns wood into ash" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasma karoti*), the meaning of the verb *karoti* consists of two results—namely, destruction qualified by counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) and production—and the activity conducive to them. Because the wood is construed with the destruction as its counter-positive and the ash with the production as its locus (*ādheyatva*), the resulting cognition is: "an existing activity conducive to the destruction whose counter-positive is the wood, which brings about the production of ash. This applies similarly in cases such as "He cooks rice into boiled rice" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*).

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that in the case of a *vikārya* (object undergoing transformation), such as in the sentence "He cooks rice into porridge" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the accusative case following the material object (*prakṛti-karman*) is "causing destruction," while the accusative following the product object (*vikṛti-karman*) signifies "bringing about production. The destruction associated with the rice and so forth is construed with the act of cooking. The bringing about of production associated with the porridge is construed with the cooking as qualified by the destruction. Furthermore, by the force of the relationship between the subject and the predicate, the fact that production is the instigator of destruction appears [in the cognition].

Therefore, although cooking destroys the conjunction that originates the rice grains, there is no such usage as "he cooks the destruction of the conjunction"; for the destruction of the conjunction that originates the rice grains is rendered superfluous (anyathāsiddha) by the destruction of the rice grains itself, which occurs upon the production of the cooked rice (odana). Thus, it is not the instrumental cause.

In reality, however, in order to prevent the usage "he cooks the conjunction" (*saṃyogaṃ pacati*)—which would otherwise occur just as in the case of "he cooks the rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*) when not co-uttered with a transformative action (*vikṛti-karman*)—the meaning of the accusative case must be stated as being the status of being a destroyer through the mediation of destruction. Thus, even though the relationship between the instigator and the instigated (*prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva*) appears in the present instance, there is no deficiency. Consequently, the cognition is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to that operation which is the producer of cooked rice (*odana*) and the destroyer of the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*). And in such cases, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is expressed by the verb ending in the passive voice (*karmākhyāta*).

For this very reason, in expressions such as "the pieces of wood are being turned into a heap of ashes," the verb agrees in number with the word "wood" (kāṣṭha), and not with a word denoting the transformation product such as "ashes," because of the rule that number must be construed with the agent of the productive operation (bhāvanā).

Now, an objection may be raised: since there is a grammatical rule stating that for roots such as *duh* (milk), the object expressed by the verbal suffix (*karmākhyāta*) refers to the non-primary object, whereas for roots such as *nī*, *hṛ*, and *kṛṣ*, it refers to the primary object—as in the rule "for *nī*, *hṛ*, and *kṛṣ*, [the suffix denotes] the primary [object]"—there is a restriction that the two types of objecthood are not denoted [simultaneously]. Consequently, in the present case, since both types of objecthood are equally present, there would be no obstacle to the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denoting even the objecthood residing in the modification (*vikṛti*). However, this would entail the undesirable consequence that the verbal suffix would have the same number (*vacana*) as the modification; for it is said: "The denoter [the suffix] does not take the number of the modification, but rather that of the original base (*prakṛti*)."

Thus, [the view] is refuted by postulating that the cause of the cognition of the number associated with the modification—which is established by the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*)—is the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)-generated expectancy (*upasthiti*), which is not grasped as being intent upon the number associated with the original base (*prakṛti*).

Otherwise, how could such usages as "the pieces of wood turn to ash" be explained? If one objects thus, we say no; for in the case of "the pot and the cloth are seen," since there is no cognition of a single common delimitor of the objecthood (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) for both, if both the modification and the modified were the objects of the verbal suffix's meaning, it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Nor can it be argued that this is an unintended consequence; for if that were the case, then just as the cognition produced by the sentence "the wood is destroyed, ash is made," the cognition produced by the sentence "the wood is made into ash" would likewise fail to eliminate the doubt as to whether ash is a modification (*vikṛti*) of wood or a modification of something else. This is because, since there is no difference in their capacity to generate a cognition based on a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), the relation of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) between wood and ash cannot be obtained from the stated sentence.

Only when there is indeed a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatā*) is it possible to obtain—by means of the restriction on the intention to express a qualified relation (*viśiṣṭānvaya*)—the state of being the instigated (*prayojya*) and the instigator (*prayojaka*) in the case of an agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*); likewise, in the case of an objective suffix (*karma-pratyaya*), by the very force of the restriction of that intention, the status of being a modification of wood (*kāṣṭhavikṛtitva*)—in the form of "having an origination instigated by the act of removing ash from the fire" (*bhasmani kāṣmaṭhocchedaprayojyotpattikatva*)—is obtained through the objective middle voice (*karmātmanepada*).

Nor does the occurrence of the accusative case follow from a word denoting a modification (*vikṛti*), because even though the status of being the object of the modification is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), the accusative cannot occur since it is admitted that such [objecthood] is merely a relation to the action which serves as a qualifier for another objecthood; for the opportunity for the accusative and other cases arises only when one intends to express objecthood and so forth as the primary qualificand of the nominal stem's meaning (*prātipadikārtha*).

But this is not the case; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) that one could say "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*). This is because we accept that an object (*karman*) appears in a relation of objective case (*karmatā*) only when its meaning possesses the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) of the agency of another action within an action that has not itself attained the status of being qualified by another [distinct] objectness. For this very reason, the expression "he makes the wood into a heap of ashes" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasmarāśiḥ karoti*) is not used, because the heap of ashes does not possess the status of being the qualificand of the agency of another action. And thus, expressions such as "look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*) are justified.

And in the present case, just as in expressions such as "the blue pot comes into being" (*nīlo ghaṭo bhavati*), where the blue color and so forth are construed with the coming-into-being—which is of the nature of an uncommon property—by way of the relationship of agency consisting in being the locus (*ādheyatva*), so too, by a peculiarity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), the object of transformation such as ashes is admitted to be construed with the effort that is the meaning of the verbal root *kṛ* (to do/make), which has become a qualifier of the object of the base (*prakṛti*), by way of the relationship of objecthood (*karmatā*). Thus, since the status of being a single sentence is established, the resolution of the aforementioned doubt is logically justified.

Thus, the understanding arising from the sentence "The wood is being turned into a heap of ash" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasmarāśiḥ kriyate*) is that the pieces of wood are the counter-correlates of a destruction brought about by an action related to ash, wherein [the wood] functions as the producer. Since the relation is not intended to be the primary qualificand of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur there either.

Thus, even in cases such as "the clay is not a pot," where there is a relationship between material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), if one accepts the rule that the accusative case is grammatically correct when it expresses an object that is construed with the meaning of the verbal root without becoming a qualifier for another object, then the aforementioned application of the accusative does not arise in that instance; nor is there any lack of justification for [the accusative] in examples such as "the cow is milked for milk."

Likewise, even in cases where there is a superimposition (āropa) of duality delimited by unity—as in "one [is known] as two" (*eko dvau jñāyeta*) and so forth—the verb must agree in number with the word denoting the superimposed object (*āropya-viśeṣya*). Poets employ such usage: "Though single, this ball appears as if three. Nor is the reading there necessarily *bhānti* (they appear); for otherwise, how could one explain: "By him his own pair of infamies was acknowledged—that his hair was bound in two tufts and remained upon his head"?

It should be stated that here Śrīharṣa has employed the verb "amāni" (was considered) as a verbal expression equivalent to the pair of his own [the king's] imposed infamies; for even there, since the pair of infamies established in the first half of the verse is real, the poet has merely imagined them as being superimposed upon the king’s two locks of hair tied with cords. Therefore, they say that even in that case, there is no room for the fault of the "unpolished predicate-part" (*amṛṣṭavidheyāṃśatā*).

On this point, some maintain that because of the usage in the *Mahābhāṣya*—"The gold ball, having returned, becomes earrings of the same color as khadira wood when joined with another form"—the verb expresses only the number of the modified (vikṛti) object. As for the statement, "The denoter does not grasp the number of the original (prakṛti), for [it belongs] to the modification," that refers exclusively to the domain of the *cvī* suffix. Thus, usages such as "pieces of wood are being made into a heap of ash" are simply ungrammatical (*asādhutva*).

Others, however, maintain that by the qualification "having the color of khadira-wood embers," the status of the two earrings as the material cause (*prakṛti*) is understood there, because an already established effect does not require further cooking. By the qualification "endowed with another form," on the other hand, the gold lump is understood as the effect (*vikṛti*), since the assumption of a different form does not necessitate its being the material cause. And this is appropriate;
for just as in the statement "Only clay is real," the status of the gold lump as an effect is understood through the perspective of dissolution by the qualification "returned again."

For instance, since the series of forms previously introduced culminates in that [gold], the eternality of gold—which was intended to be proven—is established. Therefore, it can also be argued that the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra is simply this: that gold, characterized by the form previously specified, is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the earring and so forth, while that same gold, characterized by another unspecified form, is its modification (*vikṛti*). Consequently, the mention of that [gold] does not serve as supporting evidence for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) having the same number as the modification (*vikṛti*).

In this regard, the following appears: according to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), since both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) possess agency (*kartṛtva*) in the present context, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must denote two agents. Likewise, regarding the number associated with them, since it is impossible for a single verbal suffix to express the number of those two which possess conflicting numbers, the Lord [Pāṇini] stated "the two earrings come into being" (*kuṇḍale bhavataḥ*) using only the number belonging to the modification (*vikṛti*). However, there is no decree of the Three Sages (*munitraya*) stating that the number belonging to the material cause is not to be conveyed by the verbal suffix.
And thus, by virtue of its usage, it is beyond dispute that the verb may, in turn, have the same grammatical number as either one [of the two subjects].

"Produced by an action" (*kriyākṛta*) means: being the locus of the result, while not being the locus of the objective status (*viṣayatā*) in a cognition whose qualifier is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) prompted by that action. The first part of the definition (the "locus of the result") is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to things such as the "produced" (*nirvartya*). Even there, if one were to include [only] "not being the locus of objective status," or "not being the locus of objective status in a cognition whose qualifier is a property," or that [objective status] which is composed of an uncommon property—as in "he knows the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*)—this would be impossible (*asambhava*) in the case of the jar and so forth; therefore, the term "prompted by the action" (*kriyāprayojya*) is a qualification of the property.

In that very context, the term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) is used to exclude the non-pervasion [of the definition] with respect to objects such as a village, which are the locus of the cognition of a connection with an uncommon property to be brought about by the action. The qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is used to exclude over-extension (*atiprasakti*) to that which is not the substratum of the result produced by the action.

Nor should it be argued that the general definition is over-narrow (avyāpti) because there is no fruit produced by an action in cases such as "he knows the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), and that if one were to posit the "removal of obscuration" (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*) in that case to avoid this, then—since that very removal would be an uncommon property induced by the action—the specific definition would be over-narrow due to the absence of the "existence-qualifier" (*sattvānta*), given that it becomes the object of a valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by inference, such as: "This jar has been known by him, because it is the object of his usage. [The objection fails] because [the definition applies] provided that [the agent] is distinct from the agent... provided that [the agent] is distinct from the agent... [and so on].

Since the purport of the stated definition is that [the object] is the locus of the fruit produced by an action common to both the agent and the object, and since it is also the locus of the fruit consisting of cognition by way of being its object (*viṣayatā*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the general definition. Even if the definition is applied to the objects of verbs such as "to know" (*jānāti*) by taking the fruit to be the removal of an obstruction (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*), one must nevertheless follow the aforementioned method in order to avoid the lack of pervasion in the case of the objects of verbs such as "to desire" (*icchati*). He states examples according to the order of mention, beginning with "a jar" (*ghaṭam*). "The first" (*adyam*) means that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*); the same applies to what follows.

"Not designated by other technical names" (saṃjñāntarairanākyātam) means that [the action] is not intended to be expressed through those specific forms such as "ablative-ness" (apādānatva) and so forth. In the rule *akathitaṃ ca*, the word *akathita* refers to what is "not intended to be expressed," and not to what is "non-primary. The reason for this is that if it were otherwise, the designation *karman* would undesirably apply to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the sentence "he milks [milk] into a bronze vessel with his hand" (*pāṇinā kāṃsyapātryāṃ dogdhi*). This is because, since the roots *duh* and others are specifically enumerated [in the rule], the two designations [of instrument and locus] find their scope in connection with roots such as *kṛ*. This is the underlying intention.

Thus, it should be understood that its application occurs when there is no intention to express what would otherwise be implied by a previous rule, and when that previous rule is not applicable in any way whatsoever. Although the designation "object" (*karman*) for the cow is established by the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* (Pāṇini 1.4.49) alone—since even the operation conducive to the operation conducive to separation is the meaning of the root *duh*—there is no inconsistency in this regard, because the cow is the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) by virtue of being the locus of the result which qualifies the operation residing in the agent.

Since the operation residing in the cow (*go*) that is conducive to the separation of milk (*payas*), and which is itself conducive to [the agent's] operation, is primary according to the verbal expression, this sūtra appears to have a purpose that is otherwise established; nevertheless, if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is only the operation conducive to separation, then this sūtra is necessary for the sake of [establishing] the status of the object (*karman*) when the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth is not intended, as that status would not be reached by other rules. In this sense, because of the grammatical rule "for *duh* and others, when the [object] is not primary," the suffixes *la* and so forth appear on *go* and the like.

And being a non-primary object (*apradhāna-karman*) consists in being distinct from the objects already mentioned. This remains intact for cows and the like in the aforementioned sense, because they are not the substrata of the result that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, according to this view, the meaning of the root *duh* (to milk) is an operation conducive to a separation residing in a liquid substance. In that context, when the cow is not intended to be expressed as the ablative (*apādāna*), it receives the status of an object by this rule; when it is so intended, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used. However, when the cow is construed with the milk (*payas*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. And thus, the resulting cognition is: "An operation, having a single agent, which is conducive to a separation residing in the milk, and which has the cow as its object."

The status of the cow as the object (*karmatva*) consists precisely in its being the locus of the separation (*vibhāga*). In the first alternative (*kalpa*), however, [the meaning of the verb is] an operation residing in a single agent, which is conducive to an operation residing in the cow that is itself conducive to a separation residing in the milk. In that case, the milk has the status of an object because it is the locus of the separation; whereas the cow [is the object] because it is the locus of the operation conducive to that [separation], and not because it is the locus of the separation itself, since the relation belonging to the separation residing in the milk alone serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the fruit (*phala*). This should be inferred similarly in other cases as well.

The term *anyapūrvakam* means that which is taught by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) preceded by the sublation of another technical designation (*saṃjñā*). For example, in the expression *krūram abhikrudhyati*, the designation of *sampradāna* (recipient) which would otherwise apply by the rule *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ* is sublated by the rule *krudhadruhorupasṛṣṭayoḥ karma*. The same should be understood in cases such as *vaikuṇṭham adhiśete*.

In examples such as "he causes the goat to go to the village" (*ajāṃ grāmaṃ gamayati*), "he causes the disciple to understand the scripture" (*śiṣyaṃ śāstraṃ bodhayati*), "he feeds the Brahmin food" (*brāhmaṇam annaṃ bhojayati*), "he makes the sacrificer recite the mantra" (*yajamānaṃ mantraṃ pāṭhayati*), and "he produces or destroys the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ janayati nāśayati*), the *gaty-arthādi-sūtra* prescribes the technical designation of "object" (*karma*) for the agent of the action expressed by roots such as *gam* (to go). Consequently, even in the case of the accusative case-ending associated with a causative (*ṇijanta*) root derived from such verbs as *gam*, its meaning is the locus (*āśraya*).

Although the status of *aja* (the goat) and others as the object (*karman*)—because they are the substratum of the result in the form of an activity produced by the instigation (*preraṇā*) which is the meaning of the causative root (*ṇijanta*)—is already established by the rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*), nevertheless, this sūtra is for the purpose of a restriction (*niyamārtha*). [The restriction is: if [the objecthood] occurs through the causative, it belongs only to that which is the substratum of the activity whose meaning is motion (*gati*) and so forth. Therefore, in examples such as *pācayaty odanaṃ devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to cook the rice"), [Devadatta is not the object]. As it has been said:

"Because of his independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), he who has attained the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the primary command (*preṣaṇa*) is designated by his own grammatical property (*svadharmeṇa*), due to the restriction on the technical term 'object' (*karmasaṃjñā*)."

The meaning is "by means of the third case [ending] residing in itself through the relation of denotative power (*vācakatā-sambandha*).
