In that context, the root *sic* (to pour) denotes an action conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) residing in a substance. When co-occurring with words such as "water," its meaning is merely an action conducive to conjunction. The dative suffix, however, denotes "residing in" (*vṛttitva*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "an action delimited by a conjunction residing in the tree, which belongs to the water," and so forth.

In this context, since the same cognition would arise from both the fourth (caturthī) and second (dvitīyā) case endings, the designation *sampradāna* is taught so that the second case does not occur [in such instances]. However, in examples such as *vṛkṣaṃ payasā siñcati* ("he sprinkles the tree with water"), the second case indeed occurs after the word *vṛkṣa*. In that case, the meaning of the third case is non-difference (*abheda*), which connects with the liquid substance; whereas the meaning of the second case, namely "residing in" (*vṛttitva*), connects with the conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "an action of a substance non-different from water, which is conducive to a conjunction residing in the tree."

In the expression *śatrave 'straṃ muñcati* ("He releases a weapon at the enemy"), the meaning of the dative case is "having suffering as its objective. *Mocana* (releasing) is an action delimited by separation (*vibhāga*), or rather, an operation conducive to that action. The base-meaning [of the verb] relates as a locus (*vṛtti*) to "suffering," which is one part of the meaning of the dative case. Similarly, in *mitrāya dūtaṃ preṣayati* ("He sends a messenger to a friend"), the meaning of the dative is "having the delivery of news as its objective. In *putrāya dhanaṃ preṣayati* ("He sends wealth to his son"), the meaning of the dative is "having affection as its objective. They say that such cases should be inferred accordingly.

That is not correct; for the dative case occurs in the sense of a recipient (*sampradāna*). Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the status of "recipient" as you have described it, by which the dative would apply in the case of *vṛkṣāya*. Moreover, since there is no difference in its connection with the meaning of the verbal root—namely, the action of conjunction—the dative would also result after the word *udaka* (water). As for the counter-argument that [the dative] is barred because [the water] is the object (*karman*), that remains unimpaired even in the case of the tree; thus, this [position of yours] amounts to nothing. "This very thing" means precisely that which was defined as the state of being the intended goal (*uddeśyatva*). "In the Pūrvatantre" means in the Mīmāṃsā.
"For this very reason" means precisely because the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) is the motivator for the ritual act being for the sake of another purpose.

The phrase "like the throwing away" (*prāsanavat*) means that this is according to the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] which states: "The giving of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is like the throwing away, because its purpose has been fulfilled. The analogy of the throwing away is as follows: it is heard in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: "When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been led away, he throws the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) into the *cātvāla* pit. This means that when the sacrificial fees given by the sacrificer have been received by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificer should then throw the black deer-horn held in his own hand into the pit named *cātvāla*.

In this regard, a doubt arises: is this act of throwing away (*prāsana*) a primary ritual act (*arthakarma*), or is it a disposal act (*pratipattikarma*)? It must be a primary ritual act, because it serves a purpose. As for the prima facie view that it would be purposeless if it were a disposal act due to the absence of an *apūrva* (transcendental result), [the reply is]: since the statement "he scratches himself with the black antelope horn" indicates that the horn has already served its purpose and thus requires disposal, it is logical that it is indeed a disposal act.

And it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is no lack of purpose (*anarthakya*), because even though there is no *apūrva* resulting from the act of throwing [the staff], there exists a restrictive *apūrva* (niyamāpūrva) in the rule that it must be thrown specifically into the *cātvāla* pit. The application is that, therefore, the giving of the staff is not a disposal (*pratipatti*). The phrase "in this section" (*ity adhikaraṇe*) implies "in the fourth chapter.

Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice itself, it is stated in the injunction for the Soma sacrifice, "He gives a staff to the consecrated one," which establishes the staff as a manifestor of consecration (*dīkṣābhivyañjaka*); furthermore, in the Soma sacrifice, the scripture states: "He gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest."

Regarding the doubt as to whether the giving of the staff (*daṇḍa*) is a disposal-rite (*pratipatti-karman*) or an act for the sake of attaining a purpose (*arthapratipatti-karman*): the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the staff was given by the Adhvaryu for the sake of accomplishing the initiation (*dīkṣā*), it has already served its purpose by being held by the sacrificer from the time of the purchase of Soma onwards; therefore, the giving of that used staff is merely a disposal-rite. However, because of the scriptural injunction, "The one with the staff recites the *praiṣas*," the staff is required by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest as a support while he is reciting the *praiṣas*.

And thus, because there will be a future utility [for the staff], and because the giving of the staff is a primary act (*pradhāna*) by virtue of being both the object of the act of giving and the object of the act of taking, it is appropriate that the disposal-rite (*pratipatti-karman*) consisting of the giving of the staff be considered a purposeful act (*arthakarma*). This is because it functions as a purification (*saṃskāra*) for what is about to be used, rather than a purification for what has already been used; for everywhere, the application of purificatory rites proceeds precisely for the sake of making something fit for use.

However, since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the act of acceptance would terminate merely in an act of honor (*satkāra*) once [the object] has been used, there would be no completion of the purpose; therefore, it is considered improper. Consequently, the gift is a primary ritual act (*arthakarma*) for the sake of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s refinement. This being the case, it was established in the Siddhānta that even in the case of the *nirūḍhapaśu* sacrifice, although the sacrificer is not yet initiated (*dīkṣita*), this very gift is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the preparation of the staff.

And when there is the status of being an object (*arthakarmatva*), the state of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) is the motivating factor. That [status] is understood from the Maitrāvaruṇa by means of the direct hearing of the dative case (*caturthi-śruti*); thus he says: "by the direct hearing of the dative. Now, one might raise the objection: where the root *dā* has meanings such as "bringing under control," since the recipient-status (*sampradānatva*)—defined as being the object of desire (*icchā-viṣayatva*)—is possible even for a washerman and so forth as the determiner of the result in the form of subordination (*ādhinatva*), then such usages as "he gives cloth to the washerman" (*rajakāya vastraṃ dadāti*) and "he gives a camel to the Hotṛ priest" (*hotre uṣṭraṃ dadāti*) would result as unintended consequences. This doubt is addressed by accepting the point as desired (*iṣṭāpatti*).

He avoids [the fault] by saying "for the washerman. He presents the authoritative evidence for this with the example "the teacher Khaṇḍika. His intention is that in the case of the root *dā* (to give), there exists the status of being an intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*), which consists in being the object of a desire characterized by a connection to the meaning of the verbal root *dā*, namely, the act of conjunction. In this usage, the root *dā* signifies an operation conducive to conjunction. The meaning of the word *capeṭā* (a slap) is an outstretched palm. However, in the expression "one should not give instruction to a Śūdra," the root *dā* signifies the act of making known.
It should be understood that the referent of the word *mati* (instruction/knowledge) is the Veda and other scriptures that produce such knowledge.

The operation (*vyāpāra*) consists of a desire for the destruction of one's own ownership, which is delimited by the arising of another's ownership. "Meaning" (*artham*) means the meaning of the verbal root *dā* (to give). Thus, their intention is that the status of being a recipient (*sampradāna*) is simply being the object of a desire on the part of the agent to be a participant in the result residing in the object of the action denoted by the root *dā* as previously described. Due to the force of establishing this etymologically significant technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*), and because the root *dā* does not have that [specific] meaning in the aforementioned instance, they maintain that in such cases it is only expressed as "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*).

On account of the authority of the aforementioned commentary, the fact that [the term] is etymologically meaningful is indeed unestablished. Furthermore, the employment of this great technical designation (mahāsaṃjñā) is merely out of deference to the predecessors, just as in the case of the technical designation "sarvanāmasthāna"; because of this lack of conviction, he says, "they say" (āhuḥ).

If it is argued that in the expression *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* ("he leads the goat to the village"), since the goat (*ajā*) possesses the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*) as defined [by Pāṇini 1.4.32], a dative case ending would necessarily follow from its designator—this would indeed be the case if the status of being a recipient were not sublated by the subsequent technical designation of "object" (*karman*). In expressions such as *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"), however, the dative is not used in the sense of a recipient; rather, it expresses *tādarthya*. *Tādarthya* means "having that very thing as its purpose or object. When there is a desire to express *tādarthya* with respect to a meaning co-occurring [with the word], the dative is used from the designator of that [meaning]. This is the meaning of the Vārttika: "The dative should be prescribed in the sense of *tādarthya*."

Furthermore, being a purpose (*prayojanatva*) does not consist in being produced (*janyatva*), for that would lead to the absurd conclusion that "evil is for the sake of suffering" (*duḥkhāya pāpam*). Nor does it consist in being an object of desire by virtue of being produced, for since heaven and the like are objects of desire because they are produced by merit and the like, this would lead to the absurd conclusion that "merit is for the sake of heaven" (*svargāya puṇyam*). This is not an acceptable consequence, because if that were the case, the formulation of the rule *tumarthācca* (Pāṇini 2.3.15) would be rendered useless; for that rule was formulated to justify the usage "he goes for the sake of cooking" (*pākāya vrajati*) in the sense of "he goes to cook" (*paktum vrajati*).

Since [the word] *pāka* (cooking) and the like denote the very actions such as "going" (*vrajana*) mentioned above, the dative case is justified by the Vārttika [Pāṇini 2.3.13] precisely because it expresses that meaning. Rather, [the meaning of the dative] is being the object of a desire that follows a desire for an operation residing in the referent of the word co-occurring [with the dative]. The state of being "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), which consists in having that as its purpose, is the state of being the locus of an operation that is the object of a desire dependent upon that [primary] desire. Since wood (*dāru*) possesses an operation in the form of carving and so forth, which is the object of a desire dependent upon the desire for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it has the status of being "for the sake of the post" (*yūpārtha*). With the intention to express this, the dative case is applied according to the rule *yūpāya dāru*.

The meaning of that [suffix] is the state of being the locus of an activity which is the object of a desire dependent on [another] desire. In the first desire, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth, which are the objects of the activity aimed at engagement, are construed as the objective; its locus is in the wood (*dāru*) and so forth. Some maintain that this should be understood similarly in cases such as "a pot for cooking" (*randhanāya sthālī*).

There is nothing more charming than this: for if that "being for the sake of" (tadārthyam) were of the form already stated [as mere desire], then in the expression *sukhāya hariṃ bhajati* ("He worships Hari for the sake of happiness"), the dative case would be untenable. This is because worship does not possess an activity whose object is a desire dependent on a desire for liberation; nor does liberation possess the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*), since it is not intended as the beneficiary of a result produced by an action. Therefore, being the object of a desire dependent on that [primary] desire is precisely what constitutes "being for the sake of" that. Let it be that in cases such as *svargāya puṇyam* ("merit for heaven"), it is indeed intended [in that sense].

Furthermore, because the author of the Sūtras did not proceed [to provide a rule] after seeing the Vārttika, the [separate] sūtra "tumarthāt" is also unnecessary. Even when used in conjunction with words such as *namaḥ* (salutation) and *svasti* (well-being), the fourth case ending is prescribed by the sūtra "namaḥ-svasti... from a word that denotes a specific meaning of those [words]. In this context, the meaning of the word *namaḥ* consists of both renunciation (*tyāga*) and prostration (*nati*). Among these, prostration (*nati*) is an activity conducive to making known one's own inferiority. Renunciation (*tyāga*) occurs in instances such as "salutation to Hari" (*haraye namaḥ*) and "this offering is for Śiva" (*eṣo 'rghaḥ śivāya namaḥ*). And in those cases, the fourth case ending conveys the state of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*).

If renunciation (*tyāga*) consists in the absence of the desire for one's own ownership—taking the form "let this belong to Śiva" rather than being dependent on a desire for a fruit such as "let it be mine"—then the status of being its objective (*uddeśyatva*) is the state of being the object of the volition that produces the renunciation by virtue of being the possessor of ownership.

If the very desire in the form of renunciation takes as its object the ownership residing in the thing being relinquished by virtue of it belonging to another, then its status as the objective (viṣayatva) precisely because it is the locus of ownership constitutes its status as the intended recipient (uddeśyatva); it does not consist in being the substratum of acceptance (svīkāra), for even though Śiva and others possess a physical form, they lack acceptance, and furthermore, according to the view that the mantra meditated upon in that form is the intended recipient of the renunciation, such [acceptance] is absent there as well.

Even when there is an absence of ownership as defined by Śiva and others in the case of an object being relinquished through ritual offering (*upacāra*) and so forth, the desire that arises with respect to that object is nonetheless of a nature that does not contradict the apprehension of ownership (*svatva*) therein as belonging to Him. It apprehends either the fact that the ownership of another is sublated [in favor of] being defined by Śiva and others, or it apprehends the lack of connection to that object in the case of another well-known form of ownership defined by Śiva and others which is itself sublated.

In that regard, in the first case, the meaning of the dative case is either "being produced by an intention whose mode is ownership" (*svatva-prakāraka-icchā-janyatva*) or "the state of possessing such an intention" (*tādṛśecchāvat-tva*), related by the relation of being produced (*janyatā-sambandha*). In that context, the referent of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), such as Śiva, is construed with it through the relation of a specific objecthood (*viṣayatā-viśeṣa-sambandha*). In the second case, that [meaning] is simply a specific objecthood. And in that case, the referent of the base, such as Śiva, is construed with it through the relation of being characterized (*nirūpitatva-sambandha*). The act of renunciation (*tyāga*), which is the referent of the word *namaḥ*, is construed with the substance such as the *argha* offering through the relation of a specific objecthood.

Alternatively, the connection [of the object] occurs by relinquishing its status as appearing as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the substance itself. As in examples such as *śivāyotsṛjati* ("he offers to Śiva"), there is no status of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) for one who is not the agent of rejection here, because the word *namaḥ* is not a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, by the word *namaḥ*, renunciation (*tyāga*) is understood specifically as being colored by the fact that its agent is the person who utters it; for a renunciation belonging to one person is not conveyed by the word *namaḥ* uttered by another. This is because, when a renunciation is understood from the word *namaḥ* uttered by a particular person, no doubt arises regarding the ownership of that renunciation or of the object being renounced. For this very reason, in order to convey that sense of ownership, one does not employ expressions such as "I am *namaḥ*" (ahaṃ *namaḥ*), as one would say "I give" (*ahaṃ dade*).

When an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) performs an act of renunciation of a substance belonging to another person in the form of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), he employs the word "namas" in worship only after superimposing (*āropya*) ownership upon that substance. This superimposition is justified as being a mental construct (*āhārya*) during a state in which the [actual] specific nature of the object is perceived. Just as a statement regarding a gift made by means of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) produces its result, it is not contradictory for a sentence containing the word "namas" used in worship to produce transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭa*) despite having a sublated meaning; this is due to the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra-prāmāṇya*). Further details on this are found elsewhere.

The meaning is that it is the *sampradāna* (recipient), defined by the rule "that which one aims at through an action," as indicated by the phrase "one knows this [as such]. This is to be construed with the term "threefold. The construction is as follows: that which is desired by the agent as part of the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) receives the designation *sampradāna* due to three reasons, beginning with "not being rejected by the agent. Being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the relinquishment means being perceived as a qualifier of the verbal root-meaning co-uttered with it, by way of the relation of being the determiner of the objective state (*uddeśyatā*) residing in itself.

Therefore, in expressions such as "he sprinkles water for the tree" (*vṛkṣāyodakam āsiñcati*), there is no redundancy regarding the tree and so forth. In fact, according to the view of the author of the *Vṛtti*, this distinction [between the object and the recipient] does not exist; thus, there is no harm even if the tree and so forth are not included [in the category of the object]. Consequently, it should not be explained as "in the meaning of the verbal root co-occurring [with the dative]. And this qualifier—[expressed by the phrase] "because of non-rejection" (*anirākaraṇāt*)—states the factor that determines its distinction [from other types of objects]; the meaning is: because of being devoid of an activity conducive to another activity. "That which is desired by the agent" (*karmaṇepsitam*) means: an object of desire by virtue of being a participant in the result produced by the action.

"Instigation" (*preraṇā*) means the communication to an agent who has not yet acted that a particular act is a means to a desired end; it is the impelling of an agent whose resolve has become slack due to doubts regarding the authority of that communication by presenting a means of valid cognition capable of dispelling such doubts. Alternatively, "consent" (*anumati*) is the state of possessing an activity conducive to the mere acceptance of results such as ownership (*svatva*) residing in the object of the action; the meaning [of the compound] is "by those two."

"Non-exclusion" (*anirākartṛtva*) consists in being the object of a desire [on the part of the agent] to be a recipient of a result produced by the action denoted by the verbal root, while lacking any activity conducive to either the engagement or the withdrawal of the agent. "Incitatory agency" (*prerakatva*) consists in possessing an activity that serves as a means for the cognition that the object—being such as described above—is a means to achieve a desired end, with respect to actions such as giving away [the object], which are related to the agent; other such definitions should be inferred accordingly.

Regarding the statement "he gives an *arghya* offering to the Sun," according to different philosophical views, the meaning of the root *dā-* (to give) is either a renunciation consisting of the desire for the absence of one's own ownership dependent on the desire for another's ownership, or a renunciation consisting of the desire for the absence of one's own ownership directed toward the object of another's ownership. The understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*), however, should be inferred along the lines indicated by the rule "namaḥ svasti... (*Pāṇini 2.3.16*). The phrase "in all cases" means not only in the case of words ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) prescribed by that specific rule. Regarding the phrase "non-difference is the relation" (*abhedaḥ saṃsargaḥ*), the meaning is that a relation characterized by non-difference is the "qualifier" (*viśeṣa*) that governs the cognition of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-buddhi*).

The point is that, with respect to a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the base (prakṛti) as related by identity (abheda), the cause is the mental presence (upasthiti) produced by a suffix other than one whose meaning is a relation (sambandha).

As for the claim that—since a relation is necessarily restricted by its relata, and since there is no evidence for non-difference being a relation—the relation of non-difference is a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) that is not delimited by any other relation—that is not so; for even the qualifier-qualified relationship is necessarily restricted by a [further] relation, and in the absence of that [relation], it too would be impossible. For this very reason, the author of the *Ṭīkā* states that "the state of being a qualifier is the status of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of a manifested relationality (*vaiśiṣṭya*)."

Otherwise, how could it be explained that [the word *parārthatvāt*] "requires" (its correlate) because a qualifier cannot exist without a connection to that which is intended as the qualificand—expressed by the words "even though this [reason] resides in two [loci]"? For this very reason, [the author] himself provided the explanation.

Nor should it be argued that if identity were the relation [between quality and substance], there would be the undesirable consequence of a genitive case in expressions such as *nīlo ghaṭaḥ* ("the blue pot"). For, according to the authority of the Bhāṣya—which explains the occurrence of the genitive in cases like *rāhoḥ śiraḥ* ("Rāhu’s head") by taking recourse to a relation of difference based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*)—it is understood that the genitive occurs only when the relation is rooted in difference, namely: "this part, the head, which possesses a single state, [belongs to] Rāhu, who possesses many states. Since this is the case, it is impossible for the genitive to be applied when the relation is one of non-difference (*abheda*).

Alternatively, such a commentary may not intend for the relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*) to be the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, the necessity of a relation being restricted by the difference between its relata (*sambandhibheda-niyatatva*) is simply unestablished. If one insists that it must indeed be restricted by difference, then for the sake of universal consistency, let it be accepted that the very difference in the delimiters of the relatum-ness (*sambandhitāvacchedaka-bheda*) is the regulating factor.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for that relation, because the very cognition of a qualified object—such as blue and so forth—which is established for all, serves as the proof. Furthermore, the factor that regulates the manifestation of that [relation] in verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consisting in the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of specific stems and suffixes, as well as of the referents of co-referential nominal bases (*prātipadika*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* "arthavat": "The sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is that which is the final determination upon a particularity of these words when they are functioning in a state of common reference (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)."

This is according to the view of the proponents of *anvitābhidhāna* (the theory that words denote meanings as already related), because in their system, it is only the related meaning (*anvita*) that constitutes the word-meaning. Thus, the meaning is this: words denoting relations in a general form possess the capacity to convey the specific qualification of being related to respective correlates (*anuyogi*) and counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), such as [the relation] "of this" and so forth. Due to the convergence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, that very [related meaning] becomes the sentence-meaning, which is the object of the cognition produced by the sentence. Alternatively, such a designation is made with the intention of referring to the power (*śakti*) residing in the sentence itself.

In the Bhāṣya on the *prātipadikārtha-sūtra*, regarding the statement "The co-referentiality of words (*pada-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) must be added as a supplement because [the meaning] is more than [the nominal stem]," since in examples such as "vīraḥ pūruṣaḥ" (the brave man), there is the manifestation of a relation of non-difference (*abhedasaṃsarga*)—which exceeds the meaning of the nominal stem and serves as the basis for the qualifier-qualified relationship—the first case ending (*prathamā*) would not apply because the meaning of the nominal stem alone is not present; therefore, a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the first case must indeed be initiated. Consequently, there is no contradiction with that [Bhāṣya] either.

Even Kaiyaṭa, in the context of refuting that [interpretation] with the words "na vākyārthatvāt" (not because it is the meaning of a sentence), abandoned the word *pratipādita* (established) and employed the word *ūhita* (implied). By doing so—stating that "the first case ending is prescribed after the nominal stem *vīra*, which rests solely on its own meaning (*svārthamātra*) because the state of being a qualifier is not implied by another word"—he has accepted that the relationship with something else (*itarasambandha*) alone is the determinant of the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa*) relation.

In reality, however, the status of the relation between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as a [single] relation is untenable, because—as you yourself have stated—a relation is necessarily restricted by the difference between its two relata. Furthermore, since the analysis of the term *viśeṣyaviśeṣaṇabhāva* (the state of being qualified and qualifier) results in its being nothing more than the states of being the qualified and the qualifier individually, and since these two states reside in each one of them separately, even if their co-residence (*dviṣṭhatva*) were established through the properties of the locus (*anuyogitva*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), that co-residence would belong to only one of the two, not to both together.

Because the mere following of a word [by another] determines the object—just as in the case of the relation between owner and owned—the genitive case occurs in other relations, but there is no evidence for its occurrence in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*). Therefore, the previously stated view alone is elegant. [Objection: Since it is established in other systems (*tantra*) that case-endings (*vibhakti*) denote properties (*dharma*), how can the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) be construed there through identity (*abheda*), given the lack of fitness? To this, he says: "of the case-endings," which means "of the case-endings denoting grammatical functions (*kāraka*). "Because they denote the substratum" (*dharmivācakatvāt*) means "because they are expressive of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*)" [rather than the power itself].

"Let it be that the meaning is indeed the *śakti* (power); therefore, he says: 'because [the sūtra] would suffer a violation of its natural sense (*svarasa*) regarding the denotation of the property (*dharma*). The meaning is this: since the intended sense is obtained without attributing the status of denoting a property (*dharmaparatā*) to the words *karman* and so forth contained within that sūtra, the fact that it is devoted to that [denotation of the property] clearly results in a violation of its natural sense. The implication is that if the author of the sūtra had intended such a meaning, he would have simply stated, 'the second case-ending occurs when there is the state of being an object (*karmatva*),' and so on."

[Objection: Is it not the case that in "karmaṇi" and so forth, the meaning is understood through a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*)? And thus, even if case-endings denote a property (*dharma*), since that [property] connects with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) by way of being its locus (*āśrayatā*), the action is understood from the base; therefore, even according to the view that the meaning of the accusative is simply the occurrence (*vṛtti*) in that which is connected to the result of the action, there is no violation of the natural sense of the Sūtra, because rice and the like appear as the object (*karman*)—which is the locus of the result—by virtue of being known through the same cognition. To this, he says: "having the meaning of 'object' (*karmārthaka*). [This refers to] in cases such as "the rice is cooked" (*pakvastandulaḥ*).

In the case of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), as in "a horse that is capable" (*śatyo’śvaḥ*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the *śānac* suffix, which is a substitute for the present tense marker (*laṭ*), as in "the rice being cooked" (*pacyamānastaṇḍulaḥ*).

"Because it is observed to be so" means because it is observed to denote the substratum (*dharmī*). Thus, the sense is that just as the *kta* suffixes and others prescribed by rules such as "of those [words] containing the pronoun *tat* which refer back to the object" (*karmaparamarśaka-tacchabda-ghaṭitayoḥ*) are understood to denote the substratum, here too it is logical that they denote that very same thing.

[Objection: "Granted that in those cases [of *samānādhikaraṇa* compounds] such a status [of denoting a substance] may exist because of the impossibility of coreferentiality with another word-meaning; but here, since there is no occurrence of the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*āpatti*), let it be that [the compound] denotes a property (*dharma*) itself. To this, he says: "denoting the meaning of the second case, etc. For if the second and subsequent case-endings were to denote properties, then a compound formed with words prescribed for those meanings would also necessarily denote a property. Consequently, in examples such as *prāptodakaḥ*, the meaning of the compound—the objecthood of the attainment whose agent is water—would have to be expressed by a word ending in the same case-ending [as the other member].

The point is that since the impossibility of non-differentiation (abhedānvaya) in cases such as "the village reached by foot" (*padopasthāpya-grāma*) remains active here as well, it is necessary that the words *karman* and so forth in the sūtras prescribing the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others denote the substratum (*dharmivācaka*).

[Objection: But even in your view, since the genitive case has "relation" as its meaning, there is an equal difficulty in establishing the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word-meaning for a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed with that [genitive] sense; for in that case too, coreferentiality must be explained either through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) or through a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*). Thus, if it can be resolved in that same manner elsewhere, what is the point of [positing] that case-endings denote the substratum (*dharmin*)? To this, he says: "The meanings of case-endings are also [things like] the object (*karman*) and so forth."

The point is this: if properties such as "objectness" (*karmatva*) were intended to be expressed by the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) and so forth, then one would have said, "the meanings are objectness and the rest. Since that was not stated, the status of these [properties] as the meanings of the accusative and other cases lacks authoritative support (*aprāmāṇika*), because they have not been mentioned in the three [standard] definitions [of case-meaning]. Adopting the position of the *Śaktivāda* (Doctrine of Expressed Power), he says: "Of the substratum also... The sense is that its manifestation as a substratum (*āśrayatvena bhānam*) is simply unestablished. The phrase "mere substratum-hood" (*āśrayatvamātram*) implies—by ellipsis—the accusative, instrumental, and locative cases. By the word "mere" (*mātra*), the exclusion of the substratum itself is intended.

Now, if being the locus (*āśrayatva*) is the denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*), then "locus-ness" (*āśrayatvatva*) must be stated as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); and since that is composed of the property of not occurring in anything other than locus-ness, it is cumbersome. Thus, the objection is that the very cumbersomeness of the delimitor of denotability constitutes a fault in this alternative. To this, he says: "That very [thing]"—meaning locus-ness itself. By the word "very" (*eva*), the aforementioned "locus-ness-ness" (*āśrayatvatva*) is excluded.

The sense is that since the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of that [denotatum] has been established, there is no requirement for the exclusion of other properties (*svetaradharma*) as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) only when the grasp of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) has multiple individuals as its qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*). Regarding the statement "karaṇa" (instrument), he says this because the third case ending in the word *kartṛ* (agent) signifies merely the locus (*āśrayatvamātra*). By the word "api" (also) in the phrase "vyāpāro’pi," the locus (*āśrayatva*) is conjoined with the operation (*vyāpāra*).

However, in reality, it would be more appropriate to say here as well that "the meaning is merely the operation (*vyāpāramātram arthaḥ*)," because the particle *api* functions here as a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇārthaka*).

The word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "mere separation" (*vibhāgamātram*) serves to exclude [the notion of] being a substratum (*āśrayatva*); the point is that since separation is construed as having a substratum, the status of being a limit (*avadhitva*) is obtained for the tree and so forth by that very fact. In reality, however, it has been stated that the tree and so forth are construed with the separation—which is the meaning of the ablative case—by means of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) consisting in the status of being a limit. By the phrase "mere objectivity" (*uddeśyatvamātra*), the same exclusion of being a substratum is intended. The phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) means: precisely because it has been stated that the respective case-endings express the potencies such as "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth.

The point is that it is established there [in the Siddhānta] that [the word] does not conflict [with experience], because even though both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) appear equally in the apprehension of the word's capacity (*śaktigraha*), the genus alone is the denotable meaning (*śakya*). This is due to the maxim "that which has not been apprehended as a qualifier cannot qualify" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*), and also due to the maxim "the qualified object does not go to the cognition without its qualifier. Furthermore, if the capacity belonged to the individuals, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and their infinite number; such is the sense. Having defined the meaning of the case-endings for the kārakas, the author of the *Mūla* defines the meaning of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by occasion: "relation" (*sambandha*).

From the sūtra "śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī," the meaning of the term *śeṣa* (remainder) therein is a relationship—such as that between owner and owned—which is distinct from the meanings of the case-role (*kāraka*) and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In this regard, just as there is a difference of opinion among scholars as to whether other case-endings denote the substratum (*dharmin*) or the attribute (*dharma*), one might have the misconception that this [genitive] is likewise [ambiguous]. With the intention of preventing such a delusion, the *Sāra* states: "In both views, it is simply the relation (*sambandhamātra*). This is the remainder [of the explanation].

And that [relation] is expressed in some cases as a relation in general, and in others specifically by its particular form. Among these, it is expressed in a general form in instances such as "he remembers his mother," whereas when there is an intention to express it in a specific form, the respective case-endings prevail within their own domains. However, in examples such as "the king's man," although many relations may exist, because there is an intention to express a specific relation, one uses the expression "this is not Caitra’s."

Furthermore, in all cases, a relationship is rooted solely in the relation between an action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*). Regarding the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* ("the genitive is used for the remainder"), in the example *rājñaḥ pūruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), because of the understanding that "the king gives to the man," the king is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the man is the recipient (*sampradāna*). In the example *vṛkṣasya śākhā* ("the tree's branch"), according to common worldly usage (*laukikaprasiddhi*), the tree is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the branch, as in "the branch on the tree."

"This 'own' (sva) [property] comes about in four ways: through purchase, through seizure, through begging, and through exchange in the form of barter. By this *bhāṣya*, which means that even where an action is not explicitly mentioned, the capacity for instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and so forth exists in reality because it is inferred from its connection with the result, one might suspect that the status of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) as a grammatical category is established by implication. Anticipating this, [Patañjali] stated: "In that case, then, the remainder is the non-intentional expression (*avivakṣā*) of the [other] cases such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. Thus he spoke of the "remainder."

Although the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka) exists in reality everywhere, when that which is caused by it—such as the relationship of owner and owned—is intended to be expressed as a "relationship" (sambandha), the former [the action-factor relationship] is not so intended; thus, the category of "residual" (śeṣa) meanings becomes easily available, and that is the absence [of the action-factor relationship].

Nor should it be argued that, since a relation is defined by both relata, a genitive suffix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should follow the word *puruṣa*—just as it follows the word *rājan* in the expression "the king’s servant" (*rājñaḥ pūruṣaḥ*). This is not so; for when the king's status as a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) is intended to be expressed, the genitive occurs after the word *rājan* alone; but when the servant's status as a beneficiary is intended, it occurs after the word *puruṣa* as well, as in "the king of the servant" (*puruṣasya rājā*). Thus, the genitive does not occur simultaneously in both places at once, and the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not apply. As Hari has stated:
"Though this [relation] resides in both, it is distinguished among the subordinate elements (*guṇa*) because it exists for the sake of another.
And while being expressed there [in the subordinate], it is transferred to the principal (*pradhāna*) as well."

Because it is for the sake of another—that is, because the qualities (*guṇas*) function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to another—the relation is distinguished [from other relations]; since a thing intended as a qualifier cannot be a qualifier without a relation, the relation is perceived as being predominant (*udbhūta*), and thus the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used there alone. As for the qualified (*viśeṣya*), when it is not co-uttered with another word, it is perceived by its own nature alone; therefore, there is no expectancy for a relation that would necessarily define its status as a qualified.

In that context, when it is expressed by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is employed even with respect to the primary element, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); the meaning is that, because its nature is to reside in two [relata], it serves to assist the "qualificand-ness" (*viśeṣyatā*) relative to the king, which is perceived upon the proximity of the word "king."

The phrase "by the sixth case [ending] denoting a *kāraka*" means by the sixth case prescribed by rules such as "the sixth case [is used] for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) when a *kṛt* suffix follows. The intention is that since the sixth case prescribed for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) denotes the property of being a relation (*sambandha-rūpa-dharma*), it is logical that this [sixth case] likewise denotes that very [property]. Now, one might ask: how can the third case and others, which are prescribed for *kārakas* such as the agent and the object, denote properties such as being an agent? To this he says: "the seventh and fifth cases. Thus, since even the property of being a *kāraka* is accepted in the *Bhāṣya*, there is no fault in those [cases] denoting that [property]; this is the intention.

Regarding the phrase "because of being seen" (*darśanāt*): for in that context, since the substance (*dravya*) is the agent (*kāraka*), in examples such as "Having eaten today, he will eat in two days," the agent—the person Devadatta—is one and the same. Consequently, because an intermediate designation (*madhyavyapadeśa*) is impossible, the Vārttika—"it should be stated that [the rule applies] to the middle of an action"—was formulated to justify the application of the seventh and fifth case endings where they would otherwise not apply, and was stated in order to refute [the view that the rule applies to] the interval between actions. For the commencement of an action does not occur without an instrument (*sādhana*). Furthermore, the middle of an action is also the middle of the agent (*kāraka*).

In that context, there is also the "middle of a *kāraka*. Since the point is already established by the phrase "in the middle of a *kāraka*," the term "means" (*sādhana*) therein signifies "capacity" (*śakti*). Thus, even though the substance acting as the agent—such as Devadatta—is one and the same, there is a distinction between the two capacities of agency belonging to the *kāraka*-entities inferred from the acts of eating at different times. Consequently, because the designation "middle" based on those [capacities] is not contradicted, there is no lack of justification for what was stated; therefore, the Vārttika "in the middle of an action" (*kriyāmadhye*) need not be commenced. This is the intended meaning.

This is an illustration of the commentary on the *Anabhihita-sūtra*. In that context, having established the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding "that which is not already expressed" (*anabhihita*) by means of the position that "number is the meaning of the case-ending," [the author] raises an objection: if either one of two factors of action (*kāraka*) were expressed [by the suffix], it would result in the absence of a case-ending. Where? In the examples "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*) and "he sits on the bed" (*śayane āste*). What is the reason? Having raised the doubt that the locative case would not apply because the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is already expressed by the suffix, [the author] replies: "No, because it is expressed by either one," and so forth, beginning with the statement "the rule applies when [the factor] is not already expressed."

Having set aside the objection regarding the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—whether it signifies absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) or relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—if the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) were a substance (*dravya*), then it would be only one, and since that has already been expressed [by the verb], the previously mentioned solution would not be possible. However, if the means of accomplishment is power (*śakti*), then because of its non-difference [from the substance] and the possibility of its being unexpressed, the stated solution holds. With this intention, having raised the doubt, "Is the means of accomplishment a substance or rather a quality (*guṇa*)?", he says: "What, then, is the logical means of accomplishment? It is a quality," he replies.

How is this known? For instance, someone asks, "Where is Devadatta? and another tells him, "He is in the tree. In this case, whichever tree he stands upon becomes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), yet by being connected with another word, it functions as the agent (*kartṛ*). [The rule states: "When a substance is the means (*sādhana*), that which is the object (*karman*) remains an object; that which is the instrument (*karaṇa*) remains an instrument; and that which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) remains a locus. Thus it is understood.

Kaiyaṭa also explained this as follows: "If the substance (*dravya*) were the means (*sādhana*), then, because it possesses a single form, there would be no such designations as 'bring water with the jar,' 'make a jar,' or 'the jar exists'—which are based on its performing various purposeful actions and are the objects of uncontradicted recognition; yet these are observed. Therefore, the understanding of its existence in various states is established."

And thus, since the position of the *śakti* (potency) school is accepted as authoritative, the view of those who maintain that the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) and others possess potency (*śakti*) with respect to the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth is also entirely correct; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the meanings of the nominative case prescribed by the rule *prātipadikārtha-* are, as appropriate, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), gender (*liṅga*), and measure (*parimāṇa*).

The term *mātra* (only) is included there so that the nominative case (*prathamā*) might not apply when there is an excess of factors such as the object (*karman*). Since the term *mātra* heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound is construed with each member of the compound, the syntactical split of the rule "the nominative occurs in the mere meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha-mātre prathamā*) is avoided. Furthermore, "being the meaning of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthatva*) is defined as: being the counter-correlative of a cognitive state (*viṣayitā*) which pervades the state of being an occurrence (*upasthititva*) that is the locus of the effectness (*janyatā*) determined by a generativity (*janakatā*) delimited by a power (*śakti*) residing in the name (*nāman*). Because the cognitive state whose object is the meaning of "highly" (*uccaiḥ*) etc. pervades such an occurrence, the nominative case is appropriately applied there.

Thus, in cases such as "kṛṣṇaḥ" (the word *kṛṣṇa*), it is quite evident that just as there is a necessity for the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the objectivity (*viṣayitā*) toward [the meaning] "Kṛṣṇa" and so forth, there is likewise a necessity for the presentation of the objectivity toward the masculine gender (*puṃliṅga*) and so forth. Although, under the view that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of two [factors: number and gender]," the status of gender as an object of presentation is difficult to establish, nevertheless, in accordance with empirical experience (*anubhava*), one must assume that the convergence of factors that awaken the gender occurs necessarily prior to the presentation of the denoted meaning (*śakyārtha*); thus its status as such [an object of presentation] is to be understood.

Thus, words that are genderless (*aliṅga*) and those with fixed genders (*niyataliṅga*) are examples of the rule "in the mere meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātre*). However, because the manifestation of masculine gender and so forth is not invariably present in the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by words such as *taṭa* (bank), the mention of "gender" (*liṅgagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of prescribing the nominative case where it would otherwise not apply.

In cases such as "siṃho māṇavakaḥ" ("the boy is a lion"), although there is the cognition of an additional meaning such as similarity (*sādṛśya*), the nominative case is easily obtained from that [base] which rests solely on its own primary meaning (*svārtha*) because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). In that context, the gender (*liṅga*) denoted by the nominative is construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) as a qualifier, due to both logical fitness (*yogyatā*) and actual experience (*anubhava*), since the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is postulated in exactly that manner.

Similarly, in cases such as "droṇo vrīhiḥ" ("a *droṇa* measure of rice"), because the measure (*parimāṇa*) appears as something additional beyond the meaning of the nominal base *droṇa*, the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is included there.

Nor should it be argued that, although [the measure] appears due to its co-occurrence with words such as *vrīhi* (rice), the case ending should apply to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) alone because it is more internal; for if that were so, the connection of the object denoted by the word *droṇa*—which is a measure—with [the rice] through the relation of difference would be untenable. According to the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*), however, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the connection of that [measure], which is the meaning of the nominative, with [the rice] through the relation of difference.

The moderns (navyāḥ), however, maintain that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of both the respective occasioning ground for the application of a word (*pravṛttinimitta*) and its substratum (*tadāśraya*). For this very reason, the explicit mention of gender (*liṅgagrahaṇa*) is purposeful; otherwise, since gender would also be included within the meaning of the nominal stem by virtue of the authority of the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, its separate mention would be rendered redundant. Furthermore, this status as a substratum is merely conceptual (*vaijñānika*), because it has been established elsewhere that the superimposition (*āropa*) of the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) itself constitutes the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*).

In cases such as *gopī* and others, there is no defect even if the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is indicated by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For words such as *taṭa*, gender is indeed the expressed meaning (*vācya*), while the visarga and other markers are its indicators (*dyotaka*).

And thus, regarding the phrase "the meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*), words such as *avyaya* (indeclinables), *astrīpumsa* (neuter), and others which lack gender or have gender as their cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are examples; others [words like *droṇa*, etc. are examples of the addition of mere gender. For words such as *droṇa*, whose application is caused by *droṇatva* (the property of being a *droṇa*-measure), the measure (*parimāṇa*)—like gender—is also an object that connects with the substantive (*viśeṣya*) by virtue of being a measure. And so, because it lacks the status of being the meaning of the nominal stem like gender does, the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is explicitly mentioned.

Regarding expressions such as "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), although an additional relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) appears upon the proximity of words like *puruṣa*, they say that this [relation] arises from the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with those words; prior to that co-occurrence, the word denoted its own primary meaning alone. However, the meaning of the nominative case prescribed by the rule "and in the vocative" (*saṃbodhane ca*) is "addressing" (*saṃbodhana*). Because it appears as something additional relative to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), it is not the subject matter of the preceding rule; therefore, that specific rule was commenced. Furthermore, it has been established previously that this [act of addressing] is an activity conducive to making [someone] face [the speaker], and thus it necessarily connects with a verb.

He explains the word *yathāyatha* in the phrase *yathāyathaṃ vibhaktyarthāḥ* as follows: "In the manner stated" means that in the cognition of a given object, whatever case-ending (*vibhakti*) is capable [of expressing it], its meaning is to be understood accordingly. The sense is that this was already stated previously in the passage beginning with "of the second, third, and seventh cases," and so forth. "Here" means in the context of the nominal endings (*sup*) denoting the object (*karman*) and other kārakas. "Toward the Naiyāyikas" means toward the ancient [grammarians]. How their view stands has been set forth on the occasion of the investigation into the expressive power of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*).

Now, one might object: since the Bhāṣya states that "the meanings of case-endings include [grammatical relations] such as the object," let it be granted that they possess a primary denotative power (śakti) toward the object and so forth; however, what is the obstacle to their having a secondary indicative function (lakṣaṇā) toward the state of being an object and so on?

Since the application [of the term *karman*] occurs only when there is an obstruction to its primary status as an object—defined as possessing a result produced by an action—he reveals his intention, stating "This is the point," etc., intending to present the aforementioned rule shown in the second half [of the verse] as an obstructing factor. In the rule *svaujasamauṭchaṣṭābbyasbhyāmbhyasṅebhyāmbhyasṅasosāmṅyoṣṅyossup*, because the accusative (*dvitīyā*) is mentioned first among the case-endings denoting *kārakas*, the object (*karman*) signifying that [accusative] is also mentioned first in the Vārttika. By the phrase "object and so forth" (*karmādi*), other *kārakas* are included.
By the word "also" (*api*), there is a conjunction of the powers of being an object and so forth, as stated in the position that "the power (*śakti*) is the *kāraka*."

"Likewise for *tiṅ*s" means that for *tiṅ*s as well, number, object, and so forth are the meanings; this is the sense. In that context, regarding *sup*s and *tiṅ*s, the meaning is "in the meanings already under discussion. Regarding the objection—"Since [the usage] will occur through common worldly practice (*loka*) alone in cases such as plurality for the *sup*s and *tiṅ*s, what is the purpose of the sūtra 'In the plural, the plural' (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) and so forth?"—the response is that the statement is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*), because there would otherwise be no distinction between *sup*s and *tiṅ*s and because [such usages] are observed in actual linguistic usage (*dṛṣṭaviprayoga*). This verse-verse-commentary (*ślokavārttika*) demonstrates the form of that restriction.

Alternatively, the restriction is independent of the subject matter at hand. What are the subjects at hand? They are singularity and so forth; namely, that the singular number is used for one alone, not for two, nor for many, and so on. And the commentary on that [sūtra] has the meaning "by those two."

He states the form of the restriction: "The second case [ending] is used only for the object (*karman*). This refers to the subject matter at hand. However, the isolated restriction should be understood as: "The singular number of the second case is used only for an object qualified by singularity. The same applies in subsequent instances. "In both ways" means with respect to the grammatical case ending and with respect to the meaning. The restriction regarding case endings is also twofold: that which depends on a specific meaning and that which depends on the general category.

Regarding these, the first [type of restriction] is of the form: "If a second case suffix occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is capable of expressing an object (*karman*), then it occurs only when there is an object, and not when there is an instrument (*karaṇa*) or other such factors. Likewise: "If a nominative case suffix occurs after a nominal stem capable of expressing an object and so forth, then it occurs only when that [object] is absent, and not when the object is present. And: "If a singular number suffix occurs after a nominal stem capable of expressing a number, then it occurs only when there is singularity, and not when there is duality or plurality. The second [type of restriction], however, is of the form: "If a second case suffix occurs after a nominal stem, it occurs only when there is an object."

The restriction regarding meaning (*arthaniyama*), however, is as follows: if a case-ending is to be introduced for the object (*karman*) from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is capable of denoting an object, then only the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used; if the object and so forth are absent, then only the first case (*prathamā*) is used from the nominal stem in the sense of what is appropriate to it. This is the nature [of the rule]. The phrase "by the force of the single sentence" (*ekavākyatābalena*) following the word *siddha* means this. Thus, since the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is not identical to the aforementioned technical definition of "objectness" (*karmatva*), the scripture does not prescribe the second case and so forth for it; therefore, the meaning is that the utterance of such a form with the intention of conveying that [technical] meaning would be false. "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means precisely because the assumption of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case-ending is not a motivating factor.

Now, since grammar establishes meaning through either direct denotation (*śakti*) or conventional indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), there is no obstacle to accepting indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding that which is related to the primary meaning (*śakyasaṃbandhin*) in cases where there is a recognition of the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since the cognition of knowledge having a jar or the like as its object—arising from expressions such as "he knows the jar"—is established by universal experience and would otherwise be inexplicable without a secondary function (*vṛtti*), this very fact necessitates the assumption of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). As for the common dictum that "there is no indication in an inflectional suffix" (*vibhaktau na lakṣaṇā*), it is intended to mean that one case-ending does not indicate the meaning of another case-ending; therefore, there is no pointlessness in the grammatical rules regarding the transposition of cases (*vyatyayānuśāsana*).

Nor is there any contradiction with the rule "the meanings of the *sup*-suffixes include the object and so forth," because the word "object" (*karman*) in that rule can be understood as referring to both primary and secondary (figurative) objecthood. Thus, he says: "this is merely a direction" (*dig iti*).

However, since the scripture achieves its purpose by taking the primary meaning, there is no evidence for its operation in a secondary sense. Nor should it be argued that, in accordance with the well-known usage "he knows the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), the postulation of such an operation is necessary even in a secondary sense; for in our view, the usage is possible through primary objecthood alone, as the root *jñā* has the sense of bringing about objecthood as a subordinate factor to the attainment of being an object of knowledge.

Furthermore, if one were to accept figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding an object that is accessible only through one's own experience, it would result in the futility of specifying the object, and so forth.

On this point, they argue: if one does not accept the application of the technical term "transitive" (*sakarmaka*) in a secondary sense, then in cases such as *tiṣṭhati* ("he stands"), where there is no movement (*gati*) intended as the fruit of the action, the verbal root would lack the primary status of being intransitive (*akarmaka*) because it would not be produced by an operation (*vyāpāra*) that constitutes its own meaning. Consequently, suffixes denoting the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the agent (*kartṛ*) could not be formed from such roots. Similarly, since it is universally accepted that the root *vārayati* ("he wards off") signifies an operation conducive to the absence of an operation conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it too would lack the primary status of being transitive; thus, suffixes denoting the agent or the object could not be formed from it either.

Since the introduction of verbal suffixes (lakāra) and so forth would otherwise be untenable, it must necessarily be admitted that the scope of the grammatical rule extends even to secondary (gauṇa) usage; thus, there is no lack of grammatical correctness in expressions such as "he knows the jar" (ghaṭaṃ jānāti), even when the term "jar" is used metaphorically to denote its objecthood (viṣayatva).

In reality, however, according to the view that "capacity (*śakti*) is the causal factor (*kāraka*)," there is no inconsistency even if the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) expresses the *ādheyatva* (the state of being contained) correlated with the object (*viṣayatva*), because it has already been demonstrated that in such instances the fruit in the form of the object is subordinate to the fruit expressed by the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, in that system as well, neither a contradiction of the aforementioned rule nor the possibility of its being a subject of prohibition arises; so, enough of this.

Thus, in the *Śrībhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*, the determination of the meaning of case-suffixes (*sub-artha*) has been concluded. With the intention of now presenting the determination of the meaning of nouns (*nāma-artha*), which follows in order, [the author] says: "The meaning of a noun" (*nāmārtham*). "Genus" (*jāti*) means a property that is unique to each respective word-meaning. By this, there is no deficiency even though properties such as "negativity" (*abhāvatva*) and "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*) lack the status of a genus in the sense of being eternal and residing in multiple individuals. This very [meaning] is designated by the term "own-meaning" (*svārtha*) in the technical treatises.

The proof that the universal (jāti) is the meaning of a word is the sūtra: "In the case of a name denoting a genus, the plural may optionally be used for a single [entity]"; the vārttika: "'Aṇ' is not to be understood as referring to phonemes of the same class, because it is established by the grasping of the form (ākṛti)"; and the Bhāṣya on the Sarūpa-sūtra: "Vājapyāyana [holds that the word denotes] the form. He also states the reasoning: "By way of parsimony"—the sense being that only a single power residing in a single substratum is possible.

[Objection: Surely, since the apprehension of the word’s power (śakti) occurs through usage (vyavahāra)—the crest-jewel of all means for grasping that power—only with respect to the individual (vyakti), how can its establishment be in the universal (jāti)? To this, he says: "Of many individuals" (*anekavyaktīnām*). The meaning is as follows: although the power is first grasped through usage with respect to the individual, because there is an infinity [of individuals], it is impossible to grasp the power in all of them; therefore, due to the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating multiple powers distinct for each different substratum, the power is subsequently determined to reside in the universal alone.

If one accepts that a verbal cognition regarding another individual arises from a knowledge of the word’s power (śakti) directed toward a single individual, then there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition regarding a horse arising from a knowledge of the power directed toward a cow-individual. Consequently, it must necessarily be postulated that a knowledge of the power directed toward a specific individual is the cause of a cognition regarding that very individual. Thus, since a cognition regarding another individual would not arise from a knowledge directed toward a single object, and because it would be clearly cumbersome to postulate the power in all individuals in order to account for the manifestation of all individuals, it is appropriate to postulate the power in the genus (jāti) alone.

Although the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*)—in the form "the cow is denoted by the word 'cow'" (*gaur gopadavācyaḥ*)—has the individual (*vyakti*) as its object, nevertheless, according to the maxim "for injunctions and prohibitions involving a qualified [subject] apply to the qualifier when the qualified [subject] is obstructed," it determines existence only in the universal (*jāti*). Alternatively, the apprehension of potency has the universal as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), as is evident from the very expression used in the theory that potency resides in the universal: "the cow (the universal) is denotable by the word 'cow'" (*gaur gopadaśakyaḥ*). The point is that there is no inconsistency regarding the manifestation of the individual, since that will be established later.

"Vinigamanā" means a reasoning that favors one side over another. Thus, there is an absence of a decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) in the apprehension of each individual instance, such as [the thought] "this individual is capable [of denotation], but the universal (*jāti*) is not. In the previous case, however, since the collection of individuals themselves constitutes the alternative (*koṭi*), the knowledge of complexity (*gaurava*) itself serves as the subverting factor and thus acts as the decisive factor; therefore, there is no absence of such a factor. He states "for in this way," etc., to show that even in that position, complexity alone is the subverting factor.

[Objection: But surely, since the absence of a determining factor has already been stated, the capacity (śakti) is established for all individual instances; and since there is no such thing as an "unmanifested instance" [that could not be denoted], there is no need to postulate a function residing in the individual to account for its manifestation. Thus, the position that the capacity resides in the individual (vyaktiśaktivāda) is faultless. To this, he says: "Furthermore, if it were so... Alternatively: [Objection: But surely, because we accept the capacity in all individual instances as unified by the universal (jāti) such as "cowness" (gotva), there is no fault such as infinity (anantya). To this, he says: "Furthermore, if it were so..."—that is, if one accepts the capacity in the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa).

"Without having apprehended [the qualifier]" (*nāgṛhīta*) refers to the body of the maxim: "A cognition that has not apprehended the qualifier does not reach the qualified. The meaning is that a cognition whose object is not the qualifier does not comprehend the qualified; that is to say, the property of having the qualified as its object is necessarily concomitant with the property of having the qualifier as its object.

Thus, in the theory of qualified potency (*viśiṣṭa-śakti-vāda*), since the apprehension of qualified potency necessarily has the qualifier as its object, it is more appropriate—due to parsimony (*lāghava*)—to postulate that "having the qualifier as its object" alone is the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the causality of the presentation of word-meanings and so forth, rather than postulating that "having both [qualifier and qualified] as its object" is that delimiting condition. Therefore, the intended meaning is that potency is established as residing in the universal (*jāti*) alone.

If it is objected that, in cases such as "one should give a cow" (*gāṃ dadyāt*) or "one threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the grammatical connection of the objecthood of the act of giving or threshing is untenable because a universal (*jāti*) is unfit for such a connection, some respond as follows: the connection with the objecthood of giving and so forth occurs only with respect to the individual (*vyakti*) implied by the universal. To this, [we reply] that according to the rule "suffixes [denote] the meaning of the base" (*pratyayānām*), such a connection is impossible with an individual that is not the meaning of the base. As it has been said: "And a qualification of a meaning that is merely being implied is never observed, whether by other words or by case-endings, just as one does not say 'this smoke is flaming'."* *This verse is cited from the *Vākyapadīya*. It argues that a qualifier (such as "flaming") cannot apply to something that is only inferred or implied, just as one cannot describe "smoke" (the universal) as "flaming" (a property of the individual). Thus, the universal cannot be directly qualified by the action.*

Furthermore, is this implication (ākṣepa) a case of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), or is it the state of being cognized by the same cognition? It cannot be the first, because even without an apparent inconsistency (anupapatti), there arises from the statement "the cow exists" a cognition qualified by cowness (gotva). Nor can it be the second, because since it is admitted that the apprehension of the word's power (śaktigraha) regarding the universal (jāti) is the cause of a cognition whose object is the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa), the objectivity of the universal must necessarily entail the objectivity of the individual (vyakti); no other [relation] is possible.

Furthermore, since the previously stated logical inconsistency—that [the argument] is contradicted by the fact that there is no cognition of the universal *gotva* as qualified [by the individual] in the case of "there is *gotva*"—remains unavoidable, he says: "The cognition of the individual exists. By the phrase "by means of secondary indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*), the meaning is: by means of a secondary indication consisting in the relation of being the substratum of *gotva*, which is its own primary denotation (*svaśakyagotvāśrayatva*). Thus, since the cause of verbal cognition is precisely the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the word's function (*padavṛtti*), even though the individual is not the primary denotation (*aśakyatva*), there is no logical impossibility of its being connected with the objecthood of threshing and so forth when it is presented through the function of secondary indication; this is the intended sense.

"And thus" (*evañca*) means "if one accepts [the view of] indication" (*lakṣaṇā*). "In that case" (*tatra*) refers to the individual (*vyakti*) to be indicated. "It is possible" (*upapadyate*)—the sense is that it would not be possible otherwise, based on the etymological derivation of the word *pratyaya* as "that which is otherwise" (*anyathā*). Now, an objection might be raised: if one accepts the indication of the individual, there is a contradiction regarding the simultaneous occurrence of two functions (denotation and indication), which violates the established doctrine (*siddhānta*); furthermore, the cognition of the perceived individual from the sentence "The cow exists" (*gaur asti*) would be untenable, because the "inexplicability of the syntactic connection" (*anvayānupapatti*), which is the seed of indication, is absent there. To this, he says: "The direction [is shown]" (*dig iti*).

Since everyone accepts the existence of two functions (vṛtti) in the sentence "There are a hamlet and fish in the Gaṅgā" when there is an intention (*tātparya*) toward that meaning, such a maxim is intended to mean that there is no simultaneous presence of primary denotation (*śakti*) and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding what is not the object of the intention; thus, there is no contradiction with that [maxim]. Furthermore, because the impossibility of the intention exists, there is no impossibility of secondary indication for the individual (*vyakti*). However, if one were to accept a contradiction with that [maxim], one must adopt the position of the non-difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual, and thereby establish the syntactic connection with the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). As it has been said: "Therefore, because the action is enjoined in connection with the individual indicated by that [universal]..."

"Or rather, the distinction between the universal (jāti) and the individual (vyakti) is established within the meanings of sentences. In reality, however, because it is postulated that the apprehension of the word's power (śakti) having the universal as its object is the cause for the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) of an individual qualified by the universal, there is no inconsistency in the manifestation of the individual, nor is there the contingency of the manifestation of something that is not denotable (aśakya), since the latter lacks that qualification [by the universal]. This is the conclusion of the theory of the power residing in the universal (jātiśaktivāda). More will be said on this point further below.

Others, however, have established the doctrine of the cognition of the universal (jāti) in this way: let there be no manifestation of the individual (vyakti); since actions such as bringing [an object] are impossible with respect to the universal alone, they are accomplished through association with the individual, just as the action of clapping occurs through the conjunction of the hand and the foot in their collective totality.

As it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "taddhitārthe": "Since actions such as touching (*ālambhana*) are impossible with respect to a generic form (*ākṛti*), they must apply to the substance (*dravya*) associated with it. For example, when it is said, 'Let fire be brought,' because the bringing of mere fire is impossible, a vessel is brought even though it was not explicitly enjoined. This very act of bringing the fire is what constitutes the bringing of the vessel. Likewise, when actions such as touching are enjoined with respect to a generic form, they reach the substance by virtue of its capacity and its association."

"Since every connection of the form (ākṛti) is such that the substance (dravya) is not included within it, the relationship is established as being mediated by the substance. Here, "association" (sāhacarya) means "relationship. This meaning is also clear in the Bhāṣya on the *sarūpa* sūtra. Hari also says: "When separated, [the form] undergoes grammatical operations; when combined, it conveys the universal (jāti)."

However, since the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "cow-ness" (*gotva*) resides only in the property that subsists in the substratum (the individual cow), there is no cognition in that case where the cow is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*). Even though the universal (*jāti*) is not separated from its substratum, it is not untenable for the universal alone to be the denotation of the word, just as a face seen in water and the like is understood by words such as "face" even while not separated from its own location. The delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatā*), however, belongs solely to the property residing within the universal.

This view also results in the contingency of implying the individual through the universal. And that [view] is seized by the flaw that there can be no syntactic connection (*pratyayānvaya*) with what is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*). Some, however, hold that even without being the object of a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), the universal qualifies the individual—which is presented by way of implication (*arthādhyāhāra*) due to the restriction of the relation [between the universal and the individual]—just as the eyes and other sense organs, though they are the objects of cognitions of color and so forth, are themselves grasped by the cognition "I am seeing."

With the intention that—since there is no need to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for [the word] in cases such as "cowness" (*gotva*), because the cognition of the denoted object is established solely through the force of such a causal relation (where the cognition of the denoted object follows from the cognition of the delimitor of denotability), even though there is no primary power regarding the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) just as there is no denotability (*lakṣyatā*) or delimitation of denotability (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatā*) in secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) whose nature consists in a possible relation despite the impossibility of a single [relation] between the indicated and the delimitors of indicatedness—one explains the other alternative with the words "Or rather... the individual itself," where the particle "eva" (itself) excludes the universal (*jāti*).
