[Objection: "Surely the position [that the word denotes the individual] has been stated on the authority of such rules as *savarṇe 'ṇgrahaṇam*; but what is the proof for the view that 'the individual is the meaning of the word' (*vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ*)? To this he says: "In the case of the isolated individual" (*kevalavyakti*). And regarding the rule of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*): since under the theory of the universal (*jāti-pakṣa*), it would be possible to convey two or many things by means of a single word, that [rule] would be rendered useless; therefore, its very existence serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the theory of the individual. This is the meaning.

Since the author of the Bhāṣya has rejected the inclusion of the word *āṅ* [in Pāṇini 6.1.94], and since it has been established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the rule on "similar form" (*sarūpasūtra*) is useful only for the sake of grammatical derivation (*śāstrīyaprakriyā*), how can those two [the rejection and the rule] be authoritative regarding the stated meaning? To this he says: "And this is logical," which means that this is also supported by reasoning. Furthermore, the phrase "Vyāḍi [holds] that it denotes a substance" is conjoined [by the particle *ca*] with the authority of the Bhāṣya on the *sarūpasūtra*. He states the very reasoning: "By usage" (*vyavahāreṇa*).

This truth will be explained in the *Śaktivāda* (The Doctrine of Power). In this system, he removes the previously mentioned fault of the infinity of powers (*śaktyānantya-doṣa*) by stating: "of the delimitant of relatedness" (*sambandhitāvacchedakasya*), which means "of the delimitant of the subjecthood" (*dharmmitāvacchedakasya*) in the apprehension of power. There is no logical inconsistency in the term *sambandhitāvacchedaka*, whether because it is a neuter pronoun for all genders (*liṅgasarvanāman*) or because it serves to present the subject (*uddeśya*).

Thus, since one accepts that this very same power—which is delimited by a single property—is present in various individuals made uniform by the genus that is the delimitant of relatedness, there is no complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the multiplicity of those [powers]. This is the intended meaning.

"Thus" (evam) means when one accepts that [the universal] possesses the capacity [to denote]. That is to say, it is the admission that "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth are the delimiters of the denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka) residing in the pot and so forth. "That very thing" (tadeva) means that "pot-ness" and so forth alone are the denoted (vācya), i.e., the denotable (śakya). The reason for its being denotable is stated as "on account of logic" (nyāyāt). Even though they are not causes—meaning that although "stick-ness" (daṇḍatva) and so forth are not causes because they are otherwise-established (anyathāsiddha), and although "bank-ness" (tīratva) and so forth are not related to the flowing water and the like.

The point is that even though [the property of being a jar] is the object of denotation (*lakṣya*) in that context, it is possible for [the universal *ghaṭatva* (jar-ness)] to be the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), just as one accepts a delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*)—consisting either of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) qualified by the delimitedness residing therein, or consisting of a specific kind of objectivity (*viṣayitā*)—even in the case of [the universal *ghaṭatva*] which is itself impossible [to be denoted]. This is because there is no evidence for the restrictive rule that "only that which, while being denotable, has attained the status of being a qualifier of the denotable, can be the delimitor of denotability."

He states the consensus regarding the point already mentioned with the words "And it has been said. Even though there is an infinity of entities—that is, even though individual instances are manifold and thus incognizable—it is nonetheless possible to establish a linguistic convention by accepting a single, recurring property such as a genus (*jāti*) as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), meaning by accepting it as the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Thus, a word consisting of "cow" and so forth possesses an easily established relation; that is, a relation of denotability (*vācyatā*) residing in the cow and other objects that is easy to grasp.

The meaning of "not" (*na ca*) is that it will not convey an individual instance (*vyakti*) that is not within the scope of the apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*). The intention is that, because the power is determined in all individual instances through the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*), [the word denotes them all]. More will be said on this later. Here, the individual instance itself is designated by the term "substance" (*dravya*), because it is fit to be referred to by a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). And it has been said: "Where a pronoun is employed to indicate a thing..."

"That object which is intended to be expressed as the thing to be distinguished (bhedyatvena) is called a substance (dravya). This means that a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)—which, by its very nature, denotes a property delimited by that [property] characterized as being the delimitor of the scope of a cognition—when employed with respect to a substratum (*dharmin*) by making such a property its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), is what is designated by the term "substance. In other words, it is that which is fit to be referred to by the thought "this" (*idam*). The phrase "as the thing to be distinguished" (bhedyatvena)—meaning "as the qualificand" (*viśeṣyatvena*) and so forth—is intended to provide an alternative definition; however, according to this view, even a universal (*jāti*) and the like are indeed accepted as having the status of a substance when they are not intended to be the qualificand.

Because there is a conceptual apprehension (*parāmarśa*) of the action denoted by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) through words such as *kim* ("what"), and because it possesses the status of being a substantive (*dravyatva*) insofar as it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) as determined by meanings such as *stoka* ("a little"), substance-ness indeed exists [in action]. Furthermore, in expressions such as "contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddham*), by virtue of the contextual force (*sāmarthya*), the term "substance" refers to that which is well-known in other systems (the Vaiśeṣika). In the rule "the particles beginning with *ca* [are used] when not denoting a substance" (*cādayo 'sattve*), one should understand that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) applies specifically to the kind of substance mentioned in the first alternative [of the previous definition].

And "being the delimitor of the denotatum" (śakyatāvacchedakatva) consists in appearing as the delimitor of the predication-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the denotatum. And when the power (śakti) is grasped in words such as "jar," it is jar-ness (ghaṭatva) alone that possesses this status, not earth-ness (pṛthivītva) and so on; therefore, there is no cognition of earth-ness and the like from those words. Although the word "ākāśa" lacks power with respect to being the substratum of sound, there is nevertheless a cognition of it in that very form [as the substratum of sound], because the grasp of power qualified by that [property] is the cause of that cognition. Alternatively, ākāśatva is a non-concrete (sakhāṇḍa) adventitious property (upādhi).

The conclusion for the proponent of substance (dravyavādin) is that, according to the method stated in the *Vṛddhisūtra*, either that [substance] itself or the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and thus there is no inconsistency in the usage "Ether is the substratum of sound. Now, neither of the two aforementioned positions withstands scrutiny; for instance, under the theory that the word's power resides in the universal (*jātiśaktivāda*), there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition of the object as qualified by that [universal] arising from words such as "cow" (*gotva*). This is because the apprehension of the power residing in the universal "cowness" exists as a necessary factor for the cognition of the object as qualified by it.

Furthermore, the apprehension of a word’s power (śaktigraha) where the delimiting property of the subject (dharmitāvacchedaka) is absent is not the cause for a cognition qualified by "cowness" (gotva), because at the time when there is an apprehension of a sublation regarding the delimiting property of the subject being "the state of having cowness" (gotvatva), it is possible for there to be an apprehension of power where no such delimiting property is present; this would lead to the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of a cognition qualified by "cowness" occurring. Therefore, it is necessary that the apprehension of power where the delimiting property of the subject is "the state of having cowness" (gotvatva) is the cause of such a cognition.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in "cowness" (*gotva*) without any further qualification—such that the cognition of power, which has the form "the word 'cow' is a cow," is characterized by the qualifier "cowness" through the relation of power, and has as its object the word "cow" as qualified by the property of being the word "cow," and is thus the cause for the cognition of an object qualified by cowness—even so, there would be an untenable lack of systematic restriction: why at one time there is a cognition of an object qualified by cowness through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), while at another time it occurs through a temporal or other such relation, given that the cognition of power having cowness as its object remains identical in both cases?

In my view, however, the restriction [of the relation between cause and effect] is established because the cognition of a power qualified by "cowness" (gotva) through that very relation [inherence] is the cause of a verbal cognition whose object is qualified by "cowness" through that same relation; likewise, the cognition of such a power qualified by that relation is the cause of a cognition whose object is qualified by that relation through any other relation. Thus, the restriction is logically accounted for.

Nor can it be maintained that the word *go* (cow) has its power (*śakti*) in the universal "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*), because from the apprehension of power in the form "the cow is a *gopada*," such a cognition [of cowness-ness] is not experienced; furthermore, suffixes denoting abstract states (*bhāvapratyaya*) are prescribed for the mode of the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*). If one were to accept that the denotatum (*śakyārtha*) is the cumbersome property consisting in "inherence in all cows while not inhering in anything other than cows," then the theory of the "form" (*ākṛti*)—which is based on parsimony (*lāghava*)—would suffer a collapse of its very foundation. Moreover, even under the theory of the individual (*vyaktivāda*), there would be no difference in terms of the word alone being the conveyor of the individual. Consequently, the simultaneous employment of expressions such as "the cow moves" (*gauś calati*) and "the blue cow" (*nīlo gauḥ*) would be untenable.

Furthermore, when the relation is grasped by one individual elephant-keeper (hastipaka) but not by another, there would necessarily follow the recollection [of the word] even upon seeing that other elephant-keeper who has not grasped the relation; since it is necessary that the grasp of the relation regarding a specific individual must be the regulator of its presentation, how can there be the presentation of one object from a knowledge of the expressive power (śakti) regarding a different object?

Although it is understood from the Bhāṣya—stating that "for one for whom the universal (ākṛti) is the word-meaning, the individual substance (dravya) is not the word-meaning; and for one for whom the substance is the word-meaning, the universal is not the word-meaning; thus, for both [theories], both are the word-meaning"—that the objects of the acquisition of linguistic competency (śaktigraha) are indeed the universal and the individual in isolation.

Nevertheless, upon examining the subsequent commentary—"for some [a word] has a subordinate meaning, for some a primary one"—one determines the expressive power (*śakti*) specifically from that very source; thus, its employment as such is not contradictory. Otherwise, if the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) were to be the denotable objects (*śakya*) without standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified—just as the singularity and instrumentality expressed by the third case—the cognition would result in a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) such as "the cow's individual is the cow," because there is a rule that the knowledge of expressive power, the mental presentation of the object-meaning, and the verbal cognition must possess identical modes of presentation (*samānaprakāratva*).

In the same way, this applies to the form (*ākṛti*) consisting of the conjunction of parts. Thus, Gautama formulated the sūtra: "The referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of genus (*jāti*), form (*ākṛti*), and individual (*vyakti*). The singular number used there is intended to convey that there is only one denotative power (*śakti*) residing in these three; this is also the natural implication of the Bhāṣya’s statement that [the genus] is "subordinate" (*guṇabhūta*). Its intention is that the occasional appearance of the genus as primary depends upon the apprehension of the speaker's intent (*tātparya*). It should be understood that even when the genus is primary, the use of dual or plural endings is justified by taking the number of the substance (*dravya*) into account.

This has been stated by Kaiyaṭa: "Just as in forms such as *bhavataḥ*, even though the action (*kriyā*) is predominant, there is a difference in number caused by the grammatical factor (*sādhana*), so too, even when the generic form (*ākṛti*) is predominant, there is a difference in number caused by the substance (*dravya*); thus there is no fault. Even when the substance is predominant, the number is sometimes taken from the genus (*jāti*), as in "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇaṃ na hanyāt*). Furthermore, when the genus is predominant, the individual (*vyakti*) is presented in its unqualified state, and its inclusion is achieved through the genus which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); for there is no rule that "only that which is the qualifier (*prakārin*) can be the inclusive factor (*anugamaka*). Such is the refinement of that theory.

In reality, however, it is the individual qualified by the universal (*jāti*) alone that is the denoted meaning (*śakya*). This is because the aforementioned alternative is impossible, as there is no experience of the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*) as qualified by "cow-ness" (*go*) when words such as "cow" are heard. For this very reason, it has been explained accordingly. Since there is a rule that any category distinct from a universal must be delimited by some property (*dharmāvacchinna*), it is impossible for that [individual] to appear in its aspect as a universal without being so delimited; furthermore, since cowness would not be presented under a form that serves as the delimiter of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka-rūpa*), it would be impossible for it to enter into a relation with various objects such as the accusative case.

In expressions such as "the rice is complete" (*sampanno vrīhiḥ*), however, the number one (*ekatva*) is construed with the individual denoted by the base (*prakṛtyartha-vyaktau*) itself, through the relation of possessing the delimitor of the meaning of the base which resides in its own locus. It is not correct to say that in the aforementioned instance, the multiple unities presented by the singular suffix do not construe with the rice grains; for the meaning of the singular suffix is precisely the state of being devoid of a second similar entity—where "similar" means a unity that does not delimit the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in a similar thing—and this [meaning] is sublated in that context, whereas the unity consisting of a mere number is not.

Because [the number] is obtained by implication through its commonality with the substance alone, it is useless [to state it explicitly], and because that [number] lacks the status of being the meaning of the singular suffix.

For this very reason, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the aforementioned singularity is intended by the singular suffix; therefore, the transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*) is not established from a sacrifice performed with multiple animals. Furthermore, because similarity is intended in the form of the delimitor of the primary meaning as qualified by its connection with the meanings of the co-occurring words, there is no lack of establishment of the singularity that is the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of difference residing in the jar, as in "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*).

Since this very oneness—which is the non-limiting factor (anavacchedaka) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the difference residing in the pot existing in this particular location—is understood from that [word], its establishment is possible according to the aforementioned method. And thus, since there is no inconsistency whatsoever in accepting a cognition where the individual is the qualificand (viśeṣya), and since such a cognition is impossible without the apprehension of the word's expressive power (śakti) having that individual as its qualificand, the expressive power of words such as "cow" resides precisely in the individual qualified by the universal (jāti).

The essential point is that the aforementioned defect is unavoidable if a knowledge of the word's expressive power (*śaktijñāna*)—whether having as its object the individual alone or the universal alone—is held to be the cause of the verbal cognition of an individual qualified by a universal.

Others, however, hold that based on the Bhāṣya statement "the meaning of both [the universal and the individual] is the referent of both," words such as *go* (cow) possess a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*). Nevertheless, even when there is a verbal cognition of an individual, it is the knowledge of the power residing in the universal alone that serves as the cause, because the cognition has the universal as its object. As for the power residing in the individual, it is useful only as a real entity (*svarūpasat*). If one were to admit the appearance of even an unexpressed thing in verbal cognition, then just as the unexpressed individual cow appears from the word *go*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of even unexpressed jars and other things appearing; therefore, the power residing in the individual is necessary.

This very view is designated as the "Theory of Crooked Power" (*kubja-śaktivāda*), because the requirement that the object be an individual (*vyakti*) is not included within the scope of the delimitor of the causal condition for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Thus, they say that in the case of a verbal cognition whose qualifier is "cowness" (*gotva*) and whose object is a cow, the cause is a knowledge of power (*śaktijñāna*) in the form: "The cow possesses the power of the word 'cow' with respect to cowness"; however, it is not in the form: "The cow possesses the power of the word 'cow' with respect to an object qualified by cowness. Consequently, in expressions such as "Cowness exists," there is no possibility of a cognition of something qualified by cowness, because there is an absence of such a knowledge of power whose qualifier is cowness.

That too is merely superficial, because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) if the property of "having *gotva* as its object" were included within the delimiting factor (*avacchedakakoṭi*) of the causal capacity for a grasp of denotative power (*śaktigraha*) in the form "the cow possesses the denotative power of the word 'cow' with respect to *gotva*.

[Objection: Let there be no inclusion of "having that [the individual] as its object" in the delimiting factor; rather, let the grasp of denotative power in the form "the cow possesses the denotative power of the word 'cow'" serve as the cause for a verbal cognition whose object is qualified by *gotva*, by virtue of its having *gotva* as its qualifier (*prakāra*). In this way, there is simplicity (*lāghava*), since the objective particularity (*vyaktiviṣayatā*) need not be included in the delimiting factor of the cause.

If it is argued that, because a cognition having an individual situated in another location as its qualificandum is untenable, and because a causal relation is impossible on the basis of having the same qualificandum, one must instead accept a causal relation based solely on having the same mode of presentation (*prakāra*);

This is not so; for if the individual (vyakti) were not included within the scope of the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) regarding the object of the denotation, it would follow that the acceptance of a power residing in the individual is redundant. Nor should it be argued that if such [a power in the individual] is not accepted, it is impossible for the cognition of power to have "having cow-ness as its qualifier" (*gotvaprakāraka*) as its causal nature, because such a cognition of power would be an error due to the absence of power in the individual. For power is not a cause of verbal comprehension by virtue of its mere existence (*svarūpasat*), since comprehension arises even from corrupt words (*apabhraṃśa*), and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of verbal comprehension arising from a word whose power has not been grasped. Rather, it is [the power] as known (*jñāta*) [that is the cause].

And thus, since that which is the object of the knowledge of the word’s power (*śakti*) in a particular respect is precisely what is denotable (*śakya*), the individual (*vyakti*)—just like the universal (*jāti*)—is indeed denotable; the same applies to its qualification (*tadvaiśiṣṭya*). Otherwise, if the power resided only in the individual, then because the universal would not be a qualifier (*aprakāraka*) in the knowledge of the power regarding the individual, the causal relationship between the knowledge of the power, the mental presentation of the referent (*padārthopasthiti*), and the verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*)—which requires identity of the qualifiers (*samānaprakāratva*)—would be undermined, and the concept of the word’s power would be destroyed.

Nor should it be argued that the potency (śakti) will be established regarding the individual (jāti), based on the rule that whatever is the object of a cognition of potency must necessarily be the potent (śakya). For if that were so, since the cognition of potency would have the individual as its object by virtue of being its cause, the acceptance of potency residing in the individual would be inevitable; furthermore, the citation of the Bhāṣya regarding the stated point is based solely on a failure to consider the concluding Bhāṣya which states: "For someone, one thing is primary and another is secondary. Let this matter rest for now.

[Objection: But in this way, would the position that [the word] is "one" not result in being without a basis? To this, he says: "And of the [word] 'one'... In the view that "the power is the capacity to convey meaning" (*bodhakatva*), since the meaning obtained is that power is the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) as a qualifier (*prakāritā*) in the cognition whose object is the knowledge of the capacity to convey meaning, then—because the genus (*jāti*) residing in that [capacity] is one—the capacity residing in the word itself is established. Even in the view where the status of being a power belongs also to the state of being conveyed (*bodhyatva*) residing in the object—due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*)—there is the intention: "May the cognition of this meaning arise from this word."

The meaning is that the position [that the word denotes the individual] is also tenable because there is identity (*aikya*) among the universals (*jāti*) that serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the modehood (*prakāritā*) which is the cause of verbal cognition based on the power [of the word]. Thus, since the nature of being a delimiter of such modehood resides solely in the universal that constitutes the denotable power (*śakyajāti*), the position that "the form alone (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning" is supported. Although this delimiterhood, being a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), consists of [the universal] such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) itself, the relationship between the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) is to be established through the distinction between the qualified (*upahita*) and the unqualified (*anupahita*).

In the same way, the position that "the individual is one" (the view that the individual is the denotation) must also be supported. This is because, in the causal efficacy (*kāraṇatā*) for verbal cognition residing in such a cognition, the individual is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by virtue of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) within the cognitive content. In this view, the relationship between the delimited and the delimiter is established with consistency; furthermore, since there is a unifying factor in the form of universals such as "cowness," there is no resulting infinity [of meanings]. It should be understood that in this theory, the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) regarding the individual is the cause for the cognition of the individual under a qualifier such as "cowness"; thus, the employment of a word like "cow" for the purpose of cognizing an individual cow through its movement and so forth is also rendered possible.

[Objection: But surely, from the knowledge of word-potency (*śaktijñāna*) in the form "the pot is denotable by the word 'pot'," there would result not only a qualified cognition having *ghaṭatva* (potness) as its qualifier under its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), but also a cognition having *ghaṭatva* as qualified by its being a universal (*jātitvena*). This is because [the latter] is also subsumed under the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryyatāvacchedaka*) of that [knowledge]. To this, he says: "And thus... (*tathā ca*). Regarding the phrase "in the cognition qualified by *ghaṭatva*": the meaning is a cognition having that [potness] as its qualifier under its own nature.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the relation of cause and effect, since the cognition "the jar possesses a genus" has the property of being a genus (*jātitva*) as its qualifier with respect to the aspect of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), it is not subsumed under the definition of the effect of the aforementioned knowledge of power (*śaktijñāna*). Consequently, the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) does not arise. However, for a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) that has "jar-ness" as its qualificand and the property of being a genus as its qualifier with respect to the aspect of "jar-ness," one must postulate a separate causal relationship wherein the knowledge of power having the property of being a genus as its qualifier with respect to that same aspect serves as the cause.

[Objection: But since the property consisting of "having a qualifier other than that [specific] part" is grasped by a mere collection of facts (*arthasamāja*), how can it serve as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the effect? To this, he says: "It has been explained at length. Thus, because one postulates that a cognition of the power (*śaktijñāna*) having an unconditioned (*niravacchinna*) qualifier is the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) having an unconditioned qualifier of that [object], and a cognition of the power having a conditioned (*sāvacchinna*) qualifier of that [object] is the cause of a qualified cognition having a conditioned qualifier of that [object], the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not arise.

The meaning is "as stated therein. "Having intended that" means having accepted, according to the manner described, that the qualified [entity] is the denotable object (*śakya*). "The universal and the individual" means those two as they stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*). "From the prima facie view" means from the position that [the word denotes] "the one" [the qualified entity]. For in that position, since the power (*śakti*) consists in being the delimitor of the modehood (*prakāritāvacchedakatva*) within the factor of cognition that is the cause of verbal knowledge, the universal alone is the denotable object. However, according to the view that "it is the state of being the delimitor of qualificandness (*viśeṣyitayāvacchedakatva*)," it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that the individual alone is the denotable object.

The point here is that since the state of being a qualifier (*prakāritā*) is subsumed under the state of being a subject (*viṣayitātva*), and it is accepted that the denotative power (*śakti*) consists in the state of being a delimitor (*avacchedakatva*) with respect to that [subjecthood], the status of both as word-meanings (*nāmārthatva*) is established; thus, there is no suspicion of mutual contradiction between them. Although these views are well-established in the foundational texts (*ākarārūḍha*), the position that "the individual (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning" alone withstands rigorous scrutiny. As for the determination of the specific power of each individual word, that must be ascertained from other sources.

The state of being a *liṅga* (gender) is a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) belonging to that which possesses the aforementioned qualities (*guṇa*). With the intention of explaining its specific nature as neuter gender and so forth, he says: "sattva... etc. The state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthā*) means abiding in a condition free from increase (*upacaya*) and decrease (*apacaya*). Increase refers to *buddhi* (intellection), and decrease refers to its deficiency. "Residing in those respective words" means residing in words differentiated by categories such as genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and so on.

The phrase "denotable by those respective words" means "denotable by the word that has itself as its substratum," because of the conventional usage "the word is masculine," and because of the authority of such sūtras as "tasmācchaso naḥ" and "svamornapuṃsakāt. The sense is that even though [the substance] possesses the same phonetic sequence (*anupūrvī*), it is taken as a gender (*liṅga*) consisting of mutually similar substrata (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in the form of states such as increase (*upacaya*). The phrase "they differ" means they become the objects of inference whose content is the exclusion of other things possessing genders such as masculinity.

Now, if gender (*liṅga*) consists of the states (*avasthā*) described, then since those mutually contradictory states cannot coexist in a single locus, on what basis is the linguistic usage of multiple genders for certain words established? To this, he says: "of some"—meaning of words such as *taṭa* (bank) and so forth.

The meaning is that although these [states] are in fact contradictory, the linguistic usage of multiple genders is possible due to the superimposition of non-difference based on the identity of the phonetic sequence (*samānānupūrvī*) of the words. Regarding the objective state: "A woman is defined by breasts and hair; a man is known by body hair."

However, the gender (*liṅga*) characterized by such traditional rules (*smṛti*) cannot be adopted here; for in cases such as *dārān*, since that [gender] would be absent in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of the suffix *śas*, the substitution of *n* and so forth would not occur. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "A difference in gender is observed due to the difference in words having the same referent, and also due to the difference in their constituent parts."

The meaning is that gender is something distinct residing in the word itself; for we observe a diversity of genders in a single object—as in "puṣyaḥ," "tārakā," and "nakṣatram"—and because even when the phoneme *r* is added as a constituent in words such as "kuṭīraḥ," a difference in gender is observed. The point is that if gender were resident in the object (*artha*), the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the expression "a masculine word" (*puṃliṅgaḥ śabdaḥ*) would be untenable.

The phrase "and thus" (*evañca*) means that the gender (*liṅga*) residing in technical (*pāribhāṣika*) terms is useful for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Regarding "usage": if that [gender] residing in the object were the regulator of it, then a female individual would not be denoted by the words *vastu* (thing) or *padārtha* (category), nor would a male and so forth be excluded from such denotation. The point is that since the worldly gender (*laukikaliṅga*)—consisting of breasts, hair, and so on—is absent in things like a bed (*khaṭvā*), a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) would not arise from a word denoting such a thing.

The meaning is that although words such as *taṭa* and *taṭī* possess worldly gender (*laukikaliṅga*), their respective grammatical operations are justified because they are distinct by virtue of possessing technical genders (*pāribhāṣikaliṅga*) that are not coreferential with one another.

Now, if it is argued that the aforementioned gender residing in the word itself is what serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "female," "male," and so forth, then since that [gender] exists even in the word *paśu* (animal), which denotes a female animal, one might perform a sacrifice with a female animal in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), and thereby achieve the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). This is because, like the gender denoted by words such as *vyakti* (individual), that gender—residing in the substance—is common to both female and male and thus does not determine the specific object. To this, he says: "And that... meaning that it resides precisely in the word. "The object... means that it also determines the object.

He states that very point: "That which is expressed by the word 'animal' (paśu) and so forth," the remainder being "is the gender. The meaning is as follows: if a female animal had been intended as a constituent part of the sacrifice, then [the word] would have been employed with a case-ending that does not denote the masculine gender. However, because of the use of the word "animal" ending in that [masculine] suffix, it is determined that only a male animal is a constituent part of the sacrifice.

The point is this: since the word *paśu* (animal), when denoting a feminine object, cannot take the substitution of *nā* for *āṅ* in the singular instrumental case—as prescribed by the rule *āṅo nā'striyām*—one must employ the word *paśu* ending in that [masculine] form; thus, its meaning is understood to be masculine. Now, one might object: "Just as words such as *vyakti* (individual) and others function without regard for the gender residing in their referents, so too could the word *paśu* function. Since there is no obstacle to its functioning in that way, the aforementioned fault is unavoidable. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words *na ca* and *vyaktyādi*. By the term *ādi* ("and so forth"), he includes words such as *vastu* (thing).

The commonality [of the word *paśu*] is by virtue of its relation to being denotable by its own substratum; and its occurrence in both feminine and masculine genders is due to its being eternally feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), according to the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "the suffix *ktin* is used in the feminine. Now, one might object that the Vedic usage "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) would serve as proof for its eternal masculinity; therefore, he says "paśu..."—the point being that since the word *paśu* is seen to have a feminine gender as well in the Veda, it does not share the same status as words such as *vyakti*. He cites the consensus of the Mīmāṃsakas regarding his own stated position in the passage beginning "In the Mīmāṃsā... (*mīmāṃsāyām*).

He says "in reality" (*vastutastu*) because of the lack of satisfaction with what was about to be stated. Now, one might object that if words ending in the suffix *up* were neuter, then feminine usages such as *paśvā* (with the animal) would be untenable; therefore he says, "even in the Vedabhāṣya. Thus, the meaning is that just like the gender expressed by words such as *vyakti*, the gender expressed by the word *paśu* is common to both female and male, and therefore it does not serve to delimit its own specific referent.

One might then ask: how, then, is it determined that only a male animal is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice? To this he says, "or a goat" (*chāgo vā*). By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "by reason alone" (*nyāyenaiva*), there is the exclusion of gender as a delimiter of the referent.

Just as in the case of the expression "two rams for Sarasvatī" (*sārasvatau meṣau*), where there is a doubt as to whether the base word of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is feminine or masculine, the principle "in a doubtful case, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (*sandigdhe vākyaśeṣāt*) applies; and by means of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "that is the Vāmadevya couple," both are understood through the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of two identical words). In the same way, the sense here is that the gender of the male animal is determined as being an auxiliary element of the sacrifice (*yāgāṅgatva*) based on the wording of the mantra. This has been explained in detail: the meaning of a noun is indeed its worldly gender (*laukikaliṅga*), and that consists in the specific configuration of its constituent parts.

In examples such as *dārān*, the grammatical operation conditioned by that [gender] occurs precisely through the superimposition (*āropa*) of masculinity, because the instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*)—namely, the rule "The words *rātri*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine"—serves as the authority for the stated meaning. For this very reason, one does not say "the sacrifice with the wife of a beast. Alternatively, femininity and so forth are simply universals (*jāti*). As it is said: "These three universals alone are established in certain things, existing without conflict alongside conflicting universals such as those of 'cow,' 'buffalo,' and so forth."
"Thus it has been stated therein. But others [say]:
"A woman is known by her breasts and hair; a man is known by his body hair."
And that which is the interval between these two, in the absence of those two, is the neuter."

Since the definition of gender (*liṅga*) as stated in the *Smṛti*—characterized by the possession of qualities—is not universal, there would be no occurrence of the substitution of *na* (the *natva* rule) in cases such as *dārān*; therefore, in the *sūtra* "striyām," the Bhāṣyakāra accepted a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) gender consisting of the state of qualities that is universal and capable of undergoing grammatical operations, stating: "One must certainly adopt some established conclusion (*svakṛtānta*). Nevertheless, because the application of rules such as *natva* depends on the recognition of this heavy technical designation (*gurusaṃjñā*), even the worldly (*laukika*) gender is resorted to. This is because, although the designations such as *pumān* (masculine) were introduced for the sake of including more [cases], they do not apply when their purpose is already established. "Manifestation, disappearance, and persistence—
these properties, which are subject to passing away, are established as the defining characteristics (liṅga) in all material forms."

In this context as well, Hari has included the non-worldly (*alaukika*) gender by means of the particle *api*. When possible, the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as *pumān* (man) resides only in the scriptural gender (*śāstrīyaliṅga*) as qualified by worldly masculinity (*laukikapuṃstva*), through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); it does not reside in the scriptural alone, nor in the worldly alone. However, when [worldly masculinity] is impossible, it resides in the scriptural alone. For this very reason, in cases such as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) if the sacrifice is performed with a female animal;
for in that case, the word conveys only the scriptural masculinity as qualified by worldly masculinity. Thus they say.

If it is argued that the position [of the grammarians] that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of the three factors (gender, number, and case) is untenable because gender (*liṅga*) lacks the status of being an object of the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*), we say no; for there is consistency through the acceptance of a potency-apprehension in the form: "This jar, qualified by masculine gender and so forth, is denotable by the word 'jar'," on the authority of sūtras such as *svamornapuṃsakāt*.

According to the view that "the gender (*liṅga*) resides solely in the word and is not the cause for the application [of a suffix] such as *āp*," if there is non-difference between the word and its meaning, then gender is directly [the qualifier]; otherwise, because it functions as a qualifier (*prakāraka*) with respect to the objective aspect [of the meaning] through the relation of being denoted by its own substratum, it is determined—on the strength of the observed result—that its status as the object of the apprehension of word-meaning connection (*śakti-graha*) is governed by its being co-locative with the delimitor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*).

In reality, it is more appropriate to accept that even technical gender (*pāribhāṣika-liṅga*) is based on meaning alone. In expressions such as *pumliṅgaḥ śabdaḥ* ("a word of masculine gender"), the terms *pumliṅga* and so forth are derived from the *arśa-ādyac* suffix (meaning "possessing the nature of..."). Since everything is superimposed upon the Self (*ātman*), there is, through this indirect connection, a state of solidity (*styāna*) and so forth even in that [Self]; thus, the usage of "The Self is Brahman" (*ātmā brahma*) is justified. Solidity means concealment or diminution (*apacaya*). Because the intention to express growth (*upacaya*) and so forth is what governs their specific usage, there is no contradiction in employing them for a single object, even if they are mutually exclusive.

For this very reason, the statement found here and there—"the neuter [gender] is used for the general"—is consistent. Its meaning is that it applies when excellence is not intended to be expressed, even though it exists; this and other points should be ascertained from other sources.

He raises an objection in order to establish that the triad beginning with gender (*liṅga*) constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāmadheya*): "But surely... (*nanu*). The phrase "by means of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekābhyām*) means by means of such [concomitance] as follows: when there is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of [suffixes] such as *ṭāp*, the feminine gender is understood from words like "horse" (*aśva*), whereas in its absence, it is not so understood. The same should be inferred for other cases as well. Thus, since it is determined by those two [concomitances] that gender and the rest are the meaning of the suffix, the meaning is that the triad beginning with gender does not constitute the meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*).

In the phrase "he sees curds" (*dadhi paśyati*) and so forth, the expression "and so on" (*ityādi*) includes examples such as "this one goes" (*ayaṃ yāti*) and "this one comes here" (*ityamāyāti*). The term "from cognition" (*bodhāt*) means "from the cognition of [factors] such as being an object" (*karmatvādibodhāt*). Thus, the point is that because there is a deviation from the concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) and because they are obtainable through other means, these [gender and number] cannot constitute the meaning of the suffix; therefore, it is necessary that they belong exclusively to the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāma-arthatva*). With the intention that, although by the reasoning to be stated later gender and number may be the meaning of the suffix, it is more appropriate for gender (*liṅga*) to be the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti-arthatva*), he says: "Regarding gender... (*liṅgeti*).

"From this very reason" means precisely because the logic is the same whether the expressive power belongs to either the base (*prakṛti*) or the suffix (*pratyaya*). "Insistence" (*nirbandha*) means the dogmatic adherence that this view alone is the primary one. He states that very point: "of the suffix alone. "Because it is more reasonable" means that, compared to postulating the expressive power in all infinite bases, it is simpler (*lāghava*) to postulate it in only a few, such as the suffixes beginning with *ad*.

However, some maintain that gender (*liṅga*) is indeed the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because even in the view where femininity is not derived from words such as *vāc* (speech) and the like—despite the absence of suffixes like *-ṭāp*—the cognition of masculinity and neuter-ness from words such as *rāma* and *jñāna* is established by universal experience. Furthermore, since the cognition [of number and case] is admitted even through the recollection of a deleted case-ending (*luptavibhakti*), number and grammatical relation (*kāraka*) are expressed solely by the case-endings. And it has been said:

"Meaning itself (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), and [grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*)—these five alone are the meanings of a noun (*nāman*). According to some, the first three are the primary ones."

They say that the *liṅ* (optative) endings and others are the "superior" (*agrimāḥ*). Now, since a common property such as "being in the singular number" (*ekavacanatva*) is difficult to define, how can the *svādi* (case-endings beginning with *su*) denote singularity and so forth by means of that form? To explain: first of all, denoting singularity and so forth cannot be that [property], because if denotative capacity (*vācakatā*) consists in being a power (*śakti*), it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If, however, it consists in being a cause of cognition (*bodhakatā*), then there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since even dual endings and the like could cause the cognition of singularity through an error regarding their power; furthermore, in the view that "power is the capacity to cause cognition," the fallacy of self-dependence is unavoidable.

Nor is "oneness" (ekatva) and so forth a universal (jāti), because it would overlap with [the universal] "s-ness" (sutva) and others. Nor is it the possession of the word-form "singular" and so on through a relation consisting of Pāṇini’s convention; for if such a convention were a relation by virtue of being a convention, there would be the same over-extension (atiprasaṅga), since a convention of the form "in the word 'singular' and so on, the suffix *jas* and others are to be understood" could also be possible.

If it is argued that, regarding the property of being a convention of Pāṇini, there would be no criterion for determining the delimiting factor of denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedakatva*)—since, due to the lack of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*), the property of having words such as the singular number (*ekavacana*) etc., by virtue of a conventional relation similar to Pāṇini’s convention (even if established by another person who composed a different grammar), or the property of having words such as *ḍittha* etc., by virtue of a conventional relation belonging to a specific person in the form "from the word *ḍittha*, the suffixes *su*, *au*, *jas*, etc., are to be understood"—then we say: no.

Since we accept that the singular number [of the suffix] itself possesses the capacity for denotation (*sakhya*), the aforementioned fault finds no occasion; furthermore, because "immediate succession" is included within the scope of the determinant of productivity (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the cognitions produced by each other. Nor is there a deviation in cases such as *dadhi* and *madhu*, because in those instances, cognition is accepted to arise only through the mental reconstruction (*anusandhāna*) of the elided case-ending. Otherwise, how could that [cognition] be accounted for from the bare nominal stem (*prātipadika*) even under the theory of indication (*dyotakatā*), given that the indicator itself would be absent?

Nor should it be suspected that, because of the complexity (gaurava) involved in having multiple suffixes such as the singular (*su*) as the delimitors of capacity (*śaktatva-avacchedaka*), it is more appropriate for the single status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) to serve as that [delimitor], on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*); for, according to the reasoning already stated, even the status of being a nominal stem is difficult to define as a uniform property (*anugata*), and because the cognition of singularity and so forth is established by experience even when that [status of being a nominal stem] is unknown.

If [the word] were endowed with expressive power (*śakti*) either as a *pada* (word) or as a phoneme (*varṇa*), then the suffix (*vibhakti*) itself would be established as the denoter; furthermore, since the cognition of phonemeness (*varṇatva*) is not necessarily required prior to the cognition of oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth, it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate that [expressive power] in accordance with such [phonemic] requirements. Moreover, if there were a relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*) between two word-meanings, the cognition produced by distinct words would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the jar and its oneness—both presented by the same base (*prakṛti*)—could not be related to one another as qualifier and qualified. Therefore, the point is that the suffixes (*svādi*) alone are the denoters of number and so forth.

Furthermore, the intention of those who maintain that [words] are denoters (*dyotaka*) is as follows: it is not the case that the basic stems (*prakṛti*) possess powers for "pot" and "oneness" as separate, disjointed entities—which would leave room for the aforementioned objections—but rather that [the power resides] in the pot and so forth as qualified by oneness. This is because we do not admit a separate power [for each], and thus there is no absence of syntactic connection (*anvaya*); moreover, there is no burden of postulating that infinite basic stems possess the power for oneness and so forth. Consequently, even in a state where there is a misconception regarding the power of the word "pot" to denote oneness, from a sentence such as "The pot is knowable" (*ghaṭaḥ prameyaḥ*), there arises the cognition that "oneness is knowable."

Furthermore, since it is necessary that the presentation (upasthiti) of oneness and so forth generated by words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) must be a cause for the verbal cognition whose object is oneness and so forth—this being based on the unity [of the word] with the meaning conveyed by all [inflected forms]—and moreover, according to the view that the case-ending (*vibhakti*) expresses number, both the presentation of the jar and so forth generated by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the presentation of oneness and so forth generated by the suffixes *su* and so forth must be included in the subverting condition (*pratibandhakatā*) of the causal complex for an inference having the same object. Consequently, because there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding which of these two should occupy the position of the qualifier, there would be a multiplicity of relations between the subverter and the subverted.

In my view, there is parsimony because the single unified representation (upasthiti) having as its object each of the two qualifiers [singularity and pot] is posited therein; for even such a unified representation can be posited either as possessing a pot-qualificandhood determined by a singularity-qualifierhood, or as possessing a singularity-qualifierhood determined by a pot-qualificandhood, since there is no deciding factor (vinigamaka) between these alternatives. However, this does not establish parity, because in your view, where there are three factors—the cognition of semantic competency (yogyatājñāna), the representation of the pot, and the representation of singularity—[the burden of positing multiple representations is greater].

In the case of the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there would otherwise be a lack of decisive criteria (*vinigamanāviraha*) leading to a set of six types of relationships between the sublated (*pratibadhyatva*) and the sublator (*pratibandhakatva*). However, in my view, this is avoided through parsimony (*lāghava*): in the cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*), two cases arise by introducing the qualification of the presentation of the qualified object in its two forms (the individual and the combined) respectively; and another two cases arise by introducing the qualification of the cognition of competency in each of those presentations delimited by such forms. Thus, there are four cases. Furthermore, the avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is achieved by postulating that the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of specific words is the cause for the cognition of their respective numbers.

Thus, under the view that "the case-ending has the agent (and other kārakas) as its meaning," that [agent] is to be understood by postulating that the co-occurrence with the respective case-ending following it is the cause for the cognition of each respective kāraka. And this [postulation] is necessary even for those who maintain that [the suffix] is expressive (*vācakatāvādin*), in order to prevent the cognition [of an agent] from such forms as *am ghaṭaḥ*. In this manner, the indicative nature (*dyotakatva*) of prefixes (*upasarga*) is also to be understood; thus, he cites the consensus of Hari (*harisammati*) regarding both positions with the words: "whether they are indicators (*dyotikā*) or expressives (*vācikā*). Alternatively: "The aggregate [of base and suffix] is the denoter of the object possessing number."

Thus, the meaning of the latter half of that [verse] is as follows: a collection of inflected words delimited by a specific sequence, such as "ghaṭaḥ" (the pot), is the denoter of a pot qualified by singularity and so forth; this is stated with reference to the *padasphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa). This is because the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root cannot be established through any relation other than direct identity (*abheda*), and because otherwise the systematic distinction between what is directly expressed (*abhidhāna*) and what is not would be untenable; therefore, the meaning of the case-ending (*kārakavibhakti*) [is the qualifier].

Furthermore, if the mutual connection between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root is established through their distinction, then this [objection] can be refuted simply by postulating that the knowledge of a specific sequence—such as the word *pacati* occurring in proximity to the word *taṇḍula* ending in the second case—is the cause of a cognition whose qualificandum is the cooking having rice as its object (*taṇḍulakarmakapākaviśeṣyakabodha*).

Moreover, the section concerning what is not already expressed (*anabhihitādhikāra*) is useful only under the view that number is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), because under that view, rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and "for the singular and dual" (*dvayekayoḥ*) function as a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*), and thus there is freedom in choosing the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) therein.

Regarding the action of a single [object], since the action is one, the *anabhihita* sūtra (Pāṇini 2.3.1) achieves its purpose in the first alternative for the second case-terminations (*dvitīyādi*) and for the verbal suffixes (*tiṅādi*), because when one of the two has already expressed the meaning—since either the verbal suffix or another element expresses the object—the other becomes redundant by virtue of that expression; thus, the *anabhihita* sūtra would be fruitless. However, in the second alternative, even though the object is expressed by the *kṛt* suffix, the number residing therein is not yet expressed; therefore, there is an occasion to apply the second case-ending to prevent it from occurring.

Since that [number] would not fall under the category of an unexpressed object (*anabhihita-karman*), there would be no contingency for the use of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) and so forth. Furthermore, if number were also the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), then because the aforementioned sentence-meaning would be impossible, the Sūtra itself would be rendered useless.

If it is argued that, in the absence of the *anabhihita* rule, there would be the impossibility of the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so on after words such as *bhīṣma* in examples like *bhīṣmaṃ kaṭaṃ karoti*, because the mat (*kaṭa*) and other objects, being qualified [by the adjectives], are the most desired by the action (*kriyā*), and thus the nominative (*prathamā*) would result by applying to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha-mātra*); whereas under the view of that rule, since expression (*abhidhāna*) is restricted to a specific enumeration such as *kṛt*-suffixes and the like, even though the object is expressed by the second case of the base word *kaṭa*, the application of the second case and other cases after words like *bhīṣma* is easily established—[we reply: no.

When there is a desire to enjoin a qualified [object], since there is no satisfaction with the substratum (*dharmin*) alone and because the properties (*dharmas*) themselves are what are most desired, they possess the status of the object (*karman*). Furthermore, because that [object-hood] is not expressed by the accusative case-ending following a word denoting something else [the substratum], in cases such as "the mat is made" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*), the suffix follows the verbal root; thus, it does not express the object-hood residing in the specific property denoted by the nominal stem. Consequently, since it expresses that [object-hood] residing in the substratum without distinction, the use of the nominative case is justified after words expressing qualifiers such as "Bhīṣma. Therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in not adopting that [rule].

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "The mat is also the object (*karman*), and Bhīṣma and the others are also [the object]. Therefore, let the *kāraka* (case-role) also be the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). On this view as well, some maintain that the *kāraka* is merely a qualifier of the individual denoted by the stem-meaning, since it is manifested by the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the status of the cognition produced by the nominal stem as a cause for the cognition of the case-role (*kāraka*) would be lost; for such a loss is indeed desired. In this view, since the substance qualified by genus, gender, number, and case-role is understood from the nominal stem, the aforementioned causal relationship (between the cognition of the stem-meaning and the cognition of the case-role) becomes as non-existent as a flower in the sky. Rather, it is appropriate to regard the case-role as a qualifier [of the substance], because of its conformity with actual experience and because of the requirement of its connection with the action (*kriyā*). Thus, the position of the "fivefold" (pañcaka-pakṣa) is established.

"In many places" means in the original source texts such as the *Bhāṣya* and others. Among those, the positions of the "group of five" (*pañcaka*) and the "group of four" (*catuṣka*) were presented by Kaiyaṭa under the rule *tatropapadam*, while the position of the "group of three" (*trika*) was presented by the author of the *Vṛtti*. The phrase "as the primary [position]" implies that all these positions were indeed presented by the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

By the phrase "in the Sūtra, etc.," there is an inclusion of the *anabhihita* and other rules. He addresses the objection that—since there is no evidence for the manifestation of words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) in a verbal cognition such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), it is improper to prove that such a word is the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)—by stating "The word, first of all... In this regard, he cites the statement of Hari as authority: "There is no such thing... Here, "cognition" (*pratyaya*) means a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). The phrase "due to the following of the word" (*śabdānugamāt*) means "because it has the word as its object."

The term *anuviddham* means "qualified. The meaning is that just as a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) takes as its object a cognition qualified by the actual object, so too does it take as its object [the cognition] qualified by the word. This qualification (*vaiśiṣṭhya*) should be understood as being mediated through the object.

Following the understanding generated by the word *ghaṭa*, the reflective awareness is precisely "I am verbally cognizing a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ śābdayāmi*), and not "a pot" (*kalaśam*) or "a pitcher" (*kumbham*). For this very reason, there is no tautology in such cases as "The sun rises copper-red" (*udeti savitā tāmraḥ*); for the point is that if those specific words were not employed, the uniformity of the verbal cognition regarding both rising and setting could not be established.

[Objection: Even by that much, the manifestation of the word is established, but not as the qualificand (viśeṣya); how then is the status of the word as the meaning of the word established? To this, he says: "Viṣṇum"—by stating that the utterance of the meaning is impossible, the occasion for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is also indicated. "Incoherence" (*asaṅgati*) means "impossibility. "That too"—meaning even the word—is the "meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*). The sense is that it is impossible for something presented through another mode [of cognition] to be the qualificand.

The sense is that even if one maintains that [the function] is established through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—specifically, the relation consisting in the denotability of its own denoted meaning—nevertheless, the status of being a word-meaning (*padārthatva*) is not thereby proven. Regarding the term "conventional" (*nirūḍha*): conventionality consists in the dependence of the indication upon the apprehension of an intention (*tātparya*) that is beginningless (*anādi*). And "beginninglessness" in this context means the possession of a series of successive destructions of prior cognitions that have the same form as the cognition produced by itself. The phrase "because it is not distinct from denotative power" (*śaktyanatirekāt*) implies "in our view," and so forth; the truth of this matter will be explained later.

He also states its non-universality: "jabagaḍadaśam," because the meaning is that such a collective group has no capacity whatsoever [to denote anything]. As for the phrase "due to non-apprehension" (agrahāt), the meaning is that, in my view, since such a collective group itself constitutes the denotable object (śakya) of that word, there is no logical inconsistency.

[Objection: "But even if the composite whole lacks power [to denote], since the individual phonemes such as *ja* that constitute it are established to have power for words like *jaitra* in single-syllable lexicons (*ekākṣarakośa*), there is no inconsistency regarding the definition of denotation (*vācakatva*)—which consists in being the signifier of a particular meaning—in those cases. [Response: To this he says, "of that which is unknown" (*ajñātāyāḥ*). The point is this: in the case of the word *gaṅgā*, if its actual relation—consisting in proximity to its own primary meaning, the stream—is not grasped, the cognition of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) does not arise; therefore, it is only when that relation is known that it serves as the means for the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*). Since that [relation] is not grasped in the present case, the aforementioned inconsistency remains exactly as it was.

[Objection: Surely, even if at the time immediately preceding verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) there is no apprehension of such a function (*vṛtti*), it is easy to account for such verbal cognition by means of the presentation of word-meanings through a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened by an apprehension of such a function that occurred at some time or other; to this he says: "In *gāvam*," meaning that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the imitation of the word *go* and so forth is accepted by everyone.

Regarding the phrase "paranaya" (according to the other): the "other" refers to the Naiyāyika; in his view, since those [suffixes] lack *sakti* (denotative power), a definition composed of them cannot apply either. Thus, the sense is that there would be the impossibility of their being *prātipadika*s (nominal stems) and so forth, which are based on the condition of having *arthavattva* (possessing meaning) consisting in the possession of a *vṛtti* (grammatical operation).

"Even sixfold" means including sound (*śabda*) along with the five previously mentioned categories; this refers to certain instances of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). That imitation is of two kinds: of sound (*dhvani*) and of phoneme (*varṇa*). Of these, the first is exemplified by *paṭatkaroti* and so forth; the second is exemplified by *bhuvo vuk* and so forth. "Intention to express a distinction" means that in cases such as *paṭat*, there is an intention to express the distinction between being composed of sound and being composed of phonemes, whereas in cases such as *bhuvo vuk*, there is an intention to express the distinction between being meaningless and having "word" (*śabda*) as its referent.

The word (*śabda*) is also the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus, according to the rule *matu-chaḥ sūktasāmnoḥ*, that which is recited in the Vedic corpus as the word *asyavāma-* becomes the referent of the word *āsyavāmīyam* and so forth, because it is the base for the suffix *cha*; this is the intended sense, since its status as a nominal stem is established by this very fact. In the reading found in the root-text, *arthe 'vabhāsate*, the meaning is that it "appears in the object"—that is, it appears in the form of a jar or the like, becoming the object [of cognition] as a qualifier.

In fact, the reading is: "by the consideration of the ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*), this object does not appear" (*asāv artho na bhāsate*). In that context, the word *va* signifies similarity; thus, the meaning is that just as in the theory of difference (*bhedapakṣa*) the object in the form of the original (*anukāryya*) appears as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) in verbal cognition, so too in the theory of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*) the imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) is non-different from the original. To the question of how something not [otherwise] present can appear, it is said: "by the ear and so forth" (*śrotrādibhiḥ*). Some maintain that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti-jñāna*) and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by it are included.

In reality, however, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used so that the cognition of that [word] as accompanied by its script and so forth may be fully realized in verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). The underlying intention is that the principle—"only that which is presented by a word (*pada*) appears in verbal comprehension"—is not universal. For this very reason, the author of the *Sāra* explained it by stating, "it appears as having a meaning" (*arthavad bhāsate*). By this, the objection—that under the view of non-difference (*abhedapakṣa*), since an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) lacks a meaning, it is impossible to describe its appearance in that portion [of the cognition]—is resolved.

[Objection: But even if there is non-difference [between the word and its meaning], how can the object to be imitated (anukārya) appear in verbal cognition (*śābda*), given the absence of a mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the word's function (*pada-vṛtti*)? To this, he says: "The point is as follows" (*ayam bhāvaḥ*). The ellipsis for the phrase "because it is not presented by the word" (*padānupasthitatvāt*) is to be supplied as "because its appearance in verbal cognition would be untenable. For the sake of establishing that—that is, for the sake of a presentation produced by a word which generates the verbal cognition—the ellipsis for "power" (*śakti*) is to be supplied as "because that which is unrelated does not produce the recollection thereof."

Likewise, because there exists an apprehension (upasthiti) produced by the knowledge of the word's lexical meaning (padavṛtti), its status as an object of verbal cognition (śābdaviṣayatā) is easily established. "In the case of non-difference" (abhede) means when there is an intention to express non-difference; the sense is that, on that view, since the relationship between the defined (nirūpya) and the definer (nirūpaka) is based on difference, such a relation cannot occur in the case of a mere imitation (anukaraṇa). "Because it is the cause" (hetutvāt) connects with the state of being produced residing in the apprehension.

"Of its own perception" (*svapratyakṣa*) means having the form of a perception that is an imitation [of the word itself]. "The possibility of being an object of verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhaviṣayatopapatti*) is the underlying intention: under the view of non-difference (*abheda*), just as a word appears in verbal cognition by taking up its own perceptual presentation (*upasthiti*), so too in cases such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), since it is unavoidable that words like "jar" (*ghaṭa*) also appear by taking up that same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is established that all verbal cognition has a word as its object. This is stated in the rule *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68).

In the Bhāṣya it is said: "This need not be stated. Why? Because the comprehension of an object is preceded by the word, and it is indeed preceded by the word. For even when one is called by name, if that name is not perceived [at the time], one asks: 'What did you say? Thus, the comprehension of an object is preceded by the word; and in this treatise, because the word is possible, there is the exclusion of the object."

In this context, by the passage beginning with "For [it] is preceded by word" (*śabdapūrvako hi*), the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the knowledge of the word's function in the presentation of the word-meaning and so forth are demonstrated. Then, by the conclusion of the passage beginning with "preceded by word," another method is shown; the meaning is that [the word] has the word as its qualifier. By this, the sense is that when [the word] is presented as a qualifier of the object because the [direct] application to the object is impossible, the operation [of the injunction] applies to the word. Thus, according to the aforementioned Bhāṣya, both the word and its meaning are manifested from the word itself.

In cases where there is a sublation of the connection of other word-meanings with respect to a word in a sentence, the word functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) for the meaning-component; whereas in cases where the meaning [is primary], such as in "pronounce Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇumuccāraya*) or "the suffix *ḍhak* after *agni*" (*agnerḍhak*), it is clear that the meaning functions as a qualifier for the word-component. This is because the *Vākyapadīya* states, "disregarding the status of being an object" (*viṣayatvam anādṛtya*). Regarding the term "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*): the meaning is that this is for the purpose of preventing the appearance in verbal cognition (*śābda-bhāna*) of things such as space (*ākāśa*), which might otherwise be presented through inherence (*samavāya*) or by virtue of being the object of the same cognition as the jar in the sentence "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*).

"Produced by a mental state" (*vṛttijanyā*) means "produced by the cognition of a mental state. The point is that since it is observed that the presence of such a word (*padopasthitiḥ*)—as in the case of "hearing the word 'jar' (*ghaṭapadam*)," and so on—is a cause [of verbal cognition], it would be difficult for an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) to be the object of verbal cognition in the present instance if that were absent.

"By way of being the locus (*āśrayatā*)"—this is said having accepted that "the power (*śakti*) is the state of being a signifier (*bodhakatva*). However, in the view that "it [power] is the state of being signified (*bodhyatva*)," it should be understood as being "by way of being the relatum (*nirūpakatā*). Now, one might object: if the condition for something being the object of verbal cognition is simply its possessing a linguistic function (*vṛttimatva*) through the relation of being the locus, then it would be impossible for that which possesses the function through the relation of being the relatum to appear in verbal cognition. To this he replies: "by way of being the relatum. The point is that, according to authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*), the assumption of greater complexity (*gaurava*) is not a defect.

The point is that since being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) depends solely on the capacity to convey a meaning that determines a grammatical function (*vṛtti*), there is no possibility of that designation applying under the view that it is not a word (*anabhidhāpakapakṣa*).

Now, one might ask: "Since the locus of a relation qualified by having itself as its counter-correlative is not admitted to reside in itself, how can an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) possess a grammatical function? To this he says: "of the relation. "By way of conveying that" means by way of generating a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) consisting of direct perception.

And thus, because the validity of statements by Harya and others is established, and because it is accepted that even in the present case, one's own self is the locus of such a relationship, there is no inconsistency in its manifestation in verbal cognition (śābda-bhāvanā). It is in this very manner that the manifestation of every word in verbal cognition is to be accounted for; this is the intended meaning.

Now, if being the denoter of itself is defined as being "determined by itself," then the status of being a *prātipadika* (nominal stem) would be unavoidable for an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) just as it is for other words. Furthermore, it is difficult to establish that the capacity to generate a cognition consisting of one's own direct perception constitutes a "function" (*vṛtti*), because such a function is defined specifically as a relation that serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the objecthood (*viṣayatā*) of the knowledge that generates the presentation of the word-meaning which, in turn, generates verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). And it is not the case that by such a [perceptual] knowledge, a presentation of the word-meaning in the form of a sound is generated prior to the verbal comprehension.

Nor is it the case that at that time there exists a cognition such as "the word 'pot' generates its own perception"—by which [cognition] that [self-awareness] might also be possible—because one who has not grasped the convention regarding a pot does not experience the verbal cognition of the word 'pot' from the cognition that "the word 'pot' generates its own perception. If it is asked, "How is this so?"...

On this point, they say: because there is no distinction in the relationship [of the word] with the meaning presented by the word's own function (pada-vṛtti)—as expressed in the passage beginning with "of the relation" (sambandhasya) and ending with "of the word" (śabdasya)—there is the presentation of the word [along with the meaning]; consequently, both the word and the meaning appear in the verbal cognition (śābda-bodha), since the property of being prompted by the word's function exists in both types of presentation. Thus, because the focus is on the meaning, the aforementioned inconsistency does not arise. In that context, after the phrase "just as of the meaning" (tatrārthasyeva), the words "because it is to be cognized" (bodhyatvāt) are to be supplied as the remainder. Furthermore, in the expression "by way of being its indicator" (tad-bodhakatvena), it is more appropriate to refer to the meaning of the word "meaning" (artha) which was presented immediately prior; therefore, the sense is "by way of being the indicator of the meaning. As it has been said:

"The recollection of the name (saṃjñā) that occurs therein is not itself caused by anything else; for it is only when the individual object (piṇḍa) itself is perceived that it is capable of causing the recollection of the name. Here, "perceived" (dṛṣṭaḥ) means present before the senses. However, verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) must be admitted to occur with a slight delay, on the authority of the statements of Harṣa and others which will be cited later. But in the view that the imitator (anukārya) is non-different [from the imitation], another method must be followed for its manifestation.

According to the view stated by Paretu, since it is necessary to include "being produced by a cognition possessing [the object] under a specific relation" within the scope of the determinant (avacchedaka) for the condition that the presentation of an object-entity (padārthopasthiti) is a cause of verbal comprehension (śābdabodha), there is the fault of complexity (gaurava) due to the twofold entry of the *vṛtti* (the denotative relation). However, if the relation is introduced as "either-or" (*anyataratva*), then because there is no deciding factor (vinigamanāviraha) regarding the status of the qualifier and the qualified between the two exclusions (bheda) that constitute "either-or," the same state of complexity persists.
