With respect to that [imitation], in the view that there is non-difference [between the imitation and the original], the presentation of the object to be imitated (*anukārya*) arises through the relation of similarity (*sādṛśya*). Consequently, even though it is thus presented, it appears in verbal cognition (*śābda-bhāna*) by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*). Since the condition for being produced by the knowledge of a word-derivation (*vṛtti-jñāna*) includes the exclusion of being produced by the knowledge of similarity, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding its causality. For this very reason, in examples such as *gavity ayam āha* ("He says 'cow'"), there is no production of case-endings, because [the word *go*] lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*)—defined as the capacity to convey meaning through a word-derivation—and thus is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*). This point is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *matau chaḥ sūktasāmnoḥ*. Thus they say.

Demonstrating, by means of the example of light, that the relation qualified by having itself as its counter-correlative exists in itself, he states the agreement of Hari with his own position, saying "And it has been said. "Grāhyatvam" means being cognizable; "grāhakatvam" means being a cognizer. "These two"—namely, being the object and being the subject—by the phrase "existing separately," he shows their lack of necessary concomitance. In the world, the presence of these two powers in light, such as a lamp, when in proximity to an object, is established through direct perception.

But when that [non-obstruction] is absent, there is only the state of being the apprehended object (*grāhyatva*); likewise, when the meaning of words is not obstructed, both powers mentioned [above] exist. But when it is obstructed, there is only the state of being the apprehended object—this is the meaning.

This very point is obtained even from the commentary on the sūtra *svaṃ rūpam*, as he states another verse for that purpose: "The state of being an object" (*viṣayatvam*). The meaning is that an object is not made known by words without producing its own state of being an object; that is to say, because the property of being a cognition of an object produced by itself is pervaded by the property of having itself as its object (*svaviṣayakatva*).

The intended meaning is this: according to the view that there is non-difference between word and object, because of the superimposition (adhyāsa) rooted therein, when a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of an object arises from a verbal cognition, the word also imparts its own form to that modification; thus, it is established that verbal cognition has the word as its object.

Regarding this, they say: Since it has been stated that "there is no cognition in the world [that does not have a word as its object]," is it being asserted that [all cognition] has a word as its object by virtue of the delimiting property of being a cognition (*bodhatva*), or rather, by virtue of being an apprehended object (*grāhyatva*)? From the two verses [of the *Ślokavārttika*], it appears to be the former, namely, by virtue of the delimiting property of being a word (*śabdatva*). Or perhaps it is by virtue of co-inherence with the state of being verbal (*śābdatva*). The first alternative is not tenable, because at the time immediately preceding the perception of a jar or the like, the presentation of the word "jar" or the like is not a necessity; therefore, it is impossible for such a perception to have the word "jar" as its object.

Likewise, even in the case of the inference of a jar and so forth, its presence [in the word] is not possible; for when the pervasion is grasped either as being pervaded by it or as having it as its delimiting factor, that [word] does not appear therein, and furthermore, immediately thereafter, there is no after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) such as "I perceive the word 'jar'" or "I infer the word 'jar'."

The second alternative is not tenable; for since the mental presentation (upastiti) produced by the cognition of the word "jar" lacks a word that denotes it, it is impossible for that [presentation] to be an object of verbal cognition. Furthermore, since the cognition of a word functions as a reminder of its meaning by way of being a cognition of a related entity (*sambandhijñāna*), just as the sight of the elephant-driver causes the presentation of the elephant, so too in the presentation of the meaning produced by that [word], the word itself—which is the delimitor of the capacity to awaken the memory—cannot be the object. Thus: "A jar is not the word 'jar'."

Thus, since there is no evidence for the identity of word and meaning based on universal consensus, it is impossible for a mental modification (vṛtti) having the form of an object to also possess the form of a word. Even if one were to tolerate a momentary delay because the universal experience "I am hearing the word 'jar'" occurs immediately after the cognition of the word "jar," such a thing is not actually the case; therefore, this [objection] amounts to nothing.

Furthermore, when the object is distinct [from the subject], because the causal complex for inference (*anumiti-sāmagrī*) is stronger, it is impossible to establish the manifestation of that [inference] regarding the aspect of the jar in a case where—despite the presence of such an inferential complex—a verbal cognition (*śābdadhī*) having only "jar-ness" as its qualificandum arises by the force of a desire such as "let there arise a verbal cognition of a jar. This is because the inferential complex, which has a distinct object and is qualified by the absence of a desire for a verbal cognition from the word "jar," exists as an obstructive factor (*pratibandhaka*).

Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*). This is because others accept that in cases such as "pronounce the word *Viṣṇu*," words like *Viṣṇu* are objects of verbal cognition (*śābdaviṣayatā*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, even from the aforementioned Bhāṣya, one obtains precisely the meaning that in some instances of verbal cognition, the word itself is the object. Moreover, there is no harm in accepting that, when there is an intention (*tātparya*), the word may appear in the form of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in certain other cases as well.

For this very reason, even though Nala and others are not specifically presented in their respective individual forms, the cognition of them as denotable by the word "Nala" is established according to the consensus of the ancients, based on the apprehension of a general denotative power (*sāmānya-śakti-graha*)—namely, that "there was someone denoted by the word Nala. As for the manifestation of the word itself when there is non-difference (*abheda*), this is in accordance with the view of the *Bhāṣya* cited as "others, however" (*pare tu*). For this same reason, there is a cognition of the object exactly as it is, without modification.

The words of Hari, however, serve to indicate an excellence of faith in the meditation upon the non-difference of the *praṇava* and Brahman; therefore, the establishment of a conventional (empirical) object does not result from them. Consequently, the view that the object of verbal cognition is merely the word itself is not tenable, as will become clearer further on. The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if one were to accept only the position of difference (*bheda*).

The meaning is as follows: since restrictive rules (*niyama-śāstra*) function even by way of prohibition—based on the restriction that "the base (*prakṛti*) must be employed only when followed by an affix (*pratyaya*), and never alone"—there arises the contingency of ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) due to the transgression of the prohibition "one should not employ what is not a word (*apada*)," which is rooted in that very restriction; for this prohibition applies to that which is fit for an affix, and its violation occurs when such a base is employed without an affix.

In our view, however, because that [word] lacks the fitness to be a grammatical cognition (*pratyaya*), there is an absence of its being an object of prohibition; consequently, since there is no possibility of its transgression, the substitution of *av* and so forth occurs precisely because it is correct (*sādhutva*). Otherwise, as in the case of vernacular words (*bhāṣāśabda*), such an application would not take place. This is the sense. Thus ends the determination of nouns (*nāman*) in the *Śrībhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. 4.

Intending to refute the view that there is no additional expressive power (*śakti*) in a compound (*samāsa*), which consists of a collection of names, because its function is accomplished by the very powers already established in its constituents, and wishing to define the meaning of a compound as an occasion arises, he first demonstrates its classification with the following thought in mind: "He says 'compounds' (*samāsān*). And the nature of being a compound (*samāsatva*) is either (1) the state of possessing the word-form "compound" through the relation of expressive power (*śakti*), or (2) a specific type of collection of words that has attained the state of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning).

Regarding the state of having a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) and its proof: "What, then, is meant by 'capacity' (*samartha*)? The statement of capacity refers to the becoming of a single meaning from things that have separate meanings. Where, then, are there separate meanings, and where are there single meanings? In a sentence, there are separate meanings—as in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*: 'rājapuruṣaḥ' (the king's man); and the arguments to be stated hereafter are based upon that."

In this context, "having a single meaning" (*ekārthatva*) means having as its object a single presentation (*upasthiti*). It does not mean "having a power toward a single object," because words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) would then fail to possess "single-meaningness," since they possess powers directed toward multiple objects—namely, the pot, pot-ness, and their relation. "Having distinct meanings" (*pṛthagarthakatva*) means having as their objects multiple presentations. For example, in a sentence, the word-meanings, through the assistance of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, comprehend a qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) meaning; this is according to the *Bhāṣya*: "That which has a connected meaning is *samartha* (semantically integrated)."

The apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) regarding words such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man) takes the form: "The word *rājapuruṣa* has its expressive power directed toward a person who possesses a relationship with a king. Consequently, by means of the principle of distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not yet obtained (*prāptāprāptaviveka*), the specific expressive power culminates in the meaning of the genitive case and so forth. For this very reason, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of words such as *sundara* (beautiful) with the king and so on [within the compound], because they constitute only a single part (*ekadeśatva*). However, in cases such as *devadattasya gurukulam* (Devadatta’s teacher’s family), it will be explained later that such a connection does occur due to the presence of an indicative factor (*gamakatva*).

The view that "the function of words [in a compound] is one that abandons their own meanings" (jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ) and that this results in the meaninglessness of the words is not correct; for in cases such as *mahābāhuḥ*, the substitution of *āt* (for *mahat*) would not occur. Furthermore, resorting to the notion of a "former state of existence" (bhūtapūrvagati) is improper when another explanation is available. As it has been said: "But the 'abandonment of its own meaning' occurs only where there is a conventional meaning that contradicts [the literal sense]. The meaning of this is: that [function] exists only where the collective meaning of the whole contradicts the meaning of the individual parts, as in *kṛṣṇasarpa* ("black snake") and the like. This alone is the correct position.

"In a compound (*samāsa*), there is indeed a distinct power (*śakti*), just as in the word *paṅkaja* (lotus). This view is accepted by the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*), because if that were the case, the citation of that example would be meaningful, given that opponents accept the existence of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-technical) power in words such as *paṅkaja*. For if the position that "the function [of the parts] abandons its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*) were his own accepted view, then its citation would be untenable; this is clear because, while he accepts that position in his own system, his opponents do not accept it therein. More will be said on this point further ahead.

The mention of "that which has motion" (*gatimat*) and "that which has the acute accent" (*udāttavat*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication) that also includes the rule for the analysis of the compound (*yogavibhāga*) as "a word ending in a case-suffix [is compounded] with another word ending in a case-suffix" (*saha supā*). In the example *anuvyācalat*, there is a simultaneous compounding of *anu* with *vyācalat* and of *vi* with *ācalat*, because *anu*—ending in a case-suffix—is semantically connected (*samartha*) with the entire complex *vyācalat*. Once the designation of "compound" (*samāsa*) is established, the substitution of *aṇ* (as in *śākala-pratiṣedha*) occurs, as does the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound.

Because the singular number has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), or because the operation denoted by the verbal root is incapable of being construed with number, no case-suffix (*sub*) arises from it. Furthermore, there is no occasion for the default singular number (*autsargikaikavacana*) of the *samya* [particle], since its application is impossible in Vedic usage; this is the intended meaning. Likewise, the intended meaning is that [the suffix] does not apply precisely because a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is not denotable.

The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means that one would have to accept the designation of *samāsa* (compound) prior to the production of the case-ending (*sup*). This refers to the argument beginning with "because [the word] would not be a *pada* for the purpose of the elision of *n*" (*nalopa-tyasyāpadatvāt*). Although it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *upapadam* that these two [conditions] are excluded by the rule *sup-supā*, nevertheless, the intention is that due to the force of the technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) "compound," the *samāsa* occurs only after the production of the case-ending of the preceding member. By using the expression "prior to the production of the case-ending" (*prāk subutpatteḥ*), the author has demonstrated the purpose of the *paribhāṣā* under the guise of showing the purpose of a specific portion [of the rule].

For after the production of the *sub*-suffix, since the sequence of the application of the meanings of the base (*svārtha*), the substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and case-role (*kāraka*)—which is based on the relationship between *antaraṅga* and *bahiraṅga*—is accepted as being in accordance with the commentary on the rule *kutsite* (Pāṇini 5.3.74), [the feminine suffix] *ṭāp* applies first because it is *antaraṅga*. Consequently, since the word does not end in the long vowel *ā* at that stage, the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule *krītāt karaṇapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.50) would be untenable; such is the direction of the argument.

It has been explained in the Bhāṣya; for there, having refuted by means of the principle that "a sentence is completed with respect to a whole" (vākyaparisamāptinyāya) the purpose of the word *saha*—which was to prevent the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) for each individual member—the [Bhāṣya] states: "In that case, since [the desired result] is already established, the purpose of employing the term *saha* is so that it may be understood as a constituent part of the rule (*yogāṅga*). When it is a constituent part of the rule, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: 'The word *saha* is compounded. With what? With a semantically related word (*samartha*). [Examples: *anuvyacalat*, *anuprāviśat*."

Then [it is stated]: "A *sup*-ending word is compounded with another *sup*-ending word; and this shall be the defining rule for that compound for which no other rule exists. Regarding this, the purpose of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is to be understood as the prevention of the application of the same technical name (*saṃjñā*) by means of a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as in examples such as *devadattaḥ pacati*. The meaning of "of six kinds" (*ṣāḍvidhya*) is that there are six varieties, beginning with those mentioned by the ancients.

Although, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "avyayaṃ vibhakti" (Pāṇini 2.1.6), it is stated that because the whole [compound] is what undergoes grammatical refinement (*saṃskārya*) and is therefore primary, qualifiers such as "prosperity" (*samṛddhi*) apply to that whole alone—and thus, since prosperity and so forth are understood from the whole, the same status as an *avyayībhāva* would result here as well—the author, with this intention in mind, asks: "Why does [the designation *avyayībhāva*] not apply here in cases such as *sumadrāḥ* and *sacchātraḥ*? Having raised this question, he states the definitions of compounds, beginning with: "In this case, there is a certain compound where the meaning of the prior member is predominant."

The objection that "here the predominance of the meaning of the first member of the compound is not perceived" has been resolved. Nevertheless, the sense is that there is no fault, because by introducing an alternative view with the words "Or rather," "these are not indicated as the meanings of the compounds," and so forth, he indicates a lack of strict adherence to the aforementioned definitions.

The definition of a *lakṣaṇa* (definition) is the possession of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) by that [object]. A property is "unique" if it exists in all members of that class while not existing in anything other than them. For example, the possession of a dewlap and horns is the definition of a cow. In this case, the inclusion of the terms "existence in all" (*sakalavṛttitva*) and "non-existence" (*avṛttitva*) is intended to exclude such things as the possession of horns (which applies to goats, etc. or the black color of the sky from being definitions of a cow. As it has been said: "In a definition, only those words should be employed by which the defects of under-extension (*avyāpti*), over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) are avoided."

In this context, non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) is the absence of the definition in that which is to be defined (*lakṣya*). Over-pervasion (*atīvyāpti*) is its presence in what is not to be defined. Impossibility (*asambhava*) is its failure to exist in any instance of the thing to be defined. Examples will be stated later. The result [of a definition] is the inferential cognition of the difference from others based on that property, as well as linguistic usage, arising from the knowledge that the subject possesses a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). However, in the case of a property that is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), the knowledge of that property results in mere linguistic usage.
As it has been said: "The purpose of a definition is either exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) or linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)."

The term *prāyovāda* (a statement made for the most part) means that although these [suffixes] are generally observed, some others are also found; he clarifies this very point with the words "in a previous instance" (*bhūtapūrva*) and so forth.

Even though these possess some of the characteristics to be described, they should be understood as not included because they are not taught in the sūtras governing those specific categories. For if they were included in the division governed by the sūtras concerning compounds (*samāsa*), it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Regarding the phrase "pūrvapadārtha" and so forth: primacy (*prādhānyam*) consists in being the primary qualificandum (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*) as determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) of the meaning of the constituent word of the compound. Thus, the meaning is that *avyayībhāva*-ness consists in being the generator of a cognition in which the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is the qualificandum. The same applies to what follows.

In the case of *upakumbham* ("near the jar"), since proximity as qualified by the jar is understood as the primary object (*viśeṣya*), the definition applies accordingly. Similarly, in *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the referent of the latter member (*uttarapadārtha*)—the man related to the king—is the primary object; in *pītāmbaraḥ* ("yellow-clad"), the referent of the compound as a whole (*anyapadārtha*)—one who possesses a garment identical with yellow—is the primary object; and in *dhavakhadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees"), both members of the compound—the dhava and the khadira—as joined in association (*sāhitya*) appear as the primary objects. Thus, the definition is appropriately applicable in each instance.

Regarding the phrase "due to deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*): although deviation is indeed nothing other than over-extension (*ativyāpti*), nevertheless, in this context, both are indicated by the term "deviation" as defects. As he will state later, he demonstrates that very [point] through a shift in emphasis with the words "for instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth. "The meaning of the preceding word" (*pūrvapadārtha*) means the meaning of words such as "insane" (*unmatta*). The same applies further on. "The definition of an indeclinable compound" (*avyayībhāvalakṣaṇa*) means the presence of its definition, which consists in generating a cognition where the meaning of the preceding word is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). "In a *bahuvrīhi*" means the definition of that [compound]. The same applies further on.

[Objection: "In that case, what then are the definitions of *avyayībhāva* and so forth? To this he says: "But in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), however... The delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is the state of possessing the designation *avyayībhāva* and so on through the relation of primary denotative power (*śakti*). The point is that there is no fault in not including cases such as *bhūtapūrva* (formerly been), because they are not covered by the delimiting factors of the definiendum. He introduces the root text by adopting the view that the word's function involves abandoning its own meaning (*jahatsvārthavṛtti*): "And there is the impossibility of these," where "these" refers to the definitions, and the phrase "in the view that the word's function involves abandoning its own meaning" is to be supplied.

"Impossibility" (asambhava) means non-occurrence in the mere indicated object (lakṣya). The sense is that, according to that view, since there is no occurrence of the preceding and following words anywhere in their primary sense (tattvena), those [words] which incorporate the indicated meaning cannot occur in examples such as "upakumbha."

In the *Mūla*, regarding the phrase "bhauta" in the view of those who maintain the eternality of sound (*śabdanityatāvādin*), [the author] says "so 'pi" (that too), because even the sequence beginning with "au" is impossible in compounds such as *avyayībhāva* according to the literal reading; the meaning is that "even the conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*) is intended. Regarding the term "rekhā" (line/drawing): since one thing cannot convey the nature of another, he clarifies the underlying intention in the *Sāra* with the passage beginning "rekhā-gavaya" (the line-drawn gavaya) and so forth. "Tadvad eva" means "just like the line-drawn gavaya," etc.

Just as, for instance, in the case of a *gavaya* (a wild ox) and the like, the line-shape and tail—which, though not actually present in the *gavaya*, reside in the [resembling] lines and parts of the model—are understood to denote the *gavaya* through the determination of non-difference based on similarity with the tail of the *gavaya*; likewise, the meaning is that even though primacy of the meaning of the first member and so forth—which resides in the analytical (*vigraha*) sentence—is not present in the compound (*samāsa*), it denotes the *avyayībhāva* and other types of compounds due to similarity.

However, under the view that the compound functions without abandoning its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthavṛtti*), the conventional designation of the predominance of the meaning of the first member is not difficult to establish; with this intention, he introduces the root text with the words "Now, [one might object]... (*nanu*). The phrase "as stated in various ways" refers to such passages as: "Now, among those who speak thus, is the function [of the compound] one that abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*), or rather one that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*)? and so forth. "The state of becoming a single referent (*ekārthībhāva*) and mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)"—the state of becoming a single referent has already been explained. Mutual expectancy, however, is the capacity of words—which individually terminate in their own respective meanings—to bring about the cognition of the mutual connection of their meanings by virtue of their mutual requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*).

However, upon examining the *bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* regarding semantic competency (*samartha*), it is understood that the view that "semantic competency is the state of having a single meaning" implies the acceptance of two types of *vṛtti* (derivation) according to the difference between speakers; yet, based on the *bhāṣya* passage beginning with "Now, as for those who employ *vṛtti*, what do they say?", this investigation is undertaken by adopting the position that this *vṛtti* is accomplished from the sentence itself. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "by the power of the compound alone," the exclusion of the power of the individual parts is intended. He provides an illustration: "like the words *vṛṣa* and so forth."

The meaning is as follows: since the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) qualified by the absence of being a constituent of any other sequence is the very determinant of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), the sequence inherent in "vṛṣ" and so on—which are parts of words such as "vṛṣabha"—is not a determinant of expressive power; likewise, it is impossible for the sequence of "rāja" within a compound to be a determinant of expressive power. Otherwise, from words such as "rāma," there would result the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the presentation of the meanings of the individual parts (such as fire) and their subsequent verbal cognition; there would be the consequence of the production of intermediate case-endings (*sub*); and in cases such as "dhanaṃ" and "vanaṃ," there would be the consequence of the substitution of the *jaś* suffix. However, in a sentence, the words themselves are indeed possessors of meaning.

The meaning is that, rather than postulating two distinct complex word-orders—such as "rājñaḥ pūruṣaḥ" (the king's man) and "puruṣo rājñaḥ" (the man of the king)—as having the status of delimiters for the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) in cases such as "a person related to the king," it is far more parsimonious (*laghīyas*) to simply postulate a power (*śakti*) residing in the individual words themselves.

Nor should it be argued that in this view there would be no fault in examples such as *mahābāhuḥ* and *supanthāḥ*, because they are prescribed by the rule for the assumption (*upādāna*) of a specific form (*viśiṣṭarūpa*), since they are meaningless (*anarthaka*). Likewise, one should not say that there would be no occurrence of *nalopa* (elision of *n*) due to the absence of the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) based on meaningfulness; for by superimposing meaningfulness upon what is about to occur in the compound formation (*vṛtti*), those respective grammatical operations are easily established. And this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *pratyayottarapadayośca*.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be no fault in cases such as *vāpyaśvaḥ* (a horse at a pond) because [the compound] lacks meaning under the theory of *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning), which would lead to an unavoidable contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the rule *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe*; for the intention is that, by the force of the mention of the word *artha* (meaning), an imposed meaning (*āropitārtha*) is not accepted there among the words contained within a compound.

In the case of a single word, whether it possesses meaning or lacks meaning during its occurrence and the time preceding it, the very usage [of the word] is the sole refuge. However, in instances of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional meaning), since the primary power (*śakti*) is admitted as being included within the etymological sense (*yoga*), there is no abandonment of that [meaning].

Nor should it be argued that in this view, if the words *rājan* (king) and so forth were to abandon their own meanings entirely, there would be no cognition of them, and consequently, the linguistic convention that "the meaning of one word is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the meaning of another word" would be untenable; for the first fault does not arise because the qualified [word] itself brings about the presentation of the person qualified by the king and so forth. Alternatively, the second point is also resolved by the Bhāṣya statement: "It becomes a qualifier through syntactic connection (*anvaya*)."

Just as a *campaka* flower-basket is designated as such even when the flowers have been removed, merely by virtue of the persistence of their fragrance, so too the designation of the meaning of a word like "king" as a qualifier in relation to a person occurs merely through the persistence of a similar meaning; this is the sense in which the *jahatsvārthavṛtti* (the theory that a compound abandons its own individual meanings) is established. However, it is observed in the world that when a person is engaged in the work of another, he abandons his own work; for example, a carpenter, while engaged in the king's work, abandons his own.

Thus, it is logical that according to the Bhāṣya, even in this alternative view, the "abandonment of its own meaning" (jahatsvārthatva) is obtained only for the meaning of the first member of the compound—namely, that the king, while engaging in the pursuit of human ends, might abandon his own [kingly] end, and Upagu, while engaging in the pursuit of offspring, might abandon his own [personal] end.

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if one accepts, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), that there is semantic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) in the form of syntactic dependence (*sāmarthya*). "Conjunction" (*samuccaya*) refers to that which generates a cognition characterized by a dual objective domain (*viṣayatā*), such as "the king's servant and [his] wife"—that is, two things in a single locus. Regarding the phrase "because of the consequence" (*āpatteḥ*): the point is that in our view, since [the property of being distinct from the king] is a part of the word-meaning itself, even though there is a difference, we accept a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for it; furthermore, because it is understood as being distinct from what belongs to the king, another qualifier cannot be applied to it, and thus [the aforementioned consequence] does not arise.

Since the position that the word retains its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthavṛtti*) has been established in a different manner according to the *Bhāṣya*, he says "this is the intention" by following the view of certain authorities who rely on the dictum: "some [hold] that syntactic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). The phrase "not something additional" means not something additional to the well-established individual functions [of the words]. The phrase "due to the absence of a warrant" means due to the absence of a warranting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely the impossibility of explaining the matter otherwise.

[Objection: "But surely, it is precisely the impossibility of the qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*) that will necessitate its postulation. To this, he says: "Of the postulated [power] such as that of the king, etc."—the meaning is: of the postulation of that [qualified power], namely, the postulation of a qualified capacity (*viśiṣṭaśakti*). [Objection: "This might indeed be so if, in this view, there were a postulation of a power for each individual word; but since that very thing does not exist, where is the occasion for the charge of complexity (*gaurava*)? To this, he says: "Of the postulated power"—the meaning is: the abandonment of the power of each individual word which was postulated prior to the occurrence of the *vṛtti* (the complex formation).

The sense is that even due to a difference in time, it is contradictory for a single word to possess both meaningfulness and meaninglessness; furthermore, because the determination of [grammatical operations] such as the elision of the *n* in *rājapuruṣaḥ* would otherwise be untenable, it is appropriate to accept [the presence of the whole] precisely during the state of *vṛtti* (compound formation). Now, one might object: "Even if the respective word-meanings are presented through individual powers (*śakti*), since you do not admit a power residing in the qualified [whole], that [qualified whole] is not presented; how then can it be the object of verbal cognition? To this, he says: "And thus... (*tathāca*). Regarding the term "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*): by the word "etc. (*ādi*), factors such as "compatibility" (*yogyatā*) are included; the meaning is: "due to the convergence of causes consisting in the form of the word *puruṣa* occurring immediately after the word *rājan*, and so forth."

The sense is this: since the cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭabodha*) can arise through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors aided by the presentation (*upasthiti*) of each individual word-meaning, there is no need to postulate that which would require a prior presentation of the qualified object. "This very [point]" means that it is exactly as stated in the passage beginning with "this is the intention" (*ayam abhiprāya*). The phrase "by the authors of the Bhāṣya" has the ellipsis: "by [the statement] 'some hold that mutual expectancy is semantic competency' (*parasparavyapekṣāṃ sāmarthyameke*)," and so forth. He removes the aforementioned contingency with the words "but not here" (*na cātra*).

The phrase "the contingency of connection" (*anvayāpatti*) is used according to the literal sense, because it will be stated later that there is no such contingency when there is a definition of the related (*sambandhilakṣaṇā*).

The phrase "by way of a consequence" (prasaṅgāt) means: because of possessing that property which serves as the delimiting factor for the unfitness of being a subject (pakṣa) as delimited by the time of its recollection. "Difference in function" (vṛttibhedam) means the difference in the function—such as the function of completion and so forth—caused by the meaning in the form of distinction (bheda), relation (saṃsarga), and so on. As it was stated in the Bhāṣya: "Sāmarthya is indeed distinction; that is relation. Another says: distinction and relation together constitute sāmarthya."

If difference (*bheda*) and relation (*saṃsarga*) were not present in a word-meaning complex (*vṛtti*), then there would be no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) at all, because semantic capacity consists of those two. Therefore, since that [capacity] has them as its object, their absence follows. "Difference" means the absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), which is inferred from its invariable concomitance with relation. He states this very point: "mutual absence" (*anyonyābhāva*). "Relation" means relation based on difference—the difference which is inferred from its invariable concomitance with relation. Thus, the meaning is: relation is rooted in difference.

In reality, however, the intention of the Bhāṣya statement, "The semantic capacity [of a word] consists either in difference or in relation," is that when words such as 'puruṣa' (person) are used in co-utterance with words such as 'rājan' (king), there is the cognition of a qualified object consisting precisely of a person qualified by a king; it does not mean that the [word] indicates a separate power residing in the difference, because such a cognition is never experienced, and because it is difficult to establish that difference is the expressed meaning in dual compounds such as 'Rāma-Kṛṣṇau'. This refers to the Vyapekṣā theory, which has been described in the manner stated immediately above—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The meaning is that the position (*pakṣa*) of not abandoning one’s own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*) has indeed been pointed out. The phrase “thus [by] reasoning” (*evaṃ yuktyā*) means by what has been stated and what is yet to be stated. The sense is that [this view] is refuted by the *Bhāṣya* beginning with: “There is a prohibition of the substitution of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* and of the non-accidental accent (*nighāta*) when there are various case-relations (*nānākāraka*). In the expression “merely the function” (*vṛttimātra*), the word “mere” (*mātra*) signifies “entirety. The meaning is that it brings to mind the five types of functions (*vṛtti*) through the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of not abandoning one’s own meaning. Regarding the phrase “in the denotation of the sentence-meaning” (*vākyārthābhidhāne*), the meaning is “in such a denotation. The passage from the *Bhāṣya* referred to by the word “from the *Bhāṣya*” (*bhāṣyāt*) is: “The statement regarding words (*padavacana*) applies to those that are semantically connected (*samarthānām*). etc.

The phrase "like the word *paṅkaja* at the root" employs the suffix *vat* with a locative ending, because the locative is seen in the object of comparison (*upameya*). The meaning is that just as there is a power (denotative function) distinct from the powers of the individual parts in the word *paṅkaja*, so too is there such a power in the compound. Nor is there a lack of evidence for accepting a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) in the word *paṅkaja*; for the very cognition of a lotus qualified by the property of "lotus-ness" arising from the whole word is itself the proof. This is because a fixed presentation [of a specific meaning] from a word is invariably due to convention alone; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a water-lily (*kumuda*) could be understood through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) from the word *paṅkaja*.

Even if conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is accepted, just as the word *udbhid* [denotes a tree] through etymological derivation (*yoga*), the word *paṅkaja* would also denote a water-lily (*kumuda*). Therefore, it is traditionally held that only the lotus is understood as the agent; by means of the suffix *-ḍa*, which possesses the capacity to express an agent, it is understood as the agent of the production from mud. [The phrase] "without a subverting factor" (*bādhakaṃ vinā*) [is used].

And thus, since the intention (*tātparya*) resides in the lotus (*padma*), it is that alone which is cognized even through *yoga* (etymological derivation), and not the lily (*kumuda*). However, the first alternative [that the cognition of *rūḍhi* acts as an obstacle] is not tenable, because the cognition of *rūḍhi* does not apprehend the absence of the object to be grasped, and because it is impossible for it to be an obstacle by way of subverting the generative cognition. Even if one were to accept its status as an obstacle on the grounds of established necessity—according to the maxim of "jewels, mantras, and so forth"—there is no evidence for such a construction in other cases.

And thus, because the causal complex for the apprehension of the lotus (*padma*) is present, there is the cognition of that alone, and not of the lily (*kumuda*). For, the logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that when the causal complex is complete, one must postulate an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*) to prevent the production of the other. By means of that example, the statement that "attachment (*sakti*) is necessary in the general sense of a function (*vṛtti*) within the aggregate" results in nothing other than the meaning previously stated.

If it is asked: "In the theory of *ajahatsvārthavṛtti* (retention of the individual word-meanings), since it has been stated that the capacity for the qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) ceases with respect to the relational aspect, and since they accept that even in a sentence it is only the relational aspect that is [conveyed], what then is the difference between a *vṛtti* (compound) and a sentence in the Grammarian school?"—to this they reply: "In that case, by the force of the result, at the time of the presentation of the word-meanings, the relational aspect is necessarily assumed to be present through the non-occurrence of other excitants; thus, there arises the cognition of the relation (*saṃsarga*) between two word-meanings that have been presented separately."

In the case of verbal usage (*vṛtti*), because it is postulated that the conditions for the awakening [of the relational part] necessarily coincide at the very same time as the presentation of the word-meanings, the presentation of the qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*) occurs; thus, the distinction [between the two cases] is established.

For this very reason, in cases such as *prāptodaka* ("water which has arrived"), there is no cognition when the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is reversed; for in that case, both the meaning of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) not being employed and the relation [between the two members] are to be accomplished by a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*), since they cannot be obtained through any other means. Furthermore, because the presentation of the king and so forth from words like *rāja* is possible through their established individual powers alone, it would be cumbersome to postulate a collective power in those instances. Moreover, grammatical maxims (vyutpatti) such as "the non-difference relation (*abheda-anvaya*) occurs between the meanings of nouns" refer to the meanings of nouns presented separately.

In the view that [the word] functions by abandoning its own primary meaning (*jahatsvārthavṛtti*), since the word *paṅkaja* cannot serve as an example according to the method previously stated, he introduces the root text otherwise with the words "of those who do not accept a qualified power" (*viśiṣṭaśaktayasvīkartṝṇām*). The term "proving factor" (*sādhakam*) means precisely that which proves a qualified power.

In the theory of those who maintain that meaning arises through mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), just as in expressions such as *pādapuruṣaḥ* (foot-servant), where the presentation of word-meanings occurs through the function of each individual word and a qualified meaning is understood by virtue of expectancy and so forth, so too would a qualified meaning be presented from the word *paṅkaja* (lotus) itself. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the abolition of conventional denotation (*rūḍhi*). Nor is this [abolition] desired by you; thus he says: "Even of the agent of the production from mud" (*paṅkajanikarttuḥ*), which means "even of the lotus in its form as such. "From the etymological derivation alone" (*yogādeva*) means "from the power of the individual parts alone. "There too" (*tatrāpi*) means "even in words such as *paṅkaja*. The point is: if that [etymological derivation] is accepted even there, what harm has been done to the specific power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) in a compound? That [power] is the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*).

"Of that conceptualization" means of the conceptualization based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). "Cognition in such a manner" means the cognition of the owner and so forth as being characterized by ownership and so forth. "Easy to state" means that it can be asserted that even the cognition [of the object] as a lotus and so forth occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He states there [in that context] that this also avoids contradiction with the *Rathakārādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the chariot-maker): "In this way," and so forth.

"Lakṣaṇā" means "indication" (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*); the sense is that this [indication] is equal in status to [direct] denotative power (*śakti*). "By way of etymological derivation" (*yogena*) means by way of the agency of chariot-making as presented by the function of each individual word. "In the case of feasibility" (*upapattau*) means the accomplishment of performance even without the restriction of the scriptures. "The postulation of that," etc., means the postulation of conventional usage (*rūḍhikalpanā*). This refers to having postulated that conventional usage for the sake of the "offspring born in the reverse order" (*pratilomajātayaḥ*). "Of a specific caste" (*jāti-viśeṣasya*) refers to that specific caste whose origin is from a *Māhiṣya* father and a *Karaṇī* mother, namely the *Rathakāra*.

The meaning is: "of that which is qualified by the genus (jāti) designated by convention through traditional usage. [The opponent says: "This is incorrect," because the injunction would have its purpose fulfilled even without the restriction of the scripture; such is the sense. [The author replies: But this reasoning does not establish a qualified denotative power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), because it cannot withstand a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) and because the resolution of that [objection] will be described by [the author] himself. Furthermore, even a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not easily stated for the word *paṅkaja*. To explain: would that [indication] reside in the whole word *paṅkaja*, or in the suffix *ḍa* which is a part of it? It cannot be the first, because since there is no denotative power (*śakti*) in the aggregate [as a whole], a figurative indication based upon it is impossible.

Furthermore, the *jahatsvārthā* [type of metaphorical indication] is simply impossible in that case, because there is no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) that contradicts the meaning of the individual parts. Indeed, the *jahatsvārthā* occurs only where there is a conventional usage that contradicts [the literal meaning].

Thus says the statement of the learned: as in the case of "Feed the maṇḍapa," the word *maṇḍapa* has a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) referring to a specific type of house which overrides its etymological meaning (*yoga*). Since the conventional meaning is grasped first, the etymological meaning—namely, "one who prepares a pavilion"—is sublated; for if that were accepted, the etymological sense would be contradicted. According to the well-known maxim, "Conventional meaning sets aside the etymological," it is impossible to understand the "pavilion-preparer" through direct denotation (*śakti*). Therefore, the word *maṇḍapa* possesses a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the pavilion-preparer.

And so, in that case, the cognition [of the meaning] occurs by means of "cowness" (catratva) and the like, which are grasped as the delimiters of the relation to the conventional (rūḍhi) sense; it does not occur by way of being the agent of building a pavilion. But it is not so in the present case, because when there is indication (lakṣaṇā) by way of "lotus-ness," the meaning of the individual parts is absent, and thus even *ajahatsvārthā* indication is impossible. Furthermore, *jahatsvārthā* indication cannot be asserted here, because the comprehension of the meanings of the individual parts would otherwise be untenable.

Not the latter [alternative], because it would result in the non-connection of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and because it would result in the grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutā*) of the suffix in that sense; thus, since there is no occasion for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), one must admit a distinct power (*śakti*) for the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) there due to lack of any other recourse. However, in cases such as "rājapuruṣaḥ" (the king's man), since the cognition of the qualified meaning can be accomplished through the function of each individual word, the postulation of a power for the composite whole (*samudāyaśakti*) is indeed inappropriate there.

Nor is there any contradiction with the *Rathakāra-adhikaraṇa*; for although the designation "chariot-maker" (*rathakāra*)—based on the etymological sense of "one who makes a chariot"—is simpler when applied to the *saṅkara* caste (as opposed to the specific fire-installation required for others), nevertheless, based on the wording of the mantra "Of you, the gods, the Ṛbhus... (*ṛbhūṇāṃ tvā devānām*), it is understood that the qualification for that [fire-installation] belongs specifically to the *rathakāra* who is born from the inverse union of an *Ṛbhu* and a *Saudhanvana*. Thus, disregarding the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), a specific fire-installation is postulated there in the sense of the conventional term (*rūḍhārtha*).

Nor is there the burden of postulating the study of a previously unknown science (*apūrvavidyā*), because that would be a matter pertaining to the result [of the action]. In the case at hand, regarding the complex expression such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man), there is no authority such as a lexicon (*kośa*) that establishes the [unitary] power [of the compound], by virtue of which the meaning of the individual parts (*avayavārtha*) would have to be abandoned. Because of this dissatisfaction, he introduces the root text with the words "another proof" (*sādhakāntaram*), namely "linguistic indication" (*liṅga*). The point is that in expressions such as *kukkuṭāṇḍam* (hen’s egg), the feminine gender is not perceived in the referent of the word *kukkuṭa*. As for "number" (*saṅkhyā*), in sentences such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man) or *rājñāṃ puruṣaḥ* (the men of the kings), the subordinate members of the compound are [indicated].

The meaning is that, according to the Bhāṣya, while [words] in a compound express their own specific meaning when joined with a particular number, they express the principal meaning with the specific meaning [of the number] internalized; thus, there is no perception of a specific number therein.

By the phrase "from number, etc.," the inclusion of the following points stated in the *Bhāṣya* is intended: "In that case, these would be distinctions not produced by a single referent—namely, the distinction of number, the denotation of individuals, and the non-application of qualifiers to subordinate members"—as well as the non-application [of the rule] in cases such as "the king's horses and men" (*rājño rāvaśvapuruṣāḥ*) or "the cow of Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra. By the term "by the rules" (*vacanaiḥ*), the meaning is: "by such rules as 'there is no compound formation for those accompanied by qualifiers' (*saviśeṣaṇānāṃ vṛttir na*). He clarifies this very point already stated:

The meaning is as follows: this sūtra is established by reasoning (*nyāyasiddha*). Here, when there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), a compound does not occur; and when there is a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), a sentence does not occur. Since they have distinct domains, the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is impossible; thus, the statement of an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) for what is not established by reasoning is not something new. This is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), existence and non-existence [of its application] are not intended. Its implication is that since there is an optionality regarding those things that possess a single unified meaning, there is no purpose in an optionality [for what is already established by reasoning].

The meaning is that it is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*) that [the theory of syntactic dependence] is impossible because, in a *vṛtti* (compound), the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) must denote the primary meaning; yet, when there is a requirement for its own qualification, it possesses primacy. How, then, can it simultaneously possess primacy and undergo single-meaning unification (*ekārthībhāva*), given the contradiction between being subordinate and being primary at one and the same time? The phrase "for this very reason" means precisely because the theory of syntactic dependence (*vyapekṣāvāda*) is charming only on the surface. The refutation has also been stated: "there is no prohibition of the various case-roles (*kāraka*), of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*), or of the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and so forth."

The phrase "by means of [the rule] *ayaṃ ḍhaṇḍo harānena*" and so forth is the ellipsis; [Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa] states the collection of faults as expressed by Kauṇḍa with the words "tathā" and so on. "Thus, another fault" means a fault of this nature. "Of those previously mentioned" means of those such as the statement regarding the elision of words expressing meanings like "gone beyond" (*krānta*) in examples such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. He says "another fault" because the refutation of these objections will be stated later. To reveal the breakdown of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), he says "this is the underlying intention" (*ayam āśayaḥ*). The word "in the sentence" (*vākye*) is the ellipsis for the phrase "by means of the technical term" (*lakṣaṇena*).

In cases such as "the brindled cow" (*citraguḥ*), since the sentence could be taken as indicating the owner of the cows through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), [the author] says: "the village reached by water. The phrase "even in the case of secondary signification" is according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, because they maintain that secondary signification consists precisely in the relationship between the primary denotation and the indicated object. The phrase "after the cognition" is to be understood as being qualified by "upon the apprehension of the impossibility [of the literal sense]. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even in the case of secondary signification," he indicates that secondary signification is impossible in that particular instance.

"From the acquisition of the object" (arthalābhāt) means that even when there is an acquisition of water related to the agent who has attained [the action], it is because the aforementioned object is not being experienced; this is the meaning. "In that case, it must be in grammatical coreferentiality" (tarhi samānādhikaraṇa)—here, coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) refers to having the same case-ending. Otherwise—that is, if one does not accept the coreferential connection (abhedānvaya) between the meaning of the word "water" ending in a kṛt-affix (which denotes the object) and the meaning of the verbal root—[the following would occur]. "Because of the consequence of over-extension" (baṅgāpatter)—the sense is that such a grammatical rule (vyutpatti) would be subject to deviation (vyabhicāra) precisely in this instance.

[Objection: "But surely, since that grammatical derivation (vyutpatti) involves the inclusion of the property of denoting a single referent (*ekārthābhidhāyitva*) for items in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), this [case] is not within its scope. To this he says: "Because of the impossibility of application" (*prāpteḥ*). The sense is: "Because the direct syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root through difference is not established by grammatical derivation. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if one does not accept the aforementioned grammatical derivation.

"The village is perceived"—the word "by means of a sentence" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. One might somehow postulate even a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) if the aforementioned cognition were possible; however, he says that this is not the case: "because reaching is the meaning of the verbal root. Anticipating the objection that the rule "of the base and the suffix" (*prakṛtipratyayayoḥ*) is subject to deviation in the case of number and so forth, he says: "in the word *prāpta*. [He explains: "as the meaning of the noun" (*nāmārthatvena*). The sense is that only that which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by a noun is the meaning of the noun.

"And because of the consequence of non-differentiation" (*abhedānvayāpatti*)—the meaning is that [this applies] to the referents of two nouns having the same case-ending (*samānābhaktika*). "It should be observed": in your view, even if there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the related entity after the cognition "the chariot is non-different from the object of carrying," one still fails to obtain the intended meaning, namely, "the ox is the agent of the act of carrying whose object is the chariot."

The meaning is that, according to the previously stated direction, if one were to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) for the agent in the case of the suffix *-kartṛ* when it denotes the object (*karman*), then the connection of the chariot—which is the object of the action of carrying denoted by the root-meaning—with the agent would be impossible through the relation of difference (*bheda-sambandha*), because this would contradict the aforementioned grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*). Here, the word "for" (*hi*) is to be construed with the phrase "because [the opponent] accepts such a cognition."

Regarding this, he states that if one accepts a distinct power (*śakti*) in compounds such as *ūḍharatha* (one who has brought a chariot), there is no contradiction with any rule of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). He thus demonstrates the reason for the exclusion of genitive-based *bahuvrīhi* compounds by saying "atirikta" (distinct) and so forth. The underlying intention (*bhāva*) is as follows: "power" refers to the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*). The phrase "and not there" means [not] in such a compound consisting of the preceding and following members. The sense is that this is because of the rule of derivation stating "between the meanings of two nouns in apposition," as in the case of *citrasvāmī* (the owner of variegated [cows]).

Now, it might be argued that there is a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of the word *go* in the sense of "owner of cows," and thus the cognition "the owner of a cow who is non-different from Citrā" is not untenable when *citra* is construed as a qualifier of the cow. To this, he says: "of *citrā* alone, etc. By the word "etc.," words such as *go* are included. The word *citrapada* is employed with the intention that the secondary signification resides in the first member of the compound because of its priority.

The phrase "as being a part of the object to be defined" (lakṣyaikadeśatvena) means "as being a part of the referent (padārtha) which is the cow-possessor (gosvāmin), who is the object to be defined. The reason given is "due to the impossibility of syntactic connection" (anvayāyogāt). The sense is that such a connection is impossible because it would contradict the linguistic maxim (vyutpatti) expressed as "a word-meaning connects with another word-meaning," which ultimately results in the following principle: "the presentation (upasthiti) generated by one word, related to the verbal cognition (śābdabuddhi) through the relation of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) as determined by the state of being a qualifier (prakāratā) of the meaning of a single word, is the cause [of that cognition] through the relation of being the qualificandum. Since this is the case, the aforementioned connection cannot be established.

Anticipating the opinion of someone, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not). The meaning of "sākṣāt" (directly) is "not through the mediation of 'cow'. Thus, the sense is that in a *ṣaṣṭhī-artha-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound where the genitive case-meaning is significant), there is no need to postulate a separate grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*). The sense of "in both words" is that there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) [to prefer one over the other]. The term "Naiyāyika" refers to the ancient [logicians] and so forth. Regarding the position that [the word] has partial co-referentiality (*ekadeśānvaya*), they have stated this because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the possessor appearing in two ways within the cognition (*bodha*). This is how it should be understood.

The phrase "due to the absence of a decisive criterion" (*vinigamanāviraha*) means that there is no reasoning to favor one side over the other—namely, whether it is the word *citra* or the word *go* that serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). The phrase "due to impossibility" (*asambhavāt*) means that it is impossible for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to reside in either one of the two words; the sense is that if secondary indication were applied to both words simultaneously, the aforementioned defect would follow.

Anticipating the objection that "the very impossibility of connecting the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) [with the primary sense] will serve as the determining factor for metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) in the second member," he refutes this with the words "na ca" ("and not"). He explains "evaṃ hi" ("for in this way") as meaning "if the second member alone were to indicate the meaning of the other word. He states the reason why a *bahuvrīhi* compound would be impossible with the words "anekam" ("more than one"), explaining "tadavidhānāt" ("because of its non- prescription") as meaning "because of the non-prescription of a *bahuvrīhi* [in such a case]."

The meaning is as follows: that a *vṛtti* has a specific meaning is not something cognizable solely through the technical treatises (*śāstra*). This is because, in examples such as *acatura*, no specific meaning is prescribed [by rule]; rather, it is cognizable through worldly usage (*laukikavyavahāra*). This is established by the commentary on the *sūtra* on *samartha* (Pāṇini 2.1.1), which states: "For those words which are naturally fixed upon these meanings, the grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) is performed by way of providing the formal cause (*nimitta*)."

The rules "anekamanyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24) and "cārthe dvandvaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.29), and so forth, merely prescribe the technical designations of *bahuvrīhi* and others by restating meanings already established in common usage, namely: "a collection of several words ending in the nominative case, expressing a meaning other [than their own], receives the designation *bahuvrīhi*"; and "a collection of words ending in the nominative case which functions in the sense of 'ca' (conjunction) receives the designation *dvandva*. This is because if the meaning itself were also being prescribed, it would result in the fallacy of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

To prevent the application of sentences having the same meaning as [the compound] itself, the governing rule *vibhāṣā* (optionally) would also have to be enjoined. And in that case, if a collection of *subanta* words conveys a different meaning, how could it be a *bahuvrīhi*? [Objection: But surely, when a single word conveys a different meaning, since other words are also useful as indicators of the intended sense (*tātparya*), the entire collection possesses the capacity to convey a qualified meaning; thus, [the definition] is not deficient. To this, he says: "And what [is the case] in this way?"—the meaning is: provided that only the final word of the compound functions as the indicator (*lakṣaka*).

Regarding the acceptance of this consequence, he says: "This being the case" (*evaṃ sati*) means that the final phoneme possesses the capacity to denote [the meaning]. "Even here" (*atrāpi*) means even in cases such as *prāptodaka* (where water has been reached). "The consequence" (*āpattiḥ*) refers to the fact that at the time of determining the absence of the probandum (*āpādya*), there exists a cognition of the presence of the probans (*āpādaka*) which is pervaded by that probandum; this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: Surely, from hearing only the word *udaka* (water), there is no comprehension of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), because at that time there is an absence of the presence of the preceding word—which grasps the intention (*tātparya*)—that would effect the indication (*lakṣaṇā*). To this, he says: "Elsewhere," which means in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. [The term] "in detail" refers to what was stated therein: that since the indicated meaning of the subsequent word lacks the status of being the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the affix-meaning not being syntactically connected (*anvaya*) with it, and so forth. [The phrase] "regarding proficiency" (*vyutpattau*) means that abandoning proficiency in the matter at hand is nothing other than a surrender of one's own thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).

The phrase "those who maintain the theory of mutual expectancy" (vyapekṣāvādinaḥ) means those who assert in the *Samartha-sūtra* that "expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) is precisely the capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting in the fitness for mutual syntactic connection. "There is no [additional] power in a compound" (na samāse śaktiḥ) means that there is no distinct power in a compound—that is, in a collection such as *rājapuruṣa*. The point is that the status of being the cause for the designation "compound" does not exist apart from the functions already established for each individual word.

According to the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya that "capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists in having a combined meaning," since combination (*saṃsarga*) is based on a separate presentation [of meanings], capacity is simply mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). This is because all authorities accept that the word *samartha* in the rule "isusoḥ sāmarthye" (Pāṇini 5.4.150) has such a meaning, and this is also for the sake of conforming to the treatment as if it were a subsequent member of a compound (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction: one-sidedness (*ekārthībhāva*) would apply to compounds and the like, while mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) would apply to the treatment as if it were a subsequent member and so forth, resulting in a split in the grammatical system (*vākyabheda*).

In that regard, if *vyapekṣā* (syntactic dependence) were disregarded, then in cases such as "ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāvṛtāvṛdhāvṛtaspṛśau," since the word *ṛtena* and the others would behave as if they were subordinate members (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) [to the following vocative], the rule "āmantritasya ca" (Pāṇini 8.1.19) would result in the initial syllable being accented acute (*ādyudātta*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of the application of *parāṅgavadbhāva* (the treatment as if being a member of the subsequent word) because the Vārttika—"The mention of its cause [should be made]"—restricts the rule to mean that only that which denotes the cause of the *āmantrita* (vocative) is treated as if it were a member of the subsequent word; for it is more logical to reject that Vārttika by relying on the *samartha-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding semantic competency). This is because, in the case of "ṛtena mitrāvaruṇau," since these two are connected with the action expressed in the co-occurring verb, they lack mutual semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), and thus [the rule would not apply]. "Mitram varuṇam ṛtasprśo... [is cited as an example of such usage].

However, since these two possess the capacity for meaning precisely because of the existence of the subsequent inferential cognition (*pārṣṭhikānvayabodha*), this is clearly stated in the *Vedabhāṣya*. For this very reason, even their immediate juxtaposition (*anantarapāṭha*) is purposeful; in cases such as "the king's son, Devadatta's servant," there is no possibility of compounding precisely because of the absence of the aforementioned capacity consisting of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*).

The meaning of the *samartha-sūtra*, however, should be understood as follows: a rule governing compounds (*samāsa*) and the like, which relates to words, depends upon those words that possess "capacity" (*sāmarthya*)—a term synonymous with "expectancy" (*vyapekṣā*)—defined as being the cause of a subjectivity (*viṣayatā*) that is itself characterized by a subjectivity caused by its own application. Thus, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), since the subjectivity of the word *citra* does not directly cause [the formation of the compound], it is said to do so "indirectly" (*paramparayā*).

Furthermore, in the view that maintains the existence of a single unified meaning delimited by the state of being a *vṛtti* (semantic function), there is an under-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of *vṛtti*—which consists in denoting a meaning distinct from the meanings of its constituent parts—to the *karmadhāraya* compound; for in that case, there is an absence of a meaning distinct from the meanings of the constituent parts. On the other hand, if [the definition] is taken as co-occurrent with the state of being a *vṛtti*, then since we also accept the existence of a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) established by lexicons and other authorities in cases of pure conventional terms like *rathantara* and in *yogarūḍha* terms like *paṅkaja*, this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).

His intention is that the assumption of a [unitary] denotative power (*śakti*) in a collection such as "Śuddhayogin," "Citragu," and so forth, should be rejected; for it is not mentioned in the *Kośa* and other authorities, and because its function is adequately explained by the individual word-powers residing in each constituent member of the compound. He demonstrates that there is no impossibility in postulating such a power by citing "rājapuruṣa" and so on; here, the term "rājapuruṣa" refers to a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) whose first member lacks an explicitly heard case-ending, and thus there is no fault in compounds where the case-ending is not elided, such as "dāsyāḥ putraḥ."

Nor should it be argued that "let the relation itself be the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*), and thus the popular saying that the expanded form (*vyāsa*) and the compound (*samāsa*) convey an identical cognition will also be justified; furthermore, since the relation in the form of the connection with the king and so forth can be accounted for simply by its inherence as the locus within the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound, there is no purpose in accepting a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward the relatum. This is because even in cases such as "The king [is] the man" (*rājā pūruṣaḥ*), the meaning of the word "king" and so forth stands in a relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) toward the verbal cognition produced by the relation of owner-and-owned (*svasvāmibhāva*).

Since it is necessary that the cause of [semantic] cognition must be the presentation (upasthiti) arising from either an affix (pratyaya) or a particle (nipāta), in the present case, because the meaning of the noun (*nāmārtha*)—namely, the relation with the King—is not presented by either an affix or a particle, its connection with the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth would be impossible; therefore, the qualification "other than a particle" is added. Consequently, there is no defect even in cases such as "the face is like the moon," where the similarity—which is the meaning of the particle *iva*—is a meaning of a noun, and the moon, which is the meaning of a noun other than the particle, is presented [to the mind], yet this presentation does not occur via an affix. Similarly, there is no defect regarding the similarity, which is the object of presentation for the noun "moon" (other than the particle), even though it is not the object of presentation for the face via an affix.

Because the property of being delimited by a relation other than identity has been included in the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*), that [qualifierhood] does not exist even in cases of non-difference (*abheda*) such as "the king is the man" (*rājā puruṣaḥ*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no inconsistency in the present case because the name [of the relation] is qualified by being something over and above what is compounded; for this would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and while a restriction may occasionally be adopted out of necessity, such a universal restriction is improper. Furthermore, in the present context, there exists a way out (*gati*) consisting in the acceptance of a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) based on a relationship; moreover, according to the view that particles (*nipāta*) are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), the words "pot" and so forth are accounted for simply as having the counter-correlates of pots and so forth as their secondary significations, and thus the property of being "other than a particle" is not introduced into the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). This is the intended meaning.

The phrase "for this very reason" means precisely because the preceding word possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its relation [to the primary meaning]. The thought is that there is no connection with a qualifier, because of the linguistic rule that "a word-meaning connects with another word-meaning. Now, one might object: "In cases such as 'the hamlet is on the deep river,' just as the word 'deep' connects with the river—which is a part of the river-bank signified by the word 'river'—so too here, a connection with a single part [of the signified] would be unavoidable. This is not so, because the example is unestablished.

Even in that case, according to this view, there is no fault, because it will be explained later that the word *nadī* (river) indicates a deep river (*gabhīranadī*) and the word *gabhīra* (deep) serves to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Furthermore, since such a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) concerns objects other than those related by a relation, there is no deficiency even when there is partial co-referentiality (*ekadeśānvaya*), as in the expression "Caitra’s grandson" (*caitrasya naptā*).

The meaning is as follows: since the sense has already been expressed, the prepositions such as *ni* (in *niṣkrāmati*) function merely as indicators (*dyotaka*). Consequently, it is accepted that the word *Kauśāmbī* itself possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sense of "the agent of departure delimited by Kauśāmbī. Thus, because the intended meaning is established through this alone, it is impossible to include words such as *krānta* (departed). Regarding the term "necessity" (*āvaśyakatvam*): the point is that even if those words are used in contexts such as the recitation of the entire Veda (*pārāyaṇa*) for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or for the sake of clear comprehension, there is no fault.

"Pratibandī" (the counter-objection) means the acceptance of a denotative power (*śakti*) qualified by "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*) and so forth in words such as *paṅkaja*. By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even for one who does not know the power of the parts," a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the argument (*dārṣṭāntika*) is indicated. "In the absence of the apprehension of power" (*śaktyagrahe*) means in the absence of the apprehension of the power of the individual parts. "From them" (*tebhyaḥ*) means from the constituent parts of the word *paṅkaja* and so forth. "The cognition of a qualified object" (*viśiṣṭārthapratyayaḥ*) means the understanding of a lotus and so forth in the form of "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*).

The meaning is that since secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is constituted by [the presence of] primary denotative power (*śakti*), when that [object] is presented through the power of the composite whole (*samudāyaśakti*), one must simply accept the non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) with the agent of the production of mud (*paṅkaja-nikartṛ*) presented through the power of the individual parts (*avayavaśakti*). "From this very reason" means: precisely because the knowledge of the primary denotative power of that word is the cause for grasping the secondary indication belonging to that word. By the phrase "due to being etymological" (*yaugikatvena*), he states the deciding factor (*vinigamaka*) regarding the secondary indication of the final member [of the compound]. By the phrase "because of being delayed," it is indicated that the quality of having a rapid presentation (*śīghropasthitikatva*) is the deciding factor in favor of the secondary indication of the final member.

[Objection: But surely, on the view that [words] have derivative meanings (*vyutpattipakṣa*), the status of being etymological (*yaugikatva*) is equal even for words such as *udaka* (water); therefore, he says: "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*). Since the literal sense of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is contradicted in the case of *udaka* and so on, he explains the term "meaning of the base" otherwise—as "proximate": in cases such as "bring the staff-bearer" (*daṇḍinam ānaya*), the word "proximate" is used to prevent the relation of being the object (*karmatva*) and so forth from applying to a remote referent, such as the staff (*daṇḍa*).

And thus, according to the maxim that "even a minute distinction effects a determination," the indication (lakṣaṇā) applies only to the subsequent member; therefore, the objection regarding the non-repetition of the cognition does not arise—this is the sense. He now removes another previously mentioned objection:

Regarding the phrase "and in the case of words such as 'ghaṭa'": by the expression "being postulated," he indicates that [the meaning] is not already established; the sense is that [the meaning] is determined precisely there [in the compound] through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and so forth. The remainder of the thought following "because of non-existence" is: "thereby, one would have to seek a further determining factor (*vinigamaka*) even in that case. "In the subsequent word" means "in the word 'udaka' and so forth, which constitutes the word 'udakādi' [as part of the compound]. "That" refers to the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). "The distinction" means the difference between the secondary signification of the compound and that of the word 'ghaṭa' and so forth.
