In this regard, the following should be understood: by the reasoning stated above, in cases such as *upakumbham* ("near the jar"), the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) belongs to the final member (*uttarapada*) alone in the sense of "proximity," while the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) serves merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Even in Tatpuruṣa compounds, in certain instances such as *ardhapippalī* ("half a long pepper"), that signification belongs to the final member alone in the sense of "half of the long pepper" (*pippalyardha*), while the other [preceding] member is merely indicative. However, in Karmadhāraya compounds such as *nīlotpala* ("blue lotus"), there is no such signification anywhere, because the relation of identity is easily established between the two meanings presented by the individual powers (*śakti*) of each word.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, however, it [the collective sense] resides only in the final member; this is clearly the essential point. In a *dvandva* such as *pāṇipādam* (hands and feet), where the individual referents of each word have attained a state of conjunction (*sāhitya*), that [collective sense] belongs to the final member alone. For this very reason, the connection with duality and so forth—the meaning of the dual number and so on—occurs there [in the final member]. The distinction is that in a *samāhāra-dvandva*, the conjunction is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), whereas here [in the *dvandva* of the example], it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, even in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because the sense of conjunction (*sāhitya*) is not perceived; rather, the status of being the object of the act of speaking applies directly to the two meanings presented by the power (*śakti*) of each individual word. Furthermore, according to the rule "a *dvandva* [consists of] living beings," etc., it is only a compound that has been extended [by grammatical rule] to possess singular number that is primarily designated by the term "collective" (*samāhāra*). In other cases, however, the usage of that term is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). Therefore, there is no risk of such a designation applying to a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*).

Likewise, even in the case of *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction), there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because the two meanings, presented by the two words as they are established in a single recollection, can undergo the connection with duality; furthermore, since the association—whether defined as the state of being connected to a single action or as being delimited by a single cognition—is understood only afterwards, it is impossible to grasp secondary signification there beforehand. Moreover, there is no contradiction with the rule "dvandva [is used] in the sense of *ca*," for that rule means "in a sense suitable for connection with the meaning of *ca*."

This is logical: for the Lord’s enumeration of the *dvandva* among the various types of compounds as a specific manifestation (*vibhūti*)—in the verse "The *dvandva* [is a manifestation] of all compounds" (*Gītā*)—is only consistent if the *dvandva* conveys two primary meanings delimited by their dual nature. However, if it were to convey a primary collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) through a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) or through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then the *dvandva* would be no different from other types of compounds, and the aforementioned inconsistency would be evident.

As for what is stated in the *Bhāratabhāvadīpa*: "Sama" means sitting together in one place; "samāsa" refers to the sitting together of learned persons, whether teacher and disciple, for the purpose of discussing mantras or stories. In that context, the collection of meanings known is "sāmāsika. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *cāturarthika-ṭhak*, and by the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ik* for *ṭha*; then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the final vowel. Within that [compound], there is a *dvandva*. The word "rahasya" [is used] because the word *dvandva* is well-known among grammarians as signifying a secret, according to the rule *dvandvaṃ rahasyam*. Thus it is explained.

However, for one who has understood the meaning, since [the compound] is not seen in the fourth [case] or in the sense of the four purposes (*caturartha*), it is appropriate that the meaning of a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) compound alone should be presented from the designated compound word—according to the principle of the *rathantara* section—because a collective suffix (*ṭhak*) cannot be obtained from a compound word that does not denote that [technical] meaning. Furthermore, because the *dvandva* taught in the rule "the *dvandva* [is neuter] in the sense of a secret" is invariably neuter, it is impossible for a masculine form to express that [meaning].

Furthermore, since that which expresses a compound is observed to be masculine in gender in rules such as "cārthe dvandvaḥ," and because it is a technical term (pāribhāṣika), it is more appropriate to understand by it the compound itself; thus, [the objection] is to be considered.

Nor should it be argued that if the co-existence [of the two objects] is not manifested, then when one intends to express the connection of the action with only one of them, there would result the undesirable usage "paśya dhavakhadirau chindhi" (see the *dhava* and *khadira* trees; cut them), just as in the sentence "paśya dhavam khadiram chindhi" (see the *dhava* tree; cut the *khadira* tree). For elsewhere it has been observed that the cognition of the connection of another word-meaning occurs only when that meaning is qualified by duality, which is the sense of the suffix; therefore, here too, it is appropriate that the connection occurs precisely as delimited by that [duality].

Nor should it be argued that the very connection of the number two (dvitva) would be impossible without the manifestation of a collective unity (*sāhitya*) which serves as the delimitor of the fitness for that connection; for the presentation of the delimitor of fitness is not required, since the connection occurs with whatever is fit for its presentation. For this very reason, in the sentence "Bring water with a jar," it is only the non-porous [jar] that connects by the force of fitness, yet there is no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having "non-porousness" as its qualifier; and even if the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*) itself were the delimitor of the fitness for the connection of the number two, there would be no deficiency. This has been analyzed more extensively elsewhere.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of the injunction, "The two [husband and wife], wearing linen garments, should establish the sacred fires," the attainment of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or coexistence (*sāhitya*) would not be possible; for that is established by another scriptural statement: "Whatever is to be performed, that is to be done together with her. Although mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), which consists in mutual correlative connection, is difficult to establish in a *dvandva* compound, nevertheless, the compound occurs there solely by virtue of the force of the rule "A *dvandva* [is used] in the sense of 'and' (*ca*). The meaning of the suffix *datṛ* has already been explained. Furthermore, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that a *dvandva* does not occur in the cases of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or alternative mention (*anvācaya*), precisely because these meanings are not denoted [by the word "and"].

As for the claim that "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists solely in being connected in a single form to one and the same action, that is not correct; for if one were to resort to this [definition] in some cases and to the previously mentioned [definition] in others, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) within the *Samartha* Sūtra, and because the state of being connected to a single action is not experienced from that [latter definition]. He dispels this objection by accepting the previous position as desired, stating: "It is accepted."

The phrase "of this very last phoneme" (caramavarṇasyaiva) means of the final phoneme accompanied by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) awakened by the experience of each preceding phoneme; therefore, there is no possibility of the meaning being understood from the final phoneme alone. More will be said on this later. Revealing the intention of the Bhāṣya—namely, that "when there is mutual expectancy (vyapekṣā) as the basis for semantic competency (sāmarthya), the compound would remain uncollected"—the author refutes the Naiyāyika position with the words "here it is said" (atrocyate). By the phrase "saṃjñā etc.," the status of being a word (padatva) and so forth are included.

Regarding the phrase "established by the Bhāṣya": this means that which is established by the Bhāṣya in the statement, "The mention of 'compound' (samāsa) is for the purpose of restriction regarding meaningful aggregates.

It is "clear" because, since even a sentence possesses meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), there arises the contingency of its being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); having raised the objection that a rule must therefore be commenced to exclude such cases, it is resolved by the mention of "compound" as a restrictive device. However, if one does not admit a primary expressive power (*śakti*) in a compound, then—since it lacks meaningfulness in the form of conveying meaning through a secondary function (*vṛtti*)—the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would not otherwise apply; thus, the necessity of that [mention of "compound"] for a case where the designation is not otherwise obtained would clearly contradict its status as a restrictive rule.

Therefore, the meaning is that this commentary also establishes that there is a specific expressive power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in a compound, because it has been stated therein. Nor is it the case that the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is established for a word composed of meaningful words through the capacity of those meaningful words; otherwise, since "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*) would already be obtained by the very exclusion of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth, the inclusion of that [term "meaningful"] would clearly be redundant.

It should not be argued that the phrase "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍimāni*) and similar collections of meaningless elements must necessarily be excluded; for while it is an established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the requirement of being "meaningful" (*arthavat*) serves a further purpose, this [collection] lacks such capacity. Furthermore, the *Bhāṣya* states, "The mention of 'meaningful' is for the sake of designating the named entity," showing its utility to indicate similarity by way of meaningfulness. Thus, the point is that without the acceptance of a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would be impossible in a compound.

Now, one might object: even if one does not accept a denotative power (*śakti*) for a qualified entity in cases such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), there is no inconsistency regarding the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which is based on its having a meaning. To explain: the relation with the denoted meaning (*śakyasambandha*) is not what constitutes indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because that would be impossible in cases such as "the hamlet is on the deep river" (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). In that case, first of all, the word *gabhīra* ("deep") cannot indicate the bank, because that would result in the word *nadyām* ("on the river") being syntactically unconnected. For the bank is not the river; for this very reason, the word *nadī* ("river") also cannot indicate it, because that would result in the meaning of the word *gabhīra* being unconnected.

Nor does that [indication] apply to each of the two words individually, because that would entail the non-appearance of a qualified river-bank. Nor can it be said that the bank of a deep river is indicated by the word "river" alone, while words such as "deep" merely serve to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*); for there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamakābhāva*) to determine whether the word "deep" indicates the intention or the word "river" does.

Nor should it be argued that, because the word *nadī* (river) denotes a substance (*dravya*), direct relation alone is the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For the word *gabhīra* (deep) also invariably denotes a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), and thus its meaning likewise possesses no distinction in terms of direct relation. Therefore, due to the complexity (*gaurava*) of indicating both words, indication must be accepted as residing in the composite whole (*samudāya*) itself. For this very reason, it is consistent with the principle that arthavāda sentences possess indication in the sense of excellence (*prāśastya*). However, that indication consists precisely in the form of what is signified by the words themselves.

In the sentence "There is [a person] at the deep river," that which is made known by the sentence (*vākyajñāpya*) is the relation between the river—which is non-different from "deep"—and the bank. And thus, because a compound such as *citragu* possesses meaningfulness (*arthavattva*)—insofar as it denotes, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), an object consisting of the owner of cows who is non-different from "variegated"—the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not untenable. To this, he says: "In the compound sentence. By using the term "sentence" (*vākya*), he indicates that although such [meaningfulness] might occur in some cases, it is impossible in all compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*.

The intention is this: a relation with that which is made known by itself (the primary meaning) does not constitute indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because that would lead to the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) of the definition even to the case of corrupt words (*apabhraṃśa*). Furthermore, the meaning of the phrase "made known by itself" must be stated as: "a relation with an object possessing the state of being made known, which is in turn the counter-correlate of a capacity to cause knowledge residing in itself. In this context, does "capacity to cause knowledge" mean being a signifier through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), or merely being the object of a cognition that generates [another] cognition? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that there is no indication in a sentence; for the meaning of such a sentence—namely, something non-different from "deep"—is not cognizable through any linguistic function.

Not the latter [alternative], because it would entail that each individual phoneme possesses meaning, which in turn would necessitate the application of case-endings; therefore, one must accept that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is simply the relation to what is directly denoted by itself (*sva-śakya-sambandha*). Consequently, since such a relation is impossible in a compound (*samāsa*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) remains untenable as before; thus, the acceptance of a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) for the compound is necessary. The phrase "established in the Bhāṣya" refers to the fact that this is stated therein in passages such as: "There is a prohibition regarding the single substitute for *ti* because it is treated as having the finality of the preceding element. This is the underlying intention.

The meaning of "let it be formulated as a sūtra" is that it should be formulated simply as "and what is other than a finite verb (tiṅ) or a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (sup) is a nominal stem (prātipadika). Thus, since the status of a compound (samāsa) as a nominal stem is obtained by the sense that "whatever is distinct from tiṅs and subs" is a nominal stem, the inclusion of the term "compound" (samāsagrahaṇa) is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha), meaning that [only compounds] are [to be considered nominal stems].

The phrase "in each individual phoneme" means that, under the view that phonemes are devoid of meaning, since there is no referent to be expressed when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) designation applies, suffixes would be possible for every phoneme without distinction; this is the intended sense of the expression "like indeclinables and so forth. The phrase "if they possess meaning" means that the inclusion of the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is necessary.

Nor should it be argued that even if one adopts the view that the individual phonemes constituting a meaningful aggregate are themselves meaningful—as seen in the Bhāṣya—the suffixation of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) would still be unavoidable; for even under that view, the Bhāṣya states: "Because the aggregate has a single meaning, there is no *su*-suffix [after each phoneme], but rather from the aggregate. Thus, by the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application), a single case-ending alone would convey the singularity residing in both the meaning of the aggregate and its constituent parts.
Since that single singularity is conveyed by a single *sup* suffix, there is nothing further to be expressed; hence, the sense is that the case-ending does not arise after each individual phoneme.

Now, one might object: even if a compound sentence lacks semantic unity (*arthavattva*), there is no impossibility of its being designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since that is possible by the rule "kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca" itself. For when a general rule is applicable, it is improper to assume a restrictive limitation (*niyamakalpanā*). Furthermore, the very mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in that rule is the proof that the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) exists only in compounds. However, there is no possibility of a sentence being so designated by the preceding rule, because it lacks semantic unity. Even though the relation (*saṃsarga*) is not directly denotable, its manifestation is easily established through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors.

Thus, since the aggregate of base and suffix is also devoid of meaning, the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* [suffixes] is for the purpose of prescribing a designation that would otherwise not apply; therefore, the entire sūtra is prescriptive. However, the first sūtra refers only to the form of an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) correct word, and not to aggregates such as *bahupaṭu*, because such an aggregate—where the subsequent member functions as a technical indicator (*lākṣaṇika*)—lacks meaningfulness.

Since certain forms ending in *tṛc* possess meaning yet are still verbal roots (*dhātu*), and likewise since secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *i*, *iyān*, and so forth are suffixes (*pratyaya*), the author of the Sūtras composed a second rule to prescribe the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) for such groups which are themselves meaningless and thus not covered by the preceding rule. For this very reason, the term *arthavat* ("meaningful") does not carry over here, because it is impossible [for these to be meaningful] and because there would be no purpose [in applying it].

In this context, by the term *kṛt*, there is a reference to that which ends in it (*tadanta*) through the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding suffixes, because the principle "in the formulation of a technical designation" (*saṃjñāvidhau*) is generally applicable, and because [the mention of] *kṛt* would otherwise be redundant—just as in the case of *ḍatara* and so on—since the suffix *kel* is not employed.

Although, by the reasoning already stated, the word *taddhita* is understood to refer specifically to that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix, nevertheless, in order to include forms such as *bahupaṭu* (which fall under the defining characteristic of the target), it should be explained as referring either to a *taddhita*-ending form or to a collection containing a base (*prakṛti*) qualified by a *taddhita* suffix, related by the condition of being immediately followed by it (*svāvyavahitottaratva*).

And being a *prakṛti* (base) consists in being the limit for the application of an affix (*pratyaya*). However, in cases such as *iḥ* and *ityān*, there is no fault, because the affix itself possesses that [base] as its final element. There is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *pacataki*, because the *taddhita* base included within that aggregate lacks the aforementioned qualification of being a *taddhita*. Furthermore, because the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*—which is signaled by the mention of "immediately following" (*anantara*)—is not universally applicable, there is no such over-extension in examples like *mūlakenopadaṃśam*.

Thus, since the designation *prātipadika* is established even for a compound by this rule of inclusion, the derivation of case endings such as *su* from a whole expression like *rājapuruṣa* is easily obtained; therefore, the postulation of a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in that [compound] is without proof. It has already been stated that such [power] does not belong to the sentence, because in that case, the power is determined by means of *kosa* and other [lexicons].

However, where there is a separator such as *kośa* (a sheath) and so forth—as in the case of *paṅkaja* and similar compounds—we preclude that [application of the rule] in the compound. And thus, since a sentence lacks "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) does not apply; consequently, because there is no possibility for its exclusion, it is incorrect to describe the mention of "compound" (*samāsa-grahaṇa*) as being for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). As for the description in the Bhāṣya of that [mention] as being for the sake of restriction, that is only in accordance with the view of a certain school (*ekadeśimatam*) which holds that the relation (*saṃsarga*) is the denotable meaning (*śakyatva*). Out of dissatisfaction with this, he says: "Moreover, in this way... (*kiñcaivam iti*).

"In such a compound," that is, when the acceptance of a distinct capacity (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) is not admitted; "the consequence of the non-connection of [grammatical relations] such as objecthood (*karmatva*)"—this requires the supplement "with respect to the referent of words such as 'cow'. He states the reason for this: "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*). Thus, being a base (*prakṛtitva*) consists in being the limit for the prescription of a suffix, and not in being immediately preceded by a suffix; for if it were the latter, there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *bahupaṭuḥ*, where the word *paṭu* is the base.

Nor should it be argued that, based on the Bhāṣya statement—"Those two alone are *su* and *tiṅ* which follow that [base], and that alone is the original base (*prakṛti*)"—the status of being a base is obtained only for that which immediately precedes a suffix; for this would result from a misunderstanding of its meaning. The phrase "those two alone are *su* and *tiṅ* which follow that" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) referring to all suffixes, since there is no specific rule to the contrary regarding the limit of their prescription; the meaning is that whatever [suffix] is prescribed, that alone is the base. The word "original" (*ādyā*) is used with the intention of referring to the first instance of occurrence (*abhyāsa*).

And thus, since the final member of a compound lacks the status of being a "base" (prakṛti)—defined as the limit for the application of a grammatical rule—there can be no syntactic connection (anvaya) of "object-ness" (karmatva) or other such properties with its meaning; this is because it would contradict the aforementioned linguistic principle (vyutpatti). This is the intended sense.

The derivation [of the term] *pratyaya* (suffix) is indeed accepted in cases such as *daṇḍam ānaya* ("bring the staff") in order to prevent the relation of objecthood (*karmatva*) from applying to the staff and other such items. Its meaning is: "With respect to verbal cognition, there is causality by way of being an apprehension generated by a suffix, related through the relation of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), [the suffix-apprehension] being qualified by a subjectivity (*viṣayatā*) that is itself determined by a subjectivity residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). In this context, it is argued that the base should be included merely by its presence (*sannihitatva*), for that alone prevents the aforementioned deviation (*vyabhicāra*); it should not be included by way of being a "base" (*prakṛtitva*), because that would be cumbersome. He introduces this view in order to refute it, saying: "As for what [some say]... (*yattu*).

The term *sannihita* (proximate) means being presented as immediately preceding [the word it qualifies]. The point is that since this [proximity] exists in words such as *citragu* with respect to the cow (*go*) and so forth, the aforementioned logical inconsistency does not arise. By the particle *eva* ("only") in the phrase "only the derivation" (*vyutpattireva*), there is an exclusion of the previously mentioned derivation consisting of the status of being a base (*prakṛti*). The meaning is: "even in compounds such as *upakumbha*."

In the term *ānuśāsani* (prescriptive), "proximity" (*sannihitatva*) does not mean immediate precedence, nor does it mean being connected as such [in the cognition]; for if it were the latter, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the meaning of the case-ending could not be construed with the referents of words such as *dhava* and *khadira* in expressions like *dhavakhadirau*. Rather, it is proximity as taught by the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*). And since this [proximity] exists for the referents of words such as *upādi* just as it does for the referents of words such as *dhava*, the author says "And thus" (*tathā ca*), expressing this intention.

The meaning is as follows: because the term "following the word that is being compounded" implies that a compound (*samāsa*) is a collection of multiple words, and since a collection is not distinct from its individual members, the case-ending prescribed for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the form of the compound is in proximity to each respective word.

This might be possible if the designation *prātipadika* were based on the inclusion of a compound; however, that [designation] must be stated by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) itself as a restrictive factor. Thus, with the intention that the aforementioned method is impossible, he says, "by the rule *arthavat*" (Pāṇini 1.2.45). Consequently, even the proximity (*sannihitatva*) taught by the treatise belongs only to the specific [composite] form, and not to the initial member alone; therefore, the fallacy in the case mentioned is unavoidable—this is the sense.

Even though the status of being a *prakṛti* (material cause) rests solely upon the aggregate by means of a unique relation called *paryāpti*, the property of being that [cause] can still occur in each individual part by virtue of being its exclusive substratum (*kevalāśrayatā*). With the intention that the aforementioned etymological derivation must therefore incorporate "substratum-hood" (*āśrayatā*) itself in the case of an insentient entity, he raises an objection with the words "Now, [if it be argued]... (*atha*). "In the locus of *prakṛti*-hood" (*prakṛtitvāśraye*) means "in the object that is the locus of *prakṛti*-hood."

Having raised an objection regarding the meaning of the constituent parts (*prakṛti*) when they are not proximate, he states it even when they are proximate: the objection is raised with the intention that in the case of *aghaṭam*, there is predominance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*). This point will be explained further on. The phrase "by way of being a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatayā*) means that what is already occupied by a qualifier in one place cannot be construed with another, because its expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) has been satisfied; this is the underlying sense. He refutes the literal reading that "there is connection with another [word] through a qualifier anywhere," as follows:

The meaning is that in expressions such as "blue from cooking" (*pākān nīlaḥ*), since blueness (*nīlatva*) and pleasure (*sukha*) are construed as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatayā*) within their own substrata, the causal status (*hetutva*) denoted by the ablative case (*pañcamy-artha*) in "from cooking" and so forth cannot be construed [with them]. In the phrase "being the object of the cognition produced by that" (*tajjanya-jñāna-viṣayatve*), the referent of the pronoun *tat* is the base (*prakṛti*). By the word "only" (*mātra*), the state of being conveyed through a secondary function (*vṛtti-pratipādyatva*) is excluded. Here, the meaning refers to the referent of words such as "cow" (*go*) occurring within compounds like *citragu*. "Non-contradictory" (*aviruddha*) means unrefuted (*abādhita*).

In the expression "see the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ paśya*), the root *dṛś* has the general sense of cognition. "To exclude space" means to prevent the connection of space—which is presented through association—with the status of being the object (*karman*) of the action denoted by *dṛś*. "By way of [its] occurrence as the meaning of the base" means by way of being the object of the presentation produced by the linguistic function (*vṛtti*).

According to the maxim, "as many meanings as are possible in the statement of a disputant," he explains [the passage] by way of a different meaning in order to refute the stated etymology. The sense is that [the word *kṛṣṇa*] exists within the scope of the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the word preceding the suffix, as indicated by the phrase "by occasion" (*prasaṅgāt*). Although the etymology "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*) holds true in the view that maintains a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), in our own view it is not universal, because it is impossible in the case of compounds (*samāsa*) alone. However, intending to state that in the present instance another etymology must simply be postulated, he says: "Now" (*atha*).

The phrase "the postulation of an unpostulated [cause]" (aklṛptakalpanām) means the postulation of another causal relation for the cognition produced by an affix (*pratyayajanyopasthiti*), with respect to verbal understanding (*śābdabodha*), by way of the relation of being an object as determined by the objecthood residing in the meaning of the word being compounded. Now, one might object: there is only one uniform linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) common to both compounds and non-compounds, namely that affixes convey their own meaning as it pertains to the word-meaning that is in proximity (*sannihita*). Furthermore, if "proximity" were defined as the status of being a stem (*prakṛti*)—which would involve the inclusion of the status of being a word (*padatva*)—there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and so forth; such is the general sense of the argument.

Now, since the term *pratyaya* is derived [from the root *i* with the prefix *pra-*] and thus consists of both a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*), it is difficult to specify its status as either a base or a suffix when these two are not explicitly present; consequently, one must state the relation of cause and effect according to the distinction between each specific individual instance. Thus, there is no obstacle to accepting that in the case of a compound (*samāsa*), the meaning of the word being compounded is construed with the meaning of the suffix; for this reason, he says: "Moreover... (*api ca*).

Alternatively, rather than postulating a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) for multiple compounds, it is simpler to merely postulate another rule of derivation (*vyutpatti*) aided by the abandonment of the established derivation; therefore, he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*). The phrase "the consequence of non-connection" (*ananvaya-prasaṅga*) implies the rule that "the meaning of a noun [is connected] with the meaning of a noun. He states this very non-connection with the words "of the word *rāja* and so forth. By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even in the case of secondary signification" (*lakṣaṇāyām api*), it is indicated that there is an even greater absence of connection in the case of signifying the relation itself. Nor is there a deviation from the stated rule in examples such as "white" (*śubhraḥ*), because he says: "The rice is white" (*taṇḍulaḥ śubhraḥ*).

The point is that since there is the presence of the semantic representation (upasthiti) produced by the case-ending with respect to the nominal stem-meaning associated with "rice" (*taṇḍula*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case. Anticipating and refuting a possible objection regarding deviation in instances such as *śubhreṇa taṇḍulena* ("by white rice"), he states: "having the sense of non-difference" (*abhedārthikā*). Alternatively, since the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated in the rule *anabhihita* that a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) may occur after words like *bhīṣma* when they are in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [a word] such as *kaṭa*, [there is no deviation].

The point is that since the identity (*abheda*) between two qualifiers in grammatical apposition is obtained as the meaning of the case-ending following the qualifier-word, there is no deviation [in the rule], because in that instance as well—such as in *śubhreṇa*—there exists the presence of the cognition of identity produced by the third case (*tṛtīyā*).

Now, if "non-difference" here were the absence of that which is delimited by the property of being a difference (*bhedatva*), then it would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), because difference is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) category. If, on the other hand, it were the absence having difference as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then the sentence "Fire is blue" would result in being valid (*prāmāṇya*), since the absence of the difference from blue—delimited by duality and so forth—exists in fire; furthermore, there would be the consequence that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) could not be construed with the "difference" which is a single part of the meaning of the qualifying case-ending (*viśeṣaṇavibhakti*).

Nor should it be argued that the second case suffix (*dvitīyādi*) has no expressive power (*śakti*) regarding either difference (*bheda*) or absence (*abhāva*); and that while difference is construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) as having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by the delimitor of the base-meaning, the absence of the difference residing in the base-meaning—construed with the aforementioned relation—is admitted as having a counter-correlativity delimited by [the absence] itself, and thus the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) and so forth do not arise. Why? Because [if that were the case], there would be no expressive power for the second case suffix in the case of difference, nor would there be any expressive power in the case of absence. Furthermore, it must be stated that difference is construed with the meaning of the base as having a counter-correlativity delimited by the delimitor of the base-meaning; however, since the absence of the difference residing in the base-meaning is admitted as being construed with the aforementioned relation as having a counter-correlativity delimited by that very [absence], the aforementioned undesirable consequence and so forth do not occur. This is not to be asserted.

In cases such as "the pot is cognizable" (*prameyo ghaṭaḥ*), the aforementioned method is impossible because a difference qualified by "being cognizable" (*prameyatva*) is unestablished; furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that a sentence such as "the pot is blue"—where the word "blue" is used in reference to a specific blue object like a blue cloth—would be authoritative, since the absence of a difference from "blueness" (i.e., being blue) is not sublated in the pot. Nor can the meaning of the case-ending be simply the non-difference qualified by that particularity (*tadvyaktitva*); for if that were the case, since it is impossible to know the particularity residing in a never-before-perceived individual, one could not grasp the word's power (*śakti*) regarding an absence whose counter-positive is qualified by that [ungrasped] particularity, and thus the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of non-difference with a new individual would be untenable.

This is because it is untenable for the cognition of non-existence to apprehend a qualified relation (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*), and because it is impossible for a counter-positiveness delimited by one property to appear as a relation within a non-existence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by another property. If this is argued, we reply: no; for non-difference is identity (*tādātmya*), and that is a unique property residing in itself.

And "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇya) is simply a property residing in a single entity, defined as being other than that which is qualified by difference through the two relations of "subsisting in its own counter-positive" and "co-occurrence with its own absence. The meaning of the base [the word *eka*] is construed as being inherent (*ādheyatayā*) in that [property]. Even though it is impossible to know specifically the "individuality" (*tadvyaktitva*) residing in a novel individual, it is easily grasped through the general proximity of being a property residing in a single entity; thus, everything is well-established. Regarding the term "subsequent" (*pārṣṭhika*): it means occurring at a time subsequent to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

The term "anvaya" means "cognition thereof. According to the principle established in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, all case-meanings first connect with the action; since the case-ending-generated mental presence (*upasthiti*) exists when the meaning of words such as "white" (*śubhra*) connects with that [action], there is no deviation from the stated rule of linguistic usage even in that view. This is the intended sense.

Now, although the requirement [of the definition] is necessary—based on the etymological derivation *nāmārthayoḥ* ("between the meanings of two nouns")—to prevent the application of "king" to the person in *rājā puruṣaḥ* (the king's man) or "rice" to the cooking in *taṇḍulaḥ pacati* (he cooks rice), by way of the relations of owner-ownership (*svasvāmibhāva*) and objecthood (*karmatā*), respectively; nevertheless, in order to avoid the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) where "king" is related to the person in *rājā puruṣaḥ* and "little" is related to the cooking in *stokaṃ pacati* by way of identity (*abhedasaṃbandha*), it must be stipulated that the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the noun is delimited by a relation other than identity.

Nor can it be maintained that the case-ending of the qualifier has its purpose fulfilled by signifying non-difference (*abheda*), because at the occasion of explaining the *Bhāṣya* statement "the mat itself is the object," it was stated that even though words such as *bhīṣma* are not themselves objects, the case-ending following the word *bhīṣma* must be one identical with that of the word related to the qualificandum, since they share the same grammatical status (*ekayogakṣema*). Furthermore, isolated nominal stems (*prātipadika*) are unfit for usage according to the rule "an affix [must follow] and [it must be] subsequent."

Just as the friends of a wealthy man, though themselves penniless, enjoy the fruits [of wealth] solely through his riches, so too do the qualities [of a word]. Thus, Kaiyaṭa, in commenting on the *sūtra* "anabhihite," has clearly stated that the case-ending of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) serves merely to indicate grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*). Furthermore, there is no experience of a verbal cognition where the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the meaning of the case-ending is the qualifier (*prakāra*), in instances where the qualifier and the qualificand stand in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, the word "by way of distinction" (*bhedena*) is recited in the rule of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*).

And thus, in that case, the connection of the indicated object (lakṣyārtha) with a person related to the king is not untenable; therefore, he says "furthermore" (kiñca). [He states this] because it would contradict the Vivaraṇa.

Regarding this, they argue: the analysis (*vigraha*) possesses the same meaning as that which is being analyzed (*vigṛhyamāṇa*), provided it is not [the case that] whatever generates a cognition having a particular qualificandum and a particular qualifier does not generate a cognition having that very qualificandum and that very qualifier; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that compounds ending in *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes could not function as analyses, because in those cases the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified among the word-meanings that are the objects of the cognition produced by the analysis and the cognition produced by what is being analyzed is reversed.

Nor does it consist in being the generator of a cognition that possesses as many objects as are contained in the cognition produced by that [compound], for then even the expression *puruṣasya rājñaḥ* (the king of the man) would result in being a *vigraha* (analytic expansion) of *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king’s man). Rather, that [capacity] must be defined as the capacity to generate a cognition of what is being analyzed (*vivriyamāṇa*). In the case of expressions such as *prāptam udakaṃ yam* (to whom water has come), the capacity to generate a cognition possessing as many objects as are the objects of the cognition produced by the compound *prāptodaka*, and which are the objects of the intended meaning regarding their mutual relation, constitutes that [capacity]. These objects include water and so forth.

The word "yāvat" (as much as) is used to exclude the possibility that the analysis (*vigraha*) of *ghaṭakarmatā* (the state of being the object of the pot) is merely *ghaṭakarmakānayanakṛtiḥ* (the effort of bringing the pot as the object). On the other hand, it is indeed accepted that the analysis of *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king's man) can be *rājñaḥ sundaraḥ* (the beautiful one of the king), which involves a further [qualification].

In reality, however, when a compound is employed for the purpose of grasping its semantic power (*śakti*), it is simply impossible to employ a word whose meaning is not the intended object (*atātparya-viṣaya*). The qualification "being the intended object" (*tātparya-viṣayatva*) is included [in the definition] to exclude cases such as *puruṣasya rājñaḥ* (the king of the man), which are not true *vigrahas*. In that case, "man" (*puruṣaḥ*) is not the counter-correlative (*pratiyogī*). Furthermore, a collection such as *ghaṭaḥ karmatvam* (pot-ness is the object) constitutes the *vigraha* for *ghaṭam ānaya* (bring the pot) and similar expressions. In the Nyāya system, however, only those compounds like *kumbhakāra* (pot-maker), where the agent (*kartṛ*) is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), possess the status of being a *vigraha* for expressions such as *kumbhaṃ karoti* (he makes a pot).

And in the present case, since the status of being a "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) and so forth remains intact even in the sentence "the man of the king" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), there is no impossibility of that [sentence] being the *vigraha* (analytic expansion).

The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means in the absence of having the same meaning. Therefore, [it would not be possible] from the *vigraha*-sentence; the sense is that only a sentence possessing the same meaning as that [compound] can determine its expressive power (*śakti*).

He refutes the definition of relation as "non-conceptual" (alakṣaṇa) by stating "not the latter. In order to include compounds such as *nīlotpala* ("blue lotus"), he abandons the term "having the same case-ending" (*samānavibhaktika*) and says "devoid of contradictory case-endings" (*viruddhavibhaktirahita*). He specifies "of two nominal stem meanings" (*prātipadikārthayoḥ*), because one observes non-difference (*abheda*) in the syntactic connection between the meanings of a verbal root and a nominal stem that have contradictory case-endings, as in "he cooks slightly" (*stokaṃ pacati*). Thus, [the cause] is with respect to verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of a nominal stem, which is delimited by the relation of non-difference (*abhedasaṃsarga*).

The point is that since the causal condition for [verbal] comprehension is the presentation (upasthiti) produced by words devoid of incompatible case-endings, and since such a presentation exists in relation to the referent of the final member of a compound—such as *puruṣa* in the expression *rājapuruṣaḥ*—an appositional connection (*abhedānvaya*) is unavoidable.

Now, one might object: "The absence of incompatible case-endings is common to both analytical (vyāsa) and compound (samāsa) expressions; it does not consist in the fact that the word denoting the qualificand is not the stem of the case-ending whose stem is the word denoting the qualifier, because this is absent in cases such as *nīlaṃ ghaṭam ānaya*."

Nor can it be said that the case-ending of the word denoting the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) does not have as its base a case-ending whose base is not the word denoting the qualified (viśeṣya); for in cases such as "the blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), there exists the fact that the case-ending following the word "blue" is different from the case-ending following the word "pot"—whether this be defined as not having the qualified word as its base, or as not being immediately preceded by it, or as not being perceived as such—and consequently, the syntactic relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) would be impossible there. If this is argued:

On this point, some maintain that the absence of contradictory case-endings (*viruddhavibhaktirāhitya*) in the qualifier-word (*viśeṣaṇapada*) consists simply in its not being the base for a case-ending different from the case-ending belonging to the word expressing the qualificand (*viśeṣyavācakapada*). This similarity (*sājātya*) is determined by being either a nominative (*prathamā*) or a *su*-affix (*sutva*), and so forth. Thus, in cases such as "the blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), although the case-ending of the qualifier is different from the case-ending of the qualificand, the aforementioned absence of contradictory case-endings remains intact there, because it is not different from something similar to it.

In reality, however, according to the view that the case-ending of a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*), "having a case-ending incompatible with the case-ending following the word denoting the qualified" means "having a meaning different from its own [referent]. In cases such as *nīlo ghaṭaḥ* ("the blue pot"), since the case-ending of the qualifier is devoid of meaning (*nirarthaka*), the case-ending there that has a meaning incompatible with the case-ending of the qualified is indeed one of the second type (*dvitīyā*) and so forth; because the state of not being the base (*aprakṛtitva*) of that [second-case ending] exists in the word denoting the qualifier, there is no failure to include such instances.

Thus, in cases such as "bring the blue pot" (*nīlaghaṭam ānaya*), since there is an absence of even a case-ending on the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the fact that the word denoting the qualifier is not the stem (*prakṛti*) of such a case-ending remains unchallenged. For this very reason, in expressions such as "the wealth of Caitra’s son" (*caitrasya sutasya dhanam*), there is no requirement for a relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*). This is because, in those instances, the case-endings of the qualifier and the qualified denote different types of relations. Nor is there an inclusion of examples such as "he eats little" (*stokam atti*); for in the previous theory, since the case-ending denoting the qualifier is of a different class (*vijātīya*) from the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the aforementioned requirement does not exist there, making its exclusion quite evident.

In the rule *sāre*, the phrase *prātipadikārthayoḥ* is intended precisely with reference to the present context. Thus, the resulting meaning is that in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by either a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), related to the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) through a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by a relation of non-difference residing in the meaning of a nominal stem that is neither a verbal root nor a case-ending whose suffix is contrary to what has been stated.

[Objection: But if the absence of a conflicting case-ending from what has been previously mentioned is required for the cognition of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*), then there would be such a requirement in cases like "the wealth of Caitra’s son" (*caitrasya sutasya dhanam*); therefore, he says: "It has been explained at length. It was stated therein that the aforementioned grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) applies only to the connection between the meanings of nouns (*nāmārtha*), with the meaning of the case-ending included [within the noun]. The intended sense here is that even in that case, the status of not being the base (*prakṛti*) of a meaningful case-ending must be included as a qualification for the word expressing the qualifier.

He states that even the Mīmāṃsakas must accept the theory of a specific power (viśiṣṭaśaktipakṣa): "For this very reason, [it is] not [the case]," meaning that because the unification of meaning (ekārthībhāva) in a compound is accepted by all; and "with reference to eating," meaning that the eating of the sacrificial remains enjoined in the rule "the priests eat the remnants of the oblation" is being restated.

The meaning is as follows: because it would entail the violation of *ekaprasaratā* (the requirement that a single syntactic unit must be interpreted as a whole), when there is a relation between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), their separate presentation acts as a restrictive factor; thus, if one were to accept that [separate presentation] in accordance with that [relation], it would result in the violation of *ekaprasaratā*, which consists in the capacity to generate the presentation of a qualified meaning. This is because, even if they do not accept a qualified power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), they do accept a qualified indication (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇā*), and thus *ekaprasaratā* is established in their own system.

It should not be argued: "How can that [status of being the subject] be attributed there, given that the connection with the word *yad* (‘which’), primacy, and so forth are the necessary conditions for the relation as the subject (*uddeśyatva*), while the connection with the word *tad* (‘that’), and so forth, are the necessary conditions for the relation as the predicate (*vidheyatva*), and these are absent in this case"? For when there is an intention [to convey such a relation], the relation between subject and predicate is experienced by the intellect even in cases such as "the first meal" (*prathamo bhakṣaḥ*) or "the learned Brāhmaṇa" (*paṇḍito brāhmaṇaḥ*); thus, the connection with the word *yad* and the like are merely common occurrences.

However, in such verbal cognition, the presence of meanings generated by non-compounded words (*asamasta-padajanyopasthiti*) is not the cause; for otherwise, cognitions such as "Dāmodara is to be worshipped" (*dāmodaraḥ pūjyaḥ*) or "the king’s servant is well-respected" (*rājapuruṣaḥ sunādaraḥ*) would be untenable. This is because, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), in those cases, a distinct act of eating qualified by priority (*prāthamya*) is enjoined through the primary function of the word (*śabdavṛtti*); consequently, by the principle of distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not (*prāptāprāptaviveka*), the injunction results in the prescription of priority itself. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "with three parts" (*tryaṅgaiḥ*): there arises a doubt as to whether this is an injunction for some unspecified part characterized by the remainder-ness (*śeṣabhūta*) qualified by the number three, or rather an injunction for the remaining parts qualified by the number three. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*) the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering was performed with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is a remnant, it is argued here too that the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is properly performed only with parts characterized by the number three as remnants. However, [the correct conclusion is: if one were to enjoin the number three while merely referring to certain parts that are already remnants, there would be the fault of violating the principle of "single thrust of expression" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*). Therefore...

The meaning is that it has been determined in the third section (pāda) of the tenth chapter that there is an injunction for other limbs characterized by a triad as stated in the *Kalpasūtras*. As for the eleven limbs beginning with the heart mentioned in the *Kalpasūtras*, they are: 1. heart, 2. tongue, 3. chest, 4. liver, 5. kidneys, 6. left foreleg, 7. [right foreleg], 8. both sides, 9. [both sides], 10. right hip, and 11. rectum. Among those, the triad consists of: the right shoulder, the left hip, and the rectum as the third.

Indeed, "single-sweep-ness" (*ekaprasaratva*) does not mean the capacity to generate the presentation of a qualified object; rather, its meaning is the absence of the cognition of a relation between the constituent members of a compound by way of the status of subject (*uddeśya*) and predicate (*vidheya*), because such a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) would otherwise be violated. It does not mean the non-violation of the capacity to generate the presentation of a qualified object.

The body of that grammatical rule, however, is as follows: with respect to a verbal cognition, the presentation generated by the constituent members of a compound is an inhibitor when it is related to the subjecthood (*uddeśyatā*) determined by the predicatehood (*vidheyatā*) residing in the meanings of those same constituent members of the compound.

Nor should it be argued that there is complexity (gaurava) in postulating such a relationship between the sublated and the sublator; for, compared to postulating a qualified power (viśiṣṭa-śakti) in every case, there is simplicity (lāghava) in postulating the relationship between the sublated and the sublator only in certain instances.

In reality, however, where there is a cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) by way of the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), such a relation is impossible precisely because of the absence of the respective word-orders (*ānupūrvī*) that bring about the presentation of those word-meanings; therefore, even the postulation of the aforementioned sublated and sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhaka*) is unnecessary. As for "single-syllabic force" (*ekaprasaratā*), it is simply the empirical experience of a cognition having as its qualificandum (*viśeṣyaka*) the act of eating qualified by the first word-meaning; thus, the Mīmāṃsakas should not accept a "qualified power" (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) on the grounds of the aforementioned reasoning. Therefore, he says: "And it is consistent."

Nor can it be said that [the word] "difference" (*bheda*) arises from the sentence; for its inclusion within the sentence by means of the term "sentence" is not even possible, because, being incorporeal, it cannot have a connection with actions as a factor (*kāraka*), nor with substances.

Nor should it be argued that the connection [of the quality] with the substance—by means of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), which, having referred back (*anūdya*) to the substances mentioned in the context that constitute the instruments (*karaṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, links them to the action to be performed as its delimiting factor (*paricchedaka*) by way of the quality of redness (*aruṇya*)—is not impossible; for if that were so, it would result in the collapse of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "capacity (*śakti*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). This very point he states with the words "it has been explained in detail" (*prapañcitam*). He concludes with "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

By stating "by the followers of Jaimini," the author suggests that the Nyāya view is more consistent with reason; "in accordance with the identity of meaning" means that, because of this identity of meaning, both the expanded (vyāsa) and the condensed (samāsa) forms generate a cognition having the same object as its qualificandum and the same property as its qualifier. It is in accordance with this [identity of meaning] that [the Nyāya position is favored].

The intention is revealed by the passage beginning with "yadyapi" and ending with "mīmāṃsakāḥ": although the word *rāja-* within the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in reference to its relation [to the cows], this does not undermine its status as an analytical sentence; furthermore, because a genitive case ending expressing a relation generates a cognition whose qualifier is that relation, even sentences such as *citragavo yasya* (he whose cows are brindled) possess the nature of an analytical sentence. This is the underlying thought.

It is obtained from the sūtra; for, by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "the remainder is a *bahuvrīhi*," a compound is prescribed for that which is not [otherwise] mentioned—namely, the first triplet—by rules such as "the second [case-ending] with *āśrita*, etc. Although its compounding was indeed already stated by the rule "an adjective [is compounded] with a substantive" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), nevertheless, since it was not explicitly indicated there by the word "first" (*prathamā*), the status of that triplet as the "remainder" remains intact; this is the intended meaning.

"Of that which has already been stated" means "of [sentences] such as *citragavo 'yam* (these are the brindled cows) and so forth. By the particle *eva* (only/even), there is an exclusion of [sentences] containing the word *citra* (*brindled*) in the nominative case. The explanation of the term "indicative word" is "that which conveys the meaning. "Verb" (*ākhyāta*) means that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix; the meaning is "in a paraphrase consisting of such a *tiṅ*-ending form. He states the very same transposition with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth.

[Objection: But even there, since the suffix *tip* indicates the agent (*kartṛ*), the cognition [of the sentence] as "the locus of the operation of the instrument, the eye" does not involve a loss of synonymy; therefore, he says: "In the case of a *kṛt* affix. [The term] "of the *kārakas*" refers to the agent and so forth. "Primacy" means the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*). The primacy of the *kārakas* follows from the maxim "between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the affix," whereas the primacy of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) follows from the Nirukta statement, "A verb has the efficient force as its primary meaning. The phrase "because there is no difference in possessing power" means that possessing power constitutes a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

The term *siddhāntasiddhiḥ* means the establishment (*siddhi*) of the *siddhānta*—that is, the establishment of the matter under investigation—in the sense of its fitness for practical application (*anuṣṭhānopayogārhatva*). For instance, it is heard in scripture: "One should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice."

In this regard, when the doubt arises as to whether the word *niṣādasthapati* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*, a *bahuvrīhi*, or a *karmadhāraya*: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that it must be a genitive *tatpuruṣa* because of parsimony (*lāghava*), since a *karmadhāraya* would entail the burden of assuming the study of a previously unknown branch of learning, and a *bahuvrīhi* would entail the burden of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the syntactical connection. To this, [the siddhāntin replies]: even for a *tatpuruṣa*, there is the burden of metaphorical indication in the first member; therefore, by parsimony, it is indeed a *karmadhāraya*.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since the study of a previously unknown science is to be inferred as occurring at a subsequent time, such complexity (*gaurava*) is not a fault because it pertains to the result (*phalamukha*); this [of yours] would contradict that, for in your view, even if a *tatpuruṣa* compound were accepted, there would be no room for such complexity—this is the sense.

"At that time" means by taking into account the parsimony resulting from the consideration of the internal and external relationship (*antaraṅga-vahiraṅga-bhāva*) residing in the apprehension of the word-meaning (*śaktigraha*), which occurs in the moment immediately preceding the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by such a sentence. "In the *sthapati* related to the *niṣāda*s" is the meaning; for in that case, it is accepted that there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) through the inclusion of the relation expressed by the genitive case. Since the word *sthapati* signifies a master, the meaning is: "in a man who is a master not distinct from a *niṣāda*" (*niṣādābhinnasvāmike puṃsi*).

In that context, because the acceptance of a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) occurs through the inclusion of the meanings of other words [within the compound], the phrase "when the presentation of multiple meanings has occurred" is to be understood as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the word "nānārtha. Regarding the phrase "by means of logic" (*nyāyena*), when a doubt arises as to where its intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies, [the answer is] "in the postulation of that"—that is, in the postulation of the intended meaning. [The phrase] "only in the meaning already presented" refers to the following.

The meaning of the term *niṣādasthapati* is determined as follows: because the apprehension of the compound’s own power (*śakti*)—which has as its object only those meanings presented by the individual powers of the constituent words—is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the presentation of the meaning occurs first; thus, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the intention (*tātparya*) of the word *niṣādasthapati* is understood to reside in that very [first] meaning, and thereby a specific understanding is attained. It does not, however, reside in that which is presented by the apprehension of the power pertaining to the multiple word-meanings [of the members], because the presentation of that [latter] is dependent upon the former. This is the sense of the passage.

This is also an authority for the view that the author of the *Mūla* intended "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) to mean precisely the dependence on etymological derivation (*nirukta-vyapekṣā*). Otherwise, since words would be devoid of meaning under the theory of "abandoning their own meanings" (*jahat-svārtha-vṛtti*), the presentation of the apprehension of power (*śakti-graha*) based upon them would be impossible due to the impossibility of the presentation of meaning through the function of individual words; thus, the statement regarding its "internal nature" (*antaraṅgatva*) would be entirely inconsistent—this is how it should be understood. That is the intended sense. It is "postulated"—that is, determined or ascertained.

Now, one might object: "By the statement beginning with 'Conjunction and disjunction,' etc., Hari teaches that conjunction and the rest are causes for the comprehension of specific [meanings]; how then can intention (*tātparya*) be the cause for the comprehension of a specific qualifier? If this is asked, the answer is no. For, when several meanings have been presented by multiple word-powers (*śakti*), and only one among them is determined through conjunction and so forth, there is the comprehension of a specific intention; thus, as will be explained later, there is no lack of delimitation regarding the meaning of the word.

The point is that since conjunction and the rest are useful precisely in their capacity as indicators of intention, it is universally accepted that intention is the cause for the comprehension of a specific [meaning].

[Objection: "But surely, if the view that the word-meanings reside in each individual word is accepted, the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the conclusion established by the context) follows without effort; whereas in the view that there is a single power for the qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), the difficulty in establishing such a conclusion is indeed unavoidable. To this, he says: "Even for others... The meaning is as follows: since intention (*tātparya*) alone is the regulator of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), when that [intention] exists, the understanding of a different compound through the *lakṣaṇā* of the sentence would be unavoidable; therefore, the apprehension of that [different meaning] must be prevented precisely by the absence of intention.

Now, in the case of the injunction "one should cause the Niṣādasthapati to sacrifice," the word *sthapati* is either a synonym for "master" (*svāmin*) or a synonym for "foremost" (*śreṣṭha*). In either case, it is a term expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). If this were compounded with the word *niṣāda*, which denotes a caste (*jāti*), in a *karmadhāraya* compound, then by the rule that a quality-qualifier must necessarily be placed first, the form would result as *sthapatiniṣādam*, and not *niṣādasthapatim*.

Furthermore, since the meaning of the word *sthapati* (architect/chief) necessarily depends on a correlate in both ways, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) alone is appropriate, and not a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*). How, then, does the stated conclusion apply to the present case as well? To this he says: "The direction [is indicated]. For that very reason, out of dissatisfaction with that [previous argument], the Great Sage composed the sūtra "And because of the observation of indicative marks" (*liṅgadarśanācca*) as a summary of further supporting reasons.

And this has been explained by Śabarasvāmin in the Bhāṣya: "For the trap (kūṭa) is beneficial only to the Niṣādas, not to the Āryas; and thus it is the property of the Niṣādas alone. Thus, since the compound is determined to be a *karmadhāraya* based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) being the trap, one should understand that the word *sthapati* is placed last according to the rule beginning with *rājadanta*. Furthermore, the cessation of the expectancy for a relation is justified because, by implication, the Niṣādas obtain ownership [of the trap].
In this way, the consideration of parsimony (*lāghava*) and so forth is merely a possibility in some sense; thus, everything is faultless.

Thus ends the determination of the power of compounds (*samāsa-śakti-nirūpaṇa*) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. Regarding the phrase "by way of occasion" (*prasaṅgāt*): the sense is that since the power (*śakti*) mentioned in the statement "In a compound, indeed, there is a distinct power," it is not to be neglected. For, since neither the presentation of the word-meaning nor verbal cognition is observed from a word whose relation (*vṛtti*) has not been grasped, the knowledge of a word as having for its object a relation defined by a specific property is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for a verbal cognition whose object is defined by that same property. The operation (*vyāpāra*) is the presentation of the word-meaning produced by the word through that relation, because without that [operation], the [cognition] does not arise; however—

A word (*pada*) is that which possesses a function (*vṛtti*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) could not arise because of the lack of connection with past or future words.

And this function is of two kinds, distinguished as *śakti* (primary denotation) and *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication). Among these, *śakti* is the conventional association of a word with its meaning. This consists of a divine will (*īśvarecchā*) having the word as its qualificandum, in the form: "Let this word denote this meaning"; or alternatively, it takes the form of a divine will having the word-meaning as its qualificandum, in the form: "This meaning is to be understood from this word," since there is no reason for preferring one over the other. By means of that [function], a word that denotes an object is conventionally designated as "pācaka" (cook). A convention established by the authors of technical treatises and others is called *paribhāṣā* (technical rule/metarule).

By this [definition], a word that conveys a meaning is designated as "conventional" (*pāribhāṣika*), such as the words *nadī* (river), *vṛddhi*, and so forth. Indication (*lakṣaṇā*), however, is a relation with the primary sense (*śakya*). And the basis for its postulation is the incompatibility of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), which is inferred from the sublation of the primary sense.

To explain: in the case of the expression "There is a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," since the word *gaṅgā* denotes the absence of a hamlet, its intention (*tātparya*) is inferred to be directed toward the bank. Since this verbal cognition of the bank—which is otherwise inexplicable without the recollection of the bank as the object of that intention—implies such a recollection, and since that recollection is itself inexplicable without a relation (*vṛtti*) belonging to the word *gaṅgā*, it implies the knowledge of such a relation. The relation denoted by the word *gaṅgā* in this context is not *śakti* (primary denotative power), because that [power] is absent here; therefore, some other relation, which serves as the cause of the recollection of the bank, is postulated.

And that [relation] consists precisely in being proximate to what is denoted by the word *gaṅgā*; when apprehended in that form, it causes the bank to be remembered and brings it to experience. However, the presence of the non-denotable through the denotable is not *lakṣaṇā*, because its nature as a cause of such presence is impossible. Nor is it a relation with that which is cognized by itself, according to the reasoning stated in the analysis of the power (*śakti*) of compounds. Now, one might object: "The will of God cannot be the denotative power (*śakti*), for it would follow that even the word 'jar' would possess power over a cloth, since the will—'the cloth is to be understood from the word 'jar'’—exists in the cloth as well by virtue of being its object."

If it is argued that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to the word "cloth" (paṭa), because *śakti* is defined as the state of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatva) as determined by a mode (prakāratā) consisting in being the object of a cognition produced by the word "jar" through the will of God, since—even though [the cloth] is an object of such a cognition—the state of being the qualificandum as determined by a mode residing in jar-ness is not admitted in that case; even so, since a cognition of the bank (*tīra*) also arises from the word "Gaṅgā," the state of being the qualificandum as determined by a mode consisting in being the object of a cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā" through the will of God—which has existence-in-general (*sanmātra*) as its object—subsists in the bank.

If it is argued that since the purpose is accomplished by primary denotation (*śakti*) alone, secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is redundant—this is not so. Because the conventional usage of the word *gaṅgā* as a denotative term does not apply to the bank and so forth, the primary denotation (*śakti*) of words such as *gaṅgā* resides in the current and so forth, by way of the relation of being the qualificandum (the "locatedness") determined by a modehood delimited by the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*. Furthermore, although the qualificandumhood residing in the bank and so forth is indeed determined by the modehood of being the object of a cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*, that [qualificandumhood] is not [determined] as that specific state of being an object (*tādṛśaviṣayatātvena*).

Since it is accepted that [the relation] is determined by a mode of objectivity (*viṣayatā*) as such, rather than by pure objectivity (*śuddhaviṣayatātva*) alone, there is no over-extension (*anyathāsiddhi*) of the definition by means of that [pure objectivity]. Nor is there an over-extension in the case of the word [itself], even though the relation characterized as objectivity exists both in the word and in the producer-produced relationship (*janyajanakabhāva*).

In this context, the relationship consisting of similarity (*sādṛśya*) which determines the presentation of the indicated object (*lakṣya*) is termed *gauṇī* (secondary indication); that which is distinct from it is termed *śuddhā lakṣaṇā* (pure indication). Pure indication is also twofold, distinguished as *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* (indicative inclusion) and [the other]. Among these, *upādānatva* (the state of being an inclusive indicator) is the capacity to present an object while remaining connected with the primary meaning (*mukhya*). *Lakṣaṇatva* (the state of being a pure indicator) is the capacity to generate the presentation of an indicated object that does not have the primary meaning as its domain. Examples of these are, respectively, "Enter with the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*) and "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).

Regarding this, the Naiyāyikas say that the first [type of indication] is called *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning its own meaning), while the last is called *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning); however, their other subdivisions should be understood from other sources. The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that although the aforementioned reasoning excludes the denotative function (*vācakatva*) of a word used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*), the will of God cannot be considered the primary power (*śakti*), because God himself is not accepted [by them]. Now, it might be argued that being "God's" is not a necessary requirement for a will; thus, since verbal cognition arises even from the knowledge of a modern convention, such a convention would be established as a linguistic function (*vṛtti*).

Nor does it follow that intention (*tātparya*) would also be a *vṛtti* (linguistic function) simply because it is a modern convention; for only a convention that necessitates the presentation of a word-meaning is considered a *vṛtti*, whereas intention is not such. This is because the cognition of intention produces verbal comprehension directly, without depending on an intermediate operation consisting of the presentation of the word-meaning; furthermore, it is only the meaning presented by a *vṛtti* that is determined as the intended sense through context and other factors.

However, in the case of words such as "Dittha" which are based on modern convention (*ādhunika-saṅketa*), since the previously determined modern convention acts as the regulator for the mental presentation of the word-meaning that generates the verbal cognition of the individual "Dittha" and so forth, its subsistence [in the word] does not bring about the presentation of the word-meaning; thus, its status as a *vṛtti* (relation) cannot be established. Therefore, they say that the relation which regulates the denotative-denoted relationship (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*) between a word and its meaning is indeed a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*). Nor is this relation inherent (*samaveta*), because it exists even in the case of absences (*abhāva*) and the like;
rather, it exists by means of another relation called "qualificative inherence" (*vaiśiṣṭya*). This is what they maintain.

The author of the *Dīdhiti* also followed that very view when he stated, "We shall explain how expressibility (*vācyatva*) does not possess inherence. With the intention of first demonstrating the nature of those various opinions in order to refute them, he introduces the root text with the words, "Its nature" (*tasyāḥ svarūpam*), meaning the nature of that capacity (*śakti*). He asks, "How can a jar or the like be the object of those [cognitions] which are devoid of objects? To this he replies, "Visual," and so forth; the sense is that there is no contradiction in their having a figurative (*aupacārika*) objecthood.

The term "visual" (*cākṣuṣa*) is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for sensory perception in general, such as auditory perception and so forth. Regarding the causality residing in the sense organ, its "beginninglessness" (*anāditva*) consists in its existing at the time of the destruction of each preceding cognition produced by the sense organ. Its "pervasion of [the properties] such as being visual" (*cakṣuṣṭvādivyāpakatva*) or its "independence from human effort" (*puruṣaprayatnānapekṣatva*) is intended, but not its "unproducedness" (*ajanyatva*), because that would fail to distinguish it [from other causes]. Regarding the causality of making known residing in the word, however, it consists in possessing the destruction of a preceding cognition of the same form as the cognition produced by itself. The "causality of making known" (*tadbodhakāraṇatā*) is the state of making the object known.

This [definition] is intended with reference to the word (*pada*) as it is being known as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Otherwise, the meaning should be understood as: the state of being the delimitor of such causality (*hetutā*) resides in the objectness (*viṣayatā*). One might raise the following objection: "Since the apprehension of the aforementioned capacity (*śakti*) is impossible without the knowledge of convention (*saṅketa*), and since that [convention] must necessarily be required, let convention itself be the capacity, according to the maxim 'that which is the cause of that [is itself that]'"; thus he objects with "But surely... (*nanu*). The reason for its being the capacity is stated as "modern," etc. "Modern" means qualified by a convention belonging to this present time.

The meaning is: "due to its absence"—that is, due to the absence of being a cause that conveys [the self] as qualified by the aforementioned attribute of beginninglessness.
