Even though the substantive (the self) exists, because the qualified entity is absent due to the absence of its qualifier in the present case, it is impossible for it to possess causality in the form of not being the counter-positive of that [qualified absence].

[Objection: "The phrase 'being beginningless' (anādibhūta) serves merely to demonstrate its well-known status; it has not entered into the body of its causal capacity such that its causality could be conceived in that form. Rather, in this context, its causality exists only as the cause of cognition [of meaning], and there is no sublation regarding its knowledge in that form. [Response: This would indeed be so if its apprehension occurred independently of the grasping of convention (saṅketa); however, that is not possible. Thus he says, "Otherwise" (anyathā), which means: if that [word] were the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) while being entirely independent of convention.

The meaning is that even in that case [of a word denoting a specific individual], there exists the capacity to produce cognition, despite its being beginningless. "Because it must be expected" (*āvaśyakatvāt*) means because it is the object of a cognition that must necessarily be relied upon. "That very thing" (*sa eva*) refers to the convention (*saṅketa*) itself. By the restrictive particle *eva*, the exclusion of the capacity to convey meaning [as an independent factor] is intended. He refutes the alternative options—whether the convention is a cause by its own nature or as something known, and whether that [known convention] is a cause in a general or a specific form—in the words "It is said" (*ucyate*).

"By its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*) means by its own specific property (*svāsādhāraṇadharma*), according to the etymology "that which is its own form"; that is to say, as the convention itself. The meaning is that the convention, as the cause, exists precisely as the object of cognition—just as a staff exists in a jar by way of being a "staff-ness. "From one whose power has not been grasped" means from one whose convention is unknown. "Because of the consequence of the cognition of the meaning" implies that the convention is present there [in the word].

"In a general sense" means in a form common to both that which produces [the cognition] and that which does not. "As a convention" means by way of specific properties such as being a convention of God. "Of those ignorant of that [convention]" means of those who do not know that the convention belongs to God. Regarding the phrase "of worldly Mīmāṃsakas," it is stated "worldly" because for Vedic [Mīmāṃsakas], some understanding of God is possible in some way.

Alternatively, it means "of the worldly"—that is, of the common folk (*pāmara*) who possess knowledge whose object is merely conventional things—and of the Mīmāṃsakas. "By the arising of cognition" means by the arising of the cognition of objects such as cows from the mere knowledge of that [word] as a convention (*saṅketa*).

Although, according to the view that the convention is the cause of the knowledge of the convention, the property of "belonging to God" (īśvarīyatva) and so forth is not included [in the definition], nevertheless, upon examining that author's own work, the inclusion of "belonging to God" and so forth is intended [by him] regarding cows and the like; bearing this in mind, the critique was offered. One should understand that the particle *eva* in the phrase "only for those who possess the apprehension of the production of the cognition of that object" excludes those who possess the aforementioned knowledge of the convention. And that [exclusion] is merely a restatement of the phrase "and for those devoid of that knowledge. Furthermore, the reading *eva-śūnya* is easy to understand.

And this [verse] demonstrates the cause, which consists in the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śakti*). That knowledge—namely, the knowledge of the convention (*saṅketa*)—is likewise the cause. The point is that since a word denoted by a convention is precisely what generates the cognition of the meaning, the convention serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the generative capacity residing in the word.

The meaning is as follows: by taking the causality [of the word] to reside in its being the generator of the cognition of the object (*arthadhījanakatā*), rather than in the property of being a delimitor (*avacchedakatva*) delimited by the relation of objectness (*viṣayatā*) as determined by that same generation of the cognition of the object, the position desired by the Grammarians is established. This is because, if the cognition of the convention—having the form "this word is a delimitor of the generation of the cognition of the object"—were taken as the cause by virtue of being a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is delimited by the state of being a delimitor of the generation of the cognition of the object, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); therefore, it is simpler to hold that "this word generates the cognition of the object."

The intended meaning is that it is appropriate for knowledge itself to be the cause [of recollection] by virtue of being a knowledge whose qualifier is delimited by the property of being a generator of the cognition of an object, because of parsimony (*lāghava*).

In reality, however, it should be understood that according to his [the opponent's] view, the cause is simply the convention (*saṅketa*) itself; thus, there is no occasion for the aforementioned alternatives. By the phrase "from the knowledge of the convention alone," the apprehension of its being a generator of the cognition of the object is excluded. "Of this"—that is, of the apprehension of its being a communicator—"there is deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). "Even there" means even in a case where the cognition of the object arises from the convention alone. "Apprehension of the desire" means the apprehension of a desire whose qualificandum is this word and whose qualifier is the property of being a communicator of this particular meaning. "By way of immersion" (*avagāhanena*) means by way of making it an object of awareness.

The sense is that there is a rule that a cognition whose object is [another] cognition—such as one concerning knowledge, desire, and so forth—must necessarily have that [object] as its own object. Regarding the term "svātantrye" (in independence), the meaning is "by way of not being qualified by anything else. And in the present context, the sense is that by that cognition, it is precisely the self which is the indicator, acting as a qualifier through the relation of subjectivity (*viṣayitā*) within the aspect of desire, that is made its object.

The phrase "otherwise" (anyathā) means that even through dependence on another, the cognition of the expressive capacity (*bodakatā*) is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdadhī*). To rule out the objection that this is merely an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "This [cognition] does not produce that [verbal] cognition. The phrase "from this word" (*asmācchabdāt*) means: for one who possesses a present apprehension in the form, "this object is the referent of a cognition produced by this word and directed toward this [object]."

The point is this: when there exists a cognition grasping that a word is a generator of a cognition whose object is a specific meaning (padaviśeṣyakārthadhījanakatvabodha), it is impossible for there to simultaneously exist a cognition of the form "this word is known by this person as a generator of a cognition of such-and-such a meaning," because such a cognition would involve the very same aspect—the generation of a cognition of meaning—which is already being grasped. Therefore, setting that aside, the cognition-grasping is stated in the form "from this [word]. However, in this case, the former cognition does not act as an obstacle, because it does not involve the absence of the object to be grasped (grāhyabhāva).

The phrase "due to the apprehension of that" means "due to the apprehension of verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding [objects] such as a jar. Even though the aforementioned cognition has the [object] as its content, it does not apprehend the capacity of the word-part to convey meaning, by virtue of which that [cognition] could constitute the apprehension of the word's expressive power (śaktigraha).

However, it is difficult to maintain that the fact of being produced by that word (tatpadajanyatva) resides in the object-component as nothing other than being the object of such a cognition; for by that, one would have to claim that the capacity of the word to convey the meaning is also apprehended in the word-component through "being cognized by the same cognition" (tulyavittivedyatā). This is untenable because there is no evidence for such simultaneous cognition, and because the counteracting cognition—which apprehends the absence of the apprehendable [object]—is fully present in the form: "this [word] is not the producer of the cognition of that [meaning]."

Nor can it be argued that, due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*), the state of being the object of a cognition produced by a word residing in its meaning (*arthaniṣṭha-padajanya-bodha-viṣayatva*) is also [the denotative] power (*śakti*), just as the capacity to produce a cognition of the meaning residing in the word (*padaniṣṭhārtha-dhī-janakatva*) is; for the fact that verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) arises from both types of knowledge is established by the experience of all people, and because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a verbal comprehension produced by one or the other when "immediately subsequentness" (*avyavahitottaratva*) is included in the definition of the effect-limiting property (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, if this were so, it would be easy to show that a verbal comprehension could arise from that [second apprehension of power] which consists in the second apprehension of power; for if that were the case, one could not say, "This [second apprehension] does not produce a cognition of the meaning."

The presentation of a cognition that does not apprehend the absence of the object of apprehension (grāhya) as being non-obstructive is useless. Even if it were granted that such a presentation is purposeful by accepting—on the basis of positive and negative concomitance—that both types of power constitute an obstruction despite not apprehending the absence of the object, the intended cognition would still be impossible; with this intention, he refutes [the opponent] by stating: "This is not the generator of that cognition. The meaning is that it is possible to have a cognition produced by a word whose object is a specific thing, which takes as its content the fact that [the word] is the object of such a cognition.

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: even when a sublation (*bādhagraha*) has occurred, there arises the apprehension "silver was cognized by this [cognition]," which consists in being an apprehension that has "this" (*idam*) as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and "silver" (*rajata*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*). By the phrase "of the knower of the error" (*bhrantijñasya*), the absence of defects (*doṣābhāvavattva*) is also indicated, because otherwise the status of being erroneous would follow; the point is that only one who possesses a cognition that apprehends something in what is not that thing is [erroneous].

In this regard, the following must be considered: in cases where verbal cognition arises from the mere knowledge of a convention—namely, "let this word convey this meaning"—the deviation (vyabhicāra) is unavoidable for those who maintain that the knowledge of the denotative power (*bodhakatā-śakti*) is the cause [of verbal cognition]. Nor should it be argued that in such cases the knowledge of the convention itself is the knowledge of the denotative power; for even though a cognition possessing an object has that object as its content, the qualifier (*prakāra*) of that [object] is not made an object by that [cognition] in respect to its own substantive (*viśeṣya*).

This is because, by the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I know the jar," there is the apprehension of only the state of having "jar-ness" as the qualifier (*prakāraka*) and "the jar" as the qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*) within the portion consisting of the cognition itself; otherwise, the unavoidable consequence would be that one who knows an error would themselves become erroneous.

For this very reason, although in the *Śabdacintāmaṇi* the fact that [utterance] is preceded by a cognition of the relation between the objects intended by the words is established through an inference where the words themselves are the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no establishment of the intended relation between the object of one word and the object of another word; because such an inference regarding being preceded by a cognition of a relation does not take as its object the relation between the object of that word and the object intended by the other word. It is for this lack of satisfaction (*asvarasa*) that Pabhadharamiśra introduced the inference where the word-meanings are the subject (*pakṣa*).

He states what apprehends the expressive power (*śakti*): "And this" means that which is accepted as expressive power, namely, the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*). By the phrase "father and so forth," the inclusion of a reliable person (*āpta*) is intended. The point is that because independence (*svātantrya*) is included within the scope of the delimiting condition for being an effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the cognition of the capacity to convey meaning—which consists of the knowledge of the convention—when that cognition is not produced by the knowledge of the convention itself (as it would otherwise be). He dispels the previously mentioned undesirable consequence of the elimination of metaphorical usage (*lākṣaṇika*) by treating it as acceptable: "Nor even...

The phrase "apprehending the expressive power" means that since the usage of words to apprehend the expressive power of the primary meaning is equally applicable to the metaphorical object (*lakṣya*) as well.

[Objection: Surely, because the linguistic usage of a "denotable" (*lakṣya*) would otherwise be untenable, that [word] must be denotative of what is excluded from the denotable. And thus, since the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is necessary for the presentation of the denotable, how can the aforementioned consequence be accepted? To this, he says: "Furthermore... [The phrase] "because it is not a factor in verbal cognition" means that since there is no verbal cognition of a jar or the like—presented through perception and other means—by a word such as "jar" for one who has not grasped its denotative power (*śakti*), there is a deviation in positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*); therefore, presentation through perception and other means is not a factor in verbal cognition.

Indeed, one might argue that such a degree of respect [for the rule] must be maintained due to necessity; therefore, he says "moreover" (*api ca*). The term "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) should be understood as referring to the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). He establishes this very point by stating "the apprehension produced by the word-potency" (*śaktijanyopasthitim*). Regarding the phrase "immediately preceding" (*avyavahitottaratva*), it consists in: (1) not being produced in a moment that is the locus of its own destruction, while (2) being produced in a moment that is the locus of the destruction of its own locus. Here, the word "its own" (*sva*) refers to the apprehension produced by the knowledge of the word-potency.

The qualificandum [in the definition] is for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by an object-presentation (*padārthopasthiti*) generated by a knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which itself is preceded by an object-presentation generated by a knowledge of *śakti* (denotative power). The "existence" (*sat*) clause is for the purpose of avoiding deviation in the case of a verbal cognition produced by an object-presentation generated by a knowledge of *lakṣaṇā*, which occurs immediately after a verbal cognition produced by *śakti*. The point is that in the present case—namely, a verbal cognition produced by an object-presentation generated by a knowledge of *lakṣaṇā*—there is no absence of the qualification of the object-presentation generated by the knowledge of *śakti* through the aforementioned relation; therefore, it does not fall under the scope of the defining property of that effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), and thus there is no deviation.

The meaning is as follows: since "infinity" (*anantatā*) refers to the non-universality of ownership due to its being restricted to each specific individual (*tattad-vyakti*), if one were to include "the state of having a presence through the relation of 'immediately following' as constituted by that [ownership]" within the scope of the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryyatāvacchedaka-koṭi*), there would be an infinity of causal relations (*kāryyakāraṇabhāva*). This is the intended sense.

He says "moreover" (*kiñca*) because the same logic applies: as before, there is a mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the status of these two as causes for the presentation of the word-meaning, since the meaning is presented even without knowledge of the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) due to knowledge of the primary power (*śakti*), and likewise, it is presented even without knowledge of the primary power due to knowledge of the secondary function. Furthermore, if one were to include the qualification of those respective causes by means of the relation of "immediately preceding" (*avyavahitottaratva*) within the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatā'vacchedaka*), there would be the same complexity (*gaurava*) as in that previous case; such is the meaning.

One might object: "Even for one who maintains that words possess a power to convey meaning (*bodhakatvaśaktivādin*), it is necessary to include each respective object within the definition of the causal determinant (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) in order to prevent the unwanted consequence of both the presentation of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārthopasthiti*) and the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arising from the apprehension of the power in the word 'Gaṅgā' as being a conveyor of the river-current. Thus, where is the complexity (*gaurava*) in the theory of indication (*lakṣaṇāvāda*)? Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And not" (*na ca*). The phrase "mutually" (*paraspara*) means that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and an obstruction [to the rule] regarding the cognition produced by each of them; for even without the apprehension of the power residing in the word 'Gaṅgā' to convey the bank, the cognition of the bank occurs through the apprehension of such a power residing in the word 'bank' (*tīra*) itself. Therefore, the two do not stand in a relationship of mutual necessity.

The meaning is as follows: "In accordance with the error regarding the primary power" means that since, in the state of an error regarding the primary power (*śakti-bhrama*) of the word *gaṅgā* [as referring to the bank], the presentation of the bank (*tīropasthiti*) and so forth are established in all philosophical systems, even for you it is necessary to include those respective words and their respective meanings within the scope of the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the causal conditions (*kāraṇatā*) for each instance.

The phrase "of yours" (tava) means "of one who accepts [the theory of] indication" (lakṣaṇā). One might object: "In the causal status of the knowledge of *śakti*, if *śakti* were introduced as *śakti*-ness (*śaktitva*), the aforementioned fault would indeed arise; however, since it is introduced as *vṛtti*-ness (*vṛttitva*), that possibility does not exist. To this, he raises the following doubt: "Now [atha]," etc. The sense is that it must be stated [that the fault remains], because even in the case of an apprehension produced by indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as in the case of an apprehension produced by *śakti*, there exists a state of being produced as delimited by *vṛtti*-ness, which is common to both *śakti* and *lakṣaṇā*.

"Characterized by power" (*śaktilakṣaṇā*) means that which is different from power (*śakti*) while being non-different from indication (*lakṣaṇā*); the meaning is [the state of being different from] that. "Verbal cognition" (*śābdabodha*) means conducive to that presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) which generates verbal cognition—that is, the presentation [of meanings] arising from the knowledge of the word's function (*padavṛtti*). Regarding the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatā'vacchedakatva*), he states a defect common to both [definitions]: "Because it is cumbersome" (*guruvāt*). This means that the aforementioned "either-or" nature (*anyataratva*) and so forth are more cumbersome than the "power-ness" (*śaktitva*) favored by us. He states another defect regarding the second [definition]: "The cause of verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhahetu*).

The meaning is that since the suitability for verbal cognition (śābdabodha) or its production depends upon the apprehension of the delimiting condition of causality (kāraṇatā'vacchedaka), and since that [condition] consists in the apprehension of the word-meaning through the knowledge of the word’s function (padavṛtti), such knowledge is impossible without knowing the subsistence [of the function] within its own constituents; thus, the very apprehension of the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is difficult to establish.

The point is this: if the apprehension of *vṛttitva* (the status of being a linguistic function) depends on the apprehension of the causal relation between verbal cognition and the presentation of word-meanings, and the apprehension of that *vṛttitva*—defined as the nature of the relationship between the aforementioned word and its meaning—depends on the apprehension of *vṛttitva*, then there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Consequently, the aforementioned *vṛttitva* is impossible.

In reality, however, *śakti* (denotative power) is the relationship between a word and its object that generates the presentation of a dissimilar (*vijātīya*) object. Because of the inclusion of this "dissimilarity," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to relations such as inherence (*samavāya*), which generate the presentation of space (*ākāśa*). And the indicator of such dissimilarity is the phrase "conducive to verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhānukūla*). The meaning is, however, that since even the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) functions as a cause precisely by being a knowledge of *śakti*, there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the causality of the knowledge of *śakti* in cases such as the presentation of the indicated object (*lakṣyārtha*) produced by the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā*.

If the causal relationship between the cognition of word-potency (*śaktijñāna*) and the mental presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) were possible without introducing the object (*viṣaya*) [into the relation], then the aforementioned method might indeed be valid; however, that very possibility does not exist. Thus he says: "The cognition of potency... [and so on]. The meaning is: because it is necessary, for one must necessarily postulate that the status of being a cause belongs to the cognition of potency residing in a particular word as determined by a specific meaning, with respect to the mental presentation of that same meaning.

He states the very necessity [of this condition] with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*); the meaning is: if, in the causal relation between the knowledge of word-potency (*śakti*) and the mental presentation of the object (*padārthopasthiti*), the requirement of having the same object (*samānaviṣayatva*) is not introduced. By the expression "one who does not grasp the relation," the absence of the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is indicated. "In the case of the word *gaṅgā*" means: for one who knows the potency of the word *gaṅgā* to convey an object in the form of a flowing stream. "The consequence of the cognition of the bank" (*tīrabodhaprasaṅga*) means: the undesirable contingency of the mental presentation of the bank and, through that, of the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) thereof.

Now, one might object: "In order to avoid the aforementioned undesirable consequence, let it be that the relation of cause and effect is established only between the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*) and the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), with the requirement of having the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*) being inserted therein; what is the use of inserting that requirement into the relation of cause and effect between the knowledge of the linguistic function and the mental presence of the word-meaning? To this, he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*). In order to ensure that the recollection of the elephant-driver is produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function, it is shown that the elephant itself is also an object of recollection from the sentence. In the term *samūhālambana*, the word *ālambana* refers to the object (*viṣaya*).

"Representation produced by a function" (vṛttijanyopasthitiḥ) means a representation delimited by a property that constitutes the effectness (kāryyatā) as determined by a causality residing in the knowledge of the function, which is itself delimited by having that [object] as its content. In the aforementioned instance, although the representation of the mahout is produced by the knowledge of the function, the resulting production-ness (janyatā) residing therein is not delimited by the state of having the mahout as its object.

Nor is the elephant the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) in terms of being the object (*viṣaya*) for the generative capacity residing in the cognition of the mental mode (*vṛttijñāna*), because it does not appear as the substantive (*dharmin*) within that cognition of the mental mode; thus, the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) does not arise—this is the sense. He states the point relevant to the present context: "And so" (*evaṃ ca*). The sense is that the relationship of cause and effect results from the fact that the cognition of the mental mode, the presentation (*upasthiti*), and the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) possess the same object. The phrase "impossible to assert" (*asambhavaduktika*) means that even though the cognition of the secondary function (*lakṣaṇājñāna*) has the primary power (*śakti*) as its object, it lacks the nature of being a grasp of the primary power whose object is the riverbank—this is the sense.

"By this" means either by the impossibility of the two-fold knowledge of function (*vṛtti*) being a cause in a single form, or by the fault that will be stated hereafter. "Impossible to assert" means that since the knowledge of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is dependent upon the knowledge of primary denotation (*śakti*), when the [indicated] meaning arises produced by that [knowledge of denotation], it is already governed by the primary denotation; therefore, in the view of those who maintain indication, there is no need to postulate another cause. "[Because it is] not over-extensive" means...

Since the property of being produced by [the word] exists not only in the case of an apprehension produced by the knowledge of indication (*lakṣaṇājñāna*)—just as in the case of an apprehension consisting of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that grasps a qualified relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*), such as "the place has the pot-word's denotatum" (which arises in the form of a certainty whose qualifier is the delimitor of the qualifier)—there would be the unwanted consequence (*āpatti*) that even the object of that [apprehension] would be included in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, there would be a failure to include an apprehension that is directly produced [by the word]. If, however, direct production were taken as the defining criterion, then there would be a failure to include an apprehension produced by the knowledge of indication.

The point is that since such a [relation] common to both is impossible to define—given that its nature as an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) is non-uniform (*ananugata*), making its commonality to both even more unlikely—some maintain that "being prompted by a power" (*śaktiprayojyatva*), defined as possessing a property that delimits the state of occurring immediately after the cognition of a power which is not delimited by the delimiting factor of the locus of non-establishment (*anyathāsiddhi-nirūpakatānavacchedaka-śakti-jñāna*), can be easily stated as being common to both. More will be said on this later.

On this point, they say: the discussion regarding the complexity (gaurava) or simplicity (lāghava) of the aforementioned causal relationship is possible only on the assumption that the capacity to produce verbal comprehension—which actually resides in the word—is indeed the power that regulates the linguistic convention of the signified and the signifier; however, it is not possible for that [capacity] to be identical in nature to that [power]. For instance, it is beyond dispute that the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (the denotative relation) is the cause with respect to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

Furthermore, that [definition] is not possible if the property of being the generator of the cognition of the meaning stated by you is considered the occurrence (vṛtti), because such a form of it—namely, the capacity to generate a verbal cognition residing in knowledge—is not a delimiting factor (anavacchedaka) of that very capacity. This is because it is impossible for something to be its own delimiting factor due to the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya).

Furthermore, when the cognition of the instigator’s action—such as the fetching of a jar—is inferred from the behavior of the person being instigated by an observer who perceives the relationship between the instigator and the instigated, and when it is determined that the cause of this cognition is exclusively verbal (śābda) because of the presence [of words], it is impossible for the relation postulated [to account for this] to consist in its being a generator (*janakatva*), since it is impossible for something unrelated to function as a cause; for that which is apprehended as being itself untenable cannot be grasped [as a causal factor]. Therefore, "the capacity to convey meaning" (*bodhakatva*) is not *śakti*.

Thus, according to the Nyāya school, even the state of being the object of a divine will—expressed as "let there arise from this word a cognition having this particular chariot as its qualificandum"—is not the primary denotative power (*śakti*). This is because such a state ultimately results in a *delimitingness* (*avacchedakatva*) delimited by the relation of subsistence (*ādheyatā*), which resides in the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatva*) that is itself defined by an objective reference (*uddeśyatā*) delimited by the nature of being a cognition produced by the word 'Gaṅgā' as determined by the mode (*prakāratā*) of being produced by the conventional word 'Gaṅgā'. Otherwise, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the abolition of the concept of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, because there is also the possibility of a desire on the part of the speaker (the Bhāgavata) such as "May there arise from the word *gaṅgā* a cognition having the riverbank as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*)"—since the aforementioned delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) belonging to such a desire is possible even for the riverbank as the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*)—and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate that the knowledge of the primary power (*śakti*) is a cause for verbal cognition by way of being such a delimitation.

Even though the delimitingness (avacchedakatā) residing in the bank and so forth—which terminates [the relation]—is itself delimited by the delimitingness residing in the qualificandum as previously stated, it is not delimited by that [delimitingness] in its capacity as a "delimitingness residing in the qualificandum" (viśeṣyavṛttyavacchedakatātvena); rather, it is delimited merely by pure delimitingness (śuddhāvacchedakatāmātreṇa). Therefore, the claim that such a power (śakti) does not reside in the bank is nothing but a deception of students. Furthermore, there is no decisive reason (vinigamanāviraha) to maintain that power is either the state of being an object of desire or the state of being an object of cognition; this will be explained further below.
Consequently, the relation that governs the conventional usage of the "signified-signifier" (vācyavācakabhāva) between word and meaning is indeed a distinct category of entity (padārthāntara).

Furthermore, since that [meaning] which is excluded from the indicated (lakṣya) is established by the cognition grasping the subject (dharmin), it is necessary to accept even the exclusion of the secondary indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the sake of understanding the indicated meaning. As for the complexity resulting from postulating an additional causal factor for the knowledge of that [exclusion] in verbal comprehension, it does not constitute a fault because it is "aimed at the result" (phalamukha), as otherwise [the theory] would be untenable. For this very reason, the conventional distinction between the primary power (śakya) and the indicated (lakṣya) is naturally consistent.

Alternatively, the capacity to produce verbal cognition belongs to both the knowledge of word-potency (*śakti*) and the knowledge of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) individually. To explain: with respect to that verbal cognition, the causal status [of the knowledge] consists in being a cognition whose qualificandum is that object and whose qualifier resides in the word, as determined by a relational objectivity delimited by the nature of potency (*śaktitva*). This is because, in a cognition where the word is the qualifier—whether through the relation of potency or through the relation of the indicated (*śakya*)—potency functions as the relation (*saṃsarga*).

Since pervasion (*paryāpti*) is not introduced into the delimitorhood residing in the power (*śakti*), even a cognition whose qualifier is a relation capable [of being denoted] is encompassed by that [definition]. However, because it is not accepted that the relational objectivity (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*)—which is determined by the qualifierhood residing in the word—is itself determined by the objective predication (*viśeṣyatā*) of the meaning, the knowledge of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) does not possess the property of being an inhibitor of a cognition whose qualifier is the absence of the word through the relation of power (*śakti*).

The meaning of the verse beginning with "indriyāṇām" is as follows: Just as the sense organs possess a fitness (*yogyatā*)—which is a property delimiting their causality for visual and other perceptions regarding objects such as jars, independent of human effort—likewise, the relation between words and their referents is also a fitness, which is a property delimiting the generation of that verbal cognition; it is not, however, the state of being a generator itself, according to the reasoning already stated. Thus, there is no contradiction therein, and everything is faultless.
And the means of apprehending this [fitness] are the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) and so forth. As it has been said:

The elders declare that the apprehension of the expressive power (śakti) of a word occurs through grammar, analogy, lexicons, the statements of authoritative persons, linguistic usage, the remainder of a sentence, verbal commentary, and the proximity of a known word. Thus it is said.

In this regard, the view of the Naiyāyikas is that [the meaning of] a grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth can only convey the expressive power (*śakti*) when assisted by parsimony (*lāghava*). For, by the rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) assisted by parsimony, the expressive power is determined to reside only in the action (*kriyā*), and not in the agent (*kartṛ*); thus it has been stated. Furthermore, by the lexicon entry "guṇe śuklādayaḥ" (words like *śukla* denote qualities), the expressive power is determined to reside only in the quality (*guṇa*)—assisted by parsimony—and not in the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), due to the complexity (*gaurava*) [of the latter]. Moreover, as for the cognition of the possessor of the quality from words such as *śukla*, it is stated that this occurs only through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*). And the nature of "conventional" (*nirūḍha*) has already been explained previously.

As for analogy (*upamāna*), which consists of the cognition of similarity, its function is to determine the denotative power (*śakti*)—namely, that "the gavaya and so forth are denoted by the word 'gavaya' and so forth"—by means of the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*). Furthermore, this [power] is grasped from the authoritative statement (*āptavākya*) in the form "this is the denoter of that. Authoritativeness (*āptatva*) consists in possessing a true cognition regarding the person and the subject matter of that [statement].

From worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*): for example, when the instigating elder says "Bring the jar," and the prompted elder brings the jar, the bystander infers that the action of bringing the jar, etc., was caused by the knowledge of the action of bringing the jar, etc., because in worldly transactions, the knowledge of what is to be transacted is the cause [of the activity]. Then, upon the desire to know the cause of that [knowledge], he determines that very sentence which was present [at the time] to be its cause.

And since it is impossible for that [word], which is not yet connected with the object, to be the cause of its cognition, one subsequently determines the connection of the sentence with the object; that very [connection] is designated as "capacity" (śakti).

The Naiyāyikas maintain that although he initially apprehends the sentence itself as having the power [to denote] the sentence-meaning, nevertheless, through the subsequent grasping of the power of individual words—arising from the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*) in cases such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam naya*) and "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*)—the initial grasp of the sentence's power is recognized as invalid. This is just as the initial grasp of a small measurement of the moon is superseded by the subsequent grasp of its measurement at hundreds of *yojanas* produced by the study of the *Jyotiḥśāstra*.
Their intention is that the cognition of the sentence-meaning is established solely by the grasp of the power of each individual word, assisted by factors such as expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Others, however, say that because the apprehension of the sentence-meaning depends upon the apprehension of the meaning of each individual word, and because there is no possibility of sublation by that [sentence-meaning], the previously arisen apprehension of word-meanings alone possesses greater strength.

However, by means of the *vākyaśeṣa* (complementary explanatory passage)—in the case of "He offers with barley" (*yavair juhoti*), where there arises a doubt as to where the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *yava* lies, given that Āryas use it for long-bearded grain (*dīrghaśūka*) while Mlecchas use it for *kaṅgu*—its determination is made by the *vākyaśeṣa*: "When other plants wither, these [barley] stand up as if rejoicing. How the *vivaraṇa* (explanatory paraphrase) functions to apprehend denotative power has been explained in the section on the determination of verbal root meanings (*dhātvartha*).

In such cases as "The cuckoo (*pika*) sings sweetly here on this mango tree (*sahakāra*)," the determination of the denotative power (*śakti*) of words like *pika* to refer to the *kokila* (cuckoo) occurs due to the proximity of well-known words such as *sahakāra*. This power is restricted among multiple possible meanings by means of association (*saṃyoga*) and other factors. As it is stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "Association, dissociation, companionship, opposition, context, gender, and the proximity of another word [are the factors that restrict the meaning]."
"Competence, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth, are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise undetermined. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the other [six relations] are the generators of the determination of a specific [meaning] by means of the removal of doubt when there is no delimitation of the word-meaning. The underlying idea is that their function is to produce the cognition of each respective meaning by determining the speaker’s intention toward one out of several meanings that are capable of being presented.

In this regard, "the cow with her calf" and "the cow without her calf" are, respectively, examples of association (*saṃyoga*) and dissociation (*viprayoga*). Companionship (*sāhacarya*) is similarity (*sādṛśya*), because similar things are generally used together. Thus, in cases such as "Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa," the comprehension of the specific meaning occurs through the simultaneous grasping of the intention (*tātparya*) based on the apprehension of the companionship between the two referents of the names; therefore, there is no circularity (*anyonyāśraya*). In expressions such as "the gait of Rāma and Arjuna," it [the comprehension] is based on opposition (*virodha*).

In such cases as "He offers with his joined palms" (*añjalinā juhoti*) and "He worships the sun with his joined palms" (*añjalinādityamupatiṣṭhate*), the intended meaning of the word *añjali* as an ointment applied with ghee is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of praise, namely, "Ghee is indeed splendor" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*). In such cases as "Rāma [is] Jāmadagnya," the word *rāma* refers specifically to Paraśurāma due to the proximity (*sannidhi*) of the word *jāmadagnya*. Similarly, in the statement "A maiden should be given to one who is handsome" (*abhirūpāya kanyā deyā*), it is understood through contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*) that she should be given to one who is handsome in every respect.

In the phrase "the neem tree was struck with an axe," the word *paraśu* (axe) signifies the act of cutting due to contextual propriety (*aucitya*). In the phrase "the Supreme Lord is here," the word *parameśvara* refers to a king because of the mention of a royal capital as the location.

In the phrase "Citrabhānu shines," the word *citrabhānu* denotes fire at night and the sun by day. In expressions such as "Mitra shines," the word *mitra* denotes a friend when the gender (*liṅga*) indicates an individual, and the sun in the latter case. In the phrase "a thick-spotted ox-female," the determination of whether it is a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi* compound is made from the accent (*svara*).

From the word "ādi" (and so forth), [one should understand] the substitution of *ṣatva*, *aṇatva*, and so on; for example, in the case of *susiktam*, the particle *su*—being a *karmapravacanīya*—conveys the sense of honor (*pūjā*), whereas in *suṣiktam*, the prefix (*upasarga*) conveys a different meaning. Similarly, in *praṇayakaḥ*, due to the substitution of *ṇatva*, there is the cognition of one who leads (*praṇayana-kartṛ*); in *pranāyakaḥ*, because that [substitution] is absent, there is the cognition of a leader who has gone forward (*pragata-nāyaka*). Such cases are to be inferred accordingly.

As for the relationship between word and object: that which is the meaning of the word and the object is the word, and that which is the word is the meaning; thus, there exists an identity rooted in mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*), though distinguished by difference. The designator (*vācaka*) of this [identity] is the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) and so forth, because both difference and non-difference are observed in the statement, "Om is the one-syllabled Brahman. In the first case, the genitive case is used with the intention of expressing the predominance of difference, whereas in the latter case, the nominative is used in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) with the intention of expressing the predominance of non-difference.
This very relationship is what regulates the conventional usage of the denoted and the denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between the word and its object.

The followers of Bhaṭṭa maintain that *śakti* (denotative power) is either a convention (*saṅketa*) or a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). However, that view is not tenable; for it is impossible for that [convention], which is rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and is itself unreal, to function as a relation. Furthermore, because difference and non-difference are mutually exclusive by nature, they cannot coexist in a single locus. Even if such a superimposition were possible for one particular case, there is no evidence for such a superimposition in all cases. Moreover, since a pot continues to be perceived even when the word "pot" has ceased to exist, the identity (*tādātmya*) between the two is logically untenable.

Nor should it be argued that identity and difference are not contradictory in the case of a jar that was previously dark red but becomes red through baking, because of the cognition "this is now not dark red"; for there is no escape from the contradiction when those qualities, being non-pervasive, are considered under a single delimiting condition (*ekāvacchedena*).

For this very reason, in those cases, cognitions such as "this [cloth] is not black now," "the tree does not have contact with the monkey at its root," occur precisely by way of a distinction based on the delimiters of space and time; however, there is no cognition that does not apprehend those [delimiters], such as "this jar is not black" or "the tree is not in contact with the monkey. But in the theory of non-difference (*abheda-vāda*), it would follow that upon the destruction of the word "jar," the jar itself must be destroyed. Likewise, it would follow that the meaning, like the word, is perceivable by the auditory organ, and that the word, like the meaning, is perceivable by the visual organ and other senses—thus, there would be a great deal of contradiction.
How the word is not eternal will be explained later.

Nor should one suspect that the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) is tenable because of the observation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—such as "the jar is a cloth" when there is absolute difference, or "the jar is a jar" when there is absolute non-difference—for in passages such as these, the word *akṣara* functions through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) toward its designated meaning, thereby making coreferentiality possible; furthermore, since that sentence belongs to the section on meditation (*upāsanākāṇḍa*), it is tenable as being intended for the meditation upon non-difference even where difference exists. This is explained in detail elsewhere.

That capacity (śakti) is threefold: etymology (yoga), conventional usage (rūḍhi), and etymological-conventional usage (yogarūḍhi). The capacity defined by a root and an affix with respect to their respective meanings is *yoga*; a word that conveys a meaning solely through that [capacity] is designated as *yaugika* (etymological). For example, words such as *pācaka* ("cook"), because the root and the affix contained therein are conventionally established (*vyutpanna*) in the sense of "cooking" and the "agent" (kāraka) respectively. When the meaning of the constituent parts is not perceived, the capacity of the whole alone for a specific meaning is *rūḍhi*; a word that conveys a meaning through that [capacity] is *rūḍha* (conventional).

For example, [the word] *maṇinūpura* (jeweled anklet) and so forth. However, from words such as *aśvagandhā*, there is sometimes the understanding of a medicinal herb (*oṣadhi*) based on a power (*śakti*) residing in the aggregate (*samudāya*) of its parts; but sometimes, through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which has the smell of a horse," there is the understanding of a stable for horses and the like based on the power of the individual parts (*avayavaśakti*). This derivative (*yaugika*) meaning is not mentioned separately because it is included within the two already mentioned [types of meaning].

The principle that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga)" applies only when there is an absence of context and other such factors. Others hold that in the case of the word *vājiśālā* (horse-stable), it is used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote a horse. Where the collective power of a word, assisted by the meaning of its constituent parts, conveys the sense, that is *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional); a word that conveys a meaning through such a process is *yogarūḍha*. For example, the word *paṅkaja* (lotus).

In that case, because the cognition of a lotus occurs even without the consideration of an inconsistency—since the word conveys the meaning of a thing characterized by being a locus of mud and a substratum of birth—the occasion for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not arise there; this has already been explained in detail previously.

In cases such as "The hamlet is on the Gaṅgā," when the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on proximity (*sāmīpya*)—which is not the primary denotation (*śakya*)—of the word "Gaṅgā" to the bank is apprehended, there arises a verbal cognition of a hamlet located on the bank, produced by the memory of the bank and so forth generated by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) previously acquired. This is because indication must necessarily be admitted, since the usage of the indicated meaning would otherwise be inexplicable. Furthermore, the perception of the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is the seed for postulating that [indication]; as it has been stated elsewhere, even in some cases, the absence of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) is also a seed for that [postulation].

For instance, in the verse “Her face is a face, yet the faces of others do not shine as such,” a cognition whose qualificandum-ness (viśeṣyatā) is delimited by *vadanatva* (the property of being a face) and whose qualifier-ness (prakāratā) is delimited by *vadanatva* and determined by a relation of identity (*tādātmya*) is not possible; this is because, in verbal cognition, the difference between the delimiters of the property to be predicated (*vidheyatā-avacchedaka*) is a necessary condition with respect to a qualificandum-ness delimited by a qualifier-ness determined by a relation of identity.

The expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) determined by the word *vadana* (face), which has as its referent the meaning delimited by "being a face," does not reside in the word *vadana* itself; therefore, in that context, the word *vadana* functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "that which causes delight. The non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) of that which is delimited by "delightfulness" (as presented by that indication) is connected with the face. Furthermore, even where there is an absence of expectancy as understood from grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), it may occur in such a manner, as for example:
"Having abandoned Sītā, that protector of the earth enjoyed the earth alone, [which is] girt by the ocean, the mine of jewels.
In this verse, the word *pṛthivī* (earth) lacks expectancy for another instance of *pṛthivī*, yet it occurs in such a way.

In this context, since the root *bhuj* (in the form *bhuji*), which signifies "eating," has no expectancy for the *ātmanepada* [terminations], its primary meaning is blocked from being understood; consequently, by means of that root, its own meaning—protection—is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because the rule "bhujo 'navane" (Pāṇini 1.3.66) teaches that there is a lack of expectancy (*anākāṅkṣā*) in the form of an incapacity for the cognition of protection as connected to the agent, which is understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) when co-occurring with the *ātmanepada*.

In this context, by the word *kevala* (alone), there is denoted an individual entity possessing oneness that is the non-limiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) residing in the action of enjoyment performed by a protector of the earth distinct from Rāma at that time. By the particle *eva* (only/alone), there is the exclusion of connection with anything other than the earth.

And thus, according to the Nyāya system, the sentence-meaning comprehension (*vākyārthabodha*) is as follows: "The protector of the earth who is non-different from Rāma is one who possesses the quality of being a singular entity that does not delimit the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the mutual absence residing in the act of experiencing—which has as its agent the protector of the earth who is non-different from the Rāma of that time—and which has as its object the earth; [he is] a possessor of the act of experiencing whose object is the earth, and a non-performer of the act of experiencing whose object is a woman other than the earth. However, in cases such as "the *dvirepha* sings sweetly" or "the *pika* coos in the forest," the very basis for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is precisely the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).

However, it is called "indirect indication" (lakṣitalakṣaṇā), because it is constituted by being qualified by two *repha*s that constitute the meaning of the compound which is the object of indication (*lakṣya*).

For instance, when a person has not grasped the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word *dvirepha* as referring to a particular living being, but rather grasps its etymological derivation (*yaugika*) as "that in which there are two *rephas*," they apprehend a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—in the form of a relation to the possible meaning (*śakya*)—namely, the word *bhramara* (bee), which possesses two *rephas*. Then, because the verbal cognition whose intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya*) is the agency of producing sweet sounds as qualified by that particular living being is otherwise untenable, the word *dvirepha* brings about the understanding of that particular living being through a secondary signification consisting in being denotable by a word composed of two *rephas*, which is its own [secondary] referent (*sva-lakṣya*).

They say that by the word *dvirepha* (double-*r*), the word *bhramara* (bee) is brought to mind through the connection with the property of being the producer of a sweet sound. However, it is not correct to say that this brings about the cognition of a specific living being (*prāṇiviśeṣa*), because according to the rule of etymology, "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*), the meaning of the suffix cannot be connected there [with the base]. Even if there were metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *bhramara*, the cognition of that [living being] would still not arise from it, because only that which is actually uttered can convey its meaning. This should be understood similarly in cases such as "The cuckoo (*pika*) warbles in the forest.
Likewise:
"The Ganges, when seen, drunk, or bathed in, truly carries away the sins of men."

In this context, regarding the sentence "The yellow Ganges removes sin," there is a non-comprehension of the objecthood of drinking with respect to the water—which is presented [to the mind] through the word *gaṅgā*—due to the assistance provided by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the apprehension of the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists in the relationship of part and whole between its own denoted meaning (the current) and [the water]. Alternatively, the failure of the intended meaning (*tātparya-anupapatti*) alone is the seed of secondary signification everywhere; it is precisely as the indicator of that [failure] that the aforementioned lack of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) and other factors are useful.

For this very reason, in cases such as "Bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "sticks" (*yaṣṭi*) in the sense of the person who holds them. This is because, even though there is no logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) in the sticks themselves being the object of the act of entering, the inconsistency remains active regarding their being the object of entering for the purpose of eating—this being the intended meaning inferred from the context of a meal. The same should be understood in cases such as "The spears enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*) and "The umbrella-bearers go" (*chatriṇo yānti*).

[Objection: But surely, since the word *chatri* is composed of two words and is thus a sentence according to the Nyāya system, how can it possess secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), given that its primary denotation (*śakya*) is not established? Furthermore, in this case, "being a traveler in the same caravan" cannot be the delimitor of what is to be signified (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), because it would result in the non-connection of the word "go" (*yānti*); for that which is presented as a traveler lacks the expectancy for the act of going. [Reply: This is true; however, there is no occurrence of the two aforementioned defects, because it is accepted that in this context the suffix *-matup*, which possesses the power of relation, itself signifies "one who is related to the same caravan. Thus, the stated faults do not apply.

Nor is the word *chatrī* (umbrella-bearer) redundant, for it serves a purpose by acting as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). According to the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*), "a word that possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇika*) is not merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*). Words function as causes only with respect to the experience of their own primary denotations (*svaśakya*).

In the view of those who maintain that the experience of the *tīra* (riverbank) arises from words such as *ghoṣa* (cowherd settlement) itself—since it is established that [the word] possesses the capacity to cause the experience of its own denotatum (*śakyārtha*) together with another object—and that "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) is not the presentation of the non-denotatum (*aśakyārtha*) from the denotatum, the basis for their position is this: a word is an experiencer (*anubhāvaka*) only through the relation of being connected to the presentation produced by itself, and since that [presentation] does not exist in the case of the *tīra*, the word would not be an experiencer of it. However, that is not possible; for if the *tīra* and so forth were presented by the denotatum, they would not be the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), and consequently, there could be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) with them.

In reality, however, the meaning of that [statement] is simply that a word used in a secondary sense (lākṣaṇika) does not produce a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by way of the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), because it is precisely the possession of primary denotative power (*śaktimatva*) that is the governing factor for such a connection. For this very reason, the statement "the meaning of a word in an injunction is nothing other than its primary denotation" is logically consistent.

Furthermore, since the conjunction of threads is the cause of the conjunction with the cloth, it would result in the denial of the experienced cognition of the connection in every metaphorical sentence such as "the thread produces the cloth"; therefore, it is more reasonable that even a word used in a metaphorical sense possesses the capacity to produce a direct experience. Moreover, because of the common realization—"I am experiencing the bank from the word 'Gaṅgā'"—one should not be dogmatic regarding such conventional usage.

Now, one might object that according to the maxim, "Since the employment of words is within one's own control, why should we employ a word that is not expressive?", it would be improper to use a term such as *gaṅgā*, which does not directly denote the bank. If it is argued that this term is used for the purpose of conveying [qualities] such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*) when the motive for inquiry arises, then—since that quality cannot appear in verbal cognition (*śābda-bhāna*) without a specific function (*vṛtti*)—one must also accept a third function, namely suggestion (*vyañjanā*), for that purpose. Therefore:

In this instance, even though the primary intended meaning—that unchaste women, having deprived the powerless of their wealth, sport with water-carriers—is not embraced by the conventional sense of the words, there is still a perception of another meaning. And that [perception] occurs through the medium of the literal sense as well: "O pious man, wander about with confidence; that horse has been killed by him—the naturally arrogant lion dwelling in the bower on the bank of the Godāvarī."

In such cases, for those sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) who possess creative intuition (*pratibhā*), once the speaker’s and the listener’s specific excellences have flashed forth, there arises—immediately after the cognition of the lion—the realization that the bank of the Godāvarī is unfit for the roaming of one who fears dogs. This is because, even though the meaning not connoted by the literal sense (*lūḍha-artha*) cannot be cognized through mere *yoga* (etymological derivation), its establishment is easily accomplished through *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

It is not the case that the cognition of sanctity (*pāvanatva*) and so forth is possible through *suddha-lakṣaṇā* (pure indication) alone—even if it were established by means of *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇā* (qualified indication)—because there would be no reason to accept the latter when the former suffices to resolve the logical inconsistency. Furthermore, this would lead to an over-extension even in cases such as "Bring in Naṣṭī," since the intended meaning could be understood through inference based on the metaphorical cognition (*vyañjanikabuddhi*) of the expressed sense.

In reality, however, from this [example] as well, such an intention (tātparya) is inferred—just as in the case of giving a verbal insult (*gāli*)—but there is neither a verbal comprehension (*anvaya-bodha*) nor an inference (*anumiti*), because in the case of comprehension, the two conditions of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) are absent, or else they are doubtful; for it is admitted that the manifestation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) occurs precisely in those cases where these two are impossible. This has been explained in detail elsewhere. If, on the other hand, there exists an empirical, spontaneous conviction among people that "I understand this meaning from the word," then the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*) is indeed unimpeded; thus, one should rely upon my own stated, refined conclusion.

He introduces [the objection] by its root: "Now, if the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*) alone constitutes *śakti*, then this would apply even to corrupt speech (*apabhraṃśa*), because that too possesses the capacity to convey meaning. The underlying thought is that for those who maintain that the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) and so forth constitute *śakti*, this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not occur. He states the consequence of accepting this position with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The sense is that since it would follow that corrupt speech is not the object of prohibitions and injunctions such as "One should not speak in corrupt forms," one cannot simply accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).

"Two ways" means: first, by establishing that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) lack the capacity [to convey meaning] as previously stated; and second, by providing an alternative definition of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). In the root text, the phrase "expressive by means of inference" (*anumānena vācakaḥ*)—here, "inference" (*anumāna*) refers to memory (*smṛti*), based on the etymological derivation *anu* (subsequently) + *māna* (measurement/cognition); it does not refer to the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti-jñāna*), for we observe verbal comprehension even in those who lack such [logical] knowledge.

With the intention that corrupt forms such as *gāvī* and others, by virtue of being modifications (*vikṛti*) of words like *go*, serve as immediate reminders of the original form (*prakṛti*) through the mode of an indicator (*udbodhaka*), he explains [the verse] with the words: "by means of inference, the correct word. "By means of inference" (*anumāya*) means "having remembered" (*smṛtvā*). And he will state later: "Their utility lies precisely in the recollection of the correct word. The point is that corrupt forms do not possess direct denotative power (*sākṣād bodhakatā*), either because they lack the correctness (*sādhutva*) required for generating a verbal cognition, or because the knowledge of their incorrectness acts as an obstacle.

In this regard, he states Hari’s agreement with the words "for it has been said" (*uktaṃ hi*). Those [words] are the *apabhraṃśas*. "Regarding the correct words" (*sādhuṣu*) is a locative of domain; the meaning is "by means of recollection whose object is the correct words. "Causes of cognition" (*pratyaya*) means causes for the understanding of meanings such as "cow" (*go*). He states another alternative: "identity" (*tādātmya*), which means "having brought about the status of being an object of a cognition whose qualifier is identity with the correct words 'cow' and so forth. The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "or" (*vā*).

The meaning is as follows: when the word *go* (cow) is intended to be uttered, one might utter *gāvī* due to a lack of proficiency; yet, since this is in fact the word *go* itself appearing through identity (*tādātmya*), words such as *gāvī* reveal the object in the form of "cow" and so on. Nor is there an identity with the alternative views to be mentioned later, because in those cases the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) residing in the corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*) is the delimiting factor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), whereas here the status belongs to that [sequential order] residing in the correct form (*sādhū*). This is the distinction between them.

As for the presentation of the half-verse from Hari’s *Kārikā*—beginning with "identity" (*tādātmya*)—as support for the claim that "the identity between word and meaning is the expressive power" (*śakti*), that is entirely in vain. For even if identity were the power, an identity residing in the word cannot constitute the power [of expression], since the cognition of such word-resident identity does not cause the understanding of the meaning. Rather, it is more appropriate to explain that passage as being intended to present an alternative view: namely, that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) produce the understanding of meaning through a mistaken belief in their identity with the correct form (*sādhuśabda*), as determined by a consideration of the beginning and conclusion [of the relevant discussion].

He states the reasoning for their lack of denotative power: "Not by the learned," meaning that since those corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) are not established by the learned through tradition (*smṛti*) and so forth as being correct synonyms, they are therefore not denotative. This explains the previously stated point, namely, "those [corrupt forms] are [known] in relation to the correct words. By this, [it is meant] through hearing the corrupt form which is a modification of a correct word. "In the manifest" means in the correct word which is the source (*prakṛti*) of the corrupt form. The phrase "when there is the recollection of this" is to be supplied. "The determination" means that the verbal cognition of its meaning occurs. "Thus" means in this very manner. "Correct word" refers to words such as *go* (cow). "Corrupt form" refers to words such as *gāvī*.

"By that improper word"—meaning by means of the recollection of the proper word which is mediated by it. "Somewhat well-known"—in the form of *ambā* and so forth. "Because of oneness"—the meaning is "because of belonging to the same class. The sense is that there is such a commonality of class that, due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*) even in that case, one would have to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*).

"Otherwise" means that if the homogeneity [of sounds] were not a governing factor in the postulation of expressive power (*śakti*), then, because there would be no distinction in their possessing such power, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*)—just like correct words (*sādhūni*)—would also be presented in lexicons and similar works. "Precisely according to his view" means precisely according to the view of Hari (Bhartṛhari), who stated, "They [corrupt forms] [indicate meaning] through correct words by means of inference," and so forth.

Since it has been established by the aforementioned method that comprehension arises from Apabhraṃśa, one might suspect that the postulation of a linguistic capacity (*śakti*) for it is based on a self-referential fallacy. Wishing to dispel this doubt, [the author] demonstrates the impossibility of the stated method in that case, saying: "The point is this" (*ayambhāva*). The word "them" (*tān*) means "the correct words" (*sādhuśabda*). He states the reason for their ignorance: "of the common folk" (*pāmarāṇām*). The phrase "from comprehension" (*bodhāt*) means "from the inference of their comprehension through worldly usage."

The point is this: since those who have not studied the grammatical treatises cannot possess a cognition of words characterized by their being correct (*sādhu*), it is impossible to establish verbal comprehension (*śābdabuddhi*) in them by postulating a memory of correct words. Furthermore, even if the postulation of a memory of correct words were somehow possible, it could only occur if understanding arose for them from a correct word heard through direct perception; however, that very thing does not exist, as he says: "of those [who do not know] the correct [word]. "Due to an error regarding expressive power" (*śaktibhramāt*) means due to an error regarding the expressive power residing in the correct word as determined by its meaning, [which is mistakenly attributed] to the corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*).

Does the cognition [of meaning] there arise from an error regarding the power (*śakti*) consisting in the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*), or from an error regarding the power consisting in the will of God (*īśvarecchā*)? Regarding this, he states that the first alternative is not tenable with the words "of the capacity to convey" (*bodhakatvasya*). Regarding the second, he says "the will of God" (*īśvarecchā*). The word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "mere existence" (*sanmātra*) has the sense of "entirety. Since the cognition [of meaning] arising from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) is established by the experience of everyone, and since the will of God as the capacity to convey meaning is also uncontradicted therein, even by taking that [will] into account, the knowledge of power does not attain the status of being an error.
The point is that for a cognition to be erroneous, the sublation of its object (*viṣayabādha*) alone is the determining factor.

[Objection: "But surely, since there is no usage of [the word] as denotative (*vācaka*) even in the case of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), which are like words used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*), there is no sublation for the error regarding the power (*śakti*)—which consists in the will of God (*īśvarecchā*)—in that regard. To this, he says: 'Of the power' (*śakteḥ*). And because an error is impossible: the meaning is that an error is impossible because it is impossible for a desire that has as its qualifier the property of being a generator of a cognition of a specific meaning with respect to a specific word to have as its qualificandum a different word, when that desire is apprehended as having that specific word as its qualificandum. This is according to the literal sense [of the text]."

It should be understood that there is no subverting evidence against the presence of *śakti* (denotative power) in that case—whether it takes the form of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) as refined by its adjuncts, the form of a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) delimited by its relation, or the form of a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*). Thus, since even through error (*bhrama*) comprehension would be difficult to justify otherwise, the implication is that *śakti* is indispensable for the vernacular (*bhāṣā*).

Even in this view, he shows the agreement of Hari (Patañjali) with the words "And it has been said. The suffix *ṣyañ* in *pāramparyāt* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). The term "in the case of those who are deficient" (*viguṇeṣu*) is a qualifying attribute containing a reason. This deficiency consists in the impairment of the organs of articulation (*karaṇa*), because the deficiency of the speaker is what determines the occurrence of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). Thus, the meaning is: "those meanings which have attained renown through tradition while there were speakers who were deficient. The word "divine" (*daivī*) means "of the form of Sanskrit."

"Due to incapacity"—the meaning is that it was composed by those possessing a lack of proficiency in the instruments [of speech], and thus its sequence was either intermingled or destroyed. "Of those who perceive [words] as non-eternal" refers to those who maintain the eternality of sound (*śabda*). "In this doctrine" means in the dispute regarding capacity. Now, one might object: the statement "for them, the correct word (*sādhu*) is not expressive" is untenable, because it is universally accepted that correct words possess expressiveness (*vācakatva*) with respect to whatever meaning corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are employed to convey; therefore, he explains: "not expressive" (*abodhaka*). The sense is that the correct word, though present, is not the direct communicator in that instance; rather, it is the corrupt forms themselves that are the expressors (*vācakāḥ*) by virtue of their specific respective sequences.

Surely this speech, though appearing in the form of an Apabhraṃśa and having its sequence lost due to defects in the speakers, is in fact of a divine Saṃskṛta nature. As for the Naiyāyikas, their claim that it lacks the capacity to convey meaning is merely an error; for since it has been established [by them] through tradition, it is possible for it to convey meaning via an error regarding expressive power (śakti-bhrama) rooted in a delusion of identity with the correct form (sādhutādātmya-bhrānti). Furthermore, the statement "this divine speech is undisturbed" serves as a corroboration of the final alternative mentioned previously.

Nor is it incorrect to say that "for them, the correct word is non-expressive," because in that alternative view, one does not admit that comprehension arises from the recollection of a correct word, since corrupt forms (apabhraṃśas) have superimposed correctness upon them yet possess the capacity to convey meaning. The phrase "for them" (teṣām) and so forth means that those very words, which are the objects of the superimposition of correctness, are the conveyors of well-known meanings, but they are not conveyors by virtue of possessing their respective specific sequences (ānupūrvī). Therefore, the expressiveness of corrupt forms as such is not established by the aforementioned reasoning; hence he says "furthermore" (kiñca). "Of them" (tāsām) refers to the regional dialects (bhāṣās). The term "defect" (doṣa) implies that, due to the resulting complexity (gaurava), there is no expressive power (śakti) residing in them.

The fact that [a word] is accepted by all cultured persons (*śiṣṭa*) is indeed the decisive factor; therefore, he says: “the delimiting factor” means the delimiting factor of the capacity to produce understanding. “Of those two” means of the correct form (*sādhu*) and the corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*). However, being accepted by all cultured persons is not the decisive factor, as it is said: “The root *śavati*, meaning ‘to go,’ is used among the Kambojas.”

Because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "The noble ones speak of this very [word] in its modified form (*vikāra*)," there would be no possibility of establishing a primary expressive power (*śakti*) for words fixed to specific regions [as being distinct from Sanskrit]; furthermore, it would result in the inconsistency of the examples of Prakrit languages given by the Alaṅkārikas under the heading of "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatā*) of the denotative word. For this very reason, the conviction among the learned (*śiṣṭa*) of various regions regarding the unambiguous expressive power of their respective languages is logically consistent. Nor is this a delusion, because there is no cause for such a misconception; this is the intended meaning. He concludes with the words "And thus... (*tathā ca*).

Thus, even if *apabhraṃśas* possess denotative power (*śakti*), they would have to be considered correct (*sādhu*), because the very possession of denotative power constitutes correctness; this is the underlying sense. The phrase "speaking with correct words" means that one should employ only correct words, and so forth. The phrase "not with incorrect ones" refers to the prohibition—such as "one should not speak corruptly (*apabhraṃśita*) nor in a barbarian tongue (*mlecchit*)"—which functions as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). "Capability" (*yogyatva*) consists in possessing a property that delimits the causal capacity (*janakatāvacchedaka-dharma*). In that regard, [the view is] that in a correct word, [this property] is a universal (*jāti*).

The authority for this is the Vedic scripture cited in the Bhāṣya on the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*: "A single word, when correctly understood, endowed with the science [of grammar], and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world. Here, "correctly understood" means understood as being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*). This is also supported by the statement obtainable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*): "Whatever is established here [in the world] is correct.
