"Endowed with the science" means intended according to the path of exposition provided by the science [of grammar].

The meaning is that it is "applied" by means of the path joined with well-practiced phonetics (*śikṣā*); and there is the Vedic scripture: "They, saying 'He! Alaya!', were defeated. Furthermore, if it is considered that this [quality] is not a genus (*jāti*) because of its intermixture (*sāṅkarya*) with [other qualities] such as *katva*, then let it be an adventitious condition (*upādhi*); this is the intended sense.

"Indicative of that" (tajjñāpaka) means "manifesting that. This has been explained accordingly. By the word "grammar" (vyākaraṇa) and so forth, there is the inclusion of usage by the learned (śiṣṭa). "In this very way" means precisely through the attainment of the determination of the correctness of those respective words by prioritizing their respective meanings. "Like [an action] not producing a result" implies the sense that a result is heard only for that which is performed by one who belongs to the Kṣatriya class (kṣatriyādhikārika).

The meaning of "correctness" (*sādhutva*) is that the correctness of words such as *go* consists in their being productive of merit (*puṇya*) when employed precisely with reference to objects such as a cow. Now, one might object: since words such as *Devadatta* have not been etymologically derived (*avyutpādana*) in the grammatical treatises with reference to modern individuals like Devadatta, they would lack correctness (*sādhutā*) when applied to such persons. To this, he says: "modern," etc.

"Two syllables" means: according to the traditional rule (smṛti) found in the Bhāṣya, "One should give a person a name consisting of two or four syllables that begins with a sonant and ends with a semivowel (antaḥstha), and it should be a primary derivative (kṛt), not a secondary derivative (taddhita). The sense is that names created merely in accordance with the local dialects of various regions are indeed ungrammatical (asādhutva), because they are not derived from the [Sanskrit] scriptures. "Of secondary names" means of words such as *śukla* (white) and so forth; "in a quality" means in their own denoted form, such as whiteness and so on.

Regarding the phrase "due to derivation," this refers to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "the elision of *matup* after words expressing qualities" (*guṇavacanebhyo matupo luk*), as well as the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "white and so forth are masculine when [denoting] a quality" (*guṇe śuklādayaḥ puṃsi*), and so on. With that [derivation] in view—meaning with the blue and other objects in view—their application occurs in the usage of the substratum of the quality (*guṇin*). Even though their denoted meaning (*śakyārtha*) is sublated and they bring about the presentation of a secondary meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) due to the recognition of an impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*), their status as correct words (*sādhutva*) is not untenable, provided they are taken in their primary denoted sense.

The meaning is that because they have been trained in the treatises, they prioritize the primary sense [of words]. Furthermore, since the term "secondary" (*gauṇa*) serves as an indicator for words with conventional metaphorical meanings (*nirūḍhalākṣaṇika*), the implication is that there is no lack of grammatical correctness (*asādhutva*) in cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).

"Of moderns" means those words employed by contemporary authors that do not fall within the intended scope of the treatises [of grammar], due to some slight connection [with them]. Now, one might object: since dictionaries and grammars exist as the means for grasping word-potency (śakti), the statement regarding the means for grasping potency is redundant; to this, he replies: "That which is additional," meaning that which is a means for grasping potency distinct from both dictionaries and grammars.

The sense is that, since it is possible for those who have not studied grammar to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) by means of that [usage], the author provides usage as a means for that purpose; thus, because it culminates in this, there is no pointlessness. By this, the doubt that the demonstration of the means for grasping that [power] is useless—on the grounds that the author does not accept a power distinct [from the word itself]—is also resolved. He explains the root text by supplying the word "object" (*viṣaya*): "The relation is the object."

Thus, in the linguistic usage "this is related to that," the relation (*sambandha*) is the object; regarding fitness (*yogyatā*)—in the usage of fitness such as "this is fit for this"—fitness is the object. Therefore, from that convention, there arises a cognition (*saṃvit*) of that [fitness], meaning that fitness is understood through its power (*śakti*) in the form of denotative capacity.

In this regard, the illustration is "like the connection between mother and son"; just as the usage "this is related to that" determines the relationship of produced and producer between those two, so it is here.

Others, however, explain this verse regarding the lotus-feet of Hari (*haripadma*) as follows: In the case of a relational term—namely, in the linguistic usage "this is related to that"—the object is that very relation, whether it be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or some other type, which is defined by the conventional usage of "fitness" (*yogyatā*). This fitness consists in possessing a property that delimits the capacity to produce the cognition of the meaning; it is this [relation] that is synonymous with "fitness," and this is the remainder [of the sense].

And that [relation] is beginningless; it is ascertained from the linguistic usage of elders—which is synonymous with our own conventional understanding—and not because "potency" (śakti) is simply the capacity to produce a cognition. This is because of the linguistic usage: "This [word] is fit for producing this [cognition]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śeṣa*: "Since the status of being a cause of comprehension is possible only when there is a relation, it is understood that a relation exists between the word and its meaning."
Thus, the meaning stated [previously] has been clarified by this conclusion. One should ascertain further details from other sources.
This concludes the "Definition of the Nature of Power" (*śaktisvarūpanirūpaṇa*) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. 6.

In the statement, "In a compound (*samāsa*), [the word-meaning] is indeed distinct," the author—who cites the word *paṅkaja* as an example—accepts that in a compound, the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) is assisted by the individual powers of its constituent parts (*pratyeka-śakti*), and thus possesses the nature of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). However, this is untenable; for where the individual words constituting a compound are themselves devoid of meaning, the assistance of individual powers is impossible. This is the case, for instance, with the negative particle (*nañ*) in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). As it has been said: "Indeed, there is no operation whatsoever in the denotation of the meanings of those two [constituents]."

And thus, as in the theory of *jahatsvārtha* (the abandonment of one's own meaning), there is also the problem that in such instances the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) and so forth is not naturally justified; in order to dispel this doubt, he states "the determination of the meaning of the negative particle" (*nañ-artha-nirūpaṇam*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of a *nañ*-compound" in the root text, the intention is as follows: since the verbal cognition of absence (*abhāva-śābdabodha*) in cases such as "The pot is not a cloth" (*ghaṭo na paṭaḥ*) or "The pot does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*) is established by universal consensus, it is necessary that the negative particle (*nañ*) has "absence" as its meaning. Consequently, the systematic arrangement regarding the predominance of the subsequent member and so forth becomes well-founded.

Although in cases such as "the jar is not" (*ghaṭo na*), the cognition has non-existence as its primary object (*viśeṣya*), nevertheless, in accordance with examples such as "not-all" (*asarvaḥ*), one must also admit that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of being superimposed (*āropitatva*). Thus, the *Sāra* explains by supplying the missing words: "it is established," and "for this very reason" means "precisely because primacy (*prādhānya*) is untenable.

Now, if the negative particle there has the meaning of non-existence, how is primacy untenable? To address this, he states the underlying intention (*bhāva*): "The point is this. Otherwise—that is, if one does not accept the sense of being superimposed, which amounts to saying it has the sense of difference (*bheda*)—the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) would [not apply].

The meaning is as follows: [the rule] would not apply because in the expression "asarvaḥ" (not-all), if the negative particle *nañ* has the sense of non-difference (*abheda*), then the referent of the word "sarva" (all) functions as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and is thus a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). Since words that are subordinate elements (*saṃjñopasarjana*) are excluded from the group beginning with "sarva," the rule does not apply here, just as in cases such as "atisarva. An objection might be raised: "Since we admit that the cognition in that case is 'the all that is the counter-correlate of difference,' the primary status of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*) is not lost. To this, he replies: "In cases such as 'there is no jar' (*ghaṭo nāsti*)," referring to that meaning of *nañ*. The point is that the property of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) belongs to the absence that is the meaning of *nañ*; that is what is the governing factor (*tantra*) in such instances.

[Objection: But even for you, the universally established cognition that "the cloth is not a jar" (aghaṭaḥ paṭaḥ) would be untenable as meaning "the cloth is different from the jar. To this he replies: "In our view"—that is, the cognition of difference. "Resulting from the object" (ārthaḥ) means "derived from the object," i.e., from the object presented [in consciousness]. "Mental" (mānasaḥ): the point is that in that case, the status of being a verbal cognition is simply unestablished. [Objection: But what is the harm if the word *asarva* lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). "And here" (*atra ca*) means "and in the alternative that 'being superimposed' (*āropitatvam*) is the denotation of the negative particle (*nañ*)."

The point is this: since the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is obtained through the very nature of the relation (*saṃsargamaryyādā*), the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) must be superimposition (*āropa*) alone—which cannot be obtained by any other means—and not the status of being the object of superimposition, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Now, one might object that if superimposition (*āropa*) is accepted as being denotable (*vācya*), there would be a contradiction with the root text which establishes that it is merely indicative (*dyotaka*); therefore, he says: "The mention of its being indicative. The sense is that even though it is denotable, it is only a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not the substantive (*viśeṣya*), like non-existence; it is for this very reason that it was stated in that manner. Although the root text states that the word *nañ*, when capable of forming a compound, has the meaning of superimposition, nevertheless, the statement "the jar does not exist" should be understood as an illustrative example, since here too—just as in that case—there is no experience of superimposition.

Regarding the phrase "that which is indicated by *nañ*," although *nañ* is present as a qualifier and is thus separated [from its referent], since pronouns (*tyadādi*) refer to what is currently in the mind, it is not improper to refer to that [referent] at that time; thus he says, "tadartha" (for the sake of that). By the term "sādhāraṇyena" (in a general sense), both positions are included, because in the present context the word "artha" (meaning) refers to the object of the cognition produced by it. The sense is that, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is indeed denotative (*vācakatva*); but when such a factor exists, it is also indicative (*dyotakatā*). This is because it is not denoted by *nañ*.

Even though, by virtue of the predominance of the meaning of the final member, a negative (*nañ*) *tatpuruṣa* compound would result in the bringing of a Brāhmaṇa, because of the employment of the negative particle, there will be the bringing of that which is qualified by the meaning of the negative. What, then, is this meaning of the negative? It is the cessation of the object-referent. Because one perceives qualities such as fairness of complexion seen in a Brāhmaṇa, or through instruction based on what has been seen, one first determines, "This is a Brāhmaṇa. Subsequently, one perceives, "This is not a Brāhmaṇa," and then employs the expression, "This is a non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*).

Furthermore, from the observation of qualities seen [in him] or from instruction based on what has been seen, the cognition "this is not a Brāhmaṇa" arises precisely preceded by the determination of his Brāhmaṇahood. For one does not determine "this is a Brāhmaṇa" merely upon seeing his complexion in the marketplace; rather, the true nature of the object as it exists is known by him. By examining this passage from the *Bhāṣya* on the *Nañ-sūtra*, it is established that the meaning stated by Kaiyaṭa alone is correct.

Nevertheless, since that commentary (*bhāṣya*) can be satisfactorily explained as being intended solely to demonstrate that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the reason for the perception of difference in certain cases, it lacks the capacity to support the view that the negative particle (*nañ*) denotes superimposition (*āropa*).

Otherwise, because superimposition of that [identity] would be impossible according to the aforementioned reasoning in the case of things that are absolutely dissimilar, the meaning of the negative particle could not apply there; consequently, the expression "the cloth is not a jar" (*aghaṭaḥ paṭaḥ*) would be untenable.

According to the technical dictum that "the cognition of the counter-positive and the cognition of its absence share the same fate," in cases such as "This pot is blue," the pot-part appears through identity with the referent of the word "blue. Consequently, when the negative particle *nañ* is co-occurrent, there arises—what is established by universal experience—a cognition of the absence of "blue" as delimited by the relation of identity. This would be inexplicable unless the negative particle *nañ* has "absence" as its meaning. Furthermore, since the cognitions produced by the sentences "This is not silver" and "This is silver" do not respectively apprehend that absence and that [silver], they could not stand in the relationship of mutual contradiction and non-contradiction; therefore, it is necessary that the negative particle *nañ* has "difference" (*bheda*) as its meaning.

Nor should it be argued that if the negative particle (*nañ*) has the meaning of non-difference (*abhedārthaka*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of understanding even a clod of earth or the like—distinct from a Brāhmaṇa—from such expressions as "Bring a non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*); for this is not an acceptable consequence, as it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, which states: "When it is said, 'Bring a non-Brāhmaṇa,' one does not consider his task accomplished by bringing a clod of earth. This objection is invalid because, just as a word like "pot" (which primarily denotes the universal *ghaṭatva*) brings about the cognition of a specific individual present at hand, so too, through context and other factors, the word "Brāhmaṇa"—when used here to denote anything distinct from a Brāhmaṇa—can bring about the cognition of a Kṣatriya or similar person alone.

Therefore, in expressions such as "non-pot" (*aghaṭaḥ*) and so forth, the negative particle (*nañ*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) only in difference (*bheda*), because since "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) is an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in its being the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatā'vacchedaka*). As for that [negative particle] which is a constituent of the compound, however, when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "that which is different from it," [the negative particle] merely serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhakatvam*).

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as "na brāhmaṇairetairupadrūtam" ("it was not troubled by these Brahmins"), if the negative particle *nañ* signifies difference (*bheda*), there would be an inconsistency regarding the case-terminations of the words denoting the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*), because they lack grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For the negative particle conveys difference only when there exists an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) conducive to the cognition of a non-difference relation between the counter-positive and the substratum; thus, the identity of their case-terminations is dependent upon that very expectancy.

And thus, when the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys difference, the requirement that the words expressing the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) possess identical case-endings and numbers is the regulating factor; for this very reason, there is no cognition of difference in such cases as "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale na ghaṭaḥ*).

And it is observed that in the statement, "In the *yajatis* one performs the *ye yajāmahe*; not in the *anuyājas*," there is an understanding of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by means of the negative particle (*nañ*). In the aforementioned sentence, the word *yajati* denotes the essential nature of the sacrifice (*yāga*). Thus, the meaning is: "In sacrifices other than the *anuyājas*, one utters—that is, recites—the mantra containing the words *ye yajāmahe*. For this very reason, since a single object consisting of the application of the mantra containing the term *ye yajāmahe* is enjoined here for those sacrifices distinct from the *anuyājas*, the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*)—defined as having a single intended meaning—is logically established.

The sense is that there would arise a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*)—whereby the injunction would have two distinct meanings—since one would have to enjoin the presence of the *ye yajāmahe* formula in the *yāga*s and simultaneously enjoin its absence in the *anuyāja*s; furthermore, it would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in assuming the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the *ye yajāmahe* formula [into the *anuyāja*s].

Others, however, maintain that because [the action] is both enjoined and prohibited by the scriptures, it results in an option—like the taking up or not taking up of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—and therefore, in the phrase "not in the *anuyāja*s," the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of prohibition. For instance, since an action requires an agent (or other factors), and in the absence of any specific determinant, an injunction of non-existence must be stated there with reference to a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) qualified by all its constituent factors and serving as the counter-positive. Thus, for the sake of establishing the object of reference, its prior existence is required; for a prohibition is dependent upon such prior existence.

And in some cases, [the activity] arises from attachment (*rāga*), as in the case of "One should not eat *kalañja*. In that instance, since the eating of *kalañja* and so forth has arisen through the cognition of it being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), the prohibitive scripture brings about the certainty of desisting; thus, by implication, the eating of *kalañja* is understood to be a means to an undesired end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*), and from that follows the desisting. But in the present case, however, that [activity] arises solely from the scripture: "He performs the *ye yajāmahe* [formula]."

And thus, since the prohibition possesses authority by virtue of being the subject matter of the scripture, and since the injunctional scripture also possesses authority as that upon which the former depends, it is impossible for the prohibition to completely sublate the injunction; therefore, only an option (vikalpa) results.

Furthermore, regarding the alternative [of using barley] in such cases as "one offers with rice" or "or one offers with barley," there are two faults: first, when rice is employed, the Veda would undergo subversion (viparyāsa), and since [the Veda] cannot be a producer [of knowledge in that case], one must accept the authority of the scriptural injunction for barley—which was previously unestablished—and abandon the authority already perceived [in the rice injunction]. Second, when barley is adopted in another performance, there is the abandonment of the non-authority previously accepted for the barley injunction and the acceptance of the authority previously abandoned [for it]. Thus, there are two pairs of faults.

In the fourth case, by taking *yava* (barley) as the material, there arises a twofold fault: first, the acceptance of the non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*) of the *vrīhi* (rice) scripture which had not been accepted; and second, the abandonment of the authoritativeness of that same scripture which had been accepted. Thus, with the occurrence of these eight alternative faults (*aṣṭadoṣavikalpa*), the distinction of the *anūyāja* sacrifice is understood through the two words *nañ* (negation) and *anūyāja*. This is *paryudāsa* (exclusion). And according to this view, *ye yajāmahaḥ* is not perceived as something to be performed [in the *anūyājas*], because its injunction is already established by the rule: "One performs *ye yajāmahaḥ* in the *iṣṭis*. Rather, having referred back (*anūdya*) the *ye yajāmahaḥ* enjoined by the general scripture, it is made known that its scope is restricted to those instances other than the *anūyājas*.

And thus, since a general rule (sāmānya-śāstra) is dependent upon a specific injunction (viśeṣa-vidhi), the phrase "not in the *anuyājas*" (nānuyājeṣu) assigns a scope excluding the *anuyājas*; consequently, it is understood that the *ye yajāmahe* formula is to be performed in all [offerings] except the *anuyājas*. However, in the case of the *anuyājas*, it is neither established as something to be performed, nor is it prohibited. Therefore, there is no option (*vikalpa*). Nor should it be argued that even if the negation (*nañ*) conveys a prohibition, there can be no option because the general rule—"In sacrifices, one performs the *ye yajāmahe*"—is set aside by the specific rule—"Not in the *anuyājas*," just as the rule regarding the *āhavanīya* fire is set aside by a specific scriptural injunction. This is because [the present case lacks the conditions for such sublation].

For the relationship of sublated and sublator is appropriate only between two things that are mutually independent, because the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire does not depend upon the word-injunction [regarding the *gārhapatya*]. However, the injunctive meaning of the prohibitory injunction (*niṣedha-śāstra*) does depend [on the other] for the sake of establishing its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). According to the maxim, "That which is possible is prohibited," there can be no sublation of it, because such sublation is impossible. Rather, by the reasoning already stated, there is only an option (*vikalpa*). And thus, there also follows the undesirable consequence of assuming two unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*). For it is understood from the injunction in this way:

They say that since no benefit whatsoever arises from performing the *ye yajāmaha* formula during the *anuyāja* offerings, and because its non-performance results in a prohibition—just as the non-performance of false speech does for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—that benefit must be of an entirely invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) nature; therefore, an option (*vikalpa*) between its performance and non-performance is not tenable.

On this point, some maintain that because the cognition of a negation is possible through the mere consideration of a general rule—without considering a prohibitory rule—by means of the establishment of a counter-positive (pratiyogin) consisting of an error, no such dilemma arises; and furthermore, because it is established by linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) that when there is a prohibition of a particular, a general injunction is understood to refer to "others than that," as in the cases of "Curd should be given to Brāhmaṇas" and "It should not be given to Kauṇḍinya."

Furthermore, even in that case, it is not only an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) that is conveyed by the negative particle (*nañ*); for when an exclusion is conveyed by *nañ*, the requirement for the two words expressing the qualifier and the qualified to have identical case-endings is indeed necessary, as is the requirement for them to have identical numbers (*samānavacana*). However, this [requirement of identical number] is absent in the present instance. Otherwise, just as in "not of the great king" (*na mahato rājñaḥ*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of the cognition of the difference from "great" (*mahadbheda*) even in cases such as "not of the great kings" (*na mahatāṃ rājñaḥ*).

Even if one were to somehow justify [the use of the negative particle] as "one, not two," there would still be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the injunction "curd should be given" becomes redundant; for it is argued that from the sentence "Curd should be given to Brāhmaṇas," there arises the understanding of giving curd intended for Brāhmaṇas other than Kauṇḍinya.

Furthermore, even if the fault of "optionality" (*vikalpa*) does not arise, since the contingency of "syntactical split" (*vākya-bheda*) remains acute, and since factors such as "having the same case-ending" exist as restrictors of that understanding, others maintain that in the case of "not in the *anuyāja* offerings," it is appropriate that the negative particle has the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

Let us return to the subject at hand. The phrase "otherwise" (anyathā) means in the case of accepting that superimposition (*āropitatva*) is denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*), without regard for parsimony (*lāghava*). By the phrase "of similarity, etc. (*sādṛśyādeḥ*), there is an inclusion of "smallness," and so forth, which will be mentioned later. The respective meanings [of the examples] follow this sequence: "one similar to a non-Brahmin," "absence of sin," "different from a horse," "small-bellied," "animals other than cows and horses are inferior," and "contrary to dharma," and so on.

[Objection: But if similarity and so forth are not denotable, how can there be a cognition of them from those [words]? To this, he says: "tat tu" (but that), which means "the reading of that [word]"; "abhipretya" (intending) means intending a mental cognition that occurs subsequent to the cognition of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, which has the property of being the counter-correlate of a difference as its qualifier.

The point is this: since the cognition of a *brāhmaṇa* and so forth arises from their respective words alone, the employment of words such as "non-*brāhmaṇa*" (*abrāhmaṇa*) for the purpose of cognizing a *brāhmaṇa* as the counter-correlate of a difference is intended to convey the *kṣatriya* and others through similarity and the like. Thus, the cognition of the *kṣatriya* and others based on such inference can only occur after the cognition of the primary meaning—namely, that the *brāhmaṇa* is the counter-correlate of the difference. Others, however, maintain that because one experiences the notion of verbalness (*śābdatva*) regarding that cognition, the cognition of the *brāhmaṇa* and so forth through similarity and the like occurs solely by means of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

Since a qualifier requires a qualificand, he says "pratiyoginī" (as the counter-correlative). And thus, the intended meaning is that in cases such as "abrāhmaṇaḥ," there arises a cognition in the form "a Brāhmaṇa qualified by difference, [where the Brāhmaṇa is] the counter-correlative. He states the justification for the connection of difference with the meaning of the second member as the counter-correlative by saying "tathā ca."

The connection of the four nominative forms beginning with "sarvanāmatā ca" is with the word "upapadyate. "Sarvanāmatā" means the designation (saṃjñā) of a pronoun (sarvanāman). The phrase "by the rule of tadantavidhi" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The underlying point is that otherwise, since designations and subordinate members (upasarjana) lack the status of being "sarva" etc., if that [designation] were a qualifier of the negative compound (nañ-ratha), the application of that designation would be untenable.

The point is this: if one accepts the understanding of "aneka" (many) and so forth as "that which is different from one," then because duality or plurality must necessarily exist in that which possesses a difference having "one" as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of using the dual or plural endings to express that [meaning]. Furthermore, since the meaning of oneness is sublated (*bādha*) in that context, the use of the singular ending to express it would be untenable.

Regarding the term *tatpuruṣatvam*: if there were a distinction [in the sense] of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), that would be untenable. *Pūruṣa* means "person" as designated by the triad beginning with *tva* (the second person suffix). *Vacana* means having the form of the singular number and so forth. In cases such as "you two are" (*ayuvāṃ bhavathaḥ*), since the cognition has the absence of the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* as its qualifier (*viśeṣyaka*), duality and other numbers are sublated; therefore, the dual suffix and so forth would be untenable. The point is that according to your own accepted principle—"number is construed only with that which is connected to the *bhāvanā*"—it is impossible to justify the dual suffix and so forth by taking the number residing in another referent.

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means that if the absence (*abhāva*), which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), were a qualifier of the meaning of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārtha*), then [that absence] would be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); such is the sense. "The restriction regarding persons" (*puruṣavyavasthā*) means that since the two rules beginning with "when *yuṣmad* is an upapada" (*yuṣmadyupapade*) would not apply, the rule "the first person [is used] in the remainder" (*śeṣe prathamaḥ*) would take effect, resulting in the occurrence of only the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*). "It is not untenable" (*nānupapannam*) means that, in this way, the aforementioned restriction is easily established; this is the intention.

Now, if the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) were to connect with the meaning of the subsequent word as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then in the case of "bring the non-pot" (*aghaṭam ānaya*), since the pot possesses the status of being the counter-correlate of its own absence, it would follow that even the bringing of the pot would be required after that cognition. Therefore, the root text says: "or the qualificand" (*viśeṣyo vā*). To address the requirement for a qualifier, the *Sāra* states: "the counter-correlate," which means the counter-correlate in the form of the meaning of the subsequent word.

The state of being determined (*nirūpitatva*) is expressed by the locative case. That is to say, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is that which is the substratum of the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatā*) residing in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), which is the meaning of the subsequent member [of the compound]. Now, one might object: "In that case, if the meaning of the subsequent member is not predominant, the multitude of faults mentioned previously would be difficult to avoid. To this he says: "The underlying intention is as follows" (*ayam bhāvaḥ*). The phrase "even though it is secondary" (*gauṇatve 'pi*) means even though the meaning of *etad* and so forth, which constitutes the negative compound, serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the negative particle. The phrase "due to an indicator" (*jñāpakāt*) means due to the indicator found in the mention of "negative compounds" (*anañ-samāsa*) in that rule. He elaborates on this very indicatory nature with the example: "not a Śiva" (*aśivaḥ*).

By the rule *etattadoḥ*, the elision of the case-ending *su* after the pronouns *eta-* and *tad-* when followed by a consonant (*hal*) is prescribed due to their mutual association (*sāhacarya*). Since *eta-* and *tad-* would not be considered pronominal (*sarvanāman*) when they are subordinate members (*upasarjana*) within a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the rule]; thus, the inclusion of the term *anañ-samāsa* (non-negative compound) would otherwise be redundant. However, its purpose is fulfilled by indicating that even when the meaning is subordinate in a negative compound, the initial member of the class beginning with *sarva-* retains its status as a pronoun. Suggesting that this principle of association is not universally applicable, the author states another authority for the fact that the Sūtra refers specifically to the two pronouns (*sarvanāman*) alone:

The meaning is that because *aka* is not a pronominal (*asarvanāman*), and since the suffix *akac* is prescribed for pronouns, its exclusion leads to the determination that only those two [words] which are pronouns are being referred to. In this interpretation, the meaning of the rule *etattadoḥ sulopo 'kor anañsamāse hali* is as follows. The explanation based on relying upon a relationship mediated by meaning (*arthadvārakasambandha*) is intended either according to the previous interpretation or with the intention of treating the subsequent word as a technical designation (*uttarapadalakṣaṇā*). Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the substantive" (*viśeṣyānurodhāt*):

the sense is that in the absence of an explicit grammatical rule governing the substantive, there is a fixed rule that the word expressing the qualifier must agree in number with the word expressing the substantive.

[Objection: But surely, even if the qualifier possesses a number contrary to the number of the qualified, there is no evidence for the claim that it is expressed by the word denoting the qualifier; therefore, he says "Furthermore" (kiñca). [Objection: Since the dual or plural would be established simply by the employment of the words "two" or "many," and thus the dual and plural could also serve the purpose of maintaining the convention, the employment of the singular would be entirely useless; therefore, he says "Or it is the general rule" (autsargikaṃ vā).

The meaning is that the rule "the singular number shall be used as the general rule" (*ekavacanam utsargataḥ kariṣyate*) is established by the foundational statement "not [in the case of] mere [individuals]" (*na kevalāḥ*). He states that in certain instances where there is a specific intention (*tātparya*), even a meaningful singular number is indeed accepted; this refers to the phrase "each one" (*pratyekam*), which means for the sake of producing a cognition of the connection with the act of serving each individual among the women presented as distinct from one another. He concludes with "but not... (*na tu*); "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) means because the word *aneka* has the sense of being distinct from a single entity.

"It is easily established" means that if [the compound] were to have as its referent a single object that is the counter-correlate of the difference (*bhedapratiyogī*), it would be difficult to establish; the intention is that supporting [the usage] through *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is a resort only when no other way remains. In the example cited in the Bhāṣya, "naikastiṣṭhati," the word "janaḥ" (people/person) must be supplied. Furthermore, the singular number there is for the purpose of conveying the connection with the act of staying for each individual. However, "anekojanaḥ" is simply ungrammatical. It should also be understood that designations such as "predominance of the meaning of the latter member" (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*) are merely conventional.

By the phrase "you are not" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*), "I am not" (*anahambhavāmi*) and so forth are indicated; the mention of *yuṣmad* (the word for "you") is also indicative of *asmad* (the word for "I"). Similarly, in the case of "distinct from you" (*tvadbhinnaḥ*), there is also indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, this is according to the Naiyāyikas and others, because in our own system that [notion of indication] is not accepted. The point is that since the cognition of superimposition (*āropa*) and so forth in cases such as "you are not" is contrary to universal experience, it is more appropriate that in all instances of negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*), the final member (*uttarapada*) possesses a meaning distinct from its own primary sense (*svārtha-bhinna-lākṣaṇikatva*).

He states the rule for the negative particle *nañ* when it has the sense of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*): "In this way, [in expressions] such as 'you do not cook' (*na tvaṃ pacasi*), if the referent of 'you' (*yuṣmad-artha*) were connected with the meaning of the negative particle, then the established distinction of person (*puruṣa-vyavasthā*) regarding the base form would not be established. To indicate this, the second-person pronoun is employed in the expression "you cook" (*pacasi*). More on this has already been stated at the beginning. This is also an illustration [of the problem], for in cases such as "the two pots do not exist" (*ghaṭau na staḥ*), the use of the dual number and so forth would be untenable.

The reason for [the claim that] a cognition having a specific absence whose counter-positive is an action as its qualificandum is stated: because of the previous explanation of the word *asamasta* (non-compounded), it was previously stated that the occurrence of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the cause, through the relation of being a qualificandum delimited by the nature of productive activity (*bhāvanātva*), for a cognition in which the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—namely, a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—is related to the qualificandumhood residing in such an absence denoted by the negative particle via the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*). This is the intended meaning.

Now, in what form is the denotability (*śakyatā*) of absence (*abhāva*)? It cannot be in the form of "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*), for that would result in the cognition of a difference [rather than the absence itself], as in the case of "Caitra does not cook. Even if its denotability were in the form of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the same fault would remain, because difference (*bheda*) is also an object of perception produced by the non-apprehension of the fit (*yogyānupalabdhi*). Furthermore, even when that [difference] is not present, the negative particle (*nañ*) brings about the cognition of absence; therefore, he says: "And that," which means "and absence. Thus, there is no fault, because the negative particle is assumed to have a denotative power (*śakti*) toward absence either as mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) or as absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*).

Regarding the term *atyantābhāvatva*: "extreme" (*atyanta*) means that which has transcended (*atikrānta*), i.e., deviated from, the state of being the counter-positive of an absence residing in its own counter-positive (*svapratiyoginiṣṭhābhāvapratiyogitva*). It is a compound analyzed as "that which is both this [extreme] and an absence. Its state (*bhāva*) is its essence (*tattva*). This amounts to saying: the state of being an absence that deviates from being the counter-positive of an absence similar to itself that resides in its own counter-positive. This is because Amara Siṃha, in stating "the end (*anta*) is the lowest (*jaghanya*), the last," indicates that the word *anta* functions in the sense of "lowest. And the quality of being "lowest" is understood through the word's application to the "hips" (*jaghana*), which conveys the aforementioned meaning.

The absolute absence of a jar exists in a property residing in the jar that lacks the status of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the jar itself; therefore, its [the definition's] applicability remains intact there. However, the mutual absence of a jar is excluded because it is pervaded by the status of being the counter-positive of a mutual absence residing in its own counter-positive. This is merely an illustration of the etymological derivation; the actual definition of absolute absence, however, is: "an absence whose counter-positiveness is not delimited by the relation of identity or any other relation."

Regarding the term *anyonyābhāva* (mutual non-existence): based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "non-existence" (*abhāva*) or "the state of not being" (*abhavana*) in one another through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), the nature of mutual non-existence is the state of being an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of identity. The meaning is that [the word "non-existence"] denotes these two [types of absence]. However, in reality, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is denotable only by its nature as an absence, and not by the aforementioned form [of mutual non-existence], because of the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) and because such a cognition is never experienced. For this very reason, in the rule "tatsādṛśyamabhāvaśca" (Pāṇini 5.2.11), absolute non-existence is included specifically by its nature as an absence.

Nor should it be argued that if one does not accept the denotation (*śakti*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) as being the property of "absence" (*abhāvatva*) whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then the cognition produced by the sentence "There is no jar on the ground" would fail to be an inhibitor of the cognition of a jar qualified by the ground through the relation of conjunction; for an absence-cognition can only inhibit a qualified cognition when it apprehends the counter-correlativity of that [qualifier] as being delimited by that very same relation.

Even if there were a denotative power (*śakti*) for the word *nañ* based on its being an absence (*abhāva*), since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other relations must be included in the definition [of the relation between the counter-positive and its absence] as a general form—namely, as a relation other than identity—it would be impossible for the specific property of having a counter-positivity delimited by conjunction to appear through the denotative power of the word *nañ*. Consequently, the impossibility of [the absence] being a sublater (*pratibandhaka*) would remain as it was. For, in accordance with the requirement that it be an obstacle to such a qualified cognition, one must admit—by the force of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) alone—that the state of having such a counter-positivity appears specifically as the mode of relation between the counter-positive and the absence.

Now, it might be argued that if the property of being an absence-in-general (abhāvatva), which is common to both mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) and other absences, were the basis for the application of the word *nañ*, then it would be redundant to postulate a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for mutual absence. Nor can it be said that such a postulation is necessary as the determinant of the denotation (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) in order to account for the cognition of mutual absence as having "mutual absence-ness" (*anyonyābhāvatva*) as its qualifier; otherwise, because [mutual absence] is the opposite of the cognition of the counter-positive through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), even the cognition "possessing the absence of a jar" would result in being opposed to that [cognition of identity]. [Response: This should not be said.

In that case, since the property of being an absence (*abhāvatva*) is obtained through the power of the negative particle (*nañ*) as having a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), and since this is secured by the force of the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consisting in the co-occurrence of words denoting the counter-correlate and the substratum (*anuyogin*) with identical case-endings, the status of those respective cognitions as obstructors is established simply by their apprehending the nature of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvatva*)—which is the state of being an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of identity. Therefore, it is of no consequence to postulate a separate expressive power (*śakti*) for [the negative particle] in that specific form.

Nor should it be argued that there is no power (śakti) at all for that [the word *nañ*] with respect to its delimited object, and that the separate mention [of mutual absence] is merely for the sake of obtaining the status of being the meaning of *nañ* as a general category of absence; for if that were the case, the statement "six meanings of *nañ* are proclaimed" would result in inconsistency. This would indeed be so, provided that mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) could be defined as an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). But that is not possible, because the identity of a conjunct (*saṃyogitādātmya*) is itself of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and thus the definition would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to the absolute absence of conjunction (*saṃyogātyantābhāva*).

Even if one introduces the deliminatorhood (*avacchedakatā*) residing in identity (*tādātmya*) by way of the relation, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the absolute absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the property of conjunction and delimited by the relation of conjunction remains as it was. However, if that [deliminatorhood]—refined by introducing a relationhood (*saṃsargatā*) of identity delimited by the nature of identity (*tādātmyatva*)—is taken as the deliminator of the denotable meaning (*vācyatāvacchedaka*), then the usage "the cloth is not a pot by way of identity" (*ghaṭas tādātmyena na paṭaḥ*) would be untenable.

And thus, it is also established by valid cognition that identity (*tādātmya*) is the relation that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha*) of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). This is because there is a cognition such as "This is not a pot by way of identity," just as there is the cognition "There is no pot here by way of conjunction. Furthermore, being qualified by a specific kind of objective-ness (*anuyogitāviśeṣa-prakāratā*) is precisely the determinant for a cognition having the counter-correlate as its qualifier to be opposed by a cognition through the relation of non-difference (*abheda*). Therefore, in accordance with this, it is necessary that the negative particle (*nañ*) possesses a distinct denotative power (*śakti*) toward mutual absence.

Objection: If the negative particle (*nañ*) signifies absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) without requiring a qualifier, then there would be the unwanted consequence that absolute non-existence appears in the cognition produced by sentences such as "There is no jar on the floor. Nor can you argue that this consequence does not arise because the knowledge of the co-occurrence of the locative case immediately following the word denoting the locus (*anuyogi*) is a necessary cause for the cognition of absolute non-existence generated by the negative particle; for such a causal relationship is impossible, as it is contradicted by the case of the cognition of the absolute non-existence of an action (*bhāva*) produced by sentences such as "Caitra does not cook."

On this point, they say: since it is accepted that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) only where there is an expectancy conducive to the cognition of a relation between the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) in the form of the locus-located relationship (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), there is no possibility of such a cognition in the aforementioned case, because in that instance there is an absence of the expectancy conducive to such a cognition when the negative particle is co-uttered (*samabhivyāhāra*).

In cases such as "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*) and "This is not Caitra's" (*nedaṃ caitrasya*), when the negative particle (*nañ*) is co-occurrent, there exists an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—in the form of the co-occurrence of the nominative-ending word and so forth—which serves as the basis for understanding the relation between the locus and the located between the meaning of the verbal suffix (such as *kṛti*, i.e., effort) and Caitra (presented by the nominative-ending word), and between the meaning of the word "this" (*idam*) and the genitive sense of ownership (*svatva*). Consequently, it is possible for the negative particle to convey the absence of that effort and so forth in those instances.

And thus, where the cognition of the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) between the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) is untenable without the locative case, the locative is required even from the word denoting the substratum; for example, in "There is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale na ghaṭaḥ*). As stated by the author of the *Dīdhiti*: "In reality, in cases such as 'Caitra does not cook' or 'This is not Maitra's,' the locative is not required by the negative particle (*nañ*) for the cognition of the absence of the relation of effort (*kṛti*), which is the meaning of the case-ending, but it is required for the cognition of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)."

Furthermore, there is no inconsistency regarding the dual and plural endings in sentences such as *caitro na pacati* ("Caitra does not cook") or *caitro na pacataḥ* ("Caitra and [another] do not cook"), because in your view, number must necessarily conjoin with that which the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) conjoins; thus, when the absence of productive activity—which is what the negative particle conveys—is itself the object of conjunction, it is impossible for duality and so forth to be conveyed by the dual ending and the like, since duality and so forth would be absent from that which the productive activity conjoins.

However, it must be said that according to the view of the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), since the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys precisely the absence of the action denoted by the verbal root, they accept the cognition "the absence of an action whose agent is Caitra as qualified by duality, etc."; thus, there is no such logical inconsistency.

When a negative particle (*nañ*) is employed, the number associated with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅartha-saṃkhyā*) is construed with the absence of the productive operation (*bhāvanābhāva*); this is because we accept an alternative grammatical rule (*vyutpattyantara*) that accounts for the occurrence of dual and plural endings. Furthermore, even in your own view, since it would be impossible to employ the expression "Caitra does not cook" in a case where a cooking action having Caitra as its agent is unknown—because a negative particle cannot convey an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is an action.

Nor should it be argued that in such cases the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys only a difference, and that because this [difference], qualified by Caitra and others as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), is construed with the agent—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—there is no inconsistency in such usage. For if that were so, your own established doctrine would be contradicted; for the causal relation whereby the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the uninflected negative particle is a cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the verbal root related by the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*) would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) precisely in these instances.

When used in conjunction with a negative particle (*nañ*), just as [the verb] possesses a meaning that relates to the *bhāvanā* denoted by the verbal suffix, so too, when used in conjunction with [the negative], the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*) and others possess the property of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in having a meaning that relates to the *bhāvanā*. Therefore, there is no lack of justification for the use of the second person and other persons in expressions such as "you do not cook" (*na tvaṃ pacasi*).

Alternatively, when used in conjunction with the negative particle (*nañ*), [the word] conveys its own status as the agent of cognition; however, when used in conjunction with that [negative particle], the person's [status as agent] is established by taking recourse to what was previously [the case]. This, however, should be noted: based on the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that "when used in conjunction with the negative particle, the relation between the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) appears, whereas when used in conjunction with that [negative particle], the absence of that [counter-correlative], delimited by that relation, appears in that substratum," there is no cognition of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground"; rather, the restrictive factor for that has already been stated at the outset.

However, because it is accepted that the effect-ness-determiner (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the verbal cognition of an absence qualified by a jar as its qualifier—occurring through the relation of a counter-positivehood delimited by jar-ness—is the verbal cognition of an absence qualified by jar-ness, [arising] from a word such as *nañ* co-occurring with a word that presents a jar qualified by jar-ness; and likewise, because the effect-ness-determiner for the verbal cognition of a blue jar as its qualifier—occurring through the relation of a counter-positivehood delimited by blue-jar-ness—is the verbal cognition of a blue jar, [arising] from the word *nañ* co-occurring with a word that presents a jar which requires [an adjunct] such as "blue"; therefore, the sentence "A blue jar is not a jar" does not [result].

There would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of such usages as [the sentence being interpreted as "the jar is yellow"], yet there is the justification for usages such as "the jar is yellow, not a blue jar. Intending to state that this and other matters should be understood from elsewhere, he says: "This and so forth is explained elsewhere.
Thus ends the examination of the meaning of the negative particle (nañ) in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa. || 7 ||

With the intention of providing an incidental investigation into the meanings of prefixes (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*), he introduces the root text: "The words beginning with *pra* are indicators" (*dyotaka*). This means they possess a power consisting of the nature of being indicators (*dyotakatā*). For this very reason, in expressions such as *prajati*, the meaning of excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); this is the intended sense. According to another view, however, he will explain that being an indicator consists in making the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) apprehensible.

In this context, regarding the word "yena" (by which), the pronoun "yat" does not refer solely to the reason stated in the latter half of the verse, but rather refers to other reasons as well; thus he says: "The sense is this. "Not the meaning of the verbal root" means that it is not something denotable by the verbal root occurring within that specific usage. "Because of the consequence" means because of the consequence of such cognitions as direct experience (*anubhava*) and so forth. "Not the meaning of the prefix" means that it is not something denotable by the *prādi* prefixes co-occurring with that verbal root.

Regarding the phrase "because it would lead to the fallacy of non-sequential connection" (*ananvayāpatteriti*), this is said while conceding the view that there is a mere cognition of experience (*anubhava*) and so forth. However, it should be understood that if one were to accept [the view] in reality [that experience is the meaning], then because [experience] would not have action as its meaning, experience and the like could not attain the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Now, one might object: even if experience is the meaning, since it occupies the position of the result (*phala*), there is no impossibility of [the prefix] *anu* being a verbal root, as it conveys a general activity (*vyāpāra*) connected with that [result]. To this, he says: "In cases such as *anugacchati*," etc. The meaning is that if *anu* here has experience as its meaning, then in accordance with that, one must also admit that *gam* (to go) conveys only a general activity; consequently, such a cognition [of experience] would be unavoidable.

The point is that, in reality, since the experience of connection (*anvaya-anubhava*) is sublated when the operation is already occupied by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it is impossible for there to be a connection [of the prefix], and thus there is no possibility of the prefix having the meaning of "experience. "Due to complexity" (*gauravāt*) means due to the complexity [involved] in taking a specific sequential order (*viśiṣṭānupūrvī*) as the delimiting factor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). And "likewise" (*tathāca*) means that because it is impossible for each member—whether root or prefix—individually to convey the experienced meaning as it is perceived, such is the collective sense. By the phrase "existence, etc. (*vidyamānatvādī*), "origination" (*utpatti*) is included.

The phrase "of this [word] *lakṣa*" has the word "in the sense of an object consisting of experience (*anubhava*) and so forth" as its ellipsis. The meaning is that the semantic expectancy (*tātparya-anupapatti*) which necessitates the assumption of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) depends upon the apprehension of that semantic expectancy, and that apprehension is dependent upon the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a prefix (*upasarga*). Now, one might object: by this much, it has only been established that the prefix functions as an indicator of semantic expectancy (*tātparya-grāhaka*), not as a suggester (*dyotaka*). To this he says: "And thus... (*tathā ca*). By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only the indicator of semantic expectancy," the exclusion of suggestiveness (*dyotakatva*) as a distinct mode of operation (*vṛttyantara*) is effected.

The meaning is that because the capacity of a verbal root (*dhātu*) to convey its intended sense regarding results such as experience (*anubhava*) depends upon its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a prefix (*upasarga*), even in the rule "prefixes [occur] in connection with action" (*upasargāḥ kriyāyoge*), what is intended by the phrase "in connection with action" is precisely the capacity of prefixes to convey the intended sense of that which has become a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇībhūtārtha*). This essential point will be explained further on. The word "therein" (*tatra*) means "in the case of being an indicator" (*dyotakatva*). The phrase "of transitivity" (*sakarmakatvasya*) is to be construed with the word "the non-arising of [this problem]" (*anāpatti*).

[Objection: "Let it be that [the root] is not transitive. To this, he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). The meaning is: "of the verbal root preceded by the prefix *upa*. And thus, the sense is that such usages as "Hari is worshipped" (*upāsyate hariḥ*) would be untenable. "But in the third case" means: in the view that [the prefix] expresses the meaning of the verbal root alone. The word "arrived" (*āgatam*) ends in a suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-ktānta*).

The sense is that, in the absence of the co-occurrence with the prefix *upa*, one does not observe such a cognition from the root *gam* without a specific power (*śakti*); therefore, when the root has another meaning, the prefix is obtained as the regulator (*niyāmaka*). "And in the case of *tat* etc. means: its being an indicator (*dyotakatva*). "Of those respective meanings" means: its being the communicator of those respective meanings.

The phrase "of these" (*amīṣām*) means "also of the particles (*nipāta*) such as *ca* and so forth. The expression "it certainly exists" indicates that since the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is observed in the accusative case in examples such as "the pot is being made" (*ghaṭaḥ kriyate*), there is no impossibility of the root *kṛ* having an object; thus, the intention is that there is no need for a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). The word "in these" (*eṣu*) means "in meanings consisting of direct perception and so forth. The word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means if one were to accept that the root *kṛ*, which is transitive in some instances by taking on a different meaning, were transitive in all cases.

The point is that if [the prefix *vi-*] were to express an activity conducive to modification—as in the expression "the wind transforms" (*vāyur vikurute*)—then it would follow that the verb is transitive; consequently, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), which is prescribed by the rule *akarmakācca* ("and after an intransitive verb"), would be untenable. In response to this objection regarding the inappropriateness of transitivity in cases such as "the teacher should be worshipped" (*gurur upāsyeta*), where the prefixes (*upa-ādi*) do indeed express meanings such as "worship" (*upāsanā*), he offers a resolution: "Now" (*atha*). The word "this" (*idam*) refers to the aforementioned problem concerning the inappropriateness of transitivity. "Proving" (*sādhakam*) means proving the status of the prefix as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*).

In the case of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), this undesirable consequence does not arise because of the qualification "other than a particle" (*nipātātirikta*); therefore, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*). The phrase "it might also be so" (*ity api syāt*) is a supplementary argument (*abhyuccayavāda*), because the conjunction (*samuccaya*) presented by *ca* always requires something to be conjoined, and thus the use of *ca* is impossible without employing a word that signifies conjunction. Furthermore, due to the inherent nature of linguistic power (*śabdaśakti*), prefixes (*upasarga*), which are eternally dependent on verbal roots, convey their own meaning only as qualifiers of the root-meaning; consequently, their use is impossible in co-occurrence with a demonstrative pronoun (*tad*). For this very reason, he will state later: "because they are to be resolved in the same manner."

If it is argued: "Surely, if particles (*nipāta*) are denoters (*vācaka*), the very sūtra 'a copulative compound [is used] in the sense of *ca* (and), etc. is the proof; however, since no such proof is found for the denotative power of prefixes like *pra*, it is more appropriate that they are merely indicators (*dyotaka*)," then consider this: have you perhaps covered your eyes to the proof consisting of sūtras such as 'the suffix *khal* is used after a root when preceded by *īṣat*, *duḥ*, or *su* in the sense of difficulty or ease'? By the phrase "the sixth case, etc.," the inclusion of the second case and others prescribed in those same senses is intended.

The meaning is as follows: since the presence of the semantic representation (*upasthiti*) produced by an inflection (*vibhakti*), in its capacity as the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), is the cause for that which is delimited by verbal cognition (*śābdatva*)—wherein the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) of the nominal stem-meaning is delimited by a relation other than non-difference (*abhedātirikta*)—there is no possibility of a connection based on difference (*bhedānvaya*) due to the absence of such a stem (*prakṛti*). "Otherwise" means: if the aforementioned causal relationship is not accepted. "Consequence" (*āpatti*) means: the consequence of the cognition of a connection based on difference. The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the word "etcetera" (*ādipada*) which includes connections based on difference. [End of] "Connection based on difference" (*bhedānvaya*).

The reading "the non-differential relation between the meanings of two nominal stems" (*prātipadikārthayor abhedānvayaḥ*) is questionable, because no one accepts that the cognition of such a relation has the semantic presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a case-ending as its cause, and because [the latter] has not even been introduced [as a topic]. Regarding the phrase "other than a particle" (*nipātātirikta*): the meaning is that since a particle conveys meanings such as conjunction (*samuccaya*), there is no logical impossibility of another word-meaning entering into a differential relation (*bhedānvaya*) with it.

Intending that the word *sadṛśa*—whether derived as "having an equal vision" (*samānā dṛk*) or, in the present context, as the conventional term for "similar," or as derived from the agent and object [of seeing] as in the Bhāṣya's statement "people see this one like that"—is what is being grasped, he explains: "by the similar," meaning "by the equal."

[Objection: But surely, even for that which has a different case-ending, there is the possibility of its connection [with the head-word] through identity, because it is equal [to it] in terms of being a noun (nāman) and so forth; therefore, he says "by a coreferential [word]. The meaning is that since similarity is intended to be defined as being presented by words having the same case-ending, the aforementioned fault does not arise. And thus, in the root text, after the word "anveti" (is connected), the words "through identity" (abhedena) are to be supplied.

In expressions such as "he cooks a little" (*stokam pacati*), because the meanings are presented by words with different case-endings, there is a non-identity relation (*abheda-anvaya*) even between dissimilar entities; therefore, he says "by that which has a different locus" (*asamānādhikaraṇena*). This means: [the meaning] presented by the base of a case-ending that is opposed in sense to the case-ending whose base is the word expressing the particular (*viśeṣa-vācaka-pada*).

Now, since the opponent who maintains that words possess denotative power has already stated that the grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) [of "name-meaning"] must be restricted because it excludes particles (*nipāta*), the objection is already established by that very statement. Therefore, the mention in the root-text of the derivation beginning with "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) would result in a different point being made; thus, he says: "The meaning is this," and it is as follows: By the phrase "never by way of division," which excludes the relation of non-difference between two terms in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*), the very derivation that "the meaning of a name relates to another through difference" is primarily demonstrated, and not the case of co-referential terms.
Likewise, there is another derivation; however, since that is introduced merely as an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntavidhayā*), the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Thus, the restriction regarding elements other than particles (*nipāta*) is stated specifically with respect to the primary derivation, and everything is well-established.

Now, one might object: "In the causal condition for the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns, the requirement that the words generating the presentation (*upasthiti*) must have identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktika*) should be qualified by the addition of the phrase 'other than particles' (*nipātātiriktatva*) within the word-component. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply"—this introduction (*avataraṇa*) is indeed consistent [with our position].

Nor should it be asked, "How can this be so, since such a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) has not been introduced? For by the very word "etcetera" (*ādi*) used in the root text, which demonstrates that a distinct syntactic connection (*bhedenānvaya*) is impossible without the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, the introduction of non-difference (*abheda*) as the basis for connection in cases like *dhavaśca* through the use of identical case endings (*samānavibhaktitva*) is also implicitly included; and it is precisely that co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) which is incorporated into the grammatical rule, as is evident from the way the root text is appropriately reconciled.

"Is it not the case that the very impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is the proof? To this he says: 'And [there is] prolixity' (*gauravaṃ ca*). "But is this objection not equally applicable to you as well? To this he says: "'Of us' (*asmākam*)"—meaning, of those who maintain that [particles like *ca*] are indicators (*dyotaka*). "Because they are indicators" (*dyotakatvāt*) means: because [particles] such as *ca* cause the apprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), which consists of the respective meanings appropriate to the words with which they are uttered in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*).

The point is that since [the meaning of] "it does not exist" (nāsti) and so forth is obtained by the very word co-occurring with it—as it is the qualifier of that [negation]—there is no separate presentation of it; consequently, because there is no syntactic connection (anvaya), the aforementioned instance is not within the scope of such a grammatical rule (vyutpatti). "For this very reason" means: precisely because the qualification "other than a particle" (nipātātirikta) is introduced into the rule. "Metaphorical" (lākṣaṇika): the point is that if the rule were composed of that [qualification], then resorting to metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) in that case would be entirely useless.

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that since the denotative capacity (*vācakatā*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) is sanctioned by the Bhāṣya, in cases such as "the pot is not a cloth" (*ghaṭo na paṭaḥ*) or "Caitra does not cook" (*caitro na pacati*), the absence (*bhāva*) which is the meaning of *nañ* must be construed as a qualifier with respect to the pot, Caitra, and so forth. To prevent a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from this established rule of interpretation, it is necessary to include the qualification "being other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktatva*). In this way, in expressions such as "the pot and the cloth" (*ghaṭaśca paṭaśca*), the construction of the meaning of *ca* ("and") with the pot and so forth becomes easily possible even without the presence of an expectancy generated by a case-ending (*vibhakti*).

Nor should it be argued that in the case of "the pot is not" (*ghaṭo na*), since the pot is the meaning of the noun (*nāman*), it would be impossible to avoid the difficulty that there can be no cognition of the negation (*nañ*)—which has the pot as its qualifier and the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-saṃsarga*)—without the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a case-ending; for precisely out of fear of this [difficulty], one accepts that words such as "pot" have a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the counter-correlate. This is because, according to the natural force of the dual number [in the rule], it is unestablished (*avyutpanna*) that there is a direct syntactic connection (*bhedena anvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns, provided they are other than particles (*nipāta*).

They say that the matter is consistent because one may postulate that, regarding the cognition [of the meaning], the cause is the presentation generated by the case-ending (vibhakti) through the relation of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) which does not reside in the meaning of the particle, and which is itself determined by a mode (prakāratā) delimited by the relation of difference residing in the meaning of the noun (nāman) distinct from the particle. Even if the aforementioned fault is avoided by restricting the stated grammatical rule (vyutpatti) to cases other than particles, the intention is that the impossibility of syntactic connection (anvayānupapatti) remains unavoidable in other instances under that view; with this in mind, he introduces the root text with "Moreover" (api ca).

The meaning is that this understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvayabodha*) is accepted by all; "and this" means this aforementioned understanding of the syntactic connection. "Otherwise" means if one were to accept that particles (*nipāta*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). He clarifies the contradiction with linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) [in the passage beginning] "For instance" (*tathāhi*), etc., [starting from] "from this... extraction" (*ata udīcoddharaṇe*).

[Objection: Surely, since the suffix *tṛtīyā* (instrumental case-ending) following the word *iva* easily conveys the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇa*), the connection with the meaning of *iva* is straightforward; therefore, he says: "of the word *iva*. [He explains: "by virtue of having a non-substantial referent" means by virtue of having a referent that does not admit of gender and so forth—this is to say, because it is a particle (*nipāta*). And thus, since there is no expectancy for a referent presented under a form that precludes connection with a *kāraka*, connection with a *kāraka* is impossible, and consequently, an instrumental suffix expressing such a meaning is impossible; this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "or even if [it were] possible": the disjunctive particle (*vā*) indicates a lack of firm conviction.

He states another objection—namely, "because the word *vaś* is never observed in an indeclinable form"—on the grounds that if such a form were admitted, it would be impossible to avoid hearing the case-ending and its phonetic manifestation after it. The phrase "due to the consequence of a lack of syntactic connection" (*ananvaya-prasaṅgāt*) is to be understood as referring to the view of the proponent of denotative power (*vācakatāvādin*).

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), because a third case-ending is untenable; for, just as in the case of a camel (*ustra*), the status of being the instrument of extraction (*uddharaṇakaraṇatva*) is absent in that which is merely similar in meaning to a camel. However, in our view, since the meaning of "camel" (*ustrārtha*)—which takes the form of something similar to a camel—is itself the instrument, there is no such untenability; this is the intended sense. Following that, having raised the doubt that a conjunction (*ca*) is impossible because it cannot be applied to something else when a suffix other than a case-ending (*sup*) is heard, he says: "And the hearing of case-endings (*supāṃ śravaṇam*)."

He demonstrates that the word *cakāra* (the letter 'ca') is indeclinable by stating "the third [letter] following the word *ustra*. He clarifies precisely why there is no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the meaning of that third case-ending by saying "resembling a camel," and so forth; the meaning is "of those respective word-meanings. The sense is that there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because of the established rule that the meanings of two nouns do not connect through difference (*bheda*).

[Objection: In that case, would there not be a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) there? [Response: To this he says, "because of sublation" (*bādhāt*). The sense is that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is constituted by difference (*bheda*). Here, this should be understood: for one who maintains that particles such as *iva* are denotative (*vācakatāvādin*), since the cognition of similarity and so forth arises through them, the requirement of the same case-ending (*samāna-vibhaktikatva*) for the two words denoting the correlate (*anuyogin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—even when there is a difference in gender or number—is not necessary; for there is still the status of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*). Furthermore, the case-ending for both the standard and the object of comparison is indeed the same.

Thus, by accepting the restrictive function (*niyāmakatā*) established through such instruction, the understanding that "the extraction is performed with an arrow as the instrument, which is the locus of similarity as described in relation to a camel" is easily established. As for the presentation of an alternative between difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), that stated by the author of the *Sāra* is indeed to be considered [as problematic], because the meaning of the final member [of the compound] lacks predominance (*prādhānya*); for predominance is necessarily defined in relation to something else. The phrase "the meaning to be indicated" (*dyotyārtha*) means the meaning presented by the function of indication (*dyotakatāvṛtti*). "That very same" (*tameva*) means "that which is to be indicated" (*dyotya*) alone.

The meaning of the phrase "because it possesses meaning" (*arthavattvāt*) is as follows: since even the status of being a "suggester" (*dyotakatā*) is a type of linguistic function (*vṛtti*), the possession of meaning remains intact for the suggester as well; therefore, there is no impossibility regarding the designation of "stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) based on that [possession of meaning]. For there is no rule stating that only either *śakti* (primary denotation) or *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) is the conveyor of meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "indicative-ness" (dyotakatva) consists in the word's capacity to establish a particular within a universal already presented by the word itself, rather than its capacity to present that [particular] directly? Therefore, since [the suffixes] do not possess meaning by virtue of that [direct presentation], the possibility of their having semantic value does not arise. To this, he says: "In reality... (vastutas tu).
