The point is that according to the theory of indicative-ness (dyotakatāvāda), because those [suffixes] are indeed devoid of meaning, the rule prescribing their elision (luk) after a nominal ending (sup) would otherwise be purposeless; thus, being purposeful, it serves as an indicator (jñāpaka) for the aforementioned meaning.

Now, one might object: since particles (*nipāta*) such as *svāhā* and others exist even though they do not denote sentient beings (*sattva*), that [rule] which has fulfilled its purpose by prescribing the elision of case-endings (*sub-luk*) for them cannot serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). To this, he says: "of a particle" (*nipātasya*). However, regarding the rejection of that Vārttika, he says: "kṛt-taddhita... (P. 1.2.46). The term "compendium" (*saṃgraha*) means that even a meaningless particle possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). He concludes with: "therefore" (*tasmāt*). And he cites the consensus of the Mīmāṃsakas regarding this view: "And it has been said" (*uktaṃ ca*).

"Fourfold" means that there are four types by way of the distinction between nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). "In a word" refers to those consisting of nominal suffixes (*sup*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Regarding the two types—namely, the nature of nouns and verbs—he states the reason for defining their meaning: "because doubt arises. The sense is that when doubt arises—such as whether the meaning of a noun is a genus (*jāti*) or an individual (*vyakti*), or whether the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is the activity (*vyāpāra*), the result (*phala*), or both—it is appropriate to define them. "Of those two" refers to prefixes and particles. "Operation" (*vyāpāra*) consists of either denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Those two—the prefixes (upasarga) and particles (nipāta)—are indicators of a meaning; that is, they generate the apprehension of an intentionality directed toward a specific meaning. That [meaning] consists of nouns (nāman) and verbs (ākhyāta). Since these are composed of verbal suffixes (tiṅ), primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa), their respective meanings are also investigated; such is the sense.

Although the status of being a noun (*nāmatva*) based on having a case-ending applies to prepositions (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*) as well, making their separate mention inappropriate, it is nevertheless stated thus by adopting the technical definition of "noun" as that which possesses an objecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a mode-of-being (*prakāratā*) residing in gender and number. It should be understood that even though prepositions are particles, they are included [in this context] according to the maxim of "Brāhmaṇa-Vasiṣṭha."

Now, one might object: since in the rule "the meaning of a verbal root [is modified] by a prefix" (*upasargeṇa dhātvarthaḥ*), the words *pra* and so forth are included as prefixes—which are subsumed under the category of particles (*nipāta*)—how can this serve as support for the view that particles like *ca* and others are merely indicators (*dyotaka*)? To this, he says: "The word 'prefix' (*upasargapada*). The phrase "in another word" (*padāntara*) means that in expressions such as "the face is like the moon," the term "prefix" serves as an indicator for nouns like "moon" because they possess meaning. Thus, the sense is that one should not be deluded into thinking that particles are denoters (*vācaka*) on the basis of that rule. Now, he refines the position that they are denoters, beginning with "Now, one might object" (*nanu*).

The phrase "by means of positive and negative concomitance" (anvayavyatirekābhyām) means that, as in examples such as "the face is like the moon," since the cognition of meanings such as similarity occurs when particles like *iva* are present, and does not occur when they are absent, it is logical that particles possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) just like words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*). An objection is raised: "Since they lack a power (*śakti*) consisting of intention (*icchā*) and so forth, how can they be denotative? To this he replies: "consisting of the capacity to convey understanding" (*bodhakatārūpā*). Thus, the very capacity to convey a particular meaning is what constitutes their denotative power; therefore, even particles possess denotative power just like words such as "pot."

Now, since it was previously stated that positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are useful for grasping the intended meaning (tātparya) of a word, they cannot be the cause of its denotative power (vācakatā); therefore, he says "furthermore" (kiñca). Regarding the phrase "in the manner already described" (uktarītyā): according to the principle that only what cannot be established by other means is the literal meaning of a word, in cases such as *prajayati*, the excellence (*prakṛṣṭa*) of victory is presented through the root *ji* itself by means of indication (lakṣaṇā), and thus the prefixes do not possess the meaning of excellence and so forth; rather, their utility lies solely in making the intended meaning known—this is the sense of the phrase "in the manner already described."

The sense is this: although it may be argued that verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like denote the agent and so forth—since their denotative power is established there through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—nevertheless, the same status of being denoters must also be attributed to prefixes (*pra-* etc.). However, others maintain that in cases such as *ajarghāḥ* and *acakāt*, since the agent and so forth are understood from the verbal root alone, the undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) follows if the suffixes are held to be merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

Nor does cognition in that case arise from the recollection of a lost case-ending (*luptavibhaktismaraṇāt*), because even one who is unaware of the elision (*lopa*) still possesses cognition; furthermore, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, by stating that the purpose of the rule on the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is the result of the elision itself, does not accept that cognition arises from the recollection of a lost case-ending. The scope for the restriction—that the relationship between the meanings of the base and the suffix exists only where the suffix has denotative power (*vācakatā*)—is found in cases such as *pācakaḥ* (a cook), which ends in a *kṛt* suffix.

There is no contradiction with rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* ("the *la*-suffixes [denote] the object"), because the meaning is "from a verbal root [occurring] in the context of an object or agent," and since the rule *bhāve* ("in the sense of the abstract action") is explained by all authorities as having exactly that same scope.

Nor should one suspect that because the verbal root (*dhātu*) everywhere has *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as its object, the *lakāra* suffixes would necessarily occur only there; for there is no fault, since the phrase "from that which has *bhāva* as its object" means "from that which denotes mere action alone. For this very reason, the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*—"the rules 'in the sense of *bhāva* and *karman*', 'the *parasmaipada*' from the remainder when [the agent] is the agent', 'in the sense of two or one', etc., are restrictive"—is consistent. They say that since these [suffixes] have their meanings not specifically prescribed, they are established everywhere by the maxim: "those whose meanings are not specified function in their own primary sense."

That is questionable: because in examples such as *vyatiṣe*, the agent is understood even without a verbal root (*dhātu*), the first [position] is weak; because by the same logic, it would follow that nominal suffixes (*sup*) would also be denotative; and because the dual number and so forth of a verbal root would be untenable. Furthermore, although the technical rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) results in elision, there is no obstacle to accepting that the cognition produced by the recollection of the elided case-ending is the result [of the operation]. Moreover, it contradicts your own statement that the dual suffix and so forth arise through the superimposition of duality residing in the agent expressed by the *tiṅ* suffix following the root.

According to the very method you have stated, since the meaning of *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) results in the sense that "the *l*-suffixes occur after a verbal root that denotes a *bhāvanā* qualified by an agent, a *bhāvanā* qualified by an object, or a *bhāvanā* denoting the *bhāvanā* alone," it would be impossible for the *tiṅ*-suffixes—which denote a *bhāvanā* qualified by their respective *kārakas* and so forth—to be established everywhere even by the maxim *anirdiṣṭārthāḥ*. Therefore, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) must be reconciled in a different manner; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

Now, if particles (*nipāta*) were denotative, then in expressions such as "the jar is not a cloth," the connection of the jar and so forth with the absence—which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and the connection of that absence with the jar and so forth as its locus (*āśraya*), would be untenable.

Since it is established by the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that "the meaning of two nouns is connected through difference" (*bhedena*), when there is a cognition having the meaning of a nominal stem as its qualifier (*prakāra*) by way of a relation of difference (*bhedasambandha*), the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the suffix as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*); and likewise, since the linguistic rule "of the meanings of two nouns in apposition" would result in a connection of non-difference (*abheda*), he says: "And thus... (*evañca*). "Futility of the rule" (*vidhivaiyarthyam*) means that, by such a Vārttika, the prescription of the technical name *prātipadika* (nominal stem) would be redundant.

(The phrase) "of that which is meaningless" means "useless," because since there is no deviation [from the rule], it cannot function as a qualifier; this is the intended meaning. "Because it has been rejected" means that the meaning of that [term] has already been included by the word *ca* ("and") itself in the rule "kṛt-taddhita... (Pāṇini 1.2.46); this is the intended meaning.

Out of a lack of satisfaction with what is about to be said, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*). By the phrase "from the context" (*prakaraṇāt*), the absence of *dyotakatā* (suggestiveness) as a function (*vṛtti*) is indicated. "Of us" (*asmākam*) means "of those who accept both positions. "The relation of cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) means that in the verbal cognition of a jar and so forth as a unified whole, the cause is the knowledge of the lakṣaṇā (indication) as determined by the word "jar"—this is the intended sense.

The meaning is that the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—namely, that the knowledge of the word-potency (*śakti*) regarding a pot or other object is the cause for the cognition of that object, and the knowledge of potency regarding conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth is the cause for the cognition thereof—is also necessary. "Due to the absence of any other postulation" means that there is no need to postulate anything additional beyond what is already established for each respective position, whether one adopts the view that words are *dyotaka* (indicative) or the view that they are *vācaka* (denotative).

"From this very reason" means because the reasoning is the same in both proposed alternatives. Regarding the phrase "that [prefix] is the expressive one," this is said with reference to prefixes; for Puñjarāja, in his commentary on the word *pratiṣṭhate*, explains its meaning as follows: "In the root *sthā*, the sense is the cessation of motion (*gatinivṛtti*), whereas the prefix expresses motion in the form of the absence of that [cessation]. The phrase "expressiveness alone" refers to particles (*nipātānām*), and likewise, "indicative-ness alone" refers to prefixes (*upasargāṇām*). This is the established view.

Alternatively, it is logical that particles (*nipāta*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). As for our view—that while others hold one [particle] to be denotative and the other to be indicative (*dyotaka*)—that very position is indeed not tenable; such is the fundamental construction of the argument. Now, regarding the rule *cādayo’sattve*, if one relies on a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) for the term *asattve*, there would be the consequence of an "unintegrated compound" (*asamartha-samāsa*) and the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); therefore, one must rely on an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) instead.

Thus, if one were to rely on the aforementioned definition, there would be the fault of non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding that [term] which is devoid of meaning; and if one were to include "being any one of those" (tāvad-anyatamatva), there would be the fault of prolixity (gaurava). Therefore, he says: "by means of the relation of capacity" (śakti-sambandhena). With the intention of stating the delimitor of the status of being the definiendum (lakṣyatā-avacchedaka) for that, he says: "the genus" (jāti). And the sense is that its establishment follows from its being the delimitor of the denotability (śakyatā-avacchedaka) of the word "particle" (nipāta).

Objection: Is it not the case that "nipātatva" (the state of being a particle) is not a *jāti* (universal) because of its commingling (*sāṅkarya*) with "hatva" (the state of being the letter *ha*) and so forth? To explain: "hatva" exists in that which lacks "nipātatva," namely the letter *ha* at the beginning of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and the like; "nipātatva" exists in that which lacks "hatva," namely the particle *ca*; and both coexist in the single letter *ha*. The core reason for this objection is simply the violation of the following rule: a universal (*jāti*) qualified by another universal must, by necessity, not be the counter-positive of an absence that is co-located with itself, when judged by the relation of "co-location with itself" and the relation of "inherence in what is co-located with itself. (In other words, two universals cannot occupy the same locus without one being subordinate to the other.)

The apprehension of concomitance in the absence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) is the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) for such a rule; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of those inferences that proceed solely by the force of that [concomitance], such as "the property of being a genus exists in this. For this very reason, the traditional authorities maintain that "the state of being an element (*bhūtatva*) is not a genus."

Even if one avoids the fallacy of *sāṅkarya* (overlapping) by accepting that "being a particle" (*nipātatva*)—as defined by the exclusion of "having a denotative function" (*hatvādi-vyāpya*)—is manifold, that very [property] remains unestablished because it lacks universal concomitance (*ananugatatva*), as it does not apply to all particles such as *ca* and others, and thus lacks proof. Furthermore, that [property] cannot be a genus (*jāti*), because the criteria for establishing something as a genus, such as being a delimiting factor of effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedakatva*), are absent therein. Nor is "being a delimitor of denotative capacity" (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) a prover of that [genus], for otherwise even "negativity" (*abhāvatva*) and "all-pervasiveness" (*vibhutva*) would result in being genera.

For this very reason, the author of the *Dīdhiti* refuted the generic nature (*jātitva*) of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) in his *Guṇadīdhiti*; therefore, he says: "or else, [it is] a *upādhi*. The meaning is: in a universal (*sāmānya*), that is, in a pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*).

The point is this: since both parties agree that prefixes (upasargas) must be considered either indicators (dyotaka) or denoters (vācaka), a doubt arises as to whether the property of being an indicator and so forth should be postulated as delimited by the property of being a prefix (upasargatva) or as delimited by the property of being a particle (nipātatva), given that both properties—being a prefix and being a particle—are present in the substratum. When there is a desire to determine the delimiting factor (avacchedaka), it is postulated as being delimited precisely by the property of being a particle, because that is more pervasive and thus simpler in its inclusion (saṅgraha-kalāghava).

Therefore, regarding the inference for God (*īśvarānumāna*), when there arises a desire to know the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*)—namely, whether "being produced by an agent" is delimited by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) or by "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*)—the established conclusion of the Nyāya school is that, due to the aforementioned parsimony (*lāghava*), "effect-ness" alone is that delimiting property, and not "pot-ness" and so forth.

On this point, they say: there is a partiality toward the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), where there is the complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of many properties as delimiting factors. For example, in the inference of being produced by an agent (*kartṛjanya*), "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is the delimiting factor for "being produced by an action" (*kṛtijanyatā*), rather than "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth. However, where the particular (*viśeṣa*) is also only one, then, due to the absence of the aforementioned reasoning, that very [particular] itself is the delimiting factor.

For this very reason, even though *vyāpāra* (activity) encompasses more [than *kṛti*], the Mīmāṃsakas have also accepted that *kṛtitva* (the property of being an effort) alone is the delimitor of the denotatum of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Just as, setting aside the perceptibility of substance (*dravyapratyakṣatva*), the visual perceptibility of substance (*dravyacākṣuṣatva*) alone is accepted as the delimitor of the effect of color (*rūpa*), so too in the present case, although *nipātatva* (the status of being a particle) encompasses more than its pervader, it is appropriate that *upasargatva* (the status of being a prefix) alone be the delimitor, since it is a single unitary pervader.

Because particles (nipāta) function merely as indicators (dyotaka), not as denoters (avācaka), and because their occurrence would otherwise lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) when they serve only to fill out a verse-line; and also because of the inference: "Prefixes such as *pra* and others are indicators, because they are prepositions (*upasarga*)."

Nor should it be argued that the indicative nature (*dyotakatā*) of *pra* and the other prefixes will be established by the very mark of being a particle (*nipātatva*); for that [mark] is not a prover because it possesses the property of being an "over-pervading" (*adhika*) condition, namely the state of being a prefix (*upasargatva*). Nor should it be argued that this cannot be an over-pervading condition because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) in cases such as *ceṣṭā*; for it is possible for it to be non-pervasive with respect to the pure probandum. Indeed, wherever there is indicativeness delimited by the state of being a particle, there is the state of being a prefix; whereas where the state of being a particle exists—as in the case of *nañ* and so forth—there the [state of being a prefix] is absent.

But surely [the suffix] has excellence (*prakarṣa*) and so forth as its meaning, because it is the object of a verbal cognition that conforms to the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of those [meanings]. In the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*)—"wherever something is the object of a verbal cognition that conforms to the presence and absence of another, it is denoted by that"—the examples are such things as a jar (*ghaṭa*).

Nor should it be argued that "not being obtainable by other means" (*ananyalabhyatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because while it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*)—namely, being denotable—it does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*) in cases such as the agent (*kartṛ*), which are objects of verbal cognition that follow the positive and negative concomitance of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). This argument is untenable; for, by qualifying the verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) involved in the stated reason with the attribute of "not being produced by implication (*ākṣepa*)" and the like, "not being obtainable by other means" becomes a pervader of the probans, and thus cannot function as a valid limiting condition.

Nor should it be argued that there is no "unestablished nature" (*svarūpāsiddhi*) [of the reason], because the verbal root itself has the sense of "excellent victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*), while the prefix merely grasps its intended meaning (*tātparya*); for the author himself has refuted the idea that the verbal root possesses the sense of "excellent victory. Nor can it be said that [the prefix] is the indicated object (*lakṣya*), because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) if properties such as "being posterior to *pra*" were included within the scope of the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). Therefore, one must maintain that the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) belongs to the verbal root *ji* (to conquer) and so forth, whereas excellence (*prakarṣatva*) and the like belong to the prefix. And thus, where is the lack of establishment of the reason?

Furthermore, if the meaning [of the prefix] were to be indicated by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then since there would be no distinction from the case where *ji* (the prefix *vi-*) precedes, it would follow that it must be included within the scope of the delimitor of the indicator (*lakṣakatāvacchedaka*). Nor does it entail the undesirable consequence of that meaning not being syntactically connected directly with the meaning of the root, because the aforementioned grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) qualifies [the term] with "other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktatva*). And thus, in cases such as *pratiṣṭhate*, the meaning of the root is the absence of motion, while the absence thereof is the meaning of the prefix.

If it is argued that there is thus a cognition "possessing the absence of the absence of motion" from that [perception], and that the subsequent mental cognition having "motion-ness" as its qualifier occurs later, we say no; for since the rule of grammatical derivation "pratyayānām" (of suffixes) remains active, even the cognition "possessing the absence of motion" would be as non-existent as a flower in the sky.

Furthermore, if such a theory of denotation were accepted, it would be difficult to establish the status of *pra* and other such words as *upasargas* (prepositions) in those instances, because they would not qualify the action (*kriyā*). For in these cases, the action qualifies the absence of the *upasarga*, rather than the meaning of the *upasarga* qualifying the absence of the action. The expressive function (*dyotakatā*) of *upasargas* should be understood in the same manner as the method established for *svādi* (case-endings) and others. As for certain *nipātas* (particles), however, they possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). Among them, the meaning of the negative particle *nañ* has been analyzed.

Furthermore, the meaning of *ca* (the conjunction) is fourfold—namely, conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth—as is clearly stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) under the rule "A *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of *ca*" (*cārthe dvandvaḥ*).

The meaning of *iva* is similarity (*sādṛśya*). And that [similarity] consists in possessing the attributes of that [object] while being distinct from it. As for the claim that similarity is not constituted by a negative particle (*nañ*), that is incorrect; for even in that case, its status as the meaning of *iva* is not lost, due to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "when joined with *nañ* or *iva*. The governing condition is the requirement that the two words expressing the correlate (*anuyogin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) must be in the same case-ending. Therefore, the form *candreṇeva mukham* is not correct in the sense of *candra iva mukham*.

The meaning of the particle *eva*, however, is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), and the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga-vyavaccheda*). Among these, in cases where it resides in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), as in "Pārtha alone is the archer" (*pārtha eva dhanurdharaḥ*) and so forth, the meaning is the exclusion of identity with another. And "otherness" (*anyatva*) is relative to the object denoted by the word co-occurring [with the term containing *eva*]. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Pārtha is non-different from an archer who possesses the absence of identity with anyone other than Pārtha."

In the case of the statement "fragrance exists in earth alone" (*pṛthivyāmeva gandhaḥ*), the understanding arises that "fragrance is that which lacks inherence in anything other than earth and possesses inherence in earth. In such an understanding, the co-occurrence with the locative case-ending, which functions as a qualifying inflection, is also a restrictive factor. If one does not accept the cognition of the positive concomitance (*bhāvānvaya*) here, it would follow [absurdly] that fragrance could also reside in non-earth (*pṛthivyām evākāśe*). Thus, when the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is understood through the particle *eva*, the cause is the word *eva* occurring immediately after either the word denoting the qualificand or the word denoting the qualifier ending in the locative case.

In cases where [the particle *eva*] is connected with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). For instance, in "The conch is white indeed" (*śaṅkhaḥ pāṇḍura eva*), there is the cognition of the exclusion of the absence of the inherence of whiteness as delimited by the nature of being a conch (*śaṅkhatva*). In cases where it is connected with a verb (*kriyā*), such as "Let the lotus be blue indeed" (*nīlaṃ sarojaṃ bhavaty eva*), the meaning is the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).

On this point, some say that in the case of non-connection (*ayoga*), absolute exclusion (*ātyantikatva*) is delimited; and that consists in being a pervader of the delimitor of the positive concomitance (*anvayitāvacchedaka-vyāpakatva*). Furthermore, the semantic power (*śakti*) resides there in its parts. Thus, they maintain that in the aforementioned instance, the cognition is: "the absence of the act of becoming blue, which is the counter-positive of an absence residing in the lotus."

In reality, however, the function of the particle *eva* consists solely in the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Since the apprehension of the exclusion of non-connection is understood as delimited by the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), even the co-occurrence of a verbal root meaning "to grasp" or "to study" serves as a restrictive factor; thus, while one says "knowledge grasps the object indeed," one does not say "knowledge grasps silver indeed. However, when co-occurring with another action, that [exclusion] is generally understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Thus, the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) are designated as being by way of co-existence with the delimiting property of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka-sāmānādhikaraṇyena*), whereas the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is designated as being by way of the delimiting property of the correlate itself (*anvayitāvacchedena*). However, the details should be understood from other sources.

In expressions such as "Where indeed will you eat?", even the sense of impossibility (*asambhāvanā*) is its meaning. In this way, the meanings of other meaningful particles (*nipāta*) should also be inferred. However, according to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), since it is impossible for the particle *eva* to be a direct denoter (*vācaka*), it merely brings about a specific cognition consisting of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). And that [restriction] is of various kinds, depending on the words with which it is uttered in proximity.

Just as knowledge grasps an object, in this context—since there is no grasping of the object under the delimitation of a delimiting factor—the cognition has as its object a cognition whose qualifier is a non-substratum; thus, it is understood that "grasping" has knowledge as its agent and the object as its patient. Therefore, it is composed of the aforementioned word-meanings. However, others hold that, rather than postulating a functional capacity (*vṛtti*) for various verbal roots and so forth in their respective meanings, it is more appropriate to attribute that [function] to the particle *eva* alone. Although, having introduced the topic of prefixes (*upasarga*), it has been stated:
"That [prefix] may be denotative (*vācaka*) because of the possibility of qualifiers, and it may also be indicative (*dyotaka*)."

Thus, the two categories of *hari* have been stated without distinction by the author, and he has followed that very approach. Nevertheless, certain possible distinctions, which are not indicated by the simple [roots] alone,
are manifested through their connection with prefixes (*upasarga*), such as *pra*, *sa*, and so forth.

Thus, by considering the conclusion stated therein, it is determined that prefixes (*upasarga*) possess only the function of indicators (*dyotaka*). Here, this should be understood: even for one who does not know [the technical category of] "prefixhood," because there is a cognition of "intense victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*) in cases such as *prajayati*, these [prefixes] do not have the nature of indicators. Furthermore, particles (*nipāta*) also possess denotative power (*vācakatā*) precisely by virtue of being particles, in cases where there is no way to account for the meaning without denotation. In some instances, they may also have the function of indicators, provided one does not accept the aforementioned reasoning; for example, in "with sharp arrows" (*śarairustraiḥ*). In some cases, neither [denotative nor indicative power] applies; for example, in *tu* and so forth, which serve merely to fill out the meter. As it has been said:

"Some particles are indicators (*dyotaka*), while others express distinct meanings. Some may be like suffixes (*āgama*), expressing a meaning through their combination. Here, the word "some" (*kecit*) applies to both [categories]. Thus, it being established that *pra* and so forth possess indicator-status by virtue of being prepositions (*upasarga*), while *ca* and so forth possess expressive-status (*vācaka*) by virtue of being particles (*nipāta*), the dispute—that indicator-status belongs to them as delimited by the property of being a preposition (*upasargatva*) and not as delimited by the property of being a particle (*nipātatva*)—is rooted solely in a failure to examine the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

However, *karmapravacanīyas* do not, like prepositions (*upasargas*), specify a particular action; rather, they specify a particular relation pertaining to an action. This is because their designation is etymological: they are called *karmapravacanīyas* because they "have spoken of" (*proktavantaḥ*) an object (*karman*)—that is, an action. As for *adhi* and *pari*, this [specification of a relation] follows solely from the purpose of the rule's formulation. For instance, in the example "it rained after the recitation" (*japamanuprāvarṣat*), the particle *anu* indicates the relation of the characterizer (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*), which resides in the action of raining and is defined by the recitation serving as the cause. The same should be understood in other cases as well.

For this very reason, they do not possess the status of *upasargas* (prepositions/prefixes). An *upasarga* indeed illuminates a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) inherent in the action (*kriyā*). And it has been stated by Hari:
"It illuminates the action, but it is not the denoter of the relationship;
nor does it imply the verbal root, but rather it differentiates the relationship. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: terms such as *anvādi*, which bear the technical designation *karmapravacanīya*, do not—like verbal prefixes (*upasarga*) in examples such as *prajayati*—indicate a specific quality pertaining to the action. Nor do they denote a relation, because that [relation] is already expressed by the case-ending itself. Furthermore, they do not imply an action—like the prefix *vi-* in *vilikhati* (he draws a line)—in cases such as *prādeśaṃ vilikhati* (he draws a line of one span), since in that instance the action of measuring is implied even without the prefix. If that were the case, the case-ending would have to depend solely on that specific action.

However, that relation produced by a specific action is the meaning of the case-ending (vibhakti), and [the particle] indicates that. This is because the meaning "having measured a span, he draws" is perceived; this should be understood further from other sources. Thus ends the determination of the meanings of prepositions (upasarga) and particles (nipāta) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. 8.

Having commenced the investigation into the meaning of names (*nāma*), and intending to determine the meanings of *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes that constitute names by way of an incidental introduction (*upoddhāta-saṅgati*), [the author] first states—based on the intention that the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) must be investigated because it constitutes a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—“The abstract...”. Since suffixes such as *ṣyañ* and *vuñ* also convey an abstract meaning in the form of a relation (*sambandha*), he says “of *tv* and *tal*” in order to include them. The phrase “the abstract suffix” means a *taddhita* suffix prescribed for the abstract sense. He explains the sentence beginning with “This is the meaning” and so forth.

The ellipsis for the phrase "ity uktam" (thus it has been said) is "on the occasion of the determination of the power of compound words. The meaning of "relation" (*sambandham*) is that, in the case of a compound, it is precisely the relation of the meaning of the prior member with the meaning of the subsequent member that appears as a property (*dharma*).

Regarding the position of difference (*bhedapakṣa*): the point is that according to that view, in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), the cognition is "a man distinct from one who does not belong to the king," and thus the relation to the king does not appear in the aspect of the man. Regarding "the relation between Upagu and his offspring": this means the relation consisting of the nature of producer and produced between Upagu and his offspring. Regarding "the cognition of the connection" (*anvayabodha*): the point is that the case-suffix following each respective word expresses that specific relation.

"But when there is an invariable relation" (*avyabhicaritasambandhe tu*) means: if one accepts that [the word] appears solely by way of the universal (*jāti*) which consists in an invariable relation. However, the reason for the lack of approval (*aruci*) suggested by the word "but" (*tu*) is as follows: since the suffix *aṇ* and others are prescribed after the base of the genitive case (in the rule *tasyāpatyam*) to denote a descendant in relation to [a person] such as Upagu, it must be admitted that there is a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) precisely through the inclusion of the relation denoted by the genitive. Consequently, in that instance, the relation itself functions as the qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the portion consisting of the descendant, and it is that very [relation] which constitutes the meaning of the subsequent abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

"Because it is impossible for the genus (*jāti*) not to be denotable [by the suffix]"—the meaning of "occurring in another sense" (*arthāntaravṛtti*) is that it occurs in a sense constituted by the root-meaning, such as the *ṭhak* suffix and others included within [the category] beginning with *ākṣika*. The intention is that the action, such as "playing at dice," appears as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) in relation to its agent and so forth, which are the meanings of that [suffix], through the relation of action and factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*).

The phrase "due to conventional usage" (rūḍheḥ) means that the specific meaning is well-established through some connection with the etymological parts (avayava-yoga). The phrase "from an undifferentiated form" (abhinnarūpāt) means that even though [the word] ends in a suffix, because the suffix has been elided (pratyaya-luk), it possesses the same form as the base (prakṛti); thus, according to the maxim "that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided," it expresses the meaning of the suffix as conjoined with the meaning of the base.

"From those [words] whose relation is non-deviating" means: that which has a non-deviating relation—that is, a relation consisting of inherence (*samavāya*)—is that universal (*jāti*) and so forth which is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in its own individual instances; [the word] expresses that which is qualified by such [a universal]. Therefore, [words like *rūpatva*] do not denote universals whose counter-positives are absences residing in their own substrata due to destruction by baking and the like. By the phrase "as stated," the particle "also" (*api*) indicates that even though [the word *rūpatva*] ends in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), the expression of the relation would follow through the case-ending (*bhāvapratyaya*) following that suffix.

"Because of the cognition of non-difference"—this is stated to dispel the suspicion that the suffix *matup*, prescribed in the sense of the genitive case, might signify a relation (*sambandha*). The phrase "for example" (*yathā*) is to be understood as the remainder for the illustration of the word "third" (*tṛtīyam*).

The meaning is that since, in the cognition produced by the word *sat* (existent), existence (*sattā*) appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) within the locus of the agent (*kartṛ*), that very same [existence] is also denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following it. Thus, the point is that in the aforementioned instances, because no relation appears after a word ending in an abstract suffix, the word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) has been employed in the stated sentence.

[Objection: But surely, just as in the case of "whiteness" (*śuklatvam*) or "existence" (*sattvam*), where the relation of whiteness and so forth with that which exists is not denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), so too in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), there would be no such denotation; for there too, it is possible that the king and so forth function as qualifiers (*prakāra*) toward the referent of the word "man" through relations such as ownership (*svatva*). To this, he says: "The direction [is indicated]" (*dig iti*). The meaning of that is as follows: in the rule "The state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*), the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth are prescribed to denote the abstract property (*bhāva*) which is about to be defined.

Is it not the case that there is a rule that the relation [of a suffix] occurs only with respect to a *jāti* (universal) and so forth by way of being a *jāti* itself? And thus, according to the principle: "Whatever property as a qualifier is intended by the author of the grammatical treatise to be conveyed by a base, that very property is what is denoted by the primary suffix (*tvādi*),"—since the *Bhāṣya* accepts that even from bases ending in *kṛt*-suffixes, provided they are distinct from those like *ruḍhi*, there arises a cognition whose qualifier is the relation, it is appropriate that this very [relation] be denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Therefore, the abstract suffix does not denote a *jāti* and so forth in the cases mentioned.

The reading is "denoting merely the substance qualified by the meaning of the base. By the word *mātra* (merely), the exclusion of the relation is intended. "Of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*)" means "of [suffixes] such as *-in* and so forth. The sense is that it is because they do not denote the relation, since that [relation] is not a qualifier (*aprakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "being a state" (bhāvatva) consists in being a resident of the meaning of a base while being the object of a cognition produced by that base? Since this [definition] applies to the relation with a staff (*daṇḍasaṃbandha*), its denotation will occur through the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). To this he says: "cognition produced by the base. The point is that if "being a state" were defined merely by the aforementioned [first] condition, then even the relation between a genus and a quality—such as in the case of *dāmodaratva*—would undesirably result in having the meaning of a state. He states the purpose of excluding each of the two parts of the definition in order: "otherwise," which means if only one of the two parts were adopted.

The phrase "taduttareti" means "following the words 'ghaṭa' (pot) and 'daṇḍin' (staff-bearer). Thus, the point is that just as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is not the meaning of a word in cases such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), so too in your view, "staff-relation" (*daṇḍasaṃbandha*) is likewise not the meaning of a word in cases such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*). Consequently, because it is not a qualifier (*aprakāratvāt*), it cannot possibly be the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthatva*), given that it is an absence (*abhāvatvena*). This is the intended sense.

In reality, however, the inclusion of the final case-ending (*dalopa*) is redundant; for since suffixes such as *matup* denote a relation (*sambandha*), in the cognition produced by sentences such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), it is the relation itself that serves as the qualifier (*prakāra*). Since the staff and so forth do not function as qualifiers of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), there is no over-extension (*anatiprasaṅga*). Even according to the view of a certain school of Mīmāṃsakas, who hold that possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) express a relation, one must still rely on the substratum (*āśraya*) implied by that [relation]. The intended sense of the statement "the relation is the qualifier" is that, if that were the case, suffixes such as *tva* would have to express that [relation].

He presents the Mīmāṃsaka view with the words "yattu" (as for what...). Here, in examples such as *daṇḍitvam* (the state of being a staff-bearer), [the property] is "inherent in itself"—that is, inherent in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), such as "tva" and so on. Since this is not possible in cases like *nīlatvam* (blueness), just as blueness and other qualities are not [inherently present in the word's own form], it follows that the relation itself must be accepted as the denotation of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). The point is that although the staff and so forth function as qualifiers (*prakāra*) regarding the meaning of the base, they do not constitute the "state of being" (*bhāvatva*) because they are not inherent in the base itself.

The phrase "by virtue of denoting a relatum" means that although the suffix *matup* is prescribed for expressing a relation in the rule "that which belongs to this, or is in this," the sense is that the status of denoting a relatum is necessary because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) seen in expressions such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*) would otherwise be untenable. The phrase "because there is no lack of an alternative way" means that it is possible for the relation itself to be an existent entity (*bhāvatva*). The phrase "right at the outset" refers to the *Bhūṣaṇa* commentary, specifically the section ending with the words: "In this way, the coreferentiality in cases such as *vaiśvadevī* is established precisely by the method already stated."

"Of yours as well" means "of the grammarian as well. "This" refers to the discrepancy consisting in the fact that in some cases there is denotation of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, while in other cases there is denotation of a relation (*sambandha*).

[Objection: But surely, if the adjunct (*upādhi*) is already included by the very fact of being a qualifier of the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*), then its separate mention is redundant. To this, he says: "produced by the base" (*prakṛtijanya*). And that [adjunct] is a unique property residing in the meaning of the base. Its uniqueness consists in: while not residing in anything other than that [meaning], it resides in all instances of that [meaning]. By including the positive condition (*satyanta*), the [property of] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so on—which is common to many—is excluded from being the unique property of a jar; and by including the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the exclusion of [properties such as] the individuality of that instance (*tadvayaktitva*) is achieved. It is in that form that the property is denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

In this context, since the referent of that term—such as a jar—is already obtained through the verbal root itself (e.g., *ghaṭa-*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) in respect to "not occurring in others" (*itarāvṛttitva*) and so forth, which cannot be obtained otherwise. Even there, the meaning is analytically distinct: "non-occurrence in others" is a negation (*abhāva*), while "completeness" (*sākalya*) and "possessing occurrence" (*vṛttimat*) are separate elements. This is because it is impossible for the abstract suffix to denote a qualified entity [as a single unified meaning], since the absence whose counter-positive is "occurring in others" would be over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), the absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the property of "occurring in others" (*itaravṛttitvatvāvacchinna-pratiyogitāka*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), and such a thing is contradicted in the case of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like.

In this context, regarding the cognition produced by the base (prakṛti), it should be understood that by whatever relation the property which delimits the state of being denoted (pratipādyatāvacchedakadharma) possesses the status of a qualifier (prakāratā), by that same relation it must not reside in anything else (itarāvṛttitva) and must possess occurrence (vṛttimattva). Consequently, there is no defect even if "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) occurs in time and so forth by means of the temporal relation (kālikasambandha) and the like; nor is there the manifestation of "possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth" (kambugrīvādimattva) in cases such as "pot-ness. However, in cases such as "knowability" (prameyatva), the portion consisting of "not residing in anything else" does not manifest because it is unestablished (aprasiddhatvāt); rather, there is only the fact of its occurring in all knowable things. Similarly, in the case of "oneness" (ekatva), the portion consisting of totality (sākalya) also [does not manifest].

Nor should it be argued that, under the view that the qualified is not distinct [from its constituents], there would be an impossibility [of the definition] in cases such as "existence qualified by being other than quality" (*guṇānyatva-viśiṣṭa-sattva*)—because [existence] does not reside in anything other than the qualified existence—or in "largeness" (*mahattva*) and so on, because [the property] does not reside in all large things, or in "large dimension" (*mahat-parimāṇa*) and so on. This is because there is no fault, provided the two components of the definition have the following intended meaning: the state of possessing a property that is (1) the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of an absolute non-existence that pervades what is other than that [subject], and (2) is not the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of an absolute non-existence residing in that [subject].

Regarding that, the first part [of the verse] is intended to exclude [the over-extension of the definition to] "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth in cases such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); this is the sense. "Application" (*prayoga*) means the employment of a word. "Ground" (*nimitta*) means that property (*dharma*) by virtue of which a word is employed when an object is known; that property is the ground for the application of that word. In cases such as "Dāmodara-ness," it is a genus (*jāti*), while in cases such as "whiteness" (*śuklatva*), it is simply a quality (*guṇa*). "Because it is a qualifier" (*prakāratvāt*) means because it is a property unique to pot-ness.

The meaning of the phrase "light and heavy" (*laghuguru*) is as follows: even if [the property] is denotable as the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of a substance, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the manifestation (*bhāna*) of its dimension (*parimāṇa*) and so forth in expressions such as "oneness" (*ekatva*), because the aforementioned uniqueness exists in dimension as well. Nor can it be argued that what is intended is the state of not occurring in anything other than that [substance] and the state of occurring in that [substance], qualified by being related to the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because, through that relation, dimension (*parimāṇa*) resides therein; for if that were the case, since the postulation of infinite powers would be necessary, let there simply be power in the property as such (i.e., as being a particular property), rather than by way of its being "not residing in others" and so forth—why endure such cumbersome complexity? As stated in the *Guna-dīdhiti*: "In [the word] *pṛthaktvam* and so on, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) does not intend to convey the absence of the quality which is the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*). However, the cognition occurs either in that form or as a property (*dharmatvena*). With this in mind, the author of the *Mūla* says "merely a property" (*dharmamātram*), the ellipsis being "either in that specific form or as a property."

By this, the suspicion that—on the grounds that the suffix *tva* expresses the capacity of a property (*bhāva-śaktatva*), etc.—there might be a possibility of expressing even a heavy (complex) property such as "possessing a shell-like neck" (*kambugrīvādimattva*) in cases like *kambugrīvādimattvam*, and likewise in cases like *ghātvam* by means of the suffix *tva*—is refuted as being groundless, because [in those cases] the heavy property is sublated. He states the consensus regarding a property being denotable by a *bhāva*-suffix: "qualified by those respective individuals" (*tattad-vyakty-upalakṣita*), which means "characterized by those respective individuals."

The meaning is: because [the word "pot"] has the nature of potness, pot-ness-ness, and so forth; and because it is the object of the suffix following the words "pot" and "pot-ness. He states the proof for the genus (*jāti*) being of the nature of existence (*sattā*) as described and for its being the meaning of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) with the words: "due to the difference of relata" (*sambandhibhedāt*). This serves as the proof for the position that "the genus is the word-meaning" (*jāti padārthaḥ*).

Due to the difference in its relations—that is, due to the difference in the substrata (anuyogin)—the very *sattā* (Being) residing in cows and so forth, which is perceived as distinct either by way of its inherence in all cows while not inhering in non-cows, or by way of its association with specific individuals (*tadvyakti*), is called a "universal" (*jāti*). The meaning is that all words are established as denotative of that [Being]. He clarifies this very point: "that"—meaning that Being (*sattā*) as qualified by this or that individual.

The phrase "the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*) is stated either according to the logic of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* [which holds that the word denotes the class] or with the intention of the position that "others say the action is the universal" (*jāti*). The term "great" (*mahān*) is an attribute of the self (*ātman*). By stating that in some cases it is the universal (*jāti*) and so forth, while in others it is the relation (*sambandha*), he cites the *Vārttika* as authority for the point already explained. He says "it is said" (*uktaṃ ca*) because, for the Vaiśeṣikas, the term "quality-word" (*guṇaśabda*) is well-known only in reference to color and the rest. He states its relevance to the present topic by saying "by way of being an attribute" (*viśeṣaṇatayā*). By the phrase "color and the rest" (*rūpādi*), there is an inclusion of taste and so forth, as well as qualities such as white and the like.

The phrase "in being the generator of cognition" means "because of the state of being the generator of cognition. The underlying sense is that, according to the theory of syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), since the meaning of the verbal root appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to the agent, object, and so forth—by way of the relationship between action and its factors—the [suffix] is easily established. The intention is that the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is not restricted to denoting only a genus (*jāti*), and so on. The word "therein" (*tatra*) means "among the abstract suffixes that denote a genus and the like. Regarding the phrase "of those denoting a genus," the remainder of the thought is "of the power residing in the object."

Regarding words such as "whiteness" (*śuklatva*), which denote entities whose nature consists of qualities and so forth, he says "of those denoting universals" (*jātivācakānām*) because it is possible for a universal to serve as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*). The phrase "of the abstract suffixes" (*bhāvapratyayānām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis [to complete the sentence]. The term "delimiters" (*avacchedikāḥ*) means that, due to their being present [in the cognition], they are delimiters of the power residing in universals such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) by way of a relation such as "locatedness" (*ādheyatva*), which consists in the totality of residing in itself while not residing in anything other than itself. Consequently, the power residing in universals such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is not delimited by "pot-ness."

The sense is that the unifier of the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) is precisely the property of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth. He states the resulting understanding as "subsisting in a pot" (*ghaṭavṛtti*). "Another alternative" (*pakṣāntara*) means another view, namely, that the suffix expressing the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) denotes those very words themselves. "Even for the purpose of indicating that" means even for the purpose of indicating the aforementioned Vārttika which contains the word "that" (*tat*); or alternatively, it means even for the purpose of indicating the Vārttika formulated with the word "that. By the word "even" (*api*), other alternatives are included.

In the *Vārttika*, regarding the statement "they exist by means of their own object" (*svenārthena bhavanti*), the word "own" (*sva*) signifies "one's own" (*ātmīya*). Thus, the meaning is that [the word] functions by means of its own object, such as a universal (*jāti*) and so forth. This clarifies the intention behind the following questions: how can there be another alternative view [regarding this], and how can a property (*dharma*)—namely, the word—possess the nature of being an existent (*bhāvatva*) through the recurrence of its meaning?

"This is the [intended] meaning": since it is well known that the meaning of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth functions as a qualifier for the substance-component (*dravyāṃśa*), he establishes that the word also possesses that [qualifier-status] by means of that example—*arthavat* means "like the genus and so forth. He states a unique instance (*asādhāraṇasthala*) regarding the word's status as a qualifier of the meaning: *harihareti*. By the phrase "there was someone," the impossibility of a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is a genus and so forth is suggested; this is because in the case of Hari and others, due to the absence of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*), there is no presentation (*anupasthiti*) of "Hareness" (*haritva*) and so forth as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Since a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) characterized by that [unexpressed] property as its qualifier is impossible due to the absence of the apprehension of its power (śakti), the verbal cognition must be accounted for by accepting that only the word already present [in the sentence] functions as the qualifier. The point is that how such a word is presented through its linguistic function (vṛtti) has been explained in the section on the determination of the meaning of nouns (nāmārtha).

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: the non-acceptance of the word's status as a qualifier (*prakāratva*) with respect to the objective aspect (*arthāṃśa*). It says "urbanites" (*nāgarikān*) because, for forest-dwellers (*āraṇyakas*), the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*)—which has the class-property-delimiter (*jātidharmitāvacchedaka*) [as its object]—is possible through direct sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*). "In this very way" (*evameva*) means: precisely by way of the word being a qualifier. "Unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) means: in the case of words whose potencies are not apprehended as qualified by class-ness (*jātitva*) and so forth. "By the distinction of class, etc. (*jātyādibhedena*) means: by way of those specificities. In some places, however, the reading is simply *jātyādirūpeṇaiva*. "Both" (*ubhayam*)...

The meaning is that the word has the form of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth. "Delimiting factor" (*avacchedaka*) means the delimiting factor of the [word's] denotative power (*śakti*). Now, one might object: even the apprehension of denotative power in the form "this object possesses this word" is impossible to assert at a time when the genus and so forth are not presented; therefore, he says: "not having the word as its qualifier" (*padāprakāraka*). "Specifically" (*viśiṣya*) means by way of the form of being the word "jar" (*ghaṭapadatva*) and so forth. Although, due to the employment of the word "all" in the phrase "all entities," it is understood in this theory that the word itself is the ground for the application of all words.

Nevertheless, since it is impossible to deny the universal consensus among people regarding the cognition of a pot as having "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) as its qualifier arising from words like "pot" whose power (śakti) has been grasped as such, and because one generally does not experience a cognition where the word itself is the qualifier in cases of well-known meanings, even in that [theoretical] view, it must be admitted that universals (jāti) and so forth are the grounds for the application of words (śabdapravṛttinimitta).

The *Vārttika*, however, should be interpreted as referring to a word whose meaning is not well-known (*aprasiddhārthaka*); for in that case, since there is no other cause [for the application of the term], the force of the *Vārttika* establishes that the word itself is the ground for the application of the word. For example, in the case of the five roots beginning with *ka-* (the *kādipañcaka*) which possess the power of the suffix *kup*. It is for this very reason that the statement made by the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ*—"there are two meanings for *anudātta* and *ṅit*"—and his subsequent remark in the *yathāsaṅkhya* rule, "a numerical correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśaḥ*) would result," becomes consistent.

Otherwise, since all nine [suffixes] would have the sense of *taṅ* and thus be characterized by the *ātmanepada*, they would all be understood as one; consequently, the mention of "two" (*dvau*) therein would be clearly untenable. For this very reason, the author of the *Sāra* concluded: "Both are delimiters" (*ubhayam avacchedakam*), and his intention was that "sometimes even the word [itself is a delimiter]. How, then, is the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) in that case? To this he says: "In some [cases]" (*kvacit*). The meaning is: "powerful in some [case]" means that which is the determiner of power residing in something.

And thus, in the context of the introduction of Nala and others as kings and so forth, since Nala and the rest—who are presented by way of their being kings—are manifested in the aspect of the word’s denotative power (*śakti*), it is not contradictory for the words "Nala" and so on to be manifested in that very sense; the point is that the apprehension of the word's power in the form "this is the denotation of this [word]" is what governs manifestation in a specific form. "The cognition is likewise" means that the cognition has precisely the state of being denoted by the word as its qualifier (*prakāra*). By the restrictive particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of cognitions qualified by universals (*jāti*) and the like.

And this [argument]—"this meaning is not incapable of being denoted by words such as *nala*, because it is a meaning"—is intended with reference to the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) through inference. However, if one accepts the apprehension of potency for the presented word as previously described, then the arising of a cognition having the object as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) is indeed untenable; for it must be noted that there is a rule of necessity that the knowledge of potency, the presentation of the word-meaning, and the verbal cognition possess identical modes (*samānaprakāraka*).

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that the apprehension of the specific denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "Nala" is not untenable; for there is no obstacle to the appearance of *nalatva* (the property of being Nala) and so forth—as the delimiting factor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*)—when they are the objects of the cognition of some property as being related by way of *nalatva*. Alternatively, this occurs where there is a specific cognition of the form "that which possesses [the property] through the state of being knowable (*prameyatvena prameyavān*)," wherein *nalatva* and so forth are the qualifiers.

Furthermore, regarding the aspect of cognizability (*prameyatva*), since there is no sublation to a recollection that has Nala as its qualificandum and the property of "Nala-ness" (*nalatva*) etc. as its qualifier—occurring at a time when [the cognition] is in a state of error (*moṣadaśā*)—it is easy to obtain the understanding of Nala and so forth from the word "Nala" and so forth in their respective forms, by means of the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) for "Nala" etc. specifically through those properties such as "Nala-ness" which constitute its objects. Nor is there a lack of evidence for postulating this state of error regarding the aspect of cognizability; for the very fact that the resulting verbal comprehension would otherwise fail to account for the observed qualifiers of those various properties serves as the proof.

Otherwise, how could there be a recollection of one object in a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) consisting of experience when the evocative factors for the other objects are not present? For it is more reasonable to assume a lapse (*moṣa*) regarding the aspect of knowability (*prameyatva*) in such a recollection than to assume that the word functions as a qualifier for the object-meaning—an assumption never before established. Furthermore, since a word is not a property of its meaning, it cannot possibly function as a qualifier for the object-meaning; nor is it possible for a cognition to have a word as its qualifier, because the notion that "this word has power (*śakti*) over that word" is unworldly and thus cannot occur universally. So they say.
Thus ends the ninth section, the determination of the meaning of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*.

[Objection: But surely, since the deity is obtained from words such as "Indra" and so forth, it is redundant to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for the *taddhita* suffix by including it within that [denotation]. To this, he says: "that which brings about the presentation of deityhood. The meaning is that even though the deity is presented in the form of Indra, there is no means of presenting it in the form of "deityhood" (*devatātva*). "In that form" means for the sake of presenting Indra in the form of deityhood. Otherwise:

"By the *taddhita* suffix, or by the dative case, or again by the indicative mark of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*), the connection with the deity occurs; and among these, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding."

The sense is that this is inconsistent with the established tenets of the Mīmāṃsakas. Furthermore, a substance’s relation to a deity consists in its being the object of a renunciation (*tyāga*) intended for that deity. Being the object of such a renunciation, moreover, means being the objective of a desire in a manner not contradicted by the Veda and characterized by the ownership of the substance. That alone constitutes "deity-hood" (*devatātva*). Consequently, even though the Brahmin who is the recipient (*sampradāna*) of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth is the object of the renunciation, he does not possess deity-hood.

Since that [lordship] remains uncontradicted, in cases such as "the mantra belongs to Indra" (*aindro mantraḥ*), the mantra's having that deity does not consist in its being the instrument for an offering intended for that [deity]. This is because there is no deviation [in the application of the term], since an offering intended for a deity can arise through a specific desire even without a mantra. Rather, [the meaning] consists in its being uttered as a constituent part of the offering. And this relation to the deity is the meaning of the suffix, not [the sense of] "having that deity," because otherwise the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the oblation for Indra" (*aindraṃ haviḥ*) would be untenable.

And that [suffix-meaning] is understood as a specific substance when it occurs in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as *āmikṣā*. However, the intention behind stating "the meaning of the suffix is that which is to be given" (*deya*) is that it is also understood as the object of the act of giving (*dāna-karma*) when it occurs in co-utterance with words such as *āmikṣā*. To provide support for this stated point, he says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), which means: precisely because the suffix-meaning is related to the deity. He explains "due to proximity" (*sānnidhyāt*), which means: due to its co-utterance with the word *āmikṣā* in the sentence "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*sā āmikṣā vaiśvadevī*).

The phrase "the offering of the object" (viṣayārpaṇam) means that there is the cognition of the substance consisting of the *āmikṣā* itself as the object of the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) intended for the deity. "From the mere [word]" (*kevalāt*) means from [the word] not co-occurring with words such as *soma*. "Of Agni"—that is, from the word *agni*—"appearing while reciting" means it manifests prior to the word *agni*, because it is a suffix; as in the passage: "There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni at the new moon."

The meaning is that [the word *nānya*] does not intend to convey a substance that is the object of an offering dedicated to the deity Agni as associated with Soma and others; rather, its sense is that it belongs to that deity alone. Thus, the intention is that even they (the grammarians) agree that the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is the thing to be given as qualified by the deity. Regarding the phrase "of the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyartha*), the intention is based on the linguistic maxim: "the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) connects with the meaning of another word (*padārthena*). And in this interpretation, the meaning of the base (the material) connects with the meaning of the secondary derivative (the deity) through the relation of identity (*abheda*).

And it should be understood that, according to the theory of *dyotakatva* (suggestiveness), this relates to the meaning of the subsequent word—the substance denoted by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*)—by way of the relation of being the object of a renunciation (*tyāga*) whose purpose is itself. Alternatively, according to the theory of *vācakatva* (denotativeness), since excellence (*prakarpa*) is the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*), there is no possibility of it serving as an example because one would not postulate a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the verbal root with respect to that which is qualified by it. The sense is that the status of being an example is to be understood by taking only the radical portion (*prakṛti*), as in the case of "excellent victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*).

The phrase "from the acquisition [of meaning]" (lābhāt) means that the deity, who is a related entity, is understood through the words such as "curd" (dadhi) mentioned in close proximity. Why, then, [is this so]? Because of the maxim: "The meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained from any other source. The sense is that it is more appropriate for [the suffix] to have the relation itself as its meaning. "From the cognition of that" (tatpratīteḥ) means from the cognition of the deity as a related entity. And thus, since that [cognition] would otherwise be inexplicable, it follows that the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) must necessarily have that [relation] as its meaning.

Since even the cognition of a relation [between words] when other words are not heard must be determined by the meaning [of the sentence], he says: "The *aindraṃ dadhi* [is an example]; if it were to express only the relation, there would be an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The meaning is this: "Otherwise" means if the aforementioned impossibility did not establish that [the word expresses the relation]. The point is that in the case of "the rice is cooked" (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*), the impossibility of coreferentiality indeed establishes that [the verb] denotes the agent and so forth. This is an objection directed at the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

Having cast a glance at the Mīmāṃsakas, he says: "Of the Mīmāṃsakas. The sense is that, according to their view, since the substratum (dharmin) is obtained through implication (ākṣepa) by means of the meaning of the suffix as having the form of being related to this or that [deity], the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is established. The phrase "from another word" is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of this implication. The meaning of "let the expressed object not exist" is: let agency not be the expressed object of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), or let substance not be the expressed object of the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita). The sense is that if this were accepted, it would result in the collapse of your own established doctrine: "The *āmikṣā* is conjoined with the deity."

[Objection: Since the agent (*kartṛ*) of those [karmans] cannot be obtained from anything else, it is not denoted by the suffix; rather, its status as such arises solely from its predominance (*prādhānya*). To this, he says: "The direction [is indicated]" (*digiti*). The meaning is that because the rule "between the meanings of the base and the suffix" (*prakṛtipratyayārthayoḥ*) is subject to deviation in the case of number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth, there is no predominance [of the agent] by virtue of that rule. Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency with the universally established maxim: "A verb is predominant in its action" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*), or "by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or the dative case."

Nor should it be argued that even if the secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix has that same meaning, how can the dative case be considered inferior to it, since both equally convey the deity in the form of the recipient of the sacrifice; for the meaning of the taddhita suffix is not merely the object to be given related to a deity, but rather [the deity] as defined by "deity-hood" (devatātva) as understood through the Veda.

And thus, because the nominal suffix (*taddhita*) involves an apprehension of the sacrifice’s status as a deity (*devatātva*) as being cognizable by the Veda, no suspicion of invalidity arises regarding that aspect; consequently, it possesses superior force as a means of application (*viniyojaka*). On the other hand, the dative case (*caturthī*) generates a cognition that does not involve the apprehension of the deity’s status as being cognizable by the Veda; therefore, it is subordinate (*jaghanya*), as it requires another means to dispel the suspicion of invalidity regarding that aspect.

Alternatively, when a deity is understood through its form as a deity by means of a *taddhita* suffix, there is a traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) stating, "that is its deity. However, there is no such traditional rule regarding the status of being a deity for the dative case; for the rule "the dative is used in the sense of the recipient" (*caturthī sampradāne*) establishes that it denotes only the recipient (*sampradāna*). And the state of being a recipient consists in being the receiver while having as one's objective the substance being relinquished.

And thus, although divinity (*devatātva*) is understood from that [dative case] by virtue of its constituting the status of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*), since divinity is not apprehended as primary—as it is in the case of secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) and the like—the dative is inferior to the secondary suffix. Similarly, although the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is understood from the wording of a mantra (*mantravarṇa*), since divinity is not directly apprehended, the wording of the mantra is inferior to the dative.

Thus, even though the presiding deity (adhiṣṭhāna) is understood from the wording of the mantra, since the status of being the deity itself is not directly perceived, it makes known that the wording of the mantra is secondary to the dative case. However, if one does not accept that the taddhita suffix has the deity as its meaning, then that [inconsistency] is clearly evident.

Now, one might object: since the deity is obtained through the primary power (*śakti*) itself from words such as "Indra," the acceptance of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that [deity] is useless; therefore, he says: "in the form of being a deity. Thus, according to the saying of the elders—"Secondary indication occurs when there is cognition by means of a form other than the primary power"—the intention is that although the deity whose nature is Indra is indeed the primary meaning (*śakya*), secondary indication is appropriate for the sake of making her appear as a deity distinct from Indra.

Even in the previously mentioned case of the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "Ganges" as ending at the bank—which is preceded by the cognition of its impossibility [to denote the water]—the term "conventionalized" (*nirūḍha*) is employed; thus he says "beginningless. This truth was stated earlier. Anticipating the objection regarding the contingency of partial syntactic connection (*ekadeśānvaya*), he says "playing with weapons" (*praharaṇakrīḍā*); the sense is that due to the variety of etymological derivations (*vyutpatti*), there is mutual connection even between two things presented by a single word. Intending that "one watch" (*prahara*) is also obtained through the verbal root itself, he says "merely playing" (*krīḍāmātraṃ ca*); the meaning is that it is precisely a relative [term] whose form is "play."

The word *mātra* excludes the possibility that the instrument of striking (*praharaṇa*) is the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "play characterized by an instrument of striking non-different from a staff. Regarding the suffix prescribed by this sūtra (*so'sya*), its meanings are "dwelling" (*nivāsa*) and "related to" (*sambandhin*). Here, the word *nivāsa* ends in the locative *ghañ* suffix; and by the prefix *ni*, an excellence in the form of continuity (*nairantarya*) regarding the dwelling is conveyed. Furthermore, that [continuity] is to be understood as being composed of specific durations of time, determined by context and other factors.

And thus, the understanding is: "one who has a connection with a locus of residence that is non-different from Sthurudhna. Furthermore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the act of residing (*nivāsa*) must have as its agent precisely one who is related to the meaning of the suffix. For this very reason, such a usage does not occur when the agent of the act of residing in Sthurudhna is merely occasional.

However, regarding the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) prescribed by the rule *sā 'smin* [Pāṇini 4.2.3], its referent is delimited by being composed of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). As for words such as *pauṣī* and others—ending in suffixes like *aṇ* prescribed for times associated with lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)—their meaning is "the time which is the locus of the moon’s conjunction (enjoyment) with a lunar mansion non-different from Puṣya and so forth. This [meaning] is conjoined non-differently with the full moon, which is a single part of the aforementioned referent. Thus, in cases such as "the month of Pauṣa" (*pauṣo māsaḥ*), the understanding is: "a month composed of a full moon that is non-different from the time which is the locus of the moon’s conjunction with a lunar mansion non-different from Puṣya and so forth."

Furthermore, the term *pauṣa* and others are not merely etymological (*yogika*), for there is an absence of such usage as "the month of Pauṣa is an animal" (*paśu*); rather, they are also conventional (*rūḍha*). It is precisely to indicate this that the word *saṃjñā* (name/designation) is included in the Sūtra.
