And the delimitor of the property of being a convention (*rūḍhi-nirūpakatā-avacchedaka*) is not merely "monthness," which consists in being a collection of thirty lunar days.

Even though the conventional usage of "month" and so forth applies to a collection of thirty lunar days (tithis) delimited by any given tithi, there is an absence of the conventional usage of "Pauṣa" and so on with respect to those tithis included within the thirty-day period that begins with Pauṣī—which is excluded from the Caitra-based lunar month and the solar month; rather, [the month] consists of a collection of lunar days beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad) and ending with the final day. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply; the details of this are explained elsewhere.

By the rule *tadasyāstyasmin*, a suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) is prescribed for a word ending in the nominative case, provided that it has the sense of "it exists," with respect to both the related entity (*sambandhin*) and its locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Although the mention of *asya* (of this) suggests that the prescription of suffixes such as *manu* applies specifically to a relation denoted by the genitive case, it was stated previously that—in accordance with grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in examples such as "Caitra is rich in cows" (*gomāṃścaitraḥ*)—the suffix denotes the possessor itself. Thus, in cases like "rich in cows" (*gomān*), the resulting cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) is: "one who possesses the relation of ownership characterized by cows," and so forth. And it is said: "In cases of abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, or a state of being, [the possessive suffix is used]."

One might suspect that because it is said, "When there is a desire to express a relation, the suffix *matup* and others occur," the meanings such as "abundance" (*bhūman*) are also denotable by *matup* and the like, since they are mentioned on the same footing as "relation. This would indeed be the case if a rule or similar authority were found prescribing *matup* and the like for those specific meanings; however, their status is merely that of usage (*prayoga-upapatti*), just like the word "is" (*asti*). Furthermore, the cognition of "abundance" and so forth is easily obtained through the words "cow" (*go*) and others functioning metaphorically (*lakṣaṇika*) with respect to the quality of multiplicity (*bahutva*) and so on.
Others, however, say that the meaning of *matup* is grasped from the word "is" (*asti*); the details of this are elsewhere.

The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) includes, by means of the word "etcetera," rules such as *tasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of that"), *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* ("colored by that dye"), and *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* ("prepared as food"). In cases such as *gārgiḥ*, the meaning of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), namely the offspring—which is a person produced—is construed with its constituent part, "being produced," as the relatum (*nirūpakatayā*) of the base-meaning, Garga; thus, the resulting cognition is: "a male who is the locus of being produced as related to Garga."

In cases such as *gārgyaḥ*, however, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), namely Garga, is construed with *janyatva* (the state of being born), which is a constituent part of the meaning of the patronymic (*gotrāpatya*)—that is, a person born from a person born [from the original ancestor]. In cases such as *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, the meaning of that which ends in a patronymic suffix is construed by way of being the *nirūpaka* (defining relation) with a constituent part of the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), namely the young descendant (*yuvāpatya*). However, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "But when the ancestor is living, [the suffix denotes] the young descendant," the contemporaneity with the life of Garga is also a qualifier of the primary meaning of the suffix, since that too is within the denotative power (*śakyatva*) of the suffix.
And thus, the cognition is: "This person is one who possesses the quality of being born (janyatā) in relation to a descendant of the Garga lineage, coeval with Gargajīvana.

The meaning of the suffix prescribed by the rule *na raktam* is that which is the object of the superimposition (*āropa*) of its own color, dependent upon its connection with that [color]. Such being the state of being an object of superimposition, that is what constitutes "being colored by it" (*tena raktatvam*). In order to exclude the case of a conch-shell and the like—which, by taking up the superimposition "the conch is yellow," is "colored" by the yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) that is the locus of the superimposed color—the term "dependent" (*adhīna*) is used as a qualifier for the superimposition. Furthermore, to exclude the case of a safflower-dyed cloth and the like, which is "colored" by the eye and so forth, the qualifier "having the form of belonging to it" (*tadīyatva-rūpa*) is employed.

And here, the base-meaning—such as madder (mañjiṣṭhā), which is the instrument of coloring—is construed with the referent of the secondary suffix (taddhita) as its counter-correlative in a partial relation, and with the color as its locus through the relation of superimposition. Thus, from the word *māñjiṣṭhaḥ*, the understanding is: "that which is the substratum of the objective state (viṣayatā) belonging to the superimposition of a color residing in madder, which superimposition is dependent upon the relation with madder."

In cases such as *śūlya* ("prepared on a spit") and *ukhya* ("prepared in a pot"), the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), namely the spit or the pot, is construed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the refinement (*saṃskāra*)—such as cooking—which constitutes one part of the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) prescribed by the rule *samskṛtam bhakṣāḥ*. In this very same manner, the sublation [of the primary meaning] by other secondary derivatives should be inferred.

Because secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) sometimes convey the meaning of a portion of their own referent within the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and sometimes convey only their own referent, the author introduces the root text by relying on the *jahatsvārthavṛtti* (the view that words abandon their own meanings) theory, stating "in every compound" (*vṛttimātre*). Thus, the intention is that since words would be meaningless under that theory, there would be a deviation from the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) in defining their meaning.

"In that very manner" means "in the manner of other treatises. Now, one might object: if the Vaiyākaraṇa position relies upon the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) type of function (*vṛtti*), what is the status of rules such as "na pūjanāt" and "tena raktaṃ rāgāt"? To this, he says: "superimposed," etc. [The phrase] "by a power belonging to the qualified [whole]" has the words "of the qualified meaning" as an ellipsis to be supplied.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), although the supplementation of the meanings of the constituent words is unnecessary under the *jahatsvārtha* (abandoning one's own meaning) view due to the acceptance of both sides [of the theory], it is indeed appropriate to define that [supplementation] under the *ajahatsvārtha* (not abandoning one's own meaning) view, because the apprehension of the power of the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) depends upon the determination of the individual powers. It is precisely to indicate this that the word "exceedingly" (*atīva*) is employed in the root text; such is the secret [of the author].
Thus ends the section on the meaning of the suffixes denoting deities (*devatā-pratyaya-artha-nirūpaṇa*) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. || 10 ||

One might object: "Is it not the case that while we are currently engaged in defining the meaning of the suffixes contained within a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the definition of the number 'one-ness as non-difference' (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*) is irrelevant? To this, he says: "Because of the context of the compound" (*vṛttiprasaṅgāt*). The sense is this: since we are in the process of defining the compound (*vṛtti*), it would be improper to neglect a property (*taddharma*) that has already come to mind; thus, because there is a connection by way of context (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*), the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Although it would have been more appropriate to define number immediately after the *kṛt*-affixes such as *ktvā* (which will be discussed below), since those also involve the function of *kṛt*-derivatives (*kṛdvṛtti*), nevertheless, because number does not manifest in the meaning of their base (*prakṛti*), the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) for its definition would have been interrupted; therefore, it should be understood that it is defined right here. Regarding the category of "non-dual unity" (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*), he explains it in two ways according to different views: "of particular numbers" means of those delimited by oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth. "Without division" (*avibhāgena*) means without distinction (*abhedena*), which is to say, without contradiction (*avirodhena*).

He cites the words of Hari as proof for the stated meaning: "And it has been said. The phrase *āhitaśaktayaḥ* means those by whom a power (*śakti*)—characterized by opposition and based on the distinctions between various defects—has been placed (*āhita*), that is, bestowed (*samarpitā*). In other words, they have abandoned their mutual opposition. For this very reason, *avibhāgena* means without opposition. *Tām* refers to that number of non-dual unity (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyām*). *Tādṛśīm* means similar to the state of the flavor residing in honey. [Objection: But is it not impossible for unity, duality, and so forth to coexist in one and the same place?

For two things are not conventionally designated as one, nor is one thing designated as two; this is because of the [Bhāṣya] statement, "for there is no duality in two. Furthermore, the example is also not consistent, because it is accepted that when a composite whole (avayavin) such as honey is produced from various juices possessing their respective tastes, another distinct taste of the same genus as those constituent parts is indeed produced. Therefore, he says: the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative position, namely, that it is a mere form (*ākṛti-mātra*) whose specific properties have not been apprehended.

He presents the *Vākyapadīya*, which was stated in the previous section with an underlying intention that was not explicitly expressed, as an authority even for that [present] position: "Of the distinctions... This means: due to the abandonment—that is, the non-apprehension—of the specific properties such as "oneness-ness" (*ekatvatva*), "two-ness-ness" (*dvitvatva*), and so forth. And this [non-apprehension] is construed non-differently (*abhedena*) with the category of "operation" (*vyāpāra*). "Consisting of number" (*saṃkhyātmā*) means having the very nature of number. "That" (*saḥ*) refers to oneness and so forth. "Of such a kind" (*tathāvidhaḥ*) means that which is designated as non-dual oneness. He clarifies this very point: "Of the portion belonging to the universal" (*jātibhāgasya*), meaning of "oneness-ness" and so forth.

The phrase *bhedāpohena* means that [the cognition] proceeds from that operation which consists of the exclusion (*apoha*) of difference—that is, the non-apprehension of particularity—which has the nature of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Alternatively, the meaning is that "the exclusion of difference does not occur. Thus, it proceeds from that operation which consists of the non-apprehension of difference—the exclusion of difference—which is the specific universal (*jāti*) such as oneness, and which has the nature of a qualifier. Or, if the reading is *bhedāpoho na varttate*, the sense to be understood is that the exclusion consisting of difference—that is, the exclusion of what is other than that (*atad-vyāvṛtti*)—does not occur; it does not appear.

By examining other verses, it is determined that this very reading is approved by Hari (Patañjali). The collective meaning is as follows: a numerical entity (*saṃkhyā-padārtha*) which is the object of a cognition characterized by the universal of "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*) at a time when [specific numbers] such as duality or plurality are not apprehended, becomes designated by the terms "non-difference" (*abheda*) and "oneness" (*ekatva*). Regarding this, he provides another illustration: "by that whose particularity is unapprehended"—just as a jar or similar object is perceived as "possessing color" (*rūpavān*) by means of "white" and so forth, which are the objects of a cognition characterized by the universal of "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) at a time not coinciding with a cognition characterized by the universal of "whiteness" (*śuklatva*) and so on.

The exclusion (*apoha*) that takes the form of a distinction, such as "whiteness" and so forth—which consists in the exclusion of what is not that—is not perceived [as such]. Similarly, in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), the referent of the word "king" and so forth is perceived as possessing a number; however, the meaning is that in that portion concerning number, a specific oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth does not manifest.

Since such an appearance of number is not accepted by others, how can this position be maintained? Therefore, he explains it by means of the remaining portion [of the commentary], beginning with "vaiyākaraṇānām" (of the grammarians). Now, what is the proof for the appearance of such a number in the *vṛtti*? To this he says: "The point is this. "Preceded by the knowledge of the universal" means having that as its cause. "Necessary" means that without it, the aforementioned desire to know would not arise; this is the sense.

And that number, like the relation [in a compound] between a preceding and a following word, is capable of being expressed through a *vṛtti* (compound formation) itself; for in the view that a compound does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthāvṛttipakṣa*), there is no deficiency even if the first member denotes a specific number, provided there is no means of indication [for a different number]. Therefore, in cases such as *dviputraḥ* ("having two sons"), *maudrikaḥ* ("a handful of mudga beans"), *māsajātaḥ* ("born a month ago"), *tāvakīnaḥ* ("belonging to you"), and *bhādrirāmavasaraḥ* ("the occasion of Rāma on Mount Bhadra"), there is no fault even though the number one associated with non-difference (*abhedekatvasaṃkhyā*) does not appear in the compound.

In the first case, because the prior member of the compound refers specifically to a particular number. In the second, since a single coin is unfit for purchase, a plurality is understood. In the third, because the word "month" (*māsa*) is employed to indicate a specific time, a number is determined. In the fourth, through the substitution of *tavaka* and other forms, singularity is understood. In the fifth, duality is understood from the context. The same should be inferred for expressions such as "in the midst of the factors of action" (*kārakamadhye*), since it is impossible for there to be a "midst" of a single entity.

In the presence of a specific context, even in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), there is indeed a manifestation [of number] by way of a particular number. In that case as well, it does not have the status of being the meaning of the compound’s function (*vṛttyarthatva*). "Difference" (*bheda*) refers to numbers such as duality (*dvitva*) accompanied by difference; "non-difference-unity" (*abhedaikatva*) is unity accompanied by the absence of that [difference]. According to this etymological derivation, it is unity alone that appears as number within the subordinate member of the compound.

Likewise, based on the statement "The singular number shall be used as the general rule," [the author] introduces the subsequent text with the intention that in examples such as *rājā sacitraguḥ* ("the king who has brindled cows"), the form is derived from *citrā-as-go-as*. The phrase "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) means "of that individual which is subordinate to the meaning of the word-component within the compound. The phrase "in the cognition" (*pratītau*) means "in the understanding as the qualificandum (viśeṣya) characterized by a mode (prakāratā) of singularity delimited by the property of number-ness."

The point is that he states an illustrative example for the fact that when the meaning of a subordinate term (*upasarjana*) is intended, only singularity is perceived as a number, and not duality or other numbers. The phrase "in counting" (*gaṇanāyām*) means in the enumeration of multiple things characterized by plurality. By the sentence "One should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds," the act of sacrificing *kapiñjala* birds qualified by a number subsumed under plurality is enjoined.

In this regard, when there is a doubt as to whether three or four and more [animals] are to be seized, since the property of being pervaded by plurality (bahutva) is common to all [numbers] beginning with three, it follows that they should be seized exactly as they are obtained; thus, according to the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), four and more are to be seized. This is because, in the case of the general scriptural prohibition "one must not kill," it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to assume a restriction of its intended meaning (*tātparya-saṃkoca*) to exclude only those individuals that are not fit to be seized; rather, the statement is understood as referring to the number three, which is the first to present itself in the process of counting.

It has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that, due to both functional utility (*cāritārthya*) and parsimony (*lāghava*), the meaning of the plural number is precisely three, as it is pervaded by plurality. By that same logic, here too, it is oneness alone as a number (*saṃkhyātva*) that serves as the basis for the application of the suffix; it is not oneness characterized by unperceived specific properties such as duality and so forth, because of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "non-difference" means oneness. Some further maintain that since this grammar adopts the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*) in rules such as "of the three beginning with *nija*" (*nijāṃ trayāṇām*), the perception of oneness as a number in the present context is indeed difficult to justify.

Now, it is not a rule that in the case of a desire to know (*jijñāsā*), one must necessarily have a verbal cognition whose qualifier is a general property (*sāmānyadharma*); for this is contradicted by the fact that even upon seeing the fruit of a mango tree, there arises a desire to taste its flavor. Nor should it be argued that, in such a case, the causality of a cognition qualified by a general property would be undermined; for the sight of the mango acts as an awakener (*udbodhaka*), and the resulting recollection of its flavor accounts for [the desire].

In the present case, although that [direct inquiry] is impossible, since there is the possibility of an inferential cognition of it through its invariably concomitant substancehood (*dravyatva*), and because such an inquiry is not actually experienced, the aforementioned reasoning does not prove that the *vṛtti* has the number one as its meaning. With this intention, he says: "In reality... the inquiry itself. This means that in expressions such as "the king's servant" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), there is only an inquiry regarding the first member of the compound with respect to the manner of singularity, duality, and so forth. It is established by experience.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "by which [reason], in accordance with that [view], there would necessarily be a cognition having a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) as its qualifier. The point is that the root text's statement, "the number one-ness of non-difference (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) appears in the complex formation (*vṛtti*)," is merely a restatement of the views found in ancient treatises.

Considering that the fact of being established by experience is to be determined by oath, he says: "Or if it were so. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates a lack of conviction; the meaning is "or if it were established by experience. Regarding the phrase "only by way of having the same mode of presentation" (*samānaprakārakatvenaiva*): the particle "only" (*eva*) excludes having different modes of presentation. This is because, in the case of desire for pleasure and the like, the causality of a cognition having a specific property as its mode of presentation toward a desire for that same property has already been established.

The point is this: since the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding a specific property in the present context has as its object that which possesses such a property, it necessarily involves a mode of cognition whose qualifier is that specific property; therefore, it is subsumed under the definition of the effect (*kāryatā*) of a cognition whose qualifier is a specific property of the referent of the word "that" (*tat*).

The phrase "only in those respective forms" means "only in specific forms such as oneness-ness (*ekatvatva*) and so forth. The particle *eva* (only) excludes the general property of number (*saṃkhyāsāmānyadharma*). It is not acceptable to assume that this is already established (*iṣṭāpatti*), because if it were so, the specific property would be understood from the word itself, making a desire to know it impossible. This is the intended meaning.

On this point, they say: in the defining condition (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the effect of a cognition having that property as its qualifier (*taddharmaprakāraka*), the state of having that property as its qualifier must be included independently; otherwise, the causal efficacy of a cognition having a general property as its qualifier toward the production of an inquiry (*jijñāsā*) regarding a specific property would be lost, in order to account for the fact that a cognition having a general property as its qualifier generates an inquiry regarding a specific property.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for this, because the very words of the author of the *Dīdhiti*—“When either the effect or the cause is known, the effect or the cause [is sought]”—serve as proof. In the present case, since the specific property (*viśeṣadharma*) is a qualifier (*prakāra*) of desire only through its dependence on [the general property], such a desire to know is easily established even without a cognition having that specific property as its qualifier, but rather from a cognition having the general property as its qualifier.

However, a cognition whose qualifier is a general property (sāmānyadharma) consists in a desire whose qualificandum is delimited by having a particular property as its qualifier; thus, there is no contingency of desiring pleasure and so forth from a cognition of the general property of being a quality (guṇatva). More on this should be investigated elsewhere. Consequently, since the desire to know (jijñāsā) is established in all cases here, for its justification, the occurrence of non-difference and unity in the occurrence [of the word] is necessary. And in this way, the consistency of the root text—"in the occurrence of the number non-difference and unity"—is maintained.
By this, the interpretation that the meaning [of the verse] is the absence of the cognition of difference, as well as of duality and so forth which coexist with it, and of unity, is refuted.
Thus ends the determination of the number of non-difference and unity in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. 11.

He demonstrates the connection [of this section] by stating "incidentally" (*prasaṅgāt*) while defining the intention and non-intention regarding number. The meaning is that, in the definition of the number one as non-difference, the non-intention of the number three was previously mentioned as a qualification of the injunction in the passage "one should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds," and therefore it is not fit to be neglected. Regarding the phrase "it is not intended," the sense is that if it were intended, there would be no cleansing of all the sacrificial vessels.

The phrase “*dhātoriti*” means that in the rule prescribing suffixes (*pratyaya*), the number (singular, etc. inherent in the word *dhātu* within the sūtra *dhātoḥ* is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣaṇāt*) in this system. He states—“*utpadyeta*”—that even according to the Mīmāṃsakas, it is agreed that an attribute residing in the subject (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant. [He then says] “*viśeṣyeta*”: in that case, that meaning of the suffix would be qualified by all the meanings of the verbal roots; such is the meaning.

[Objection: But surely this reasoning does not establish the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), because such a collection [of sounds] lacks the status of being a verbal root denoting an action; thus, since the production of an affix from it would be as impossible as a flower in the sky, the intended meaning exists by its very nature. To this, he says: "By the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeṅ valādeḥ*," and "and because it is intended. The sense is that otherwise, the inclusion of that [term] would result in futility. "In this way" means that the specific quality of the subject of the restatement (*anuvādya*) is indeed unintended; the meaning is that it is due to not relying on a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), when the sacrifice—the meaning of the root *yaj*—requires an instrument (*karaṇa*), the animal is enjoined as that means. Thus, since the word "animal" (*paśu*) serves to present the thing to be enjoined, there is no evidence for accepting some of the properties presented by it while rejecting others; consequently, singularity—as well as animality, being an animal, and so forth—is intended to be a means of the sacrifice. Therefore, the transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*) is not accomplished through a sacrifice performed with multiple animals. In this same way, in other cases as well, the qualifiers of the thing to be enjoined are intended to be significant.

"In this case, because there is an absence of any reason for not intending [the number]," such is the path traversed by the Mīmāṃsakas; however, we have no obligation to follow that path. He demonstrates the undesirable consequence of resorting to that [Mīmāṃsaka] view in this treatise with the words "radābhyām" (P. 8.2.42). The meaning is that since the prescription would not otherwise apply, even the singularity presented by the singular number in "na" (*naḥ*) would, as a qualifier of the thing to be prescribed, be intended to be significant; consequently, the prescription of two *nakāra*s would not take place.

[Objection: Let there not be the prescription of two *na*s; to this he says, "And thus" (*tathā ca*). This is with the intention that the prescription is by way of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*); however, regarding the view that the prescription is by way of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), he says, "in cases such as *ād guṇaḥ*" (*ādguṇa ityādau*). "Precisely by the intention of singularity" means: precisely by the intention of the singularity residing in the quality (*guṇa*) which is the object of the prescription. Thus, the meaning is that the very mention of the word "one" (*eka*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the stated point.

Anticipating the objection that since Jaimini’s reasons for intending the singularity of the animal and so forth are well-established, his reliance upon them cannot be considered unauthoritative, the author sets aside this doubt by explaining the meaning of the *pāda* (section) under the guise of demonstrating the interpretation, beginning with the words "But the meaning of the word," etc.

The meaning is: "of the reasons stated in the section concerning the singularity of the animal" (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*). In the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), if the singularity inherent in the object of prescription were not intended to be significant, then the following defects would arise as reasons: (1) the impossibility of performing the sacrifice due to the sublation of the requirement for a single performance if another animal were seized; (2) the consequence of violating the primacy of the principal act (*pradhāna*) by repeating the sacrifice for the sake of the subordinate quality (*guṇa*); and (3) the impossibility of a sacrifice performed with as many animals as exist. These are the defects that serve as the reasons.

The phrase "established by the Siddhānta" means established by the *Mahābhāṣya* and other works that expound the meaning of the Siddhānta. Regarding the expression "to prevent [the application of] different substitutes": in reality, the inclusion of the word "one" (*eka*) is not the decisive factor for the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the qualifier of the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*). This is because, as in the case of "Make a mat from two bundles of grass" (*anyoḥ pūlayoḥ kaṭaṃ kuru*), even in rules such as "guṇa is substituted for [the vowels] *ā* and *i*" (*ād guṇaḥ*), since both [vowels] are mentioned together in a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) via the dual compound "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*), it is possible to prescribe a single substitute in place of both; thus, due to the difference in the substituends (*sthānin*), there is no need for multiple guṇas. This is the secret [of the matter], as the inclusion of the word "one" is rejected in the *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the phrase "vākyabheda-ādi" (and so forth, including sentence-splitting): by the statement "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), the cleansing (*sammārga*) is enjoined with reference to the cups prescribed by the sentence "The nine cups belong to Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyā navagrahāḥ*). In that context, if one were to enjoin the singularity of the cup—which is the object of the restatement (*anuvādya*)—there would be a contradiction with the number [nine] contained in the original productive injunction (*utpattivākya*). Therefore, there would be a "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*), meaning the sentence would produce a cognition having distinct subjects; this is the sense of the word "ādi. Others, however, state that there is the contingency of a sentence-splitting of the form: "He cleanses the cup" and "that [cup] is one."

Because the meaning of the word *graha* (cup) is delimited by the number nine occurring in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)—and thus there is an absence of any need for further delimitation—and because the accusative case in the word *graham* conveys a predominance characterized by being the object of a sanctification (*saṃskārya*), [the principle] "the repetition of a subordinate element applies to each principal" (*pratipradhānaṃ guṇāvṛttiḥ*) does not apply; furthermore, since there is no basis for selection (*vinigamanāviraha*) and the cleansing (*sammārga*) which has the result of removing the remnants of Soma requires all the cups, it lacks the status of being a subsidiary to the action (*kriyāṅgatva*) like the qualifying attributes of the animal to be sacrificed (*paśu*).

Furthermore, there is the inclusion of the seed for the absence of the speaker’s intention [to apply the rule], because there is no possibility of a deficiency in the operation caused by a deficiency in that [intention]; the phrase "without a source" (*anākaram*) is as explained previously. By the words "of the augment *iṭ*, etc.," the inclusion of the prohibition of *it* (the substitution of *i*) is intended, according to the rule "for the place of *ā* of the Northern Grammarians, when preceded by *ya* or *ka*" (*udīcām ātaḥ sthāne yakapūrvāyāḥ*). This is because in that case, the substitution of *it* is prescribed with reference to an *āt* that has *ā* as its locus. For this very reason, in the rule *ekāj* which prescribes the prohibition of *iṇ*, the commentators have explained the text as excluding the teaching of multi-syllabic roots (*anekāckopadeśa*), out of regard for the singular number in the word *acaḥ*.

In reality, however, by the analogy of the "singularity of the cup" (*grahaikatva*), let it be granted that in some cases there is a lack of intention (*avivakṣā*) regarding numbers and other qualifiers used as attributes of a restatement (*anuvāda*). This lack of intention is appropriate because those other qualifiers are understood from the sentence itself and are thus merely incidental (*anuṣaṅgika*). But it should be understood that this is not the case in the present instance. Thus ends the determination of the non-intentionality of number and so forth in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*. 12.

He demonstrates the contextual connection (*avasarasaṅgati*) in the investigation of the meaning of suffixes such as *ktvā* with the words "of the suffix *ktvā*, etc. Since the term *prakṛtyartha* (the meaning of the base) exists even in the result (*phala*), he says "bhāva" (the action/state). Even there, it refers only to the operation (*vyāpāra*) which has attained the status of a being (*sattvabhūta*), and not to [factors] such as prior time; this is the meaning. The point is that, unlike in cases such as "pākaḥ" (cooking), one does not experience the aspect of the action (*bhāvāṃśa*) in the cognition produced by forms such as "paktum" (to cook) or "paktvā" (having cooked).

In reality, however, in the cognition produced by [words such as] *paktvā* ("having cooked"), it is indeed experienced that the abstract action (*bhāva*) lacks connection with gender and number. Similarly, in cases such as *paktum*, since it is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by means of the suffix *tumun*, which denotes the result, this has already been largely explained.

As for the question "What is the recourse?"—the point there is that because [the rule] mentions "prior time" (*pūrvakāle*) and so forth, the denotability (*vācyatā*) of prior time and the like is perceived; whereas if [the suffixes] were to denote mere abstract action (*bhāvamātra*), that would be untenable. [The phrase] "samānakartṛkatvādi" (having the same agent, etc.)...

And thus, when there is an expectancy for meaning—namely, that the suffix *ktvā* expresses the sense of "between two verbal root-meanings having the same agent, that which is connected with the earlier time"—and since the rule *kartari kṛt* would otherwise apply, the commencement of the Vārttika serves to determine that the state (*bhāva*) alone is the expressed meaning (*vācyatā*), in order to set aside that [general rule]. If the agent were intended as a qualifier of the suffix, however, he would have simply said "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛka*). The point is that those [meanings] included in the Sūtra are merely indicated (*dyotyatva*), just like [the notions of] presentness and so forth.

In reality, however, there is no insistence even on the status of being "expressed" (dyotyatā), because its manifestation is possible through the very constraints of syntactic relation (saṃsargamaryādā); thus he says: "This is the sense."

The point is that rules such as *samānakartṛkayoḥ* fall under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the connection between verbal roots (*dhātusaṃbandha*). The sense of the phrase "is untenable" is that since the roles of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) require a corresponding nature in their objective status (*viṣayatā*) regarding the relation (*saṃsarga*), a determinate cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) is impossible without a relation; thus, the manifestation of the relation is established even without its being denoted by the word. The meaning of "otherwise" is: if one were to admit syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) even in the absence of the relation between the qualified and the qualifier.

"Co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) means having a single substratum. "The relation of prior and posterior" (*pūrvottarabhāva*) means either being produced immediately after itself or existing at a time preceding itself. "Pervadedness" (*vyāpyatva*) means invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*). He states the verbal cognition resulting from words ending in suffixes such as *tumun* with the words "And thus" (*tathāca*).

The statement "the producer of eating" (*bhojanajanikā*) is made in order to clarify that here the relation of being a producer (*janakatva*) functions as a relational connector (*saṃsarga*). However, the form of the cognition is simply "qualified by eating" (*bhojanaviśiṣṭā*), because since being a producer is not a word-meaning (*apadārthatayā*), it cannot function as a qualifier (*aprakāratvāt*). He provides the reasoning for why even the relationship of being produced and being a producer between two actions is considered a relation: "for this very reason. This means precisely because one accepts that being produced (*janyatva*) functions as a relational connector. By the phrase "of the immediate succession of drinking water" (*jalapānāntaryasya*), the existence of a connection between the preceding and following sentences is indicated.

The point is that while the intention to express being produced by that [action] is indeed desired in such usage, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) itself is not the intended meaning. Rather, the acceptance of co-referentiality as a relation—rather than being the object of the apprehension of the word-meanings involved—is for the purpose of excluding the usage "having eaten, he is satisfied" (*bhuktvā tṛpyati*) in cases where there is a lack of co-referentiality between the acts of eating and satisfaction occurring in a temporal sequence (prior and posterior). Furthermore, the inclusion of "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*) is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ktvā* when it refers to an action such as eating that occurs at a prior time separated by another day, even though it is co-referential with the main action.

And the interval [between actions] should be understood as being determined by the speaker's intention (tātparya) to be one of a *daṇḍa*, a *muhūrta*, or the like; therefore, it should be noted that even if there is an interval of a *daṇḍa* or similar duration after eating, there is no logical inconsistency in such usage.

[Objection: But surely, if one accepts that the relation of "prior and posterior" (pūrvottarabhāva) constitutes the connection [between two actions], then the usage "having studied, he remains" (*adhītya tiṣṭhati*) would be untenable at the time of study, because there is no immediate succession (*anantarya*) of study with respect to remaining. Similarly, the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*) would not be possible; for if sleep were present at the very moment of opening—the separation of the lips—then such a usage would be desired precisely because the opening is not preceded by sleep. To this, he says: "Having studied, he remains," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "kālaviśeṣe" (in a specific time): since there is no relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) constituted by the temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*) between two things belonging to different times, one must accept that the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) as delimited by that very relation also functions as a relational connector (*saṃsarga*). It is not only the state of being pervaded that serves as the relational connector in that case, but also co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); thus he says, "and co-occurrence. Consequently, there is no risk of the aforementioned linguistic usage occurring by taking as its basis a single-time study performed by different agents.

And thus, in cases governed by the rule "samānakartṛkayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.21), where a suffix ending in *ktvā* is prescribed, the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in having a common agent is universally a constituent of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). The point is that relations such as being produced (*janyatva*), however, appear in the verbal cognition only occasionally, depending on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

Others, however, maintain that the relation of *pūrvottarabhāva* (antecedence and consequence) is everywhere the object of the cognition produced by a suffix ending in *-ktvā*, just like coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In examples such as "having opened his mouth" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya*), just as in "having slept, he opens his mouth" (*suptvā mukhaṃ vyādatte*), the usage is justified by taking the temporal sequence in view of the persistence of sleep even after the opening of the mouth. Thus, they say that the manifestation of a relation other than these two mentioned relations is merely occasional. And [it is not the case that] "Since you despise me, therefore it shall not be for you... [is unaccounted for].

Regarding the passage, "He cursed you, saying: 'Your progeny shall not exist without having propitiated my offspring,'" one should not argue that the requirement of a single agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) for the suffix *ktvā* is not universal, since we observe *ktvā* even when the agents are different—namely, "your progeny shall not exist" (*te prajā na bhaviṣyati*), where the implied agent of the first clause differs from the second. This is because, according to the natural sense of the grammatical rule (*sūtra-svārasya*), in such cases one supplies an intermediate action such as "remaining" (*sthitvā*), thereby accepting the understanding: "of one who remains [in this state] without having propitiated. Thus, the universality of the rule is not compromised.

The phrase "because it is obtainable elsewhere" (*anyalabhyatvāt*) means either because it is restricted by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā-niyamyatvāt*) or because it is obtainable through the syntactic connection of the sentence (*vākya-sakti-labhyatvāt*).

The meaning is that although "the connection between two actions" (kriyayoḥ saṃsargaḥ)—in the form of being a qualifier of the primary meaning of the verbal root—is impossible here, that very definition [of the *samānakartṛka* relationship] should nevertheless be understood in this context. "For this very reason" means precisely because the suffix *ktvā* indicates such things as having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). Regarding the phrase "the introductory citation from the Bhāṣya," it refers to the Bhāṣya passage: "Why does [the suffix *ktvā*] not occur here—'He eats first, then he goes'? Because [the sequence] is expressed by its own word (*svaśabdenopāttatvāt*). In that instance, the application of *ktvā* is based on the presence of a common agent and a prior temporal sequence.

"But not the object" means "not that which is denoted by any word whatsoever contained within the application [of the rule]"; the sense is that this follows from the maxim, "That which has already expressed its meaning is not employed. Thus, Kaiyaṭa’s intention is that in the expression "samānakartṛkayoḥ," the genitive case is used for the purpose of specification (*nirddhāraṇa*), and in "pūrvakāla," a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed in the sense of the genitive. The meaning of the sentence has already been stated previously.

Nor should it be argued that if the word *pūrva* and others denote "prior time," then the suffix *ktvā* would be ungrammatical, and thus the application of *ktvā* in the sentence "having first eaten, he afterwards goes" (*pūrvaṃ bhuktvā paścād vrajati*) would remain untenable; for the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself has provided the solution to this. Thus says the *Bhāṣya*: "This is not the priority of the action, but rather the priority of the agent—this person, having first eaten before other goers, afterwards goes."

The intention [of the author] is that, in the sense of "having first eaten from these previous eaters, he goes after [those] subsequent goers," the possibility of the suffix *ktvā* arises by taking the priority (*paurvakālya*) as depending on the action of another means (*sādhanāntara*), according to the rule *vibhāṣā graha*. However, the moderns (*navyāḥ*) maintain that *pūrvakāla* is a *karmadhāraya* compound; the word *bhūta*, however, is not mentioned because it is a synonym and because there is no experience of cognition in that form.

Thus, the meaning of the rule is that between two actions having the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* occurs after a verbal root denoting the action qualified by the earlier time. Consequently, the earlier time is the meaning of *ktvā*, and it is indeed a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root. For this very reason, having raised the objection regarding the suffix *ktvā* in the sentence "He eats first and then he goes" (*pūrvabhuṅkte paścād vrajati*) on the grounds of the actions having the same agent, the *Bhāṣya* resolves it by stating: "It does not occur because [the sequence] is already expressed by its own word (*svaśabdenopāttatvāt*)."

The word *pūrva* has "prior time" as its meaning, but the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not function in that sense; therefore, its meaning [is not expressed by the suffix], for it is not the case that words whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed. For this very reason, there is no room for the subsequent objection: "Why does [the suffix] not occur here in *āsyate bhoktum*? Otherwise, since the prior time of the action of sitting (*āsikriyā*) would be indicated by the *tumun* suffix used in the sense of a result, the lack of application [of the suffix] would be obvious. However, if the prior time were not understood from that [suffix], how could the suffix *ktvā* be introduced? It is another matter that it is established by the present tense (*laṭ*) according to the rule of "optionality due to dissimilarity" (*vā'sarūpa*).
And thus they say that, just as the genitive case expresses a relation (*sambandha*), it is equally easy to state that these [kṛt suffixes] also express a relation.

Here, however, this must be considered: the introduction of the example *upaṣṭambhaka* (supporter) is weakened for the purpose of supporting the argument that the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not function there [in the sense of "is seated"], because the subsequent doubt—"it is sat upon in order to eat" (*āsyate bhoktum*)"—would otherwise be untenable. For even in Kaiyaṭa’s view, since the relation to the prior time is perceived [in the compound], the maxim "there is no use of a word whose meaning has already been expressed" (*uktārthānāmaprayogaḥ*) does not apply; therefore, the possibility of raising the doubt remains.

Furthermore, since even the Neo-Naiyāyikas accept that in instances involving *kṛt* suffixes, that which is denoted by the suffix stands as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the root-meaning, there would be a contradiction with the preceding text which states: "The meaning of the *ktvā* suffix is [an action] occurring at a prior time, and it is indeed a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the root-meaning. Nor can the aforementioned consistency be maintained by accepting that the *ktvā* suffix denotes agency (*kartṛtva*), because this would contradict the subsequent text which states: "Just as the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a relation (*sambandha*), so too do these [suffixes] denote a relation."

Nor is that [position] easily maintainable, because the denotability (*vācyatā*) of factors such as having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is not obtained from the Sūtra. Therefore, Kaiyaṭa’s statement alone is correct: that suffixes such as *ktvā* merely specify particular relations with the action, like the term *karmapacanīya*.

He introduces another view in order to refute it with the words "yattu" (as for what [has been said]). The meaning is that since there is no reason for a disparity—whereby the time preceding [the action] would be the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of both terms in the rule "samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle" (Pāṇini 3.4.21) while the other [the agent] would be merely indicated (*dyotya*)—because there is no difference in their being *bahuvrīhi* compounds, [the agent must be expressed]. He states the subverting argument against such a disparity with the words "anyathā" (otherwise); the meaning is: if that [agent] were not expressed by the *ktvā* suffix. And the consequence of the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) follows; the sense is that the agent is not denoted by the *ktvā* suffix.

One might object: "In the rule *anabhihite*, since the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of a simple prohibition (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), there is no occurrence of the third case here, because the agent is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "and not" (*na ca*). The term *anabhihite* does not signify a simple prohibition, because that would entail faults such as the splitting of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Nor can one accept that [interpretation] on the grounds of logical necessity alone, because it contradicts the Bhāṣya which will be cited later.

And thus, even if [the agent] is not denoted by one [word], because it is not denoted by the other, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is unavoidable; with this intention, he says "of the performer of a sinful act," etc., ending with "due to its absence," which means "because it is distinct from what has been denoted. "For this very reason" means "precisely because the negative particle (*nañ*) in that sūtra has the sense of *paryudāsa* (exclusion). The word "in the Bhāṣya" is to be completed as "in the [Bhāṣya] on the *anabhihita* sūtra. "Of that" means "of the state of having a common agent."

The meaning is that, by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound based on the dual number, the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is indeed a qualifier of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*). And from the employment of the word "common" (*samāna*), the identity of the two agents is obtained. [The objection] that there would be a *nyāsa* (a formal grammatical rule) is like the rule "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). However, in reality, that is not possible; for the point is already established by the very sūtra "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent," and because it would contradict the Vārttika "indeclinable kṛt-affixes [denote] the action" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*). He refutes the aforementioned undesirable consequence with the words: "But the introduction of the third case... (*tṛtīyāpādanaṃ tu*).

The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "of the action denoted by the verb" (*ākhyātārthakriyāyāḥ*), although there is a multiplicity of agent-powers (*kartṛśakti*) defined by two actions, when the agent-power defined by the primary action denoted by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is expressed by the verb, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the status of being "expressed" (*abhihitatva*) to that power defined by the action denoted by the nominal suffix (*kṛdanta*), even though it is not itself expressed. Conversely, when it is not expressed, there is an extension of the status of being "unexpressed" (*anabhihitatva*). Since this is accepted on the authority of the aforementioned Bhāṣya, there is no contingency for the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the present instance.

The phrase "of the primary and the other" means that the power (śakti) determined by the qualities of the subordinate and the principal actions conforms to the property of the power determined by the principal action. Regarding the aforementioned transfer (atideśa), he states their agreement: "having the principal as its object. This means that when that power, which has the principal as its object—that is, that which determines it—is expressed by a verbal suffix (tiṅ), then even though it is not expressed by the suffix following the root denoting the subordinate action, it is understood as if it were expressed.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), because even that which has been expressed is perceived as unexpressed. In this regard, one should cite the example: *prāsāde āste* ("He sits in the palace"). This must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, even if one avoids the occurrence of the instrumental case in the aforementioned instance by accepting that the agent is the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā*, the occurrence of the accusative case after the word *odana* in the sentence *paktvaudano mayā bhujyate* ("Having cooked, rice is eaten by me") would be unavoidable.

In this regard, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*), because, according to the aforementioned method, the capacity for the status of being an object (*karmatva*) as defined by the act of cooking (*pākakriyā*) cannot be expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix due to its non-expression. Here, this should be understood: if what is intended is that only the status of being an object as defined by the act of cooking is the objective domain of the verbal expression (*śābdaviṣayatva*) with respect to the rice (*odana*), and not also the status of being an object as defined by the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*), then the construction "having cooked the rice, it is eaten" (*odanaṃ paktvā bhujyate*) is also correct, because the rice's status as the object of eating is merely implied (*ārthikatva*).

However, when it is intended that the verbal object consists solely of both actions, then the accusative case after the word *odana* (rice) is indeed incorrect, according to the established rule stated above. Nevertheless, because the action expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*) is primary, all actions presented by the suffix *-ktvā* become subordinate to it alone; there is no mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) among those actions themselves, in accordance with the maxim: "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*). And thus, constructions such as *snātvā pītvā bhuktvā vrajati* ("having bathed, drunk, and eaten, he goes") are used without [mutual] qualification.

The state of being an object (*uddeśyatva*), which consists in being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*), is also manifested by the suffix *tum*, because of the rule "when there is an action for the sake of another action. Its extraction is exactly as before. Furthermore, the relationship between the meaning of the verbal root of the *tum* suffix and the meaning of the subordinate word (*upapada*) includes not only being for the sake of that, but also having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) and so forth. Thus, from the sentence "He goes to see Hari" (*hariṃ draṣṭuṃ yāti*), the verbal cognition is: "going, whose agent is the agent of seeing, has as its intended object a future seeing of which Hari is the object.
In this very manner, the cognition from "He goes to fetch fuel" (*edhānāhārako vrajati*) is to be inferred.
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of *katva* and so forth in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*.

In this manner, since verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is not observed to arise from a collection of words whose expressive power (*śakti*) has been grasped through grammar and other means, provided that they are non-proximate (*anāsanna*), their intended meaning has not been grasped (*agṛhītārthatātparyaka*), they are semantically incompatible (*ayogya*), or they lack mutual expectancy (*anākāṅkṣa*), proximity (*āsatti*) and the other factors are also auxiliary causes for the production of cognition, following upon the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) generated by the knowledge of expressive power. And proximity (*āsatti*) consists in the absence of an intervention between words that is conducive to the intended cognition.

Furthermore, in the sentence "The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), there is such non-interruption of words; however, in "The mountain was eaten by Devadatta, [and] it possesses fire" (*girir bhuktaṃ vahnimān devadattena*), there is not, and thus no understanding arises from that. For this very reason, in the sentence "He cooks rice in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), there is no lack of proximity (*anāsannatā*) regarding the understanding of an action whose object is rice and whose locus is the pot, because all the words constituting it are conducive to such an understanding. But in the case of the understanding of merely "He cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*), it is indeed a lack of proximity.

However, in the case of a verse (*śloka*) and the like, understanding arises precisely from the sentence of the *yojanā* (the syntactic connection). According to the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*), since understanding is observed even when there is no immediate proximity due to error, the knowledge of that [proximity] itself is the cause. The moderns (*navyāḥ*), however, argue that "proximity" (*āsatti*) cannot be defined as the aforementioned lack of intervention, because it would follow that no understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) could arise from a "silent verse" (*mauniśloka*). This is because, provided there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, and given the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), understanding is observed to occur both from what is intervened by a pause and from what is not; furthermore, there is no delay in verbal comprehension corresponding to a delay in the knowledge of that [proximity].

However, they say that this [cause] is the speaker’s intention (*abhisandhi*) in the form of a desire to convey the meaning of the words—specifically, the intention that "this word, together with this word, shall produce the cognition of the syntactic relation"—and not merely the desire of the speaker; for otherwise, defects would remain as they are in cases such as the verses of a mute person. As for the speech of a parrot, its interpretation proceeds only by taking the intention of the Blessed One (the Buddha) as the basis.

In reality, however, since there is no delay in verbal cognition when one knows the speaker’s intention regarding the meaning despite a delay in knowing the word’s intention, it follows that "proximity" (*āsatti*)—defined as the immediate presentation of the word-meanings produced by the words through their respective functions (*vṛtti*)—is the cause for the arising of a cognition of syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*), provided that this [proximity] exists in its own right (*svarūpasat*). For no one ever experiences a cognition of the relation of word-meanings when those meanings have not been presented. This "intention regarding the meaning," moreover, is the desire of the communicator: "May these words cause the understanding of the syntactic relation of word-meanings with respect to this particular meaning."

In the case of the words of a trustworthy parrot, however, that [causality] belongs to the Lord alone; whereas in the case of those that are inconsistent, it belongs to the instructor. Since there is no understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) when there is doubt or when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is ascertained, and because one observes the occurrence of the understanding of the positive concomitance through error regarding that [inconsistency], the knowledge of that [trustworthiness] is also a cause for the understanding of the positive concomitance. More will be said on this later.

"Many hold that the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā*) is a cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). And this [compatibility] is simply the possession by one word-meaning of such a relation with another word-meaning as exists; that is to say, the possession of the relation that is the object of the verbal cognition in question. And in the case of 'He sprinkles with water,' there exists the relation of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) of water with the act of sprinkling."

For this very reason, the sentence "she sprinkles with water [contained] in a jar" (payaḥ) as intended by the speaker is not semantically appropriate, because the substance denoted by the word *payaḥ* lacks the status of being the instrument of sprinkling when it resides in the jar. Furthermore, due to the qualification "of such a kind," the sentence "space is sound" (*ākāśaṃ śabdaḥ*) is not appropriate for a relation of identity, even if one takes the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) into account. Since a cognition of semantic fitness is also a cause, for even when there is no fitness, one observes the occurrence of a cognitive connection through error regarding this [fitness].

If it is objected: "Since the sentence-meaning consists of the relation (*saṃsarga*), how can that relation exist [in the cognition] prior to its being presented, given that it is not yet presented before the cognition of that meaning arises?"—we do not assert that the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā*) is a cause for verbal comprehension by way of being a certainty (*niścaya*), which would allow room for the aforementioned defect.

However, [the cognition] is characterized as a knowledge that is common to both doubt and certainty, and it is not difficult to obtain; for this is evident because such a cognition occurs prior [to the final conclusion] in cases like "he sprinkles with milk," where there is a doubt as to whether the act of sprinkling has milk as its instrument or not, and also in cases like "there is a jar on the ground," where it takes the form of a perceptual certainty. This is possible because the very verbal cognition produced by itself acts as an obstacle to the subsequent inferential cognition (anvaya-bodha).

However, some argue that since the absence of the cognition of the absence of a property (tadabhāvavattājñānābhāva) is the cause for a cognition of possessing that property (tadvattābuddhi) which is not produced by a worldly sense-contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*) and is qualified by being a specific defect, and since verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is also included within the scope of its effect-ness (*kāryyatāvacchedaka*), the occurrence of verbal cognition is prevented simply by the presence of the cognition of incompatibility (*ayogyatājñāna*). Thus, it is argued that there is no need for the cognition of compatibility (*yogyatājñāna*) as a cause for it.

In this view, although worldly perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) is excluded by including "being other than perception" (*pratyakṣānyatva*) in the definition of the effect-ness delimiter, the two terms beginning with "not produced by" (*ajanyānta*) are introduced instead of that [perceptual exclusion] in order to include cases of "presented cognition" (*upanītabhāna*) such as that of a jar.

Nor should it be argued that there is parsimony (lāghava) in taking the cognition of fitness—which is common to both doubt and certainty—as the cause, rather than the absence of the certainty of sublation (bādhaniścaya). This would indeed be the case if the verbal nature of the absence of sublation were postulated as the delimiting factor of the effect; however, since the verbal comprehension itself is already pervaded by the state of being an effect of the absence of sublation, we deny [the necessity of such a separate factor] at that stage.

For this very reason, there is no defect even in cases such as "the pot is denotable" (*ghaṭo 'bhidheyaḥ*), despite the fact that the sublation (*bādha*) and the lack of prior establishment (*aprasiddhi*) [of the property] have been mentioned; because the nature of a cognition having that [denotability] as its qualifier and that [pot] as its qualificandum, as delimited by the relation [of denotability], is precisely what delimits the effect-ness (*kāryatā*) of that [cognition]. Furthermore, they say that even the absence of that [denotability] is established by taking into account the state of an error regarding the absence of a pot, wherein denotability is mistakenly apprehended as being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

On this point, they argue: the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) is not the cause for the general class of cognitions qualified by that [object]; rather, since the arising of an *āhārya* (voluntary) perception occurs when there is a desire even in the presence of sublation, it is necessary to accept that perceptuality itself (*pratyakṣatva*) is the delimiting factor of the state of being obstructed (*pratibandhyatā’vacchedakatva*), because an obstruction common to the case of "presentation" (*upanītabhāna*) is impossible in the case of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). This is due to the requirement that desire acts as an excitatory factor (*uttejaka*).

Nor can it be doubted that the state of being the object to be negated (*pratibadhyatā*), which is common to inference, is also common to verbal cognition; for if "being a cognition other than perception" (*pratyakṣānyajñānatva*)—which is common to both—were the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that state of being the object to be negated, there would result a multiplicity of relations between the objects to be negated and their negators due to the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between "being other than perception" and "being a cognition. Furthermore, this would entail the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in the delimiting factor of the state of being the object to be negated, whereas [the state of being the object to be negated] is [properly delimited] by "inference-ness" (*anumititva*) alone.

Since that [absence] must be accepted as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka), it must therefore be asserted that the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) only in its own right. In that case, due to the aforementioned complexity (*gaurava*), it is more appropriate to hold that the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā*)—in the form of a relation—is itself the cause. Furthermore, in verbal cognition, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate to hold that the knowledge of compatibility alone is the cause, rather than postulating the status of obstructors (*pratibandhaka*) such as the knowledge of the mutual absence of those [terms] or the knowledge of the presence of their pervaders (*vyāpyavat*).

Furthermore, regarding the sentence "he sprinkles with milk" (*payasā siñcati*), at the time when the causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābdasāmagrī*) is present, there arises the mental [cognition] that "the act of sprinkling lacks the property of having milk as its instrument. To prevent this, if one were to postulate that the causal complex for verbal cognition acts as an inhibitor (*pratibandhaka*) in that case, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). In my view, since the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) is indispensable in that instance, and since the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) is the cause of perception following a contrary cognition, the aforementioned mental cognition is prevented simply by the absence of that competency-knowledge. Moreover, when the perception of a specific feature is present, there exists an inhibitor in the form of a definitive judgment (*nirṇaya*) that the object possesses a property pervaded by the absence of that [instrumentality]. Consequently, the causal complex for verbal cognition itself is absent; thus, such a mental cognition is accepted as a desired outcome (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Nor should it be argued that, since the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) is a cause for certainty (*nirṇaya*) alone, when the causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābda-sāmagrī*) is present, one must postulate that this complex acts as an inhibitor (*pratibandhaka*) to prevent mental doubt (*mānasa-saṃśaya*). In doing so, rather than including "doubt-ness" (*saṃśayatva*) in the definition of what is to be inhibited, one could simply take "mental-cognition-ness qualified by the absence of the state of being a water-pot (as the predicate) with respect to a subject qualified by oneness" as the delimitor of the state of being inhibited (*pratibandhyatāvacchedaka*). Thus, there would be no need to postulate an additional relation between the inhibited and the inhibitor. This cannot be maintained.

Since both [theories] must postulate a distinct capacity for the mental cognition—whose qualificandum is delimited by the property of being a substance (*sekatva*) and whose qualifier is the state of having milk as its instrument (*payaḥkaraṇakatva*)—to obstruct the conditions for verbal cognition (*śābdasāmagrī*), it is sufficient to prevent such doubt by that very capacity; there is no need to postulate a further obstructive capacity for that doubt.

Nor should it be argued that the causal status of the cognition of fitness (*yogyatājñāna*) is established only upon the establishment of the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) as the cause for a perceptual cognition that sublates a contrary cognition; for it is more appropriate to postulate its causal status than to postulate the counteracting force of the cumbersome verbal causal complex (*śābdasāmagrī*). By this very line of reasoning, the causal status of cognitions such as "this is a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) in regard to purposeful activity is established; therefore, enough with the description of the opponent's view.

In the case of the expression "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), since there is no comprehension that "the pot-ness is the object" arising from a sentence lacking expectancy due to the absence of a relationship between locus and located, *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is also a necessary auxiliary factor. And this *ākāṅkṣā* is defined as: the capacity of a word to generate a cognition characterized by a particular qualificandum, a particular relation, and a particular qualifier, which capacity is brought about by its co-occurrence with another word. This is the *ākāṅkṣā* of one word relative to another.

For example, in the sentence "he brings the jar" (*ghaṭam ānayati*), there is a word-based expectancy (*padanirūpitākāṅkṣā*) residing in the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), which is conducive to the cognition that "the jar-ness is the objecthood characterized by the relation of inherence. Without this, the cognition "the jar is objecthood" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) would not be produced by the word "jar. Similarly, in the case of a verbal root (*dhātu*), one must likewise posit an expectancy directed toward the finite verb (*ākhyāta*). For this very reason, from the expression "bringing is an effort" (*ānayanaṃ kṛtiḥ*), there arises no cognition such as "an effort conducive to bringing," because the verbal root is not co-occurrent with a finite verb.

This very expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is what is established by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). Thus, it results that this [expectancy] is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) consisting of the specific sequential order of various words relative to one another. Even though the aforementioned expectancies might exist without it, when there is the delusion that the word *karmatva* (the state of being an object) is not a case-ending (*sup*), the cognition "the objecthood of the pot" arises because of the co-occurrence consisting of the specific sequential order of those respective words related to the pot; therefore, the knowledge of that [co-occurrence] is necessary.

It is not the case that this [expectancy] exists as an intrinsic property (*svarūpasatī*), for it is merely a cause. Nor should it be argued that there would be the recurrence of such a cognition from a sentence that has already produced an understanding of the connection, because the aforementioned expectancy remains unimpaired even at that time. This is not so, because expectancy is defined as the state of not being accompanied by a cognition of the same form as the cognition of the connection currently under discussion; since this condition is absent in a case where a connection has already been produced, the recurrence of the cognition is impossible. Furthermore, the cognition is qualified by "being under discussion," which consists in its being the object of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

Because there exists an intention (*tātparya*) that "two cognitions may arise," when a subsequent cognition is produced following a prior one, the first cognition lacks expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) with respect to a second cognition. Furthermore, due to the expression "its own" (*svasamāna-*), a cognition that has already been produced does not possess the status of being a constituent part (*avāntara-bodha*) for the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*). For this very reason, in cases such as "The king's son is coming; let the man be removed," there is always an absence of expectancy once the cognition of the connection between the king and the man has been generated.

The modern [logicians], however, hold that the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between one word and another consists in the latter's lack of capacity to produce a cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) that is the object of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), which is necessitated by the absence of the former word. In the sentence "This son of the king comes, [and] the man," when uttered with the desire to convey the connection between the king and the man, the condition "being the object of the intention toward the cognition of the relation" is included as a qualifier [in the definition] in order to exclude the expectancy of the word *rājñaḥ* (of the king) with respect to *puruṣaḥ* (the man).

They say that if there is an intention (*tātparya*) regarding the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with a person, then there is indeed expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). Thus, the cognition of intention does not have a separate causal status toward verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), because in cases where the intention concerns a connected meaning, the absence of the aforementioned cognition of expectancy itself prevents the occurrence of a comprehension of the connection. Consequently, since the manifestation of the sentence-meaning—which consists of the connection—is established even prior to verbal comprehension by relying solely on the expectancy consisting of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the respective words (which is necessarily assumed), the Naiyāyikas maintain that the sentence has no power (*śakti*) in that regard, as there is no evidence for it.

However, the Mīmāṃsakas and others maintain that in that case there is only *lakṣaṇā* (indication) of the sentence, and not *śakti* (denotative power). With the intention of refuting their view, the author introduces the root text with the words "siddhānta" (the established conclusion), stating that it is for the purpose of defining *sphoṭa*.

Alternatively, one might raise the following objection: "According to the reasoning already stated, it is untenable for grammar to establish that the *prakṛtis* (bases) and *pratyayas* (suffixes) possess the power to convey their respective meanings. Since *prakṛtis* and *pratyayas* consist of a sequence of momentary and perishable phonemes, they are unstable and imperceptible; thus, it is impossible in any way to apprehend the linguistic capacity (*śakti*) therein. Consequently, this treatise which purports to establish such [a capacity] would fall into the error of being invalid. With the intention of resolving this doubt by defining *sphoṭa*, he introduces the root text, saying:

It should be noted that the summary of the final conclusion (*siddhāntaniṣkarṣa*) is thus connected to the introduction (*upoddhāta*). The refutation of those respective views is clearly evident in the root text itself. With the intention that the exclusion of those [other sphoṭas] would not be achieved because the eight types of sphoṭas are already included within the "etcetera" (*ādi*), he says: "useless" (*anarthaka*), meaning it serves no purpose; and "meaningless" (*durarthaka*), the sense being that if those were included, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of failing to include things other than the sentence. He provides the resolution with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*); the meaning is "of the others," namely the five sphoṭas beginning with phonemes (*varṇa*).

In this context, "sphoṭatva" (the nature of sphoṭa) consists in being a manifestor of meaning, derived from the etymology "that from which meaning bursts forth" (*sphuṭati*)—that is, becomes clearly manifested. And "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is knowledge (*jñāna*). Thus, it ultimately results in the state of possessing a power that brings about the objective reference (*viṣayatā*) residing in the object. When the status of being such [a manifestor] is accepted for phonemes alone, there is the usage "phoneme-sphoṭa" (*varṇasphoṭa*); but when its status is accepted for words and so forth, there is the usage "word-sphoṭa" (*padādisphoṭa*) and so on.

Regarding the term "unreal" (*avāstavatva*): since the phoneme-sphoṭa (*varṇasphoṭa*) and others lack the capacity to resolve expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), they are unreal; their acceptance in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) is merely for the sake of establishing the technical procedures of the science (*śāstra*). The sense is that ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), however, belongs to the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*) alone. As for the term "disagreement" (*vipratipatti*): it means a statement that brings to mind all the possible alternatives (*koṭi*) of a doubt; it does not mean that the statement which actually generates the doubt is itself the disagreement.

According to the traditional doctrine of the ancients that indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is necessarily of a determinate nature (*niścayātmaka*), it is impossible for a sentence to produce doubt; however, in reality, the state of being a "contradictory statement" (*vipratipatti*) consists precisely in its capacity to generate doubt. This is because, as noted in the sūtra *samānānekadharmopapatter* and others, it is explicitly stated that contradictory statements are a cause of doubt, just like the cognition of a property that coexists with both that property and its absence. This is how it should be understood.

Considering that at the root [of the argument] there is no relevance to an investigation into whether individual phonemes contained within an incorrect word (*asādhuśabda*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), [the author states: "In the phrase *sādhu* (correct), if one were to prove denotative power and so forth by way of its co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the state of being a phoneme contained within a correct word, it would be impossible for that sentence to constitute a formal contradiction (*vipratipatti*), because even the Naiyāyikas accept that some phonemes contained within a correct word possess denotative power."

If, however, one were to prove that denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) and so forth are restricted to such phonemes [as those in correct words], then there would be a contradiction for the Grammarians regarding other [phonemes] which are modifications (*vikāra*); therefore, he says: "They are remembered as such" (*tat-smṛtāḥ*).
