Now, an objection: according to the literal meaning, the sense obtained is that the denotator is contained within the correct word, but it is not the case that the phonemes contained therein are what cause the memory [of the word]. Since this sentence thus refers to different subjects (*dharmī*), the very possibility of a disagreement (*vipratipatti*) is absent; for a disagreement is defined as that which generates a doubt characterized by contradictory alternatives regarding a single subject. Therefore, he explains [the passage] as follows:

The meaning is that [the letters] are included within correct words (*sādhvantargata*), i.e., they are letters included within correct words. For if taken literally, since no one accepts that letters occurring in an incorrect sequence—such as those not included within correct words—are denotative, there would result the fallacies of contradiction (*bādha*) and proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, "being remembered by that" (being remembered by the letters in a correct word) occurs through either of the two relations: the relation of substitute and original (*ādeśādeśibhāva*) or the relation of cause and effect (*nimittanimittibhāva*) as taught by the grammatical treatise. By this, there is no failure to include cases such as *asyāpatyam* ("his offspring") or *iyān* ("so much").

The term *koṭi* is used to indicate that in a doubt (*saṃśaya*), a "limit" (*kāṭitā*)—a cognitive state (*viṣayatā*) excluded from the category of synthesis (*samuccaya*)—is necessary. This is stated to point out that for others—the Naiyāyikas—it is only the suffixes prescribed by rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* and *svaujasamauṭ* that possess denotative power (*vācakatva*); whereas forms such as *tib* and the visarga possess only the capacity to cause cognition (*bodhakatva*) by means of recollecting their substitutes (*ādeśin*), just like written letters (*lipivat*).

The sense is that, since both [the proponent and the opponent] establish [the capacity of words] according to their respective views by way of the property of being a phoneme recalled by a phoneme included within a correct word (*sādhvantargatavarṇasmāritavarṇatva*), the aforementioned fault does not apply. However, following the disagreement (*vipratipatti*) stated in the root-text as heard, he says "the correct word" (*sādhuśabda*), and so forth. Now, even if the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*) is established for the phonemes included within a correct word, the status of being a denoter (*vācakatva*) is not yet proven; therefore, he says "those which convey meaning are denoters. The phrase "of that very [thing]" means "of the capacity to convey meaning itself. The word "previously" (*prāk*) means "at the occasion of defining expressive power (*śakti*)."

The sense is that once it is established that [words] possess the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*), then by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*), a potency (*śakti*) consisting of a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*) would also be established; however, in the absence of that [conveying capacity], that [potency] too would not exist, and thus the non-existence of the general property of being a denoter (*vācakatva*) is established. He sets forth the Nyāya position in order to refute it with the words "But those who... (*ye tu*). He states the reason for the absence of denotative power in them with the words "For them... (*teṣām iti*).

The phrase "by way of plurality" (*bahutvena*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indicator), implying also the absence of a unifying property (*anugamakadharma*). This is because properties such as *tiṅtva* (the state of being a *tiṅ*-suffix) or *suptva* (the state of being a *sup*-suffix) cannot function as unifiers, just as singular-numberhood (*ekavacanatva*) and so on do not unify all suffixes. Furthermore, it should be understood that since the meaning of the verbal root (*kṛtyādi*) is understood even without the cognition of *tiṅtva* and so forth, these properties lack the status of being delimiters of expressive power (*śaktatānavacchedakatva*) due to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Now, one might object: "Even for those [suffixes] designated as *tiP* and so forth, there is multiplicity due to the difference between their respective *anubandhas* (indicatory letters); therefore, they cannot be denotative according to the method stated above. To this, he says: "In the case of *edhāṃ*... etc.

Since the meaning of that [suffix] can also be understood through elements such as *edh* following a root that is being applied (anuprayujyamāna), the aforementioned fault does not arise; therefore, he says "brahma" etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as "adya tiṣyo liṅdhuk" are included. By the phrase "of *lug* etc.," the meaning is "by those substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *lub* and *lopa*. Anticipating the aforementioned objection, he says "of the *la*-ness" (*latvasya*). His intention is that its establishment occurs through the uniform cognition of "la-" in *laṭ* and so on, by virtue of its being a universal (*jāti*).

The moderns (navya), however, say: its establishment [as the denotatum] does not occur by way of being the delimitor of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). This is because the property of *latva* (the *la*-suffixhood) common to all verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) is over-pervasive (*atiprasakta*), and because a suffix occurring in only ten verbal suffixes (*daśalakāra*) has not been apprehended prior to the grasp of the word's capacity; furthermore, since it would follow that there would be a cognition of effort (*kṛti*) in cases such as *pacan*, it is impossible for that [property] to be the delimitor of capacity. Rather, they say that *tit*, *pat*, *tvat*, and so on, are themselves the delimiters of that capacity. Thus, it should be understood that regarding the aforementioned dispute, there is indeed a disagreement with the ancients (*prācīna*).

The point is this: because the apprehension of the denotative power delimited by *la*-ness (*latvāvacchinna-śaktigraha*) necessarily exists prior to the cognition of the effort (*kṛti*), there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*). However, if *tip*-ness (*tiptva*) and so forth were taken as the delimiters of the denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), then—even without the apprehension of the power delimited by those [specific suffixes]—the cognition of effort would occur just as it does from the apprehension of the power of *tas* and other substitutes; thus, in the view that the substitutes (*adeśa*) are the expressive agents (*vācaka*), the deviation would be unavoidable. Now, one might object: "This undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) does not arise if 'immediate succession' (*avyavahitottaratva*) is included within the scope of the effect-delimiter (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). To this, he says: "By the rule *laḥ karmaṇi*... (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

Thus they say; therefore, the meaning is that the denotative power belongs only to the substitutes (ādeśins), as established by proof. The term *svasādhaka* means "that which nourishes its own [logical] support. Demonstrating how the three ablative endings in the phrase beginning with *vyavasthiteḥ* connect with the meaning of the word *bodhaka* found in the preceding verse, he first explains *vyavasthiteḥ*: "In accordance with the fixed rule (*vyavasthā*). The meaning is: "Because otherwise, the determination of word-meanings through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be inexplicable. This is the sense of *vyavasthā*.

The phrase "due to the error regarding capacity" (śaktibhramāt) means that the denotative power (vācakatva), which resides in that which is delimited by the property of being a *l*-sound, is superimposed upon it. The phrase "due to the absence of evidence" (mānābhāvāt) implies that, since the sublation of the object (*viṣayabādha*) is the sole determinant of an error, in the present case there is no sublation of the denotative capacity residing therein.

[Objection: Surely the very multiplicity of substitutes (*ādeśa*) constitutes an obstacle to accepting their expressive power (*śakti*). To this, he says: "Of the substituends (*ādeśin*) also... The meaning is that for grammarians such as Śākaṭāyana and others, there can be no determination (*nirddhāraṇa*) that "this alone is the expressive [element]," because the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) exists everywhere [for both substituends and substitutes]. The intention is that since it applies to all, there is no deciding factor (*vinigamaka*) [to favor one over the other]. [Objection: Even so, since the substituends are fewer than the substitutes, the expressive power will be established in the substituends due to the resulting parsimony (*lāghava*). To this, he says: "And there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*)."

[Objection: But surely, the status of the substitutes (*ādeśa*) as denoters is established precisely because there is no deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*). To this, he says: "Of the substitutes" (*ādeśānām*). Thus, although both [positions] are equal in terms of the defects such as prolixity (*gaurava*) and the avoidance thereof, the very fact that the usage is restricted—aided by the parsimony (*lāghava*) resulting from the absence of the postulation of a recollection of the substituendum (*uddeśin*)—is the deciding factor for the status of the substituenda (*uddeśin*) as denoters; this is the meaning of the refutation (*ākhaṇḍalārtha*). [Objection: But the aforementioned arrangement is only tenable if the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatā*) is itself the expressive power (*śakti*).

Furthermore, it is not established in their own system that the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*) constitutes *śakti* (the expressive power); rather, they maintain that it is either convention (*saṅketa*) or a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*). Thus, since [the opponent] accepts that [power] only where it is indicated by grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*), how could it be established for the suffixes *tiP* and so forth? As for the objection regarding the "burden of postulation" (*kalpanā-gaurava*) involved in the theory of recollection (*smaraṇa*), it is not defective because it is supported by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*). For this reason, stating that there is another proof, he introduces a further argument to establish that the *tiP* and other suffixes heard in actual usage are indeed expressive. He says: "another proof."

Regarding the term "primary" (*mukhya*): its primacy consists in its independence from other means of apprehending the word's expressive power (*śakti*), because when the expressive power is apprehended through grammar and such means, one invariably depends on those other apprehending factors.

The meaning is that if the apprehension of expressive power (*śaktigraha*) arises from linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). The point is that although that [power] might be apprehended previously through usage in relation to *tiṅ* suffixes and so forth alone—as in the preceding sentence—later, by means of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), its determination is made specifically with respect to those *tiṅ* suffixes and so forth that constitute the word. Objection: If the apprehension of expressive power were established through universally accepted usage regarding the individual phonemes included within a word, then it would follow that even the *śap* augment and so forth contained within words such as "ghaṭam ānaya" (bring the jar) would possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). But this is not desirable, as it would contradict the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇas*) lack denotative power (*nairarthakya*).

Furthermore, since linguistic practices such as bringing [an object] are impossible without the employment of words ending in *loṭ* and other suffixes, even if the expressive power (*vācakatva*) of the phonemes contained within such usages is not established by that practice, the expressive power of the phonemes contained within sentences devoid of those suffixes must nonetheless be accepted on the basis of the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) themselves. Thus, once the expressive power of the original forms (*ādeśin*) is established therein, it may be inferred for the substitutes (*ādeśa*) elsewhere as well; however, because this is not the intended position, he says, "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). This principle—"When the effect is produced by that very cause, what is the use of another?"—is based on the economy of means (*lāghava*).

Because there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) if both were causes, he connects that [point] with the words "of the letter *l*" (*lakārasya*). The phrase "the consequence of the cognition [of the agent]" (*bodhāpatti*) means the consequence of the cognition of the agent of the action (*bhavana*). By the maxim "not alone" (*na kevala*), since the letter *l* alone is unfit for usage, the word "root" (*bha*) is mentioned. Since the suffix *śap* is impossible at the stage when the letter *l* is present, the word "does not occur" (*na bhavati*) is employed. Thus, the sense is this: just as there is a cognition of the agent from the letter *l* when it is mentally supplied (*anusaṃhita*) in the case of "he is" (*bhavati*), so too there would be a consequence of the cognition of the agent from the letter *l* which is actually heard (*pratyakṣaśruta*).

The point is this: the cognition of ungrammaticality (*asādhutvajñāna*) is not an impediment [to comprehension], because grammaticality (*sādhutā*), which consists in the possession of expressive power (*śakti*), is present even in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), and since comprehension arises even from such forms, the cognition of their ungrammaticality cannot act as an obstacle. The term "of that kind" (*tādṛśa*) means "in the case of the agent-comprehension brought about. "Co-occurrence" (*samabhivyāhāra*) means a collection of phonemes arranged in a temporal sequence; the meaning is that such co-occurrence is necessary because, in its absence, no comprehension can arise even through the verbal suffix (*lakāra*).

"Denotative power" (*vācakatva-śakti*) means the power consisting in the capacity to convey meaning. Nor is there the fault of "premature timing" (*aprāptakālatā*), because that [power] is useful for the manifestation of the *dhvani* (phoneme-sphoṭa); this is the sense. He demonstrates the complexity (*gaurava*) in the view that maintains the power resides in the substituend (*ādeśin*)—that is, in the case of not accepting the denotative power of the aforementioned co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*)—with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: in the event of not accepting the denotative power of the aforementioned co-occurrence.

Regarding the term "gaurava" (complexity): although in the view that holds that substitutes (*ādeśa*) denote meaning, one must necessarily postulate that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the word "bhavati" is the cause for the cognition of an existing agent of the action of becoming—thereby preventing the understanding of "bhūti" as such an agent—and thus the complexity is indeed equal, nevertheless, the advantage resulting from not having to postulate the recollection of the substituendum (*ādeśin*) remains entirely intact; this is the intended sense.

But surely, by this much, it follows that the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) itself is the expressive unit, and not the individual phonemes (*varṇa*) that constitute the verbal root and suffix within the usage; therefore, he says "and thus" (*tathā ca*), meaning "due to the absence of a decisive factor" (*vinigamanāviraha*). Nor is the mere plurality of phonemes the deciding factor, because the aforementioned sequence (*ānupūrvī*) is what governs them—this is the sense.

In reality, however, it should be understood that if the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) were the expressive unit (*vācaka*), there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of multiple phonemes within it serving as its delimiters; whereas if the phonemes themselves are the expressives, the simplicity (*lāghava*) of a single such sequence (*ānupūrvī*) being the expressive unit serves as the decisive factor. Now, an objection may be raised: if expressiveness is established as delimited by the property of "being remembered from a phoneme occurring within an actual usage," then, in the present context, it would be improper to claim that the word *bhū* causes the cognition of the agent of the action of becoming (*bhavana*), for the purpose of proving the absence of expressiveness [in the suffix]; this is because such a verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is not remembered from a phoneme occurring within an actual usage.

And thus, the aforementioned reasoning does not establish that co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) is expressive; nor is there any scope here for the principle of "the cause of that" (*taddhetunyāya*). For although co-occurrence may be a cause of verbal cognition by virtue of its utility in apprehending expressiveness, since there is no evidence for its being the expresser itself, it cannot be otherwise established as such by that [co-occurrence]. However, regarding the expressiveness of the *lakāra* suffix, the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) itself is the proof. Because of this lack of complete satisfaction, the author introduces the root text with the words "Moreover" (*apica*).

The sense is that [the agent] would not [be expressed], because the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in its original form (*sthānin*) is identical in both cases. However, according to the modern Naiyāyikas, this undesirable consequence does not arise, because they accept that only the *tiP* and other affixes occurring within the actual usage (*prayoga*) possess denotative power (*vācakatā*). It should be noted that the justification for the comprehension of the respective meanings in instances where there is elision (*lopa*) of a verbal root or an affix requires equal effort from both [schools]. As for the phrase "let it be so" (*ityastu*), the meaning is that the agent is obtained precisely through the denotative power of those two [the *tiP* and the *lakāra*], since agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs only to the substratum of the action (*kṛti*).

The phrase "anyeti" means "even when there is no expectation for the application of the treatise"; the sense is that the delimitors of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) remain distinct even in that case. The phrase "sāmānādhikaraṇyānurodhāt" means that if the suffix *śānac* were to denote effort (*kṛti*), it would be untenable to account for the cognition of non-differentiation (*abhedānvaya*) established by universal experience. It should be understood that the result of teaching the meaning of [tenses] such as the *laṅ* (imperfect) is simply the cognition of presentness with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The example "pacatikalpam" is given following the view that this is a noun ending in a nominal suffix (*svādyanta*).

According to the *Nirukta*, "names have substance as their primary referent"; thus, being a name (*nāmatva*) consists in generating a cognition whose qualificand is a substance (*dravya*). And this very quality is what constitutes the semantic role of a name in the rule of word-formation (*vyutpatti*). For this reason, others maintain that this objection applies to the view that the meaning of a particle (*nipāta*) undergoes a relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*). The phrase "of the definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) has the word "of the suffix" (*lasya*) as its ellipsis.

The sense is that [the view] regarding the [individual letters as the] cause of the offense is not desired by you. Now, if the substitutes (ādeśas) possess denotative power, then rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* which establish the expressive power of the original bases (ādeśins) would be rendered useless; therefore, he says: *laḥ karmaṇi*. The phrase "it has been stated" refers to the occasion of defining the expressive power of the verb (*ākhyāta*), this being the understood remainder. And thus, the conclusion is that the expressive power resides in the phonemes constituting the stem and suffix as they are heard in actual usage; this is the definition of the Phoneme-Sphoṭa (*varṇasphoṭa*). || 13 ||

In the investigation of *padasphoṭa*, the author introduces the root text while indicating that the relationship of the "supported and the supporter" (*upajīvyopajīvakabhāva*) also constitutes a logical connection (*saṅgati*). He says, "In this way," which means "in the manner already described. Since some substitutes (*ādeśa*) are also included within actual usage, he says, "the *tiṅ*-suffixes, visarga, and so forth," meaning all the phonemes occurring within linguistic usage. Now, if all such phonemes were the denoters (*vācaka*), how could the *padasphoṭa* be established? Therefore, he states the intended sense: "This [is the word]," while the phrase "co-uttered" (*samabhivyāhṛta*) has already been explained.

The meaning is as follows: since phonemes (*varṇa*) possessing a specific sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) are not denotative, the hope that a word-form (*pada*) consisting of such a sequence might be denotative is a vain hope. Now, one might object: "Since a collection (*samudāya*) is not distinct from its individual members, the denotative capacity must ultimately rest upon each individual phoneme; therefore, how can a word-form consisting of such phonemes in combination be denotative? To this, he refutes the denotative capacity of each individual phoneme with the words "prativarṇam" (with respect to each phoneme).

The phrase "because it contradicts experience" means that the cognition occurs precisely as "I understand this meaning from the word *ghaṭa*. He states another refutation with the words "individually," etc.; the meaning is that [the opponent] accepts that [the parts] possess meaning. By the phrase "elision of *n*, etc.," the inclusion of *jaś*-substitution and so forth is intended.

Consequently, one must accept that either those [parts] taken together are the expressive agents (*vācaka*). And in that case, by the reasoning already stated, the expressiveness of that collection is beyond dispute. The point is that this very [collection] is what we designate by the term "word" (*pada*).

[Objection: Since the denotative capacity of individual phonemes is impossible precisely because it is refuted by the principle of prolixity (*gaurava*), it will necessarily follow that this capacity belongs to the collection [of phonemes] alone; thus, the presentation of the argument that "phonemes uttered together" are the cause for the denotative capacity of phonemes is futile, as any suspicion of it being the ravings of a madman is dispelled by this very fact. To this, he says: "And this," meaning the presentation of the denotative capacity of phonemes uttered together. "In the final phoneme alone" means in the phoneme heard at the end of the word.

By the particle *eva*, there is the exclusion of the preceding phonemes within the word-complex. He states the reason for this: "because of capacity" (*śakteḥ*). This means that since it is impossible for the causal capacity for cognition—which consists of an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*)—to be fully present (*paryāpti*) [in the preceding phonemes], and because cognition arises from the final phoneme alone, there is no evidence for its existence elsewhere. This is the meaning.

[Objection: But if that [word] alone were the expressive unit, would it not follow that the meaning would be understood from hearing only that much? To this he says: "by each preceding letter," which means by each preceding letter constituting that word. "In another view" (matāntare) means for the purpose of refuting that other view according to which, if the individual phonemes uttered together are not expressive, then the word in the form of their aggregate is all the more not expressive. The word "stated" (uktam) has "in the root text" as its ellipsis. In reality, however, this undesirable consequence does not arise.

He states another objection regarding that [view of] the awakener (*udbodhaka*), beginning with "Rāma exists," etc. Regarding the phrase "by the occurrence of the cognition of the meaning": since the co-presence of the awakener is to be inferred from its effect, it should be understood that in such a case, due to the absence of the effect, there is an absence of the awakened latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Now, one might object: "Co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) is not a collection, because it is impossible for letters—which are sequential and rapidly perishable—to constitute one; therefore, it cannot be the state of possessing preceding letters related by the relation of 'immediately following,' precisely because that [collection] does not exist."

Nor is there another distinct entity (padārthāntara) inherent in the phonemes (*varṇa*), because there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*). Otherwise, since the phonemes themselves—when followed by such specific properties (*dharma*)—would suffice as the denoters (*vācaka*), it would follow that the *pada-sphoṭa* is without a basis (*nirālambanatā*). Furthermore, since the effects produced by words (*pada-prayukta-kārya*) are observed in the phonemes themselves, how could the *pada-sphoṭa* be established? To this, he says: "The direction [is indicated]" (*dig iti*). Its meaning is as follows: a word (*pada*) is a collection of properties (*dharma-samudāya*), not the phoneme itself; for one accepts a word consisting of a collection of those [phonemes] arranged in a prior-to-later sequence, which is distinct from the individual phonemes, based on the cognition [of the word as such].

This is necessary; for this very reason, even the common usage "a phoneme in a word" (*pade varṇaḥ*) is naturally consistent. Furthermore, the phonemes are eternal, and their sequence (*paurvāparyam*) exists because—according to the method to be described regarding the *vākya-sphoṭa*—the recollection of each preceding phoneme stands in a relation of immediate succession to the recollection of the following phoneme. Thus, [the sequence] consists in being the object of a recollection qualified by a recollection whose own object is that [preceding phoneme]; therefore, there is no inconsistency. How this is so will be explained in the determination of the *vākya-sphoṭa*.

Thus, in the view of *pada-sphoṭa*, it results in the conclusion that "the collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) is the expressive unit," which is technical in nature; this means it is designated by Pāṇini and others. However, earlier [authorities], having rejected the idea that the phonemes recalled through substitutes (*ādeśa*) possess the capacity to convey meaning, stated that the expressive power belongs to that which consists of the collection of phonemes forming the base (*prakṛti*) and the collection of phonemes forming the suffix (*pratyaya*). Now, however, the distinction is that the expressive power belongs precisely to the collection of phonemes constituting both [the base and the suffix].

The construction should be understood as follows: since it is impossible to know the distinction between the stem (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*)—such that "ghaṭ" is the stem and "ena" is the suffix—the Bhāṣya statement "all [words] are all words" establishes the eternity of phonemes (*varṇa-nityatā*). He says "by way of a pretext" because forms such as *vas* and *nas* are also included within the subject (*pakṣa*). Thus, the point is that since the possession of the property to be proven (*sādhyavatva*) is the essential factor for being an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), its status as an example is not untenable even if it is not distinct from the subject (*pakṣa*). In that context—that is, in cases such as *vas*, *nas*, and so on.

The meaning is the determination of the distinction between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). The phrase "even for grammarians" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Others, however, argue that since the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*) is observed in cases such as *ām* (the genitive plural ending), it is impossible—in the manner previously stated—to infer that in forms like *vām* (the dual ending), the portion beginning with *va* (as in *āmo vaḥ*) is a suffix while the other portion is the base; thus, the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of the composite consisting of base, suffix, and affix (*upapada*) is not established.

In the case of *ghaṭena*, however, the fact that the word *na* is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *ṭā* has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself; therefore, there is no failure to establish the division [of meaning] there. In examples such as *ajarghāḥ* and *acakāt*, however, since there is no other way, the expressive power belongs to the base (*prakṛti*) alone, according to the maxim: "That which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided. Alternatively, let it be that even in those cases, comprehension arises from the recollection of the elided suffix. Or else, let there be a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the base itself in the sense of the suffix qualified by its own meaning.

They say that even the principle "all substitutes are in place of all [original] words" is far removed from the view of those who maintain the non-eternality of phonemes (*varṇa*), because of the identity of the reasoning [involved]. With the intention that the determination of the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākya-sphoṭa*) follows in the sequence [of topics], he introduces the root text with the words *suptiṅanta-*. That [refers to] the capacity to denote. "In the aggregate" means in the sentence, which consists of an aggregate of words. "In this way" means like the expressive power of the sentence (*vākya-śakti*). "Specifically" means in the form provided by the sūtra. By the phrase "when they are not being cognized," it is indicated that the cognition of the denotative capacity residing in them is impossible.

It is indicated by the phrase "by the comprehension of the whole" (*samudāyavyutpattyā*), which means by the apprehension of the denotative power of the whole. "From the cognition" (*bodhāt*) means from the cognition of the meaning of the suffix as qualified by the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). "Even there" (*tatrāpi*) means that even in the case of a word-form consisting of a *sup* or *tiṅ* suffix, there is a [separate] expressive power; thus, the postulation of that [power] is intended. Now, an objection is raised: since the root text beginning with "by the jar" (*ghaṭena*) introduces two types of *sphoṭa* along with their supporting arguments, how can the sentence-*sphoṭa* serve as an illustrative example when the word-*sphoṭa* is the thesis to be proven?

Furthermore, since the word-sphoṭa (padasphoṭa) is not established, and because the meaning of a sentence—which consists of the relationship between the meanings of those words—is consequently unestablished, there is no occasion for postulating a power residing in the sentence-meaning; thus, due to this initial dissatisfaction, [the author] sets aside the word-sphoṭa and establishes the power of the sentence, stating "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*). Accordingly, since the apprehension of the power of word-meanings occurs precisely within the words, and since the presence of the words makes possible the apprehension of the power of the words, the understanding of the sentence-meaning arises through that very power of the words.

In cases such as "hare's horn" (*śaśaviṣāṇa*), where that [word-meaning] is impossible, this understanding arises through the power of the sentence itself due to necessity. Although the two positions are established by the greatness of the word *vyavasthitau*, nevertheless, since the explanation is possible through the necessary sentence-sphoṭa alone, the postulation of a word-sphoṭa is not required; thus, it should be understood that in the final conclusion, it results in the sentence-sphoṭa alone.

He demonstrates the necessity of the sentence-sphoṭa (vākya-sphoṭa) itself with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*), meaning: in the absence of the acceptance of sentence-power (*vākya-śakti*). "Of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*) means: even for one who lacks the knowledge of sentence-power characterized by its being the generator of the cognition of the sentence-meaning. The intention is that when that [sentence-power] exists, a cognition is indeed desired even in that case. "The contingency of cognition" (*bodha-prasaṅga*) means: the undesirable consequence of the cognition of an effort conducive to the bringing of the pot as the object. The intention is that this occurs because the presence of the mental representation of word-meanings produced by the knowledge of word-powers (*pada-vṛtti-jñāna*) exists. "Just as in 'bring the pot'" (*ghaṭam ānaya* iva).

In this context, the phrase "of one who lacks such proficiency" is to be supplied. Now, one might object: "The absence of comprehension occurs simply because of the lack of another auxiliary cause, namely the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), which is a cause for verbal cognition. To this he replies: "Even when [the other causes are present]. The phrase "due to the absence of comprehension" means "due to the absence of such a comprehension. Thus, the point is that since the absence of the effect follows from the absence of something, that thing must necessarily be the cause; therefore, the power of the sentence (*vākya-śakti*) is indispensable. By this, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) that establishes causality has been demonstrated.

Demonstrating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he establishes the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*): "In that very [instance]" means "in the case of 'bring the jar' (*ghaṭam ānaya*) itself. By the word "from cognition" (*bodhāt*), he excludes [the idea] that causality exists merely by virtue of the [sentence's] own nature (*svarūpasataḥ*). In our view, the power of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣāśakti*) is defined as the power of the sentence residing in such a cognition that possesses expectancy and which serves as the cause of comprehension; thus, even though there is a difference in technical terminology (*paribhāṣābheda*), the establishment of the *vākyasphoṭa* remains unassailable—this is what he intends to say with the words "then" (*tarhi*). Now, one might object: "The nature of power (*śaktitva*) consists in being the generator of the apprehension of meaning (*arthopasthiti*) which is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*)."

That [denotative function] resides in the word alone and not in the sentence, because the denotative capacity residing in that [sentence] does not produce such an apprehension; therefore, he says "that which brings about the apprehension of the meaning. The phrase "residing in the word" means the causality of denotation that resides in the word. Thus, since there is no purpose for including the status of being a cause of verbal cognition within the apprehension in this view, the nature of *śakti* (denotative power) remains intact even if the knowledge of that [word] does not produce such an apprehension. Furthermore, by including the denotative word as "word-ness" (*śabdatva*), the intention is that even corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are included.

Now, in the view of those who maintain that the power resides in the sentence (*vākyaśaktivāda*), since the sentence-meaning consists of a relation and is manifold, there would be an infinity of powers corresponding to its various differences. Furthermore, because the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises through the function of individual words even without the power of the sentence, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the claim that the apprehension of sentence-power is the cause of that cognition. Moreover, the position that the sentence is an indivisible unit (*akhaṇḍavākyapakṣa*) has not been introduced at this point.

If it is argued: "Even if that [over-extension] is avoided by including 'immediate succession' (*avyavahitottaratva*) in the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryyatāvacchedaka*), how can the apprehension of the sentence-meaning's power (*vākyaśaktigraha*) regarding a relation that has not been presented [priorly] serve as a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) before such a cognition occurs? [The answer is: True; even though the relation is not presented in its specific form, there is a general apprehension of it—just as in the case of pronouns like *tad*—in the form: "A verbal root-word qualified by a case-ending is expressive of an action qualified by a kāraka. For you too, the apprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparyagraha*) must be stated in exactly this same way.

Immediately thereafter, through the co-utterance of specific words and by virtue of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), there arises the manifestation of that action as qualified by those factors (*kāraka*) through a specific relation (*saṃsarga*). Nor does this entail an infinity of potencies (*śakti*) caused by the infinity of relations; for the capacity of a unifying relation to act as a regulator is equal in both cases—such is the summary of his view. Now, one might object: this aforementioned method would be tenable only if it were established by proof that the denotative power residing in the sentence is indeed "potency" (*śakti*); but that is not the case. To this, he replies: "And this is logical."

This is the definition of "power" (śakti) as the capacity to convey meaning residing in the sentence. He states the reasoning itself: "as the object-domain" (viṣayatā); the meaning is that this is common to all verbal cognition (śābdabodha). "Of the knowledge of the relation" (vṛttijñānasya) means "the presentation (upasthiti) produced by the knowledge of the relation. The phrase "by way of the relation of object-domain" (viṣayatāsambandhena) is to be supplied [to complete the sense].

Regarding the term *lāghavena* (by way of parsimony): otherwise, since a person who does not know the word-potency (*śakti*) of the word "pot" but knows that word, or one who knows some other word-potency, would still experience a cognition from the sentence "Bring the pot," it would have to be stated that the cause for the verbal cognition of a pot is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the word-potency of a word whose meaning is a pot. This would result in the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating an infinite number of cause-and-effect relationships due to the diversity of meanings. In our view, however, because the mental presence produced by the knowledge of the word-potency of "pot" does not exist [in those cases]—due to the absence of the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā-sambandha*)—there is no manifestation of it in the verbal cognition; thus, only a single cause-and-effect relationship needs to be postulated. This is the meaning of *lāghavena*.

Now, one might object: since the relation between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) between "pot" and "pot-ness" can be reversed, an understanding qualified by pot-ness would arise from the command "bring the pot. To prevent this, one must necessarily admit that for an understanding qualified by pot-ness, the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) of pot-ness as qualified by it, which is produced by the knowledge of the word-pot's denotative function (*vṛtti*). Since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is thus avoided by this alone, there is no evidence for the aforementioned causal relationship [between the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning]. To this he replies: "And this should be discerned," meaning that, in view of the infinite causal relationships involving the entry of the denotative function (*vṛtti*) due to the distinction between each word and its respective object.

Since the apprehension (*upasthiti*) [of a word-meaning] is produced by the knowledge of the word, it is appropriate that it enter into the scope of the causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābdasāmagrī*). This being the case, in order to prevent the appearance in verbal cognition of space—which is apprehended as a cause by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*)—and of Devadatta and others, one must state that the apprehension produced by a *vṛtti* (denotative function) is the cause of verbal cognition in general, specifically as the object (*viṣayatā*) [of that cognition]. Furthermore, in accordance with the requirement for the relation (*saṃsarga*) to appear in verbal cognition, it is necessary to postulate a *vṛtti* even with respect to the relation itself.

And thus, it has been analyzed there that the phrase "of the knowledge of the *vṛtti*" (vṛttijñānasya) carries its literal meaning, namely, "because of the cognition of word-meanings by means of words and the cognition of sentence-meaning by means of a sentence. In reality, however, the term *vṛttijñāna* retains its literal sense; immediately after "of the knowledge of the *vṛtti*," the phrase "by means of the relation of the subject-matter which is implied" (*anuṣaktaviṣayatāsambandhena*) means "by means of the relation of the subject-matter belonging to the cognition that constitutes the capacity of the knowledge of the *vṛtti* to convey the meaning."

Otherwise, since the cognition of sentence-meaning (*śābdabodha*) would consist solely of the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the function of the sentence, it would be impossible for that [sentence] to be the cause of that [presentation] through that relation; thus, the "power of the sentence" (*vākyaśakti*) would result in a miscarriage. This is how it should be understood. On this point, they say: since verbal comprehension does not arise without the presentation of word-meanings produced by words, it is beyond dispute that the presentation of such word-meanings is the cause of verbal comprehension.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for a word—consisting of a stem (*prakṛti*) and so forth—to bring about the cognition of its meaning without a relation, a relation in the form of a *vṛtti* (linguistic function) is also necessarily required for that [meaning]. However, such a relation does not exist between the conventional word (*pada*), which is a collection of those [constituents], and the sentence (*vākya*), which is a collection of those words, with respect to the qualified meaning; for even without that [relation], the cognition of the qualified meaning is established simply through the convergence of causes such as expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). This is because the very nature of the effect to be produced is defined as "the state of being a verbal cognition whose object is the meaning of one word qualified by the meaning of another word."

As for the claim that parsimony (*lāghava*) serves as the proof for the existence of sentence-meaning (*vākyaśakti*), based on the fact that the cause [of verbal cognition] is simply the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of word-meaning relations, connected by the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), that is not correct; for the causality of that [sentence-meaning] independently remains unestablished. To explain: in such a causal relationship, would the "word-meaning relation" (*padavṛtti*) be introduced as a property of the word, or as a property of the sentence, or as the general property of "relation" (*vṛttisāmānya*)? It cannot be the first, because everyone accepts that the mental presence produced by the knowledge of the word-meaning relation is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

Not the second, because the function of the sentence (*vākyavṛtti*) is not established prior to that. For this very reason, not the third; moreover, since in your view the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the power of the sentence is of the nature of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is impossible for it to have that [sentence] as its object; thus, the aforementioned method is not tenable.

Furthermore, the knowledge of the syntactic function (*vākyavṛtti*) does not independently serve as a cause for verbal cognition (*śābda*) in general; for there is a deviation [from this rule] when, at some time, even for one who does not know the sentence-potency (*vākyaśakti*) of "Bring the jar," a verbal cognition arises due to the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, during the stage of the presentation of word-meanings produced by the knowledge of the potencies of words such as "jar. As for the claim that the sentence is nothing other than the expectancy consisting in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), that too is not correct; for if that were the case, then in the cognition "the objectness belonging to the jar," the sentence "Bring the jar" would have to be considered expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*).

Furthermore, there would be an impossibility of all established linguistic usage, such as the expression "the jar is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), which lacks expectancy. Thus, even if co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) were the cause of verbal cognition, it remains difficult to establish that this constitutes a sentence; where, then, could the existence of the power of a sentence be proven? Moreover, the claim that for one who has grasped the capacity to generate cognition residing in co-occurrence, the knowledge of that [capacity] is the cause of the cognition, is an empty statement.

Because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is the knowledge of the co-utterance itself that is the cause of verbal cognition, there is no basis for asserting that the knowledge of its being a generator of understanding is the cause. Nor is even that possible, because prior to the verbal cognition, the relation itself has not yet been presented. Even if it were presented in a general form, since the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) and so forth would still be required for its manifestation in a specific form, the very root of your position would be undermined; consequently, the existence of the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) itself would be rendered unestablished.

If one accepts the presence [of the sentence-meaning] prior to verbal cognition in the manner to be explained hereafter, or if one accepts verbal cognition immediately after the presence produced by the knowledge of the sentence's function (*vākya-vṛtti*), there would be the consequence of the collapse of the validity of verbal testimony (*śābdaprāmāṇya-bhaṅga*), because the nature of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists in its being the cause for grasping an object not already known. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras included the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*; otherwise, if the power of the sentence were [the sole basis], that inclusion would clearly be redundant.

"The cognition of meaning from a word occurs simultaneously [with the word]"—because of this statement by Kaṇāda, and because it is impossible to grasp that [simultaneity] due to the absence of any grammatical rule or other means for grasping the power of a sentence, the sentence-sphoṭa is merely superficially attractive. With the intention of keeping in mind the weakness of the previously mentioned method of grasping the power [of words], the author says "Now then" (*nanu*) in order to state another method regarding that [sentence-sphoṭa]. "Because of its being unprecedented" (*apūrvatvāt*) means because it is not present prior to the verbal cognition.

[Objection: Is it not the case that prior to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) residing in a word—defined by the object-meaning presented through perception and other means—is quite easy? Thus, the root text’s statement that "it is the same regarding the word" appears untenable. To clarify the intended meaning, [the author] states: "In the word itself. The expressive power of words resides only in the related object-meaning (*anvitapadārtha*). Furthermore, this relation (*anvaya*) is known in its general form. For this very reason, when an object such as a jar is presented in relation to something else upon hearing a word like "jar," there necessarily arises an expectancy for its correlate (*tatpratiyogī*): "With what is the jar related? or "With what is [this] related?"

The [cognition] has the form "being an object" (*karmatvam*) and so forth; for a cognition whose qualifier is a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) generates a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*). As for its manifestation in a specific form, however, the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as *tvam* (you) is the restrictive factor; therefore, it manifests in verbal cognition (*śābda*), because it is the object of the word's function (*padavṛtti*), since otherwise there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of manifesting even that which is not denotable (*aśakya*).

Nor does it follow that, in a case such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the relation appearing in multiple ways—such as "the objecthood [is] connected with the other"—because even though the respective meanings are presented by their respective words, they are necessarily manifested in only one way due to the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Nor should it be argued that since expectancy is necessarily the regulator of that manifestation, it is pointless to postulate a linguistic function (*vṛtti*) there; for that [function] is accepted precisely out of fear that what is not denotable (*aśakya*) might otherwise be manifested.

Thus, since the manifestation of the relation (*saṃsarga*) is established by the power of the word alone, there is no power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) therein; furthermore, this is because "sentence-ness" (*vākyatva*) is more complex than "word-ness" (*padatva*). Such is their view. Consequently, even in the theory that [the meaning] is denoted by what is not yet known (*ajñātābhidhāna*), the impossibility of grasping the power of the sentence-meaning in a single word is the same. This is the sense. The point is that, because the word-meanings are already present beforehand, it is possible to grasp the power of the word-meanings therein. As for the acceptance of a function (*vṛtti*) where [the meaning] is indeed unknown, the point is that this is due solely to the impossibility of its manifestation in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

The suffix *vat* is used here with a locative ending, as seen in the locative case of the object of comparison (*upameya*). "In the sentence-meaning" means even in the relation (*saṃsarga*). This [term] is stated with the intention that this capacity to be understood (*bodhyatva*) is the "power" (*śakti*); thus he says "the apprehension of power" (*śaktigraha*). Since the word *lakṣaṇa* is well-known in the sense of a "mark" (*cihna*) and so forth, he explains it by taking it to mean "that which is useful for the subject at hand"—namely, "it is characterized" (*lakṣyate*). In the root text, in the phrase "in the meaning" (*arthe*), the locative case signifies "being defined" (*nirūpitatva*).

Intending that [the word] "that" (tat) connects with the cognition of the word's power (*śakti*), he explains [the verse] with the words "even in the case of a word," etc. The meaning of "its apprehension" (*tad-graha*) is the apprehension of the power as determined by the sentence-meaning. This is the underlying idea: for one who has determined the power of a word toward its referent through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) in such cases as "Bring the jar," when that sentence is heard, the presentation of the word-meanings by means of the words leads to the presentation of their mutual relation; thus, the presentation of that relation is not untenable.

However, since mental [cognition] generally possesses a doubtful nature, there is a reliance on words for the sake of certainty; for in that case, because there exists a determinative factor such as the indicative mark (liṅga) which is the cause of grasping the word’s power (śakti), doubt is impossible. Now, one might object: since it has been established that the ascertainment of the power residing in the word itself is the cause of verbal cognition (śābdabodha), and since—according to the aforementioned reasoning—that [ascertainment] is impossible prior to the verbal cognition, it is difficult to maintain that the power of the sentence (vākyaśakti) is the cause of verbal cognition. To this, he says: "In reality, however... (vastutastu).

The apprehension of that [relation] is the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of the sentence as a whole possessing a specific meaning. Thus, since the apprehension of power occurs first in the sentence itself through usage—which is the crest-jewel among the apprehenders of power—and it is determined that this [sentence-level apprehension] alone is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is no deviation regarding the causality of the knowledge of the relation (*vṛtti*) in verbal cognition. This is because the state of being qualified by both relations—namely, having its own locus as its object and co-occurrence with a manifested latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is itself—is unimpaired even in the present knowledge of the sentence.

The point is that since the presentation of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) does not depend on [the individual word-meanings] in the middle [of the process], there is no occasion for the aforementioned defect. Now, one might object: "In that case, the *padasphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa) would result in being without a basis. To this he says: "By means of insertion and deletion" (*āvāpodvāpābhyām*). This means by means of bringing in and removing—that is, by the inclusion of one word and the non-inclusion of another word. "Its apprehension" (*tadgrahaḥ*) refers to the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of each individual word-meaning in each individual word.

The sense is that two views result: when the verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from the individual word-potencies aided by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, then there is the *pada-sphoṭa*; but when it produces that cognition independently of those [word-potencies], then there is the *vākya-sphoṭa*. Some, however, maintain that the causes of verbal cognition are the presented word-meanings or their presentation, but not even the knowledge of the words, because there is deviation—since verbal cognition arises even without it.

As it has been said: "For one who sees the white form and hears the sound of neighing, as well as the sound of the hooves striking the ground, there arises the cognition: 'A white horse is running. This is not correct, because it would follow that even the visual perception of a jar or other objects, which arises without sound, would be verbal in nature.

In that case, if [you argue] that there is no verbal nature (śābdatva) because of the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I see there, I do not hear," then the same applies to the present case as well, since the aforementioned cognition is established by means of inference alone; thus, the existence of a verbal cognition (*śābdapratyaya*) therein is simply unproven, and so forth—you should understand this yourself. Furthermore, in your own view, the term "indication" (*upalakṣaṇa*) refers to [the process in cases like] "A hamlet on a deep river," where [the meaning is derived] through the individual word-powers (*padashakti*).

The sense is that, because it is impossible to have a cognition of the intended meaning through *lakṣaṇā*—which consists of a relation possible for [the word] itself—in the manner stated, one must accept that the relation of being cognized by [the word] is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) [of *lakṣaṇā*]; thus, *lakṣaṇā* of the sentence is admitted with respect to the entire sentence-meaning alone. "The two positions" means the two types of *sphoṭa* established according to the distinction between words and sentences. He states the difference in logical inconsistency: "of those produced and unproduced"—in the view of those who maintain the non-eternality of phonemes (*varṇa*), since phonemes are particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of eternal and all-pervading substances (*yogyavibhu*), they are destroyed by the quality produced immediately after them; therefore, their simultaneous existence is impossible.

Regarding the view that maintains their eternity, he says: "Of those manifested. The phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, but their manifestation alone is non-eternal; for it is accepted that the very factors intended by others to be the producers of phonemes—such as the impact on the throat and so forth—are actually their manifestors. The meaning is that simultaneous existence is simply impossible. Now, one might object: "Let it be that phonemes do not exist simultaneously; what is undesirable for us [in this]? To this, he says: "The aggregate of phonemes. He states the same even regarding the theory of the *sphoṭa* of the sentence: "And thus..."

The meaning of the phrase "the impossibility of knowledge" (*jñānāsambhava*) is as follows: because a conjunction of momentary parts is impossible, at the time of the production of the final phoneme—or at the time of its manifestation—the preceding phonemes, whether already manifested or not, cannot persist. Consequently, since there is no cause for perception through identity with that aggregate form of a word or a sentence, perception itself is impossible; thus, the apprehension of the aforementioned capacity (of words) therein is as non-existent as a flower in the sky. This is the summary of the argument.

Adopting the position that [the letters] are manifested (*abhivyakti*), he offers a solution: "The perception of the subsequent letter" (*uttaravarṇapratyakṣa*). According to this view, since all letters are eternal, they would all exist without interval in the time immediately following their own substratum-moments; thus, to avoid the consequence of a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*), the state of being "immediately subsequent" must be predicated only of their respective manifestations. It is precisely through the superimposition (*āropa*) of that [manifestation-property] onto the letters themselves that the linguistic usage of "being immediately subsequent" occurs with respect to the letters. For this very reason, it is introduced as a qualifier in the context of its presence there.

And that [subsequentness] consists in being subsequent while being non-intervened. Non-intervention, moreover, is the state of being connected with a moment that is not a locus for the destruction of itself. Consequently, in expressions such as *te ghaṭita-ghaṭaḥ*, the portion *śīdhu* does not possess the status of a word (*pada*).

Since the absence of intervention (avyavadhāna) and so forth as defined by one [letter] cannot constitute a relation with another, they enter [the definition] merely as indicators (*paricāyaka*) of their own [relation]; thus, there is no suspicion of a lack of universal applicability (*anugama*). This is because each subsequent letter, upon its presentation, possesses the aforementioned relation—being related to the whole while not being the locus of the destruction of the presentation of each preceding letter, and being the locus of the moment of that [presentation's] destruction; therefore, its possession of that [relation] remains intact.

And thus, since worldly perception (laukikapratyakṣa) is possible regarding the final phoneme—given that there has been a non-worldly cognition (alaukikasaṃvitti) regarding each preceding phoneme—it follows that the power (śakti) consisting in the capacity to convey meaning can be easily grasped therein; therefore, the establishment of the aforementioned word-sphoṭa and sentence-sphoṭa is free from objection. This is the sense.
Thus ends the exposition on the sphoṭa of words and sentences. || 18 ||

Indicating that the occasion for the exposition of the indivisible *sphoṭa* constitutes a logical connection (*saṅgati*), he says: "Now" (*idānīm*), which means immediately following the exposition of the divisible *sphoṭa*. Regarding the term "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*), the indivisibility of words and sentences consists in their having no constituent parts (*avidyamānāvayavakatva*).

Since it is also intended to prove that phonemes (*varṇas*) are not composed of parts, he says "dṛṣṭānta" (example). Raising the objection—given the rule that an example-sentence must necessarily contain words such as *iva* and so forth, how can there be the status [of being an example] for the phrase "in the phonemes" (*varmeṣu*) and so on?—he explains the root text by including the word *yathā*: "yathā. The phrase "ivetī" means "like the parts" (*avayavā iva*). Thus, the status of being an example for the literal wording itself is not untenable.

The meaning of the word *praviveka*—derived from the root *vi-cir* in the sense of "separation" (*pṛthagbhāve*), with the prefixes *pra* and *vi*, and the suffix *ghañ* used as an abstract noun—is that it culminates in "difference. With this intention, he says: "Difference. Now, since the phonemes, which are its constituent parts, are perceived when words and so forth are cognized, how can they be non-existent? To this, he replies: "The point is this. He clarifies what is excluded by the particle *eva* in the phrase "indeed indivisible" (*akhaṇḍameva*) for the sake of explaining the meaning: "Not, however... The term "infinite" (*ananta*) means "many" (*aneka*).

Is it not the case that the very cognition "this is the letter *ka*, this is the letter *ga*" is the proof for the postulation of phonemes (*varṇa*)? Even if it is maintained that such a cognition has as its object the *sphoṭa* manifested by specific conjunctions of air—which are intended either as the manifestors or the producers of the phonemes—then still, cognitions such as "the letter *ka* has arisen" or "the letter *ka* has perished" would be untenable; for you do not admit the existence of letters like *ka* as entities distinct from the *sphoṭa*.

And since that [sphoṭa] is eternal, if its object were the production residing in the manifestor, then it would follow that pleasure and so forth are also eternal; therefore, he says: "by way of being the producer of each respective phoneme. He shows the proof for this specific difference (vaijātya) with the words: "of the non-productivity of phonemes," and so on. Thus, when such a specific difference is taken and superimposed upon a portion of the sphoṭa by means of inherence (samavāya), the distinctness of the aforementioned cognition is established; consequently, there is no lack of justification for that [cognition], nor does it serve as a proof for the existence of additional phonemes such as 'ka' and so forth.

Nor is there such a cognition as "What is this that has arisen? and so forth; for, since there exists a subverting factor in the form of non-differential recognition—namely, "This is that very one"—such a cognition is an error. Furthermore, there is no contingency of pleasure and the like being eternal, because their destroyer—the specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) of the self that arises immediately after them—is fully present. This is the intended meaning. In the *Bhāmatī*—that is, in the work of Vācaspati Miśra bearing that name—the phrase "taking [it] as the starting point" (*ādāya*) is explained as being directed toward superimposition (*āropa*), in accordance with the expression "is superimposed" (*āropyate*).

The view of another school will be stated as follows: "It is merely the conjunction with air"—meaning that it is merely the conjunction with air resulting from the impact of the palate and so forth. By the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of the sphoṭa consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), because it is simpler [to assume] that the non-superimposed inherence (*samavāya*) is the delimitor of denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedakatva*). Nevertheless, the meaning is: let the nature of *ka* and other phonemes belong to that very conjunction itself. He provides the solution: "Because of perception," etc. The underlying intention is this: if the phonemes *ka* and others were of the nature of the aforementioned conjunction, they would result in being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

Nor is that [singularity] desired, because it contradicts experience. Nor should it be argued: "How can the aforementioned singularity, being a supersensible property, be an object of direct perception? For just as in the cognition "fragrant sandalwood," fragrance and the like—which are unsuitable for the eye—are nevertheless objects of visual perception, so too it is possible for this [singularity] to be grasped by the auditory organ. It is only due to a contradiction regarding the object [of the word-sound itself] that the cognition of singularity in respect to the *sphoṭa* is considered erroneous.

Others, however, hold that if the cognition of "ka" and so forth were to apprehend the property of *katva* (the universal "ka-ness") as residing in a portion of the *sphoṭa*, then there would be the possibility of its being non-erroneous; but rather, in that portion, there is a distinct class-character (*vaijātya*) through the relation of being manifested by its own substratum. Nor is there a lack of proof for the relation of being manifested by its own substratum, because the very cognition of "ka" and so forth serves as the evidence; for a relation is indeed a specific factor that determines a qualified cognition.

For this very reason, they maintain that the cognition "the crystal is red" has the conjunction with its own substratum as its relation. Nor is that erroneous cognition one whose object is inherence; for when a cognition can be established as valid through some means of apprehension, it is improper to assume it to be an error—more on this will be stated later, they say.

He summarizes: "And likewise" means that because expressiveness is untenable; that is to say, since words and sentences consist of aggregates of phonemes, and because—according to the reasoning already stated—it is impossible for phonemes to exist simultaneously, the apprehension of their expressiveness is untenable. Even if one were to somehow establish the apprehension of expressive power by the aforementioned method, the point is that since words and sentences composed of phonemes are non-eternal, the impossibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) remains difficult to avoid.

"By this" connects with "is refuted"; the meaning is: by establishing that the indivisible *sphoṭa*—which is proven through the impossibility of recognition—is the expressive agent (*vācaka*). "Because of non-experience" implies that, since there is no evidence for such [a view] in that very case, the status of being an expressive agent is decisively rejected. The meaning of "distinct from the *sphoṭa*" regarding those phonemes such as *ga* is that we accept the expressiveness of the *sphoṭa* which is the object of a cognition having the universal *gatva* (the property of being *ga*) as its qualifier. It is stated "of those possessing sequence" because a collection of things that perish very rapidly and arise simultaneously is impossible.

Regarding those [letters] that are sequential yet endure, it is stated "occurring more swiftly" (*āśutarā*), which means they are counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction occurring in the third moment. The sense is that [the formation of a word] is "impossible" because, in perception, the object serves as the cause by way of identity (*tādātmya*), and thus a collective form of object simply does not exist. [Objection: Regarding the phrase "of the preceding and following," one might ask: in the view of those who maintain the non-eternality of phonemes (*varṇa-anityatāvādin*), since perception itself is impossible for those phonemes—which are counter-correlatives of destruction occurring in the third moment—how can there be the possibility of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by them acting as a cooperative cause?

For instance, the cognition of "k" and so forth apprehends the property of being "k" (kāditva) as a qualifier in respect to the letter "k" and so forth. Since the knowledge of a qualifier is a cause for the cognition of a qualified object, one must admit that after the production of the letter "k" and so forth, there is a non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) perception in the second moment, and a qualified cognition in the third moment; however, this is not possible, because of the statement of the elders: "That which is connected [to the senses] and present is perceived by the eye and other [senses]."

If it is argued that in perception, because the object serves as a cause by existing simultaneously with its effect, the object in the form of the letter *ta* (or *ka*, etc. is absent in the third moment; and that it need not be said that a determinate cognition (*savikalpakajñāna*) arises in the second moment itself through the recollection of "k-ness" (*katva*) and so forth produced at the moment of the letter *ka*'s arising—for even so, the initial qualified cognition remains difficult to establish.

On this point, they argue as follows: because saṃsāra is beginningless, there is no impossibility [of such a memory], since it is possible for a memory that produces a specific cognition—characterized by being "first" and so forth—to arise, just as there arises a memory of the fact that something is a means to a desired end, which is the cause for an infant's inclination toward suckling at the breast. Furthermore, the very specific cognition that "this is the letter *ka*" or "this is the letter *ga*" immediately after the production of the letter *ka* and so on, serves as the proof for such a postulation.

If, on the other hand, such a specific quality were a cause in a general sense, it would follow that the perception of the letter *ka* and so forth would be impossible; yet this is not the case, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the destruction of the final sound and in the destruction of cognitions and other factors produced prior to deep sleep. However, in the destruction of qualities belonging to a different class (*vijātīya*), there is a generic difference (*vaijātya*) that excludes the final sound and the like, and which likewise excludes the phonemes that are the objects of the first determinate cognition.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for such a specific universal (*vaijātya*), since it is established precisely by its inclusion within the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of perishability. Thus, in the destruction of the final sound, it is the second moment itself that serves as the cause; and even in the destruction of that particular phoneme, because the cause is postulated as having the nature of that specific individual existing in the third moment, they say that there is no impossibility of perceiving it persisting into the third moment, even if the aforementioned causal relation is accepted.

"An over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)" means that there would arise the cognition of the *rasa* [sentiment] from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the letter *sa*, the vowel *a*, the *repha* (the sound *r*), and the *visarga* contained within the word *saras*. "Indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*) means not composed of phonemes (*varṇa*). "Manifested by *nāda*" means manifested by the phonemes included within the resonance (*dhvani*). The phrase "because it has been established" implies the remainder of the sense: "on the occasion of the definition of the divisible *sphoṭa*."

The meaning is that such a perception has been established as being worldly (*laukika*) with respect to the final phoneme-part and non-worldly (*alaukika*) with respect to the past phoneme-parts; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as "sara" and "rasa. He states the refutation of the view that something additional [to the phonemes] is the expressive agent: "of the phonemes," etc. [He says] "because of being swallowed by the dilemma (*vikalpa*). For if each [phoneme] were individually manifesting, then since the manifestation could occur from the first phoneme alone, the utterance of the others would result in futility, and there would also be an over-extension.

The meaning is that since it is difficult to establish the existence of a "whole" (*samudāya*) in the manner described, its capacity to manifest [the word-meaning] is likewise impossible to assert. However, the followers of Kaiyaṭa argue: if the production of the second and subsequent phonemes were possible at the time of each preceding phoneme, then perhaps—though only with difficulty—the perception of words and sentences could be accounted for according to your method; but that is not the case. For, as it is said: "As long as the voice remains on the sound *ra*, it does not reach the sound *au*; by that very effort, only one phoneme is articulated."

This is because of the authority of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ*, which states: "When that first phoneme has been cut off, having withdrawn that effort, one undertakes another effort and the second [phoneme] proceeds. Thus, it is accepted that immediately after the destruction of the preceding phoneme, the second phoneme arises through a different effort. Furthermore, in your view, the perception of phonemes is untenable; for since they perish as soon as they are uttered, there is no production or manifestation of them, as they are momentary and delimited by imperceptible moments.

And thus, the usage of priority and posteriority—expressed by the word *idam* (this) as the object of perception in the form "this is prior" and "this is posterior"—which is required for the application of rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, is impossible. Likewise, since it is impossible to state that the state of being immediately followed constitutes a relationship between two related entities where one has perished and the other exists, the perception of a word (*pada*) remains unestablished according to the reasoning previously stated.

Furthermore, according to the rule that only that which has its capacity grasped possesses the power to convey meaning, it is impossible to grasp the capacity for words in the case of individual utterances due to their difference. This is because sequence (*ānupūrvī*), being constituted by the "immediately following" relation delimited by specific points in time, lacks uniformity (*ananugamakatva*) and thus cannot serve as the delimiting factor of the expressive capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). However, if one accepts the indivisible *sphoṭa*, then since it is that [entity] delimited by each respective phoneme that serves as the object of conventional usage such as priority and posteriority, the aforementioned logical inconsistency does not arise.

And they say that although all the letters included in the sequence are indeed the manifestors of that [cognition], nevertheless, it is only when the final letter is manifested that it becomes the cause of that cognition; thus, there is no occasion even for the aforementioned dilemma.

Now, even if it is accepted that each conjunction with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*) is individually a manifester, one might object: "In the word *gauḥ*, the sphoṭa would be manifested as both *ga*-ness and *au*-ness. To this, he says: "But rather... (*parantu*). The meaning is that there is no such fault, because it is accepted that a specific type of air-conjunction is the manifester of the sphoṭa qualified by the universal *ga*-ness (*gatva*). "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means: precisely because it is accepted that a specific air-conjunction manifests the sphoṭa in its respective form.

The point is that there is no acceptance of anything additional to that; for since the cognition of the letter *ka* as having "k-ness" and other qualifiers is accounted for by those respective conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) alone, there is no evidence for postulating a *sphoṭa* distinct from them.

[Objection: But surely the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains exactly as it was in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, because the conjunctions with the manifesting air, in their form as *sa*-ness and so on, are equal in both instances. To this, he says: "And thus," [referring to] "the state of being *gha*. That is to say, by taking into account a difference based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*), just as there is the status of being the referent of the word *ghaṭa* in that very same [phoneme] consisting of the letter *ṭa*—which is the object of a cognition having *gha*-ness as its qualifier and which is the object of a grasp of non-intervention—so too, in the case of the *sphoṭa* consisting of the letter *ra*, [there is such status] in the grasp of non-intervention which is the object of a cognition having *sa*-ness as its qualifier.

The sense is that, because it is the object of the linguistic usage "lake," the sphoṭa whose essence is the lake does not have the nature of taste (*rasa*). Now, an objection: in your view, since phonemes such as *ga* are of the nature of the eternal sphoṭa and are thus eternal, they cannot possess the property of being "immediately subsequent" (defined as the state of occurring in a moment that is qualified by the non-arising of the moment of its destruction, etc., and the state of occurring in a moment that is the locus of that [destruction]). Therefore, how is the aforementioned method possible? To this, he says: "But rather... (*parantu*). Thus, even though the phonemes are eternal, their manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is non-eternal.

The sense is that since this [order] is also accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, there is no contradiction in its being the state of immediate succession (avyavahitottaratva) following one phoneme in the manifestation of another; thus, by taking this into account, the cognition of words such as "ghaṭa" is established. The meaning of "ata eva" is precisely because the state of immediate succession relative to manifestation is the regulator of the conventional usage of "sequence" (ānupūrvī). He says "by the elders" (vṛddhaiḥ), because the moderns do not accept it in that way. The meaning of "etena" is by means of establishing that the sphoṭa, consisting of phonemes delimited by sequence, is the expressive agent (vācaka).

This is connected with the word "rejected" (*apāstam*). "Sphoṭa" means an indivisible word-meaning that is intended to be the denoter. "Not the first" means not one [of the two options]. He states the refutation of that position: "In the case of the word 'ghaṭa'"—the meaning is: for one who has grasped the expressive power (*śakti*) in the sphoṭa delimited by the sequence "ghaṭa. "From the word 'kalaśa'" means from that which has not grasped the expressive power in the sphoṭa delimited by that [same sequence], and so forth.
