The meaning is as follows: [the opponent argues that] because of the consequence of [constant] cognition [of meaning], since the *sphoṭa* delimited by the sequence "kalaśa"—which has the status of a cause established for denoting a jar—exists at that time due to its being eternally of one form, there would be no such fault if a word consisting of a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) were the denoter. Regarding the phrase "the cause of the cognition of meaning": in the aforementioned case, because the *sphoṭa* is not the object of the apprehension of a power delimited by the manifestation of the synonym "kalaśa," there is no consequence of the cognition of meaning [from that synonym]. This is the intended sense.

"Thus" (evam) means that one accepts the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) as delimited by the manifestation of the synonym (*tatparyyāya*) as the cause for the verbal cognition produced by that synonym. "By the necessity of the apprehension of power" means that, according to the maxim *nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇa* ("one does not grasp what is qualified unless the qualifier is grasped"), the apprehension of power in the synonym must necessarily be admitted. "Because it is appropriate" (*ucitatvāt*): he states this very appropriateness [by saying] "that being so. "As the apprehension of power" means "as the apprehension of power residing in the synonym."

"Due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*) means that this [sphoṭa] is the cause because it is simpler than the aforementioned form; this is the meaning. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. With the words "otherwise," he reveals the complexity (*gaurava*) in the previous theory; this is merely a stylistic variation in expression. "Not the second" means that even the position that there is a plurality of sphoṭas in the case of synonyms is not accepted. "Otherwise" means the postulation of distinct sphoṭas for each synonym. "The capacity" (*śaktim*) means the postulation of infinite capacities, distinguished by those respective differences, in the words.

"Various" (aneka) means differentiated by various synonyms (paryāya-bheda). "Because it is established for all" (sarvasiddhatvāt): thus, since the postulation of multiple powers in the case of synonyms is not something new (apūrva), there is no fault. This is the underlying intention: the aforementioned objection has an opportunity only if one accepts that phonemes (varṇas) are the manifestors of the sphoṭa; however, this is not the case under the view that the sphoṭa is non-different from the phonemes, because in that case, since there is no separate postulation of power, the charge of prolixity (gaurava) is impossible.

The avoidance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by including "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*) within the scope of the determinant of the effect (*kāryatā’vacchedaka*) for the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) regarding synonyms is common to both [theories]. Now, an objection: in your view, since phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal and distinct from the *sphoṭa*, it is impossible for there to be a sequential order (*ānupūrvī*)—which consists in the property of having each preceding phoneme as its constituent—to serve as the determinant of the power (*śaktatā’vacchedaka*) with respect to the phonemes that follow immediately after them. To this, he says: "that determinant," meaning the determinant of the power.

The phrase "prior" (prāk) refers to the remainder of the argument in the text: "the state of being the object of a manifestation produced at the moment that constitutes its own locus of manifestation. Now, if one accepts the eternity of phonemes (varṇas), then since the effect of the sphoṭa would be produced by those very eternal phonemes, the sphoṭa itself remains unestablished.

Thus he says: "Because these [phonemes] have been established by you in their proper sequence, it is easy to establish the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) for those very phonemes as qualified by that [sequence], since they possess the status of being words; and because the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that 'this very word is the sentence' is thus possible. To this he replies with the word "dig" (direction/indication). The meaning of that is: if phonemes were independent and eternal, then indeed the *sphoṭa* could be established through them as an alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*).

However, since the sphoṭa itself, as perceived through [the process of] *kṛti* and so forth, is accepted as being the phoneme *ka* and the rest, the aforementioned possibility of an alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*) is impossible; for this very reason, there is also no suspicion of the cumbersome complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of multiple phonemes.

If it is asked, "What indeed is this *sphoṭa*, such that the phonemes (*varṇas*) are not distinct from it? they reply: It is called *sphoṭa*—the *nāda* (sound) designated by terms such as *parā* and so forth—which originates from the *avyakta* (the unmanifest), which consists of the three *guṇas* and is synonymous with *māyā* and *īśvara-sisṛkṣā* (the Lord’s desire to create); it is another name for *śabda-brahman*, presided over by consciousness, and is a resonance in which specific phonemes are not yet manifested. Although it is all-pervading, it is manifested by the vital air (*pavana*) located in the *mūlādhāra*, which is impelled by the effort dependent upon the speaker’s desire to express a known object.

It is conventionally designated as "para" (the supreme). It is manifested by that [speech] when it has reached the heart; thus they say, "they see. Furthermore, when it returns to the heart and is manifested by that very same [speech], it becomes the object of a cognition that delineates various meanings; because it is not perceptible to the ears of others, it is subtle and is called "madhyamā" (the intermediate) speech. However, for the speaker, it is heard when the ears are covered due to the impact of even subtler air, or during the utterance of a whisper.

That very [subtle sound], having reached the end of the mouth by means of that air moving toward it, goes to the region of the throat, strikes the head, turns back, and becomes manifested in various locations; it is then termed *vaikharī*, which is capable of being perceived even by the hearing of another.

And the proof for the stated meaning is the Śruti: "Speech has four measured quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech humans speak. And there is the Purāṇic statement: "From that Bindu, as it was being divided, there arose the unmanifest essence of sound. That very thing, when perfected through the Śruti, is celebrated as Śabdabrahman. This meaning is also clear at the beginning of the eleventh skandha of the Bhāgavata.

In the *Śikṣā* as well, it is stated: "The self (ātman), having united with the intellect (buddhi), joins the mind (manas) with the desire to speak; the mind strikes the fire of the body (kāyāgni), which impels the vital air (māruta); that air, being driven upward and struck at the head, reaches the mouth and produces the phonemes (varṇas). Accordingly, it is the very portion of sound (nādāṃśa) within the *madhyamā* state, delimited by the heart and consisting of the internal *praṇava*, that is the signifier (*vācaka*). This is because of the Vedic revelation: "The syllable *Oṃ* alone is all speech; this [speech], when manifested by the consonants (sparśas) and sibilants (ūṣmans), becomes manifold in form."

"Because it resides in the hearts of all living beings, it is also designated by the term 'Brahman'"—this is explained at length elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "because of such cognition": the implication is that otherwise, since a *mālā* (a garland) consisting of a succession of phonemes is not distinct from the words (*pada*) that constitute its aggregate, the cognition apprehending the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) would be untenable. "Otherwise" means: if such cognition were not a proof for the existence of the word-meaning (*padārtha*).

The existence [of the pot] is established by the cognition "the pot is in the shards," which apprehends a difference; however, if that cognition were not a proof for it, then the non-establishment of the pot and so forth would be evident, because such a cognition can be accounted for by taking into account only the shards and their conjunctions—this is the sense. By the word "tu" (but) in the phrase "In the Kausetubha, however," a lack of approval is indicated. The reason for this is that even if one does not accept a sphoṭa distinct from the phonemes, there is no inconsistency in the aforementioned cognition.

Because the word *mālā* (garland) refers to a series of varṇas delimited by their sequential order, it is possible for the term "sequential" (*ānupūrvi*) to stand in a relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) with respect to that [series]. Furthermore, since the constituent parts such as the potsherds are produced by heterogeneous causes, their difference cannot be denied; thus, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not apply. Others, however, maintain that the varṇas do not have the nature of *sphoṭa*, but rather that *sphoṭa* is simply that which is manifested (*abhivyaṅgya*) by the varṇas.

Nor does the fault mentioned regarding the view that each [letter] is an individual manifester apply here; for since all the letters included within the utterance are perceived as being colored by the very form produced by the reflection of that manifesting form, the perception of multiplicity is merely adventitious (*aupādhikī*), just as a single face is perceived as long, round, and so forth due to the influence of various manifesters such as a sword or a mirror. For this very reason, there is no need even to postulate a genus (*jāti*) therein for the sake of providing a unifying factor.

Furthermore, because there is no manifestor distinct from the phonemes, there is never a cognition of that [word] devoid of phonemes; and the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) themselves are what provide its reflection. And since it is accepted that it [the word] is colored by the form of the manifestor in the very same sequence in which they reside in the mind, there is no lack of distinction between the words *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*.

Because the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of that [sphoṭa] occurs only when it is colored by the manifesting forms (phonemes), there is no contingency of semantic comprehension upon hearing an unfamiliar word for one who has already grasped the power in the sphoṭa manifested by synonyms such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*). For this very reason, they say that the common usage—"this is one word," "this is one sentence"—naturally accords with reality. The phrase "in this way" (*evam*) means: provided that the indivisible sphoṭa alone is the signifier. He explains the consequence of invalidity itself with the words "of the word" (*padasya*); this is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the sentence (*vākya*).

"Because it is indivisible" means that it is devoid of any division between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*). The implication is that you yourselves have established that only such an [indivisible] entity possesses denotative capacity (*vācakatā*). "Of the treatise" refers to the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). "By means of the base and the suffix" means that its sole purpose is the derivation (*vyutpādana*)—that is, the communication of the expressive power (*śakti*)—from those two.

And thus, the sense is that if the word were an indivisible unit (*akhaṇḍa*), this science—which teaches the denotation of word-meanings through the division into stem and suffix—would result in invalidity. The phrase "for the sake of understanding the goal" (from *upeyapratipattyartha*) is to be construed with the subsequent text as well by changing its grammatical form. The remainder is: "This conceptual construction was resorted to and accepted by the Sage for the sake of the comprehension of the goal—that which is to be understood. Having asked [the question], he [the teacher] replied, "Food is Brahman"; and having understood that even that [food] is of such a nature, he asked again, "The mind is Brahman."

The food eaten by that [breath] also becomes threefold: "Breath is Brahman. Having understood its nature to be likewise, he was asked again: "Mind is Brahman. The food eaten by that [mind] also becomes threefold, according to the scriptural statement: "That which is coarse becomes feces; that which is middling becomes flesh; that which is subtle becomes mind. Having ascertained its impermanence from this, he was asked again. When he was asked once more, it was taught to him: "Consciousness (vijñāna) is Brahman. Having understood that even this is conditioned by its own functions (vṛtti), he was asked again, and it was taught: "Bliss (ānanda) is Brahman."

He understood. Thus it is established that [the Self] remains having attained the state of being the Reality (vastutva). Now, one might object: "This *Vallī* does not expound the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), because the fifth is not a means, is not a sheath, and because it is taught therein as the very thing to be known. Anticipating this doubt, he provides an example of the five sheaths found in the *Ānandavallī*, saying: "Or just as... For the five sheaths mentioned there are indeed means; moreover, even the sheath of bliss (*ānandakośa*) which was taught there is not Brahman, because it is worldly and impermanent. Rather, [it says]: "Brahman is the tail, the support."

In this context, the word *brahman* as it is heard [in the text] refers exclusively to the primary Brahman. For this very reason, the word *puccha* (tail), which signifies a support (*ādhāra*), is also appropriate, since its primary meaning of "tail" is sublated. Thus, just as in the *Ānandavallī*, the five sheaths (*pañca-kośas*) are employed as means for the cognition of Brahman, which is the ultimate substratum of all, yet they do not possess actual Brahman-hood; so too here, the unreal suffixes and stems—which produce the notion of denotative power—are sublated by the actual denotative power residing in the *sphoṭa*, and thus the meaning is the indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) whole. By the phrase "from hearing and so forth" (*śravaṇāditaḥ*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes reflection (*manana*) and the rest.

The meaning is that [the objection] "it is not the scripture" arises because there is deviation even without this scripture through means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*). He states the reasoning, along with an illustration, regarding how one means does not invalidate another: "And so" (*tathā ca*). The state of being the knowledge of *sphoṭa* is not the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the study of grammar; rather, it is a specific class-character (*vaijātya*) residing in that knowledge. And that which is delimited by such a character is not [attained] from another means; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The point is that even if the specific difference (*vaijātya*) has not been previously presented, the apprehension of its causal status is to be understood according to the direction stated in the *Vidhivāda*. "As if produced by a mantra" means as if it were delimited by being produced by a mantra; the same applies to what follows. Now, one might object that there is a futility in producing that which does not accomplish a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, he says: "And of that," meaning of the cognition of the *sphoṭa*. "Of the sacrifices and so forth" means of those [sacrifices] which are enjoined with the renunciation of desire.

By the phrase "sacrifice and so forth," there is the inclusion of giving and other acts mentioned in the Śruti: "They seek to know that Brahman through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by giving, and by austerity. By the phrase "the body and so forth," there is the inclusion of the organ of speech. Now, one might object: since even the purification of the body and such is not an end in itself for a person (*apuruṣārtha*), it would be difficult to initiate activity even with that as a goal. To this he says: "directly," and by the phrase "heaven and so forth," there is the inclusion of liberation (*apavarga*). The meaning is that [these acts] are direct causes of heaven and indirect causes of liberation.

Regarding its being the cause of the [knowledge of] musical notes (svaraga), the scriptural authority cited in the Bhāṣya is the Śruti passage, "One is the Word" (*ekaḥ śabdaḥ*); and regarding its being the cause of liberation (mokṣa) through a traditional succession, the Smṛti passage, "Two Brahmans are to be known," is the authority. It should be understood that the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvajñāna*), which constitutes the link in this succession, is established by the Śruti, "Only by knowing Him," because this scripture teaches the exclusion of anything other than that [Self-knowledge] as being the direct cause of liberation. To provide support for the stated meaning from the consensus of Hari (Bhartṛhari), he says, "It has been said. That refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) which expounds the Sphoṭa consisting of sound (*nāda*).
"Of liberation" (apavargasya) means "of mokṣa. "The door" (dvāram) means "that which is conducive to it. He states a qualification containing a reason: "of the impurities of speech" (vāṅmalānām).

"Cikitsitam" (the science of healing) is derived from the root *kit* with the suffix *san* in the sense of "removing," followed by the suffix *kta*. Thus, its meaning is that which is the means for removing the impurities of speech; therefore, it is the gateway to liberation (*mokṣadvāra*). The underlying idea is that, just as sacrifices and other rites are for the purification of the body, this [grammar] is used specifically for the purification of speech. Since it is the most purifying among all branches of knowledge, it is called "adhividyam," meaning it shines pre-eminently among the sciences (*vidyāsu*). Accordingly, it has been said: "And the great seers declare that among the Sāmas, Ṛks, and Yajus, grammar is the ultimate."

"This" refers to the first step among the stages of the ladder of the perfected ones (*siddha-sopāna*); the meaning is that this is the foundational section for abiding in the state [of the word]. Here, "one whose delusions have passed away regarding the *sphoṭa*" means one who is free from error—that is, one who possesses knowledge of this reality. "The absolute," meaning the one called *parā*, he perceives directly through the dharma born of yoga. Thus, once his status as a yogi is established, what remains? It means that the knowledge of reality remains. As it is said in the twelfth book of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, following the description of the *nāda*:
By worshipping which, yogis shake off the impurity of the self known as substance, action, and agent, and attain the state from which there is no rebirth.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "because falsity is not established": the meaning is that, since the division into base and suffix—like the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so forth—is itself illusory (*māyika*), it does not possess the same degree of falsity as an absolutely non-existent thing such as a rabbit's horn; this is because [the author] will state this point extensively later on. Furthermore, the intention is that even though it is unreal, just as the reflection of a jewel's luster is useful for obtaining the actual jewel, so too is this [division] useful for the vision of the Supreme Self. The phrase "by the word 'etcetera'" (*ādipadena*) means by the word *ādi* employed in the expression "like the five sheaths etcetera."

The reasoning has been elaborated upon in the discussion on compounding (*samāsavāda*). The root text introduces [the following] with "Now then" (*nanu*) for the purpose of resolving the objection that the impermanence of phonemes (*varṇa*), which is witnessed by the perception of their arising and destruction, would entail the impermanence of the *sphoṭa* as well if one were to accept that the *sphoṭa* consists of such phonemes. [The phrase] "of the phoneme-classes" (*varṇajātīnām*) means of the phonemes and of the classes residing in them, such as [the class] "being-a-vowel" (*tad-vṛttikatva*) and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: the cognition, "the phoneme *ka* has arisen," or "it has perished," must have as its object either the *sphoṭa* consisting of the phoneme *ka*, or the universal (*jāti*) residing therein, by virtue of their possessing the properties of arising and so forth. However, this is not possible; for since both [the *sphoṭa* and the universal] are eternal, such a cognition would necessarily be an error due to the sublation of its object. To address the objection that one might simply accept such a cognition as erroneous, he says: "due to the conjunction with air" (*vāyusaṃyoga*). This refers to the cognitions of *ka*, *ga*, and so on—that is, the mental states such as "the phoneme *ka*" and "the phoneme *ga*."

The objection that this would result in [the cognition being] erroneous is made according to the literal sense [of the opponent's position], for in the previously mentioned alternative, such error does not follow. Nor should it be argued that, even in your own view, the status of *katva* (the property of being *ka*) and so forth as objects of ordinary perception (*laukika-viṣayatva*) is untenable because there is no ordinary sense-contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*), namely the inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-auditory-organ (*śrotra-samaveta-samavāya*) which manifests them; for in your system, since *katva* and so forth reside in the conjunction with air (*vāyu-saṃyoga-vṛtti-dharma*), the cognition "I perceive *katva*" leads you to accept that the relation [between the organ and the object] is precisely the inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-manifestor (*sva-samaveta-vyañjaka-samavāya*).

Because there is no loss of its status as an object of the worldly realm; for, according to the maxim "when there is a superimposition, one seeks the cause," this very hypothesis is more appropriate than postulating that such numerous cognitions are erroneous.

The root of that view, however, should be introduced as follows: [Objection: But surely no one accepts that inherence residing in a manifestor inherent in itself can function as a relation; to this he says, "of the imagined" (*kalpitānām*). The meaning is this: even those specific properties residing in the air-conjunctions—which do not themselves reside [in the phoneme]—are imagined to exist there by way of the relation of inherence; they serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), meaning they produce the cognition of the vowel *ai* as being acute (*udātta*) and so forth. More will be said on this later.

To clarify the illustration, he states the Mīmāṃsaka position: "udāttatvādi" (high-pitchedness, etc.), where "ādi" (etc. includes low-pitchedness (*anudāttatva*). Because high-pitchedness and low-pitchedness are mutually exclusive, their existence must be predicated of distinct phonemes (*varṇa*). And such distinction between phonemes would only occur if they were non-eternal or multiple; however, that is not possible, as he says: "tasyaikatvāt" (because of its unity), and so forth. He provides the proof for its eternity: "tacca" (and that), meaning both eternity and unity.

"Because of the impossibility of abandonment" means because of the impossibility of [the universal] being an object [of cognition]. "Sublating" means that the cognition [of identity] when there is no difference between individuals is the sublater. "Provided there was prior non-existence," etc., means [the absence] whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of possessing the destruction of its own locus-time, and which takes the form of a temporal qualifier-relation (kālika-viśeṣaṇatā) delimited by the state of possessing such an absence. Since the relation of the second and subsequent moments possesses itself through the aforementioned relation, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in that case.

"From this very reason" means precisely because it contradicts experience. "Cognition" (pratyaya) refers to knowledge; "usage" (vyavahāra) refers to the employment of words. Now, one might object: even the act of utterance is indeed an activity conducive to the production of that [sound]; thus, every cognition would prove the non-eternality of phonemes. To this, he says: "And the state of being uttered" means the state of being qualified by manifestation, which is its [the sound's] objective content.

Thus, the meaning is that what is apprehended is precisely the objectivity (viṣayitva) residing in the manifestation of such a cognition as determined by the phoneme, and not the state of residing in the production [of the phoneme]; therefore, that [manifestation] does not prove impermanence. Now, one might ask: what is the proof for the claim that the term "utterance" (uccāraṇa) refers only to the impact of the throat, palate, and so forth, which causes the manifestation of the phonemes, and not to that which causes their production?

Some [opponents] might argue that for those who maintain the impermanence of phonemes (*varṇa*), logical applications such as "a phoneme arises" or "a phoneme produces another phoneme" are indeed accepted, and thus there is no contradiction with experience; to this he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*). By the phrase "of arising, etc.," the destruction witnessed by the cognition "the phoneme has perished" is included. "By way of succession" means by way of being manifested by its own constituent sounds (*dhvani*). "Not something additional" means not something additional to the proof of the impermanence of phonemes; however, it does not mean "not additional to the *sphoṭa*," because they do not admit the existence of the *sphoṭa*.

[Objection: But in this way, if the letters are apprehended through such a cognition [of the sound], there would be the consequence of their being erroneous due to the production of the sound and so forth; therefore, he says: "indirectly, the letters... The sense is that just as the cognition "the crystal is red," which apprehends its own substrate's conjunction [with a red object], is not an error, so too is this [cognition of the letters]. The remainder of the phrase "it remains" is to be supplied as "because of the cognition that 'the letter has been produced. [Objection: But to postulate that such a cognition invariably has a mediated (paramparā) relation as its object involves unnecessary complexity (gaurava); therefore, he says: "But rather..."

"Excessive" (*atirikta*) means "additional" (*adhika*). Thus, the sense is that, compared to the postulation of multiple phonemes (*varṇa*), their destructions (*dhvaṃsa*), and so forth, it is far more parsimonious (*laghīyasī*) to simply postulate that the cognition of those [phonemes] invariably involves a relation to their destructions. One might object: "If there were a necessity for sound (*dhvani*) in the case of phonemes, then the production of the phoneme would indeed reside in the phoneme itself through a mediated relation consisting of that [sound]. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the words "if not," meaning that sound is not experienced as distinct from the phoneme.

He states that its existence is not tenable even because of the lack of connection with a cause: "tadutpādaka... (by that which produces it), meaning by the conjunction of air arising from the striking of the conch and the lips, and so forth. "Varṇānutpatteḥ" (due to the non-production of phonemes) means due to the non-manifestation of phonemes. "Darśanāt" (because of seeing/perceiving): the root *dṛś* has the general sense of cognition.

The meaning is as follows: since there exists a distinct perception [of the phoneme] and its cause—the contact of the tongue with the palate and the air in the throat—there is no invariable concomitance (*naiyatyam*) between the manifestation of a phoneme and sound (*dhvani*) in the case of phonemes; thus, the aforementioned cognition regarding the relationship [between the two] remains unimpeded. The phrase "for you alone" (*tavaiva*) means for one who maintains that sound (*dhvani*) does not exist in the case of phonemes.

"Reversed complexity" (*viparītagaurava*) means that [the theory] is beset by a greater complexity than the economy resulting from the assumption that the causal complex producing phonemes acts as an obstacle to the sound (*dhvani*) arising from its own cause. "Of them" (*teṣām*) refers to the Mīmāṃsakas who maintain the eternity of phonemes. "And thus" (*evañca*) means that production and so forth do not reside in the phoneme.

The meaning is that the response is "by way of a counter-objection" (*pratibandyaiva*), which is to say, it is a reply that must be accepted by the opponent as a valid refutation. Thus, the intention is that whatever solution the Mīmāṃsakas have adopted regarding the validity of the cognition of [word-meanings] such as "origination" (*utpatti*) and so forth, that very same solution should be followed by us as well. Consequently, the result is that there is no obstacle whatsoever to accepting the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍavākyasphoṭa*). [Objection: But in this theory, since words do not exist, does this not contradict the established doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas?

For instance, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhiryajeta*), since the word "sacrifice" implies the mere substance [required for the rite], the mention of "rice" serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*): "with rice alone, and not with others. In that context, so that there may be no omission of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite or the commenced optional (*kāmya*) rite in the absence of rice, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is employed. This is because, since the generic property of being rice (*vrīhitva*) serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the ritual efficacy, the substitute is also considered to be scripturally sanctioned (*śrauta*).

In your view, if a substitute were employed there, the performance of the meaning of that scriptural injunction would not be accomplished, resulting in the nullification of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and others, because the action performed with *nīvāra* grains is a different action altogether. Furthermore, this would entail the abandonment of the established maxim: "The action is not substituted; rather, it is the substance alone that is substituted. Likewise, regarding the rule "only with rice, not with others": since the absence of rice would otherwise lead to the loss of both the obligatory rite and the commenced optional rite (*kāmya*), a substitute is indeed taken up.

Because the action that serves as the indicator of the capacity (*śakti*) for the nature of rice (*brīhitva*) is distinct [from the action of the substitute], there would also be the abolition of the maxim: "Action is not substituted, but substance is indeed substituted. Likewise, in the injunction "One should sacrifice a white goat," the connection of the action with the substance, the goat, is based on direct Vedic revelation (*śrauta*), since it is directly expressed by the accusative case-ending; however, the connection of the quality of whiteness is based on syntactical context (*vākyīya*).

Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that, it is impossible for that substance to be devoid of qualities or for that quality to be without a substratum. Since the connection of the quality "white" with the action depends solely upon its dependence on the connection of the white quality with the goat—and because the connection with the quality established by the sentence is weaker than the connection with the substance established by direct audition (*śruti*), due to the white quality's dependence on its connection with the goat for its own connection with the action, and due to the substance's connection [with the action] being established by direct audition rather than the sentence's presentation of the quality.

Because of its weakness, in the absence of a white goat, a goat possessing other qualities may be sacrificed, but not a ram endowed with the quality of whiteness, for that would result in the sublation of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), and such a thing is impossible under the view that [the compound] is an indivisible unit (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*). In this very same way, there is likewise an impossibility of applying the principles of Mīmāṃsā based on other constituent words.

If it is asked, "In your view, since the indivisible *sphoṭa* itself possesses the nature of an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*), how could there be a sublation of one by another?", they reply as follows: Through the analogy of the "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavaya*), by means of the addition and removal of words and word-meanings from the indivisible sentence and its respective indivisible meanings, one adopts imagined words and word-meanings; thus, the employment of substitutes is justified. This is because, even though the sages possess knowledge of the ultimate reality (*tattva*), practical linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) cannot be carried out through that reality as it truly is.

At the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), because words and their meanings are employed in various ways whose true reality remains undetermined, the words do not possess an ultimate reality regarding those words and word-meanings; even the meaning of a sentence is merely relative to that [usage], since in the state of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-daśā*), everything belonging to the realm of linguistic convention is unreal. The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that all this would be possible only if phonemes were eternal; yet there is no proof for that very point, because sound in general has space as its inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).

Furthermore, just as the conjunction of a drum and its stick is the cause for sound consisting of resonance (*dhvani*), so too the impact of air against the vocal organs such as the throat is established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the cause for sound consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*).

And thus, since a phoneme uttered at a different moment is not perceived as the cause—by way of the relation of identity (*tādātmya*)—of a produced entity delimited by the nature of destruction (*dhvaṃsatva*) through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), and since the cognition "the phoneme has perished" arises [only when it is gone], one must postulate that only the phoneme immediately following itself is the destroyer. This involves postulating that, with respect to the destruction of a capable particular quality of an all-pervading substance (*vibhu*) through the relation of counter-correlativity, the cause is the phoneme immediately following itself, established by the relations of co-location (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) and immediate succession.

Furthermore, it is because the causal role of a fit specific quality of an all-pervading substance (*yogyavibhuviśeṣaguṇa*) with respect to the destruction of another such quality—occurring through the relation of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*)—is established in cases such as cognition, by way of the two relations of co-location (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) and being immediately antecedent (*svāvyavahitapūrvavartitva*). Nor should it be argued that the impact of the throat, palate, and so forth has the universal *ka-tva* (the property of being the letter *ka*) as its effect, for that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving a cacophony (*kolāhala*).

Indeed, auditory perception of noise does not have "soundness" (*kāṭva*) and so forth as its object, such that the worldly objective presence (*laukika-viṣayatā*) of that [quality] could possibly be included within the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatā-avacchedaka*). Furthermore, if even the staff and other instruments that produce a jar were to have "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) alone as the delimiting factor of their effect, it would follow that jars and the like are also eternal; thus, there would be a great deal of contradiction with established doctrine. Nor should it be argued that this consequence is acceptable because one adopts the Sāṅkhya position that only what already exists is manifested, for that doctrine itself is merely superficially pleasing.

To explain: is manifestation (abhivyakti) existent or non-existent? It cannot be the former, because, like a jar, it would exist even at the time when the jar has not yet arisen; consequently, the cognition "this is a jar" would arise [even then]. If one were to accept a further manifestation of this manifestation, then since that too would be an effect and thus existent, the aforementioned fault would indeed be unavoidable. In the latter case (if it is non-existent), there is a contradiction with your own tenet, because by the same logic, the production of other categories of entities would also be established.

Just as the impermanence of jars and other such things is established by the cognition "the jar has arisen" and "the jar has perished," so too the impermanence of the letter *ka* and others is determined precisely by the non-distinctive cognition "the letter *ka* has arisen" and "it has perished. Furthermore, it is impossible to establish that properties such as being a *ka*-letter (*katva*) are qualities inhering in conjunction (*saṃyoga-dharma*), for this would entail the absurd consequence that they could not be perceived by the auditory organ, since they would be non-material (*amūrta*). Nor can the perception of them be explained through the aforementioned sense-object contact alone; if that were the case, the perception of "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) and other such universals would likewise fail to occur.

Furthermore, there is no evidence for the appearance of that relation [between the letter and its inherence] in the cognition "I hear the letter *ka*"; for since the cognition "I hear a sound" has inherence as its object, the aforementioned cognition is likewise explained as having that same object. Nor can it be argued that all such cognitions regarding the aspect of inherence are erroneous, because the inherence of the phoneme is admitted therein, and thus there is no sublation of the object.

Furthermore, since there are multiple phonemes (*varṇa*), the perception of accentuation (*udātta*) and so forth therein would naturally be consistent; thus, the example itself is flawed. Moreover, since the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of phonemes are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), they cannot be denied, and therefore there is no burden of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) in postulating them.

Furthermore, in the view that maintains the impermanence of phonemes (*varṇa*), the recognition "this is that same letter *ga*" would be untenable. If one attempts to justify this recognition by claiming its object is merely "belonging to that class" (*tajjātīyatva*), then the form of the cognition would have to be "this belongs to that class" (*tajjātīyo 'yam*); however, in that case, one must admit that the cognition actually takes the form "this is that very same thing" (*so 'yam eva*) with respect to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Moreover, such a recognition which apprehends the non-difference from that very same individual—taking the form "this is that very same thing"—is established for everyone. Therefore, the claim that the *sphoṭa* consisting of phonemes is the expressive agent (*vācaka*) is simply impossible to maintain.

Furthermore, because *sphoṭa* lacks existence as something distinct from sound (*dhvani*), its description in the Yoga-śāstra and other texts is merely for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), as has been largely stated previously. As for the *sakhaṇḍa-sphoṭa*, it has already been refuted; therefore, they maintain that the denotative capacity belongs to the phonemes (*varṇa*) as delimited by their sequential order (*ānupūrvī*). The word "thus" (*ittham*) means "by the aforementioned methods. "In five ways" (*pañcadhā*) means distinguished by the divisions of phoneme, word, sentence, indivisible word, and indivisible sentence.
Thus ends the exposition of the *vyakti-sphoṭa* in the *Bhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*.

He defines the *jāti-sphoṭa* (the universal sphoṭa), which follows in sequence [from the previous discussion], with the words "as in the case of being denotable" (*śakyatva iva*). Now, one might object: since, according to the reasoning already stated, there are no phonemes (*varṇa*) apart from the sphoṭa, an investigation into whether a universal (*jāti*) residing therein is the denoter is like examining the teeth of a crow; therefore, he says in the *Sāra*: "This is the underlying point. He provides the proof for the non-difference between the phoneme *ha* and the phoneme *ga* with the words "because of the unity of the sphoṭa" (*sphoṭasyaikatvāt*). The meaning is that, by the rule that "what is non-different from what is non-different from x is itself non-different from x," there would result the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the cognition apprehending the non-difference [of *ga*] from the *ha*-constituted sphoṭa would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), since the *ga* is non-different from the sphoṭa which is non-different from the *ha*.

"And because there is no non-offense" means that precisely because there is no difference [between the phonemes], it is impossible for a cognition apprehending such a difference to be valid. Now, one might object: "Even if the sphoṭa consisting of phonemes is unitary, there is no inconsistency in the perception of difference rooted in the presence of contradictory properties such as *g*-ness (*gatva*) and so forth; however, its validity is certainly cast far away in the doctrine of the unity of phonemes. To this he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*), meaning: "insofar as *g*-ness and so forth are intended to be limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In the first case—the position that accepts *g*-ness in the sphoṭa—it is that very thing, namely *g*-ness itself.

[Objection: But since *g-ness* (*gatva*) and so forth are properties of the phoneme *ga*, how can they be identical to it? To this he replies: "by those who maintain the non-eternality of phonemes" means by the Mīmāṃsakas and others. "Extraneous" means because they accept the non-difference between property and substrate (*dharma* and *dharmin*). "Complexity" (*gaurava*) means that the cognitions of *ga* and so forth cannot be accounted for unless they have as their objects the *ga* phonemes qualified by *g-ness* and so forth. "In the latter case" means in the alternative theory which does not admit *g-ness* and so forth in the *sphoṭa*. "Contradiction" [means...].

The meaning is that the cognition [of the word] as "ga," and so forth, would be untenable. The point is that since the property *gatva* (the universal of being *ga*) does not reside in the *sphoṭa*, a cognition whose object is qualified by it is impossible. Regarding the phrases "not residing in the conjunctions of air" (*vāyusaṃyogāvṛtti*) and "residing in the sound-manifestation" (*dhvanivṛtti*), the former refers to his own view, while the latter refers to another school's position. He says "by way of superimposition" (*āropya*) because, according to the previously mentioned method, such a cognition can be easily established through the superimposition of that specific generic character (*vaijātya*). The reason given is "because error is impossible" (*bhramatvāyogāt*); the sense is that when a cognition can be established as valid (*pramā*) through a direct relation, there is no evidence for its having as its object a superimposed relation.

[Objection: "But surely, rather than postulating multiple additional phonemes (*varṇa*), it is more logical that such cognitions are simply erroneous. To this he says: "Or let it be so," meaning that since the validity of the cognition can be established otherwise, there is no need for the postulation of *sphoṭa*. [The word] "of that" refers to the conjunction (*saṃyoga*). "Transcendence of the senses" (*atīndriyatva*) means being devoid of ordinary objective presence (*laukika-viṣayatā*). "Defect" (*doṣa*) means a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

He answers by way of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*): "Like a property" (*dharmavat*). The meaning is this: just as you do not accept that the state of being a property residing solely in supersensible (*atīndriya*) entities is pervaded by the state of not being an object of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), so too, I [do not accept] such a specific difference (*vaijātya*) residing in supersensible conjunction (*saṃyoga*). The point is that if the possession of sensory perceptibility (*aindriyakatva*) by something supersensible is utterly impossible to assert, then likewise, the possession of such a specific difference as a property of the *sphoṭa* is also impossible, precisely because its perception would be unaccountable.

If it is argued that even though properties such as *katva* (the property of being the letter *ka*) are beyond the senses, there is no obstacle to their manifestation when they appear in the cognition of *ka* through the "characteristic of knowledge" (*jñānalakṣaṇā*), we say no. This is because in the cognition "this is the letter *ka*" (*kakāraḥ*), the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)—"I am directly perceiving *katva*"—involves the apprehension of the aspect of *katva* as an object of ordinary sensory perception (*laukika-viṣayatva*); thus, the aforementioned mode [of supersensuous apprehension] is impossible. Furthermore, the cognition "I see yellowness," which arises immediately after the cognition "The conch is yellow," is merely an error.

It should be considered that it is due to the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating that a specific defect (*doṣaviśeṣa*) is the regulator of such objectivity (*viṣayatā*). He concludes: "They indeed exist" means that phonemes (*varṇa*) distinct from the *sphoṭa* you favor certainly exist. "But" (*param*) means "however. "Due to complexity" means due to the complexity of postulating infinite powers (*śakti*) differentiated by the various individual phonemes.

[Objection: Since it is accepted that there is only a single power (*śakti*) with respect to those [words] which are subsumed under universals (*jāti*) such as "being a word occurring in wool" (*ūrṇagatapadatva*), there is no complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from multiplicity; therefore, he says: "In the section on *ākṛti*. This logic has been explained in detail in the determination of the meaning of nouns (*nāmārthanirūpaṇa*). [Objection: But there is no proof for such a universal; therefore, he says: "The word 'Hari'. The sense is that without a recurring property (*anugatadharma*), a uniform cognition of that kind would be impossible across all such words.

[Objection: If the mere fact of being apprehended as a recurring cognition (*anugatapratīti*) were sufficient to establish a universal (*jāti*), then even omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and other such properties would result in being universals. Therefore, its status must be established by means of being a delimiting factor of causal efficacy (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*) and so forth; since that is absent in the present case, how can it be a universal? To this, he says: "Necessarily" (*avaśyam*). The sense is that otherwise, because those respective words would have to be causes in their specific individual forms (*tattadvyaktitvena*), it would be impossible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [The phrase] "of being the delimitors of the cognition" means "of being the delimiters of the recurring cognition."

"By the sequence of phonemes" (varṇānupūrvyā) means by that [sequence] which must necessarily be postulated as the manifestor of such a genus (jāti). "Resolution" (nirvāha) means that since it is possible for the sequence—defined as the delimiting factor of the necessary antecedence—to serve as the delimiting factor of the causality of the uniform cognition, the causality [of the word] would consist in the presentation of the word as qualified by that form; thus, [the opponent's position] is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddhi). The sense is that this is not desired because it would entail the fallacy of being otherwise established, as it contradicts means of valid cognition such as perception.

Now, if the genus (*jāti*) is the locus of expressive power (*śakti*), then "genus-ness" (*jātitva*) must be stated as the delimiting factor of that power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Since that [genus-ness] consists in residing in all instances of the genus while not residing in anything other than them, its status as such is impossible due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*); therefore, he says: "by way of identity" (*tādātmyena*), which means "non-differently" (*abhedenā*). The sense is that, in this way, the aforementioned defect does not arise. This essential point was explained previously.

The meaning is as follows: since those two words (*jāti* and *jātyoḥ*) are indistinguishable insofar as they both consist of the phonemes *ra*, *a*, *sa*, and *visarga*, there is no criterion for determining whether the delimitor of the presentation of that which is qualified by the property of being a *rasa* (taste) or the delimitor of the presentation of that which is qualified by the property of being a *saras* (lake) is present. Consequently, because there is no deciding factor (*vinigamaka*), the cognition of a distinct meaning from them would be untenable. He dispels the misconception that the word *vā* implies an alternative position, stating: "The word *vā* means 'only' (*avadhāraṇe*). This means it functions as a restrictive particle.

Regarding the term "distinction" (*bheda*): likewise, even though there is identity of phonemes (*varṇa*) in those cases, because the *ānupūrvī* (sequential order) differs, it is precisely the *ānupūrvī*—consisting of the letters 'ra', 'vi', 'śa', 'ṣa', 'tva', etc.—that serves as the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), by virtue of being delimited by the aforementioned relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*) as the delimitor of the class (*jāti*) that brings about the cognition qualified by *rasatva*. Since that [specific *ānupūrvī*] is absent in the word *saraḥ*, there is no possibility of the cognition of something qualified by *rasatva* arising from the word *saraḥ*; such is the sense of the phrase "even here" (*evamapyatrāpi*). In the root text, in the expression "like high and low" (*tāramandavat*), the words *tāra* and *manda* refer to the properties (*dharma*).

And thus, the meaning is that it is just as in the view that phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal and unitary: when there is an impact by a dissimilar wind on the palate and other [articulatory organs], there is a perception of difference through properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*), and so forth. With reference to the *sphoṭa* consisting of the genus (*jāti*) of phonemes, the *Sāra* raises an objection with the words "Now, an objection... (*nanu*). "Of the genus" (*jāteḥ*) means "of the genus that conveys the meaning. "Respectively" (*pratyekam*) means "in each of those individual phonemes contained within a word," and the same applies hereafter. "The consequence of the cognition of meaning" (*arthabodhāpattiḥ*) implies that this would occur because the phonemes that manifest it are present.

"By way of its etymological meaning (*yogārthatayā*)" means by the etymological derivation of its constituent parts (*avayavavyutpatti*) which will be stated later, namely, "the object (*artha*) is manifested (*sphuṭati*) from this [word]. By the phrase "by this" (*etena*), the meaning is: by accepting that the universal (*jāti*) manifested by all the phonemes (*varṇa*) constituting that word is the denoter (*vācaka*). "Always" (*sarvadā*) means even when the word is not being heard. It is "refuted" (*apapāstam*); the sense is that although the universal is eternal (*sanātana*), because the manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*) is absent in the aforementioned instance, there is no manifestation of it, and thus it is impossible to establish a contradiction (*bādha*).

Now, on the view that the sphoṭa consists of the genus (*jāti*) of letters, it must be admitted that the meanings are conveyed by the very genera residing in all the letters that constitute a word. In that case, since the genus residing in one letter cannot be manifested by another letter, each individual letter itself must be said to be the manifestor. Consequently, the aforementioned defect remains exactly as it was; therefore, he says: "The meaning is this" (*ayam bhāvaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned defect": the sense is that because [that view] is thus defective, that position should not be adopted. "Therein" (*tatra*) means in the word and in the sentence; "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) refers to the genus such as "wordhood" (*padatva*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of having a distributive occurrence" (*vyāsajyavṛttitvasya*): the meaning is "of an occurrence by way of a distinct relation called pervasion" (*paryāpti*). Now, since a universal (*jāti*) is universally established as being merely inherent (*samaveta*), how can it have this quality of pervasion? To this he says: "by the evidence that apprehends the locus" (*dharmigrāhaka*). The meaning is: a universal is that which possesses a property; the evidence that apprehends it is the impossibility of [the word] being expressive [if it were not so], whether it be the state of being a word (*padatva*) or the state of being a sentence (*vākyatva*), because that [expressiveness] is established thereby.

Since the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of a genus that resides in each individual letter has been swallowed by the aforementioned refutations, it is impossible; thus, if the genus "word-ness" (*padatva*) and so forth, which is postulated because denotative capacity cannot otherwise be established, were to reside in each [letter] individually, then its very establishment would be impossible, as the failure to account for denotative capacity would remain unremedied. Therefore, the sense is that the phrase "manifested by multiple individuals" (*anekavyaktyabhivyaṅgyā*)—which does not prove that [the genus] is restricted to a single [individual]—means rather that it is "restricted to multiple individuals" (*anekavyaktiparyāptā*). This is the intended meaning.

In reality, however, let it be granted that the property of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth resides in each individual instance, based on the universal consensus and linguistic usage of the cognition "this is a pot" regarding each individual object such as a jar. For there is no linguistic usage of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) with respect to a single phoneme, by virtue of which the property of being a "word" (*padatva*) would reside in each individual [phoneme]. Rather, one should consider the opposite: that the term "word" does not apply to a single phoneme. This point must be kept in mind.

It should be noted that the inference "wordhood is not pervasive because it is a genus" is unconvincing (*aprayojaka*), as there is no supporting reason (*anukūlatarka*). Furthermore, this point must be observed here: the phrase "manifested by multiple individuals" refers to being manifested by phonemes delimited by their specific sequence (*ānupūrvī*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the cognition of different meanings in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*. Thus, this is merely an elaboration of the previously stated point; the only difference lies in the reversal of the qualifier and the qualified status between the sequence and the phoneme.

For this very reason, there is a connection with what follows. Intending that the meaning of the word *vyakti* (individual manifestation) is the phoneme (*varṇa*)—based on the etymological derivation "that by which something is manifested"—he says, "of sound and phonemes. Because phonemes are invariably concomitant with sound (*dhvani*), there is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between them; for this same reason, in the *Paspaśā* [section of the Mahābhāṣya], in response to the question "Now, in the word 'cow' (*gauḥ*), what is the word? it is stated that it is "the collection consisting of sound and phonemes, apprehended in common usage as that which conveys meaning. Alternatively, the sense is that it was said: "Or, sound (*dhvani*) whose object has been understood is the word (*śabda*)."

The phrase "the remaining meaning" (*śeṣārtha*) means the meaning of the second half of the present verse. He cites the consensus regarding the conventional usage of the term *dhvani* with respect to phonemes (*varṇa*), saying "for it has been said" (*uktaṃ hi*). The reference is to the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, specifically to the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the verse: "This is called 'dhvani' by the wise when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) excels the expressed meaning (*vācya*). The word "here" (*sara*) is the remainder [of the citation].

Regarding the phrase "manifested by the *sphoṭa*": the meaning is that it refers to the word consisting of the phonemes (*varṇa*) which are the manifestors (*vyañjaka*) of that which is manifested (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of the *sphoṭa*. Now, one might raise the objection: "Is not this entire elaborate argumentation regarding the establishment of the generic nature (*jātitva*) of 'wordhood' (*padatva*) and so forth, as well as its denotative capacity (*tadvācakatva*), fruitless? For it serves no purpose for human goals (*puruṣārtha*). Anticipating this doubt, the author introduces the root text with the intent of providing a resolution: "But what is that? The construction is: "What is that generic nature (*jāti*) which is intended as the denotator (*vācaka*)?"

"Real aspect" (*satyāṃśa*) means reality—namely, being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time; its opposite is unreality (*asatyatva*). He states the final meaning: "characterized by that manifestation" (*tad-vyakty-upalakṣita*), which means characterized by that manifestation; for it is impossible for there to be a specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) between the ultimate Brahman and manifestations. Therefore, it should be understood that [scriptures] declare that the world-creatorship and other attributes are merely characterizations (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that [Brahman]. "Universal" (*jāti*) means the object of the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding that [manifestation].

"Having unreal adjuncts" (*asatyopādhi*) means that the status of being an adjunct belongs to individual instances (*vyakti*); in reality, even for a single [universal], its capacity to produce various cognitions is delimited by—that is, characterized by—that [adjunct]. "The word 'substance'" (*dravyaśabda*) means the word "cow" (*go*) and so forth. Since the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept a genus residing in qualities (*guṇajāti*), or alternatively, it means "that which is expressed by the word whose nature is substance," because the Mīmāṃsakas admit that sound (*śabda*) is a substance. "By way of the nature of sound" (*śabdasvarūpatayā*) means by way of having the form of sound consisting of audition (*śruti*).

This is based on the Vedic scripture: "Two Brahmans are to be known. The underlying intention is as follows: Since the Taittirīyaka scripture—beginning with "From that, from this very Self, space was produced"—declares that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, and since it is well-known in the world that the effect is non-different from its material cause, it is firmly established that both name and object are non-different from their own non-different material cause, and thus non-different from one another. Consequently, when the world, which appears as distinct, is firmly sublated by the scriptural text "There is no diversity here," [the identity of name and object is realized].

Since the cognition of a sublated object is necessarily restricted to the existence of its substratum, Brahman—which remains as the reality whose nature is *sat* (Being)—cannot be known directly; therefore, the utility of the scripture (*śāstra*) lies in providing knowledge of Him by means of defining His names and forms, which serve as secondary characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*). How this is consistent with the [scriptural] statement "How could it be so? is the intended meaning, given the contradiction between the preceding and following parts. He says "superimposed" (*āvidyaka*) because it is impossible for that [form]—which consists of false knowledge or the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by it—to be a genus (*jāti*); "superimposed" means "fashioned by ignorance" (*avidyā-kalpita*).

Regarding the term *dharmaviśeṣa* (particular property): here, the word *dharma* is used to exclude [the relation of] subsistence (*vṛtti*), and the word *viśeṣa* is used to exclude that [subsistence] as well as individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) and so forth. This is another alternative view; thus, since both meanings are established in the original source according to different opinions, the sense is that there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

In reality, however, it should be understood that the very nature of existence (*sattātva*) as delimited by adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as "cow" and so forth, is what governs the linguistic usage of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like. Furthermore, in the Advaita philosophy, because there is an absence of delimiters such as "cow" and so forth, existence does not possess the character of "qualified existence" (*viśiṣṭasattātva*) at that time, since it abides solely in its state of being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmakatva*). Thus, the contradiction is easily resolved even when the text is interpreted in this sense. Although two types of *sphoṭa*—the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa and the *sphoṭa* consisting of the universal produced by the cognition arising from that sentence—have been mentioned regarding the subject matter of sentences without qualifiers, nevertheless, in the theory of the *sphoṭa* consisting of sound (*nādātmaka-sphoṭa*), [this is the case] for the scripture.

The root text introduces [the subject] with the intention that, while [these categories] are useful for human goals through a traditional succession, in the final view they are directly so; thus, that alone possesses primacy. The meaning is as follows: "That very [nature]" refers to that which has been stated by the phrase "that genus," which is established by such scriptural passages as "This Self" and "That is Truth. In the root text, the word "thus" (*ittham*) means in the manner previously described; it is being distinguished from the bases (*prakṛti*) and other terms which denote the superimposed. For this very reason, it is "spotless" (*nirañjana*), meaning free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Therefore, it is "imperishable" (akṣara), meaning indestructible, according to the Smṛti: "That which does not perish when all beings perish. Since only that which possesses limiting adjuncts (upādhi) can be subject to destruction, the term "Word-principle" (śabda-tattva) or "Word-state" (śabda-pada) is also an indication for form (rūpa).

By that [statement], through the use of the restrictive particle *eva* conjoined with the qualifier "Brahman alone," it is taught—that they declare (*prāhuḥ*)—that the material cause of name-and-form (*nāmarūpopādāna*) is Brahman itself; specifically, this teaches the pervasiveness of the non-limiting property (*anavacchedaka*), which is the essence of the Word (*śabdatattva*), over the exclusion of the absence of identity with Brahman regarding the qualifier. They declare it, meaning they know it as non-different from Brahman. In that context, the material cause of name-and-form is what is declared; they declare it, meaning they know it as non-different from Brahman. That is the meaning.

In this regard, having raised the objection—given that in other systems (tantrāntara) the property of being the material cause of sound is well-established in the case of space and so forth, how can Brahman be its material cause?—the author says: "The meaning is as follows," and so on. "Name and form" means established by the Śruti passage: "Entering with this living self, let me evolve names and forms. "Twofold" means consisting of an aggregate of two parts, namely name and form. "Therein" means between the two creations; "just as in the case of form" means just as in the case of the object consisting of ether and so forth.

The phrase "of the name" (nāmnaḥ) means "of the word that denotes it. "That very reality" (tattvam) means that Brahman alone is the material cause (upādāna), according to such scriptural passages as, "From this very Self... Since [the ether] ultimately results from having the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) as its material cause, Brahman is the material cause of both. For this very reason, their mutual non-difference is established, because they are non-different from Brahman, which is their own material cause.

Nor does the fact that Brahman is the material cause of the world entail its being subject to modification (*vikāritva*), for this has already been resolved by the author of the root-text himself when he states, "this world is a vivarta (illusory manifestation) [of Brahman]. Thus, by the elimination of empirical and apparent objects, Brahman alone remains as the residue according to the Śruti; such is the very meaning stated previously.

[Objection: But if multiplicity is entirely false in every respect, how is it that there is such a cognition among people? To this he says: "But the portion consisting of the *prakriyā*"—the meaning is: the portion consisting of linguistic usage such as roots (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), and so forth. The meaning is that it is merely a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by impure *sattva*. Thus, even though these [categories] do not exist apart from Brahman, their perception as distinct entities is caused solely by ignorance regarding the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*); the point is that as long as there is ignorance regarding the substratum, the appearance of multiplicity does not cease.

[Objection: But how can the scriptures be of use for the knowledge of such a Brahman? To this he says: "The portion concerning the *prakriyā*," which means the exposition of roots (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth. [He explains] "as ignorance" (*avidyā*): thus, the utility of the scriptures is according to the logic of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so on; the point is that they are not directly useful for the knowledge of That (Brahman) itself. Immediately after the *Vākyapadīya* statement "Ignorance alone is described," there is the verse: "The means [of instruction] are mere consolations for children who are being taught; having established them on an unreal path, one subsequently strives for the Real."

Regarding the phrase "the commencement of entities," its first half is as follows: "The world is determined to be finite through the observation of jars and the like. Its meaning is this: just as, having seen a jar or similar object, people infer that the entire phenomenal universe is finite because it possesses the nature of being an effect whose causality resides in something specific; in the same way, the "commencement of entities"—that is, the "proper commencement" (samārambhaḥ), meaning the birth—of entities such as space and so forth [is understood].

The meaning of the words is that the designation is primarily based on the state (*bhāva*), because [the world] has its origin in that; that is to say, because it has that as its material cause (*upādāna*). Alternatively, the reason is identity (*tādātmya*). Regarding the phrase "because of undertaking" (*samārambhāt*), it is understood that even Brahman, which is eternal and constant, appears as if it were something with a beginning and as if it were uncaused. If one were to accept that Brahman is a transforming material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*), there would be the suspicion of the consequence of its being subject to modification (*vikāritva*).

In reality, there is no such contingency, because that very [Brahman] is accepted as the material cause by way of being an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), just like the illusory snake in a rope; this is the sense. Regarding the reading "the beginningless Brahman is eternal," since it would render the mention of the material cause redundant due to the qualification of either one or the other, he says "by Brahman. Thus, in the present context, the word "Brahman" refers to Brahman in its self-luminous form, and therefore there is no aforementioned inconsistency; this is the sense.

Regarding the phrase "tameva bhāntam" ("shining upon that very [Self]"), the preceding portion is: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. The mention of "Śruti" (Scripture) is illustrative; it includes such Smṛti passages as: "The splendor residing in the sun which illuminates the entire world," and so forth. Thus, its nature as both self-luminous and luminous to others is established. Regarding its luminosity to others, I have already spoken. Its self-luminosity, however, means being luminous while not being illuminated by anything other than itself; in other words, being the object of eternal knowledge whose essence is identical to itself.

Because the scripture, "Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss," establishes that Brahman has the nature of eternal knowledge and bliss, the present scriptural passage, as well as the Smṛti text, "O Puruṣottama, you alone know yourself by yourself," serve as authority for its self-luminosity and its non-luminosity by another; likewise, the Smṛti text, "The sun does not illuminate it," and others are authoritative. Further details should be sought elsewhere.

The phrase "it indicates" (sūcayati) means that it makes known the synonymy between the terms *sphoṭa* and *svaprakāśa*. Thus, it is established that according to the doctrine of the *jātisphoṭa*, grammar serves the purpose of human welfare through knowledge consisting of the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), by means of the removal of adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*). The manner in which it serves a purpose according to the doctrine of the *nādasphoṭa* has already been explained previously. The term "unimpededly" (*nirvidhna*) means for the sake of the unobstructed dissemination of one's own work. "At the end" (*ante*) means at the conclusion of the treatise.

The meaning is that "auspiciousness" (maṅgala) consists of salutation (natyātmaka). The intention is based on the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya: "Treatises that begin with auspiciousness, end with auspiciousness, and have auspiciousness in their midst, flourish. It should be understood that "fullness" (pūrṇatva) means being indivisible (akhaṇḍārthatva) or having unimpeded power (apratihatecchatva); and salutation in that form is for the sake of accomplishing the desired object of one's wish for the propagation of one's own work.

Having thoroughly examined the incomparable web of statements by the venerable Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), as well as the assertions of the Naiyāyikas, and having mastered the system of Mīmāṃsā, [this has been done] by me in the Darpaṇa, which has been properly composed.
In this [work], the wise man perceives the essence of ornamentation and a display of clever wit; for a mirror made of the dust of breath is incapable of revealing the true nature of reality. || 1 ||
On Mount Kūrma there was an eminent Brāhmaṇa named Śrīvallabha, a scholar in the Vedāntas whose intellect was renowned as the "Cluster of Delight.
His son, Harivallabha, has joyfully composed this *Śrīmad-bhūṣaṇa-sāra-darpaṇa*, radiant with the jewels of its own splendor, for the delight of the learned.

For an object of mere imagination does not lead to true joy, even when practiced intensely; that [imagination] is likewise for the wise. Having considered this, I have set forth here both [theories], established by logic and authoritative means of knowledge. || 3 ||
Although every subject has been touched upon here by the wise, nevertheless, who can ward off my sense of ownership toward this work, which is expanded by the excellence of its composition? || 4 ||

Thus ends the *Sphoṭavāda* (Discourse on Sphoṭa) in the *Bhūṣaṇasāradarpaṇa*, composed by Harivallabha, son of the venerable Vallabha, whose ancestral lineage is from the illustrious Kūrmacala and who bears the secondary name Uprabhātīya.
